Junk e-mails are on the rise, with the number of spam messages increasing for the first time in three years, according to a security software firm.
Symantec said that in 2010 the average number of spam e-mails each user received stood at 56 per cent of all e-mail traffic.
That figure rose to 56.5 per cent in 2011, the first increase since 2008.
The security software firm said that social media was "the spammer's favourite new playground".
Symantec said that spammers were using sites such as Facebook and Twitter to promote themselves and recruit members to their cause.
It said that spam was also spreading to other forms of social media, including YouTube and Flickr.
"Spammers have always adopted techniques that allow them to reach the most people, in the most efficient way possible," said Symantec researcher Paul Wood.
"Reaching users on social media platforms is just another step in that direction, using tools they know users will see and click on.

"

The research, based on data collected by more than 200 million Symantec security software users, showed that e-mail was still the preferred method of spamming.
More than 90 per cent of spam messages were sent by e-mail, with only about 5 per cent sent via social media, Symantec said.
But it added that the proportion of spam delivered by social media was likely to increase over the coming year.
Ask Jeeves has joined the web log market with the acquisition of Bloglines.
The company has also launched Ask Blog, a custom search-powered weblog, and re-designed Bloglines to work more smoothly with the new service.
Bloglines boasts three million users who use the free service to track more than 300 million feeds.
It is the latest company to enter the blog search market, following Google's acquisition of Blogsearch.org, and Technorati's new blog search service.
Ask Blog and Bloglines are being promoted as a package, although they can be used separately.
The weblog comes with a choice of themes, and users can roll their own with HTML and CSS.
There is also an option to add Google AdSense so the owner can make money from the blog.
Ask Blog has a sidebar on the right with links to Bloglines, a to-do list, and a list of "hot" searches on Ask.com.
The searches are powered by Teoma technology, which Ask Jeeves bought last year.

"We believe there are going to be lots of niches in the weblog space, just like there are going to be lots of niches in the RSS (Really Simple Syndication) reader space," said Jason Shellen, co-founder of Bloglines, based in San Francisco.

"We feel there's going to be a place for simple, basic weblog services where you can get up and running quickly, and probably a place for much more elaborate, much more feature-rich products," he added.
Bloglines, which will remain a separate service, has also been re-designed with a greater emphasis on "search per feed", and each feed can be searched individually.
"If you look at weblog search today, it's really returning searches based on the meta-data of weblogs, the titles of weblogs, and the brief descriptions," said Mr Shellen.
"What we're trying to do is allow people to search the full text of every single feed that's in the system," he added.

The latest version of the Opera web browser can now read aloud any news article or website you visit.
The Norwegian software firm behind Opera said the feature was introduced to make surfing the web more accessible.
The browser can also be given commands verbally, making it possible to browse the web without touching the keyboard.

"This introduces a new way of interacting with browsers, making web content more accessible and bridging the gap between sites and applications," said Håkon Wium, the company's chief technology officer.
"It makes the desktop web experience a lot more like using a tablet or smartphone.

"

To read text out loud, users simply need to select it with their mouse and click on a speaker icon that appears in the browser's address bar.
They can also click on any link and have the content read aloud without leaving the page they are on.
Opera's "native speech" technology is based on the same browser engine that is used by Google's Chrome browser, but Wium said Opera was the first to make use of it in this way.
"We are trying to make the PC experience more like how tablets work, where you can enjoy the web without having to stare at the screen all the time," he said.
"This is an important step towards that.

"

However, the speech function does not work with all websites because it relies on them to be written in a way that is compatible with the speech API in Opera.
At the moment, it works best with news articles and stories on e-commerce websites, Wium said.
"We support the W3C's speech API, but not all sites implement this API," he said.
"As this technology advances, we expect more sites to implement it, making more web content accessible.

"

Napster has launched a subscription service offering access to millions of songs for a monthly fee.
The service, Napster Unlimited, is priced at $5 a month for broadband subscribers.
Napster, originally a free music file-sharing service, was shut down in 2001.
It was bought by Roxio, now known as Roxio/Napster, which hopes the new service will help it compete with market leader iTunes.
The service was announced at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas.
Napster Unlimited offers unlimited access to Napster's library of more than eight million songs.
Users will be able to play songs on up to three computers and burn up to three songs a day onto CDs.
The service will be available in the US before the end of January, with a UK launch to follow shortly afterwards, a Napster spokeswoman said.

Roxio competitor iTunes offers a subscription service in conjunction with phone company Verizon, but it is only available to Verizon broadband subscribers and is more expensive than Napster Unlimited.
iTunes is the market leader in legal digital music sales.
It sold more than 70 million songs in 2004 and accounts for more than 70% of online music sales, according to media analyst firm Nielsen SoundScan.
Roxio has struggled to compete.
It sold just over two million songs last year, according to Nielsen SoundScan.
Roxio's chief executive, Chris Gorog, said Napster Unlimited would "create a new model for digital music".
"It is perfect for people who love music, it is affordable, and it provides unlimited access to a massive library of music," he said.
In addition to the monthly subscription fee, users will have to pay a one-off $0.99 fee to register their computers.
Each song downloaded will come with "digital rights management" software that limits its use.
The new Napster service will be available in the US through such broadband providers as Comcast, Time Warner, and Cox.
Comcast executive vice-president David Cohen said the partnership offered customers "a great new way to access a broad array of music".

Vision will be available in three packages, with prices ranging from £99 to £299.

John Pluthero, the chief executive of Telewest, said Vision represented a "major advance" in digital TV.
"This will be the UK's first true video-on-demand service," he said.

"

Cats are enigmatic creatures and, just like the felines that adorn this game, the follow-up to 2002's innovative Blinx has arrived with little fanfare and no real explanation.
The original was a groundbreaking game that redefined the rules of 3D platform gaming with its fast and furious gameplay, and inventive use of gravity.
Its eponymous hero was a cat with a special pair of glasses that allowed him to view different planes of reality and, as a result, walk on walls, ceilings and any other surface.
The sequel, Blinx 2: Masters of Time and Space, is every bit as groundbreaking and inventive as the original, and will redefine the rules of gaming in much the same way.
The graphics have been given a bit of a face-lift and now have a distinctive, cell-shaded look, similar to that of the fantastic Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time.
They are just as smooth and the addition of a few extra layers of texture and a bit of gloss has definitely improved the overall look of the game.
The gameplay is where this game really pushes the envelope.
The original was already at the forefront of innovation and this simply takes things to a new level.

The story, such as it is, sees our feline friend transported to a parallel world and forced to hunt down a number of mysterious time-distorting orbs that are threatening to unravel the very fabric of time and space.
It's a typically convoluted and absurd story that does little other than provide an excuse to send our furry friend on a massive treasure hunt through a series of beautifully designed levels.
The real star of the show is the ingenious way the rules of gravity are manipulated.

There are plenty of puzzles to keep you occupied, and a huge variety of enemies to keep you on your toes.

Chris Harris, chief executive of the firm, said: "The auto-pod combines pioneering sensor technologies with the latest in computer vision to ensure that it operates safely on public roads and footpaths, without compromising the safety of pedestrians or other road users.

"

Mr Harris said the pods could "revolutionise" the way people travel around airports.

"The auto-pod can drive around airports without the need to ever expand the existing infrastructure, creating a fast, convenient and low-cost way of moving people around quickly and efficiently," he said.

Microsoft is launching a tool to help computer users keep track of their favourite blogs and make their own postings.
The software, to be released as a free download on Wednesday, is called Windows Live Writer.
It is the latest element in Microsoft's Windows Live strategy, which is aimed at countering the threat from Google's fast-growing webmail and other services.
Blog writers can use the tool to compose entries, and to add images or videos, regardless of which blogging service they use.
Once they have posted an entry, the writer can also use the tool to view statistics on readership, and for reposting to other blogs.
More than 27 million people have created blogs in the US alone, according to market research firm Nielsen Online.
However, many either use a web-based interface or proprietary software supplied by their blogging service.
Windows Live Writer will work with popular blog services, such as Blogger, LiveJournal and TypePad.
Microsoft has its own Windows Live Spaces blog service, and the software will work seamlessly with this.

"Until now, blogging has been a disconnected experience where you had to start by visiting a website, logging in, and then typing your blog post using an online form," said Brian Hall, who heads Microsoft's Windows Live efforts.
"With Windows Live Writer, the blogging experience is brought back to your computer, where you can blog to your heart's content, and then publish when you're ready," he added.
The software has an "offline" mode, allowing writers to compose entries when their computers are not connected to the internet.

They found that in 2008 more than half of spam emails were sent from email accounts that were maintained by their owners in such a way as to allow spammers to use them.

The researchers said that more than half of the spam they analyzed in 2008 was sent using accounts that had been registered with fake information.
But of the spam that came from accounts with real information, about 60 percent were sent from accounts that were being maintained in such a way as to allow spammers to send messages.
They found that people tended to use single email addresses for long periods of time, and tended not to cancel email accounts even when they were no longer active.
The team found evidence that spammers were taking advantage of this by searching through old email accounts for ones that were still active, and then using them.
"People do a poor job of unsubscribing from things they no longer find valuable," said Eric Zielinski, one of the researchers.

Technology giant Microsoft is planning to roll out a new user authentication system, aiming to make the internet a "safer place".
The "safer ID" system will rely on physical tokens, such as a mobile phone, as well as biometric data, such as a fingerprint.
The idea is that passwords - easily hacked or forgotten - will become a thing of the past.
The project is open-source, meaning outside developers can contribute to it.
Microsoft's announcement was timed to coincide with the RSA cyber security conference in San Francisco.
It comes amid a sharp rise in cyber attacks against companies and governments.
The "safer ID" system is still in its early stages, with no release date available, although Microsoft said it would start testing the technology with select customers in the coming months.
The system will also let users log in to a service with a one-time password generated by their phone, and let websites confirm a user's identity with a token rather than a password.
Microsoft said it had been working on the project for several months, but it had been developed independently of its acquisition of Nokia's devices and services business.

The "safer ID" system will work with Microsoft's cloud-based computing service, Azure, as well as with its Windows, Outlook.com and Skype services.
Once online, the system will compete with similar offerings from Google and Amazon.
What's more, the project will be open-source, meaning outside developers can contribute to it.
Experts said the move was a significant step for Microsoft.
"This eliminates the need for passwords altogether and that is a great thing," said Richard Stiennon, a security industry expert.

"

Mr Stiennon said the open-sourcing of the system was "forward thinking" and would generate support for the project.

The United Kingdom is losing its allure for movie makers, figures suggest.
The British Film Institute (BFI) said production was down 40% in the first half of 2020, with only 46 films made.

The streets of major cities across the UK have been colourful and vibrant this week as people have gathered to pay tribute to Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, following his death on Friday.
Among the many heartfelt messages, some of the most moving have come from members of the Commonwealth.

Prime Minister Boris Johnson described the duke as "the grandfather of the nation", while Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison spoke of the "strong values" his late father, John, shared with Philip.
And, as the world reflects on the legacy of the man who was married to the Queen for more than 70 years, there is no doubt that his influence will be long-lasting.
So what was it about the duke that has made him such an enduring figure, not only in the UK but across the globe?
Born in 1921, Philip was born a prince of Greece and Denmark, before becoming a British citizen in 1947 and going on to become one of the most prominent members of the Royal Family.
He joined the Royal Navy in 1939 and was mentioned in dispatches for his service during World War Two.

He went on to become a champion of conservation and the environment, and was a leading figure in the development of the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, which has inspired young people around the world to serve their communities and gain new skills.
The duke was also known for his sense of humour and his many gaffes, which often made the front pages of the newspapers.
He was also a regular presence at major events, such as the annual Remembrance Day service, and was a strong supporter of the armed forces.
In tribute to the duke, the Royal Family's official Twitter account posted a photo of him with the Queen, saying he would be "greatly missed".
And, as the world continues to mourn his loss, it seems likely that Philip's legacy will continue to be felt for many years to come.

The managing director of Germany's flagship classical music station has warned that the country's entire music industry is "slowly dying" and in danger of being replaced by American and British imports.
Dr Klaus Zehelein, from Deutschlandradio, said that without urgent state intervention, the nation's entire musical culture was at risk of being swallowed up by foreign competitors.
His comments come as orchestras and opera houses across Germany are facing cuts and threats of closure.

Dr Zehelein said that in the field of classical music, the problem originated in the early 1990s, when the major radio stations all but stopped playing classical music, with the result that a whole generation of young people was unaware of the genre.
He said: "They do not know the works of Johann Sebastian Bach, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart or Richard Wagner.

'A whole generation is musically illiterate'
"They simply do not possess the musical knowledge of the previous generation.
They are musically illiterate.
"On top of that, classical music in Germany is slowly dying, and it must be recognised that this is a cultural tragedy for our country."
Dr Zehelein called for national radio stations to be obliged by law to play a certain percentage of German music, and for the state to increase its funding of the classical music sector.
Without such measures, he said, Germany's musical culture was threatened by a flood of cheap imports from the US and the UK, and could even be replaced by Asian competitors.
He said: "Germany is slowly turning into a cultural colony with cheap imports replacing local products, and if people allow this to happen, then soon there will be no-one making music in Germany."
His comments were welcomed by the musical community, who said that they reflected a growing sense of alarm over the state of Germany's music industry.
Prof Martin Staehelin, the director of the Lucerne Festival, told the Neue Zuercher Zeitung that Dr Zehelein's warning was "a wake-up call for everyone who cares about musical culture in Germany".

A mysterious, unpublished novel by Leonardo da Vinci - the most recent of his works to be found - will be released in France on Thursday.
French historian Jean-Luc Marion discovered the manuscript in the archives of the Louvre museum in Paris in 2005.
Entitled "The Siege of Malta", it is believed to have been written by da Vinci in the early 1570s, and is his only work of fiction.
It tells the story of a sea battle, and is said to foreshadow the inventions and ideas that would appear in da Vinci's treatises on warfare.
Marion spent years researching and decoding the manuscript, which was written in Italian and includes many technical drawings and diagrams.
It was published in France last year, but the release of the book - which has been translated into English, Spanish and Italian - marks its first appearance in bookshops.
While the work is credited to da Vinci, Marion told the AFP news agency that it was likely written by one of the artist's disciples.
"For me, there are two possibilities," he said.
"Either Leonardo gave the order to write it, or he wrote it himself.
But it's more likely that he gave the order, because he knew how to write, but didn't like doing it.
The book is the second major work by da Vinci to be published in recent years.
In 2012, a lost book by the polymath was found in a French library, containing sketches and notes about the design of hydraulic turbines, flying machines and other inventions.
Born in Vinci, Italy in 1452, da Vinci died in 1519.
As well as being an artist, he was a scientist, engineer and inventor.

No charges against TV's Cosby

Bill Cosby has been cleared of all charges in a Pennsylvania court, prompting cheers and applause from the comedian and a relieved smile.
The 80-year-old stood quietly in court as the judge announced the jury's verdict in the trial over allegations he had sexually assaulted a woman more than a decade ago.
The jury cleared him of all three charges after less than 10 hours of deliberations spread over two days.
The judge had told them they could consider only whether Cosby put the woman in fear of immediate bodily harm, not whether he had sexually assaulted her.
Cosby, who did not testify, showed little emotion during the brief hearing, but his wife, Camille, smiled and squeezed his hand as they left the courtroom.
"I'm thrilled, thrilled," he told reporters outside.
"I'm overwhelmed with emotion.
I owe you guys.
I owe you."
Asked if he was angry at the accuser, he replied: "I don't think she deserves anybody's anger.
She's young, and she went through a lot of pain."
The comedian denied ever putting his sexual demands on any woman and said he had been victimized by "conspiracy theories, innuendo, and lies".

The accuser, Camille Cosby, had testified that Cosby gave her alcohol and pills and sexually assaulted her at his home in January 2004, two years after the comedian was acquitted of similar charges in a trial held in Massachusetts.
She wept on the stand as she described how he had put his hand over her mouth, but her account was challenged by defence cross-examination.
Bill Cosby gave a brief statement outside the court house, thanking his family and supporters: "I've always maintained my innocence and I'm glad it's all over," he said.
"I've never been through this before and I never want to see anyone go through this."
"I love my wife, for standing with me, and the children of ours.
My grandkids, for being brave enough to allow me to talk to them while all this was going on.
And my friends, for praying for me."
The jury had been sequestered since the trial began on 24 November and allowed little contact with the outside world.
They will now be permitted to speak to reporters but are not allowed to disclose any details of their deliberations.

Media company Viacom has been fined £1.8m ($2.6m) for broadcasting an episode of the adult cartoon South Park that included a fictional scene of former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair having sex with a doll.
London's Royal Courts of Justice heard that the episode, which aired in 2007, caused "distress" to Blair and his wife, Cherie.
Viacom, which owns the Channel 5 network that showed the cartoon, pleaded guilty to breaching the 2003 Communications Act for airing offensive material.
However, the fine was far lower than the £5m demanded by Blair, who gave his approval for the prosecution to go ahead.
The fine is the largest ever for a case of this kind.
Blair's lawyer, Jenny Afia, had argued that the episode, entitled "Trapped in the Closet", had caused "significant distress" to the Blairs and "undermined his credibility as a public figure".
She added that there had been more than 450 complaints to media watchdog Ofcom and more than 200 complaints to Channel 5.

Viacom said in a statement after the hearing: "Channel 5 admitted liability in relation to the broadcasting of the South Park episode 'Trapped in the Closet' in 2007, and deeply regrets the distress the episode caused to Tony Blair and his wife, Cherie.

"Today's settlement marks a fair and reasonable conclusion to this legacy case, and Channel 5 considers the matter closed."

Jenny Afia, who also represented the former prime minister, said her client was "pleased" with the fine, saying it was "a landmark case which demonstrates that no one is above the law, whatever their position".

She added: "We are delighted that Channel 5 acknowledged its liability and hope that this will lead other broadcasters to think carefully in future about the responsibility they have to consider the effects of their programming on the public.

"

In the episode, Blair is shown struggling to have sex with his wife, before turning his attention to a doll designed to look like former US President George W Bush.

Obituary: Dame Alicia Markova

Born: December 1, 1910; died: December 25, 2004, in Bath, England

Ballerina
Alicia Markova was one of the greatest English dancers of the 20th century.
She was best known for her extraordinary versatility, mastering many different styles, from classical and romantic to modern and character dance.
Markova was born in London in 1910 and began her dance training at an early age.
She studied at the Legat School of Ballet in London and made her debut as a soloist with the Markova-Dolin Ballet in 1931.

She became the prima ballerina assoluta of the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo in 1932, where she achieved international fame and worked with renowned choreographers such as George Balanchine and Michel Fokine.
Markova was known for her technical precision, grace, and musicality.
She was also a talented choreographer and teacher.
She taught at the School of American Ballet and established the Markova-Nicholson School of Ballet in London in 1935.
She was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1949 and was also awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Coronation Medal in 1953.
Markova retired from dancing in 1963 and died in 2004 at the age of 94.
She is widely regarded as one of the greatest ballerinas of all time and her legacy continues to inspire and influence dancers and choreographers today.

The study also revealed that 92% of people now own a mobile, a jump from 88% last year.
This proliferation of mobiles has helped fuel a 28% jump in the amount of time each day that people spend on phones - from 88 minutes to 114 minutes each day over the past year, Ofcom said.
The study also showed that texting is the most popular activity on mobiles - one in five texts are sent or received every day, with the typical mobile user sending 41 texts each month.
In contrast, the number of voice calls made on mobiles has fallen for the first time, dropping from 102 calls each month to 96.

Millions of users click on the top couple of results, where the ads are clearly labelled - and a similar number on the "related searches" where the ad label is fainter.

Google has run tests to check the ad labels' effectiveness.

The company says the test proved that the existing labelling is working well, because few people click on the bottom ads even when the label is there.

The EU's competition commissioner, Neelie Kroes, has given the go-ahead for an investigation into whether Italy has given Alitalia illegal state aid.
The probe follows the Italian government's announcement that it is to pump another €300m ($430m; £260m) into the loss-making airline.
Ms. Kroes said there were "serious doubts" about the investment being compliant with the EU rules on state aid.
She said the decision to open the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.
Alitalia has been losing about €1m a day, but the government has insisted the airline will not be allowed to fail.

The commissioner's decision on Tuesday to open the investigation follows a complaint by the Association of European Airlines (AEA), which claimed that the Italian government had not demonstrated that its plan for Alitalia complied with EU state-aid rules.
These require a government to demonstrate that any injection of public funds does not distort competition in the single market.
In a statement on Tuesday, Ms. Kroes said that she agreed with the association's assessment that there were "serious doubts" about the investment being compliant with state-aid rules.
"Consequently, the commission will open proceedings pursuant to Article 88(2) of the EC Treaty
[the basis of EU state-aid rules]," she said.
"This decision does not prejudge the outcome of the proceeding.

"

The commission has given Italy 20 days to respond to its concerns.
Last week, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi defended the government's decision to inject more funds into Alitalia, despite the airline making successive losses.
"Alitalia is a national interest," he said.
"We will not allow it to collapse.
The government has said that it wants to draw a line under the various bail-outs of the past, and has appointed advisers to help find a partner for the airline.
Manchester United have offered Harry Maguire a deal worth up to 500,000 pounds a week to stay at the club.
The centre-back has been linked with a move to Premier League rivals Newcastle this summer.
The BBC's Simon Stone reports United have made it clear to Maguire they do not want him to leave and are willing to reward him with a double-your-money deal.
Stone says the offer is worth 300,000 pounds a week basic with various add-ons.
One source told the BBC the offer has taken Maguire by surprise.

The UK's new terrorism prevention and investigation measures, which give authorities wide-ranging stop-and-search powers and allow suspects to be detained without charge, face their first test in court.
The measures - part of the government's new counter-terrorism strategy - were unveiled by Home Secretary Theresa May in February.
They are being challenged in the High Court by two men, who are arguing that they violate the UK's human rights laws.
The men - one from Lancashire, the other from Dorset - are seeking a judicial review of the measures, claiming they undermine the "fundamental rights of free citizens".
Their case is being supported by human rights group Liberty and public law experts from Bhatt Murphy solicitors.
The men, who cannot be named for legal reasons, are seeking a declaration that the measures are unlawful and should not be enforced.
The Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005 (PTA), which the men successfully challenged in the High Court in 2011, was due to expire in July.

The new measures replaced the PTA with a set of temporary stop-and-search powers and a new regime of "investigative detention" - which allows suspects to be held for up to 14 days without being charged.
The men's legal team claim that the new measures breach the European Convention on Human Rights - which protects rights to liberty, security and a fair trial.
They also argue that the powers are too broad and give police the ability to stop people at random without reasonable grounds for suspicion.
The judicial review, which begins on Monday, is expected to last three days.

The men's lawyers will argue that the measures do not provide "sufficient clarity as to the circumstances in which the new powers may be exercised, and sufficient safeguards as to how they may be exercised".
They will also claim there is no effective independent oversight of the new regime and that the measures breach the right to a fair trial.
A Home Office spokesperson said: "The government is determined to tackle terrorism and protect the public.

"But as the Court of Appeal recognised when it gave the go-ahead for these vital powers, there are strong safeguards in place - including independent oversight by a senior judge, Code of Practice and a new Stop and Search Scrutiny Panel."
Air China has launched its $1.3bn (£820m) float on the London Stock Exchange, becoming the first Chinese airline to list in the UK.
The company sold about 4.5 billion shares at 67p each, valuing the total stock at £802 million.
The shares began trading in London on Wednesday morning, and were trading up 3% at 69.75p at 1305 GMT.
The flotation is a rare example of a Chinese company choosing to list in London following a string of high-profile cancellations.

There are growing concerns in the UK that Beijing is trying to discourage Chinese firms from listing in London, which until recently was the world's most popular venue for initial public offerings (IPOs).

In the six months to the end of June this year, a total of 13 Chinese firms cancelled London IPO plans, according to data from Refinitiv, higher than the 11 that scrapped them in the first six months of last year.
Air China's listing comes as the UK government has been trying to calm investor jitters ahead of Brexit on 31 October.
The airline, which has a fleet of 580 aircraft, is headquartered in Beijing and is a member of the Star Alliance.
It flies to more than 170 destinations, with a particular focus on China's fast-growing domestic market.
Air China's listing is a secondary listing, with the company already listed on the Hong Kong and Shanghai stock exchanges.
The firm said it would not be raising any new money from the London float, but would instead be allowing existing shareholders to sell their shares.
About eight per cent of the company is being made available in the float, which is expected to raise about £65 million for the selling shareholders.
The company's two largest shareholders are the China National Aviation Holding Company Ltd, which owns 28.1%, and Citic Group Corporation, which owns 18.5%.
The airline has been hit by the coronavirus pandemic, which has led to a sharp decline in air travel.
In the first half of the year, it carried just over 11 million passengers, down 55% from a year earlier.
It reported a net loss of about CNY2.5 billion (£293 million) in the first half of 2020, compared with a net profit of CNY1.3 billion (£162 million) a year earlier.

Czech Republic goalkeeper Petr Koubek has been banned from football for two years after being found guilty of taking illegal drugs.
The Czech Football Federation (CFF) suspended Koubek, 34, after he tested positive for the banned substance Methamphetamine.
"I did not expect this and I am shocked by the decision," Koubek told Czech newspaper Mlada fronta Dnes.
"I am innocent and I will use all legal means to restore my reputation," added the former Czech Republic number one.
Koubek, who plays for top-flight side Slavia Prague, returned a positive A-sample following a random test by the CFF.

UK prime minister Boris Johnson has insisted he had "no option but to suspend parliament" ahead of Brexit, denying it was a "coup".
The prime minister suspended - or prorogued - parliament for five weeks in September, prompting legal challenges from some MPs.
Mr Johnson was interviewed for BBC's Political Thinking podcast, where he said the "people of this country have had enough" of parliament's delay to Brexit.
"There is no option but to obey the law, and the law requires me to prorogue parliament," he said.
"It's absolutely untrue to suggest this is some kind of constitutional outrage, or a coup, or whatever people want to call it.

"

He added that the UK parliament would still sit again - on Monday - following the suspension.
The prime minister's decision to suspend parliament sparked anger across the political spectrum and he was accused of trying to silence opposition to a no-deal Brexit.
Mr Johnson also suggested the BBC could have shown "a little more enthusiasm" for Brexit, as he defended his decision to threaten to cut its funding.
The BBC has been accused by some Brexit supporters of having a pro-EU agenda, with Mr Johnson previously saying it had "failed to speak up for this country".
The prime minister said the BBC's news coverage now had a "totally unbiased" feel, but that this had not always been the case.
"Sometimes it seemed to me that the BBC slightly, you know, wanted to keep us in the EU if they could," he said.
"Now they've totally got an open mind about it, I think."
When asked if the BBC had been "too woke", Mr Johnson said: "I think the real problem, frankly, is that occasionally, the BBC has maybe not shown enough love for this country."
Mr Johnson denied that his threats to the BBC's funding were an attempt to influence its coverage, saying he was only following through on manifesto promises.
"Sometimes, I think people accuse me of being some kind of dictator or something, because they think I'm trying to bully the BBC," he said.
"But it's simply not true.

"

He added that, despite the threats, the BBC was still expected to deliver on its promises for "proper, free-ranging journalism".

Samir Hariri, the brother of former Lebanese prime minister Rafik Hariri, gestures to supporters at the site of the bombing in Beirut on Monday.

Mr Hariri was one of the main shareholders in Lebanon's largest bank, Byblos Bank, as well as in the country's only mobile phone operator, Touch.

Mr Hariri had reportedly been considering reinvesting in Lebanon after years of war and instability.
Instead, investors now face fresh uncertainty.

Halloween writer Debra Hill has died at the age of 65.
Hill, who wrote the 1978 horror classic alongside John Carpenter, died on Sunday at her home in Los Angeles, her publicist has confirmed.
Her other writing credits include the Steve Martin comedy The Man with Two Brains.
She also produced a string of Hill-related films including Escape from New York, Halloween III: Season of the Witch and The Funhouse.
Her publicist did not reveal a cause of death.
Hill was born in Los Angeles in 1951.
She studied theatre at the University of California and then embarked on a career as a writer and producer in Hollywood.
Her most famous screenplay was for Halloween, a low-budget slasher movie that has gone on to be a huge influence on the horror genre.
It starred Donald Pleasence and Jamie Lee Curtis and told the story of psychotic killer Michael Myers' revenge on Halloween night.
Hill was credited as Nancy Loomis, her mother's maiden name, on the film because the producers did not think a female screenwriter would be taken seriously, Hill told website IndieWire in 2018.
"It was a very different time," she said.
"I really didn't care about credit, and I realise that might sound silly, but it's true.
I was just happy to have a job and to be able to pay my rent.

"

Carpenter, who directed the film, told the website it was "one of the great partnerships in cinema history".

Debra and I created the movie from nothing," he said.
"It literally was a green-screen shot in Michigan in the middle of winter.
So it was not only memorable, but it was mandatory that we be collaborative and creative because there was nothing else to fall back on.

"

Hill wrote the script for The Man with Two Brains with the movie's star Steve Martin, and they won a Saturn Award for best writing.
Her producing credits included House Arrest, starring Kevin Bacon, and The Big Green, featuring Walter Matthau.
In later years, she founded independent film company Medusa Productions and continued to write, most recently on the 2010 TV movie A Nightmare on Elm Street.

"But he was also one of the most effective political operators of his generation," he added.

CEO Doug Parker said in a memo to employees the agreement saves about $600 million a year and puts the company "on a more viable cost structure."

Glastonbury fans will be able to buy ID cards featuring images of the festival's stages.
Organizers say the cards will be needed to gain entry to the 2023 event, following disruption caused by so-called "fake fans" last year.
The cards will be personalised and feature a photo and information about what the ticket-holder purchased.
Glastonbury 2023 will take place from 21 to 25 June.
Tickets for the 2022 festival sold out in 33 minutes but many were then resold on sites like eBay for thousands of pounds.
Organizers say the photo ID cards will be introduced "to fight against theft" and "to make sure tickets get into the right hands".
They will also be needed to access "pre-sale tickets" for the 50th anniversary festival in 2024.

In a post on Instagram, Glastonbury Festival said: "Following disruption we saw from 'fake fans' last year - when tickets were purchased by people who hadn't any intention of coming to the festival, but instead resold them on secondary sites as soon as they got them - we are introducing personalised photo ID cards for all ticket holders in 2023.
"That means that every ticket holder will now need to have their photo taken when they collect their ticket, in order to receive their personalised photo ID card.
"These cards will be needed for entry into the festival, and will also be required to access any pre-sale tickets for the 50th anniversary festival in 2024.

"

The post adds the photo cards will fight theft and "make sure tickets get into the right hands".
It is not yet known whether you will be able to opt out of having your photo taken.
In 2021, Glastonbury was one of the first big festivals to return after the lifting of coronavirus restrictions.
Headliner Paul McCartney had to appeal to fans to "look after each other" after a number of medical incidents were reported during the festival.

The following year, the festival introduced more measures to keep attendees safe, including setting up a "safe haven" area, where people could recharge their phone if they needed to contact friends or family, or charge a power bank.
There were also increased medical facilities, including an on-site hospital, with more staff, equipment and treatment areas, as well as an increased presence of security and police.
The chief executive, chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Aer Lingus have stepped down.
The Irish airline said Sean Doyle, Colin Murphy and Peter Hamilton had left "with immediate effect" following "a formal review" of the company's executive team.
Aer Lingus, which is owned by International Airlines Group (IAG), added that the move was part of a "refreshed leadership team" at the carrier.
The departures come weeks after the airline announced a new expansion plan.
Mr Doyle had been chief executive since August 2015.
Aer Lingus said Michael Cawley, who has been chairman of the airline since May 2019, would lead the management team until a new chief executive is appointed.
The airline also said it was beginning the search for a new chief financial officer and chief operating officer "in the coming days".
Last month, Aer Lingus launched a new expansion plan which it said would see it fly to Manchester, Birmingham and Bristol from Dublin, and to Birmingham and Bristol from Cork, by 2021.
At the time, Mr Doyle said the plans would deliver more than 400 new jobs in direct employment.
Aer Lingus also announced in December that it would cease its service between Dublin and Hartford, Connecticut, in the summer of 2019.
Founded in 1936, Aer Lingus is the flag carrier of Ireland and operates flights to more than 100 destinations, including destinations in the UK, Europe and North America.
It was bought by IAG, which also owns British Airways and Iberia, in 2015.
Apple has unveiled a pocket-sized version of its iPod music player, aimed at taking on Sony's market-leading Walkman devices.
The new iPod shuffle is the smallest music player Apple has made to date and is about the same size as a pack of chewing gum.
Apple said it was the first music player in the world that talks to the user.
The 1GB device, which holds about 240 songs, will go on sale in the US from 1 March for $149.
Apple is hoping the shuffle, which is priced lower than its other iPods, will appeal to a mass market that is not necessarily interested in all the features of its other music players.
"We're introducing iPod shuffle, the newest member of the iPod family.
With iPod shuffle, you can now have a compact, wearable iPod that talks to you," said Steve Jobs, Apple's chief executive, at the launch at the company's headquarters in Cupertino, California.
"With its wearable, compact size, iPod shuffle is the first iPod that can be used as an audio companion to all your activities," he added.
The 2GB version of Sony's Walkman MP3 player is currently the market leader and is priced at $130.
Apple's shuffle is encased in aluminium and comes in three colours - platinum, blue and green.

It can be attached to clothing via a new range of lanyards and belts to be sold by Apple, and features the same "voiceover" feature found on Apple's other iPods that tells the user the name of the song and the artist.
Apple said the device could play up to 15 hours of music on a single battery charge.
The shuffle does not feature the displays found on Apple's other iPods, instead there are three buttons on the device to control the music - volume up, play/pause and volume down.
To select a song, the user presses the play/pause button and the device will randomly choose another track from the playlist.
The shuffle joins Apple's expanding iPod family, which includes the iPod mini, iPod, iPod photo and the iPod video.
Apple said it now had a 70% share of the digital music player market and sold more than 22 million iPods in 2005.
The company also said it sold more than 50 million songs through its iTunes online music store last year.
Shredding in Whitehall has increased since 2005, according to a new report by the National Audit Office.
The report, presented to Parliament, showed that central government departments spent £80m on shredding in 2005-06.
The Department of Work and Pensions accounted for nearly half of that - £35.4m. The department said it was getting rid of 3 million cases of old paperwork each year.
That figure has now risen to 4.5 million.
The Department of Health spent £2.7m on shredding - £700,000 more than in 2005-06.
Nearly two-thirds of the 26 departments increased their spending on shredding.
The NAO said the overall increase may be due to departments shredding more material on site instead of sending it to commercial companies.

Ad firm WPP posts rise in annual profits for the first time in four years - BBC News

WPP has posted its first annual rise in profits for four years thanks to cost cuts and increased revenue.
The advertising giant said pre-tax profits rose by 15% to £306m ($408m) for the year to 31 December.
It marks a turnaround for the firm, which has been hit by economic uncertainty and competition from digital rivals.
The world's biggest advertising agency said it had made a "solid start" to 2023.
WPP's shares rose more than 5% in morning trading in London.
The group said it had won new business, with net new bookings up by more than 50% compared to 2021.

Chief executive Mark Read said: "We are making good progress against our strategy, delivering meaningful growth for our clients and continuing to invest in creative capabilities and talent, despite a more difficult economic backdrop.

"We are making a solid start to 2023, with strong new business momentum and important client wins, and are well positioned to continue delivering for our clients as the global economy undergoes a transformation.

"

WPP's results come as rivals grapple with the impact of the economic downturn, although the industry has so far avoided major fallout from the conflict in Ukraine.
Last week, rival firm Omnicom reported its profits had fallen by nearly a third, while Publicis Groupe raised its profit forecasts on the back of "strong" demand.
At 09:00 GMT, WPP's shares were up 5.1% at 718p.
Britain's economy is likely to be the fastest growing in the G7 this year, chancellor Jeremy Hunt has said.
In a speech in London, he said the country's recovery from the Covid crisis was "well under way", with unemployment returning to pre-pandemic levels and a record number of people in work.
But the independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has warned that the UK's cost of living crisis is set to continue, with inflation remaining high for longer than expected.
Speaking at the Mansion House in London on Friday evening, Mr Hunt celebrated the "incredible strength and resilience of the British people" following the difficulties of the pandemic.
He said the economy was likely to grow by 4% this year, faster than any other G7 country, although he warned there were "storm clouds on the horizon".

The chancellor said the government was "standing ready" to help households through the cost of living crisis with a £1bn support package, including discounts on energy bills and cuts to rail ticket prices.
But he said "most of all" people needed stability in politics following the turmoil of the last few months, warning that the public "have had quite enough of turbulence and chaos".

Beer giant swallows Russian firm for $7.8bn

Anheuser-Busch InBev (AB InBev) has completed its takeover of the Russian beer firm Sibirskaya Korona.
The deal, first announced in February, sees AB InBev pay $7.8bn (£4.7bn) to buy out the company's minority shareholders.
Sibirskaya Korona is the maker of Russia's number two beer, Sibirskaya Korona, and number three, Ershovsky.
AB InBev, which owns more than 200 brands of beer, already owned a controlling stake in the firm.
The Belgian-based company said it would finance the deal with a combination of cash and shares in its subsidiary, AB InBev Russia.
At the end of last year, AB InBev made an offer to buy the 54% of Sibirskaya Korona that it did not already own for $3.4bn.
That offer was increased to $7.8bn earlier this year to buy out the company's two main minority shareholders - the Russian government and the company's chairman, Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The deal has been approved by regulators in Russia and Belgium.
Mr Chernomyrdin will remain as chairman of the board of directors of AB InBev Russia.
AB InBev was formed in 2008 through the merger of Belgium's InBev and U.S. beer maker Anheuser-Busch.
It makes more than 200 beer brands including Budweiser, Stella Artois and Beck's.
Its products are sold in more than 130 countries and it employs about 70,000 people.
The company's revenues were $47.9bn last year.
Three-time world champion Catherine Chepkemei has been banned from the sport for four years after breaching athletics' anti-doping rules.
The 31-year-old Kenyan runner, who won the 5,000m and 10,000m world titles in 2003 and 2005, failed an out-of-competition test in November 2006.
The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) said she had taken the banned blood-booster EPO.

Chepkemei, who won five consecutive world cross-country titles between 2004 and 2008, has been disqualified from the 2007 World Championships in Osaka, where she finished 11th in the 10,000m.

She also loses the silver medal she won at the 2005 World Championships in Helsinki, where she was runner-up in the 5,000m behind Tirunesh Dibaba of Ethiopia.
Chepkemei's ban runs until 23 September 2010.
IAAF president Lamine Diack said: "Once again the IAAF has been forced to take tough action against those who believe they can flout the system and that they are above the rules.

"This is a clear message to all athletes - there is no place in our sport for those who do not play by the rules."

Chepkemei, who became a mother for the first time last year, has been one of Kenya's most successful female runners, also winning the world junior 3,000m title in 1996, two Commonwealth golds and three consecutive IAAF World Cup titles.
Kenya is one of the leading countries when it comes to doping scandals.

Last month, former 10,000m world champion David Obrado and wife Lucy Wangui Kabuu, who finished fourth in the 2008 Olympic marathon, were banned for two years after both tested positive for the banned blood-booster CERA.
In August, former Olympic 1,500m champion Rashid Ramzi, who won gold in Athens in 2004, was banned for two years after testing positive for the anabolic steroid nandrolone.

The Wales international, 28, will leave the Gunners at the end of the season and has been ruled out until then with a hamstring injury.
Arsenal's players and staff went to Ramsey at the final whistle to commiserate, with Mourinho focusing on that rather than his side's 2-0 loss.
"I would do it if it was the opposite way around," he said.
"If I was them, I would do the same thing.

"

Mourinho felt the Gunners were already treating Ramsey's injury as if it were a pre-season friendly and had criticised their attitude before the game.

"

Arsene Wenger has signed a new two-year contract as Arsenal manager, the club have announced.
The 65-year-old's new deal will keep him at Emirates Stadium until at least the end of the 2019-20 season.
"This is a significant moment for our club," said Arsenal chairman Sir Chips Keswick.

"Arsene Wenger's continue involvement is good for our fans, our club and our game - and we are delighted that he will continue to manage Arsenal for the next two years," added Sir Chips, who was appointed chairman last October.
The Frenchman, who took over as Arsenal manager in October 1996, won a record seventh FA Cup with the club last season - ending their nine-year wait for a trophy.
They also finished runners-up in the Premier League in 2002, 2004, 2005 and 2006 under Wenger.
"I am happy to continue to work with our staff, players and everyone at the club to bring success to Arsenal in the years to come," said Wenger.
"I love this club and feel privileged to be its manager.
"There is so much to come in the future.
We are all excited about what we can achieve - all together."
Wenger made a total of 1,235 appearances as a player for Nancy, Monaco and Paris St-Germain.
He has taken charge of more than 1,500 games as a manager and has won 10 major trophies since joining Arsenal.
"He has conducted himself with dignity and honesty and has been fully committed to the club throughout his time here," said Sir Chips.
"It is a measure of his dedication to Arsenal that he has agreed to continue to serve as our manager despite having no longer been obliged to do so."
The US has taken the top spot in a supercomputing ranking for the first time in 10 years after building a machine that is eight times faster than China's number one.

The US Department of Energy said its new Summit supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee took the top spot in the Top500 list, with a computational speed of 200 quadrillion – or 200,000,000,000,000 – calculations per second.
It knocked China's Sunway TaihuLight, which came out number one in the previous list, down to number two.
The US has struggled to keep up with China in supercomputing in recent years.
In November 2013, China took the top two spots in the Top500 with the Tianhe-2A and the Tianhe-1A.
The US didn't have a machine in the top 10.
Since then, China has built two more machines in the top five.
But the US has caught up thanks in part to a $500m (£380m) investment in the Summit machine, which is powered by IBM POWER9 chips and NVIDIA GPUs.
It is also the first system to break the exaflop barrier, meaning it can perform 200,000,000,000,000,000 (200 exaflops) floating point operations per second.
An exaflop is a measure of a computer's processing speed.
What is a supercomputer?
Supercomputers are extremely fast and powerful machines.
They are designed to do complex calculations and work that requires a lot of number-crunching.
They are used by scientists to predict the weather, by engineers to design aircraft and by mathematicians to try to crack encryption.
Although they are incredibly powerful, supercomputers are generally not as flexible as a desktop computer or a smartphone.
And despite their name, they are actually fairly common.
There are supercomputers in many countries around the world.

Supercomputers are often used by scientists to run complex simulations.

The Bank of England has decided to keep interest rates on hold, despite predictions that it would raise them to tame soaring prices.
Some economists had expected a rise in the base rate from the record low of 0.1% to 0.25% - the level it stood at before the pandemic.
But in a statement, the Bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) said that, despite recent inflationary pressures, "now was not the right time to raise interest rates".
It put the decision down to "supply conditions" which have "improved" and "short-term inflationary pressures" which "should subside" as the economy opens up.
It also said that, while there had been some positive labour market trends, "there were still a few million people with underlying employment vulnerabilities".
It is the second time in a row that the MPC has voted to hold rates at 0.1%.
Construction company Galliford Try has said it is setting aside £131m to deal with historic asbestos claims.
The firm, which built the Olympic village, announced the charge alongside half-year results.
It said the money would cover the cost of compensation payments to current and future claimants, and the purchase of insurance cover.
Asbestos is a material that was once widely used in construction, but can cause the lung disease mesothelioma.
Galliford Try said the provision related to allegations dating back as far as the 1960s, when its businesses were involved in construction and property development.
"We have always maintained that our policies and procedures in respect of asbestos were and are appropriate," said chief executive Peter Truscott.
"This provision is a reflection of the current legal environment in this field.

"

The firm said it had not been possible to obtain insurance to cover the full cost of the claims, so it was putting the money aside.
It said it had been contacted by about 650 claimants, but expected that number to rise to about 2,000.
Galliford Try made an operating profit of £86m in the six months to 31 December, up from £77m a year earlier.
The company, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, also announced an interim dividend of 7.6p a share, up from 7.2p at the same time last year.

Pornographers, hackers and virus writers have emerged as the top cyber criminals in 2004, according to a report by security software firm Symantec.
The report reveals a growing trend in the criminal use of the internet, with one US server alone being used to distribute 33 million spam emails.
Symantec's annual Internet Security Threat Report details a year of "rapid change and massive growth" in cyber crime.
The report shows a significant rise in the exploitation of web services and vulnerabilities in mobile devices and other consumer electronics.
During 2004, Symantec processed more than 370,000 malicious code samples, almost triple the number from the previous year.
Malicious code is any program or code designed to gain unauthorized access to computer systems.
The report reveals that although the US is still the primary source of originating e-mail spam, other countries are fast catching up.
Symantec discovered that during 2004, spam emissions from the US dropped from 61% to 54%, whilst spam emissions from China rose from 9% to 13%.
"The sheer volume of spam being produced by these groups is phenomenal," said Vincent Weafer, senior director of Symantec's Security Response group.
"We are seeing a change in the way that spam is being used, with a large number of spammers now using it to promote their own commercial services and products," he added.
The report also highlights the growth in "phishing" - fraudulent emails designed to lure people to fake websites in order to steal their passwords, credit card numbers and other personal information.
Symantec found a sharp increase in phishing attacks, primarily through emails impersonating major corporations such as eBay.
"Both the number of attacks and the level of sophistication are increasing," the report said, warning that phishing would be a major concern in 2005.
The report also highlights a shift in the way viruses and worms are written.
It says virus writers are increasingly using a technique called "polymorphic" or "metamorphic" code to disguise the core code of their programs in each new release.
This makes it increasingly difficult for antivirus companies to detect and clean up the infected files.

Bank payout to Pinochet victims

Bank Julius Baer has agreed to pay former Chilean dictator General Augusto Pinochet $23.8m in a long-running case relating to money deposited in Swiss bank accounts.
The BBC's Sebastian Bell in Santiago says this is likely to be the final chapter in a historic case.
For years, thousands of victims of General Pinochet's military regime had demanded the return of $44m of state funds that were deposited in several Swiss banks.

In 2004, Swiss authorities ordered Bank Julius Baer to return $15m to the Chilean state, but the bank appealed, insisting that it had been advised by its lawyers that the funds deposited were legitimate.
The case has gone through several iterations.
In 2010, a court ordered the bank to pay $50m in compensation, with $24m going to the Chilean state and $26m to 600 victims.
The victims then took the case to Switzerland, demanding that the bank return the full $44m. Last October, a Swiss court ruled that the bank had to pay $90m in compensation.
Now, Bank Julius Baer says it will pay a total of $23.8m to both the Chilean state and the victims.
The bank said it had reached a "friendly agreement" with the victims.
It is not clear if this latest agreement will be the final chapter in the case.
Our correspondent says that even though Bank Julius Baer has agreed to pay $23.8m, more than half of the originally disputed amount, there is no guarantee this will be the end of the story.
He says both the Chilean government and the victims still have the right to appeal against the amount, although neither side has said yet if they will do so.
Chelsea made it three Premier League wins from four matches under Guus Hiddink with a 2-0 victory at home to Stoke City.
The Blues dominated throughout but lacked the finishing touch until Willian Robben scored with a fine shot early in the second half.
Stoke's frustration grew when Jon Moss sent off Charlie Adam for a challenge on Cesc Fabregas shortly before the hour mark.
The 10 men of the Potters held out until the 81st minute, when Diego Costa scored a second for Chelsea from Fabregas's pass.
It was no more than the hosts deserved, having created numerous chances, with Stoke failing to register a shot on target.
Hiddink's side remain 10th in the table, while Stoke slip a place to 12th.
Robben was given the space to fire in a shot from 25 yards after a one-two with Costa and the ball beat the diving Asmir Begovic.
The Netherlands international almost created a second for himself moments later but was twice denied by Begovic, who also did well to tip a header from Kurt Zouma over the bar.
The visitors had created nothing in attack but almost took an unlikely lead when Ryan Shawcross's header from a corner was cleared off the line by Fabregas.
And they were handed an even greater chance to take something from the game when Adam was sent off after a challenge on Fabregas.
The Scotland international appeared to win the ball but his follow-through caught the Chelsea man on the knee and Moss had no option but to produce a red card.
Hiddink responded by replacing Eden Hazard with Nemanja Matic for the final 15 minutes, and it was the Serbian's pass that released Fabregas to set up Costa for the killer second goal.
The Spanish striker controlled the ball with his right foot before firing low into the corner with his left to seal the victory.
It could have been even better for the hosts in the final minutes but Begovic made a superb save to deny Costa a second and Shawcross headed another chance off the line.

MPs' murder sentence concern

MPs have questioned the judge's decision to hand down a life sentence to a man who murdered an MP.
WA Corke, who killed Jo Cox, was given a minimum term of 35 years in December.
The Sentencing Council said it will examine whether the sentencing guidelines for murder are "fit for purpose".
Its statement came after a number of MPs raised concerns over the "vague" and "incomprehensible" law.
The Labour MP for Batley and Spen, who was pregnant, was attacked by Corke in Birstall in June 2016.
He was charged with her murder and the murder of Labour councillor Bernard Carter outside a library in Birstall.
At the time of the attack, Corke gave his name as "Death to Traitors, Freedom for Britain", which was also written on his baseball bat.
He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 35 years, which is variable and can be increased or decreased depending on behaviour.
The judge said the minimum term would have been 30 years but it was increased because the murder was "a terrorist act" and carried out "in pursuance of extremist ideology".
On Friday, Labour MP Yvette Cooper, who chairs the Home Affairs Select Committee, tabled a debate on the sentencing guidelines for murder, calling them "vague and incomprehensible".
She said the law needed to be changed so the public could have confidence it acted as a deterrent.
Her comments were echoed by Tory MP Bob
Seely, who said the law was an "absolute mess" and needed to be simplified.
The Sentencing Council said it will examine the sentencing guidelines over the next few months "to ensure they are fit for purpose and clearly articulated".
"This review will commence shortly and the council will engage with stakeholders ahead of publishing any changes to the guidelines," it added in a statement.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "The justice system has always allowed for sentences for violent crimes to be increased or decreased in accordance with behaviour, and this was a rare case because of the terrorist connection.

"

They added that the ministry had asked the Sentencing Council to "keep the guidelines under review".

Cork woman Mary McAleese has been elected to the largely ceremonial post, beating the favourite, Fianna Fail leader Michael Woods.
Mrs McAleese, a former senator and lawyer, received 62% of the vote.

In the top 100 films of 2019 just over a third (34%) of the lead characters were women, according to the study.

Have hackers recruited your PC?
It's a painful fact that computers get slower as they age - but did you know that it's often malware that's to blame?
Security firm Avast has looked into the issue, and found that almost one in three Windows PCs is running slower than it should due to malicious programs that have made their way onto the machine.
And these are programs that the owners themselves have deliberately installed, largely through ignorance of the risks involved.
Avast's researchers found that the typical victim was exposed to an average of six different ad-displaying programs.
These are often presented as useful downloads such as PDF readers or software to help you download other programs.
In addition, four different programs were found to be mining virtual currencies such as Bitcoin on the users' computers, without their knowledge.
"Most people assume that these are isolated incidents, but our data shows that millions of people worldwide are actually affected," said Avast chief operations officer Ondrej Vlcek.
The infections themselves are usually caused by downloads that look useful or interesting, and are presented by legitimate-looking websites.
However, the programs come with a hidden payload - advertising software that displays intrusive pop-up ads, or in some cases, cryptocurrency-mining programs.
These typically use up to half of the computer's processing power, and as a result, the machine starts to run more slowly.
And it's nearly always the case that these programs haven't been installed by the computer's owner.
Instead, they've come bundled with another program that the user did want.
Security firm Kaspersky Lab recently reported similar findings - it said that a quarter of Windows 10 users had been affected.
It also found that one in ten Android devices had been hit by crypto-mining software, and that the problem was getting worse.
So what can you do to avoid becoming a victim?
Firstly, get a good security package.
Both Avast and Kaspersky offer free versions of their software that will protect you from such attacks.
Secondly, think twice before you install a program that you don't absolutely need.
PDF readers and software download assistants may be useful, but they aren't essential.
And finally, if a website offers you a program for download, make sure you know what it is before you install it - and think about whether you really need it.

The lawsuit accuses Eric L. Jones of being the "principal architect" of a spamming operation that sent tens of millions of illegal spam messages advertising diet pills, cheap cigarettes and online porn.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), which filed the lawsuit, said Jones operated through two companies he controlled, Affordable Media and The Public Group.
The FTC said Jones' operation has generated at least $1.8m (£1.1m) in revenue since November 2003.

"We will track them down and hold them accountable.

"

The lawsuit was filed on Tuesday in US District Court in Las Vegas.
The court issued a temporary restraining order against Jones, Affordable Media and The Public Group, and froze their assets.
Jones could not be reached for comment.
The US Can-Spam Act, which took effect on January 1, 2004, prohibits the sending of unsolicited commercial email and allows state attorneys general and the FTC to enforce the law.
Spam is unsolicited email that is sent in bulk.
It has become a major headache for Internet services providers, which have struggled to find effective ways of dealing with the flood of unwanted messages.

Washington: The US trade gap hit a record $725.8 billion in 2004, as a booming American economy sucked in imports at a faster pace than exports, official data showed on Friday.

The Commerce Department reported that the gap between what the United States buys from abroad and what it sells to other countries widened by a revised 7.5 percent to a record $41.6 billion in December.
November's trade gap was revised to $40.9 billion from the previously estimated $40.6 billion.
For the year, the trade gap expanded by 12.7 percent to a record $725.8 billion, underscoring how much the US economy depends on foreign produced goods.
The trend, which has been exacerbated by the strong dollar, bodes ill for the US trade deficit, as Americans snap up foreign cars and consumer electronics, and rely on imported oil.
A shrinking trade gap is seen as crucial to bringing down the large federal budget deficit.
But with oil prices rising, the trade gap may get wider in 2005.
The gap with China, the fastest growing US trade partner, hit a record $124.9 billion, swelling by more than 23 percent in 2004.
US trade officials say they are pressing Beijing to rein in its currency, which they claim is undervalued, making Chinese exports artificially cheap and US goods expensive in China.
President Bush recently threatened to brand China a "currency manipulator" if it does not act to narrow the trade gap.

It also expects the UK economy to grow by 3.2% this year, down from its previous forecast of 4.0%.

An Alabama rapper has filmed a music video at a jail in Georgia, US, where he's serving time for a 2019 murder.
American rapper FC Gucci, real name Ferrando Calvache, is seen in the clip waving wads of cash and flashing expensive jewellery.

He's serving a 25-year sentence for the murder-for-hire of a man in Birmingham, Alabama.

Gucci, 32, has been housed in the Walker County Jail in Rock Spring, Georgia, since his conviction because he faces charges there too, including attempted murder.
The video, called Prison Vision, was filmed in February this year, but has just been released.
In it, he raps about his continued love for his girlfriend, known as "Melody", who he says "meant the world" to him.
"I never thought I'd be stuck in a cell, separated from my lover," he says.
"This ain't supposed to be like this, I keep telling myself every night.

"

Gucci was convicted of killing Demarco Baker in Birmingham, Alabama, in 2019.
Baker was shot dead in September 2018, after he was allegedly paid $15,000 (£12,000) by Gucci to kill a man in a feud over a love interest.
Gucci was arrested seven months after the killing in Miami, Florida, and was later extradited to Alabama.
Baker's mother, Karen Baker-Bradley, told reporters at the time of his conviction that "justice has been served".
"This is not a happy day, but it's a good day," she said.
"Now I can have some closure.

"

Gucci's lawyer, Lawrence Kendrick, has asked for a new trial, claiming that crucial evidence that could have cleared his client was not heard at his trial.
The judge has yet to rule on that motion.
Gucci's lawyers have also asked for bail while the appeal is heard.
The role of a controversial "fee factor" in possible student fee increases has been played down by the universities minister.
Chris Skidmore said the figure - used to calculate tuition fee increases - was not a "magic number" and that a government green paper on fee increases would not be "led by" the figure.
He said it was "a total myth" that the fee factor - which stands at 3% - would be used to raise fees every year.
The minister said it was "not a decision" for him to take on fee levels.

Speaking to the BBC, he added that it was for universities to decide what they thought was "reasonable" in terms of fee levels, and that he wanted a debate with the sector on what those levels should be.
The green paper on the future of university fees in England will be published later this month.
It comes after universities were accused of using the fee factor - the maximum fee increase universities can impose - to suggest they could raise fees by as much as £250 per year from 2022.

Several universities - including some of the most prestigious in the country - have announced increases in tuition fees for the 2022/23 academic year using the fee factor, with some setting hikes of up to 6.5%.
These increases are well in excess of the rate of inflation - which stands at 3.1% - and apply to students who are already enrolled on courses as well as those about to start.
Labour has described the increases as a "kick in the teeth" for students.
Shadow universities minister Emma Hardy has urged the government to "step in" and stop the increases.
University leaders have defended the rises - which they say are needed to tackle a funding crisis - and some have offered disadvantaged students rebates or extra financial help.

President Kennedy begins a pre-election tour of the South, speaking at the Municipal Auditorium in Mobile, Alabama.
Mr. Kennedy arrived in Alabama yesterday afternoon, and went to Mobile - a Democratic stronghold in a state whose voters strongly favour his Republican opponent, Senator Barry Goldwater of Arizona.
The president was introduced by Senator James O. Eastland, Democrat of Mississippi, one of the most conservative members of the Senate.
In his speech, the president urged the crowd to send him back to the White House for another four years.
He said he was confident that America could win its fight against Communism if it had the leadership of the Democratic Party for another term.
Speaking of the Republican candidate, Senator Goldwater, the president said that those who favoured his policies were "ready to sell out the United States" and "abandon its mission".
He said he did not believe that Senator Goldwater or his supporters reflected the views of the majority of Republican voters, and he appealed to Republicans to vote for him in November.
UK state pension should be overhauled to include a "good conduct" clause, The Pensions Advisory Service has said.
The government-backed pensions group said too many people still did not understand their retirement options.
Its report called for a simplification of the state pension, including the proposed "good conduct" clause.
This would see the government take into account people's lifestyles and contributions when working out their state pension.
Currently, the state pension is calculated on the number of years a person has worked and the amount they have paid in national insurance contributions.

But the report said this did not take into account whether people had taken active steps to save for their retirement or whether they had taken time out of work to care for children or elderly relatives.
It said the state pension should be "fairer" to these groups of people.
The report also called for a "default" retirement option to be offered to workers, to make sure they did not spend too long in low-return savings vehicles.
At the moment, too many people were staying in the same pension scheme throughout their career, when they would be better off moving to a different scheme, it said.
Default options would help people make better decisions about their retirement savings, it added.
The report's authors also called for the automatic enrollment into workplace pensions, which the government is planning to introduce in 2012, to be extended to the self-employed.
At the moment, the scheme is expected to cover only workers in large and medium-sized firms.
Small businesses will be exempt from the scheme, as will the self-employed.
But the Pensions Advisory Service said the self-employed would have to be included if the pension system was to be fair.
Its report said: "Automatic enrollment offers a real opportunity to increase pension savings, but this will only be successful if it is available to the self-employed as well as the employed.

Andy Murray's hopes of a fairytale finish at Wimbledon were ended by Marin Cilic, who fought back to beat the British favourite into retirement.
The Croatian world number nine produced a powerful display to win 6-7 (6) 4-6 6-3 6-4 6-2 and reach the final.
Defeat ended the hopes of a Murray win on his final Wimbledon appearance, with the roof closed on Centre Court to silence the crowd.
Cilic, who reached the Wimbledon final in 2017, hitting 51 winners and 18 aces on his way to victory.
He will face Nick Kyrgios in Sunday's final after the Australian beat Brandon Nakashima in the other semi-final.
It had been hoped Murray might be able to emulate his hero Fred Perry, who won his final match at Wimbledon, and then farewell the tournament with a lap of honour on Sunday.
But, despite a brilliant battle in which he produced moments of his old magic, the 39-year-old could not quite pull off his dream end.
Instead, it was Cilic who progressed to his first major final since the 2019 US Open, where he lost to Rafael Nadal.

Voters "reject EU by two to one"

The BBC has seen an exclusive poll it commissioned which suggests that a third of people in the UK would vote to leave the EU if there was a referendum tomorrow.
The poll puts support for the EU at 39%, with 51% opposed and 10% don't knows or wouldn't votes.
The findings will concern EU supporters who hope an in/out referendum will not be held tomorrow, or anytime soon.
The poll, carried out by ComRes, asked people how they would vote if a referendum on EU membership were held tomorrow.
Some 39% of respondents said they would vote to stay in the EU, with 51% saying they would vote to leave, and 10% saying they did not know or would not vote.
ComRes chairman Andrew Hawkins said the finding suggested that the country was still divided on the issue.

"There is no doubt that this is an extremely sensitive issue for the British public, with a clear divide in attitudes, and it is clear that there are very strong feelings on both sides of the debate," he said.
"As the government continues to weigh up its policy on this issue, it is clear that it faces a tricky decision with strong feelings on both sides.

"

The poll questioned 1,000 people aged 18 and over on 18 and 19 November.
It came as Prime Minister David Cameron prepared to meet European leaders in Brussels on Thursday to discuss his proposed EU reforms ahead of a summit in December.
Mr Cameron hopes the reforms - on the single market, welfare and immigration - will be enough for him to recommend that the UK stays in the EU at an in/out referendum by the end of 2017.
Several recent polls on the issue have indicated that the public is divided on the issue, with those in favour of withdrawal gaining ground.
Last week, a poll for the Sun newspaper put support for withdrawal at 44%, with 42% wanting to stay in, and 14% don't knows.
