Humanoid robot learns how to run

A humanoid robot has been taught how to jog and jump, in a development that could eventually lead to robots being used for search and rescue missions.
The robot, called Atlas, performs a range of athletic movements, including doing a high jump and squatting to pick up a heavy box.
It was developed by Boston Dynamics, a company owned by Google parent firm Alphabet.
Boston Dynamics has been refining the robot's movements over several years.
"Now that we have laid the foundation for dynamic mobility, we will be building out a suite of advanced mobility capabilities," said the company's founder, Marc Raibert.
"These will include everything from highly dynamic mobility in rough terrain to manipulating objects in the environment.

"

At present, Atlas weighs just under 80kg (175lb) and is powered by an internal combustion engine.
In the future, the company hopes to create an electric version that is lighter and faster.
Film critics in the US have showered praise on the comedy Sideways, which opened in American cinemas last week.

The film, which stars Paul Giamatti and Thomas Haden Church, is set in the California wine country and tells the story of two friends on a road trip who venture to the valley to celebrate one's upcoming wedding.

Los Angeles Times critic Kenneth Turan called the film "smart, insightful and funny" and added: "Thomas Haden Church and Paul Giamatti are absolutely perfect, capturing the hell-bent sense of the inevitable that runs through the movie.

"

In the New York Times, Manohla Dargis called the film "deceptively complex and insightful".
She added: "Though centred on the male mid-life crisis, it's really about all sorts of longing, fulfilled and unfulfilled, and the compromises, large and small, that we make to survive."
In the Wall Street Journal, Joe Morgenstern called the film "smart, insightful and hilarious...
a sideways look at love and marriage, ageing and addiction, men and women, and the good and bad chemicals that course through them".
However, in the Daily News, Joe Brown was less enthusiastic, calling the film "a lot of fun, but it's not Oscar material".
"I'm glad I saw it, but I don't need to see it a second time," he added.
In Variety, Todd McCarthy called it "smart, insightful, witty, observant and amusing".
"This comedy hits the mark on every level," he concluded.
Liverpool's injury nightmare has worsened with the news that striker Daniel Sturridge is now a major doubt for this Sunday's visit of Manchester United.

Sturridge joins Luis Suarez, Steven Gerrard and Jonjo Shelvey on the treatment table, with captain Gerrard ruled out for a month with a hamstring injury picked up in the win over United.
Midfielder Shelvey is out for at least three weeks with a thigh problem, while striker Suarez has not trained all week because of a knee injury and is rated as highly unlikely to be available.
That leaves Sturridge, who has already had surgery this season on his hip and a thigh injury, as the only senior striker available.
And he only returned against United last week following two months out after picking up a hamstring injury against Swansea in early February.
The news will be a huge concern to Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers, who is already trying to cope with defensive injuries to Sebastian Coates, Martin Skrtel and Daniel Agger.
Coates is out for the rest of the season with a knee injury while Skrtel faces a fight to be fit for United after picking up a hamstring problem in the 2-1 win at Old Trafford.
Agger has been out for more than a month with a similar problem and is not expected back any time soon.
Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has defended the club's decision to spend so much money on Robbie Keane, despite the Irish striker's recent dip in form.
Keane joined the Reds from Tottenham for £20m in the summer, but has failed to score from open play this season.
The 28-year-old came in for criticism following Liverpool's 1-0 defeat at Fulham on Sunday.
Benitez said: "Robbie is a good player.
We were following him before he went to Tottenham.

"
Keane joined Spurs from Leeds for £7m in July 2002 and scored 56 goals in 131 games for the north London club.
He signed a four-and-a-half-year contract with Liverpool in August and has scored four goals in 21 appearances for the club.
Benitez added: "He has experience, he is hungry to win things and he wants to win things with us.
"He is a good player and he will score goals here."
Keane was largely ineffective at Craven Cottage and was substituted 55 minutes into the 1-0 defeat.
He has now gone 11 games without a goal and has failed to score from open play since his strike against Portsmouth on 17 March.
Benitez said: "I know he can score more goals but at the moment he is not doing that.
"But he is trying and making efforts for the team.
Against Fulham he was working hard and involved in the game.
"He is a player who will score goals, I am sure about that.

"
Meanwhile, Liverpool have confirmed that they will appeal against the sending-off of Spanish midfielder Xabi Alonso in Sunday's defeat at Fulham.
Alonso was dismissed in the 75th minute for a professional foul on Clint Dempsey, but Benitez said the 27-year-old did not deserve to be given his second yellow card.
He said: "It was a tactical foul and it was not a second booking.
"We have seen the DVD and we will appeal.

"
If the club's appeal is unsuccessful, Alonso will miss the FA Cup fourth-round replay at Birmingham on Tuesday, as well as the league games against West Ham and Aston Villa.

Senior US and Russian trade officials have held "constructive" talks on Moscow's wish to join the WTO, officials say.
Russia's entry to the World Trade Organization (WTO) has been blocked for years by Georgia and other ex-Soviet states.
But US Trade Representative Susan Schwab and Russian Economic Development and Trade Minister German Gref said they had made progress in clearing obstacles to Russia's entry.
"We exchanged specific ideas about the remaining issues that must be resolved," Ms Schwab said in a statement after the meeting in Washington.
"We agreed that the two sides would continue to work towards resolving these issues so that Russia can join the WTO," she added.
Mr Gref said: "We made progress in clearing obstacles remaining in the way of Russia's accession to the WTO."
The Russian minister said one of the issues that still needed to be tackled was the "transparency" of Russia's laws on intellectual property.
Ms Schwab said she planned to visit Russia in April to continue the talks.
Russia has been trying to join the WTO since 1996, and US backing for its membership bid has been a key factor in the negotiations.

But Washington has become increasingly frustrated with Russia's lack of progress in adopting reforms to its trade policies, and there were reports last year that the US might withdraw its support for Russia's membership.
US President George W Bush and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed the issue at a summit in Bratislava last year, and agreed to intensify efforts to try to resolve the remaining obstacles.

Given the recent deterioration in Russia's relations with Georgia, and the ongoing tensions between Moscow and ex-Soviet states, it appears unlikely that they will continue to stand in the way of Russia's WTO membership.
Greek pole vaulters Ekaterina Stefanidi and Andrej Melu have had their appeals against suspensions from the sport's governing body, cleared by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).
Stefanidi, who won gold at Rio 2016, and Melu had been suspended by the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) in June last year for allegedly violating anti-doping rules.
The IAAF said at the time that the athletes had allegedly missed four out-of-competition tests between June 2017 and January 2018.
But Cas said the suspensions were "not necessary" and that there was "insufficient evidence" that the athletes had ever missed a test.
In a statement, Cas said the IAAF's "failing to properly serve notices" to the athletes for the tests in question was an "obvious" and "critical" flaw in the process.
Both athletes have consistently denied doping violations and have said they were not at the addresses provided to the doping control officers on the day of the alleged missed tests.

Cas' ruling said the athletes - who have been cleared to return to competition immediately - had provided "reliable telephone data" to show they could not have been at the addresses provided to doping control officers on the days of the tests.
The athletics body said it would not appeal against the Cas' decision.
In a statement, Stefanidi, who also won bronze at London 2012, said she was "delighted" with the outcome.
"I have said from the beginning that this case was not about whether I was a clean athlete or not, but about the procedures that should be followed in anti-doping," she said.
"Unfortunately, these were not followed and this decision shows that.
I'm looking forward to getting back to training and competing again as soon as possible."
The Conservative Party has published details of its policy to send asylum seekers to Rwanda.
The cost of the policy, which aims to deter people crossing the English Channel in small boats, would be about £1.4bn a year, the party says.
Under the scheme, announced earlier this month, arrivals would be given a choice of either being sent to Rwanda or leaving the UK for a "safe third country" where they would be granted asylum.
Those who chose to go to Rwanda would be processed there and, if successful, would be resettled in the east African country.
Unsuccessful applicants would be offered accommodation in Rwanda and encouraged to apply again, the policy says.
The cost of the policy would be about £1.4bn in the first full year, then £1.2bn a year afterwards, the party says.
About £106m of that money would be for accommodation for those waiting for decisions on their asylum claims.
The remainder would be for airline contracts and "support on the ground" in Rwanda.
The party says it has received advice from the Migration Advisory Committee on the cost of the policy and that the committee's members agreed with their calculations.
The policy has been widely criticised by churches, charities and opposition parties.
The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, said it was immoral and unjust while the Prime Minister's wife, Carrie Johnson, said it was "unethical and dangerous".
The UN's refugee chief called the policy "catastrophic" and the US government described it as "wrong" and a "waste of human life".
The policy says the government could consider further "safe destination" agreements for asylum seekers in the future.
Andy Roddick reached the final of the SAP Open in San Jose with a straight-set victory over Russia's Mikhail Youzhny.
The third seed beat the world number 18 6-4 7-5 to set up a final meeting with either Serbia's Janko Tipsarevic or France's Richard Gasquet.
Tipsarevic reached the semi-finals with a 6-4 6-2 victory over Germany's Tommy Haas.
Roddick, 27, has yet to drop a set in the tournament.
Oil company Yukos has lost its bankruptcy battle in a US court, leaving its former owners with nothing.
The former Russian oil giant had been appealing against a court ruling last year that cleared the way for its assets to be sold off to pay off debt.
The Texas court rejected the appeal, saying Yukos had filed too late and failed to provide sufficient evidence.
Former Yukos shareholders including its former chief executive Mikhail Khodorkovsky had hoped to share in the proceeds.
They were jailed in Russia but have since been released.
The case dates back to 2004 when Yukos was broken up and its main production unit was sold to state-owned gas giant Gazprom for $9.35bn (£5.8bn).
The company was placed into bankruptcy protection, with its main assets sold to a company called Baikal Finance Group.
Last year, a US court ruled that the sale of Yukos' main production unit could go ahead, clearing the way for its assets to be sold off to pay off debt.
Yukos had argued that the sale was merely an attempt by the Russian government to seize its assets and that it was politically motivated.
However, the US court rejected this argument, saying that there was "sufficient evidence" that Yukos had filed its appeal too late.
The former shareholders plan to appeal on Monday.
The former owner of Russian oil company Yukos has filed a lawsuit against Russia at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in Washington.
Mikhail Khodorkovsky is seeking $28bn in compensation for his firm's breakup and for being detained and jailed for a decade.
Yukos, once Russia's largest oil company, was broken up after being hit with huge tax bills.
Mr Khodorkovsky said the suit was "to defend my good name and my rights".
The suit claims that Russia violated the Energy Charter, a global energy treaty, by expropriating Yukos.
"I decided to file a claim today to defend my good name and my rights, as well as the rights of all Yukos shareholders," Mr Khodorkovsky said at the ICSID.
"I hope that the Russian authorities will realise that their unlawful behaviour has consequences."
Yukos, once the largest oil producer in Russia, was broken up after the government issued huge tax claims against it.
The firm owed billions in back taxes, according to the Russian authorities, although Yukos said the claims were politically motivated.
Yukos' assets were sold to state oil company Rosneft and private firm Gazprom Neft.
Mr Khodorkovsky, who had employed former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev as a consultant, was Russia's richest man at the time of his arrest in 2003.
He was found guilty of fraud and tax evasion and sentenced to 10 years in jail.
He was released in 2013 and flew to Switzerland, where he had lived prior to his imprisonment.
The Russian government has previously indicated it would not recognise any claims by Yukos.
"The suit will not be without consequences for Khodorkovsky himself," said Vladimir Milov, a former deputy energy minister and an adviser to Mr Khodorkovsky.
"He is not any more a Russian citizen, but the chances are high that he will not be able to travel to Russia anyway.
So it is not a matter of choice for him."
The European Parliament has ordered a reboot of its ambitious plans to create a unified patent system across Europe.
The assembly's legal affairs committee said the package, known as the unitary patent, would be rewritten to try to address critics' concerns.
These centred on the involvement of the European Court of Justice, the need for translation and whether patents would be valid in all EU states.
The legislation aims to simplify patent protection by allowing inventors to gain patent protection in a single, unified patent court.
The legislation has faced resistance from Italy, Spain and Poland.
They have threatened to block the legislation unless changes are made.
The committee said it planned to split the unitary patent package into two bills.
One would deal with the unitary patent itself while the other would establish a new court to handle patent disputes, known as the Unified Patent Court (UPC).
Italian socialist Guido Sacconi, who led the work on the report, said the committee had decided to "take the bull by the horns".
"We have decided to modify the two pillars of the unitary patent package: the unitary patent itself and the Unified Patent Court," he said.
"The two elements will be split and this will allow us to proceed with the patent court and a bit later discuss the unitary patent."
The committee's proposal will now go before the full parliament for a vote.
If passed, it will then be up to the EU's 28 member states to decide whether to proceed with the plan.
Currently, inventors must apply for patent protection in each EU country where they want patent protection.
The court would have the power to rule on patent disputes for the entire EU, making it easier for inventors to protect their patents across the EU.
The court would be made up of a main branch, based in Paris, with branches in London and Munich.
It would have the power to rule on patent disputes for the entire EU, making it easier for inventors to protect their patents in multiple countries.
The economic situation in Britain is likely to deteriorate over the next 12 months, according to a poll of economists carried out by the BBC.
The survey comes as official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% in the three months to September, compared with 0.4% growth in the three months to June.
The BBC's poll suggests that economists do not expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates before the second half of 2023.
Inflation is expected to be above 4% until the second quarter of 2023, the poll of about 40 economists found.
The Bank of England has predicted that consumer price inflation - the rate at which prices rise - could hit 5% by the end of the year, and analysts expect it to stay elevated well into 2023.
The BBC's poll came as official figures showed that the cost of living rose by 4.1% in the 12 months to September, down from a 5.1% rise in the 12 months to August.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said warmer clothing and increased spending on footwear helped to push down the rate of inflation, but it remains high by historical standards.

Richest 1% of Colombia's population has grabbed nearly half the money set aside for the nation's anti-poverty programme, alarming officials in a country where wealth inequality is among the widest in the world.
The enriched families withdrew nearly $750m (£656m) from the so-called "solidarity dividend" over the past six years.
The dividend is paid by the government from taxes on the nation's largest banks and telephone and utilities companies.
It is meant to help some of Colombia's neediest citizens.
But the fund has instead become a windfall for the wealthy, according to the head of the national tax office, Juan Carlos Velez.
"This is unacceptable," he told local media.
"We are going to implement measures to avoid this happening again.
The fund was set up more than 20 years ago as part of a landmark peace deal between the government and guerrilla group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
But in recent years the rules governing the programme have been loosened and the money is now used by some as an alternative pension scheme, or to pay for private education and healthcare.
The head of the tax office plans to restrict the use of the funds, and increase controls over them.
Several former directors of the fund have been accused of taking bribes in exchange for allowing wealthy Colombians to withdraw money.
One former official was arrested last week as part of the investigation.
The fund is officially called the Solidarity Intergenerational Savings Programme, and was modelled on a similar scheme in Chile.
It is funded by a tax on the largest local and foreign companies operating in Colombia.
The money is meant to incentivise businesses to invest in the country.
Colombia has one of the highest rates of wealth inequality in the world, according to the World Inequality Report 2022.
The report found that the top 1% of earners in the country earn more than 20% of the total national income.
Manchester United will allow executive co-chairman Joel Glazer to be interviewed by independent advisers as part of the review into the European Super League (ESL).
The Premier League club say they have received more than 200 pieces of evidence from fans, shareholders and other interested parties.
The ESL was launched on 18 April but collapsed within 72 hours due to widespread opposition.
United, Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City and Tottenham were the six Premier League clubs who signed up to the breakaway league.
Last month, the clubs faced heavy criticism after they were revealed to have signed 'letterheads' that would have seen them become founding members of the ESL.
United's involvement in the ESL proposal saw their plans for a £1.3bn ($1.7bn) float on the Singapore stock exchange delayed, while the Glazers received criticism for their involvement.
The family, who have been United owners since 2005, were understood to have been key players in the formation of the ESL.
In a statement, United said: "Independent advisers, supported by global legal firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton, will conduct a review of the club's involvement in the European Super League.

"The review will consider evidence gathered from fans, shareholders and other interested parties and will include input from independent advisers, supported by global legal firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP, as well as from the club itself.

"All evidence will be scrutinised and considered as part of the review process and the advisers will be afforded access to senior executives and non-executive directors of the club, including executive co-chairman Joel Glazer."
United added that evidence can be provided until Wednesday, 21 July, with an online portal set up to allow fans to submit any evidence they feel is relevant.
"The Sands of Time" almost didn't get made.
Universal Pictures didn't believe in the script and balked at making the film because it featured a video-game character who was relatively unknown to moviegoers.
Almost 10 years later, the studio has learned its lesson.
On Thursday, it announced it was moving forward with a sequel to the 2010 "Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time," which grossed $336 million at the box office.
The follow-up is slated for release on August 5, 2022.
"Prince of Persia" stars Jake Gyllenhaal as the title character, with Ben Affleck, Gemma Arterton, and Sir Ben Kingsley also attached to return.

The announcement comes after Disney rebranded its 20th Century Fox film production as 20th Century Studios, and amid continued interest in video game adaptations including Universal's "Warcraft" and Sony's "The Last of Us" television series.
There's no word on whether the sequel will be based on a video game.

Britain left the EU on 31 January and is currently in an 11-month transition period.
It is due to end on 31 December, and could be extended.
The proposed changes to the EU's asylum system will be discussed at a meeting of interior ministers in Brussels on Thursday.
The ministers are hoping to finally agree a deal on how to handle asylum seekers - including those who enter the EU illegally.

The current rules state that refugees must stay in the first country they set foot in - but this has caused a political row, with countries on the EU's external border such as Greece struggling to cope with the influx.
The UK has already refused to take part in an emergency meeting on the issue on Tuesday.
A government spokesperson said the proposal was "a departure from the initial proposal agreed last summer" and would "not be in the best interests" of the UK.
The spokesperson said: "We have been clear that we need a pragmatic approach to asylum that ensures refugees are shared fairly across the continent."
The spokesperson added the UK would "continue to engage" with the proposal but said any future system had to "meet the interests of the whole community" in the UK.

Defiant American hunters put wolf ban to the test

Two men have headed to court to challenge a federal law that bans the hunting of wolves in the US.
William Perry and Jason Molnar say the 1966 Endangered Species Act is an unconstitutional infringement on citizens' rights.
The pair want to renew a tradition of wolf hunting on their property in north-eastern Utah.
At issue is whether a long-standing federal law can overrule a state's right to manage wildlife within its own borders.
Their lawsuit has been backed by several hunting groups, who say the wolves are harming their livestock and that the predators should be managed by the state.
"It is time for this court to stop federal bureaucrats from trampling on state's rights to manage and regulate their own wildlife," the groups say in their court filing.
"This case is not about the ethics of hunting wolves.
Nor is this case about the importance of preserving wolves...

It is about who gets to decide these questions: state governments or federal bureaucrats?"

The US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), which manages the endangered species list, says the pair's challenge is without merit.
"Returning wolf management to the states will not only benefit the species, it will also benefit the ecosystems in which they occur," the USFWS said in court documents.

"There is no scientific or legal basis for continuing to list wolves as a threatened species, and USFWS's determination that wolf populations in the lower-48 states should be delisted was reasonable and not arbitrary and capricious."
The wolves were hunted nearly to extinction in the US by the mid-20th Century.
They were placed under federal protection in the 1970s and 80s, allowing their populations to grow.
More recently, they have been the subject of bitter debates between those who say they should be protected and those who say they represent a threat to livestock and wild game.
The USFWS announced in March that it would remove protections for wolves in the contiguous US, prompting several states to schedule hunts for next year.
The move has been challenged by several groups, and a federal court recently restored protections for the animals while the legal challenges play out.
Regardless of the outcome of this case, the wolf's legal status is likely to remain a contentious issue for years to come.

Industrial output falls in Japan

Official data shows the monthly fall in October was 0.6%, compared with a 0.2% gain in September.
The figure for October was also down 3.2% on the same month last year.
Japan has been hit by supply chain problems, which have been exacerbated by the pandemic.
But the government has insisted that the country's economy will recover soon.
Data also shows falls in industrial production across Asia.
In October, output fell in Malaysia, South Korea and Thailand, while it rose in China and Indonesia.
Japan's government has urged businesses to raise pay for workers which it hopes will help the economy recover.
Last week, data showed that Japan's unemployment rate had fallen to 2.7%, while job vacancies hit a record high.
Japan's economy has been recovering from the initial hit it took during the pandemic, thanks to strong exports and household spending.
Tech firms should be held responsible for harmful content on their platforms, the EU's internal market commissioner has said.
Thierry Brighton said EU laws could be used to force tech companies to remove illegal content.
The UK government has proposed holding firms "directly accountable" for harmful content.
Mr Brighton said the EU had "all the tools in the toolbox" to make sure action was taken.
The BBC has learned that Mr Brighton made the comments in a private meeting with journalists on Friday.
In recent years, the EU has struggled to agree on how best to regulate online companies.
A draft of a digital services act, due to be published in December, is likely to include measures that would force tech firms to be more proactive in removing illegal content.
But it is not clear whether the legislation will include a mandate for speedier removal of content, which the UK government has called for.

Speaking at the Internet Governance Forum in Berlin, Mr Brighton said the EU had three key tools at its disposal:

"One is of course the Digital Services Act that we are working on.
The second one is the Electronic Commerce Directive that already exists and that could be reinforced, and the third one is competition law."
Mr Brighton's comments are significant because he is responsible for proposing new EU laws on the digital single market.
The digital single market is an EU initiative to regulate the online economy across the 27-member bloc.

"When it comes to the responsibility of platforms, I think platforms have a responsibility to behave better on illegal content, on hate speech, on terrorist content and on copyright infringement," Mr Brighton said.
"And I think they have a responsibility to analyse and assess the risks that are linked to the platforms themselves.

"

Earlier this year the father of a girl who was killed in the 2015 Sousse terror attack in Tunisia, said large technology firms were " aiding and abetting" terrorism by allowing extremist material to be broadcast on their platforms.
Mike Haines said companies such as Facebook and Google had "monopolies" on content and advertising and should be forced to do more.
In response, Google said it was working "tirelessly" to remove extremist content from its platforms "as quickly as possible".
A Facebook spokesman said: "There is no place for terrorism on Facebook - we take swift action to remove terrorist content, and we make it easy for people to report this content."

An Irish Athletics Year

The year 2004 was a memorable one for Irish athletics, with a number of notable performances and achievements.
At the Olympic Games in Athens, Ireland's athletes recorded their best ever finish, with Brian Carroll winning a bronze medal in the 3000m steeplechase.
This was followed by a silver medal in the same event at the World Athletics Championships in Helsinki, won by David Gillick.
At the European Championships in Athens, Ireland won four gold medals, with Robert Heffernan winning the 10,000m, Maria McCambridge winning the 800m, and Derval O'Rourke winning the 100m hurdles.
The men's 4x100m relay team also won gold, with Paul Hession, Tom Comyns, Paul Brizzell, and Darren Campbell winning in a time of 39.82s.
At the World Junior Championships in Italy, Ireland won two silver medals, with Derval O'Rourke finishing second in the 100m hurdles, and Roisin McGettigan finishing second in the 3000m steeplechase.
Overall, it was a successful year for Irish athletics, with a number of notable performances and achievements at the highest levels of the sport.
The London Stock Exchange has set 30 July as the date it will decide whether to recommend an £8.2bn ($12bn) takeover offer from a consortium of investors.
The board of the exchange will meet on that day to consider the proposal from a group led by the London Stock Exchange Group and including hedge funds Citadel and Hoxton.
The consortium launched its surprise bid for the exchange last month.
At that stage, the LSE said the proposal was "highly conditional" and "unsolicited".
But on Tuesday it announced it was considering the offer and that its directors intended to vote in favour of it.
The consortium has made clear it does not expect to win support from the LSE's management and board without the backing of at least 50% of shareholders.
When the bid was announced last month, LSE shares jumped by more than 20% to more than £75.40.
They have since slipped back to about £72, still some way above the offer price of 3,250p per share.
The London Stock Exchange is the world's oldest stock exchange and is home to a number of leading indices, including the FTSE 100.

The exchange operates two trading platforms - one for its customers to trade shares and another, called Turquoise, which allows investors to trade shares, bonds, derivatives and exchange-traded funds.
The LSE also offers trading in shares on other stock exchanges through its Borsa Italiana and Turquoise businesses.
A US federal judge has set a trial date for the Balco case, in which major league baseball players are accused of using steroids.
The trial, which could be the biggest doping case in American sporting history, will begin on 12 January.
Forty-four players face evidence alleging they used steroids and human growth hormone between 1996 and 2001.
They include star names such as Jose Canseco, Juan Gonzalez and Jason Giambi.
The players have all denied the allegations.
The trial was set after hearings in US District Court in San Francisco on Wednesday.
Judge Harold Baer set the trial date after lawyers for the players and the Office of the US Attorney agreed to avoid a trial this year.
That would have clashed with the baseball playoffs and World Series, which finish in late October.
The players' lawyers had asked for a trial in February 2005 but the court rejected that proposal.
The players face evidence including secret recordings of conversations at the Laboratory for Athletic Performance, or Balco, in the San Francisco Bay area.
The US government filed charges in February, accusing the players of cheating, lying to officials and conspiring to cover up their doping violations.
They face potential fines of up to $250,000 (£150,000) and up to two years in jail.
The players say they are victims of a conspiracy by steroids dealer Victor Conte, who has already been convicted of supplying steroids to athletes.
The UK has retained its position as the world's biggest buyer of music, spending $1.3bn last year, according to a report by music industry body the IFPI.
The figure represented a 7% rise on 2021 and coincided with increased sales of vinyl records and CDs, as well as a surge in streams.
The IFPI said vinyl sales in the UK were up by 23% while CD sales rose by 6%.
UK listeners also led the world in audio streaming, with 148 billion songs played in the 12 months to the end of 2022, up by 11%.

The IFPI, which represents the recorded music industry worldwide, published the figures on the same day that the UK's Official Charts Company announced the Beatles were the biggest artist of the 21st century so far, based on sales of their recordings.
The IFPI's report said that the top five markets in terms of trade value - the UK, US, Japan, Germany and Australia - accounted for more than half (54%) of the global total.
The IFPI's chief executive, Frances Moore, said the figures demonstrated "the resilience of the fan-driven music ecosystem".
"In an age of unlimited choice, fans around the world turned to music in record numbers," she added.
The figures were compiled for the IFPI by Nielsen Music for the year to the end of 2022.
The total volume of vinyl sales in the world last year increased by 11% to $1.08 billion, while CD sales rose by 4% to $1.5 billion.
However, the rise in vinyl sales was lower than the huge surge in popularity the format enjoyed in the first decade of this century, when sales increased by 170% between 2000 and 2009.

The IFPI said vinyl's revival had been driven by a tilt in the format's sales towards more recent releases, with vinyl copies of albums by Adele, Taylor Swift, Elton John, Fleetwood Mac and Dave being sold alongside classics by the Beatles, Pink Floyd and Nirvana.
The UK's national fraud and cyber crime reporting centre has issued an alert over an increase in the theft of card details.
The centre, run by the City of London Police, said criminals were targeting web browsers and passwords.
It issued advice on how to reduce the risk of fraud, but no specific incidents had been reported.
The warning came after months of similar alerts from banks.
In a statement, the centre said it wanted to make the public aware of "increasing reports" of a new technique being used by criminals to steal people's card details.
"Fraudsters are targeting the computers of consumers, as well as businesses and retailers, by infecting web browsers with malicious malware," it said.
"This malware is known to be difficult to detect, and allows criminals to capture card details as a customer enters them online.

"

It urged people to protect themselves when shopping online by using websites that were "secure and authentic".
"We would also encourage people to be wary of clicking on promotional banners, pop-ups or attachments in emails - as these are commonly used as a vehicle to transmit the malware," it added.
"Ensuring you have antivirus software installed on your computer and keeping web browsers up to date is also vital in combating this type of malware.

"

The centre said it had also alerted the banking and retail industry to the threat.

A number of major banks have issued warnings about the threat of so-called "card-not-present" fraud - where a stolen card is used to buy goods or services over the phone or internet - in recent months.
The warning came on "Cyber Monday", the busiest day of the year for online shopping.
The ban on hunting with dogs has robust support in England and Wales, a minister has told the BBC.
Animal welfare minister Lord Goldsmith said "not everyone agrees" with the 2004 Hunting Act but it had wide support.
He said he remained committed to the "principle of the ban" following a review.

Lord Mancroft said the current law was "not working" and was "widely ignored".

The review came after the Conservative Party included a pledge to "legislate to allow hunting of foxes and other wild animals with dogs" in its 2019 general election manifesto.
Lord Goldsmith told the BBC's Newsnight programme that the review would ensure the law was "working as intended".
"Not everyone agrees with the Hunting Act, but it is important to recognise that it did have very wide support at the time it was passed, and it continues to have wide support today," he said.
"That is why the principle of the ban is still in place.
We recognise there are some who don't like it, but it is an important part of our legislation."
The Hunting Act 2004 bans hunting wild mammals with dogs in England and Wales - but not in Scotland.
The act does not prohibit chasing wild mammals without dogs, or training dogs to hunt.
Nor does it make it illegal to kill wild mammals that are "injuring or threatening" livestock, game or poultry.
The Countryside Alliance, a pro-hunting campaign group, said the ban had failed and called for it to be repealed.
Its head of hunting, Liam Stokes, said: "The Hunting Act is inherently flawed.
It has failed in its intention to curb hunting and has instead criminalised those who abide by the law.
"The solution is to repeal the act and replace it with a sensible alternative that will deliver its original aim."
But Lord Goldsmith said the current law was "important for animal welfare" and "the principle of the ban is there for a good reason".
He added that the review would make sure the legislation was "working as intended and… it is properly enforced".
But he said the issue was "not about re-opening the debate" over whether to have a ban.

Title: Bath faced with Tindall ultimatum

Subtitle: Sport: Rugby union: Bath have been given until Friday to resolve their dispute with England centre Mike Tindall.
If they can't reach an agreement the 26-year-old will leave the club.
Tindall wants to stay at The Rec but has been frustrated by the lack of a new contract offer.
He has been offered a deal by French giants Stade Francais.
The BBC's Jim Bear on Tindall: "He is one of the best centres in the country, if not the best.
There is no doubt he is a world-class player.
"He is also a local boy who has come through the ranks at Bath and is very popular with the fans.
It would be a big blow to the club if he were to leave.

"

Bear on the offers Tindall has received: "There has been a lot of interest from France and even though Stade Francais are not one of the top clubs in France, the offer they have made to Tindall is worth around £350,000 a year.
"That is about double what he is currently earning at Bath and the kind of money the club cannot really match.

"You are also looking at the fact he is married to Zara Phillips, Princess Anne's daughter, and they have just had a baby son, so the attraction of staying in this country may not be as great for him as it once was.

"

Tindall was reportedly unhappy that he was not offered a new contract during the summer and, with less than a year left on his current deal, he is free to talk to other clubs.

The BBC's Bear adds: "There is a feeling that Tindall could have been offered a new contract during the summer to keep the peace and from the club's point of view they would have been happy for him to stay.
But for whatever reason that offer never came.
"Now he has basically said, if I don't get an offer by Friday, I am going.

"

If Bath do not offer Tindall a new deal, they will receive nothing if he moves to France but could receive up to £350,000 if he moves to another English club.
Bear concludes: "There is a feeling that his preferred option would be to stay at Bath but that possibility is looking less likely with every passing day."

The 61-year-old left his role as a pundit with BBC Sport last month and has signed a three-year contract with the Championship club.
He will work closely with the first team and assist manager Mick McCarthy, who was appointed last month.
Hoddle said: "It is a massive opportunity and I'm very excited about the challenge."

and I can't wait to get started.

"

He was in charge for 18 months before moving to Tottenham but said he "always wanted to come back" to the club.
"When this opportunity arose it was something I couldn't turn down," he said.
Wolves chairman Steve Morgan said: "We are delighted to have secured the services of someone of Glenn's calibre and experience to become an integral part of our backroom team.
"He will provide invaluable support to Mick McCarthy and the other members of the coaching staff, and will also assist with the development of our young players and academy."
Tata Steel aims to cut up to 15,000 jobs in Britain over the next decade as part of a restructuring plan.
The company, which employs about 20,000 people in the UK, said it had begun consultations that could lead to compulsory redundancies.
Unions said they were "disappointed" and called on the company to improve its offer on jobs and investment.
As part of the plans, Tata Steel is also selling its specialty steel making operation in South Yorkshire.

As part of the latest plans, the company is aiming to deliver another £50-65m of annual savings to its European operations by the end of March 2026, on top of the £65m it aims to achieve this year.

NTL is offering the service on its digital television platform, which is available in 70% of UK households.
Customers with digital set-top boxes can purchase films for £2.99, or TV programmes for £1.75.
The company said it intended to increase the choice of films and programmes available, and intended to offer more interactive services in the future.
NTL has had more than 1.2 million digital TV customers since it was launched in October 1999.

Krispy Kreme shares hit by doughnut overdose

Glazed and confused investors dumped shares in Krispy Kreme after the doughnut chain warned that it had suffered an "overdose" of popularity.
The company, best known for its Original Glazed doughnuts, said it had been overwhelmed by demand since the beginning of the year.
Shares in the company fell 12% in response to the news.
Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Mike Tattersfield said the company was working to resolve the supply chain issues, but it would take time.
"In the last few weeks, we have experienced several supply chain challenges, including ingredient shortages and delivery delays," he said.
"While we expect most of these issues to be resolved soon, they may impact us in the coming months," he added.
Krispy Kreme cited delivery delays and shortages of ingredients such as chocolate and packaging materials among its problems.
The company, which has 397 stores in 31 countries, said it suffered from an "overdose of success" after sales jumped 17% in the first financial quarter ending on 31 March.
It warned that this had put its supply chain under significant pressure, with some stores selling out of doughnuts.
Mr. Tattersfield said that an increase in delivery costs - caused by a shortage of drivers - had also hit the firm.
In recent months, several major companies have warned that they have been hit by a perfect storm of supply chain problems and shortages.
Last month, Nestle warned that its supply chain issues could last until 2022.
And supermarket chain Morrisons recently said its supply chain crisis had worsened, with the supermarket industry struggling to recruit drivers.
Krispy Kreme, which is headquartered in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, was founded in 1937 and has been owned by investment group JAB Holding Company since 2016.
In an effort to fix its supply chain issues, the company said it was opening more delivery routes to its shops and warehouses and was hiring more workers.
It is also trying to make its doughnut-making processes more efficient, for example by simplifying its recipes.

"The attitude, application and desire of the players has been first class in Europe," said McClaren.

Mr Yates was giving evidence against ex-Worldcom accountants Troy Normand and David Myers, who are accused of cooking the books to hide the firm's true financial state.

"

The judge then cleared the court and discussed the matter with both the defence and prosecution.

US prosecutors have alleged that the two men created false documents to hide hundreds of millions of dollars of expenses, giving Worldcom an inaccurate picture of its financial health.

Labour have been attacked for "glorifying" the memory of a mass murderer after using an image of Myra Hindley in an election poster.
The party has been criticised for including an image of the Moors Murderer - imprisoned for killing five children in the 1960s - in a poster highlighting the sentences served by child killers.
The poster lists the sentences given to killers Mary Bell, Jon Venables and Robert Thompson, and Hindley - who spent 15 years in jail for her crimes - alongside pictures of Labour politicians.
The party said it was highlighting the difference between Labour and the Tories on the issue.
But shadow home secretary David Davis said it was a "grotesque" decision which "glorified a murderer".
"This is not the first time that Labour have used evil figures from our past in this way and I am furious that they have done it again," he said.
"To compare Myra Hindley with those children is disgusting and grotesque.
To suggest that Labour MPs are in some way similar to her is disgusting.

"

Hindley, who died in 2002, spent more than 40 years in prison after being jailed alongside her lover Ian Brady for killing five children between 1963 and 1965.
The pair buried four of their victims on Saddleworth Moor in the Pennines and the bodies of Keith Bennett and Pauline Reade have never been found.
A Labour Party spokesman said: "Our poster focuses on the difference between Labour and the Tories on criminal justice - it's the Tories who set the sentence, Labour who votes to review it.
"Myra Hindley served more than 15 years in jail, five times longer than the worst cases of child killers under the last Tory government who were allowed out after serving just months.
"This is the factual comparison Labour is making - we make no apology for it.

"

The Liberal Democrats have also criticised the poster, with home affairs spokesman Mark Oaten calling it "disgusting and inappropriate".

But Conservative leader Michael Howard said his party had a "very clear" policy on the issue.

"We will not be swayed by the Labour Party's silly politics."
Barclays shares have risen after the UK bank confirmed it was in talks to buy the credit card business of US lender Credit Suisse.

British Airways will suspend its two direct flights to Saudi Arabia next month due to a "diminishing commercial outlook," the airline says.

The move comes as Saudi Arabia continues to pursue budget cuts as part of plans to diversify its economy.
British Airways said it was "sorry" to customers who would be affected by the cancellations.

BT has announced it will be offering free internet phone calls to customers, the BBC reported.
The UK's largest telecoms provider said calls would be free whether made to fixed-line or mobile phones, or even international numbers.
However, calls will only be free if they are made via broadband and not via the mobile phone network, BT said.
The company said it wanted to "future-proof" its customers' phone bills and "evolve" the traditional landline.

Industry regulator Ofcom said it would "carefully review" the offer, to ensure it complied with its rules, which state that providers must be clear about any price differences between using a landline or internet service.
In its statement, BT said its customers would need to have an active subscription to BT Broadband and a compatible router to benefit from the offer.
Once they had signed up, they would be able to make free calls anytime, anywhere, the company said.
Landline and broadband customers will be able to sign up from November, while EE mobile customers can do so in January.
It comes as BT, which still boasts 12 million landline customers, recently reported a quarterly rise in profits, boosted by growth in its broadband and mobile services.
The company said it wanted to "reward our loyal customers and attract new ones".
A spokesman for BT told the BBC the company was "confident" the offer would not result in a "material decline" in the number of calls made via the landline network.

Landlines continue to be used by many customers for regular phone calls, as well as taking advantage of offers such as free weekends and cheap evening calls, said Marc Allera, CEO of BT's consumer division.
Millions of textile workers in Asia risk losing their jobs as fashion brands pledge to reduce their carbon footprints, according to a new study.
The Textile Exchange, a non-profit group based in the US, surveyed 40 leading brands.
It found that one-third of chief executive officers (CEOs) planned to decrease their fabric carbon footprint by at least 26% by the end of 2030.
If achieved, that would result in the closure of hundreds of textile factories in Asia, which is the main region where clothing is produced.
It added that environmental sustainability was important for about half of the CEOs when it came to selecting a textile supplier.
But 90% of the executives were concerned that proposed changes to fibres could lead to higher costs and affect the quality of their clothes.
Textile Exchange's chief executive La Rhea Pepper said: "The industry has never seen this amount of change in such a short amount of time.
"There is going to be a real shift in the materials landscape.
A lot of the fibres that are more carbon intensive are going to start to decline.
The survey highlighted a number of fibres that fashion brands were planning to decrease.
Synthetic fibres such as acrylic, nylon and polyester were among those materials, which the Textile Exchange described as "carbon-intensive".
The Textile Exchange also said that more than half of the CEOs it surveyed planned to increase their use of preferred fibres, such as cotton, hemp, linen and recycled polyester.
However, the study noted that cotton production was "extremely water intensive", adding that increases in its use could lead to higher water consumption.
The Textile Exchange's survey was conducted with 40 brands, including Adidas, Patagonia, H&M and C&A.
The group said the CEOs it surveyed represented brands that collectively produce more than $100bn in annual sales.

The economy of EuroDisney's key market, France, is finally showing signs of improvement, prompting the company to issue the bonds.
The Financial Markets Regulator (AMF) announced on Tuesday that it had cleared EuroDisney's plan to sell debt securities worth up to 2.259 billion euros ($2.8 billion).

The theme park, which employs 15,000 people, is an important tourist attraction for France, drawing more than 14 million visitors a year.
But it has struggled in recent years, hit by the weak eurozone economy, the aftermath of terrorist attacks in France, and competition from cheaper leisure alternatives.
Disneyland Paris's finances have been strained by the construction of a new Disney-branded hotel, as well as the refurbishment of its parks.
The company has embarked on a cost-cutting drive, including a major restructuring of its operations, to help restore its profitability.
Disneyland Paris's management has also implemented a range of measures to boost visitor numbers and increase revenue, including introducing new attractions and improving its marketing efforts.
The economy in France, the company's main market, is now showing signs of recovery, with unemployment falling and consumer confidence rising, which is encouraging Disneyland Paris to issue more debt.
Disneyland Paris has been profitable in the past, and its management believes that the company can return to profitability once its debt has been refinanced and its cost-cutting measures take effect.
The company said it would use the proceeds from the debt sale to pay off its existing loans, which have fallen sharply in value as a result of the company's financial difficulties.
Disneyland Paris's management said it believed that the company's new financial plan would help it to return to profitability and continue operating as a major tourist attraction in France.

Oil company Shell has paid $1.3m (£960,000) to former boss Ben van Beurden for losing his job last year.
Mr van Beurden, who was chief executive from 2014-21, was paid the sum in lieu of 12 months' notice after he was unexpectedly sacked in February last year.
The company said it had advised the 58-year-old "there was no need for a non-compete obligation".
But in July last year, Shell changed its mind and told him to leave the company.
The firm said it had made a "mutual agreement" with Mr van Beurden, who is Dutch, over his departure.
At the time of his sacking, Shell said it wanted a change in leadership as it began a "turnaround plan" to improve profitability and halt a decline in output.
The oil giant has been under pressure from investors to improve profitability and reverse a decline in output after a decade of overspending on mega-projects.
Mr van Beurden received £1.4m in basic pay and a £4.2m bonus for 2021 - his final year in the role.
The former boss received a £110,000 lump sum in lieu of notice and remains bound by the terms of the "reasons of leaving" as well as "post-termination restrictions".
These include a six-month period during which he is not allowed to work for a competing firm or hire staff from Shell.
According to the company's annual report for 2021, Mr van Beurden received £1.4m in basic pay and a £4.2m bonus - his annual bonus was equal to 133% of his basic salary.
The first reviews of Microsoft's new browser, Edge, have appeared online - and they are promising.
The browser had a troubled development, with the initial version released with Windows 10 last year withdrawn shortly after arrival.
Rebuilt from scratch, the new version of Edge is included in a preview of Windows 10 released at the weekend.
Tech sites praised its speed and battery life but criticised its lack of features.
Edge is set to replace Internet Explorer as the company's default browser.
Internet Explorer has been an integral part of the Windows operating system for 20 years but its market share has plummeted in recent years.
It once had more than 90% of the market but last month had just 8.5% of desktop browsers, according to analytics firm StatCounter.
Firefox has 4.2% and Chrome, which is also the most-used browser on mobile, has 44.5%.
Microsoft said in January that it was withdrawing Internet Explorer from its list of supported browsers.
While some businesses will continue to use it, the majority of consumers will switch to Edge as it is the only browser that will be supported by Microsoft's new operating system.
Reaction to the new browser has been positive, with most reviews noting its speed and efficiency.
"It's fast.
It's really fast.
It feels faster than Chrome, and if true, that's a very good thing," wrote ZDNet's David Gewirtz.
The browser uses the same engine as Chrome, and in some tests it was faster than Google's browser.
"Microsoft's rebuilt Edge browser delivers a fast, efficient, and capable browsing experience," wrote Engadget.
"It's too early to tell whether it will become a favourite but it's certainly a good start," said PCWorld.
But the new browser does not yet have the full range of features associated with Chrome and Firefox.
There is no extension store - although one is promised for the final version - and the home page lacks customisation options.
"Unless you're a Windows Insider obsessed with trying new things, there's little reason to switch from Chrome or Firefox," wrote Gizmodo.
Microsoft said the new browser would not arrive in its final form until after the release of Windows 10, which is expected in the autumn.
Chinese leaders are trying to balance expectations as the country's rapid growth slows.
The world's second-biggest economy grew by 6.5% in the three months ending in September, down from the previous quarter's 7%.
It is China's weakest growth in nearly three years, and falls short of forecasts.
The announcement sparked a sell-off on stock markets, but analysts say the data is not all bad news.
The latest figures show that growth in the giant services sector slowed to 8.4% over a year earlier, down from 9.5% in the second quarter.
Factory output and investment growth also weakened, but analysts said the data was not as bad as some had feared.
"The national team has done a stellar job in stabilising the markets," said Zhang Xiaomin, chief strategist at China Securities International in Hong Kong.
"But the economy is still facing considerable downward pressure and the central bank will need to step up support for growth," he added.
The Chinese economy expanded by 6.7% in 2016, its slowest pace for 26 years, as it continued its transition from a period of spectacular growth to one of more moderate expansion.
The government has set a modest growth target for 2017 of around 6.5%, which it looks set to achieve.

Halliburton informed the ministry on Sunday that it would not seek to extend the contract for the development of the field in southern Iraq, a ministry statement said.

Ireland have finalised their 2023 fixtures with the confirmation of their final home game of the year.
The rugby federation has secured the use of the Aviva Stadium in Dublin for a November test against Australia.

The match, which will be the fourth and final Test in the summer international window, will take place on 19 November, with the Australians travelling to Dublin following their meetings with England, Wales and Scotland.

The UK's fastest broadband is being trialled in Aberdeen, with speeds of up to 20 gigabits per second (Gbps).
The city is one of the UK's "smart cities" and is seen as an ideal location to test the benefits of very high-speed internet.
The trial is part of a programme run by a UK company called CityFibre.
It is due to be completed by summer 2024.
What does it involve?
The company has created a network of more than 100 "spines" - small, sealed units filled with optical fibre and electronic equipment.
These are being installed around the city, never more than a few hundred metres away from each other.
Once turned on, each spine has the potential to provide internet speeds of up to 20Gbps.
This is faster than any other current broadband network in the UK.
CityFibre said the spines would be able to offer "near infinite bandwidth" and would never need to be upgraded.
How is it being used?

The network has already been used to film a live performance of a ballet at the city's Music Hall, which was then streamed over the internet in ultra-high definition 3D.

It has also been used to connect schools, universities and hospitals in the city.

CityFibre said the network would be capable of streaming hundreds of Netflix movies to thousands of homes simultaneously, or every game from a major football tournament such as the Euros or the World Cup, to every screen in people's homes, all at the same time.
The company's chief executive, Greg Mesch, said the network could eventually be used to power all kinds of new technologies.
"From smart transportation and traffic systems to digital healthcare, ultra-high definition video, and even augmented and virtual reality," he said.

Why is it being trialled in Aberdeen?
Aberdeen has been named as a "smart city", as part of a project run by the UK government.
The project aims to make cities more efficient, using the internet of things - a network of internet-connected objects or devices.
CityFibre has been working in Aberdeen since 2019, and the city was chosen as the first to trial the new network.
The company said it planned to expand the network to other cities in the UK, including Edinburgh, Glasgow, Newcastle, Leeds and Manchester.
But it has not yet said when this might happen.
Mr Blair said he would serve out his third term as Labour leader.
The BBC's political editor, Nick Robinson, said he had seen a letter in which Mr Blair promised to go at or before the next election.

"He has always said that he will serve a full third term - that remains his position."
Mr Blair's spokesman accused the BBC of making "a very serious mistake" and said it had breached its own guidelines on accuracy.

"

The letter is dated April 2005, around the time of the last election, and refers to "the coming years".

Mr Blair added: "I should also say - because I sometimes think people forget this - that in the end, it is for the party to decide who should be leader, just as it is for the party membership to decide who should be member of Parliament."
The prime minister's spokesman again attacked the BBC for publishing what he described as "a pretty fundamental error of judgment".
He said: "They [the BBC] have breached their own guidelines on serious factual errors and serious breaches of fairness.
"We have made it clear to the BBC that not only has information been released, but that it was released by the BBC themselves.

"

The number of people with broadband will double in the next four years, with most of the growth coming from the developing world, according to a new study.
By 2010, there will be nearly 1.3 billion broadband subscribers, with almost 700 million of these in China and India, said market research group Strategy Analytics.
"The next few years will see broadband accelerating beyond the rich nations and into the developing world," said David Kerr, vice-president of the firm's digital consumer practice.

Chinese engineers have started work on a controversial dam project that Beijing had tried to stop, according to a state-run newspaper.

The $1.6bn (£980m) project, which is owned by China's largest hydropower firm, China Three Gorges Corporation (CTGC), was suspended in March amid protests over resettlement issues.

It said that the local government in Yunnan had asked the subsidiary to "speed up" construction.
Work on the dam was "defying the central government's instruction and representing the actual situation that 'the local region is governing the central government'," it added.

The suspension order was issued by the Ministry of Environmental Protection days after the protests began.
But the Securities Times report suggests that the order may never have been officially issued, despite confirmation from the company at the time that it had received it.
It said that the ministry had told CTGC to report back on issues relating to the relocation, and that this had been misinterpreted as an official suspension order.

TV viewing figures on all formats have fallen year on year for the first time since records began, official data shows.
The audience research body Barb said analogue and digital TV viewers watched an average of 3.4 hours of television a day in April, down from 3.6 hours in 2007.

The figures reflect the growing popularity of the internet as a source of news, entertainment and communication.
They also show the average UK adult now spends almost four hours a day using the internet, compared with less than three hours watching TV.
Of those, more than 80% use the internet daily compared with 60% who watch TV every day.
The data also reveals the average time spent online has increased by at least a quarter in the last year, with the average user spending 14.7 hours a week online, up from 11.8 hours in 2007.

"However, it's too early to state that the age of TV is over, or that the future is solely online," she added.
TV still attracts the largest audiences, but the data does suggest that people are watching less television as they spend more time using the internet.
The research also shows that the way people watch TV is changing as they time-shift programmes using digital video recorders (DVRs) such as Sky Plus or Virgin Plus.
This allows them to watch what they want, when they want, and fast forward through the adverts.
Some 42.5% of TV sets in the UK are now connected to DVRs, an increase of more than a quarter in the last year, according to the data.
The average number of channels viewed by each TV set is also falling, from 26.1 in 2007 to 24.9 last month.
But TV still dominates the media landscape, attracting far larger audiences than the internet.

US retail sales surged in December, recording their largest increase since early 2021, as spending was boosted by purchases of toys, video games, and clothing, according to Commerce Department data released on Wednesday.
Total retail sales in December rose 3.3% from the previous month, well above analysts' expectations of a 1.9% increase.
Sales at general merchandise stores, which include big box retailers such as Walmart and Target, increased 7.0% from November and were up 11.5% from December 2021.
Sales at clothing stores rose 2.2% month-over-month and were up 10.2% from a year earlier.
Electronics and appliance stores saw sales climb 1.2% from November and were up 8.0% from a year earlier.
Sales at online retailers were up 1.4% from November and increased 7.0% from a year earlier.
The retail sales report covers only about a third of overall consumer spending, but it is still a widely watched indicator of the strength of the US economy.
The Commerce Department reported last week that gross domestic product increased at a 2.6% annualized rate in the third quarter of 2022, marking a downward revision from the 2.9% previously reported.
Fiat's board has approved a deal to give GM a $2.8bn (£1.7bn) stake in its auto business, clearing a major obstacle to a merger of the two carmakers.
The deal had been delayed as Fiat's board debated GM's offer and fought off a rival bid from Ford.
The merger will create the world's third-biggest carmaker by sales.
The combined company will be called Fiat-GM and be headed by Fiat's CEO, Sergio Marchionne.
The deal must still be approved by regulators and shareholders.
If it goes through, GM will get a 20% stake in Fiat, while Fiat will get a 1.5% stake in GM.
The companies said the deal would save them $2.8bn a year by 2015.
The merger has been approved by the boards of both companies but still needs the go-ahead from regulators and shareholders.
If the merger is approved, the new company would be worth about $140bn, based on the companies' current market values.
By comparison, Toyota is currently the world's biggest carmaker with sales of 10.2 million vehicles last year, followed by Volkswagen with 8.3 million.
Fiat-GM would sell about 8.6 million cars a year.
The merger deal comes as the auto industry struggles to recover from a sharp drop in sales in the US and Europe.
The combined company will have about $132bn in debt, ranking it as one of the most indebted companies in the world.
GM sold a record 4.7 million cars and trucks in 2010 but analysts say it needs to expand to survive as sales growth slows in its main markets.

Russian oil giant Yukos has been accused of lying to a Moscow court about the size of its debt.

The rise of broadband has helped to fuel an explosion of blogs, online video and digital photography, the head of the BBC's interactive division has said.
Paul Russell said broadband had become a "fundamental human right" and that online expression formed a "crucial part" of modern life.
In a speech to the Royal Television Society in Cambridge, he said interactive TV would eventually be viewed as "quaint".
Mr Russell said the BBC had to be ready to embrace new technologies as they emerged.
In his speech, entitled The Future of Public Service Television, he said the BBC had to be prepared to "surrender" some of its services in the face of new technology.

"We will have to be ready to surrender some services as the market takes them on, and be ready to replace them with new services where we feel we can add value - that may be on mobile, it may be on screens we cannot even imagine yet," he said.
Mr Russell added that the BBC had to be ready to make content available on as many platforms as possible - including digital television, the internet and mobile phones.
He said TV would continue to have a crucial role - but that it would have to "change faster than ever before" to meet the challenges ahead.
Mr Russell predicted that within 10 years, computers would be built into furniture and walls, with all content - television, radio and internet - being accessed through a single box.
"We are moving into an era where all content will be available all of the time, anywhere, on any device," he said.
"The challenge for public service broadcasters is not to fight the future but to understand our unique role in it.

"

Mr Russell said the BBC had a "crucial role" to play in ensuring that the burgeoning number of videos, photographs and blogs did not become a "cacophony of mediocrity".
He said the BBC's role was to "supercharge" the most talented content makers and give them global reach.
"If we can do that, then we won't be worrying about our future - because we will be busy making it," he said.
Three-month-old Rumi, who stars in "Beasts of the Southern Wild" has become a favourite to win Oscar's best actress gong, despite rumours of a shake-up to the category's rules.
If she were to win, Rumi would be the youngest ever recipient of an Oscar.
She has received rave reviews for her performance in the film, which centres on a young girl's coming-of-age in a dangerous, primal world.
Her co-star Quvenzhané Wallis is also nominated for best actress, making them the third pair of co-stars to receive nominations in the same year.
The last time this happened was in 1991, when Jessica Tandy and Dan Aykroyd were nominated for "Driving Miss Daisy" and "Ghostbusters," respectively.

There has been debate over whether the best actress category should be scrapped altogether and replaced with a "best leading performance" category to recognise the growing number of male actors taking female roles.

Several high-profile stars, including Michelle Williams and Kristen Stewart, have been snubbed by the Academy in the best actress category, with some speculating whether gender has played a part in their omission.
However, the Academy has said it is committed to honouring the best performances, regardless of an actor's gender.
The controversial £1.4bn Crossrail link to Heathrow Airport is expected to get the go-ahead after months of delay.
Ministers were expected to approve the project - which has been hit by funding problems and delays - at a meeting on Friday.
The link, connecting the western hub of Heathrow with Reading, Slough and Maidenhead in the east, is seen as vital to the airport's future development.
But it has also been criticised for the use of public money and the impact on local residents.
Business Secretary John Hutton said in June the project's "economic case remained strong" and the government was still committed to the scheme.
But he said the government was considering asking banks and other financial institutions to share the risk of the project, which is expected to attract about 18 million passengers a year.
The Department for Transport refused to comment on Friday's expected go-ahead for the project, which has been hit by a series of setbacks over the last year.
In July, Transport Secretary Ruth Kelly announced a review of all major transport projects in the wake of the successful campaign against the government's plan for a third runway at Heathrow.
And in April this year, the government was forced to give a £170m bail-out to the project, after it emerged that its costs had soared by more than a quarter to £1.76bn.

The project - dubbed the "Elizabeth Line" - will link Heathrow Airport, west of London, with stations in Reading, Slough and Maidenhead to the east, and as far as Paddington, Bond Street and Liverpool Street stations in central London.
The link faces strong opposition from local residents who say it will spark massive house demolitions and could cause house prices to plummet.
A public inquiry into the project ended last year and Minister of State for Transport Tony McNulty announced in January that he planned to give the go-ahead for the scheme "as soon as possible".
Cardiff and Wales prop Dillon Lewis has been banned for three weeks after admitting a charge of eye-gouging against Exeter.
The 22-year-old committed the offence in the 74th minute of the Blues' 18-13 Champions Cup win on Saturday.
Lewis, who has won 13 caps, will miss his club's European games against Toulouse and Harlequins.
The prop accepted the charge on the day of the game and has been sanctioned by a European Professional Club Rugby tribunal.

Failing to plan for staff being infected with HIV is costing British businesses millions of pounds, according to a leading charity.
Terrence Higgins Trust said employers were not providing adequate training on HIV and were paying out for unnecessary testing.
It said this was leading to inefficient use of NHS resources and infringement of HIV patients' rights.
The trust launched its HIV and Employment Guide for employers on World AIDS Day, 1 December.
The charity is concerned that because of a lack of knowledge, some employers demand that all applicants who are HIV-positive take a HIV test - something that is voluntary.
Those who are HIV-positive and who do disclose their status may face discrimination in the workplace, the charity said.
This includes being passed over for promotion or being unable to do their job properly because of a lack of understanding among colleagues and managers.
The trust is also concerned that some employers are not providing adequate training on how to avoid unnecessary risk of HIV transmission in the workplace.
This means employees are not always able to do their jobs safely, it said.
The guide advises employers on how to avoid unnecessary costs caused by HIV, including the cost of replacing staff who have contracted the virus and who need to take long-term sick leave.
It says inadequate planning for staff who are HIV-positive is wasting NHS resources because of unnecessary testing and follow-up treatment.
The guide also warns that employers who fail to carry out a proper risk assessment could face legal action.

The future of Rover looks uncertain as the company's owners, BMW, have given it until the middle of November to find a buyer.
The German car giant has agreed to continue funding Rover's loss-making Longbridge plant in Birmingham, central England, until then.
But the company has made it clear it will not do so indefinitely and has not ruled out closing the plant.
About 6,000 people work at Longbridge but only 2,000 are certain to keep their jobs until November.
The uncertainty over the future has prompted speculation that BMW may pull out before November if a buyer is not found.

'Improving competitiveness'

Rover has been seeking a partner to share the high costs of making cars and has had talks with a number of companies, including Honda, General Motors and Ford.
But these have not been successful and the company's managing director, Kevin Howe, said on Wednesday that it was now looking for a buyer.
In a statement, BMW said it was in talks with three possible partners but these had not progressed as far as it had hoped.
"Based on intensive analyses of all alternatives for the future of Rover, the BMW board has decided to explore the option of a sale of Rover," it said.
"This process will be carried out in parallel with ongoing efforts to improve the competitiveness of the Rover Group.
The statement said BMW would not fund losses at Rover indefinitely and the company's management would "continue to explore all options for the future of Rover".
This has led to speculation that BMW may pull the plug on Rover if a buyer is not found by November.

"The court in Greece has decided to overwrite key parts of the global regulatory system for athletics," the IAAF statement added.

"

In an interview with the BBC last week, Lebedeva said she was "happy" with the decision and hoped it would help other Russians.
"It was a long journey, but I am happy it is over," she said.

"

The IAAF has not said if it will appeal against the ruling.

portable video equipment, despite heavy promotion and the endorsement of film and television stars, is disappearing from the marketplace, according to a new study in the us.

The study, which was conducted by the investment bank morgan stanley, found that the $1bn (£670m) portable video market in the us has failed to take off, with sales of personal video recorders (PVRs) and digital video cameras (DVCs) falling short of manufacturers' expectations.
The bank concluded that, despite the widespread promotion of such products by celebrities such as the american actor tom hanks, the public saw the devices as "cumbersome and difficult to use".
Morgan stanley also found that prices of the products had been falling faster than expected, reducing the potential profits of manufacturers.
Portable video was once seen as one of the most promising sectors of the electronics industry, with analysts talking of a "billion-dollar market".
But the study found that the market for the devices was "smaller, slower growing, and much more saturated than we had expected".
Tom kristensen, an analyst with the bank, said that portable video equipment was now a "commodity business" and that the market was "mature".
He said that there was now little difference in the performance of the products from different manufacturers, and that customers were simply buying on price.
Mr kristensen said falling prices had been driven by intense competition and "heavy, heavy" discounting by retailers.

The morgan stanley study found that PVRs, which allow television programmes to be recorded and played back, had been particularly hard hit, with sales falling by 27 percent in 1999, compared with the previous year.
