A student who has been blind since birth can now see colours, following a groundbreaking surgery.
The surgery involved a unique "tongue display" which stimulated the brain, enabling the patient to see colours.
The patient, who was born with a form of congenital blindness that affects 1 in every 10,000 people, underwent the experimental surgery in November last year.

The operation, which was led by Dr. Ron Pelias, assistant professor of ophthalmology at Stanford University, stimulated the tongue's nerve fibres, which in turn stimulated the brain's visual cortex, allowing the patient to perceive colours.
"We're trying to work out the neural mechanisms of colour vision by stimulating the brain in this very precise way," said Dr Pelias.
The patient can now see colours, but still does not have any form of visual acuity, meaning they can't see shapes or outlines.
The surgery was carried out on a patient with complete colour blindness and involves a small, 1.5mm square electrode, which is placed on the tongue.
The electrode is linked to a small, wearable computer, which transforms images from a camera into "tongue maps", consisting of eight different regions, each stimulated by a different colour.
When the patient looks at an object, the computer converts the image into a "tongue map", which stimulates the brain in such a way that the patient can perceive colours.

"We're trying to stimulate the brain so that it interprets stimuli as colour, by coaxing neurons in the brain to respond in a way that would normally only occur when a sighted person sees colour," said Dr Pelias.
The device needs to be calibrated against a "tongue colour chart", which the patient uses to tune the colours on the device, ensuring they are seeing the right colours.
So far, the patient has been able to identify colours in experiments, but the team is still working on improving the clarity of the images produced.
"This is a very early stage of the research.
We're a long way from understanding how the brain encodes colour and even further from understanding how to restore that ability through electrical stimulation," Dr Pelias said.
"But it's a very exciting proof of concept that brings us a little bit closer to helping patients with congenital colour blindness.

"
The team hopes to carry out the procedure on other patients in the future and believes the technology could also be used to help people who have lost their sight to retinal degeneration.
The UK government has pledged £1bn ($1.4bn) to the international effort to develop a vaccine for coronavirus.
The sum - for research and development - will be paid in UK aid, Chancellor Rishi Sunak announced in his budget on Wednesday.
Mr Sunak said the money would help "create a vaccine" for Covid-19 "that will ensure we can protect people here in the UK and around the world".
UK aid, the Department for International Development (DfID), will also provide £388m to help end the pandemic and distribute treatments and vaccines.
It will spend £300m on the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a global alliance working on Covid-19 vaccines.
Cepi has already funded three promising candidates, according to Mr Sunak.
Additionally, DfID will give £38m to the WHO to help distribute coronavirus vaccines, treatments and tests.
It will also spend £62m on research and development, including testing new treatments.
The budget also included £1.35bn to accelerate the rollout of coronavirus vaccines, including helping the NHS to become ready to distribute a vaccine next month.
This included £150m to fund 50 million doses of a vaccine, if one becomes available, Mr Sunak said.
The budget also pledged £5bn for testing and tracing over the next six months.
The Santy worm, which has been around for years but was dormant for a while, has made an unwelcome visit to Android phones.
Security experts have said that the worm, one of the first Android worms, is sophisticated and can bypass security defences.
The discovery was made by researchers at Zimperium, an Arizona-based mobile security company.
It affects "almost all Android 4 devices" which is around 95% of Android phones and tablets.
The discovery was announced at the Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas.
Ian Beer, from Google's Project Zero security team, said that the bug was "one of the worst I've seen in terms of potential impact".
Google has released a fix for the vulnerability and is working with partners to get it to all users.
The worm was first seen in the wild in 2011 and is also known as Axiom, it targeted computers and networks in the Middle East and Korea.
Antivirus firm Bitdefender says the Android version is a "near identical copy" of the Windows version, just under a different name - instead of Santy.
It is hard to detect and very difficult to remove and, once one device is infected, it tries to spread to other devices connected to the same network.
It does this by cracking the password used to secure the wireless network.
It then harvests email addresses from the infected device and sends itself to all these addresses with a message containing a link to download a fake version of the Android operating system.
Anyone clicking on the link would become infected.
Researchers at Zimperium found the worm when a customer in Germany asked them to investigate why many of his company's Android devices were crashing.
The team was able to recreate the scenario and realised that the Santy worm was the cause.
Zimperium has created a free app, zANTI, which can be used to detect if a phone is infected.
Microsoft has launched a new version of its Windows operating system in India, aimed at curbing software piracy.
Windows 10 "Core", as it has been named, is an edition of Windows 10 that contains minimal features.
While users will be able to run apps, they will not be able to access Microsoft's Windows Store to download programmes.
The move aims to offer a low-cost alternative to Windows, making it easier for Microsoft to compete with cheap pirated versions of its software, which are widely used in the country.
It also hopes the new version will encourage users of pirated Windows to move towards legal versions, by offering a more affordable option.

"It has always been our endeavour to ensure that customers have the best possible experience on our platform, and as a part of this, we are bringing the Windows 10 'Core' edition to India," said Bhaskar Pramanik, chairman of Microsoft India.
"This edition offers a no-frills Windows 10 experience to our customers at an affordable price, and we believe this edition will be attractive to both desktop and mobile customers in the country."
The Indian computer market is currently dominated by software pirates, who buy a single copy of Windows and install it on multiple computers, rather than buying separate licences for each.

According to industry body National Association of Software and Services Companies (Nasscom), the rate of software piracy in India in 2016 was more than 59%, costing the country more than $1.7bn (£1.2bn) in lost revenue.
Microsoft has launched several initiatives in India to curb the practice.
It launched a programme called "Digital-Life Alliance" in 2016, aimed at educating Indians about the dangers of downloading pirated software.
In addition, Microsoft's Indian subsidiary launched a website this year, Buy Genuine Software, which describes the risks of using pirated software, and offers alternatives.
According to Microsoft, users of Windows 10 Core will have the ability to "unlock" additional features in the future.
However, the company has not detailed how this will be possible.

It could fly from New York to London in less than three hours, and was a favourite of celebrities and business leaders.

The US created 235,000 jobs in February, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
That was the most jobs created in a month since March 2022.
But it is still considered slow growth, especially considering that the US economy needs to create roughly 150,000 jobs a month to keep up with the growth of the working-age population.
The unemployment rate remained flat at 3.6%, near a 50-year low.
Average hourly earnings increased 0.1% in February, raising wages by 5.1% from a year earlier, compared with a 5.7% annual increase in January.
The report showed that there are still more jobs than there are workers to fill them.
In February, there were 1.8 job openings for every unemployed person.
The labor force participation rate, which measures the share of working-age Americans who are working or looking for work, was 62.4% - unchanged from January.
The jobs gains in February were broad-based.
Professional and business services added 74,000 jobs; transportation and warehousing added 60,000; education added 48,000; and manufacturing added 44,000.
Job growth was also strong in the leisure and hospitality sector, which added 112,000.
However, the number of restaurant and bar jobs still has not returned to its pre-pandemic level.
The sector remains about 426,000 jobs below its February 2020 level.
The report showed that the number of people working remotely because of the pandemic declined by 150,000 to 15.4 million in February.
But that is still significantly higher than the 12.4 million in February 2020.
The jobs report comes as inflation is showing signs of moderating.
The consumer price index rose 6.4% in January from a year earlier, the smallest increase in nearly a year.
But it is still significantly higher than the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell told lawmakers this week that he expects inflation to fall further in the coming months as the Fed continues to raise interest rates.
The central bank is expected to raise rates by 25 basis points when it meets next week.

Search wars hit desktop PCs

Google and Microsoft are battling for desktop search supremacy -- but are desktop users ready for search?
That's the question both companies are hoping to answer with new desktop search applications designed to help users find anything stored on their PCs.
Google has introduced Google Desktop Search, a free application that scans the contents of a PC and displays find results in a Google-style page.
The application, which works on Windows machines, indexes the contents of a PC's hard drive, including email archives, and allows users to search them quickly.

Microsoft, which introduced its own desktop search tool, Windows Desktop Search, as a downloadable beta application last year, plans to release the final version of the product, also for Windows PCs, later this year.
Unlike Google's offering, Microsoft's will be integrated with the next version of Windows, code-named "Longhorn," due out sometime in 2006.
Google's move has raised the stakes in the ongoing battle between the two companies for search dominance.
Microsoft is still well ahead of Google in overall search share with more than 62% of searches conducted in the US performed on Microsoft sites, according to latest data from ComScore Networks.
But Google is nipping at its heels.
In February, Google sites accounted for 34.6% of US searches, up from 30.5% a year ago, ComScore said.
Now the two companies are battling for search supremacy on the desktop.
Microsoft has had a desktop search tool since 1995, when it introduced Windows 95.

But Google's new tool is seen as a significant upgrade, since it allows users to search information stored in many different applications, including Outlook, Outlook Express, and Netscape Messenger, as well as PDF and Word files.
It also lets users search across multiple PCs -- a boon for businesses.
All of this has Microsoft scrambling to catch up.

"Google has jumped into the desktop search market in a way that is sure to get Microsoft's attention," said Matt Rosoff, an analyst with Directions on Microsoft, a research firm that tracks the software giant.
"It's clear that Google views desktop search as a platform, and Microsoft will have to respond," he added.

Police have issued an alert after "suspicious" devices were found attached to cash machines in Bath.
The devices, believed to be skimming equipment, were discovered attached to the front of the ATMs in windows of banks in the city.
Avon and Somerset police have issued an appeal for information and urged people to be vigilant.
PC Chris Burgess said cash points were being targeted nationwide.
"Skimming incidents usually occur at ATMs in secluded areas, often late at night," he said.
"Or alternatively, they are installed overnight while the banks are closed and the ATMs are unattended.

"

The police have asked anyone who thinks they may have information about the devices to get in touch.

South African car demand surges

South Africa's new car market is booming, confounding economists' predictions that borrowing costs would choke off demand as the central bank tightened monetary policy to curb inflation.
They are predicting record sales this year of more than 150,000 units, with growth in the motor sector outpacing the economy's expansion.
The demand has been fuelled by low interest rates and people opting to buy instead of renting.
But some analysts are questioning how long the boom can last.
Already, the used car market is showing signs of overheating.
And with interest rates expected to rise further - and economic growth likely to slow - the new car market is likely to cool off.
South Africa's car market is an important barometer of the country's economic health.
Not only does it employ about 14% of the country's workforce, but it is also a key indicator of the strength of consumer demand and confidence.

When the economy started to grow again after the 2009 recession, car sales took off, climbing by more than 70% in five years to 556,000 units in 2014, according to data from the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa.

But economists had expected the boom to end when the South African Reserve Bank started raising interest rates in early 2014 to curb rising inflation - increasing them five times over the subsequent year-and-a-half.
However, instead of choking off demand, higher borrowing costs have so far had little impact on the appetite of South Africans to buy new cars.
Official figures show that total vehicle sales last year grew 5.2% to 152,488 units, with the new car market up by more than 8% to 136,385 units.
The figures include sales of demonstration vehicles and pre-owned cars, but exclude sales to car rental companies.
Some in the industry believe the growth can be sustained.

"All the factors that drove sales in 2014 are still in place - low interest rates, good value for money, great model offerings, a growing economy and positive consumer sentiment," says Johan van Velden, the chairman of the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa.
However, not everyone is so optimistic.
"The market is likely to cool off this year," says Arno van der Veen, a senior economist at RMB.

England midfielder Danny Pountney has been banned from football for four years and fined £100,000 after being found guilty of placing 1,260 bets on matches between 2006 and 2011.
The former Grimsby, Norwich and Charlton player, now aged 35, broke FA rules by betting on matches involving his own club, as well as games in the Championship, League One and League Two.
He also placed bets on the outcome of games in Australia, Scotland, Ireland and Wales.
However, Pountney, who was charged in July, denied seven of the eight charges against him.
He has been fined £30,000 for betting on games involving his own club, with a further £70,000 penalty for placing bets on the outcome of other games.
All of the money will go to the FA's funding for grassroots football.
"It was deeply unfair to professional footballers who rightly expect strict rules against gambling to be enforced," said Adam French, the FA's integrity adviser.
Pountney last played in England for Crawley in 2015.
He has also had spells with Huddersfield, Blackpool, Sheffield United and Bristol City.
The FA said he had been "fully cooperative" with the investigation.
He said in a statement: "I have loved my career as a professional footballer and I regret what has happened.
"I appreciate that my actions call into question my integrity as a sportsman and I apologise to anyone who believes that my behaviour has brought the game into disrepute.

"

In 2007, the former England Under-21 international was banned from football for three months after admitting placing bets on 1,427 matches over a two-year period.
Pountney was also fined £20,000 and warned about his future conduct.
He was originally suspended by the FA in June, with chairman Greg Clarke saying the organisation had to be "careful" when considering the case.
"This is a difficult area," he said.
"There is a difference in my mind between gambling and match-fixing.
"If people are betting on their own games, it is difficult to see that that is not cheating."
Former Charlton team-mate Sam Sodje was banned from football for two years in 2012 after he was found guilty of placing bets on games.
The Nigeria international was also fined £20,000.
The Bank of England is set to keep interest rates on hold as it weighs up the prospects of a slowdown in the global economy and the impact of Brexit.
The Bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is expected to keep the cost of borrowing at 0.5% when it announces its decision at midday on Thursday.
Since the MPC's last meeting in February, the mood in the global economy has changed markedly, with risks from mainland Europe, the US and China.
While the UK economy has continued to grow, analysts say the MPC is likely to want to see the impact of the Brexit negotiations on the UK's economic performance before making any moves.
At its last meeting, the MPC voted unanimously to keep rates at their current level, but two members, Ian McCafferty and Michael Saunders, voted to raise rates in February.
What's more, the MPC said that "some withdrawal of monetary stimulus was likely to be appropriate over the coming months" if the economy evolved as expected.
But since then, figures showing a slowdown in the economy towards the end of last year have raised questions about the strength of the UK's economic performance.
The MPC's decision will be announced at 12pm, with Governor Mark Carney giving a press conference at 12:30pm.

Chapel Down CEO Frazer Thompson said: "We're thrilled that Wine For Dogs has been awarded the Comedy Award at the Decanter World Wine Awards.

"

The comedy award was a new category at this year's Decanter World Wine Awards, which were founded in 2004 and are considered among the most prestigious in the industry.

The party's election manifesto will promise to introduce compulsory attendance - with parents fined if their children persistently play truant.

Pyotr Ofitser, an anti-corruption campaigner, was accused of trying to steal funds from a charity founded by Navalny.
Ofitser's lawyer said the case was politically motivated and that his client planned to appeal.
The hearing came on the same day that Russia's highest court upheld a decision to block Navalny's website.
The 44-year-old opposition leader is currently serving a jail sentence for breaking the terms of a suspended jail term for fraud.
Navalny says the case was politically motivated like the rest of his legal battles since he became the leading opposition figure challenging President Vladimir Putin.
Ofitser is one of several people close to Navalny who have been targeted by Russian authorities in recent months.
His brother Oleg, a politician in Moscow, was handed a prison sentence last month after arguing with Putin's supporters on Instagram.
And Navalny's wife Yulia was given a fine this week for failing to explain why she had not registered her marriage to the opposition leader.
On Tuesday, Russia's highest court upheld a decision to block Navalny's popular website, saying the decision by authorities was legal.
The website's defence team plan to appeal, saying the block was an attack on freedom of speech.

I still think that, despite the fact the Spaniard has not come close to delivering the Premier League title that everyone associated with Liverpool wanted so badly.

They are among seven athletes and sports figures who were scheduled to go on trial in Washington on 7 January.
US district judge Reggie Walton set the new date on Thursday, saying the delay was needed to give defence lawyers more time to prepare.
They all pleaded not guilty to charges they lied to congressional investigators about steroid use in baseball.
Clemens and Bonds, baseball's all-time leader in career home runs, face charges they deceived Congress in 2003 about the use of performance-enhancing drugs.

Art fans can now browse more than 150,000 works in London's National Gallery with a new smart search tool.
The tool, created by Google Arts and Culture and launched on Tuesday, reveals paintings in the gallery's collection not currently on display.
It allows users to construct personalised tours and includes details such as artists' biographies.
The gallery said the new feature reflected its "commitment to digital innovation".

Users of the new tool can choose from a variety of curatorial approaches, from themes such as "take a walk in the woods" or "explore the world", to more specific searches for particular artists, art forms and art mediums.
The tool also provides information on more than 1,500 artists, including videos and written content about their lives and the context in which they worked.
There are also details about each painting, including the materials used and the year the work was created.
Will Cooper, the gallery's head of digital infrastructure, said the new feature was "a great way to see our collection in a new and engaging way".

"We're always looking for new ways to help people get closer to our collection and we hope people will enjoy using the app as much as we've enjoyed working with Google Arts and Culture on this project," he said.
The tool is available in the gallery and can be accessed via smartphones and other devices.

This would include a transition period for licensees to adapt, and further discussions on the practicalities of the new regime, said the first minister.

They will ask for views on the best way to enforce the ban, and on potential exemptions for pavements outside premises.

The number of jobs created in the US in January was much higher than expected, according to official data.
Figures from the Labor Department showed that the US economy added 678,000 jobs during the month, beating predictions of 400,000.
It said employment continued to trend up in leisure and hospitality, in professional and business services, in manufacturing and in construction.
But the data also showed that the unemployment rate had edged up from 3.9% to 4%, partly because of a surge in people entering the labour market.
Average hourly earnings for all workers also increased, rising to 5.1% compared with a year earlier.
But compared with December, they fell by 0.5% to $32.09.
"This was a solid report with a very strong headline number and is likely to be well received on Wall Street," said Richard Flynn, managing director at Charles Schwab.
"The unemployment rate did edge up, but it was for good reasons as more people entered the workforce, and the participation rate rose as well.
"With earnings growth remaining steady and the Fed's inflation target still distant, there is no reason for the central bank to accelerate its tightening cycle.

"

The jobs data follows on from Wednesday's inflation report, which showed that prices rose by their fastest rate in 40 years in December, increasing by an annualised 7%.
The strong jobs growth also comes in the wake of December's mixed jobs report, which showed a loss of 227,000 jobs in the month.
That figure was revised up to a gain of 768,000.

In the report for January, the Labor Department said that job gains had occurred in several industries, including leisure and hospitality, professional and business services, retail trade and manufacturing.
Construction employment continued to trend up, rising by 4%, or 78,000, in January, with job gains occurring in both residential and non-residential construction, the report said.
But it added that employment in local government education declined by 63,000 in January, mainly because of job losses in elementary and secondary schools.
The report also showed that the number of unemployed people rose by 187,000 to 6.1 million in January, while the labour force participation rate increased by 0.2 percentage points to 62.4%.

England's failure to beat Australia in the Rugby World Cup final has prompted fresh criticism of the team's performance from one of its most high-profile female fans.
Barbara Campagna, an Italian socialite and girlfriend of England coach Eddie Jones, took to Instagram to vent her frustration.
In a lengthy post, she appeared to criticise England's display in the 32-12 defeat in Tokyo on Saturday.
"It's been a tough week... a tough second half of the season," she wrote.
"Sometimes it feels like people and things are put in your path to test you, push you to your limits, and show you that you can be better, stronger, and wiser.

It is the first time Campagna has commented on England's performance since the final.

"It's been the most incredible, rewarding and emotional journey," she wrote.
"These boys have worked so hard, they deserve this final - they deserve the opportunity to shine.

"Bring it home for all of us, you've got this."

Campagna and Jones have been in a relationship since 2016, after being introduced by mutual friend, the late rugby player Andy Ripley.
Jones has previously said that Campagna provides a "nice balance" to his life, allowing him to "switch off" from rugby.

Tim Henman gave Britain a winning start at the ATP Finals with a straight-set victory over Frenchman Arnaud Clement in Shanghai.
The British number one, 29, beat the world number nine 6-2 6-4 in one hour and 23 minutes.
It was a confident display from Henman, who had lost in the first round on his two previous appearances in the year-ending tournament.
The win meant he topped his group after the opening day's play and booked a quarter-final meeting with Roger Federer.
Henman became the first British player to win the title when the event was last held in Shanghai, in 2005.
The ATP Finals is the season-ending tournament for the top eight players in the world.
This year it is being held in Shanghai for the first time, after seven years in Madrid.
Henman went into the match as the underdog with Clement claiming five titles this year, including Masters 1000 events in Paris and Madrid.
The first set went with serve until the eighth game when Henman earned the first break of the match with a stunning cross-court forehand winner.
Henman served out the first set and broke again at the start of the second to take a 2-0 lead.

The United States has agreed to delay a new set of tariffs on some imported products from Europe, following an announcement that both parties had agreed to start talks early next month.
The tariffs, which were due to come into force on Tuesday, have been postponed for up to six months.
They would have hit a range of products, from large aircraft to dairy products and wine.
The move comes after the US and EU agreed to start talks later this month aimed at resolving a 17-year dispute over state subsidies for aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Boeing.

The US announced in May that it was imposing tariffs on imports of aluminium and steel from the EU, along with imports of a range of other products, including gouda cheese, single-malt whiskey and large aircraft.
The EU responded with its own tariffs on more than $3.2bn worth of US goods, including corn, peanut butter, motorcycles and denim.
The two sides have now agreed to "pause" the tariffs for six months, according to a joint statement released by the US Trade Representative (USTR) and the EU on Friday.
If talks to resolve the dispute over aircraft subsidies are not successful within six months, the US will move forward with the tariffs on the $7.5bn worth of EU goods.
The EU will also do the same with its tariffs on more than $4bn worth of US goods.
The BBC's news website has launched a version specifically for mobile phones using the 3G wireless internet standard.
The BBC's executive producer for multimedia news, Emma Nagraba, said she was "delighted" by the launch.
"We're offering a rich, multimedia experience, with the same mix of news, sport, entertainment and information as the website," she said.
The mobile site will enable users to access the same information as the website, but it has been redesigned for the smaller screen of a mobile phone.
Ms Nagraba said the redesign would ensure the service was easy to use on the "smaller screen and limited navigation" of a phone.
The mobile site includes stories from the BBC's international, UK, and technology news sections, and users can also access the sports, entertainment and lifestyle sections.
They can also contribute their own content, including pictures and video.
"We're aiming to engage people by providing the tools for them to contribute, so we will be encouraging users to upload their content," said Ms Nagraba.
"We want to make it easy for people to use the BBC's mobile services, and we will be promoting the site through our other outlets, such as Radio 1 and BBC TV."
The mobile site also offers access to BBC Sounds, the corporation's digital radio station, and users can watch video footage and catch up on BBC Three programming.
The launch of the mobile service follows the BBC's recent decision to make its news output "digital first", meaning that its website will be the first place that BBC news stories appear.
"We want to deliver our content to as many people as possible, and this is another step towards that," said Ms Nagraba.
The mobile site can be accessed via the BBC's main website or through an internet search.
Former home secretary David Blunkett says he is proud of his time in Tony Blair's government and does not regret the introduction of university top-up fees or the Iraq war.
The Sheffield Brightside MP also denied his decision to resign as education secretary in 2001 over the widening child benefit scandal was a factor in the subsequent inquiry's findings.
And he defended his record as home secretary, saying he had been "a good reforming minister".
Mr Blunkett was speaking as he launched his autobiography, 'Beyond the Clouds', at the Labour Party conference in Brighton.
He told the BBC that the current Labour leadership had to accept that the party had moved on since Mr Blair's time in charge and it could not simply recreate the 'New Labour' era.
But he added that he did not believe Ed Miliband could lead the party to victory at the next general election and said the situation was 'desperate'.

Mr Blunkett served in the Cabinet for seven years from 2001 to 2008, first as education and employment secretary, then as home secretary and finally as secretary of state for communities and local government.
He was forced to resign from the Cabinet after revealing he had accidentally failed to declare a series of interests in a parliamentary register.

'Blind faith'
In his autobiography, Mr Blunkett reveals that he was one of only a handful of ministers who supported the Iraq war from the beginning.

He said there was no evidence of weapons of mass destruction immediately prior to the invasion of Iraq, but that it was his belief that the intelligence services were correct in their original assessments.

Additionally, some players have expressed concerns about the increased risk of injuries, particularly related to the increased friction and impact on joints.
Despite these concerns, Uefa's decision to approve artificial turf reflects a growing acceptance of this type of playing surface in professional football.
It is expected that more clubs and stadiums will now consider installing fake grass, especially those looking to improve the durability and consistency of their playing surfaces.

The Federal National Mortgage Association, commonly known as Fannie Mae, should restate its books, according to a report by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The report, released on Tuesday, found that Fannie Mae had engaged in improper accounting practices, leading to an overstatement of its earnings by billions of dollars.
The SEC's investigation focused on Fannie Mae's use of "cookie jar" reserves, which allowed the company to smooth out its earnings over time.
This practice, while not illegal, is considered to be misleading to investors.
The report also found that Fannie Mae had failed to properly account for certain derivatives transactions, resulting in further misstatements of its financial position.
The SEC has recommended that Fannie Mae restate its financial statements to correct these errors.
Fannie Mae, which is a government-sponsored enterprise, has been under scrutiny since 2004, when it was revealed that the company had manipulated its earnings to meet Wall Street expectations.
The scandal led to the resignation of several top executives and the imposition of a $400 million fine by the SEC.
Fannie Mae has since implemented a number of reforms to improve its accounting practices, but the latest report suggests that further action is needed.
The company's current CEO, Hugh R. Frater, has acknowledged the findings of the report and stated that Fannie Mae will work with the SEC to address the issues raised.
The SEC's report comes at a time when Fannie Mae is facing increased scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators.
The company, which was created by Congress in 1938 to provide liquidity to the mortgage market, has been under pressure to reform its operations and reduce its risk to taxpayers.

Fannie Mae and its sister company, Freddie Mac, were taken into conservatorship by the US government during the financial crisis of 2008 and have since received billions of dollars in taxpayer-funded bailouts.
The Trump administration has called for the privatization of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, but progress on this front has been slow.
The SEC's report is likely to add to the pressure on Fannie Mae to address its accounting issues and improve its governance.

In an increasingly digital world, cash is slowly losing its reign as the preferred method of payment.
The rise of contactless payments and mobile wallets has paved the way for a new era of convenience and flexibility.
As a result, the trusty old wallet is being replaced by its more adaptable counterpart - the flexible friend.
Gone are the days of fumbling for loose change or waiting in line at the ATM.
With the tap of a card or the swipe of a smartphone, consumers can now make quick and seamless transactions.
This shift towards digital payments has been accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, as people seek to minimize physical contact and reduce the risk of spreading the virus.
The benefits of the flexible friend are manifold.
Not only does it eliminate the need for carrying cash, but it also offers enhanced security.
Lost or stolen cards can be easily cancelled and replaced, providing peace of mind to consumers.
Additionally, digital transactions leave a digital trail, making it easier to track and manage expenses.
Furthermore, the flexible friend opens up a world of possibilities for businesses.
Small vendors and independent sellers can now accept card payments without the need for expensive point-of-sale systems.
This democratization of payment methods levels the playing field and allows for greater financial inclusion.
However, the transition to a cashless society is not without its challenges.
While digital payments offer convenience, they also raise concerns about privacy and data security.
As more personal information is stored and transmitted electronically, the risk of identity theft and fraud increases.
It is crucial for both consumers and businesses to remain vigilant and adopt robust security measures to protect sensitive information.
Moreover, the move away from cash may have unintended consequences for vulnerable populations who rely heavily on physical currency.
The elderly, homeless individuals, and those without access to banking services may find themselves marginalized in a cashless society.
Efforts must be made to ensure that everyone has equal access to digital payment options and the necessary infrastructure to support them.
As the world becomes increasingly interconnected, the flexible friend is set to become an integral part of our daily lives.
While cash may still have its place in certain situations, the convenience and flexibility offered by digital payments are hard to ignore.
As technology continues to advance, it is likely that the flexible friend will only become more prevalent, reshaping the way we think about money and transactions.

There is growing concern over the use of RFID tags, with critics arguing that they pose a threat to privacy and security.
RFID, or radio-frequency identification, technology uses small electronic devices to track and identify objects remotely.
These tags are embedded in various items, such as clothing, passports, and credit cards.
One of the main concerns surrounding RFID tags is the potential for unauthorized tracking and surveillance.
As these tags can be read from a distance, there is a fear that individuals could be monitored without their knowledge or consent.
This raises serious privacy issues, as people may not be aware that their movements and activities are being tracked.
Another worry is the vulnerability of RFID tags to hacking and data breaches.
As these tags transmit information wirelessly, they can be intercepted by malicious actors who can then access sensitive data.
This could include personal information, financial details, or even location data.
The risk of identity theft and fraud is a significant concern for many.
Furthermore, critics argue that the widespread use of RFID tags could lead to a loss of control over personal information.
With these tags embedded in everyday items, individuals may unknowingly disclose personal data to various entities, such as retailers or government agencies.
This lack of transparency and control over one's own information is seen as a threat to individual autonomy and privacy.
Despite these concerns, proponents of RFID technology argue that it offers numerous benefits, such as improved inventory management and enhanced security measures.
For example, RFID tags can help retailers track their inventory more efficiently, reducing costs and improving customer satisfaction.
In the healthcare sector, RFID tags can be used to monitor patients and ensure their safety.
However, it is crucial to strike a balance between the advantages of RFID technology and the potential risks it poses to privacy and security.
Robust safeguards and regulations must be in place to protect individuals from unauthorized tracking and data breaches.
Transparency and informed consent should also be prioritized to ensure that individuals have control over their personal information.
As the use of RFID tags becomes more prevalent in our daily lives, it is essential to address the concerns surrounding their use.
Striking the right balance between convenience and privacy is crucial to ensure that individuals' rights are protected in an increasingly connected world.
The days of slow and unreliable wi-fi connections may soon be a thing of the past, as researchers are working on developing a souped-up version of the technology.

A team of scientists from the University of California, Irvine, have successfully achieved wireless speeds of up to 186 gigabits per second (Gbps), which is around 100 times faster than the current average wi-fi speed.
The breakthrough was made possible by using a combination of new hardware and software techniques.

The researchers used a combination of multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology, which allows multiple antennas to transmit and receive data simultaneously, and orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), a method of encoding data that allows for faster transmission speeds.
The team also developed a new type of wireless transceiver, which is capable of transmitting and receiving data at such high speeds.
This transceiver uses a combination of analog and digital signal processing techniques to achieve the high data rates.
The potential applications of this new technology are vast.

With faster and more reliable wi-fi connections, users will be able to download large files in a matter of seconds, stream high-definition videos without buffering, and connect multiple devices to the internet without experiencing any slowdowns.
In addition to improving the user experience, this new technology could also have significant implications for industries such as healthcare, transportation, and entertainment.
For example, in healthcare, faster wi-fi connections could enable remote monitoring of patients, allowing doctors to provide real-time care from a distance.
In transportation, it could enable the development of autonomous vehicles that rely on high-speed wireless connections to communicate with each other and with infrastructure.
However, there are still some challenges to overcome before this souped-up wi-fi becomes a reality.
One of the main challenges is ensuring that the technology can be implemented on a large scale without causing interference with other wireless devices.
The researchers are currently working on developing algorithms and protocols that will allow for efficient coexistence with other wireless networks.
Despite these challenges, the researchers are optimistic about the future of souped-up wi-fi.
They believe that their breakthrough could pave the way for a new era of wireless communication, where fast and reliable internet connections are the norm.
With further development and refinement, this technology could soon become a reality, revolutionizing the way we connect to the internet.

The number of junk e-mails being sent worldwide is on a relentless rise, according to a new report.
The study, conducted by cybersecurity firm Symantec, found that the global spam rate reached 55% in 2020, up from 53% in the previous year.
This means that more than half of all e-mails sent last year were unwanted and potentially harmful.
The increase in spam e-mails can be attributed to various factors, including the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.
Cybercriminals have been taking advantage of the global health crisis to launch phishing attacks and spread malware through spam e-mails.

These malicious e-mails often disguise themselves as legitimate messages from health organizations or government agencies, tricking unsuspecting recipients into clicking on malicious links or downloading harmful attachments.
Symantec's report also highlighted the role of botnets in the rise of spam e-mails.
Botnets are networks of infected computers that cybercriminals use to send out massive volumes of spam.
These botnets can be rented or sold on the dark web, making it easier for anyone with malicious intent to launch spam campaigns.
The consequences of spam e-mails can be severe.
They not only waste time and resources for individuals and businesses but also pose significant security risks.
Clicking on a malicious link or downloading a harmful attachment can lead to identity theft, financial loss, or even the compromise of sensitive data.
To combat the rising tide of spam e-mails, cybersecurity experts recommend several measures.
First and foremost, individuals should exercise caution when opening e-mails from unknown senders or those that seem suspicious.
It is crucial to avoid clicking on links or downloading attachments from such e-mails.
Additionally, organizations should invest in robust cybersecurity measures, including spam filters and antivirus software, to detect and block spam e-mails.
Regular employee training on cybersecurity best practices can also help raise awareness and reduce the risk of falling victim to spam attacks.

While the fight against spam e-mails may seem never-ending, it is essential for individuals, businesses, and governments to remain vigilant and take proactive steps to protect themselves from these unwanted and potentially harmful messages.

Web logs, or blogs, are proving to be a valuable tool in aiding disaster recovery efforts around the world.
These online platforms allow individuals and organizations to share real-time information, updates, and resources during times of crisis.
During natural disasters such as hurricanes, earthquakes, or wildfires, traditional communication channels can often become overwhelmed or disrupted.
This is where blogs step in, providing a decentralized and accessible platform for people to share critical information.
From emergency response teams to local residents, blogs have become a go-to source for up-to-date news and instructions.
One of the key advantages of blogs is their ability to provide real-time updates.
Unlike traditional news outlets, which may have limited resources or face logistical challenges during a disaster, blogs can be updated instantly by anyone with an internet connection.
This means that affected communities can receive the latest information on evacuation routes, shelter locations, and emergency services without delay.
Furthermore, blogs allow for two-way communication, enabling individuals to share their experiences, needs, and offers of assistance.
This creates a sense of community and solidarity among those affected by the disaster, fostering a spirit of collaboration and support.
Bloggers can also provide firsthand accounts of the situation on the ground, giving a more personal and relatable perspective to the recovery efforts.
In addition to disseminating information, blogs also serve as a platform for resource coordination.
People can share information about available supplies, such as food, water, and medical aid, and connect those in need with those who can provide assistance.
This helps to streamline the distribution of resources and ensures that help reaches those who need it most.
Moreover, blogs have proven to be a valuable tool for documenting and preserving the stories and experiences of disaster survivors.
These firsthand accounts can serve as a historical record and provide valuable insights for future disaster preparedness and response efforts.
While blogs have become an essential tool in disaster recovery, it is important to note that they are not without their challenges.
The spread of misinformation and rumors can be a concern, as anyone can create a blog and share information without verification.
However, many organizations and authorities have recognized this issue and are working to establish trusted sources and guidelines for bloggers during emergencies.
In conclusion, web logs have emerged as a powerful tool in aiding disaster recovery efforts.
Their ability to provide real-time updates, facilitate communication and resource coordination, and document experiences make them an invaluable asset during times of crisis.
As technology continues to advance, it is likely that blogs will play an even greater role in future disaster response and recovery efforts.

The app allows users to purchase bus tickets and store them on their phones, eliminating the need for physical tickets or Oyster cards.

The app will then deduct the appropriate fare from the user's account.
This new system is not only more convenient for passengers, but it also reduces the risk of lost or forgotten tickets.

Stan Lee, the legendary comic book writer and editor, has passed away at the age of 95.
Lee, who co-created iconic superheroes such as Spider-Man, Iron Man, and the X-Men, revolutionized the comic book industry and left an indelible mark on popular culture.
Born Stanley Martin Lieber in 1922, Lee began his career in the comic book industry in 1939, working as an assistant at Timely Comics, which would later become Marvel Comics.
Over the years, he worked his way up to become the editor-in-chief and eventually the publisher of Marvel Comics.
Lee's creative vision and innovative storytelling transformed the comic book medium.
He introduced flawed and relatable characters, breaking away from the traditional archetype of the infallible superhero.
His characters faced real-world problems and grappled with their own personal demons, making them more relatable to readers.
Spider-Man, one of Lee's most beloved creations, exemplifies this approach.

A recent study has revealed that many internet users are failing to identify online advertisements, despite considering themselves to be savvy searchers.

The research, conducted by a team at a leading university, found that a significant number of participants were unable to distinguish between organic search results and paid advertisements on search engine results pages.
The study involved a group of participants who were asked to perform various search tasks on popular search engines.
The researchers closely monitored their eye movements and recorded their interactions with the search results.
Surprisingly, the results showed that a large proportion of participants were unable to identify the paid advertisements that appeared at the top of the search results.
The researchers believe that this lack of awareness could be attributed to the increasing sophistication of online advertising techniques.
Paid advertisements are now designed to closely resemble organic search results, making it difficult for users to differentiate between the two.
Additionally, the placement of ads at the top of search results, often accompanied by a small "Ad" label, can easily go unnoticed by users who are focused on finding relevant information.
This lack of awareness has significant implications for both users and advertisers.
Users may unknowingly click on paid advertisements, thinking they are clicking on organic search results, which can lead to frustration and a loss of trust in search engines.
On the other hand, advertisers may not be getting the desired return on investment if their ads are not being noticed or clicked on by users.
The study suggests that search engines and advertisers need to find ways to make paid advertisements more distinguishable from organic search results.
This could include clearer labeling or visual cues that clearly indicate the presence of an advertisement.
Additionally, user education and awareness campaigns could help users become more discerning when it comes to identifying online advertisements.
In conclusion, the study highlights the need for internet users to be more vigilant when it comes to identifying online advertisements.
Despite considering themselves to be savvy searchers, many users are failing to spot paid advertisements on search engine results pages.
This lack of awareness has implications for both users and advertisers, and calls for improved strategies to make advertisements more distinguishable.

The Bank of England has decided to keep interest rates on hold at 0.1% amid concerns over the economic impact of the ongoing coronavirus pandemic.
The decision comes as the central bank assesses the effectiveness of its current monetary policy measures and weighs the need for further stimulus.
The Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted unanimously to maintain the historically low interest rates, which have been in place since March 2020.
The decision was widely expected by economists, who believe that the Bank will continue to prioritize supporting the economy as it recovers from the effects of the pandemic.
The decision to leave rates unchanged comes as the UK faces a surge in COVID-19 cases driven by the highly transmissible Delta variant.
The Bank has acknowledged the potential risks to the economic outlook posed by the variant and the possibility of further restrictions being imposed to contain its spread.
In addition to keeping interest rates on hold, the Bank also maintained its quantitative easing (QE) program at £895 billion ($1.2 trillion).
The program involves the purchase of government bonds and corporate debt to inject liquidity into the financial system and support borrowing and spending.
The Bank's decision reflects its cautious approach to monetary policy amid the uncertain economic landscape.

While the UK economy has shown signs of recovery, with GDP growing by 2.3% in April, there are concerns about the sustainability of the rebound as government support measures, such as the furlough scheme, wind down.
The Bank's Governor, Andrew Bailey, has previously stated that the central bank is ready to take further action if necessary to support the economy.
However, he has also emphasized the need for a balanced approach, considering the potential risks of excessive stimulus, such as inflationary pressures.
The decision to leave rates on hold is likely to be welcomed by businesses and households, as it helps to keep borrowing costs low.
However, savers will continue to face the challenge of finding attractive returns on their deposits in a low-interest-rate environment.
Looking ahead, the Bank will closely monitor the evolving economic situation and the impact of the Delta variant on the recovery.
The next MPC meeting is scheduled for August, where the Bank will reassess its monetary policy stance and consider any necessary adjustments to support the UK's economic revival.

Cybersecurity experts are warning computer users about the increasing threat of hackers recruiting their PCs for malicious activities.
With the rise of botnets, hackers are able to take control of thousands, if not millions, of computers and use them to carry out cyberattacks without the owners' knowledge.
Botnets are networks of infected computers that are controlled remotely by hackers.
These compromised computers, also known as "zombies," can be used to launch distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, send spam emails, mine cryptocurrencies, or even steal sensitive information.
The owners of these infected computers are often unaware that their devices have been compromised and are being used for illegal activities.
One of the most common ways hackers recruit PCs is through malware infections.
Malware can be disguised as legitimate software or hidden within malicious websites, emails, or downloads.
Once a computer is infected, the hacker gains control and can use it as part of their botnet.
The consequences of having your PC recruited by hackers can be severe.
Not only can it lead to financial loss or identity theft, but it can also result in legal consequences if the compromised computer is used for illegal activities.
Additionally, the reputation of individuals or businesses can be tarnished if their computers are involved in cyberattacks.
To protect against PC recruitment, cybersecurity experts recommend taking several precautions.
First and foremost, it is crucial to keep all software, including operating systems and antivirus programs, up to date.
Regularly installing security patches and updates can help prevent malware infections.
Furthermore, it is essential to exercise caution when browsing the internet and opening emails or attachments from unknown sources.
Avoid clicking on suspicious links or downloading files from untrusted websites.
Using strong, unique passwords and enabling two-factor authentication can also help protect against unauthorized access to your PC.
In addition to these preventive measures, it is advisable to invest in reliable antivirus software and regularly scan your computer for malware.
Antivirus programs can detect and remove malicious software, reducing the risk of PC recruitment.
Overall, the threat of hackers recruiting PCs is a growing concern in the digital age.
By staying vigilant and implementing cybersecurity best practices, computer users can minimize the risk of their devices being used for malicious activities.

The researchers argue that universities should focus on promoting the quality of their teaching and learning, as well as highlighting the unique opportunities and resources available to students.

Overall, the study challenges the notion that tuition fees are the deciding factor for students when choosing a university.

The report concludes that while the rise in online card fraud is concerning, it is not a reason to avoid online shopping altogether.

The visionary behind the creation of the first Apple Mac, Douglas Engelbart, has passed away at the age of 88.
Engelbart, who was widely regarded as a pioneer in the field of computer technology, revolutionized the way we interact with computers and laid the foundation for the modern personal computer.
His groundbreaking work paved the way for the development of the mouse, graphical user interfaces, and hypertext, all of which are now integral parts of our everyday computing experience.
Engelbart's most notable achievement came in 1968 when he unveiled the "Mother of All Demos," a live demonstration of his revolutionary ideas at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco.
During the demo, he showcased a range of technologies that were far ahead of their time, including video conferencing, word processing, and the use of a mouse to navigate a computer screen.
This demonstration not only impressed the audience but also inspired a generation of computer scientists and engineers.
Born in 1925 in Oregon, Engelbart showed an early interest in technology and pursued a career in electrical engineering.
He joined the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) in the 1950s, where he began his groundbreaking research on human-computer interaction.
It was during his time at SRI that he developed the concept of the mouse, which he believed would provide a more intuitive way for users to interact with computers.
Engelbart's work caught the attention of Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, who were in the process of developing the first Apple Macintosh.
They were inspired by Engelbart's ideas and incorporated many of his concepts into their design.
The Macintosh, which was released in 1984, featured a graphical user interface and a mouse, making it more user-friendly and accessible to a wider audience.
Despite his significant contributions to the field of computer technology, Engelbart's work went largely unrecognized for many years.
However, in 2000, he was awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation by President Bill Clinton for his pioneering work.
His legacy continues to shape the way we interact with computers and his impact on the industry cannot be overstated.
Engelbart's death marks the end of an era in computer technology.
His vision and innovation have left an indelible mark on the industry, and his contributions will continue to shape the future of computing for generations to come.
As we mourn the loss of a true pioneer, we also celebrate his remarkable achievements and the lasting impact he has had on our lives.

Scientists have long known about synesthesia, a condition where the stimulation of one sense triggers an involuntary experience in another sense.
However, Daniel's case is particularly intriguing as he is blind and therefore lacks the visual input that typically triggers synesthetic experiences.
To investigate further, Daniel participated in a series of experiments conducted by researchers at the university.
They found that his ability to "hear in colour" was consistent across different musical instruments and even extended to non-musical sounds.
For example, he associated the sound of a car engine with the colour red and the sound of rain with the colour blue.
The researchers believe that Daniel's brain has developed alternative neural pathways to compensate for his lack of vision.
These pathways may be responsible for the cross-wiring of his senses, allowing him to experience sound as colour.
This discovery has significant implications for our understanding of the human brain and the potential for sensory compensation in individuals with disabilities.
It also raises questions about the nature of perception and the boundaries of our senses.
Daniel's unique ability has not only fascinated scientists but has also opened up new possibilities for artistic expression.
He has started composing music that aims to capture the colours he perceives through sound, creating a truly immersive and multi-sensory experience for his audience.

The September reading suggests that the sector is not only expanding but doing so at an accelerated pace.
The report also revealed that new orders, production, and employment all increased in September.
New orders rose to 64.6, up from 60.3 in August, while production increased to 62.2, up from 61 in the previous month.

These positive figures come as welcome news for the US economy, which has been grappling with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Windows ATMs, which are widely used across the globe, are raising concerns among experts due to their vulnerability to cyber attacks.
The machines, which run on the Windows operating system, have become a prime target for hackers looking to exploit security flaws and gain unauthorized access to sensitive financial information.
Recent incidents have highlighted the risks associated with Windows ATMs.
In 2019, a group of cybercriminals known as "Carbanak" managed to steal over $1.2 billion from banks worldwide by exploiting vulnerabilities in Windows-based ATMs.
The group used sophisticated malware to gain control of the machines remotely, allowing them to dispense cash on demand.
The main issue with Windows ATMs is their outdated software.
Many of these machines are still running on older versions of the Windows operating system, such as Windows XP, which is no longer supported by Microsoft.
This means that security patches and updates are not available, leaving the ATMs exposed to known vulnerabilities.
Furthermore, the lack of encryption in Windows ATMs makes them an easy target for hackers.
Without proper encryption, sensitive data, including PIN numbers and card details, can be easily intercepted and used for fraudulent activities.
This poses a significant risk to both financial institutions and their customers.
Experts are urging banks and ATM manufacturers to take immediate action to address these security concerns.
Upgrading the operating system to a more secure version, such as Windows 10, is a crucial step in mitigating the risks associated with Windows ATMs.
Additionally, implementing strong encryption protocols and regularly updating the software are essential to ensure the security of these machines.
In response to these concerns, some banks have already started taking measures to enhance the security of their ATMs.
For instance, they are implementing multi-factor authentication systems and conducting regular security audits to identify and fix any vulnerabilities.
However, the transition to more secure systems may take time and require significant investments.
Financial institutions must weigh the costs of upgrading their ATMs against the potential losses resulting from cyber attacks.
Nevertheless, the importance of safeguarding customer data and maintaining public trust in the banking system cannot be overstated.
As the use of digital banking and cashless transactions continues to grow, the security of ATMs becomes even more critical.
It is imperative that banks and ATM manufacturers work together to address the vulnerabilities of Windows ATMs and ensure the protection of customer information.
Failure to do so could have severe consequences for both financial institutions and their customers.
