Public support for a ban on hunting in the UK appears to be dwindling, according to a recent survey.
The poll, conducted by Ipsos MORI, suggests that the number of people in favour of maintaining the Hunting Act has fallen significantly over the past decade.
The Hunting Act, which came into effect in 2005, outlawed the hunting of wild mammals with dogs in England and Wales.
However, the new survey indicates that public opinion may be shifting, with fewer people now supporting the ban.
According to the poll, 49% of respondents were in favour of keeping the ban, down from 58% in a similar survey conducted in 2016.
Meanwhile, the proportion of people who believe the ban should be lifted has risen from 31% to 37%.
The survey also revealed a generational divide in attitudes towards hunting.
Younger respondents were more likely to support the ban, with 57% of those aged 18-24 in favour, compared to just 41% of those aged 55 and over.
The results of the survey have been welcomed by pro-hunting groups, who argue that the Hunting Act is outdated and ineffective.
The Countryside Alliance, a group that advocates for rural issues including hunting, said the findings showed a "growing recognition of the Act's failure".
However, animal rights groups have disputed the survey's findings.
The League Against Cruel Sports argued that the majority of the public still supports the ban, and accused pro-hunting groups of trying to "manipulate" public opinion.
The debate over hunting has been a contentious issue in the UK for many years.
Supporters argue that it is a traditional rural activity that helps control pest populations, while opponents believe it is cruel and unnecessary.
The latest survey suggests that while public opinion may be shifting, the issue remains deeply divisive.
With both sides of the debate likely to seize on these findings to support their cause, the future of the Hunting Act remains uncertain.

The rise of broadband internet has significantly transformed the way people express themselves online, according to a recent study.

The study highlights how the availability of high-speed internet has given rise to a new era of digital expression, enabling individuals to share their thoughts, ideas, and creativity more freely and widely than ever before.
Broadband internet, with its high-speed data transmission, has made it possible for people to upload and share large files such as videos, music, and high-resolution images.
This has led to an explosion of user-generated content on platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, where individuals can showcase their talents, opinions, and experiences to a global audience.
The study, conducted by the University of Oxford, analysed the online behaviour of more than 10,000 internet users across the globe.
It found that the availability of broadband internet was directly linked to an increase in online expression.
"Before the advent of broadband, the internet was a largely passive medium.
People would browse websites, send emails, maybe participate in a forum or two.
But the ability to easily upload and share content has fundamentally changed the way we use the internet," said Dr. Sarah Roberts, the lead author of the study.
The study also found that broadband internet has democratised online expression.
In the past, creating and sharing high-quality digital content required expensive equipment and technical expertise.
But today, anyone with a smartphone and a broadband connection can become a content creator.
"Broadband has levelled the playing field.
It's given a voice to people who might not have been heard otherwise," said Dr. Roberts.
The rise of social media platforms has also played a significant role in fuelling online expression.
These platforms, combined with broadband internet, have created a space where people can express themselves in real-time, engage with others, and participate in global conversations.
However, the study also warns of the potential downsides of this increased online expression.
The ease of sharing content can also lead to the spread of misinformation, hate speech, and online harassment.
"Like any tool, the internet can be used for good or ill.
It's important that we continue to develop strategies for dealing with the darker side of online expression," said Dr. Roberts.
Despite these challenges, the study concludes that the rise of broadband internet has overall been a positive force for online expression.
It has enabled a new generation of digital creators, fostered global conversations, and given a voice to those who might not have been heard otherwise.

A significant number of businesses are failing to prepare for the impact of HIV on their workforce, according to a new report.

The study, conducted by the International Labour Organization (ILO), suggests that many companies are not taking adequate steps to protect their employees and their operations from the potential effects of the virus.
The report reveals that despite the fact that HIV can have a significant impact on a company's productivity and profitability, many businesses are not implementing HIV workplace policies.
These policies are designed to prevent new infections, manage the impact of the virus on employees, and reduce the stigma associated with HIV.
The ILO study surveyed over 1,000 businesses across various sectors in different parts of the world.
It found that only 42% of the businesses had a comprehensive HIV policy in place.
This is despite the fact that HIV can lead to increased absenteeism, higher healthcare costs, and a loss of skills and experience.
The report also highlighted that many businesses are not providing their employees with access to HIV testing, treatment, and support services.
This is a critical issue as early diagnosis and treatment can significantly improve the health outcomes for people living with HIV and can also reduce the risk of transmission.
The ILO has called on businesses to take action to address this issue.
"Businesses have a key role to play in the global response to HIV," said Manuela Tomei, Director of the ILO's Conditions of Work and Equality Department.
"By implementing HIV workplace policies, businesses can protect their employees and their bottom line.

"

The report also emphasised the importance of businesses working in partnership with their employees, trade unions, and HIV service providers to develop and implement these policies.
The ILO has developed guidelines to help businesses create effective HIV workplace policies.

These guidelines include providing employees with access to voluntary and confidential HIV testing, ensuring that employees living with HIV are not discriminated against, and providing employees with access to HIV prevention and treatment services.
The report's findings highlight the need for businesses to take HIV seriously and to take proactive steps to protect their employees and their operations.
As the global fight against HIV continues, it is clear that businesses have a crucial role to play.

A blind student from the University of Oxford has developed a unique ability to 'hear in colour', thanks to a revolutionary device that translates colours into sound.
Tommy Edison, a 22-year-old physics student, lost his sight at birth due to a rare genetic disorder.
However, his world has been transformed by a groundbreaking piece of technology known as the 'Eyeborg'.
The Eyeborg, developed by Canadian artist Neil Harbisson, is a device that converts colours into sound frequencies.
Harbisson, who himself is colour-blind, invented the device to help him perceive colours.
Edison wears the Eyeborg, which resembles a small, flexible antenna, over his forehead.
The device scans the colours in front of him and translates them into different sound frequencies, which he hears through bone conduction headphones.
Over time, Edison has learned to associate specific frequencies with certain colours.
For instance, he knows that a high-pitched sound corresponds to blue, while a lower frequency indicates red.
"It's like learning a new language," Edison explained.
"At first, it was just noise.
But over time, I've learned to understand what each sound means.
Now, I can 'hear' a sunset or a painting.
It's incredible.

"

Edison's unique ability has not only enriched his personal life but also his academic pursuits.
As a physics student, he can now 'hear' and understand complex colour-coded data and diagrams, which were previously inaccessible to him.
His story has sparked interest among scientists and researchers, who believe that this technology could open up new possibilities for visually impaired individuals.
Dr. Hannah Smith, a neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, said, "This is a fascinating example of neuroplasticity – the brain's ability to adapt and learn new skills.
It shows that even when one sense is lost, others can be enhanced or adapted in remarkable ways.

"

While the Eyeborg is not yet commercially available, its success with Edison and Harbisson suggests a promising future.
As technology continues to advance, it offers new hope for those living with sensory impairments, potentially transforming their experience of the world.
For Edison, the Eyeborg has already made a significant impact.
"I may not be able to see colours," he said, "but I can hear them.
And that's a beautiful thing."

Banks worldwide are facing growing concerns over the use of Windows-based Automated Teller Machines (ATMs), as the operating system is increasingly becoming a target for cybercriminals.
The majority of ATMs around the globe run on versions of Microsoft's Windows operating system, primarily Windows 7.
However, with Microsoft ending support for Windows 7 in January 2020, these machines are no longer receiving security updates, leaving them vulnerable to hacking and malware attacks.
Cybersecurity experts have warned that this could potentially lead to a surge in ATM fraud.
Criminals could exploit the outdated software to steal card details, manipulate transactions, or even take control of the entire ATM network.
The issue is further compounded by the fact that upgrading these machines to a newer operating system is not a straightforward task.
ATMs are complex machines that require specific software to interact with their hardware components, such as card readers and cash dispensers.
Upgrading the operating system could potentially disrupt these interactions, leading to machine malfunctions.
Moreover, the cost of upgrading is another significant hurdle.
Banks would need to invest heavily in new hardware, software, and the necessary testing to ensure the upgraded ATMs function correctly.
This is a cost that many banks, particularly smaller ones, may struggle to afford.
The situation has prompted calls for banks to move away from Windows-based ATMs altogether.
Some experts suggest that Linux, an open-source operating system, could be a more secure and cost-effective alternative.
However, this would still require a significant investment in terms of time and resources to implement.
In the meantime, banks are being urged to take immediate action to secure their ATM networks.
This includes regularly monitoring and updating their systems, implementing strong firewalls, and educating customers about the risks of ATM fraud.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has also issued guidance to banks, advising them to assess the risks associated with their current ATM operating systems and to take appropriate measures to mitigate these risks.
The concerns over Windows ATMs highlight the broader issue of cybersecurity in the banking sector.
As banks continue to digitise their services, they must also invest in robust security measures to protect their systems and their customers' data from cyber threats.

It's astonishing how many people still haven't learned proper email etiquette.

Are you guilty of any of these?

Not including an unsubscribe link: If you're sending an email to a list of people, you should always include an unsubscribe link.

This is a legal requirement in many countries.

Not getting permission: If you're sending an email to someone, make sure they've given you permission to do so.
Don't buy email lists or send emails to people who haven't opted in to receive them.
This is the best way to get marked as spam.
Not using a real email address: If you're sending an email, use a real email address that people can reply to.
Don't use a fake or anonymous email address.
This just looks suspicious and can get your email marked as spam.
Not including a signature: If you're sending an email, include a signature with your name, title, and contact information.
This helps people identify who you are and why they're receiving an email from you.
Not proofreading: Before you hit send, make sure you proofread your email for any spelling or grammar mistakes.

France will this week become the first country to require televisions to include digital tuners, in a move that could boost sales of LCD and plasma screens.

From Tuesday, broadcasters will stop broadcasting on the country's four analogue channels, which for years have been able to be received anywhere in France.
Full details of the digitisation process, and the names of the towns where analogue transmission will end, can be found on the website of France's public service broadcaster, France Televisions.
Those who do not receive their television signal via satellite or cable, and who watch analogue broadcasts on a cathode ray tube TV, face having to buy a digital decoder or a new digital TV.
Digital decoders, which cost about €100 (£65), are slightly cheaper than a basic LCD TV, which starts at about €150.
Digital tuners are already included in all LCD and plasma TVs and sales have benefited from the run-up to the switchover.

"This catalyst for digitising television has allowed us to regain market share in television sales, which had been slipping since the beginning of the year," said Patrice Brehmer, an executive at Fnac, the French high-street electronics retailer.
About half of all French households already have digital television, either because they receive satellite or cable television, or because they have bought a TV with a digital tuner.
According to the latest figures from GfK, a market research company, about 40 per cent of the French population plan to buy a digital TV or decoder in the next year.

"The French have reacted reasonably to information campaigns conducted by broadcasters since the beginning of the year," said François Barrault, the director of the digital economy at the Ministry of Industry.
"The French are aware of the digitisation process."
The experience in France will be closely watched in Britain, where a digital switchover is due to take place in 2010.
British broadcasters have already started to run information campaigns, but full-scale trials will not take place until next year.
Michael Grade, the BBC's chairman, said last week that the corporation was working on the assumption that people would have digital television by 2010.
"That is why we have consciously driven forward the take-up of digital television," he said.
"Some 52 per cent of the population has already converted, and that will grow."

Few names are as synonymous with comic books as Stan Lee.
As the co-creator of Marvel Comics' instantly recognizable stable of superheroes, including the Fantastic Four, Spider-Man, the Avengers, and the X-Men, Lee's impact on the genre is undeniable.
Yet, for all of his success, Lee remained grounded, and was known for his trademark wit, and an ability to connect with fans that transcended the page.
Born as Stanley Martin Lieber on December 28, 1922, in New York City, Lee grew up in a vibrant neighborhood filled with immigrants from around the world.
As a child, he was fascinated by movies and books, and dreamed of one day becoming a writer.
After graduating from high school in 1939, Lee got his start in the comic book industry as an assistant at Timely Comics, which would eventually become Marvel Comics.
Initially, he performed menial tasks, such as filling in watercolors and proofreading, but soon began writing his own scripts.
Lee's career took off in the early 1960s when he and artist Jack Kirby created the Fantastic Four.
The title's success spurred Lee to create even more superheroes, including the Hulk, Thor, and Iron Man.
What set Lee's creations apart from other comic book heroes was their relatable, human qualities.
Despite their superhuman powers, characters like Spider-Man and the X-Men faced the same struggles as everyday people, such as paying rent and dealing with relationships.
Lee's impact on the comic book industry was unparalleled.
He introduced a level of complexity and emotional depth to his characters that set them apart from the traditional archetypes of the time.
Additionally, he was a master of the cliffhanger, and his stories were filled with twists and turns that kept readers coming back for more.
Lee was also a pioneer in the realm of multimedia franchising.
He saw the potential for his characters to thrive in other formats, and successfully expanded the Marvel Universe into television, film, and even video games.
As Lee's fame grew, so did his reputation as a pop culture icon.
He made appearances in numerous Marvel films, and was beloved by fans for his trademark wit and charm.
Lee's legacy extends far beyond the page.
He was a true pioneer in the world of superhero comics, and his creations have become a timeless part of popular culture.
He will be remembered as a true visionary who helped to shape the industry into what it is today.

"The infrastructure is collapsing.

"

Barenboim, who was born in Buenos Aires in 1942, said that he had moved to Germany in 1982 because he had been offered the chance to establish the Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra as a world-class ensemble - a dream that had been realised.

"There is not enough being done in Germany to help young musicians find their place," he said.

But the era of the home phone may be coming to an end - signalled by telecoms giant BT's decision to stop selling them altogether.

It found that even older people, who might have relied on landlines in the past, were turning to mobile phones.

Since then, many have decided they do not need an additional phone socket in their homes, and have cancelled their landlines, or not taken one out when moving into a new property.
Some have even ripped out the wiring altogether.
BT's decision to stop selling landlines - which Ofcom approved - is not expected to have an immediate impact on existing customers.

The company said landline connections were increasingly being used only for broadband, and that its focus would be on providing digital phone services, such as VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol), which allows people to make calls over the internet.
But what does the disappearance of the home phone mean for Britain - and could it leave people behind?

Less socially inclusive

It pointed to older people and those on low incomes as potentially being most affected, because they are less likely to own a mobile phone.

A study carried out by the University of Texas showed that people were unable to correctly identify the sponsored advertisements on search engine results pages (SERPs).
When shown screenshots of Google search results, participants pointed out advertisements as fewer than 25% of the time, despite the presence of cues like "Ad" or "Sponsored."

One of the authors of the study, Amanda Broderick, commented on the low number of participants able to discern between ads and search results, noting that "just because something is labeled 'Ad' doesn't mean that people will notice that it's an advertisement."
This failure to identify advertisements relates to a concept from psychology known as inattentional blindness, which causes people to miss obvious facts when their attention is focused elsewhere.
The authors of the study suggest that the low ability to recognize ads is due to the design of SERPs, which often place ads and search results in similar formats.
Additionally, people may be more focused on the search results themselves rather than the ads that appear on the page.
The authors suggest that search engine designers should make ads more distinct from search results to improve transparency and help users make more informed decisions.
The study's findings highlight the need for search engine users to be more vigilant in identifying advertisements and interpreting information on SERPs.
It is important to be aware of the potential for ads to influence search results and to consider the motivations of the companies behind the advertisements.

Overall, the study suggests that people are unable to reliably identify advertisements on SERPs, which has implications for the credibility of information and the influence of advertising on search engine users.

Gazprom, the Russian state-controlled energy company, has been accused of avoiding more than $36m in taxes in Moldova, according to the country's prosecutor general.
The claim relates to the period when Gazprom controlled the gas transmitted through Moldova towards Europe.
It is the latest in a number of disputes between the company and European countries.

The prosecutor's office said in a statement that an investigation had found that Gazprom had been transporting gas across Moldova "without observing the formalities of customs clearance" at the southern endpoint of the pipeline that goes through the country.
The statement added that the company had failed to comply with "the requirements of Moldovan tax legislation... for the payment of excise duties and VAT" for the five years from 2014 to 2019.
The total amount of back taxes claimed is 7.2 billion lei ($1.35bn; £1.06bn).
The company has been in dispute with a number of European countries over supplies of gas.
It has reduced or completely cut off supplies to countries including Poland, Bulgaria and Finland after they approved plans to diversify their energy sources away from Russia.

Germany rejected this explanation and accused Russia of using gas as a political weapon.

Furthermore, "blog" became a focal point for debates surrounding the future of the English language and the influence of technology on communication.
Some welcomed "blog" as a fresh and innovative addition to the language, while others expressed concerns about the potential decline of traditional writing forms.

In conclusion, the selection of "blog" as the word of the year for 2023 reflects its widespread use and the debates it sparked regarding the evolution of language in the digital age.

Shredding in Whitehall has increased under the Conservative government, according to a Freedom of Information request submitted by the Labour Party.
The party obtained data from the Cabinet Office, which oversees the civil service, showing that the monthly amount of shredding across government departments has increased year after year since 2016.
The data does not include the Prime Minister's Office.
In 2016, the monthly average of shredded documents was around 12 tonnes.
This increased to over 13 tonnes in 2017, 15 tonnes in 2018, and 17 tonnes in 2019.
Data for 2020 is unavailable, but in the first three months of this year, an average of 16 tonnes of documents were shredded each month.
The highest monthly amount of shredding in the past four years was in March 2019, when over 19 tonnes of documents were destroyed.
April and May of this year saw similar levels, with just under 19 tonnes of paper being shredded both months.
A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “The Cabinet Office does not recognise these figures.
Shredding is carried out on a bank basis by our clearing contractor and any paper that is shredded is recycled.”
The Labour Party has criticized the government for shredding documents that should be preserved for future generations.
Shadow Cabinet Office minister Rachel Reeves said: “The shredding spree in Theresa May’s Downing Street reached new heights today.
Shifting from denial to sarcasm, ministers now admit they shred policies and important documents but insist it’s all to save the planet.
“Labour has uncovered a vast and growing culture of shredding within Whitehall.
From Universal Credit to the 'no deal' Brexit papers, it seems this government is happy to destroy vital documents to hide their failures from the public.”

The rules, which were introduced in 2011 and have since been revised, required female athletes with testosterone levels above a certain threshold to take medication to reduce them to be allowed to compete.
Ms Chand welcomed the Athens court's decision, saying it was a "victory for all women athletes".
The government has unveiled plans to reform the asylum system, including a proposal to send some asylum seekers to a "third country" while their application is processed.
The plan, which was announced by Home Secretary Priti Patel, would see applicants sent to countries such as Rwanda, Ghana, and Kenya.
Under the plans, some asylum seekers could be charged up to £1,000 to fund their flight.
The government says the scheme will cost £120 million in the first year and will "deter illegal entry" to the UK.
The plans have been criticised by opposition parties and human rights groups, who have described them as "inhumane" and "unethical".
They add that the government has not provided any details on how the scheme would work or how much it would cost.
Former world number one Andy Roddick defeated Russia's Marat Safin to reach the San Jose final.
The American, 29, beat the world number 39 6-4 7-6 (7-2) in one hour and 48 minutes.
Roddick will now play Serbia's Novak Djokovic, who saw off the challenge of France's Jo-Wilfried Tsonga.
The top seed beat his French opponent - who had beaten him in their last two meetings - 6-3 6-4.
The final is set to be an interesting clash of styles, with Roddick's power against Djokovic's craft and guile.
Russian oil giant Yukos has lost its bankruptcy battle in a US court, leaving investors with few options for recouping the $3bn they are owed.
The company was once Russia's largest oil producer, but saw its assets frozen after being hit with a $42bn tax bill, later reduced to $9bn.
Yukos filed for bankruptcy in August 2006, leaving many investors from the US, Europe and Asia owed huge sums.
US bankruptcy judge Robert Drain approved a settlement proposed by Yukos' primary secured creditor, the Russian Deposit Insurance Agency, and the company's management.
It will see the agency convert its $3.5bn debt into 99.4% of Yukos' stock.
The plan does not allow for any money to be paid out to unsecured creditors, such as investors who bought Yukos' international bonds.
These investors are expected to receive just 0.2% of the company, and will have to wait for several years to receive any payment.
The decision leaves Russia as the sole jurisdiction in which Yukos investors can pursue claims for their losses.
Yukos was declared bankrupt by a Russian court in August 2007.
The firm's chief executive, Steven Theede, said he was pleased the case had been resolved.
"We are very pleased that the court has confirmed the settlement, bringing to an end a long period of uncertainty for Yukos' stakeholders," he said in a statement.
"We will now work to ensure the most effective realisation of Yukos' assets for the benefit of creditors."
One of the founders of the now-defunct Russian oil company Yukos has filed a lawsuit against Russia seeking $28bn in compensation for his firm's bankruptcy.
Mikhail Khodorkovsky, who spent a decade in jail in Russia on charges of fraud and tax evasion, filed the claim on Tuesday at the Supreme Court in The Hague.
The claim alleges that Russia violated an investment protection treaty when it seized Yukos' assets.
Mr Khodorkovsky, who now lives in London, alleges that the Russian government "expropriated" his investment in Yukos "without compensation or justification".
Yukos, once Russia's largest oil company, was placed into bankruptcy by the Russian government in 2004.
The firm's assets were subsequently sold off to Russian state companies, notably Rosneft, now one of the world's biggest oil producers.
Mr Khodorkovsky, who denies the fraud and tax evasion charges against him, had claimed that the Russian legal system was biased against him.
He had been released from prison in 2013 and flew to Berlin, where he had been given asylum.

His lawsuit claims that the Russian government "forced the Yukos group into bankruptcy" and that this was "an orchestrated campaign" which "culminated in malicious, large-scale, multi-faceted raids on Yukos' principal production, refining and retail facilities".
The claim argues that this campaign constituted "expropriation" and that the Russian government is liable for damages.
Mr Khodorkovsky is seeking $28.7bn in compensation, as well as interest and costs.
His lawyers wrote that "calculations of the claim are based on a valuation of Yukos as of end-2004, being the date of the expropriation".

They added that the claim takes into account the fact that Yukos' assets were sold at "substantially discounted prices" and that the firm also had assets which it had not been able to sell at the time of its bankruptcy.

Mr Khodorkovsky's lawyers also argued that the claim is made against Russia, rather than any specific Russian officials, because the actions which led to Yukos' bankruptcy "were undertaken by the Russian state".
They said that no compensation had been paid to Yukos' shareholders and that Russia had "failed to recognise any liability for the expropriation".
The EU patent reform, known as the Unitary Patent Package, is due for completion this year.

The reform, which has been over a decade in the making, aims to create a single, unified patent regime across all EU member states, and is considered to be the most significant change to EU patent law in decades.
However, the project has faced several delays and setbacks over the years, and most recently, the UK's departure from the EU has thrown the project into doubt.
The UK's Patent Office has said that it will not be joining the unitary patent regime, which has raised concerns about the project's viability.

In light of these developments, the EU's Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) has announced that it will be rebooting the project, and has invited stakeholders to provide their input on how to move forward with the reform.
The EUIPO has said that it hopes to complete the project by the end of the year, and has stressed the importance of the reform in supporting Europe's economic recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic.
The reboot of the EU patent reform is being seen as a positive step towards ensuring that the project is completed in a timely and effective manner.
It is hoped that the renewed focus on the project will result in a successful and robust patent regime that supports innovation and competitiveness in the EU.
The BBC has released the results of a new poll that indicates growing concern among UK citizens about the economy.
The poll, which was conducted by the market research company Ipsos MORI, found that 42% of people believe the country is heading in the wrong direction.
This represents an increase of 6% since January.
The results of the poll come as the UK economy continues to struggle with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine.
The country has seen a sharp increase in inflation, with prices rising by 10.1% in the 12 months to September.
This has led to a decrease in real wages and increased pressure on household budgets.
The poll also found that people are increasingly worried about their personal financial situation.
43% of people said they are concerned about their finances, an increase of 6% since January.
This is likely due to a combination of rising prices and the end of government support schemes such as furlough.
The BBC poll indicates that people are concerned about the direction the UK economy is heading in and their personal financial situation.
With inflation continuing to rise and no end in sight to the conflict in Ukraine, it seems likely that these concerns will continue to grow.
The very poorest people in Colombia are having their savings eaten away by inflation, forcing them to eat less and turn to child labour, the country's central bank has said.
The bank's survey - based on interviews with more than 17,000 people - found that nearly half of the country's poorest had lost money because of inflation.
Households earning less than 375,000 pesos (£63; $75) a month - around the minimum wage - lost an average of 13% of their savings in the past year, it found.
Many said they were eating less, or eating lower-quality food.
Some reported having to send their children to work.
The survey was carried out in October 2021.
"I want to eat three meals a day
but I can't," said one respondent.
"Sometimes I eat only once and that's in the morning.
When I can I eat lunch, otherwise I don't.

"

The statistics are the latest to highlight the impact that decades of conflict, climate change and the pandemic have had on some of the country's most vulnerable people.
Colombia's statistical agency said that the country's poverty rate - which stood at 52% in 2019 - had likely increased during the pandemic.
And the country's National Planning Department said that 8.4 million people were living in conditions of extreme poverty, defined as living on less than $1 a day.
The central bank's survey found that poverty and inflation were higher in rural and urban areas than in small towns.
The bank's governor, Leonardo Villar, said that the findings showed that "price dynamics are affecting the poorest households the most".
"This tells us we have to redouble our efforts, not only to bring down inflation, but also to find mechanisms to protect the most vulnerable households," he told reporters.
The bank has been raising interest rates to try to reduce inflation, which currently stands at nearly 11%, one of the highest rates in the world.
But it has warned that inflation - which is also being hit by the war in Ukraine - is likely to remain high for some time.
The decision to allow the Glazer family to buy Manchester United was based on "inaccurate and flawed" information, according to a report published by the Independent Football Ombudsman (IFO).

The IFO investigation into the process concluded that there were "multiple failures" in the system for ensuring that the purchase of football clubs by offshore trusts was transparent and in the best interests of the game.
The report said there was insufficient scrutiny of the Glazers' ownership and suitability to own Manchester United.
The panel found that the club's board had failed to carry out proper due diligence on the Glazers before the takeover went ahead and that the club had broken its own procedures.
The IFO has called for the introduction of stronger checks and balances to prevent a similar situation occurring in the future.
The iconic platforming hero, Prince of Persia, returns in a gritty, realistic new adventure.
Having been away from the throne for over a decade, Prince Dastan finally returns to the legendary city of Alamut with his brother, the newly crowned King Sharaman.
However, amid the lavish pomp and celebrations of the king's coronation, the brothers are suddenly thrust into a treacherous plot that threatens to tear them apart and plunge the kingdom into chaos.
Trapped in a dangerous game of cat and mouse, the Prince finds himself drawn to the beautiful and enigmatic Princess Tamina.
But before he can win her heart, he must first defeat her father, the evil Vizier, who will stop at nothing to burn the Prince's kingdom to the ground and seize the all-powerful Dagger of Time.
With the help of a mysterious, ancient ally who possesses the gift of eternal youth, the Prince sets out on a journey to unveil the Vizier's secrets and save his kingdom from destruction.
But with each step, he uncovers a deeper, darker truth about his family and his own destiny.
As he battles his way through the deadly terrain of Alamut, the Prince must confront his own demons and decide who he can trust.
With the fate of his kingdom and his own soul at stake, the Prince must confront his past and finally come to terms with his legacy.
This gritty, realistic take on the classic platforming adventure is a must-play for fans of the series and newcomers alike.
With its stunning visuals, immersive gameplay, and deep, emotional story, Prince of Persia is a journey worth taking.
The mayor of a town in Austria has refused to retract a Nazi jibe at a local politician of Turkish descent, despite a criminal complaint.
The comment by mayor Herbert Dorfmann, from Vöcklabruck, was made during a town council meeting on 23 November.
He responded to a question from independent councillor Gulcin Ozcan by saying: “I have just returned from Istanbul, where I admired Erdogan’s palace.
It was so magnificent that I would have voted yes
if I had been asked whether I am a Führer or not.”
Mr Dorfmann later apologised for his comments but said he would not resign.
He claimed his words had been misinterpreted.
“I have enormous respect for Chancellor Erdogan and the people in Turkey,” he added.
The municipality’s website was subsequently hacked and a false statement attributed to Mr Dorfmann, which claimed that “an Islamic takeover of Europe is inevitable”.
The hacker also claimed that “the Turks are finally turning us into slaves”.
The town’s deputy mayor, Günter Steinbauer, has requested that Mr Dorfmann retract his comments and apologise to Ms Ozcan.
However, the mayor has refused to do so.
Mr Dorfmann said that he had already issued an apology and that “no-one can claim they did not understand the irony of my statement”.
He added: “I will not resign.
I have other things to do in my life than constantly being tormented by a woman who wants to get ahead in politics.”
The mayor’s comments come amid a rise in political rhetoric criticising immigration in Austria.
The far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) has recently increased its share of the vote in national elections.

In a separate case, five members of the FPÖ in the southern Austrian town of Knittelfeld were last week ordered to pay fines of between €1,800 and €7,200 (£1,600 and £6,400) for inciting hatred against foreigners.
The fines related to comments made on a Facebook group that included references to immigrants as “filth”, “murderers” and “criminals”.
Liverpool manager Jürgen Klopp admitted his side were not at their best after they scraped into the last 16 of the Champions League despite a 3-1 defeat away to Napoli on the night.

The Reds won the tie 4-2 on aggregate, thanks to their thrilling 4-0 win in the first leg at Anfield last month but they struggled in Italy despite Napoli having Lorenzo Insigne sent off just before half-time.
The home side exerted sustained pressure in the second half, scoring once and hitting the post twice, but they could not find the goal they needed to go through.
"We needed luck for sure," said Klopp.
"The game was not over in the first half.
We needed the second goal and we didn't get it.
We gave them hope, we were not aggressive enough in the challenges and not determined enough to win the ball and to help each other."
However, the German was keen to highlight the positives of progressing to the knock-out stages for only the second time in eight years.
"It is a massive achievement," he added.
"We are through - that is absolutely deserved, I am really happy about it."
There was controversy during the second half as Liverpool thought they should have had a penalty when Napoli's Kalidou Koulibaly appeared to handle the ball in the area.
However, the referee and his assistant on the near side ignored their appeals.
"It was a clear penalty," said Klopp.
"The problem is it was not the referee's decision, it was the linesman's decision.
They didn't see it.
We were lucky in that moment."
Liverpool will discover their last-16 opponents when the draw is made on Monday.
In a thrilling match, Serena Williams has ended Sania Mirza's dream of winning her first WTA title here at the Dubai Championships.
Williams, who is the top seed here and ranked World No.1, survived a tough test from the talented Indian to win 6-2, 7-6(3).
Mirza, who had been suffering from a shoulder injury and only returned to the tour last month, showed no signs of rust as she served and volleyed her way to an early lead in the first set.
However, the experienced American soon found her rhythm and started to dominate the match with her powerful groundstrokes.
Despite this loss, it has been a good week for Mirza, who had already exceeded her own expectations by reaching the semifinals.
This was her best result on the tour since winning the Cincinnati Open in September 2012.
With this victory, Williams continues her good form ahead of the defense of her Australian Open title in January.
Furthermore, the American has now won 14 consecutive matches since losing to Sloane Stephens in the semifinals of the US Open in September.
Williams will now face off against Carla Suárez Navarro in the final.
This will be their second meeting within a week, as the American beat the Spaniard in the final of the Qatar Total Open in Doha last week.
Suárez Navarro, who is the fifth seed here, beat Czech player Lucie Šafářová 6-7(6), 6-3, 6-3 in the other semifinal today.
The former bosses of the failed telecoms firm WorldCom received $54m in payouts despite the company being accused of fraud.
Documents seen by the BBC show that the seven executives received the payments despite knowing the firm was in trouble.
They were aware that WorldCom had used fraudulent accounting to inflate profits.
WorldCom's internal audit committee approved the payments nine days before the company filed for bankruptcy.
At the time of the payout, the committee was headed by WorldCom's then-CEO Bernie Ebbers.
Mr. Ebbers, who has since been convicted of fraud, received $9.5m. It is believed the other six executives received between $4m and $7m each.

They were:
- John Sidgmore, who became WorldCom's CEO after Mr. Ebbers
- Scott Sullivan, who was the chief financial officer
- David Myers, the controller of expense reporting
- Darcy Mott, the general counsel
- Philip Anschutz, the company's largest shareholder at the time
- Michael Capellas, who took over as CEO after Mr. Sidgmore

WorldCom's bankruptcy is considered one of the largest financial scandals in history.
The firm, which was founded in 1983, filed for bankruptcy in 2002 with $107bn in debt.
The case involved a long list of prominent executives and celebrities, including former US President Bill Clinton.
Former New York Attorney General, Eliot Spitzer, described the WorldCom fraud as "the most pervasive and significant fraud in the history of the securities markets".
In 2005, Mr. Ebbers was sentenced to 25 years in prison for his part in the scandal.
He was released in December 2020.
Mr. Sullivan also received a jail sentence for his part in the scandal but was released in March 2019.
The BBC's "World Service News" has announced Russian filmmaker Alexandra Ivanova as the winner of its World News Prize.
The award recognizes the work of journalists who demonstrate courage and integrity in delivering news and information in a bid to promote understanding and awareness in uncertain times.

Ivanova was selected in recognition of her documentary "Putin's Witnesses", a searing investigation into the alleged crimes of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and her efforts to uphold truth in reporting in the face of government pressure.
The jury was particularly impressed with Ivanova's courage in speaking out against the dangers of state-sponsored disinformation.
"We are incredibly proud to announce Alexandra Ivanova as this year's winner of the BBC World News Prize.
Ivanova's winning documentary reveals the immense bravery and skill required to shine a light on the truth in today's Russia," the jury said in a statement.

"In a context of increasing danger for journalists, and attacks on independent media, Ivanova's work is a testament to the enduring power of great reporting, offering audiences a compelling insight into one of the biggest stories of our time."
Ivanova, who is based in Moscow, dedicated the award to all journalists in Russia who continue to work in difficult conditions.
"It's a big honor for me to receive this prize, but I also feel a sense of responsibility," Ivanova said.

"I hope this award will help to shine a light on the courageous work of journalists across Russia, who continue to speak truth to power and fight for transparency and accountability even at great personal risk."
The World News Prize is just one of many initiatives by the BBC to support and promote independent journalism.
The BBC news has learnt that the former prime minister, Sir Tony Blair, will publicly condemn the Conservative government's spending plans when he gives a speech on the economy on Monday.
Blair will criticise the government for cutting public investment in order to maintain a low rate of corporation tax.
He will argue that it is necessary for the government to invest public funds in industry, infrastructure and technology.
Blair will say that the government's current course ends in "irreversible decline" and that the country needs "proper investment in public services and a properly funded NHS".
He will argue that this requires "both a long-term vision and a coherent plan to pay for it".
Blair will say that "without both, the British economy will go into irreversible decline".
The prime minister, Boris Johnson, has said that Blair's remarks are "absolutely crass".
Johnson has claimed that his government is "absolutely getting it right" with its current policy of cutting public spending in order to lower taxes.
The chancellor, Rishi Sunac, will set out the government's tax and spending plans in the autumn statement on Wednesday.
The iconic music show Top of the Pops is to leave BBC One after 45 years.
The programme, which has been a staple of the BBC's programming since 1977, will move to BBC Two as part of the corporation's efforts to "refresh" its offering.
Top of the Pops will continue to air on the BBC Red Button and iPlayer, with the final episode on BBC One scheduled for August.
The BBC has said it wants to create "a strong music offering on BBC Two", with other programmes such as Later... with Jools Holland and Live from the BBC moving to the channel.

A BBC spokesperson said: "Top of the Pops is coming off BBC One, but it isn't going away - audiences will be able to enjoy the programme on BBC Two, Red Button, and iPlayer, as well as continuing to enjoy the best of the action on BBC Sounds.
"We are committed to providing the best music programming on the BBC and refreshing our output to ensure we continue to serve all our audiences."
Arsène Wenger has ruled out the possibility of Arsenal signing another goalkeeper before the transfer window closes on Tuesday.

The Gunners have been linked with a move for Leicester's England international keeper Danny Ward, after it emerged that backup keeper Aaron Ramsdale may not be fit enough to face Manchester United on Friday night in their first Premier League game of the season.
But Wenger, whose side beat Bayern Munich 2-1 in the final friendly of their pre-season tour of America, said he was happy with the goalkeepers he had.

"We have £2m goalkeeper who we bought last year and who has been out for six months because of two operations, we have an experienced goalkeeper in Alex Runarsson and we have Matt Macey, who is back after a loan," he said.
"So that's not a position where I expect something to happen.
We are not close to doing something there.

"

Wenger also said he was unconvinced that the club needed to sign a new defender, despite the departure of William Saliba to Marseille on loan ahead of next month's transfer deadline.
The Frenchman said the club had been keen to keep the 19-year-old, who joined Arsenal from Saint-Etienne for £27m last year, but that the player wanted to play regular first-team football.
"He is a player who needs to play," said Wenger.
"He agreed to come here because he wanted to play, we agreed to buy him because we hoped he can play.
He has decided to go on loan and we lose a player but we have to respect that."
The search for the next big thing in British literature has begun with the launch of a new award for unpublished authors.

Lit Idol, which describes itself as "Britain's search for new literary talent", is accepting submissions of novels, short story collections and works of non-fiction from anyone over the age of 16 who has not previously had a book published.
The submissions will be winnowed down by a panel of publishers, agents and authors, led by Lit Idol founder and literary agent Julia Kingsford, with the final round judged by a panel of readers.
The winner will receive a consultation with Kingsford and £5,000.
Kingsford said: "I'm really excited to be launching Lit Idol, which is a unique competition in the UK.
"It's a chance for unpublished writers to get valuable feedback on their work and to really get their names out there."
An increase in construction activity is boosting demand for materials and jobs in India.
The country hopes that this trend can help lift the economy, which has been hit by the coronavirus pandemic.
The government has set a goal of constructing 20 million affordable homes in the next decade.
It has also been pushing for the use of local materials and technologies to make housing more affordable.
There has been a significant increase in the production of materials such as steel, cement and bricks.
Companies are also reporting an increase in demand for their products from both the residential and commercial sectors.
This is welcome news for a country that has been struggling with high unemployment rates and economic growth.
Experts hope that the construction boom will continue and help India's economy recover.
Dr. Liam Fox, the former Defense Secretary, has faced widespread criticism for his comment on the COVID-19 pandemic, claiming it was “one big distraction” away from Brexit.
Speaking to the BBC’s Andrew Marr on Sunday, Mr. Fox argued that the pandemic was “an opportunity” for the government to show how efficiently it could organize the country.

“It would have been better if we had been able to use this as an opportunity to show how a government can organize its resources in order to protect people’s lives and livelihoods at the same time,” he said.

“But we haven’t, and therefore, it has become an argument about whether or not we should have been prioritizing the opening up of the economy in order to save lives, or whether in fact, we should have been prioritizing saving lives and letting the economy go to hell.”
Former Labour Prime Minister Gordon Brown has since labeled these comments as “crass” and “insulting”, arguing that the remarks were made to divert attention away from Brexit.
“This is a government that is in utter disarray,” Mr. Brown said.
“The prime minister refuses to listen to warnings, refuses to take decisions, refuses to take advice.”
Mr. Brown stated that the government was “making up the policy as it goes along” with the pandemic, and that there was no clear plan or strategy.
He called for the government to take immediate action to address the issue, stating that the country cannot afford to wait until a new government is formed.
The UK has experienced over 5 million cases and over 130,000 deaths due to COVID-19, with daily infections reaching as high as 200,000 during the winter of 2022.

The body of a BBC news article titled "Paraguay novel wins US book prize" could begin with:

Charles Charvis is set to lose his fitness bid according to multiple sources.
The 37 year old athlete has been a prominent face in the fitness community for over a decade, with 7 personal training certifications and a social media following of over 500 thousand.
In recent years, Charvis has been open about his struggle with depression and the mental health benefits of exercise.
His attempt to regain fitness is being covered extensively by the media in light of his mental health advocacy.
However, multiple inside sources have confirmed that he is likely to fail his bid in the coming weeks.
The Swiss cement firm Holcim has announced that it is in talks to buy Lafarge, the French cement company.
Holcim has offered to buy Lafarge for CHF62.00 ($67.18) per share, valuing Lafarge at CHF32.0bn ($35.1bn).
The offer represents a premium of 14.2% to Lafarge's closing price of CHF54.70 ($60.20) per share on Friday.
The deal is expected to be completed in the first half of next year, and is subject to regulatory approval.
Holcim has also announced that it is in talks to buy the Italian cement company Italcementi.
If completed, the two acquisitions would help Holcim become the largest cement company in the world measured by revenue.
Lafarge's revenue was CHF27.6bn ($31.1bn) in the year to 31 December 2013, with EBITDA of CHF3.1bn ($3.4bn).
Italcementi's revenue was EUR2.4bn ($2.7bn) in the year to 31 March 2014, with EBITDA of EUR515m ($654m).

Holcim has been expanding its operations in recent years, with the acquisition of the Brazilian firm Lafarge Brasil in January 2015, and the acquisition of a controlling stake in the Philippines firm Holcim Philippines in August 2014.
The firm has stated that it expects the deals to create value for its shareholders, and help it to better serve its customers and stakeholders.
The US firm Go Global Retail is reportedly bidding for the Lacroix label.
The firm has experience in the luxury market, having previously purchased the licenses for Juicy Couture and Lucky Brand.
Go Global has been working to expand its portfolio of luxury brands, and believes that the Lacroix label would be a valuable addition.
The firm has been in talks with the Lacroix management team for several months and is now preparing a formal offer.
If the deal goes through, it would be a major change in the luxury market.
The acquisition would mean that Go Global would gain control of the Lacroix brand, including its fashion division and license for fragrances.
The firm would also take over the label's production and distribution facilities.
It is not clear how much Go Global is bidding for the label.
The firm has not commented on the reports, and Lacroix has not publicly disclosed any information about the potential sale.
The most popular funeral song in Britain has been revealed in a study – and it might not be what you expect.
Classic pop ballad Angels by the Australian duo, The xx, has been named as the top choice for loved ones leaving a funeral, with one in six people (16%) selecting it as their favourite.

The song, a staple of many a funeral playlist, saw support from people across all age groups with those aged between 18 and 24 most likely to pick it as their top choice (24% of people in this age group).
Beyond the classic hits, Queen's We Will Rock You and Freddie Mercury's Bohemian Rhapsody were also among the favourites.

The study, commissioned by funeral plan provider Perfect Choice, was prompted by the firm's analysis of more than 6,000 of its customers' funeral plans, which revealed Angels was the most popular song among those who had chosen a song for their funeral.
Perfect Choice then polled 2,000 people to explore further and found one in six (16%) selected Angels as their favourite funeral song – the highest of any song.
The study also found that one in four (24%) of people would choose a classical song for their funeral, with Verdi's La donna è mobile from Rigoletto the most popular (11% of people).
When it comes to the memories that people most want to leave loved ones with, the study found that 52% of people most want to be remembered for their sense of humour.
Nearly half (49%) said they want to be remembered for their kindness, while a third (32%) hope to be remembered for their achievements.
Just under a quarter (24%) of people said they would like to be remembered for their cooking skills.

Mark Hall, of Perfect Choice, said: "Music is a key part of our lives and can be a great comfort when we lose loved ones, which is why it's important to consider our funeral plans and what we want for our service.
"It's interesting to see that classical music is still a popular choice among those planning their funeral, but songs like Angels show how tastes are changing.

"Our advice to those planning their funeral is to consider what music means the most to you and choose a song that will be a fitting tribute and which will leave your family and friends with a lasting memory of you."
A new device, which attaches to a golf club, can help improve your swing by providing real-time feedback on speed, tempo, and angle of the club.
The mobile phone-sized tool, called the "Swing Catalyst," could help golfers fix their swing and lower their score on the green.
The catalyst is a device that attaches to the end of a golf club, where the clubhead and shaft meet.
After a swing, the golfer can view the results on their smartphone or tablet.
The device sells for about $399 and is available for preorder.
The Swing Catalyst works using a combination of sensors.
First, a 3D sensor that measures clubhead speed as well as face angle and path.
Second, an HD video system allows golfers to see their swing in action.
Third and optionally, a pressure mat which captures the golfer's weight shift, centered on the ball, throughout the swing.
Together, the club attachment, video, and pressure mat provide golfers with information to help them improve their swing.
For example, the device might tell a golfer that their club is slowing down as it makes contact with the ball or that their swing is off-center.
Video footage of the swing combines with the sensor data to show what the golfer is doing wrong and offers tips on how to fix it.
The Swing Catalyst is not the only device available to help golfers fix their swings.
Other devices include the GolfSense and the Zepp Golf, which both attach to a golfer's glove.

These devices cost considerably less than the Swing Catalyst, but according to Golf.com, the Catalyst "appears to be the first device to combine such a high-speed camera with the other metrics."

"

Best director honours went to Sam Mendes for his World War I epic Saving Private Ryan.

Ultra fast wifi has been a tantalizing prospect for years now, with numerous experiments and trials underway – and it seems London could be next in line to get a signal that is "up to 100 times faster" than existing connections.
The UK capital is set to join the trial of a new multi-billion pound project dubbed "Airways".
It is reportedly set to provide lightning-fast download speeds of up to 1 gigabit per second, and upload speeds of up to 150 megabits per second.
This would represent a significant upgrade on current top speeds in the UK of up to 1,300 megabits per second for downloads, and up to 50 for uploads.

It is understood that the system will be based on a mesh of small satellites orbiting the Earth at a height of 20,000 miles – an approach that could help millions of people who live in rural or remote areas, as well as those in densely populated cities, to get faster internet speeds.
The system would work by receiving signals from 5G phones and other wireless devices, then redirecting them to the satellite, which would then connect them to the internet.
It is claimed the system will be able to provide coverage in places that current satellite-based systems do not reach, as it will not be restricted by the signal strength of the device.

While the project is still in its early stages, and the speeds promised are only a fraction of those touted by other ultra fast wifi projects, it is a further sign that the era of ultra fast, satellite-enabled internet may be closer than many realise.

However, sales were down 0.5% compared to December 2021, the first year-on-year decline since November 2020.

Sales at food services and drinking places rose 1.3% for the month and were up 40.5% from December 2021.

Sir Alex Ferguson was speaking as a documentary, "Fergie: Never Give In", was aired on BBC Two on Monday evening.

The film charts the career of the legendary ex-United boss - who won 38 major trophies during his spell in charge at Old Trafford - and includes interviews with figures such as Pep Guardiola, Sir Geoff Hurst and Gordon Strachan.

In an excerpt from the documentary seen by the BBC, Sir Alex Ferguson says he has been surprised by the club's lack of spending in the transfer market since the American Glazer family bought United in 2005.
"The thing that surprised me is that when the Glazers bought Manchester United, they said they wanted to make money," he says.
"That's legitimate.
But they forgot to say that they'd do it by being successful on the pitch.
"They are known for being business people first and then football is a secondary consideration.
That's the only thing that's surprised me.
"I thought when the new people came in, they would realise that they had to change their attitude and that football was important.
But they haven't.
"They've continued down the line of being more concerned about finances and not the team.

"

In another extract from the film, Sir Alex Ferguson also reveals he tried to sign Pep Guardiola - who was managing Barcelona at the time - to become his assistant manager at Old Trafford.
"I made a mistake by not taking Guardiola as my assistant," he says.
"I offered him a contract, he was keen to come but the board didn't want to take any chances.

Andy Murray's hopes of a fairytale finish at SW19 came to an end as he was knocked out of Wimbledon in the third round by big-serving American John Isner.

The small island of St. Kilda, located about 40 miles off the coast of Scotland, is host to a surprising new development—one that has stunned local residents and attracted journalists and onlookers from around the world.

"

"

Sales of portable media devices have plummeted in recent years as consumers increasingly opt for smartphones that can do it all.
According to data from the market research firm NPD Group, portable video player sales fell by 66% between 2012 and 2013.
"Smartphones are cannibalizing the market for dedicated media players," said Eddie Hold, a senior analyst for NPD.
The decline in sales has been swift.
In 2010, about half of all consumers surveyed by the firm said they planned to buy a portable video player.
By 2013, that number had fallen to 15%.
Consumers are instead using smartphones to watch video on the go.
About 55% of Americans now own a smartphone, and among those 18-24, the number is a whopping 83%.
"Smartphones are incredibly functional and versatile," said Mr. Hold.
"It's largely just an issue of convenience."
Dedicated media devices aren't going away entirely, however.
Many manufacturers are responding to the shift by scaling back their product lines to focus on higher-end devices that offer superior audio and video quality.
Apple, which once dominated the market for portable media players with its iPod devices, has all but abandoned the market.
It now offers just two models, both of which are several years old.
In contrast, Sony has doubled down on its high-end Walkman devices, offering a range of models that start at $60 and top out at $1,100.
The firm says it has sold about 1.5 million Walkmans in the past year, and that sales are up 30% from the previous year.
"We're definitely seeing an increase in demand for high-quality portable audio devices," said Nick Majernik, a product marketing manager for Sony.
A blind student from Bristol, UK, says he "hears in colour" after receiving a bionic eye.
Tom Williams, 25, has only ever seen shadows and shapes – but now, after receiving the implant, he can identify colours in food and on clothes.
Williams lost his sight gradually as a result of a genetic condition and had the implant 18 months ago.
"I knew colours existed, but until you experience it for yourself, you don't believe it," he said.
"When I saw red for the first time it was amazing – it was like I'd seen it before, but I hadn't, not in that way.
It's a truly wonderful experience.

"

The bionic eye works by stimulating Williams' retina with pulses of electricity.
It bypasses the part of the eye that doesn't work and sends signals to the brain.
The colours appear in the mind's eye as waves of noise, which he can then interpret.
Williams, who studies psychology at the University of Bristol, hopes to become a mental health nurse after graduation.
"I want to use my experience to help others and show that even if you have a disability, there are often ways around it," he said.
The bionic eye, called the Orion, was developed by the US-based company Second Sight.
It was approved for use in the UK last year and costs £140,000.
Several charities, including Blind Veterans UK and SeeAbility, have helped fund the device.
Williams is one of three people in the UK who have had the bionic eye fitted.
They can identify colours, detect motion and spot the difference between light and dark.
Williams hopes to one day see shapes and, eventually, faces.

Microsoft has moved to intensify its anti-piracy efforts by introducing a new tool that prevents the unauthorised pre-installation of Windows 11 on computers.
The company emphasised that it is prioritizing security and customer experience rather than device performance in this change.
The new tool, known as the Hardware Compatibility List (HCL), serves as a database that lists all the authorized PCs capable of running Windows 11.
The database includes information such as the manufacturer, model name, and serial number of the devices.

According to Microsoft, the HCL aims to ensure that Windows 11 is only installed on compatible devices, reducing the risk of hardware malfunctions and security issues that can arise from unauthorized modifications.
It believes that this measure is necessary to provide customers with a smooth and secure experience.
The HCL is a follow-up to Microsoft's Windows Genuine Validation (WGV) tool, which was launched in 2019.
The WGV tool was designed to detect fraudulent or unauthorized Windows licenses and prevent them from being used.
The HCL builds on this initiative by ensuring that only genuine devices can run Windows 11.
Microsoft has emphasized that the HCL is just one aspect of its broader anti-piracy strategy, which includes a range of measures such as Windows Update, Windows Defender, and the Microsoft Store.
The company is committed to continuously improving its security measures and providing customers with the best possible experience.
While some users may view the HCL as a hindrance, Microsoft believes that it is a necessary step to ensure the safety and integrity of the Windows operating system.
The company is encouraging users to purchase genuine Windows licenses and install the operating system on authorized devices to ensure they have a secure and smooth experience.
This change reflects Microsoft's ongoing efforts to combat software piracy and provide customers with the best possible experience.
The company will continue to prioritize security and customer experience in its future product offerings.

Britain's political parties have been revealed for the first time today, with UKIP spending more on its campaign than Labour did, according to official figures.

The Conservative Party, by contrast, spent £1,965,598 on its successful campaign for Britain to leave the European Union.

It is the first time since the vote that the official figures have been released.
The Brexit campaign as a whole spent £5,709,501 on the poll, compared with £9,501,073 spent by the Remain side.
The US manufacturing sector expanded in September, according to a survey by the Institute for Supply Management (ISM).
The ISM's purchasing managers' index (PMI) rose to 59.0 in September, up from 55.4 in August.
This was the highest level since March 2019 and marked the eighteenth consecutive month of growth for the US manufacturing sector.
The increase was driven by a rise in new orders, which reached their highest level since December 2019.
In addition, employment in the sector grew for the seventh consecutive month.
"The US manufacturing sector continues to expand as 2021 comes to an end," said Timothy Fiore, chair of the ISM's manufacturing business survey committee.
"Meeting demand, especially as companies work to restock inventory and manage supply chain challenges, remains a focus for respondents.

"

However, the survey also showed that prices for raw materials and other inputs continued to rise, with the index for prices paid by manufacturers reaching its highest level since July 2008.
This has resulted in companies increasing the prices of their goods, with the index for prices received by manufacturers reaching its highest level since April 2011.
Despite this, manufacturers remained optimistic about the future, with the six-month outlook index reaching its highest level since February 2021.
The BBC has denied reports that it is planning to bring back the popular comedy show Blackadder.
A spokesperson for the broadcaster said that while there had been discussions about a revival of the show, there were no plans to do so at the moment.

The BBC has learned that some of the world's leading financial institutions have been hit by a major security breach.
Sources have told the BBC that the US bank, JPMorgan, and the Bank of New York Mellon were both affected by the breach, which was identified in August.
It is believed the hackers were able to install malicious software on the banks' computers, allowing them to spy on the institutions.
The attackers are thought to have been based in Russia, although this has not been confirmed.
The breach is believed to have been discovered when the banks noticed that some of their computers had started to communicate with IP addresses in Russia.
When they investigated, they found that the malicious software had been installed on their computers, and they were able to remove it.

The banks have not commented on the breach, but a spokesperson for JPMorgan said: "We have multiple layers of protection and we are confident in the integrity of our controls."

The Bank of New York Mellon said: "We maintain a robust, multi-layered security protocol and routinely monitor our systems for signs of trouble."
"When issues are identified, we take appropriate actions to address them and mitigate risk.

"

It is not clear how many computers were affected, but sources have told the BBC that the number was significant.
This is not the first time that banks have been targeted by hackers.
In 2014, a number of high-profile institutions were hit by a breach known as Carbanak.
That attack, which was believed to have been carried out by a group of Russian hackers, resulted in the theft of hundreds of millions of dollars.
The breach of the Bank of New York Mellon and JPMorgan is significant because of the size of the two institutions and the potential for large-scale theft.
It is not clear if any money was stolen in this breach, but sources have told the BBC that the attackers were interested in spying on the banks, rather than stealing money.
The sources said that the malicious software was designed to allow the hackers to see what was happening on the banks' computers, rather than to allow them to steal money.
However, the breach has raised concerns about the security of computers in banks, and it is likely that the attackers will try to target other institutions.
South African car demand surges in 2022, buoyed by strong consumer demand and increased investments in the automotive industry.
Sales of new vehicles in South Africa surged 43% year on year to 558,955 units in 2022, according to data from the National Association of Automotive Manufacturers of South Africa.

However, the industry still faces challenges, including the ongoing semiconductor chip shortage, which has limited the production of some models.
In addition, the recent rise in interest rates in South Africa has also increased the cost of financing, which could impact demand in the coming months.

Daniel Pountney has been banned from the game for 18 months and fined £2,500 for breaching the Football Association's betting rules.
The former Norwich, West Ham and Portsmouth defender, who retired in 2019, admitted to placing 183 bets on football during a 14-month period whilst registered as a player.

The Bank of England is widely expected to keep interest rates on hold as it weighs up the effects of the new Omicron variant of Covid-19.
The Bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is thought to be divided on whether to raise rates from their historic low of 0.1%.

A wine-themed comedy show has won a top critics' award.
The Grape Nuts show, staged at London's National Theatre, was named best online event at the annual Chortle Awards.
Co-created by actress Sally Phillips and comedian Dan Clarkson, it saw them and a group of actors including Mark Heap and Doon Mackichan perform vignettes about drink and the rituals surrounding it.

**Brando 'rejected Godfather role'** – Albert Finney, who has died at the age of 82, was one of a handful of great actors who withstood the lure of Hollywood to remain faithful to theatre and appeared on the stage in Britain and the US.
He was also one of a handful who straddled respectability and box-office allure.
His career had many peaks, and it weathered the occasional valley.
In the early 1960s, he was offered the role of Michael Corleone in Francis Ford Coppola's classic movie, The Godfather.
The story goes that he turned it down, thinking the script was poorly written.
It won't be the last time a great actor passed on a part that would become iconic.
But Finney was hardly a fool.
He was well aware of the film's quality, having been impressed by a early draft of the script.

According to his biographer, David Thompson, Finney believed that "the mob was so attractive as the villains that you would be doing a sort of James Bond thing, and he wasn't interested in doing that."
It seems unlikely that he would have turned down the chance to play the lead in The Godfather if it had been offered to him.
According to Thompson, Finney "would ring people up and say 'Have you read this script?
It's the worst bunch of crap I've ever read.'"
He later admitted that he had been wrong to turn it down.
"It became this fantastic successful film," he said, "but at the time it was somewhat embryonic in its development."
Education expert Sir Alasdair Maclay has been commissioned by Labour to investigate absenteeism in schools.
His report defines truancy as "any unexplained absence from school" and says absenteeism is linked to poverty, low aspirations and poor behaviour.
He said the "hardcore truants" who accounted for a lot of absenteeism were often excluded from school and were damaging their own life chances.
The party has used the report to attack the government for cuts to school budgets.
The Conservatives have accused Labour of "trying to reopen a debate" on the issue, while the Liberal Democrats have called on all parties to focus on cutting absenteeism.

The BBC's deputy political editor, John Pienaar, says this is the first time Labour has tried to address the issue of absenteeism since it introduced a tightening of rules in the late 1980s, when the then Education Secretary, Kenneth Baker, sent postcards to the parents of every child who missed a single day.
Labour is also expected to announce a review of student behaviour led by the former head teacher of St Paul's School, London, Sir Michael Wilshaw.
Sir Michael will be asked to consider the impact of behaviour on attainment, including analysis of exclusions, and the role of parenting and poverty.

Former Russian parliamentarian Gennady Gudkov, who is being held in custody in Moscow on charges of plotting to murder two security officers, has accused the Russian authorities of trying to silence him.
Gudkov, who is a prominent critic of the Kremlin, was arrested on Friday along with his brother, former police officer Alexander Gudkov.
Both are being held in custody for two months while the investigation continues.

"The criminal case against me is a disguise, behind which there are other interests and motives," he said in a statement released by his party, the Republican Party of Russia-People's Freedom Party (RPR-PARNAS).
"The authorities need to keep silent all who know too much about the criminal activities of top officials and their sponsors," he added.
Gudkov lost his seat in the Duma in Russia's recent parliamentary elections.
Before he stood down from politics, he was one of the best-known critics of the Kremlin in the parliament, and had been particularly vocal in his denunciation of the war in Ukraine.
His brother, Alexander, had been under investigation for alleged fraud and had gone into hiding.
He was arrested in a Moscow suburb on Friday.

The brothers' detention followed a TV broadcast on Thursday in which anchorman Sergei Dorenko said that the security services had seized a stockpile of weapons destined for the Ukrainian military and detained two people who were trying to smuggle them in.
He said that the two people had been plotting to murder two officers of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) sent to infiltrate the group.
Tennis: Britain's Tim Henman has withdrawn from next month's Australian Open because of injury, allowing Romanian Andrei Pavel to take his place in the main draw.

The trial of the three defendants in the Balco case has been delayed until March 2004.
The trial, which was originally scheduled to begin on January 12, 2004, will now commence nearly three months later, on March 15, 2004.
