Browsing the collections of national museums from the comfort of your own home is set to get a whole lot easier.

The BBC is reporting that its research and development unit, in partnership with the National Museum of Scotland, has developed an AI-powered tool that allows users to search for specific objects in museum collections using everyday language.
The tool, called Smartify, is designed to make museum collections more accessible to the public.
Users can search for an object by describing it in natural language, such as "vase with flowers", rather than using technical or formal language typically found in museum catalogues.
Smartify uses machine learning to interpret the user's description and retrieve the most relevant results from the museum's collection.
The tool is trained on a large amount of text and image data, including the museum's catalogue and other sources such as Wikipedia.
It is able to understand the relationship between words and images, allowing it to identify objects that are similar in appearance or meaning.
Smartify has been trained on multiple languages, including English, Scottish Gaelic, and Scots.
This will enable the tool to be used by people who speak different languages and have different cultural backgrounds.
The tool is currently in the testing phase and is being used by a small group of users.
It is expected to be made available to the public in the near future.
A smoking ban being planned by the Scottish government for next year will be widened to include hospitals, care homes, and school grounds, ministers have said.
The original plan was to ban smoking in playgrounds and outdoor areas of cafes, pubs and restaurants.
Health Secretary Humza Yousaf said the phased ban would not come into force until next spring at the earliest.
The Scottish government aims to bring "smoking-free" standards to hospitals, care homes and schools by April 2024.
This will require NHS boards to create smoke-free policies, and care homes and schools will need to have smoke-free policies in place by April 2022.
Ministers expect most hospitals to prevent smoking on their grounds, with exceptions in specialised circumstances, by April 2023.
The number of jobs added to the US economy rose above expectations in the first week of 2023, according to new data.
The labor market showed promise as the week closed on February 19, with the addition of 479,000 jobs, compared to the 350,000 estimates.
The figures suggest that the US economy is on a steady path to recovery from its shortest recession on record, caused by the pandemic and subsequent lockdowns.
The hospitality industry saw a particular boost, reflecting the renewed consumer demand following the lifting of restrictions.
Hotels and restaurants added 146,000 jobs, bringing the total to pre-pandemic levels.
Meanwhile, professional and business services contributed to a gain of 100,000, with employment in the sector now surpassing its February 2020 level.
The labor market participation rate remained unchanged at 62.4 percent, with the unemployment rate holding steady at 3.8 percent.
These figures indicate a tight labor market, marked by a shortage of available workers despite the robust job growth.
The data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed a steady trend of job growth over the past year.
In the past three months, the US has added an average of 550,000 jobs per month.
That said, there are still about 5 million fewer jobs than before the pandemic.
The data showed a slight increase in the average hourly earnings from the previous month, up to $32.10, indicating a potential rise in wages due to the increasing demand for labor.
The job numbers come as the Federal Reserve continues to raise interest rates to combat inflation, with the latest increase of 0.25 percent taking the rate to 4.5 percent.
These moves are intended to slow down the economy and reduce the demand for goods and services, which could potentially lead to job losses.
However, the data suggests that the labor market remains robust despite the rate hikes.
As the job market continues to evolve, the focus shifts to the upcoming wage growth data and the consumer price index, which will provide further insight into the state of the economy.
The report is a positive start to the year, showing a much better-than-expected job market performance and indicating a resilient US economy.

England's ill-disciplined World Cup campaign ended with a whimper as they were out-played and out-muscled by a young, vibrant and skilful Australia side, who booked a semi-final meeting with Trans-Tasman rivals New Zealand.

A ninth defeat in a row - the team's worst run for 34 years - was assured before halftime as a 13-6 scoreline reflected the dominance of the Southern Hemisphere side, who scored four tries to England's two.
But it was the manner in which England surrendered meekly that will cause most concern for director of rugby Clive Woodward, whose side were out-thought and out-fought in every department.
For much of the first half, England were buoyed by a partisan crowd who cheered their every move but, once again, they were unable to deliver on the promise of their early play.
A well-taken try from Jason Robinson and a penalty from Jonny Wilkinson after just eight minutes gave England an early lead but that was as good as it got for the home side.
The introduction of Elton Flatley at fly-half for the Australians proved an inspired move as his precise kicking and calm authority helped turn the tide.
A well-taken try from centre Matt Giteau, who exploited acres of space in the English defence, and a Flatley penalty put the Wallabies ahead after 21 minutes.
Winger Chris Latham then scored Australia's second try in the corner, Flatley missed the conversion but added a penalty goal minutes later to give his side a 13-6 half-time lead.
England's lack of discipline was once again their downfall as Wilkinson, Robinson and captain Martin Johnson were all sin-binned as the pressure finally told.
The crowd's fervour was dampened by the sight of England's star centre Mike Tindall being helped from the field after injuring his shoulder in a tackle early in the second half.
It was Australia who extended their lead when left-wing Latham scored his second try, again in the corner, Flatley missing the conversion.
England's cause was not helped by the loss of Wilkinson with a hamstring injury, the young Wilkinson replacing his father, who had an indifferent game.

But replacement Charlie Hodgson, who has had an excellent season with Newcastle and was among the few English players to enhance his reputation, scored a try which he converted himself to give England a glimmer of hope with 10 minutes remaining.

"
Tuilagi has scored 20 tries in his 57 England tests and was among the 46 players trained by the RFU ahead of the Six Nations.

England's manager Roy Hodgson said he took "full responsibility" for his side's early exit from Euro 2016 after their loss to Iceland.
The 61-year-old admitted he was "extremely sorry for the fans" after the 2-1 defeat in Nice.
England's performance was one of the most disappointing in their history, says BBC sports editor Dan Roan.

The Euro 2016 surprise package led through Ragnar Sigurdsson's header before Kolbeinn Sigthorsson's clinical finish extended their lead.

We all wanted to do better than we did.
I'm extremely sorry for the fans.

"

England suffered their earliest exit from a major tournament since the 1958 World Cup - when they were beaten by the Soviet Union in the quarter-finals.
Their only previous tournament meeting with Iceland had been a 2-1 victory for England in the last 16 of Euro 2004, but this time it was Iceland who progressed.

Henman, who has never gone beyond the round-robin stage, faces a repeat clash with Carlos Moya in his second match tomorrow.
The Spanish world number nine beat Dutchman Sjeng Schalken 6-4 7-5 in the first match of the evening session.

The US has announced that it will allow foreign firms in Russia and Belarus to continue to operate for an additional six months, until May 31, 2024.

China has blocked the Google news site, according to a report in The New York Times.
The move comes as Beijing continues to tighten controls over information and the internet, including recent regulations that have slowed down internet traffic in the country.

The Nintendo 3DS will launch in Europe on March 25, priced at £229.99.
In Europe, Nintendo is calling the device a "platform", reflecting its two screens and 360-degree viewing angle.

The row comes after the National Lottery announced a partnership with the Saudi government-owned Saudi Sports Company to promote sporting events in the kingdom.
The partnership has been criticized by human rights activists and opposition politicians for being inappropriate given the Saudi government's poor human rights record.
When asked for comment, a National Lottery spokesperson said that the partnership had been "conducted in line with the UK government's guidance on trade with Saudi Arabia."
They added that "all parties are bound by a non-disclosure agreement, so we are unable to comment further."

Chelsea have announced the signing of Sweden defender Magdalena Johansson from Kopparbergs/Goteborg on a deal until 2025.
The 21-year-old has joined the Women's Super League club after leaving Swedish side Kopparbergs/Goteborg, where she came through the academy and went on to make more than 70 appearances.
Johansson made her Sweden debut in November 2020 and has gone on to earn 17 caps for her country.
"It's a great feeling to sign for Chelsea," Johansson said.
"It's a fantastic club with a great history and amazing fans.
I'm excited to get started and hopefully I'll be able to win silverware with the club."
The claim made by Aaliyah's estate that the singer's music was used without permission in the soundtrack of the new Marvel series "Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur" has been dismissed by a court.
The estate of the late R&B star, who died in a plane crash in 2001, claimed that elements of her music were used in the series without the estate's permission.
The estate said that it owned half of the copyright to the songs, including the song "Are You That Somebody," because Aaliyah helped write and produce them.
The judge ruled that the estate failed to provide sufficient evidence that Aaliyah was involved in the creation of the songs and therefore did not have a legal stake in them.
The estate has said it will appeal the decision.
This decision is a major setback for the estate, which has been seeking to increase its control over Aaliyah's music and brand.
The judge's ruling states that the estate's claim for copyright infringement was based on "speculation and conjecture."
It is unclear if the estate will continue to pursue legal action against Marvel and other involved parties.
This development comes as a surprise to many, as Aaliyah's music has been widely used in popular culture for decades, including in films and television shows.
The estate has reportedly earned millions of dollars in royalties from Aaliyah's music, and it appears that this decision may significantly impact those earnings.
Ireland welcome England to the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Sunday with both sides in search of a win to round out the year.
The hosts currently top the Six Nations table on try difference after their 25-24 victory over Wales in Cardiff last weekend.
England were on the wrong end of a thrilling encounter with France, going down 22-16 despite scoring the first 17 points of the match.
Ireland have selected their team with no changes from the win in Cardiff, with captain Johnny Sexton and his half-back partner Conor Murray both included despite concerns over their fitness.
England head coach Eddie Jones has made two changes to his side with captain Owen Farrell and centre Jonathan Joseph returning to the starting line-up.
Farrell will resume his partnership with George Ford at half-back after the pair combined well in attack for Leicester in their victory over Saracens on Saturday.
Joseph's return means Ben Te'o is dropped to the bench, with Farrell shifting to inside centre.
Ireland head coach Joe Schmidt said he was excited by the prospect of facing England's attacking threats.
"They have got the ability to threat everywhere on the park.
They have got threats through their set-piece, through their attacking prowess, and they will challenge our defensive system," he said.

"That is something we have been working on this week, but we have also been working on our attacking game to make sure we can get the upper hand on what is going to be a very physical and athletic English side."
Multi-award-winning Northern Irish band Snow Patrol have announced that their bassist, Paul Wilson, is to leave the group after almost 30 years.
The departure comes after the release of the band's ninth studio album, 'Transitions'.
It is not known why Wilson is leaving, or if he will pursue a solo career.
Snow Patrol's remaining members, Johnny Mcdaid, Tom Simpson, Josh Macdonald, and Johnny Quinn, have not yet commented on Wilson's departure.
Shares in the US pharmaceutical company Biogen fell in aftermarket trading after it suspended sales of its newly approved Alzheimer's drug.
The company said it would temporarily stop marketing the drug, Aduhelm, after a slow start to prescriptions prompted an analysis of the drug's use.
The move comes as a surprise just a few months after the drug was approved by the FDA in June.
US officials had very recently begun outreach efforts to increase adoption of the drug.
In a statement, the company said it would "continue to listen to the evolving needs of the Alzheimer's disease community" and "follow the science" of the drug.
The company added that it was committed to "the patients currently being treated with Aduhelm".
Biogen had predicted that the drug would generate $7bn in annual sales by 2026, but so far only around 300 patients have received it, according to reports.
The company's stock fell by around 22% after the announcement.
Rory McIlroy won the indoor 800m title for St Patrick's Academy in Armagh on Wednesday.

The BBC Sport NI reporter Ryan Sidley tweeted a video of the event, with the caption "Rory McIlroy wins indoor 800m title for St Pat's Armagh!!"

McIlroy, who is from Holywood in County Down, is better known for his prowess in golf.
The 29-year-old is a four-time major winner, most recently securing the Wells Fargo Championship in May 2021.
He has 19 PGA Tour titles to his name and has won three European Tour titles, too.
On Tuesday, McIlroy pulled out of the Abu Dhabi HSBC Championship as he recovers from a hairline fracture to his rib.
Manchester City manager Joe Royle hopes the arrival of Andy Smith will help improve the team's poor away form.
The 28-year-old striker joins from Queens Park Rangers for £800,000 and City hope he will benefit from the freedom offered by his three-year contract.
"Away from home we haven't been good enough," said Royle.
"Hopefully Andy can help turn that around.
"He's got all the attributes of a good centre forward.
He's strong and brave and works hard.
"He's got a good touch and hopefully he'll bring a bit of respect back to the club."
Smith said a telephone call from Royle convinced him his future lay at Maine Road.
"Joe rang me on Thursday night and that swayed it for me," said Smith.
"He told me where he wanted me to play and what he wanted me to do.
"He said he saw me as a centre forward and not a striker playing off a big centre forward.
"He told me I'd be the main man and that he wanted me to get 20-25 goals a season.
"That's what I'm aiming for.
I'm confident I can do it."
BBC Sport - Andy Murray's hopes of a deep run at the Australian Open received a boost with the announcement that Dan Evans and Kyle Edmund have received wild cards for the Grand Slam.
British number one Evans and world number 50
Edmund join Murray and Cameron Norrie in a strong contingent from these shores in Melbourne.
Evans' ranking of 33 is higher than his career-high of 39, while Edmund has climbed from 68th to 50th in the world since September.
The wild cards for Evans and Edmund were announced at lunchtime on Sunday UK time ahead of the 2 February start of the 2022 tournament.
Australian Open tournament director Craig Tiley said the British pair were given the wild cards because "they help elevate the tournament".
"We get to see some amazing matches and with the way they can play, we feel they can go deep into the second week.

"

Evans, who has earned £1.8m this year, reached the third round of the Australian Open in 2017 and won the ATP title in Melbourne in 2017.
He said: "I am really excited to be playing in Melbourne again.
I have great memories from winning here in 2017 and I can't wait to step back out on court at Melbourne Park."
Edmund, 25, has yet to progress beyond the third round of a Grand Slam but reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open in 2018.
He is ranked ahead of Evans and has earned £2.5m this year, with his best result a run to the final of the ATP event in Vienna in October.
"I have good memories of playing in Australia and hopefully I can play well again," said Edmund.
"I'd like to thank Craig and all those involved for the opportunity.

"

It is the first time in a decade that Britain has had four representatives in the main draw of a Grand Slam.
The last time was at Wimbledon in 2013 when Murray, Evans, Edmund and James Ward were all in action.
Murray is still on the comeback trail following surgery on his hip in January 2019 and having had two rounds of chemotherapy after testing positive for Covid-19 in March 2020.

Justine Henin-Hardenne's comeback ended in defeat as she lost to Russia's Anna Chakvetadze in the third round of the WTA tournament in Warsaw.
The Belgian, who retired in 2008, was trailing 6-2 2-0 when she withdrew with a knee injury she sustained in the warm-up.
"I can't explain how disappointed I am," said Henin-Hardenne.
"I wanted to play until the end
but I couldn't."
The 28-year-old needed treatment on her knee after just six games and eventually threw in the towel after 89 minutes of action.
Second seed Chakvetadze, who will replace Henin-Hardenne as world number 10 on Monday, faces Poland's Agnieszka Radwanska in the last eight.
"I am sorry it ended like this but these things happen in life," added the Russian.
"The court was very slow and bouncing high so it was difficult for me to make winners.

"

Former world number one Henin-Hardenne, who won the French Open and US Open in 2007 before retiring two years ago, had been suffering from a virus ahead of the match.
And her woes increased when she injured her knee during her pre-match warm-up.
She required treatment on the court after just six games and again at the end of the first set but, despite fighting back to 4-5, could not continue.
Former football coach Jimmy Jones has filed a lawsuit against Conte Sports, a sports marketing firm.
Jones claims that the company failed to pay him for work done under his former contract with the company.
The lawsuit seeks compensation for the unpaid wages, as well as damages for breach of contract.
Jones was contracted to provide coaching services to Conte Sports' football team, as well as to assist in the development of the company's training facilities.
According to the lawsuit, Jones performed all of the services required under the contract, but Conte Sports failed to pay him for his work.
The lawsuit also claims that the company breached the contract by failing to provide the agreed-upon compensation.
Conte Sports has yet to comment on the lawsuit.
Roddick, who has yet to drop a set in the tournament, is bidding to win his second title of the year after his success in Memphis in February.
The American number two is playing in only his second clay court event of 2006 - and his first since reaching the semi-finals in Rome last month.
Saulnier, who beat Spain's Fernando Vicente in the semi-finals on Saturday, has already beaten Roddick once on clay, in the first round of the 2004 French Open.
The Frenchman has shown signs of his former promise this week, having come through the qualifying tournament to reach the main draw.
Former footballer Ryan Jones has filed a lawsuit against Conte for "bullying and discrimination".
The former Wales international, who played for Cardiff City, Swansea City and Wigan Athletic, claims that Conte used racist language towards him during his time as a player at Chelsea.
Jones, who is mixed race, says he was subjected to "repeatedly" being called "King Kong" and other racist names by Conte, who was in charge of the Premier League club at the time.
In his legal complaint, Jones also claims that Conte bullied and discriminated against him because of his race, colour and nationality.
He says he was subjected to "unwelcome physical contact" by Conte, who would often poke him on the shoulder and grab his neck.
Jones also claims that Conte treated him differently from other players because of his race, and that he was not given the same opportunities as his white teammates.
He has decided to take legal action against Conte after failing to resolve the matter directly with the Italian manager.
A spokesman for Conte said: "Mr Conte totally refutes the allegations made by Mr Jones.
They are completely without merit and are not true.

"

Jones is seeking financial compensation from Conte, as well as an apology.

A spokesman for Jones said: "Ryan has not come to this decision lightly, but despite attempting to resolve this issue directly with Mr Conte, his legal team have been left with no choice but to pursue the matter further in order to obtain justice for Ryan and to prevent others from experiencing similar discrimination in the future."
This is not the first time that Conte has been accused of using racist language towards players.
In 2016, he was accused of using racist language towards then-Chelsea player Diego Costa, who he managed at the time.
Conte denied the allegations and said that he was not a "racist".
Former player Jones played for Cardiff City between 2011 and 2013, and subsequently for Swansea City and Wigan Athletic before retiring in 2016.

Liverpool midfielder Emre Can will be out of action for up to seven weeks after sustaining a knee injury during the 5-0 win over Manchester City in the Champions League, says manager Jurgen Klopp.
The German midfielder was forced off in the first half at Anfield on Wednesday with a knee problem and subsequent tests have revealed a "serious" injury.
"It is not a small thing, it is a proper injury," Klopp said.

"He has seen the specialist and from what I heard it is not as serious as it could have been but it is serious enough to keep him out for maybe six, seven weeks."

Can has made 35 appearances for Liverpool this season, with his absence likely to mean more game time for England midfielder James Milner.
Klopp also revealed that Georginio Wijnaldum and Daniel Sturridge are both in contention to feature in Saturday's FA Cup fourth-round replay at Plymouth.
Wijnaldum has been struggling with a knee injury while Sturridge has been out with a hip problem.
"They are both in a really good way.
It looks really good so far," said Klopp.

"In this moment, they are both available and we will see what we do with that."

Adam Lallana and Roberto Firmino are also likely to feature after being left out of the squad for the City game with slight muscle problems.
"It is good news for us.
We have no real new injuries and the two boys who were injured in the last few days are now available," added Klopp.
"We have a few difficult games coming up but it is good that we are not too busy in the treatment room."
Liverpool face AC Milan in the last 16 of the Champions League, with the first leg to be played on 15 February.
The second leg at the San Siro is on 7 March with the winner facing either Bayern Munich or Real Madrid in the quarter-finals.
Klopp's side are through to the last 16 of the FA Cup, with the replay at Plymouth followed by the visit of West Ham United in the last 32 of the Europa League.
Liverpool are also still in contention for a top-four finish in the Premier League despite dropping to fifth following Sunday's 2-0 defeat at Manchester United.
They are two points behind fourth-placed Manchester City with two games in hand.

Ireland have won the Six Nations Championship after a nerve-jangling 19-16 victory over England in Dublin.
The hosts scored three tries to England's one, but victory was secured by the Irish half-backs, who scored all their side's points through kicks.
Conor O'Shea's men led 19-9 with 10 minutes left, but Owen Farrell's penalty brought England to within two points and they dominated the closing stages.
However, Ireland managed to see out the game, clinching the title with one round remaining.
It was a remarkable triumph for a team that had not won a match in this year's competition going into the fifth weekend of action.
Ireland's previous victory was a 20-10 win over Australia on 29 November, and they had lost their first four Six Nations matches, including a 57-15 thrashing by England at Twickenham in Round 4.

Their title bid looked to have found a major obstacle when centre Robbie Henshaw went off with a shoulder injury after just three minutes, but his replacement, fit-again Garry Ringrose, scored a try with his first touch.
England, who needed to win to keep their title hopes alive, played with ambition but made a series of uncharacteristic mistakes, with Maro Itoje's looping pass intercepted by Ringrose for the try.

Ireland capitalised on another English error when Johnny Sexton's expertly-angled cross-field kick was collected by Simon Zebo for his side's second try, with the fly-half converting to give his side a 13-3 half-time lead.
England had been limited to three Owen Farrell penalties in the opening 40 minutes, with the first of those coming in the first minute.
The visitors came out firing after the break, and a scrum penalty awarded within sight of the Irish line allowed Farrell to reduce the deficit to just four points.
But Ireland hit back with a penalty of their own when England were penalised for not rolling away, and Sexton made it 16-6.

The fly-half had the chance to extend the lead further but skewed his penalty wide, and England took full advantage to score their first try when Ben Te'o touched down after a superb break from Jonathan Joseph.
Farrell's conversion brought England to within a point, and his subsequent penalty meant Steve Borthwick's men had the opportunity to win the game in the final
David Ferrer's victory over Russia's Dmitry Tursunov gave Spain an unassailable 3-0 lead in the best-of-five tie and sent them through to the World Group play-offs.
It also meant that Carlos Moya, the world number 12, did not have to play in the final dead rubber against Marat Safin.
The 29-year-old Moya has struggled with a knee injury in recent months and his place in the Spanish team had been a source of controversy.
He pulled out of the tie against Russia with a back injury after originally being named in the squad.
Moya's place was taken by Francisco Clavet, who lost a tight five-setter to Younes El Aynaoui in the opening day's play.
But the former world number one returned for Sunday's singles matches and looked to be moving freely as he watched Spain secure victory.
Ferrer, who is ranked 14 in the world, saw three match points slip by before taking his opportunity in the deciding set tiebreak.
The 24-year-old Spaniard dropped to his knees and wept tears of relief after finally seeing off Tursunov 7-6 (7-5) 6-7 (6-8) 7-6 (7-2) 6-4.
"I don't think it was the best match of my career but it was very important for me," said Ferrer.

"Maybe it was a mistake to miss those three match points but I have won matches before when I have missed more."

Spain will now play away to Australia in September's World Group play-offs, with the winners securing a place in the eight-team World Group in 2006.
Cardiff manager Neil Warnock has criticised "disrespectful" comments made by club owner Vincent Tan, who has questioned the manager's ability to attract players.
Tan, who appointed Warnock in 2011, said the 70-year-old might struggle to handle "big names" in the future.
The Welsh side avoided relegation from the Premier League on the final day of the season despite finishing 18th in the table.
They have already announced the departures of midfielder Peter Whittingham and goalkeeper David Marshall, who are out of contract.
Speaking on BBC Radio Wales' Scrum V podcast, Tan said: "That's the problem.
When you go to a higher level, when you go to a bigger name, can he handle it?
We will have to see.

"

 Warnock reacted to Tan's remarks on Friday, saying: "I think it is a little bit disrespectful.
"You can question my tactics, you can question my team selection, you can question lots of things, but not the players I have brought in - that is a bit disrespectful.
"Even managers with far more experience - Man City recently - get sacked with top, top players.
It's the way it is.
"You need an owner who trusts you.
I think Vincent trusts me - he has questioned me before on certain things and he is well within his rights to do so.
"But when it comes to the players, I have never brought a player in that was not of value.
That is a little bit disrespectful.

"

Tan bought a controlling interest in Cardiff City in 2010 and, at the end of the following season, sacked manager Dave Jones - who had led the club to the Championship play-off final - despite having previously said he would remain in charge regardless of the outcome.
In the summer of 2011, Tan appointed Warnock - then 61 - as manager and the club were promoted to the Premier League in 2013, though they were relegated after just one season.
The Bluebirds returned to the top flight in 2018 under Neil Harris, but he was replaced by Warnock - who had originally taken over when Harris became manager - towards the end of the campaign.
This year they have again struggled, even going into the final game of the season against Manchester United needing a point to be sure of survival.
They achieved that aim despite being beaten 2-0, with Fulham and Huddersfield Town going down instead.

Spain coach Luis Enrique faces a racism investigation after he was filmed greeting fans with a handshake mimicking the anti-racism gesture.
The Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) has begun an investigation into the incident.
Enrique, who is not of Spanish nationality, waved and shook hands with supporters imitating an Asian person's facial features.
He appeared to squint his eyes and pull down his eyelids, while moving his head from side to side.
The 57-year-old subsequently apologised for "any hurt caused" by his "unacceptable" behaviour.
In a statement released on social media, he added it was "not my intention to offend anyone".
Enrique, who has coached Spain since 2018 and led them to the 2020 Olympic title, was reportedly on a family holiday in Japan when the footage was taken.

The RFEF has begun proceedings against him and said in a statement: "RFEF will open disciplinary proceedings against Luis Enrique for recognisable disrespect towards the values of the sport with regards to racism.

"

The Spanish football authorities can impose a range of sanctions, from a verbal warning to point deductions or even expulsion.
The former Spain international is yet to comment publicly on the incident since he issued his apology on Wednesday.
Enrique succeeded Julen Lopetegui as Spain coach in 2018 and led Spain to the semi-finals of the Nations League the following year.
They also reached the last four of the European Championship in 2020, before eventually losing to champions Italy in the final.
Spain won the Olympic title in Tokyo last year after beating Brazil in the final.

England's white-ball captain Eoin Morgan and his predecessor, Joe Root, have both made themselves available for the tour of Pakistan planned for early next year but Ben Stokes and Jos Buttler are unlikely to be included in the squad, and Sam Curran is currently recovering from knee surgery.
It has also been reported that Yorkshire's Harry Brook is a possibility to be considered for the tour as a backup wicketkeeper batsman.
The PCB has invited England to play three ODIs and as many T20s in Pakistan from 13-22 October 2023 and the ECB has said it is "committed" to playing in the country.
The last time England played a limited-overs series in Pakistan was in 2015, when they played four matches including a T20 and won the series 3-0.

England players have not been averse to visiting Pakistan in the past with some of them playing in the Pakistan Super League but since an attack on the Sri Lankan team's bus in March 2009, England have been reluctant to play there with the ECB taking into account the players' and staff's welfare and security.

But with Pakistan successfully hosting the ICC World Cup 2023 matches - including the final at the Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore on 13 November - in a safe and secure environment and the PCB making every effort to make sure that all the visiting teams are comfortable and get top-class security, the ECB's concerns have been allayed to some extent.
The PCB has also informed the ECB that it will hire a charter flight to take the England team to Pakistan and avoid any exposure of the players to commercial travel.
"The safety and welfare of our players and staff is our first priority and we will not hesitate to postpone the tour if we do not feel it is safe to proceed," said an ECB spokesperson.
"We are in ongoing discussions with the PCB around conditions for the tour, working together to deliver a safe environment for the players and staff.
We will continue to take guidance from the UK government and relevant security teams.

"

The PCB, on its part, has promised to look after the visiting team in the best possible manner and is trying to convince the ECB that all the concerns it might have are addressed adequately and that the players and staff will be completely safe in Pakistan.

"We have assured them that we will host them with the same love and warmth as we did with the ICC events and our team is actively engaged with the ECB and are in constant touch with their security consultant firm as well," a PCB source told ESPN
Liverpool manager Rafael Benítez has played down fresh speculation about the future of captain Steven Gerrard.
The Spain coach said he was not concerned by reports the England midfielder, 30, had told teammates he wanted to join Real Madrid.
"I don't worry about that - the important thing is that he knows how important he is for us," said Benítez.
Gerrard has been linked with a move to the Spanish giants in the past.
The Liverpool captain signed a new contract in February 2012 which runs until 2015.
Gerrard is currently injured and missed Sunday's 1-0 Premier League win over Manchester United.
Benítez said he did not know when the midfielder would return from the hamstring injury he sustained against Hull on 9 February.
"He is getting better but it is a difficult injury," said the Liverpool boss.
"It is not just the time out, but the intensity of the training when you come back.

"

The Reds manager also said he was happy with the way his team were performing, despite drawing four of their last five Premier League matches.
"We are creating chances in every game and that is a positive thing," he added.
"Maybe we are not getting the results that we want but the performances have been good.
"We were playing against a good team in United, who are fighting for the title, and I was happy with the performance.
We created chances and that is positive for the team."
Martina Navratilova has urged tennis' governing bodies to do more to fight sexism in the sport, saying the game had not moved on from the era of "bullshit politics".
The 18-time grand slam tennis champion said women were still being treated like "second-class citizens" in the sport.
Speaking to the BBC, she said women's tournaments were still paid less and players subjected to sexism from officials.
Navratilova, who won 59 grand slam titles, said women were treated like "pieces of meat" by the media.
"I don't think we've changed.
On the outside, we've changed but on the inside, we're still the same," she said.
"There is still pay disparity.
When you look at the grand slams, the men play best of five sets and we play best of three.
"In most tournaments, the men get paid more.
They still make more money even though we bring in $1.2bn which is roughly half of what the men bring in but our prize money is less than half.
"And it's still the same old, same old from officials.
It's always the women players who get punished for their emotions.
The men do ten times worse and get away with it.

"

Navratilova was speaking as the BBC revealed its latest list of the 100 most influential women in the world.
The former world number one purchased a stake in the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) last year and has been a vocal campaigner for gender equality in sport.
She successfully campaigned for the equalisation of prizemoney in all events up to the quarter-finals.
But the two-time Wimbledon champion said there was still a long way to go.
"There are double standards that I notice.
Officials tend to baby the men, not the women.
When women players react, they get punished for it," she added.
"It's always about how we look, how we dress, instead of being professionals like the men.
"Even in the media, we are still objectified.
We are treated like pieces of meat.
If we were treated as athletes, I'd be happy.

"

Navratilova also warned that any player who transgressed the new dress code at this year's French Open, which bans the skirts worn by many women players, would be "hurting themselves".

Ireland have overtaken Scotland in their annual new year's rugby clash for the first time since 2010.
Twenty-eight points from fly-half Johnny Sexton helped Ireland run out 49-7 winners in Dublin.
It was a disappointing start to the year for Scotland, who have now won only one of their last 10 matches.
The visitors were outplayed in most areas of the pitch and, despite having most of the possession in the first half, only managed to score one try through stand-off Finn Russell.
Ireland, who led 26-7 at the break, scored six tries as they ran in seven touchdowns.

It was a memorable debut for Ulster's Craig Casey, who scored a second-half try and produced an impressive performance, while fellow newcomer Stephen Archer, who wins his 50th cap, also shone in the second row.

For Scotland, the only positives were that they avoided a fourth successive defeat by Ireland and retained the Centenary Quaich trophy, which was introduced in 1989 and is awarded to the winner of the annual match between the two sides.
Dundee United ended Aberdeen's nine-match unbeaten run in the Premiership with a 4-1 victory at Tannadice.
Peter Pawlett gave the hosts the lead with a close-range finish in the 14th minute.
United doubled their advantage five minutes later when Ryan Edwards headed in from eight yards.
Niall McGinn pulled one back for Aberdeen just before the half-hour mark, firing into the bottom corner.
And the Dons were back on level terms seven minutes into the second half when Vicente Besuijen scored with a looping header.
But James Keatings restored United's lead in the 64th minute with a superb strike from just inside the box and the hosts sealed the win 11 minutes from time through Marc McNulty.
It was a first defeat in 10 matches in all competitions for Jim Goodwin's side, who remained fifth in the table, four points behind United in fourth.
Scotland's top referee has told BBC Scotland he is "surprised" and "disappointed" at being removed from this season's Premier League campaign.
Barry Cook was dropped from the list of top-flight officials for matches in Scotland and England.
The Scottish Football Association (SFA) has stood by his decision to cancel a match between Motherwell and Celtic in November 2011.
Cook felt he was the subject of racial abuse from players and fans during the game.
The SFA says his decision to abandon the match was "correct".
And Cook, 44, says he has not been given a reason for his omission from the list of top-flight referees.
"I am surprised and disappointed at being removed from the Premier League list but I can't complain as I have enjoyed a wonderful career," he said.
"I never thought in my wildest dreams that I would be appointed to referee a match involving the Old Firm clubs, never mind the amount of times I have been lucky enough to do so.
"I remain extremely grateful to the SFA for this.

"

Cook was in charge when he stopped the match at Motherwell's Fir Park ground after Celtic's Leigh Griffiths claimed he had been the target of racist abuse from fans.
The official said he heard "monkey noises" aimed at Griffiths and his decision to abandon the game was supported by the SFA.
Celtic manager Neil Lennon said he was "100% certain" that his player had been the target of racial abuse.
However, Cook has been told he will not be refereeing top-flight matches involving the Old Firm clubs or any other match in the Premier League this season.
The referee says he has not been given a reason for the decision, but understands that he can reapply for his place on the list next season.
"I have spoken to the head of referee development at the SFA and he told me I had been removed from the list," Cook said.
"I have served as a referee in the Premier League for many years now and never once has a club, player or manager complained to the SFA about my performances.
"I feel I still have a lot to offer and hope to continue refereeing for many more years yet."
Harry Potter actor Daniel Radcliffe is to compete in the 2022 Cazoo World Cup Gala, held at the Royal Albert Hall in London on Sunday.
The £125,000 purchase By Hand, ridden by David Egan, will line up in the showpiece event of the equestrian year.
It will be the first time the actor has competed at the venue.
The news comes after Egan teamed up with the actor to win at the Land Rover Burghley Horse Trials in September 2022.

Newcastle boosted their Premier League survival hopes with a crucial 2-1 victory over Bolton at St James' Park.
The Magpies took the lead when Yohan Cabaye scored with a 25-yard drive early in the second half.
Midfielder Darren Pratley equalised for Bolton with a superb volley from 20 yards.
But Newcastle regained the lead when Papiss Cisse scored with an angled finish in the 82nd minute.
The win takes Newcastle out of the bottom three and to within two points of Bolton, who drop to 17th.
Before the game, Bolton manager Dougie Freedman had said a draw would be a good result for his side, who had not won away from home in the league since August.
And for large parts of the game it looked like that would be the case as Newcastle struggled to create chances against a resolute Bolton defence.
When Newcastle did break through they found Bolton keeper Adam Bogdan in inspired form.
The Hungarian, who signed from Liverpool during the week, made a host of fine saves.

He did not have much to do in the first half as Newcastle produced little in the way of chances, but in the second half he made a fantastic one-handed save to deny Leon Best and prevented the home side from taking the lead.
Newcastle's goal finally came when Cabaye collected the ball just inside the Bolton half and drove towards the visiting defence.
The Frenchman moved inside Pratley and hit a low right-footed shot that flew past Bogdan and into the corner.
The visitors equalised with their first effort on target eight minutes later.
Pratley, who had scored just one goal this season, connected sweetly with a volley from the edge of the area after Tim Ream had headed a free-kick into his path.
Newcastle responded and Bogdan was forced into another good save to tip a Hatem Ben Arfa shot over the bar.
The Magpies kept pressing and finally broke through when Cisse scored with a clinical finish after being set up by Ben Arfa.
It was a crucial win for Newcastle, who moved above Bolton and out of the bottom three for the first time since October.
Canadian tennis player Bianca Andreescu has pulled out of the Australian Open, with a leg injury that she says was caused by "complications" from a blood clot in her arm.

Canadian tennis player Bianca Andreescu has withdrawn from the Australian Open with a leg injury

"

Andreescu - who has not played a competitive match since September - said she began feeling "sharp pain" in her leg during training and a MRI scan on Saturday evening local time revealed a "small lesion" on her lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

"

Andreescu won her first Grand Slam in New York three years ago and followed that with a victory at the WTA Finals in Shenzhen.

Prior to the Australian Open, Andreescu - who has been ranked as high as fourth in the world - said she was "hungry for more".
Amelie Mauresmo's comeback ended with a victory as the French former world number one beat Poland's Magdalena Rybarikova in the first round of the WTA tournament in Los Angeles.
The 31-year-old, who gave birth to her first child in August, overcame world number 58 Rybarikova 6-2 6-4.
"I was nervous in the beginning but I played solid and my serve was good," said Mauresmo, who is unranked.
"I feel I'm getting better and I'm happy to win.

"

The 2006 Wimbledon champion plans to return to the French Open in May.
Mauresmo, who married Frenchman Richard Gasquet - herself a former top 10 player - last year, has not played competitive tennis since Wimbledon in 2009.

"I've been working hard in the last few months to get back in shape.
I'm not there yet
but I'm on the right way."

Newcastle have joined the race to sign Real Madrid and Spain striker Alvaro Morata, 32, on loan from Atletico Madrid.
The forward has struggled to establish himself under Diego Simeone this season, making just six starts in La Liga with six goals.
Newcastle's attempt to bring in the former Juventus man is a sign they plan to fight to stay in the Premier League.

Zambia's president has said he is "confident and cautious" as the country becomes the first on the African continent to receive COVID-19 vaccines through the UN-backed COVAX scheme.
Ruling party leader Edgar Lungu received his shot live on TV on Friday, urging others to follow suit.
But the event itself was not without controversy.
Main opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema criticised the handling of the process, and questioned the timing of the president's vaccination.
Mr Hichilema, who disputed last year's presidential election results, said the vaccine should have been administered at a hospital, rather than at State House.
He added that as the leader of an opposition party, he did not believe Mr Lungu should have been given "preferential treatment" in receiving the vaccine ahead of healthcare workers.
Hasn't Zambia had its share of tragedy?
Yes.
Zambia is among the African countries that have suffered countless tragedies as a result of the pandemic.
It has recorded more than 27,000 cases and over 220 deaths - but the actual numbers are thought to be higher as testing is limited.
In the capital, Lusaka, mortuaries ran out of space for bodies in December, and funeral parlours say they are overrun.
Reverend Pauline Nalley, a senior administrator at the University of Zambia, said she had seen an increase in the number of funerals at her church.
She said it was a race against time to bury bodies because of the rapid decomposition of the deceased.
"We are now afraid of handling the bodies because of the risk of infection, so we have urged the government to do something about the situation," Rev Nalley said.
As for the arrival of the vaccines, she said she was "cautiously optimistic" that things would start to get better.
What about the controversy?
The delivery of just under a quarter of a million doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine has been greeted with a sense of relief in Zambia - but also some concern.
There are worries about how the vaccine will be transported to the more remote parts of the country, and stored in countries with frequent power cuts.
There is also a lack of trust in the safety of the vaccine, and confusion about its effectiveness.

"

"

Italian tennis player Francesca "Farina" Schiavone achieved one of the most surprising victories in Venus Williams' grand slam career when she knocked the American out of the French Open in the third round.

"I know everybody is equal when it comes to decisions

Footballer Gareth Bale has been praised in Wales after becoming the most-capped player in the country's history.

"

"

The PRO14 season would be shortened to 16 games and a semi-final play-off involving the four top-ranked teams introduced under a new format proposed by tournament organisers.
The current structure comprises 142 matches, including the finals, played across 21 weekends.
The new plan would feature 84 games over 18 weeks, with each team playing home and away fixtures against the other 13 teams.
The two highest-ranked teams would receive a bye to the semi-finals.
The proposal, from Pro14 Rugby, aims to have more top-tier fixtures played over the Christmas and New Year period.
Under the current structure, teams play their divisional rivals home and away, plus three sides from the other division.
The new model would see each club play home and away fixtures against every other team.

"We believe the new format delivers on our objective to provide our fans with more of the derby matches and local rivalries that they want to see, while maintaining the unique character of our competitions," said Pro14 Rugby's chief executive officer, Martin Anayi.
"It also allows us to have a simpler and more equalised format in terms of fixtures.

"

Pro14 Rugby expects the new structure to be in place by the 2022-23 season but needs the approval of the Pro14 Board, which comprises representatives of the Celtic Rugby Union, the Welsh Rugby Union and SRU.
The board will meet on Monday to discuss the proposal.
If agreed, it could be put to an SRU general meeting for ratification on 30 May.
The Pro14 was due to introduce its first 'wildcard' side - South Africa's Southern Kings - this season but the plan was shelved because of financial difficulties.
The new structure does not mention the possibility of introducing a fifth franchise.

France striker Nicolas Anelka is hoping to leave Manchester City in the January transfer window, with several clubs including Tottenham, Juventus and Borussia Dortmund interested in signing him.
The 33-year-old's agent said "several giants" of the game are interested in the former Arsenal and Chelsea player.
City signed Anelka for £12m from Bolton in July 2008.
But the former France international has started only four Premier League games for City this season.
"Nicolas is looking to leave in January," said Anelka's agent Andy Savić.

"There are several giants of European football interested in him and he hopes to make a decision in the next few days."

Anelka, who has scored 13 goals in 56 games for City, has struggled to establish himself in manager Roberto Mancini's first team plans at Eastlands.
The press in Brazil are describing Carlos Tevez as "the most expensive player in Brazilian football history" after Shanghai Shenhua agreed to sell the Argentine striker to Corinthians.

The Chinese club have confirmed they have agreed a deal with the Brazilian club, thought to be about £3.6m.

The move brings to an end a turbulent 10 months for Tevez in the Chinese Super League.
He argued with coach Gregorio Manzano and club officials in October and was banned from the squad, before being reinstated in February.
Corinthians president Roberto de Andrade said the club had been interested in Tevez for a long time and that he was happy with the signing.
"We have managed to sign a top-level player, who is in great shape and can contribute immediately," the Brazilian added.
Tevez is expected to link up with his new club after the international break.
He will be available to play in the Copa Libertadores, the South American equivalent of the Champions League, which starts next month.
The 32-year-old former Manchester United, Manchester City and Juventus striker has also agreed a deal to stay at Corinthians until the end of 2019.
Corinthians are owned by the church and have won the Copa Libertadores three times, most recently in 2012.
They finished ninth in this year's Brazilian Championship, won by Flamengo, and were knocked out of the Copa Brasil at the quarter-final stage.
Tevez scored just four goals in 19 Chinese Super League appearances for Shanghai Shenhua.
His last game was on 4 November, near the end of the Chinese season.
He was banned for four months by Shanghai Shenhua in December after arguing with coach Gregorio Manzano during a training session.
An arbitration court ruling ended his Super League ban in February and Tevez made his comeback in March.
But he made just four more appearances before talks over a move to Corinthians began in June.
BBC Sport - Leeds United midfielder Adam Prutton has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his involvement in an alleged altercation with a fan after a match.
The FA has charged Prutton with "misconduct in relation to media and improper conduct".
If found guilty, the 28-year-old is facing a ban of up to six matches and a fine of £25,000.
Prutton, who has made 14 appearances for Leeds this season, has until 18:00 GMT on Wednesday, 18 March to respond to the charge.
In the FA's charge sheet, it is claimed that Prutton's "conduct in the vicinity of the tunnel at the end of the fixture was improper".
It is also claimed he breached FA Rule E3, which relates to "misconduct in relation to media".
Leeds United have confirmed they will be conducting their own investigation into the incident.

Ireland's housing market has had a rollercoaster year, with prices rising sharply - by more than 20% in Dublin - before a new tax aimed at curbing buy-to-let investment kicked in, and then falling back slightly.
Prices are still rising in Dublin, but the trend is reversing in the rest of the country, with prices falling modestly.
The number of mortgages approved for house purchase fell by 15% in the year to September, according to the Central Bank.
One of the biggest challenges facing the new government, which takes office this week, will be to tackle the housing shortage.
There were 34,400 people registered as officially homeless at the end of October, though this is widely believed to be an undercount.
Taoiseach (prime minister)

Leo Varadkar has said that the government will try to build more than 50,000 new homes over the next five years, and to make 100,000 homes available through local authorities and approved housing bodies.
One of the government's first challenges will be to pass a budget for 2020 through the newly-elected parliament.
Expect to hear a lot about "Brexit" in the coming year, as the deadline for the UK's exit from the European Union draws nearer.
The Irish government has been keen to ensure that the country is prepared for all possible outcomes, including a no-deal Brexit.
The UK's departure from the EU has already had a significant impact on the Irish economy.

The Irish government has said that it is working to ensure that there is a "soft landing" for the country as it leaves the EU, but there are still significant uncertainties about how the departure will affect Ireland.
One thing that's certain is that the issue will continue to dominate the headlines in the coming year.
No-deal Brexit aside, the Irish economy has continued to grow strongly in 2019, with GDP up by about 5% in the first three quarters of the year.

Consumer spending is down, and business investment has been weak.

The Athletics Kenya (AK) disciplinary committee has lifted the five-year ban imposed on 3000m steeplechase runner Lydia Chepkemei in 2018 for allegedly doping.
The decision was made after an appeal by Chepkemei, who is a two-time world champion and three-time Olympic medallist.
The committee said it was satisfied with her explanation that her positive test was the result of a contaminated supplement.
The AK committee also took into account that Chepkemei had "cooperated fully" with the doping authorities.
Her results from 24 February 2017, when the alleged doping occurred, have been disqualified.
Chepkemei welcomed the decision, saying she had "suffered emotionally and financially" during her two-year court battle.
Last year, the 30-year-old filed an appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), seeking to overturn the ban.
But Cas decided to delay a decision on her case until after the outcome of her second appeal to AK, which has now ruled in her favour.
Chepkemei is now expected to return to competition soon, with her lawyer Victor Rabei saying they will seek compensation for the period she was suspended.

The Scotland Under-21 coach has been mentioned as a possible candidate to replace Gordon Strachan, who was sacked in October.
And Souness, who managed his country from 1986 to 90, says he "wouldn't say no" to the job himself.

"

Why is Smith regarded as a contender?
The former Rangers and Everton defender has worked with Scotland's youth teams since 2011 and has had spells in charge of the under-19s and the under-21s.
Along with Billy Stark - who was appointed as Strachan's assistant in October - Smith has been credited with improving the pathway for young players to the first team.

Their complaint is that too much red tape remains, making it difficult to use the new transit route.

Qantas has reported a healthier balance sheet and a return to profit for the first time in seven years, boosted by rising travel demand and the partial recovery of international routes.
The Australian airline said it made a net profit of Aus$497m (£268m) in the 12 months to 31 March, compared with a loss of Aus$1.73bn the previous year.
It described the result as "remarkable", given the pandemic's impact on global travel.
However, the company's debt has increased to more than Aus$6.5bn from Aus$5bn a year earlier.

French police have now released Lactalis chairman Emmanuel Besnier, who was being held in custody over the scandal, after he was questioned for two days.
Mr Besnier was detained on Tuesday under a European warrant.
The detention order was issued in 2013 when Italian authorities requested his arrest for alleged fraud in the collapse of the dairy group Parmalat two decades ago.
Parmalat, once one of the world's biggest dairy producers, collapsed in 2003 after admitting it had found €14bn ($15.3bn) hole in its accounts through the systematic use of fraudulent accounting.
The company, which operated in more than 30 countries, was placed into administration and eventually split up.
Thousands of investors lost money, including small shareholders and pensioners who were unable to recover their savings.

"I wish to tell the thousands of small investors in Italy and elsewhere in Europe who were harmed that I am sincerely sorry they suffered such injustice," Mr Besnier said in a statement released by his lawyers on Thursday.
He said he had always declared that he had "nothing to do" with the events which led to the crisis and that he had "never been charged with any offence in France or elsewhere".
Mr Besnier described his detention as "a mistake" and said he had immediately agreed to be interviewed by police once he was made aware of the warrant.
His lawyers said that he had been released without any charges being laid and that he would soon return to France.
A spokesperson for the Italian justice ministry said Mr Besnier could still face an extradition request from Italy in the coming days.
Sri Lanka's economy has been hit by a sharp increase in oil prices, the island's central bank has said.
It said the surge in oil prices, caused by the war in Ukraine, had slowed growth in Asia's fastest growing economy.
The island nation is heavily dependent on imported oil, which is used in factories and to generate electricity.
The bank left its main interest rate unchanged at 9.5% earlier this month, saying the rate was "adequate" given the current conditions.
It now expects the economy to expand by 5.5% this year, down from its previous forecast of 6.0%.
The update came as official data showed the economy grew by 8.8% in the first three months of 2022, compared with 11.8% in the same period last year.
"The increase in commodity prices, particularly of crude oil, reduced the growth of output in the manufacturing and construction sectors," the bank said in its statement.
It also said that the economy had been hit by a reduction in tourist numbers because of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Before the pandemic, tourism was a major revenue earner for the country, accounting for about 11% of its GDP.

The central bank now expects tourism to rebound this year, with the country set to reopen to tourists on 1 June, more than three months after the country closed its borders in the face of the third wave of Covid-19.

Turkey turns on the economic charm

ANKARA (BBC) - Turkey's government has approved a draft law that would pave the way for Kurdish parties to enter parliament - if approved in a referendum.
The bill would change the way Turkey's political parties are formed, allowing them to appeal to voters from a specific ethnic background.
Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan has promised to deliver "a new, democratised political system" to voters in the referendum.
The changes would also limit the powers of the president - albeit after Erdogan himself assumed the office.
The draft law approved by ministers on Tuesday will be put to a referendum, probably in March.
If passed, it would make Turkey the latest country to adopt what politicians call a "proportional representation" system.
Currently, parties in Turkey elect MPs from closed lists of candidates, a system that often results in vote-winning parties winning far more seats than their share of the vote.
The new system would lower the threshold for winning seats in parliament - currently set at 10% - giving smaller parties a better chance of representation.

One of the consequences of the change would be to allow the pro-Kurdish Democratic Society Party (DTP) - closed down last year for alleged ties with the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) - to re-enter parliament.
The DTP won almost six percent of the vote in 2007, but took no seats because the 10% threshold ruled them out.
The change is one element in a package of reforms put forward by the government designed to address concerns over Turkey's democracy.
Another element, also to be put to a referendum, would change the way the president is elected, reducing the powers of the office.
The changes were agreed in a consensus between the government and opposition parties, but critics say the reforms do not go far enough.
"This system will bring about change, a new, democratised political system," Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said last week.
"Our people will decide on this change, on these reforms in a referendum," he said.
"I am confident our people will give the right decision.
The reforms have been closely watched by Europe, as Turkey seeks to begin accession talks with the European Union.
The EU has made clear that it wants to see the democratisation package passed into law.

Five million Germans out of work:

Germany has seen its biggest annual rise in unemployment for 25 years.
The number of people out of work rose by 130,000 to 5.1 million in February, the biggest monthly increase since November 2002, officials said.
The unemployment rate rose to 11.3% from 11.1% in January.
Youth unemployment stood at 18.2% from 17.7% in the previous month.

The strong rise in unemployment has been attributed to Germany's steep coronavirus lockdown, with economists saying that without the restrictions in place the figure might have been closer to 4.8 million.
The lockdown is due to be relaxed gradually over the next few months.

Germany has been less affected by the coronavirus pandemic than some other European countries, with its total official death toll standing at 69,000, according to data from the Johns Hopkins University.
The UK, for example, has recorded more than 150,000 deaths, and Spain has seen more than 120,000 deaths.
However, as in other countries, the real death toll is believed to be significantly higher.
Germany posted its first annual decline in GDP for six years in 2020 and its biggest fall since the financial crisis, according to preliminary data from its statistics office.
The German economy shrank by 4.9% in 2020 as coronavirus restrictions slowed activity.
The country's statistics office said the impact of the pandemic became evident in the second quarter of the year, when the economy contracted by 10.1%.
It said the decline in the fourth quarter was smaller, at 1.3%, following a rebound in activity in the summer and autumn.
The German government has predicted that the economy will grow by 4.2% this year, and the country's central bank says it could expand by as much as 5.2%.

The German unemployment figures come a day after it was announced that the number of people in the US who have filed for first-time unemployment benefits rose last week to 770,000, from 730,000 the week before.
Financial services group MetLife has agreed to buy the life insurance division of Citigroup for $12.5bn (£7.4bn).
The deal includes the sale of Citigroup's interest in the joint venture, Citigroup Insurance Holdings, as well as the sale of Metropolitan Insurance & Annuity Company, and MetLife Asia.
The transaction excludes Citigroup's foreign insurance businesses in Korea, India, and Japan.
New York-based MetLife is the largest life insurer in the US.
It has about 70 million customers in nearly 50 countries.
Citigroup's insurance division, which offers life insurance, annuities and asset management, has about 130 million customers in North America, Japan and other parts of Asia.
MetLife said the deal would increase its presence in Asia and add to its portfolio of individual life insurance products in the US.
It added the acquisition would make it "one of the world's leading insurance and financial services companies".

"MetLife and Citigroup's insurance businesses have highly complementary franchises, and this acquisition demonstrates our commitment to our clients and shareholders," said MetLife chief executive Steven A. Kandarian.

"This transaction offers substantial long-term value for our shareholders, with the strategic and financial benefits of size and scale, improved financial flexibility due to the lower amount of capital required to support the business, and the opportunity to realize approximately $1.5 billion of value over time through the monetization of the tax benefits generated by the transaction," he added.
MetLife is funding the deal with the cash it holds overseas as well as by issuing stock.
The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2016, subject to regulatory approval.
German carmaker Daimler faces a drop in profit this year as the global economic downturn hits demand for luxury cars.
The world's largest maker of luxury cars said on Thursday that group earnings would "significantly" fall in 2023.
Daimler, which owns the Mercedes-Benz brand, put the blame on falling car sales in the second half of 2022 as well as a "cost explosion" in the industry.
It added that efforts to green its fleet by shifting to battery-powered cars would be a "significant headwind" and a "major challenge" in 2023.
Daimler's prediction of lower profits follows similar warnings from other carmakers, including BMW and Volkswagen.
On Wednesday, BMW said it expected its full-year profit to drop by as much as a quarter, while VW said it was trimming its workforce in a bid to save costs.
Daimler's prediction also came as it posted its first annual loss since 2008.
For the year 2022, the group reported a loss after taxes of €1.4bn (£1.2bn), compared to a profit of €7.9bn (£6.9bn) a year earlier.
The group said it would not propose a dividend for 2022 to save cash, and aimed to make a profit of between €7bn (£6.4bn) and €7.5bn (£6.8bn) in 2024.
At the same time, Mercedes-Benz Cars & Vans division saw a fall in 2022 sales, down 5% to 2,093,498 vehicles.
Profits at the division, which makes the Mercedes-Benz cars as well as vans, fell 35% to €2.8bn (£2.5bn).
The company said it had faced "continued supply bottlenecks" during the year, which had been felt particularly in the second half.
It added that pricing actions had so far not been enough to completely offset the increased costs, mainly due to inflation.

Sara Nathan has told how her father, who died in 2016, "would be thrilled" with the progress of their Indian beer venture.
Sara Nathan is the daughter of Stanley Metcalf Nathan, who founded the company in 1740.
The family business - which has been controlled by descendants of the same family since it began 280 years ago - has expanded rapidly in India in recent years.
It now expects to see further growth after unveiling a £100m investment plan.
S&N said it would invest in a new brewery and a "state-of-the-art" bottle manufacturing plant in the southern Indian state of Karnataka.
The firm did not reveal an exact location for the new facilities, but said they would be developed in "close proximity" to its existing brewery near Bangalore, the state's capital.

'Metcalf's moment'

Ms. Nathan, S&N's interim chief executive, said: "My father, who passed away in 2016, would be thrilled with how well our Indian business has performed.
"This feels like Metcalf's moment - investing in our Indian beer business to create a long-term sustainable future for our flagship ale brand, Newcastle Brown Ale.

"

She said the company had undertaken "extensive due diligence" before deciding to invest.
"This includes comprehensive research into the premium beer segment in India, which demonstrates the potential for our business to continue to grow sustainably.

"

S&N's Indian subsidiary, United Breweries, is the country's second-largest beer company by market share.
It was founded in 1915 by Sir Thomas Leishman, a Scottish businessman who settled in Bangalore.

It is now controlled by his descendants, who are joint shareholders with the Nathens and the Primos in S&N.

China has suspended approval for 26 coal-fired power projects in Guizhou province, amid efforts to cut down on carbon emissions, according to reports.
The suspension came after local authorities submitted a list of projects for review, an anonymous source told the Reuters news agency.

It follows a notice issued by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) in February, according to which provinces were ordered to stop building coal-fired power projects that were suspended or had not started construction.
The notice followed a key meeting of the Communist Party's top leadership, where a reduction in carbon emissions was agreed as a priority.
China is the world's largest emitter of carbon dioxide and has been under pressure to take firmer action to tackle climate change.
It previously announced that it would aim to peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.
However, it has been facing an energy supply crunch that has seen power outages in many regions, and authorities have been pushing for a rapid increase in coal production.
The suspension of the 26 projects, with a total capacity of 129.2 gigawatts, is a significant step in reducing coal consumption, according to Greenpeace.

"This remarkable suspension of projects shows the beginning of the end of China's energy glut, and signals a clear move towards energy conservation and carbon neutrality," said Greenpeace East Asia climate and energy campaigner Huang Wei in a statement.
Japan's bank shares have risen after media reports that the country's government is considering linking its interest rates with those of other major economies.
The reports come as Japan's central bank is under pressure to normalise monetary policy.
The Nikkei 225 index was up 1.4% in early trading, with bank shares leading the gainers.
Media reports over the weekend said that Japan was considering a "negative interest rate" policy.
Under such a policy, commercial banks would be charged a fee for holding large amounts of cash at the central bank.
The move is being considered by the government as a way to encourage banks to increase lending and stimulate the economy.
Japan's interest rates have been near zero for years, and the country has struggled to generate any significant economic growth.
A negative interest rate policy would be a further step away from normalisation, and could hurt the country's banking sector.
However, analysts said that the reports had led to speculation that the government could be planning to increase economic ties with other countries.
"There is a growing sense that Japan should team up with other major economies to normalise its monetary policy," said Hiroaki Hayashi, an economist at Morgan Stanley.

The dollar's decline ahead of this week's G7 meeting in London prompted European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde to blame the US for not doing enough to bolster the world's primary reserve currency, whose global strength is seen as vital for economic stability.
"It is more reflective of the US economic situation and the US economic policy choices than it is on the international community and on the choices that have been made abroad," she said.
Ms. Lagarde, who will step down as ECB president at the end of her eight-year term in October, made the remarks in a question-and-answer session in the Dutch parliament.
Her comments come as central bankers and finance ministers from the G7 group of wealthy nations meet in London on Thursday and Friday.
The US dollar is widely regarded as a haven currency, and its decline has been accelerated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
This has led to a marked increase in volatility across financial markets.
A weakening dollar can help US exporters and reduce imported inflation, but it can also lead to financial instability in some emerging markets that have borrowed in dollars.
It can also roil global markets as investors reassess what is supposed to be the safest asset of all.
This creates problems for markets such as government bonds.
Interest rate differentials between the US and other major economies have been a key driver of the dollar's decline.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, is expected to raise interest rates by 50 basis points next month, but the ECB is not expected to raise rates at all this year.
In the Netherlands, Ms. Lagarde also spoke about the importance of the independence of central banks.
She said that political interference in central banking had led in the past "to disastrous consequences".
She cited the example of the Austrian central bank before the First World War and more recent examples of "political interference leading to outcomes that many would regret".
Tech giant Google's parent company Alphabet has seen its shares drop 2.3% after its employees were offered the chance to sell shares worth up to $45,000 each.
The sale came as part of a pre-arranged trading plan, which lets staff sell a certain number of shares at pre-set times.
It comes as several tech firms, including Google, face challenges due to the economic crisis sparked by the Covid-19 pandemic and changing consumer habits.
Alphabet's shares were down ($15.90) to $695.85 in afternoon trading in New York.
The stock has fallen substantially from last year when it was trading above $1,300.

He added that the trading plan had been in place for a while and was not a result of current economic conditions.
In a note to employees, Alphabet and Google's chief financial officer Ruth Porat said that staff need to exercise caution when trading shares, "given the volatility in the stock market".
"While we are in a period of uncertainty, it's important to remember that our business fundamentals remain strong," she wrote.
The drop in Alphabet's share price has been driven partly by the advertising market being hit by the pandemic as companies cut marketing budgets.
Google makes the majority of its money from advertising and like much of the tech sector is facing questions over its business practices.
The company has been the subject of antitrust lawsuits from the US government and regulators in India and Europe, who say it has abused its dominance in search and other areas.
The company's YouTube subsidiary is also facing questions over its role in political campaigning ahead of the US presidential election in November.
Last week, US President Donald Trump accused the video-sharing platform of "tying" political ad placements to favourable news coverage.
YouTube rejected the claim and said it had introduced measures to protect against misinformation in political ads.

A French billionaire has challenged the London Stock Exchange's (LSE) rejection of his £1.5bn ($2.1bn) takeover bid.
Xavier Niel - a telecoms and technology entrepreneur who is also a minority shareholder in the LSE - held talks with the exchange's management on Thursday.
The LSE said earlier this month that Mr. Niel's bid was not in the "best interests" of the company or its shareholders.
Mr. Niel has until 19 October to make an offer or announce a firm intention to make an offer.
The LSE's rejection came after the UK government announced plans to increase its shareholding in the exchange to up to 25% .
The move was part of a plan to keep London as a global financial hub after the UK leaves the European Union.

Stock exchanges in the EU are required to be regulated by the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), and many fear that London will lose its access to the EU single market because of Brexit.

Last week, EU officials also announced that they were working on plans to lure the LSE to Amsterdam.
Why is Mr. Niel interested?
Mr. Niel is the founder of telecoms company Iliad, which operates the low-cost Free Mobile service in France.
He also owns about 4% of the LSE, and is its largest shareholder who is not a member of the exchange's board.

His interest in taking over the exchange has been seen as an attempt to ward off a takeover by the Shanghai Stock Exchange, which last month entered into an agreement to access the LSE's trading technology.
What has the LSE said?
The LSE said it had noted Mr. Niel's statement regarding his meeting with senior management on Thursday and that its response to his proposal "remains the same".
"The London Stock Exchange Group Board is confident that it can deliver greater value for shareholders as a listed company than would be available from the offer," it added in a statement.
Former President Donald Trump's senior aide Jason Miller says the so-called "golden rule" of journalism is still intact.
Mr Miller, who was Trump's spokesman, made the comment in response to questions about whether the media had treated the Republican favorably enough during his presidency.
"Maybe you guys should spend less time defending yourselves and focusing on the real enemy, and that's the Biden administration," he told a journalism conference on Thursday.

"I think it's a belief that's shared by the majority of Americans, that you guys are fair, you're balanced, you're impartial," he said.

"
