Bombardier's chief executive will step down on June 30, the company has announced.
Alain Bellemare - who led the aerospace company for the past seven years - will be replaced by Éric Martel.
Mr Martel has been president of Bombardier's rail division since November 2019.
The change comes as the company continues to recover from bankruptcy protection, which it entered in 2019.
Last month, Bombardier announced a $250m (£180m) deal to supply aircraft to NetJets.

"With the turnaround plan delivered, the company positioned to execute its growth plan and the rail business back on a path to profitability, the board has determined that this is the right time to transition to a new CEO," Mr Bellemare, 60, said in a statement.

JP Morgan has admitted for the first time that two of its predecessor firms owned slaves in the past.
The bank said its two largest antecedents, JPMorgan Chase and Chase Manhattan, had owned slaves prior to the Civil War and used discriminatory practices against them.
The admission came in a letter to Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who had queried the bank's ties to slavery.
The disclosure is extremely rare for a modern American bank, and reflects a growing willingness of companies to confront their historical ties to slavery.

Last year, New York Life, the nation's largest life insurance company, released a report on its historical ties to slavery, saying that many of its founders were slave owners and that the insurer profited from the slave economy through investments in slave-owning clients.

In its letter to Senator Wyden, JP Morgan said that its predecessor firms had owned at least 267 slaves, and that a pair of plantations the banks owned used the forced labor of slaves to produce cotton and rice.
The bank said that many of the slaves were sold in order to keep the plantation running, a common practice at the time.
The letter also detailed the ways in which JP Morgan's predecessor firms used discriminatory practices against African Americans, including denying them mortgages and loans.
The bank said it would donate more than $5 million to organizations dedicated to helping African Americans.
In a statement, JP Morgan said that the revelations were "extremely disappointing" but that the bank was "proud of the actions" it was taking to address them.
"We understand that our firm's history is linked to some shameful aspects of America's past," the bank said.
India's Deccan Aviation has signed a $1.8bn (£1.1bn) deal to sell a stake in itself to US-based private equity firm General Atlantic.

The head of the UN's food security agency has warned that billions of dollars of subsidies for fossil fuels are putting healthy food out of the reach of millions of people.
Qu Dongyu, director-general of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), said the subsidies were skewing markets and harming farmers.
He said energy prices were affecting the cost of fertilisers, pesticides and farming equipment.
Mr Dongyu called for the reform of energy subsidies to help protect farmers and consumers.
His comments came as the FAO released its annual State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report.
It showed that global hunger remains higher than before the Covid-19 pandemic, with around 1 in 10 people - 680 million - going hungry.
The report said hunger had increased in around 40 countries last year, with acute hunger rising in Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Haiti, Somalia and Sudan.
It also warned that other forms of malnutrition - such as obesity - were on the rise, with nearly a billion people overweight.
Mr Dongyu said the cost of fossil fuels was making it impossible for many people to maintain a healthy diet.
"Forty percent of the world's population cannot afford a healthy diet and healthy diets are getting more and more expensive," he said.

"This is not only a crisis of food affordability, but it is also a crisis of affordability of healthy diets and the cost of energy, the cost of fertilisers, the cost of pesticides, the cost of equipment, the cost of logistics and these are all converging and affecting each other.

"

He said the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine - which together account for about 30% of global wheat exports - had played a role in increasing food prices.
The war has also affected fertiliser prices, as Russia is a major exporter of natural gas, which is used to produce fertiliser.
Mr Dongyu called for an end to "distorted and harmful" subsidies for fossil fuels that were benefiting big businesses, and for the money to instead be used to help farmers and consumers.
He said there was a need to support small farmers, who produce most of the world's food and are most vulnerable to food price hikes.
The FAO chief said it was important to ensure farmers received a fair price for what they produced to avoid another "food crisis".

The Securities and Exchange Commission has charged Kansas City-based asset management firm Waddell & Reed with "massive failures" in its handling of mutual funds, according to a lawsuit filed in US District Court.
The regulator's complaint centres on how Waddell & Reed managed a portfolio of complex mortgage securities in a series of mutual funds it offered to investors.

"

Waddell & Reed manages the Near-Term Tax-Free Fund and the Intermediate Tax-Free Fund, which together held more than $2.4bn in assets as of mid-2007.

Ibrahim told the BBC that the EU had raised about $2 trillion in the past seven years by issuing bonds on the capital markets.

Ibrahim, a Sudanese-British mobile phone entrepreneur who made his fortune in Africa, said the continent needed to be more ambitious.
"It's a question of political will and understanding the importance of our continents developing together.

The scheme, which was supposed to start on Friday, would have charged drivers of non-electric vehicles 3 yuan (£0.32; $0.43) each time they entered the district.

Many also questioned why two-wheeled motorbikes were not included in the plan.
"I thought Beijing was about to become a world city, but it turns out we're still living in a feudal society where the rich get special treatment," one person wrote on China's Twitter-like Weibo.

Drivers entering the area in Beijing's east would have had to pay the charge every working day.
The city government says the fees were intended to reduce traffic congestion and pollution in the area.
But the plan quickly sparked an online backlash, with many complaining that they were being charged for going to work.
On Sunday, a group of a few dozen people gathered at a major road in the CBD to protest the plan, according to a photo blog on Sina Weibo.
The blogger said that some protesters were taken away by police.
The city's government announced on Tuesday that the plan had been suspended and that the policy would be revised.

"After listening to opinions…the relevant plan shall be thoroughly revised, and the revision shall be reported to the standing committee of the municipal people's congress for decision," a statement published online said.
The statement also said that the government would crack down on "maliciously fabricating rumours and causing chaos".
But suspending the plan has not quelled all the anger, with many Beijingers complaining that they still had no solution for parking in the area.
"Now I'm happy that the policy has been cancelled, but where are we supposed to park?"

Parmalat filed a lawsuit against the banks in 2011, but a number of legal issues meant that it has only now got to court.
The company is seeking €480m in damages.

The company alleges that this was part of a larger plan to short-sell its stock "to buy it back later at a lower price".
Parmalat has also accused the banks of "disseminating false information" to clients and shareholders about the company's financial health "in order to justify their conduct".
The dairy group ran into trouble in 2003 after revealing that it had found a €4bn hole in its finances.
This led to the bankruptcy of its Finanziaria Nazionale unit and the jailing of its founder, Tanzi.

Japan's economy has shrunk in the last quarter, ending more than a year of growth as rising prices and falling exports hit activity.
The world's third-largest economy contracted by 0.2% in the three months to the end of September, compared with the previous quarter.
That ended a streak of eight consecutive quarters of growth, as the country recovered from the economic hit it took from the pandemic.
However, Japan has been hit by rising costs for raw materials and fuel, which has pushed up prices.
And analysts say the country has been hit by a combination of weakening global demand and the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, as well as the war in Ukraine.
Capital expenditure, which is generally a good indicator of how businesses expect the economy to perform in the future, also increased by 1.1%.
However, households and businesses are under pressure from rising prices, with the country's core consumer price index (CPI) rising by 3% in September, the fastest pace since 2008.
Meanwhile, exports of goods and services fell by 1.1% in September, the biggest fall since March 2021.

Swedish appliance maker Electrolux is to cut thousands of jobs in Europe over the next two years as it shifts production to Hungary and Thailand.

Electrolux, which is based in Stockholm, said it would close a refrigerator factory in Motala, Sweden, and consolidate production at a facility in Hungary.
It also plans to move the production of oven doors to Thailand.
The company said it was taking the measures to adapt to changes in the market and improve its competitiveness.

Still, the company has seen rising profits in recent months, thanks in part to strong sales in North America and Asia.

The dollar jumped and US bond yields surged on Thursday after data showed that the US economy added far more jobs than expected in January, while wages recorded their largest annual increase in four decades, sparking worries about inflation.

The employment report added to indications that the world's biggest economy is recovering from the coronavirus pandemic, but it also raised the prospect of sharply higher interest rates coming sooner than thought.

Financial markets had been expecting several interest rate rises this year, but the strong jobs data pointed to the need for tighter monetary policy, which tends to push up bond yields and boost the dollar.
The figures raised concerns because the large increase in wages could fuel inflation, as companies may have to pay more to hire workers.
Annual wage growth accelerated to 5.7% in January from 4.4% in December, the largest increase since June 1982, the Labour Department said.
But the data was collected before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which has driven up oil prices and added to concerns about inflation.
The strong jobs report could make the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, even more hawkish, analysts said.
"This is going to be rocket fuel for Fed tightening expectations," said Brian Coulton, an economist at Fitch Ratings.
The prospect of faster rate rises pushed up the dollar's value against other major currencies, as it tends to attract investors seeking a higher return on their money.
The dollar index, which measures the currency against six major rivals, was up 0.8% on the day.
The 10-year US Treasury yield, which tends to move in the opposite direction to the price, was up sharply at 2.14% compared with just 1.92% late on Tuesday.
The two-year yield, which is more sensitive to interest rate expectations, also jumped, rising to 1.62% from 1.44% on Tuesday.

US consumer confidence up - but spending trends cautious

The Conference Board's monthly consumer confidence survey points to improved confidence in the US during December, albeit at a slightly slower pace.
The index stands at 115.8, down from 117.5 in November, but above market expectations of 111.
"Consumers are entering 2023 with stout savings, the job market is robust, and inflation is moderating," said Conference Board chief economist Lynn Franco.
"Given these foundational factors, we anticipate that consumers will continue to spend, though perhaps at a slower pace than in 2022," she added.
The survey measuring current economic conditions stood at 144.4, down from 153.8 in November.
The expectations index stood at 99.7, up from 96.4.
The numbers point to improved confidence in the US economy, with consumers more optimistic about the future, although inflation remains a concern.
However, the survey also showed that while confidence improved, consumer spending trends remained cautious.

The percentage of consumers planning to make a major purchase in the next six months fell to 12.1 percent, while those intending to purchase a car stood at 9.6 percent, down from 10.6 percent in November.
The survey also showed that consumer expectations for inflation over the next 12 months stood at 6.7 percent, down from 7.3 percent in November, but still high.
The Conference Board's survey is conducted monthly and measures consumer attitudes on the current economy and future expectations.
The latest report shows that while confidence improved, consumers remain cautious about their spending habits as they continue to feel the impact of high inflation.

Data from Chile's Copper Commission, known as Cochilco, shows the country produced some 5.6 million tonnes of copper in 2021, up from 5.2 million tonnes in 2020.
The boost was driven by Chilean mines such as Escondida, which recorded a 22% increase in production compared with 2020, and Collahuasi, which saw output rise by more than third.

But Cochilco said that output at the world's biggest copper mine, Escondida - which accounts for 7% of global copper production - would fall by more than 43,000 tonnes this year, to 1.48 million tonnes, because of the lowering of operational parameters.
It did not give a reason.

A number of mines in Chile were also affected by protests and wildfires last year.

British drug giant GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) has announced plans to sell a cheaper version of its HIV treatment in Africa.
The company said it would offer a version of its bestselling HIV drug, Epivir, at a lower cost in all least 70 countries.
The drug will be sold for about $700 per year, compared to $10,000 for the original version in the United States.
GSK said it was responding to criticism that it was not doing enough to increase access to its drugs in the developing world.
The company said it planned to "take innovative approaches to help reduce the impact of HIV/AIDS".
The cheaper version of Epivir will be available in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
These regions account for about 95% of all HIV infections worldwide.
GSK is also donating large quantities of the drug Combivir to the United Nations-backed programme to fight HIV/Aids in Africa.
Combivir is a combination of Epivir and another GSK drug, Zovirax.
A tsunami warning has been issued for banks in Sri Lanka after fishermen reported seeing a large wave off the country's coast, the island's navy said.
The warning came after fishermen in northwestern Sri Lanka reported seeing a sudden rise in the water level early on Friday, the navy said in a statement.
Navy spokesman Indika de Silva said that the island's naval forces were ordered to evacuate families of naval personnel residing in coastal areas.
The tsunami warning centre in Colombo also issued an advisory notice to India's southern states of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh to keep fishermen out of the water.
There were no immediate reports of damage or casualties.

A major MCI shareholder is suing to stop the telecommunications company's $37 billion takeover by Verizon Communications (VZ), arguing that the deal undervalues MCI and robs shareholders of a better offer.

The complaint, filed late Friday in Delaware Chancery Court on behalf of shareholder Robert M. Wason, claims that Verizon and MCI violated their fiduciary duties by entering into the merger agreement.
The proposed deal, which was announced Oct. 7, has already been approved by the MCI board and is expected to close by the middle of next year, pending regulatory and shareholder approval.
Mr. Wason, who owns 2.3 million shares of MCI, is seeking an injunction to prevent the companies from proceeding with the merger until they disclose more information about the deal's terms.

His lawyer, David A. Katz, a partner with Cohen Milstein Hausfeld & Toll PLLC, said Monday that they believe MCI's management orchestrated a bidding process that effectively shut out other potential buyers and forced shareholders to accept an unfair price.
"Our allegation is that this process was rigged from the beginning," Mr. Katz said.
"The merger agreement contains a $750 million termination fee, which is so high that no other bidder could afford to top Verizon's offer and still expect to make a profit.

"

An MCI spokesman wasn't immediately available for comment.
Mr. Wason's lawsuit comes after another MCI shareholder, the University of Illinois Board of Trustees, filed a similar complaint against MCI and Verizon in Illinois state court last week.
The University of Illinois, which owns more than 400,000 shares of MCI, is seeking an injunction to stop the merger, as well as unspecified damages.
Like Mr. Wason, the university claims that MCI and Verizon violated their fiduciary duties by agreeing to the deal without shopping around for the highest bidder.
MCI has said it believes the complaints are without merit.
Verizon declined to comment on the lawsuits.
One of the largest state-owned companies in China has reported a significant increase in profits, despite a slowdown in the country's economy.
The electrical equipment maker, Yangtze Electric, said its net profit for the first nine months of 2022 rose 112% to 31.5bn yuan ($4.6bn: £3.7bn).
The company benefited from rising prices of its products, including transformers and electrical relays, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
But it is not the only company in China to have experienced a boost to its bottom line.
Other major state-owned firms, including PetroChina and Sinopec, have reported strong financial results.
Meanwhile, China's economy, the second biggest in the world, has been hit by months of Covid lockdowns and a real estate crisis.
Growth is expected to slow to 3.3% this year, according to the IMF, down from 8.1% in 2021.
But analysts say that China's economy could be worse had it not been for the stimulus packages introduced by Beijing.
Recent data has also suggested that the country's economy may be starting to recover.
China's trade data for October, released last week, showed that exports rose faster than expected, while imports slowed but beat forecasts.
Continental warned on Thursday it may run out of cash as the German automotive supplier continued to struggle with a global shortage of semiconductors, which has led to a sharp fall in production.
The news weighed on Continental's shares, which were down 6.5% in early trade, wiping off about €1.6bn ($1.8bn) of the company's market value.
Chief Financial Officer Wolfgang Schäfer said Continental had seen a significant recovery in its operations in the second quarter as lockdowns were eased, including in key markets such as China.
But he said that recovery had stalled in the third quarter due to the shortage of semiconductors, as well as rising costs and supply chain problems that were causing delays in production.
"We currently expect that we will generate positive cash flow in the third quarter, but that this will be significantly lower than in the second quarter," Schäfer said.
"We are doing everything in our power to ensure that Continental does not run out of cash.
At the same time, we are making advances in securing additional financing for the company.

"

 Continental, which is due to report third-quarter results on Oct. 28, had cash and cash equivalents of €4.3bn ($4.9bn) at the end of June.
The automotive industry has been hit by a global shortage of semiconductors, which are key components in electronic devices used in cars, including power steering and cruise control systems.
The problem has led major carmakers such as Volkswagen, Toyota and General Motors to cut production and warn of a significant hit to their sales and profits.
At the same time, automakers are facing rising costs for raw materials such as copper, as well as higher shipping costs.

Continental, which is due to spin off its interior unit, is looking to save costs by cutting jobs and investing in new technologies such as hydrogen fuel cells and battery management systems for electric vehicles.
The company has said it expects the global semiconductor shortage to remain a major challenge through 2023.
The German economy has avoided a recession after official data showed it grew by 1% in the third quarter of this year.
Quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.5% in the three months to September, beating expectations of a 0.4% contraction.
It comes after Germany's economy shrank by 0.2% in the three months to June, and by 1.2% in the second quarter.
The data provided a boost to the new German government, which has been in office for just over a week.
One factor in the rebound was likely the reduction in VAT - Germany's version of sales tax - which took effect in July, experts said.
The reduction in VAT - from 19% to 16% - was part of a package of measures announced in September to help protect Germany's economy as it faces soaring energy prices and supply chain problems.
While the tax cut gave a short-term boost, it will start to reverse next year, and Germany faces a long-term challenge of adapting its economy as it moves away from coal and towards green energy.
In response to the data, Chancellor Olaf Scholz - who took office last week - said the recession had been averted "despite major challenges".
"We have managed to achieve positive growth in both industry and private consumption," he added.
Mr Scholz also said that his government would "do everything necessary" to ensure the German economy continues to recover.
The Venezuelan government has started to identify "idle" farms in the country in a bid to boost food production in the crisis-hit nation.
Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez announced the measure following a meeting with farmers and producers.
She said the "identification week" would help the government take back land and give it to "productive" farmers.
Many farms have been abandoned during the economic crisis, as farmers cannot afford to produce.
Ms Rodriguez said the land would be given to "those who work it, so that we can all have something to eat".
She added that the government would "not allow the country to be left without food".
The identification process began on Monday and is due to end on 15 April.
Official figures released last year showed that Venezuela produced less than half the quantity of maize and rice it did eight years earlier.
Maize production fell from 163,000 hectares (613 sq km) in 2010 to 72,000 hectares in 2017, while rice production dropped from 116,000 hectares to 49,000 hectares in the same period.
The drop has been attributed to a lack of fertiliser, pesticides and seeds, as well as a shortage of petrol needed to operate farm machinery.
What's more, US sanctions prevent Venezuela from selling its crude oil to repay debts to China for farming equipment.
The move to take back unproductive land comes after the government last year launched an "agricultural offensive" aimed at increasing domestic production of corn, rice and vegetables.
In January, Agriculture Minister Luis Fernando Benazero said that in 2018, some 3.3m hectares of agricultural land had been identified, of which only 800,000 were being used.
The figure, he said, was increasing month by month.

Mr. Maduro said the company had not met its commitments to develop the project.

Ukraine has trimmed its target for privatisation revenues this year by more than half to $1.5bn (£1.2bn), according to the ministry of economy.
The aim had earlier been set at $3.7bn.
There are few investors keen on Ukraine's state-owned enterprises.
The ministry said it had revised its targets lower, because plans to sell large state assets had failed to materialise.
It is also looking to speed up the sale of smaller assets.
"We are not going to wait for the big privatisations.
Small and medium-sized privatisations will speed up Ukraine's economic growth," said Economy Minister Yulia Svyrydenko.

Privatisation proceeds aimed at helping Ukraine recover from war

The ministry said it was retaining its goal of raising $281m from the sale of state-owned stakes in agricultural firms.
That would include the sale of 100% plus one share in agricultural company Mriya.
The ministry said it was also aiming to raise $322m through the sale of other state assets, including aircraft engine maker Motor Sich and Ukraine's largest chemical plant, Azot.
However, Ukraine's previous attempts to sell state enterprises have largely failed because of investor wariness about corruption and the country's poor business climate.
Last year, a deal to sell Ukraine's largest lender, Privatbank, to the state fell apart because of legal challenges.
The war has also disrupted Ukraine's economy and industrial production has plummeted, making it difficult to find willing investors for state enterprises.
Many of Ukraine's state-owned enterprises were built up under former President Viktor Yanukovych, whose regime was ousted in 2014.
Mr Yanukovych amassed huge debts, leaving the enterprises indebted and in need of repair.
Ukraine's government has been trying to overhaul the state-owned sector since a debt crisis erupted in 2015.
But progress has been slow.
Ask Jeeves has launched a new service which offers small businesses affordable and simple internet advertising.
The company said its new service, Ask Ad Solutions, fills a gap in the market.
"Many small and medium sized businesses have been left behind by the complexities and costs associated with online advertising," said Greg Sterling from the Interactive Advertising Bureau.
"While search engines, online directories and other web sites offer a range of advertising options, they are still difficult and too expensive for many small businesses," he added.
Ask Jeeves said it had developed its new service after research revealed many small businesses felt "left out" of online advertising.

"We saw a need to streamline and simplify the process, making it easy and cost-effective for local businesses to tap into the power of internet search and attract new customers," said Brian McAndrews, chief executive of Ask Jeeves.
"We believe this service will be particularly appealing to the vast majority of local businesses that do not have websites," he added.
Ask Ad Solutions allows businesses to create and place ads on the Ask Jeeves website, and appears alongside search results when users look for a particular product or service in a specific region.
The ads can be updated daily, to feature special offers or to announce new services.
Mr Sterling said small businesses had been "underserved" by the online advertising industry.
"Most local businesses don't have websites, and the cost and complexity of buying online ads has been a barrier for them," he said.
But other experts have warned that small firms could still be put off by the cost of maintaining a campaign.
"The reality is that maintaining a consistent and effective ad campaign, even with these simplified tools, requires time and money," said Kate Morris, chief executive of Buy.com.
"Until there is better education on how to market online, many small businesses will continue to struggle with the idea of investing in a medium they don't understand and can't quantify," she added.
Deutsche Boerse has reported a record first-quarter net profit of 699m euros ($807m; £626m), as volatility related to Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up revenues.
The German stock exchange's quarterly result was up by nearly a third on the same period a year earlier.
Chief executive Theodor Weimer said the firm was boosting its dividend by 23% due to the strong performance.
Shares in the group, which owns the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, rose 2.5% on the news.
The exchange has benefited from trading surges since Russia's invasion, as investors have reacted to the resulting economic uncertainty.

Volumes on Deutsche Boerse's Eurex derivatives exchange, where investors can bet on price movements in shares, bonds or indexes, were up 41% on the year earlier.

EBIT, which strips out exceptional items and financial derivatives, rose to 723m euros from 570m euros a year earlier.
The company, which in March reached a $5.2bn deal to buy the London Stock Exchange Group, said it was sticking to its full-year guidance.

A statement released by the FA said it would "continue to monitor the situation" alongside the EFL but that the consortium had asked for its "positive consideration" in respect of the change of control and ownership conditions of the league.
In a statement released by the club, Sunderland said discussions with the consortium had been "positive" and that "further announcements will be made in due course".

The BBC is aware of several further interested parties, both in the UK and abroad, who are awaiting further developments.

The club, who have been in existence for 134 years, were relegated from the Championship last season with a -26 points deduction for breaching EFL rules on spending on player wages and transfer fees.
They have suffered from turmoil on and off the field in recent years, with five managers passing through the Stadium of Light in the space of three years.
At the end of August, they were given a 15-point deduction for being in breach of the EFL's profitability and sustainability rules.
The Wearsiders began the season with a 12-point deduction, which was halved following an appeal, and subsequently sacked manager Jack Ross on the eve of the campaign.
Former England manager Steve McClaren subsequently took charge but was sacked after less than three months in charge, with Andrew Taylor placed in temporary charge.
The club's owner, Ellis Short, announced in June that he was willing to consider offers for the club.

The American businessman, who has been the club's owner for 10 years, said he had hoped to sell the club to new owners by the end of the season, but that he had been unable to find buyers "who share my aspirations or who are prepared to meet my valuation".

A judge has fined US agrochemical giant Monsanto $1.5m for bribing Argentine officials.
Monsanto pleaded guilty to the bribery charges in March.
US District Judge Jeffery White also fined the company's former head of global sustainability, Hugh Grant, $78,000 for his role in the scheme.
According to the Justice Department, Grant authorized a $50,000 bribe to an official in Argentina's agriculture ministry in order to preserve commercial permits for Monsanto.
The company also admitted to transferring $200,000 to a former official in Argentina's environmental and sustainable development ministry.
"Monsanto chose to illegally bribe foreign officials instead of complying with antitrust laws," said Assistant Attorney General Brian Benczkowski.
"This behaviour threatens our system of international law and commerce and we will hold accountable companies that corrupt the integrity of foreign elections and democratic institutions."
In a statement, Monsanto said it took "full responsibility" for its employees' actions and said the fines would not be passed on to its customers.
"This resolution with the DOJ concludes this investigation," the company said.
"Monsanto strongly opposes bribery of any government official and has taken steps to ensure that such behaviour does not occur.

"

The Justice Department said Grant had authorized bribes to Argentine officials in exchange for inside information on pesticide regulations and the timing of government actions.
According to the department, Grant and other Monsanto executives used an intermediary to provide $70,000 in bribes to the official in the agriculture ministry.
The company also admitted to transferring $200,000 to the former official in the environmental and sustainable development ministry.
That money was to be used for environmental consulting, but the official instead kept $98,000 for himself and shared the rest with other government officials, the Justice Department said.

House prices suffered a festive fall as inflation and rising interest rates put the brakes on the property market, according to an industry survey.
The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) said its monthly price balance fell to -44 in December, its lowest level since May 2020.
It said that demand from potential buyers and the number of properties on the market were also flat.
The survey comes a day after data from lender Nationwide showed a surprise pick-up in UK house prices in November, but that was before the Bank of England's recent interest rate rises.
Rics said that, taking into account its monthly data going back to 2006, house prices were now close to "peak-to-trough" trends.
The organisation's chief economist, Simon Rubin, said the market had seen a "significant shift" in the last three months.
"Following a long period of imbalance between demand and supply, the recent rise in interest rates has helped tilt the balance more towards homeowners," he said.
"Going forward, we expect that trend to continue, but it remains too early to say if this will be reflected in a material decline in house prices."
The trend was reflected in all parts of the UK, with London seeing a particularly sharp drop, the survey suggested.
Mr Rubin said that, in the capital, prices were falling at a faster pace than elsewhere in the country "due to the combination of base rate hikes and a shift in investor activity".
He said that, while London house prices had surged in the years after the global financial crisis due to demand from investors, that had now changed.
"Following a trend which began last year, investor demand has now turned into a negative, dragging down activity levels and prices," he added.
But estate agents also reported that buyers were still in the market in December, despite the traditional Christmas slowdown.
The report said that 44% of respondents had seen an increase in the number of properties for sale, while 11% said that figure had decreased.
That was the lowest proportion of respondents reporting a fall in supply since January 2015, it said.
Standard Life has become the latest insurer to cut policy bonuses in response to new regulations that are due to come into force next year.
The changes, which will impact about 7,000 with-profit policyholders, will see the company's bonus rate fall by about 1% for its pension and bond products.
Standard Life said the move would ensure its financial strength following Brexit.
The changes will take effect from December.
The company joins a number of other insurers that have cut bonuses recently, including Aviva, LV= and Aegon.
Standard Life's move comes after the regulator, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), announced plans to limit the bonuses that can be offered by insurers to policyholders.
The PRA's new rules, which are due to come into force in January, will require insurers to hold more capital in reserve in order to protect policyholders in the event of an emergency.
Standard Life said the changes would not affect its financial strength or its ability to pay claims.

The company said: "As we have consistently said, we must operate a prudent and sustainable with-profits fund, which is appropriately capitalised at all times to ensure we can meet our promises to all our policyholders."

"In response to the PRA's changes, we have conducted a review of our with-profits bonuses and decided to reduce the bonus rate on our pension and bond products."

"This reduction, which is fully reflected in our capital modelling, ensures we maintain our financial strength and ability to pay claims, as well as supporting the long-term interests of all our policyholders."

"We will write to policyholders who are affected by these changes in early December."

Standard Life's with-profits business offers a variety of policies to customers, including life insurance, critical illness cover and pensions.
The with-profits sector has been hit by a number of challenges in recent years, including low interest rates and changing regulations.
These challenges have led to a number of companies cutting bonuses and benefits, and in some cases, closing their with-profits businesses altogether.
Gold prices have dropped to a four-month low after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) announced that it plans to sell more than a third of its gold reserves.
The IMF said it would sell more than $6bn of gold over the next five years to boost its reserves.
Analysts said news of the sale - which comes after the IMF recently sold most of its stake in the BIS - hit sentiment.
Spokeswoman Caroline Atkinson said most of the proceeds from the sale would be used to bolster the IMF's lending capacity.
She said the sale "will contribute to IMF's ability to lend freely in all its currencies".
Gold prices hit their lowest level since early November, dropping below the key $1,200 an ounce mark.
They were trading at $1,194.90 an ounce in New York.
In late trade on Thursday, spot gold was down 0.5% at $1,197.70 an ounce.

"The market was already ripe for a sell-off on the back of a strong dollar and rising bond yields, and the news from the IMF provided additional impetus for the sell-off," said Capital Economics analyst Ross Strachan.
The IMF said it would sell 13 million ounces of gold, worth about $6.6bn at current prices, although it did not reveal which vaults it plans to empty.
The fund said it would only sell in the market "when conditions are favourable, and with prior transparent notice to the market".
The IMF has been selling gold regularly since 2009, and has already reduced its holdings from 94.5 million ounces to around 38 million ounces.
However, it has come under fire for continuing to sell despite a rising gold price.

"The IMF selling even a small portion of its gold reserves makes the headline 'IMF sells gold' irresistible for the media, and will immediately create concerns over central bank gold selling and long-term sentiment," said Gain Capital analyst Edward Meir.

"

The EU's newest members are helping to underpin growth in the bloc, although Britain's economic output lags behind, according to a report from the European Commission.

The annual report on the evolution of the European Union's economy said that 13 of the EU's newest members, mostly from eastern Europe, had raised their output by an average of 3.6% a year between 2004 and 2010.
That compared with average growth of 2.2% in the EU's original 15 members before Greece and Portugal joined in 1981.
Seven of the 13 new members saw their economies grow by more than 3% a year between 2004 and 2010, led by Lithuania, which saw annual growth of 7.6%.

The report said that several factors explained the new members' stronger performance, including reforms and lower unemployment rates, as well as the fact that many had a lot of ground to make up after years of stagnation.
Bulgaria and Romania joined the EU in 2007, and Poland, the largest of the new members, joined in 2004.
The report said there were also indications that the investment rate and productivity were gradually increasing in the new member states, although they were still below the average of the EU-15.
Croatia is set to become the EU's 28th member on 1 July.

The report said that the eurozone was outperforming the EU as a whole, but noted that Britain continued to lag behind, with growth forecast at 1.2% this year and 1.7% in 2014, compared with average growth across the EU of 1.6% in 2013 and 2.0% in 2014.
Olivier Blanchard, the International Monetary Fund's chief economist, said that the British economy's weakness was among the biggest surprises of the global crisis.
"In 2003, everybody agreed that Britain had managed the macroeconomic policies better than any other country in the EU," he said.
"Ten years later, it is Britain that has suffered the largest output losses, and the only one among the G7 economies that is yet to return to pre-crisis output levels."
The report said that Britain's output was still almost 3% below its previous path.

Archbishop Francis George, who heads the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, on Sunday criticised the cost of the Iraq war as a "moral disaster".
The archbishop said that the war had done "unthinkable harm" to the US economy.
The cost of the Iraq war has been estimated at $450bn (£290bn).
The archbishop was speaking at the University of Notre Dame in South Bend, Indiana.
He criticised both main US political parties for getting the nation into a "terrible bind" on the war.
He said that the US had "squandered" a projected half-trillion dollars on the war.
"The price tag of the Iraq war is not simply the expenditure of public funds, though that is bad enough," he said.
"It is a moral disaster borne by our nation with unfathomable consequences for the poor here and abroad.
The archbishop said that the money spent on the war could have been used to "feed the hungry, shelter the homeless, educate our young people and care for the sick".
He said that the war had done "unthinkable harm" to the US economy and that it had done "irreparable harm" to US credibility abroad.
Archbishop George criticised the administration of President George W Bush for taking the US to war "on what proved to be a false premise".
But he also criticised the Democratic-controlled Congress for not doing more to stop the war.

The UK government will announce a reduction in the legal driving limit for alcohol in England and Wales, the BBC can reveal.
It says the move, to cut the drink-drive limit to 50mg of alcohol per 100ml of blood, will save up to 95 lives a year.
The current limit, of 80mg, is one of the highest in Europe.
The planned change, to take effect in spring 2022, has been welcomed by road safety and medical groups.
But the British Beer and Pub Association said the move would punish responsible drinkers.

The Department for Transport said the reduction would bring England and Wales into line with the other devolved nations of Scotland and Northern Ireland, where the limit was reduced to 50mg in December 2014.
The new limit will apply to motorists in England and Wales who drive on Sunday morning, after a Saturday night out.
The government estimates that the current limit of 80mg sees an estimated 300 people killed in alcohol-related crashes each year.

The decision comes as global inflation - the rate at which prices rise - is soaring, driven up by the war in Ukraine and the pandemic.
Inflation in the UK - as measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) - was 9.1% in the 12 months to May, the highest level for 40 years.
Financial markets had expected UK interest rates to be increased, but by a smaller margin of 0.25%.
The Bank of England said the move was designed to control inflation, by reducing the demand for goods and services.
It said inflation was now the "biggest threat" to the financial stability of the UK.
The Bank also warned that the cost of living was likely to rise further, with inflation expected to be around 9% in the coming months.
It said the increase in the base rate would help to control inflation by making it more expensive for people to borrow money.
This would then reduce the demand for goods and services, which in turn would help to control price rises.
The Bank also said it would continue to monitor the situation and take further action if necessary.
The announcement comes as the UK economy is already facing a slowdown, with the country set to enter a recession later this year.
The increase in the base rate is likely to make it more expensive for people to borrow money, which could lead to a further slowdown in the economy.
However, the Bank of England said it was necessary to take action on inflation now, as it was likely to be "elevated" for the next two years.

"I think people voted for us to keep delivering on that ambitious agenda we set out," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Tory MP Sayeeda Warsi is to stand down at the next general election.
The former cabinet minister announced her decision to step down as MP for Batley and Spen in West Yorkshire following discussions with her family.
The 51-year-old said it had been a "great honour" to serve her constituency.
Warsi became the first Muslim woman to serve in a British cabinet in 2010.
She was appointed by former prime minister David Cameron as minister without portfolio and shadow minister for faith and communities.
"I have decided not to stand at the next general election, although that is some years away," she said.

"That's a decision I have taken in conjunction with my family, particularly as my son is now 10 years old and they should not grow up solely with the weekends as the time they can see their mum."

Warsi was elected to Parliament in 2010, and became the first Muslim woman to serve in a British cabinet, as minister without portfolio and shadow minister for faith and communities.
She stepped down from the frontbench after voting against the government on the issue of airstrikes in Syria in 2015.
She was among several Tory MPs to criticise Boris Johnson over his handling of the partygate scandal earlier this year.
In January, she called for him to resign, saying she was "deeply disturbed" by the behaviour on display in Downing Street.
"The reason you become an MP is to make a difference, that's the only reason you do it," she said in the video statement.
"And when you can no longer make that difference it is time to step back and that is a very difficult decision for any MP to make.

"

Warsi said she did not know what the future held for her, but that she was "excited" by the possibilities.

The father of a controversial play about Adolf Hitler has defended his right to a £20,000 arts grant - despite complaints that it glorifies the Nazi leader.
In January, the Arts Council of Wales gave the money to Jeff James for his play Führer, about the last days of Hitler's life.
The council received 34 complaints - 24 from the public and 10 from artists and academics.
One complainant, the historian Nigel Jones, has asked for the grant to be reinvestigated.
But Mr James, whose company is called No Fit State, said: "I think there's a kind of prurience about the way in which we approach the past."
He said the complaints were a form of censorship and that he was proud of his work.
"I think there's a very strong case for saying that this is a very important part of our recent past and that it deserves to be examined," he said.
"And if it is examined in a popular form, like a play, then I think that is a good thing.

"

Complainant Nigel Jones said he was "astounded" that the Arts Council gave over £20,000 to a play containing such "toxic" material.
"They are glorifying Hitler.
It's madness," he said.

"You have got a situation where you have got a company called No Fit State, fronted by someone called Jeff James, who is apparently doing all sorts of things around the country, who have got very good at manipulating the system.

"

An Arts Council of Wales spokeswoman said the complaint would be "investigated through the appropriate channels" but said the matter was now with its independent adjudication panel.
The spokeswoman said the council had awarded £198,000 from its arts portfolio to No Fit State in the past.
Mr James said any criticism of his past work was "like comparing apples with oranges".
He said: "This is a new play, it hasn't been seen.

How can you possibly censure something that doesn't exist?"

Police have long had the power to shut down pubs, restaurants and leisure centres to prevent crime and anti-social behaviour.
But now they want the ability to shut down shops and businesses too.
Britain's biggest police force, the Metropolitan Police, says it wants to double the number of premises it can close.
It says the powers are a vital tool in preventing serious crime.
But businesses say they are being treated as a soft target.
The Met is seeking to add another 100 closure orders to its existing list of 173, which include pubs, clubs, restaurants and leisure centres.
Superintendent Jane Scotchbrook says the Met is also seeking to extend the scope of the orders to include "any business where the nuisance or annoyance is caused".
"The legislation could be used for any business where we have evidence that it is causing a nuisance or annoyance to members of the public," she said.
"That could be pubs, bars, restaurants, it could be businesses that have a lot of comings and goings, causing anti-social behaviour.
Any business could potentially be included.

"

She said the closure orders, introduced in 2003, had been a "really useful tool" but were under-used.
"They are certainly a last resort.
Officers have to provide evidence that crime is being committed or is likely to be committed and the business owner does have the right to appeal."
But Tony Cohen, national officer for the Federation of Small Businesses, expressed concern about the plans.
"It seems to be the easy option to go for the small businesses which are struggling in any case, rather than going for the big supermarkets which have a lot of causes of crime near them," he said.
"They (small businesses) are not causing crime, they are not encouraging it and many are victimised by it.
I think it is wrong to target them.

"

Supt Scotchbrook said the Met was also seeking to streamline the process which can take up to three months to obtain a closure order.
"That can be too long.
By the time you have gone through that process, the problem business can be defunct because it has had its licence removed or because the crime has moved on," she said.

Mr Chirac made the comment at a news conference in Paris after talks with Germany's Chancellor, Gerhard Schroeder.
The UK currently enjoys the largest rebate of all the EU member states, worth about £2.5bn ($4.5bn) a year.
London has always said it will not countenance any change to the arrangement, which was negotiated by the then Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher, in 1984.
Mr Chirac said the issue would be among those to be addressed at a European summit in December.
"Concerning the British question, the British rebate, it is obvious that this question is one that upsets a number of people, namely the other members states of the European Union," he said.

"Everybody understands that the United Kingdom when it joined the Community had a special situation, that certain efforts were demanded of it and that consequently advantages were granted to it on this point.
"But nowadays, there is a different situation and it seems to us necessary to re-examine the question of the British rebate in the context of the preparation of the 2007-13 financial perspective.

"

Mr Chirac said the issue would be on the agenda at the EU summit in Brussels on 16 and 17 December.
But a UK government spokesman said there was "no discussion" about the rebate and pointed out that it was enshrined in the EU's own treaties.
"It is not up for negotiation," he said.

His period as prime minister is generally considered to have been unsuccessful, and he was defeated by Mrs Thatcher in the general election of 1979.

"

The United Nations has told the UK it "discriminated" against Roma migrants during the pandemic by failing to provide any accommodation or support for them.
The UK had argued such provisions would encourage others to make dangerous journeys.
The UN's anti-racism panel, CERD, made the ruling after examining evidence from the UK, which argued its policies were a proportionate response to the pandemic.
The UK's delegation to the committee in Geneva argued the government had "gone above and beyond" its obligations to protect the group.

But in a decision released on Monday, the UN's Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) said the UK had "failed" to provide any accommodation or support to Roma during the pandemic.
It also criticised the government for its "overly broad" use of public health orders which allowed local authorities to close down campsites and evict Roma.
The UN said it was "particularly concerned" that such measures resulted in the forced eviction of Roma, "exposing them to great hardship and distress and impacting their right to health".

Like many others, I remember exactly where I was and what I was doing when I first heard about HIV and AIDS.
I was in high school, and for myself and my peers, it was a crisis occurring among adults that felt very distant.
In the decades since, I've worked with a series of HIV/AIDS organisations, most recently the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
From that vantage point, I have seen the crisis unfold and watched the remarkable progress that has been made to overcome it.
I remember speaking to a colleague working in Swaziland, one of the most HIV-affected countries in the world, about the fear that HIV causes, and how that thwarts efforts to fight it.
And yet, despite the terrible toll HIV has taken, the tide has turned.
The number of new HIV infections has dropped by one-third since 2000; the number of AIDS-related deaths has fallen by one-half.
These achievements did not happen spontaneously.
They are the result of long-term, well-funded, committed responses, both in terms of policy and funding.
But today, against the backdrop of the Covid-19 pandemic, that progress is at risk.

According to UNAIDS, the global response to HIV/AIDS has already been disrupted by Covid-19, with supply chain disruptions, access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) and HIV services, as well as interruptions in prevention programmes, including suspension of sexual education programmes and the cancellation of mass testing campaigns.
The fund has calculated that Covid-19 will reverse the progress against HIV/AIDS by at least seven years.
Seven years of progress that has been painstakingly achieved through the concerted efforts of governments, private sector and civil society.
That is unconscionable.
As the Covid-19 pandemic waxes and wanes, we must not allow HIV to stage a comeback.
The fight against HIV/AIDS must not fall off the agenda.
Instead, we must redouble our efforts to keep the momentum going - governments, the private sector, civil society and donors.
The Global Fund has just hosted its sixth replenishment conference where we asked donors to step up to ensure the fight against HIV/AIDS remains a priority.
We are grateful to the United Kingdom for its increased pledge.
As the world refocuses on Covid-19, we must not forget the ongoing fight against HIV/AIDS.

What high-definition will do to DVDs

If you have a library of DVDs, you might want to think about transferring them to a hard drive before the discs become obsolete.
It's happening already.
Even a modestly-sized HD television will reveal dust particles on the DVD and the blocks of pixels that make up the image.
The picture is often blurred, and there's a softness to the image that is absent from high-definition (HD).
This is not the fault of the DVD format, which is of excellent quality, particularly for the standard definition (SD) television sets for which they were designed.
It's the television that is at fault.
The picture information stored on a DVD is a series of dots, known in the trade as pixels.
In SD, there are 352,000 pixels, or blocks of colour, across the screen, while in HD there are 1,920,000.
That's more than five times as many.
A DVD player sends the information on the disc to a television at a constant rate of 25 megabits per second.
This information includes not only the pixels but also other data, such as sound.
To accommodate all this information, the data is compressed.
When it is decompressed inside the television, the picture is reconstructed from the dots.
Each dot relates to a point on the screen where a beam of light - a pixel - is required.
The position of the pixel and its colour is calculated from the dot.
That's fine for SD television, which has fewer pixels and therefore less information to handle.
But with HD, the television has to calculate almost six times as many positions for the pixels on the screen, and thus needs much more information, or data, from the disc.
The result is that a DVD will not give you a high-definition picture, however good the disc might be.
Some new machines are advertised as up-converting your DVDs, giving you a higher resolution picture.
In fact, they are simply sharpening the image, and the result is often disappointing.
A sharp, crisp HD image is a beauty to behold - but it needs a lot of data.
To get it, you will need to think about copying your DVDs on to a hard drive and compressing them to a format that can be played back through an HD television set.

DVD review: Spider-Man 2

Released: 26 April 2004
Director: Sam Raimi
Stars:

Tobey Maguire, Kirsten Dunst, Alfred Molina

In this eagerly awaited sequel, Spider-Man (Maguire) is struggling to come to terms with his dual life as a super hero and as Peter Parker, ordinary teenager.
Things look promising when he meets up with M.J. (Kirsten Dunst) at a party but his hopes are dashed when she fails to show up at the next couple of meetings.
It becomes apparent that she is being forced by her possessive and controlling father (Alfred Molina) to end the relationship.

This is the least of Spider-Man's problems, as he faces a powerful new foe, Doctor Octopus (Molina again), who has harnessed the power of four genetically modified tentacles that he controls with his mind.
The good doctor is plotting to steal a cache of missiles from the launch site at Coney Island and bring them into the city.

As Spider-Man battles to save innocent lives, he is forced to ask himself what it is that really matters: his dedication to being a super hero, or his love for M.J.

This is a hugely enjoyable adventure, with breathtaking action sequences and a genuine emotional core.
The spider suit has been redesigned and allows for even more flexibility than before, while the introduction of organic web shooters is a welcome addition.
Doctor Octopus is an awesome opponent, and the climactic battle between the two in an arena of swinging chains is a masterpiece of special effects.
The dialogue is snappy, and there are some nice comic touches, as when Spider-Man wraps a subway robber in web and gives him a hug, telling him to "take a chill pill".

Maguire makes an engaging hero, investing Peter Parker with humility and self-doubt, and there is strong support from Dunst, who manages to overcome the clunky script and deliver a credible performance as M.J.
However, it is Molina who really stands out, investing the doctor with a malevolence that is genuinely chilling.

The disk includes a number of interesting featurettes, including a look at the development of the story and the effects, a tour of the Spider-Man exhibit at Universal Studios, and a piece on the music.
There is also a trailer for the next installment, Spider-Man 3.
While this is unlikely to convert the sceptics, for fans of the web slinger this is essential viewing.

The Son, which depicts Adam Lanza's 2012 massacre of 26 people in Connecticut, has won a top prize at a controversial film festival in France.

"It's not cutting-edge fiction, it's a documentary.

"

The brothers grew up in the same small town as Lanza and knew his parents.

"It's difficult, it's dangerous, but I believe that our duty is to look at things, to try to understand things, to analyse things, and not to lock ourselves in a kind of self-righteousness where we say 'this is good, this is bad'."

A campaign has been launched to help independent music retailers compete with larger rivals in the digital downloads market.

"It is increasingly difficult for independent retailers to compete against digital downloads from the likes of Amazon and iTunes which are sold below cost price," he said.
"This is particularly difficult for the independent retailer who cannot buy the downloads as cheaply as the multiples can.
"We are levelling the playing field by offering a digital download service to independent retailers at the same price as the multiples.

"

The downloads will be available from 150 independent stores around the UK, with more stores being added to the scheme soon.

"

The BBC should allow more scrutiny of its news output, a House of Lords select committee has said.
The committee suggested the broadcaster could be given a statutory basis to assure its future.
The BBC's outgoing director general, Mark Thompson, told the committee the corporation was "confident" it would survive the digital age.
He said the BBC had a "bright future" as a "major multimedia provider".
But the committee said the BBC would have to demonstrate it was entitled to the £3.6bn licence fee from taxpayers every year.
The BBC's commercial operations, such as BBC Worldwide, should be "more explicitly" separated from its public service activities, said the committee.
The committee's report, entitled "The Future of the BBC", was published on Wednesday.
It said the BBC should be ready to "open up" its news operations to scrutiny and challenge from other media outlets, to demonstrate it was fulfilling its mission.
The committee recognised the BBC was already "under considerable scrutiny", but this should be extended to include other broadcasters and newspapers, to show it was not "dominating" the news agenda.

The report said: "To demonstrate its continuing relevance and value to viewers and listeners, the BBC should be open to as much scrutiny as possible - not merely of its performance, but also of its output.
"This should include scrutiny by other broadcasters and the press, provided that the BBC is not disadvantaged so as to undermine its ability to fulfil its mission.
"However, the committee recognises that the BBC already operates in a highly competitive market and is subject to a high degree of scrutiny and challenge.
"It must be ready to open up further in this area in order to demonstrate that it is fulfilling its mission, and to show that it is entitled to the licence fee."
Mark Thompson told the committee the BBC was "confident" it could survive the digital revolution, with services including the iPlayer and high-definition programming.

A fierce debate is underway in the United States over raising the government's borrowing limit, with potentially severe economic consequences should Congress fail to act.
The US government is bound by law to pay its debts, but a failure to raise the cap on borrowing - known as the debt ceiling - could force it to default on its loans.
That would likely have ripple effects on the global economy and financial markets.
What is the debt ceiling?
In simple terms, the debt ceiling is a cap on how much money the US government is allowed to borrow.
It is an aggregate figure that applies to gross debt, which includes debt that has already been borrowed, as well as any additional debt that has been approved but not yet borrowed.
The US government is the largest borrower in the world and tends to pay relatively low interest rates on its debt because of the US dollar's status as the de facto global currency.
About one-third of the US federal debt is held by foreign investors, while the rest is held by US investors such as the Federal Reserve and individual investors.
When does the US debt ceiling need to be raised?
The US debt ceiling has been temporarily raised several times in recent years, but it has not been permanently lifted.
The US Treasury Department says that the current ceiling of $28.4tn will be reached on 3 August, though analysts believe that it could be breached as soon as next month.
The Biden administration has begun to employ "extraordinary measures" - financial tools that push the deadline back a few months, but do not address the underlying problem.
Without a rise in the debt ceiling, economists say the US government will lack the cash to pay its bills, which could trigger a default on its loans.
What happens if the US defaults on its debt?
This scenario would be unprecedented in US history.
A default could trigger a financial crisis, as investors would lose confidence in the US government's ability to meet its debt obligations.
That could lead to a downgrade in the US government's credit rating, which would increase the cost of borrowing money for the government and consumers.
It could also cause turmoil in financial markets, as investors seek safer investments, and lead to a decline in the value of the US dollar.
The Biden administration and many lawmakers have argued that a default could trigger a recession.

Madrid coach Bernd Schuster has made no secret of his desire to sign Essien, who has three years left on his current Chelsea contract.
He said this week: "Michael Essien is a player that we like and perhaps we can do something.

"

Chelsea manager Jose Mourinho has said he will not stand in the way of any player who wants to leave the club.
But the Portuguese has also said he wants to keep the squad which won the Premier League and League Cup double last season intact.
If a fee, believed to be in the region of £12m, cannot be agreed between the two clubs, Madrid are ready to step aside and allow Essien to join French club Paris St-Germain.
PSG have already had a £16.2m bid for the player rejected by Chelsea, who rate Essien at £22m.
BBC Sport - Tom Holmes scored a try and kicked five conversions as Championship leaders Leicester defeated second-placed Toulouse 31-12 to reach the European Champions Cup quarter-finals.
The Tigers led 19-0 at half-time at Welford Road thanks to tries from Julian Salvi and Greg Bateman and 10 points from the boot of Holmes.
Toulouse came out strongly in the second half, with Maxime Médard scoring their only try, but Holmes' penalty and drop-goal kept them at bay.
A 66th-minute try from Matt Toomua and Holmes' conversion put the game beyond the visitors' reach.
Toulouse's defeat meant they finished runners-up in Pool 3 behind the Tigers, who qualified for the last eight as the best runner-up.
Leinster and Wasps also secured qualification as the top two teams in the other three pools.
The Irish province topped Pool 1 after thrashing Montpellier 47-7 in Dublin, while Wasps beat already-qualified Saracens 23-6 at Allianz Park to finish top of Pool 2.
In the final round of pool games, Ulster defeated Ospreys 13-3 in Belfast to secure a quarter-final berth despite finishing second in Pool 4 behind Saracens.
Former Germany striker Lukas Podolski has tipped his former team-mate Thomas Hitzlsperger to be a success in management.
The ex-Aston Villa and West Ham United midfielder has been linked with the vacant managerial post at Irish side Aston Villa.
German Podolski played with Hitzlsperger at club and international level.
"He's a guy who's very interested in the game, he knows a lot about the game, he's got the personality, he's got the will," Podolski said.
"He's already been a captain at Aston Villa, so he's got the experience.
I think for him
it's maybe the next step
and I think he can do very well.

"

Hitzlsperger, who won 54 caps for Germany and played at the 2006 World Cup, has been without a job since leaving Villa in 2016.
The 38-year-old has been linked with the vacant manager's job at League of Ireland side Dundalk, but Podolski believes his friend would be better off waiting for a job in England or Germany.
"He knows the football, the players, the teams, the clubs, everything about England, and Germany as well," Podolski added.
"I think it's not easy to go to another country and another league and start from scratch.
"He's still young, he's only 38, so he can still wait a little bit and get a good job in England or in Germany and do a good job there."
Middle distance runner Hassane El Guerrouj has announced he will compete in the cross country discipline at the IAAF World Cross Country Championships in March.
The 36-year-old, who won gold in the 1500m and 5000m at the 2004 Olympics, has not competed in the event since he was 16.
He will be one of seven Moroccan runners taking part in the championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland on 30 March.
"I am not coming to Bydgoszcz to win but to gain experience," said El Guerrouj.
"I have been speaking a lot with [coach]
Jama Aden and he is confident I can do well."

El Guerrouj has competed at the Olympics five times and also won four world titles indoors and outdoors over 1,500m as well as the 2003 world title over 5,000m.
He retired from the track in August 2012 after suffering from a series of injuries but returned to competition in March last year and has set a series of world best times in the 3,000m this winter.
"I never thought I would return to competition, never mind cross country," added El Guerrouj, who spent nearly three months last year receiving treatment in Spain for a chronic back problem.
"I am not afraid of the mud and I have always enjoyed cross country.
It is something new and I wanted to have a go."
Should we be worried about "spy chips"?
RFID tags can be used to track people and objects, but experts say concerns about "spy chips" are overblown.
RFID stands for "radio-frequency identification".
Tags are small circuits that can be used to store and remotely retrieve data.
They are usually attached to objects, but can also be implanted in living things.
Experts say RFID holds great promise.
It can be used to track goods in the supply chain, and to streamline inventory.
It is also being used in innovative ways - to prevent poaching of elephants, and to track birds migrating across continents.
But concerns about "spy chips" have been raised in the popular media, and by privacy advocates.
Journalist Katherine Albrecht, who has written extensively on the issue, said the tags could be used to track individuals' movements.
"It's a spy chip - it can be used to track your movements, your behaviour," she told the BBC.
"It can be used to allow retailers to track what you buy, what you wear, how often you wear it, how often you purchase something, what your eating habits are, what your dietary habits are."
Ms Albrecht, who co-authored a book called Spychips, said RFID was an invasion of privacy.
"Your privacy is being violated when this spy chip is placed on products," she said.
"It's essentially a barcode that you can't get off the product, that contains a lot of information about you.

"

But experts say fears about "spy chips" are overblown, and that RFID tags can be encrypted to prevent unauthorised access.
Prof. Peter Ryan, an expert on RFID at the University of Birmingham, said the technology was very limited.
"It's not a transmitter.
It's a transponder.
It has no power of its own, it simply reflects back a signal," he said.

"So if you want to use it to track somebody secretly, you would have to have a reader that was small enough to be concealed on their person, and you'd have to get within 10cm (four inches) of them, which I think is quite difficult."

Former US President George W Bush and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair have agreed on a joint statement about the war in Iraq, describing it as "justified" and "successful".
The two leaders said that Iraq was now safer and that the world was safer without Saddam Hussein in power.
The statement came on the 10th anniversary of the US-led invasion, which toppled Saddam.
Mr Blair said the war had been "better" and "stronger" than people thought it would be.
But critics said the men were "living in cloud cuckoo land".
The statement came after Mr Blair, who was prime minister when the UK joined the US-led invasion, spent about two hours with Mr Bush at the former president's home in Dallas, Texas.

Speaking after the meeting, Mr Blair, who is now an envoy for the Middle East, said the two men "have always been agreed" on the decision to go to war but that he had "never properly explained" his reasoning.
"I think people will see this as a historic statement," he added.
"I can say that the decisions I took, including on Iraq, are ones that I would take again," he said.
Mr Bush said the two had talked about "how we reached a decision as to what we would do about Iraq".
"It's been a tough decision but the decisions we made were the right decisions," he said.
The former president argued that the Iraq war had helped to spread freedom in the Middle East and that it was "worth every life that was lost".
The invasion - which began on 20 March 2003 - was "justified" because Saddam was a "threat", Mr Bush said.
"Today, the situation is better, safer and the world is better off without Saddam Hussein," he added.

Mr Blair said that when people "look back at the history of this decade... the service that President Bush and the Americans rendered... in the context of 9/11, in the context of what happened in Iraq, in the context of what is happening in Afghanistan - it is a historic service for which people should be grateful".
He added that the world "is a better and safer place" because of the actions that were taken.
But the pair faced strong criticism for the statement, with Plaid Cymru's leader in the Welsh Assembly, Leanne Wood, calling for both men to be tried for war crimes
Malaysia's securities commission has lifted a limit on the amount of equity that Islamic banks can hold in a single company.
The change is part of efforts to help Malaysia's Islamic finance industry grow and expand overseas.
For years, the country's two full-fledged Islamic banks have been restricted to holding a maximum of 15% of any company's shares.
That limit has now been removed for investment in firms related to Islamic activities.
And it has been raised to 30% for investment in firms not related to Islam.
The move is seen as a major boost for the Islamic finance industry, which has been growing rapidly in recent years.
It is expected to lead to more mergers and acquisitions as Islamic banks expand their operations.
The change was announced by Malaysia's Securities Commission on Monday.
It said the move would help Islamic banks "expand their investment banking activities, and enhance their role in the country's capital market".
Mitsubishi Motors has confirmed that it is in talks with Peugeot SA about a possible merger.
The Japanese car maker said it has asked Peugeot - which is itself preparing to merge with Fiat Chrysler - to "jointly study" a merger plan.
A merger between Mitsubishi and Peugeot would create the world's fourth-largest auto maker by sales, behind Volkswagen, Toyota and Renault-Nissan.
In a statement, Mitsubishi said the two companies plan to hold talks "from a long-term perspective".
Last month, Peugeot revealed that it was in talks to buy Fiat Chrysler, in a deal that would create the world's fourth-largest car maker.
Peugeot's board was meeting on Thursday to discuss the proposal, amid growing speculation that a deal could be announced as early as next week.
Last week, Peugeot's chief executive, Carlos Tavares, said the company was open to a "friendly" merger with Mitsubishi Motors.
Mitsubishi was once part of the Renault-Nissan alliance, but sold a controlling stake to Nissan in 2016.
Mr Tavares said a merger with Mitsubishi would help his company expand its presence in Asia.
Mitsubishi Motors was hit hard by a scandal in 2016 over data cheating that affected some of its cars.
The company sold 930,000 vehicles worldwide in 2018, compared to the 3.9 million sold by Peugeot.

Kraft Foods has announced it is no longer going to advertise its snack brands to children under the age of 12 in the US.
The company, which owns Cadbury and Oreo, said it was "aligning with the goals of the Healthy Kids programme".
The Children's Food and Beverage Advertising Initiative (CFBAI) said Kraft was the first food company to make such a pledge.
Kraft said it would define childhood as under 12 years of age based on the US Census definition.

"As part of this commitment, we will expand our definition of 'child-directed' advertising to include not only commercials on children's television programmes but also advertising placed on other children's media, such as websites and video games, that are directed to children under 12," the company said in a statement.
CFBAI said the decision was "a significant step forward in the effort to improve the nutritional profile of food advertised to children".
"Kraft's commitment serves as an example of the industry's ability to self-regulate and improve its practices to promote healthier dietary habits among children," said CFBAI president Lisa Gable.

The number of text messages sent in the UK has surpassed 20 billion a year for the first time.
Comms regulator Ofcom said the number of texts sent in March broke the record, with 20.5 billion sent.
It said half of all mobile phone users sent 250 or more text messages a month.
Ofcom said nearly 90% of mobile phone users now owned a smartphone.
The report said that the average UK household owned 7.2 internet-connected devices.
These included TVs, laptops, tablets and games consoles.
The report said that overall, UK households owned an average of 25 connected devices, which included everything from smartwatches to virtual reality headsets.

Industrial revival hope for Japan

Japan's once-booming manufacturing industry has been on the decline for nearly 30 years.
But could "smart factories" help it stage a comeback?
Akio Toyoda is proud of the car he is about to show me.
It is not yet another hybrid, or an electric vehicle, but a petrol-engine sports utility vehicle (SUV).
"I love SUVs, because people who like SUVs are people who like to have fun," says the chief executive of Toyota, the world's largest car maker.
"This is a car that brings together the know-how and the technology of Toyota engines, and Toyota teamwork.

"

The new Toyota Highlander SUV will soon be making its way to car dealerships in the US and elsewhere.
It is one of dozens of models Toyota hopes will revive its fortunes in global car markets.
Toyota has invested billions of dollars in new plants and equipment in the US and Asia.
It has also raised wages and streamlined production lines.
Mr Toyoda says that these changes, along with the new models, will help turn around Toyota's sales which have been falling in the US and Europe.
"We are confident that we can regain sales momentum to reach our target of selling 10 million cars by the end of 2016," he says.

"
