Former England captain Mike Atherton has been impressed by the early-season form of Somerset's Tom Banton and Hampshire's James Vince, but says opener Sibley must improve.

Ex-Somerset captain Atherton said: "If England are going to go to The Ashes with another opener, then Sibley needs to be scoring a lot of runs.

" simultaneosly, other players are making cases for selection.
Vince, for example, was very good yesterday and Banton has an array of strokes.

"

Nottinghamshire's Ben Duckett made a century in England's second warm-up, as did Hampshire's Vince in the first.
Atherton said: "Duckett has worked hard on his game and is another who has come into some form.

"

The BBC cricket expert added: "The difficulty for England is that when you pick your squad, you are picking a group of players you think will win the Ashes, but you also need to keep one eye on the future.
"That is particularly the case when you pick the opener, because you are also picking the next opener as well."
SBC, the former British Telecom, has said it will cut its workforce by 15% after taking over the struggling mobile firm EE.
About 2,500 jobs are expected to go, mainly in back-office functions.
The announcements comes after SBC completed its £12.5bn ($16.3bn) takeover of EE on 30 January.
The firm said there was a "significant overlap" in the two firms' operations.
In a statement, SBC said it would start a consultation that could lead to redundancies "in certain areas" of the business.
It added that it would "explore alternative solutions wherever possible" and that "every effort will be made" to avoid compulsory redundancies.
SBC, which completed its acquisition of the telecoms firm EE in January, said most of the jobs lost would be from the enterprise and legacy consumer divisions.
The company said it would "invest significantly" in training and developing its workforce in "key strategic areas".
In a statement, the company said: "This is a business with a great history and a brilliant future ahead of it.
"However, the market is changing rapidly and to maintain our competitiveness and grow sustainably, we need to become a leaner and more agile business.

"

The announcement came as SBC reported a 3% fall in third-quarter revenue, to £5.8bn, which it said was in line with expectations as its £500m cost-cutting plan continued.

The company said it was "on track with the delivery" of the cost-cutting plan, which would "complete by the end of this year".

SBC, which has offices in London and Manchester, said its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased by 5% to £1.4bn, as it "benefited from lower pension expenses".
The company's net debt stood at £1.6bn, including £1.3bn of acquired EE debt.
SBC said it would "continue to review the level of the EE debt and consider options to optimise its capital structure", which could include a sale and leaseback of its mast portfolio.
The firm added that it would "continue to assess M&A opportunities closely, including those that may be transformative in nature".
An FBI agent admitted using his position to collude with an analyst to send pornographic emails to colleagues, police and judges.

Straford Wood Jr., 54, sent the emails over a period of eight months from his FBI account and through an unclassified computer system at the FBI office in Springfield, Illinois, according to court documents.
The court heard how Wood and analyst Amy Chang, who also faces charges, would take turns pressing the "send" button after drafting the emails together.
He admitted sending an email to a state police officer with the header "Disgusting pic... worth every second of your time" and a photo of a woman wearing only a jacket made from dollar bills.
Other emails had headers such as "Sexy Nurse", "Big Boobs" and "Nice".
The court heard how Wood and Chang took "great care" in drafting the emails and would use Google to determine which keywords would result in the emails being filtered through to government computers.
He admitted to sending the emails to about 20 people, including state police officers and federal judges.
Wood had been working under cover in an organized crime investigation and had been assigned to a task force investigating cyber-crime.
He has been charged with corruption and obstructing justice.
The charges against him were unsealed in federal court in Illinois on Wednesday.
Israel is looking to the United States to fill the post of governor of its central bank, according to media reports.
The job has been vacant since Stanley Fischer stepped down last month.

Media reports say Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked US President Donald Trump to nominate Marvin Goodfriend, a professor at Carnegie Mellon University and a former official at the Federal Reserve, for the role.
The appointment needs to be approved by the Israeli parliament.
Mr Goodfriend has not responded to the reports.
The Bank of Israel has had just seven governors since it was founded in 1954, and all have been career central bankers, rather than political appointments, according to Reuters.
The post is regarded as one of the most important in the country's economic leadership.
The bank's responsibilities include conducting monetary policy, regulating banks and financial institutions, and overseeing payments systems.
Former world tennis number one Andy Roddick is in talks with renowned coach Patrick Mouratoglou about formalising their player-coach relationship.
Roddick, who has been working with Mouratoglou since November, is set to officially appoint the coach who boasts Naomi Osaka and Serena Williams among his clients.
The American, who is now ranked 69th in the world, has not won a title since the 2012 US Open when he beat Roger Federer in the final.

"I have been very impressed with his overall knowledge of the game, his technical expertise and the way he has been able to explain some complex ideas to me in a simple and concise way," Roddick said.
"But more importantly, he has already pushed me to look at tennis in a different way and it has brought back that hunger to compete and get better every day."
Roddick has won 32 titles - including one Masters and US Open singles crown - and reached four Grand Slam singles finals.
He retired from tennis in 2012 and since then has worked as a TV pundit and also helped to launch a sports media production company with his wife, Brooklyn Decker.
Mouratoglou first emerged as a coach having guided Serena Williams to 10 of her 23 Grand Slam singles titles.
His most successful partnership was with Andre Agassi between 2012 and 2014, during which time the American won the ATP World Tour Finals in London and reached the final of the French Open.
Conservative MP Leo Docherty has defended his decision to resign from the British army after 18 years in order to stand for parliament, saying the move was endorsed by the chief of the defence staff.
The 38-year-old soldier announced he was standing for the safe Tory seat of Aldershot in Hampshire and quitting the army in a statement released by the Conservative Party on Monday night.
But in an interview with the BBC's Newsnight programme, Air Chief Marshal Sir Mike Wigston said he did "not have a memory" of signing a letter of support for the father-of-three's departure.
"I don't recall seeing that letter myself," Sir Mike said.

"I have had a chat with Leo, as indeed I have done with other people in the past who have felt that their service career should end and that they wish to pursue a political path, and I wish him well in that endeavour.

"

Docherty served in the Special Air Service (SAS) as a troop commander and is considered to be a rising star in the Conservative Party.
He has been endorsed by Tory MPs Scott Mann and Mark Pawsey, as well as party leader Boris Johnson.

But his move has been questioned by some former army colleagues who have described it as an "absolutely staggering" and "unethical" breach of the armed forces' motto of "soldier first, last and always".
The MP candidate said he had "loved" his career in the army and it had been a "huge privilege" to serve, but that he had "reached the limit of what I can achieve" and was "ready for a new challenge".

Docherty served in the Gulf, Iraq and Afghanistan and was awarded the Military Cross (MC) for bravery in 2012.

Grocery chain Winn-Dixie Stores Inc has filed for bankruptcy, the company said on Thursday.
The Jacksonville, Florida-based company operates 560 stores in the US Southeast, employing some 38,000 people.
It has been hit hard by the coronavirus pandemic, as customers flock to supermarkets and warehouse stores like Costco, where they can buy groceries in bulk at affordable prices.
Winn-Dixie said it will continue to operate throughout the court-supervised process.
It expects the process to last several months.
"The coronavirus pandemic has created unprecedented challenges for Winn-Dixie, as it has for so many other businesses and industries," the company said in a statement.
Winn-Dixie said it has obtained approximately $560m in financing to support its operations during the court-supervised process.
The bankruptcy filing comes as the US holiday season kicks into gear.
Retailers have been pushing for shoppers to buy early this year, as people avoid gathering in large crowds due to the pandemic.
Yet, sales growth has been slow.
Last week, luxury department store chain Neiman Marcus Group filed for bankruptcy, becoming the first major US retailer to do so since the pandemic.
Other retailers facing bankruptcy this year include the UK's Arcadia Group, which owns Topshop and other brands, and the US-based J Crew.

Tories 'would cut number of MPs'

The Conservatives would reduce the number of MPs in Parliament - but not immediately.
The party's election manifesto says it will appoint a boundary review commission to look at cutting the number of seats.
The plan would not come into effect until the 2030s, with the aim of saving £100m in taxpayers' money.
The review would involve merging constituencies in England, to bring the number of MPs representing English seats down from 523 to 502.
The MPs representing constituencies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland would be unaffected.
The decision was criticised by opponents, who described it as a "con" that would prevent voters from having a say on the issue in a referendum.
The manifesto says the review would be carried out on the basis of "equal electorate".
This means that seats would be drawn up so that each one has roughly the same number of voters - with a 5% tolerance.
At the moment, the size of constituencies varies hugely.
For example, the Isle of Wight, which has a population of 132,000, has slightly more constituents than the safe Tory seat of Chelsea and Fulham, which has 127,000.
The boundary review - also known as a redrawing of constituency boundaries - is traditionally carried out every 10 years, to even out any changes in population across the country.
The process is already under way - but the Tories said they would put it on hold, as it could lead to Labour gaining seats at the next election, due to the way the new boundaries have been drawn up.
Labour has already accused the Tories of trying to "fudge the numbers" by putting the review on hold, as it would allow them to move voters in Tory seats to neighbouring Labour constituencies.
The manifesto does not say how the review commission would be appointed.
It does not say whether the appointments would be made by the Conservative Party, or whether other parties would be asked to nominate members.

Ms. Pidcock was elected in 2017 to the constituency, which includes the towns of Burnopfield, Consett, Stanley, and Chester-le-Street, and parts of Durham City.

"But politics is changing.

"

Ms. Pidcock said Labour needed to "offer a clear, hopeful alternative" and that she believed the party needed "a different candidate to win again in North West Durham".
"I have decided to stand down as the Labour candidate for the forthcoming general election," she added.

"It has been a difficult decision but I am confident that it is the right one."

Ms. Pidcock was elected to the shadow cabinet in March 2019, becoming the party's spokeswoman on employment rights and pensions.
She resigned from the role the following year, calling Sir Keir "a terrible leader".
Reacting to her decision to stand down, Labour MP Jessica Morden said she was "a brilliant colleague and campaigner".
"Laura has been a fantastic constituency MP, dedicated to serving her constituents and fighting for Labour values," she added.

The tune for Book 1's Prelude in C was fed into an AI system, which generated a new score.

"I didn't want it to be a pastiche, I wanted it to be something that could stand on its own," he said.
The new score was performed at the Boston Early Music Festival over the weekend.
Bach wrote Well-Tempered Clavier – a set of 48 preludes and fugues in each major and minor key – in the 1700s.

Neave is a pianist and composer who graduated from Boston's Berklee College of Music, and is currently artist in residence at the University of Arkansas.

"We'll take a melody, assign some numbers to it, and then the computer will generate thousands of responses based on those numbers," he said.
The team then worked to refine the results, balancing the desire to use AI with making sure the new music sounded like something Bach could have written.

"There were a lot of wrong turns, but eventually we got something where I felt like it captured the spirit of what Bach might do, if he had been given infinite amounts of time, and used this technology," Neave explained.

The regulation in question says that for a name to be protected it has to be "clearly distinguishable, capable of being pronounced by consumers, and not devoid of any distinctive character".

Growth has been fairly sluggish in the wake of the financial crisis, and there are few signs that a sustained acceleration is about to begin.

Norwegian file-sharing website Megaupload has won a landmark case challenging whether internet service providers (ISPs) can be held responsible for content uploaded by users.
The nation's highest court ruled that the ISP was not liable for copyright breaches carried out by its customers.
The decision could have a major impact on the way in which copyright laws are enforced online.
The entertainment industry has argued that ISPs should be responsible for banning access to sites offering illegal content.
Megaupload was sued in Norway by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) and Norwegian collection society Tono for allowing users to share songs online.
The lower courts had ruled that the ISP was liable for the actions of its customers.
But the Norwegian Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that the ISP was not liable for direct copyright infringement carried out by its customers.
The court said that indirect infringement - for example, failure to take down copyrighted content - was not sufficient to hold the ISP responsible.
The case turned on whether the ISP could be said to have "authorized" the copyright breaches.

"File-sharing services have argued that they are unable to monitor all the content that is being uploaded and downloaded, and that any obligation on their part to remove copyright violations or make sure that they do not appear would be impractical and unreasonably costly," the court said in its decision.
The ruling said that copyright holders instead should target the individuals who commit the breaches.
Megaupload was represented by lawyer Jon Wessel Tonning.
He said the ruling was a victory for ISPs who did not want to be held responsible for the actions of customers.
"They [the ISPs] have the responsibility to provide access to a network, but they should not be responsible for the information that is transmitted," he told the BBC.
The case is the latest in a series of legal battles over online copyright.
Last year, the US Supreme Court ruled that ISPs could be held responsible for copyright breaches carried out by customers.
That case, which involved college students who had shared music online, reversed a ruling that said the ISP could not be held responsible.
And in a recent case in the UK, the High Court ordered British ISPs to block access to file-sharing website The Pirate Bay.
A restored copy of what is thought to be Dutch painter Vincent Van Gogh's last film has made its debut at a festival in France.
The artist filmed the landscape of France in the early 1890s using a lenticular camera - a precursor to the modern-day flip book.
The film was discovered in 2014 in the Netherlands and recently restored by the National Film Board of Canada.
It was shown at the Van Gogh exhibit at the Auvers-sur-Oise festival, outside Paris.
Museum official Emilie Gordenker told AFP news agency it was "exciting" to think it might be the final film Van Gogh made.
"We know he wanted to make a movie with moving images of peasants working in the fields," she said.
"We hope we will discover some day that there is another film...
but for now this is the only existing one.

"

The 55-second long film shows peasants walking through a field and digging up potatoes.
It was shot in the French town of Auvers-sur-Oise, where the artist spent his final months and is buried.
The camera used to make the film rotates between two lenses, creating an effect similar to that of a flip book.
It was likely that Van Gogh had to stop and change the lens, meaning the filming process was probably quite slow, Ms Gordenker said.

Van Gogh is known to have made one other film, also using a lenticular camera, which showed his friend and fellow artist Paul Gauguin, though some experts have questioned whether that can really be classed as a movie.
The restored film was shown at the festival on Friday and again on Saturday.

The number of people in work rose to a record 89.9 million, the agency said.
The data was dated 31 March but was only made public on Tuesday.
Despite the low unemployment rate, Brazil is still struggling to absorb into the workforce millions who left it during the pandemic.
Some have retired early, while others have started their own businesses.

"We still have about 1.5 million people who should be looking for work, but they are not doing so," said Jose Vilela, an economist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation, a Brazilian think tank.
The labour ministry says that of the 11 million people who lost their jobs in 2020, nine million have found work again.
Unemployment in Brazil usually rises in the run-up to elections as political uncertainty deters companies from creating new jobs.
This year, the first round of the presidential election takes place on 2 October.
But analysts say this year's drop in the unemployment rate is linked to the expansion of the informal economy, which has been fuelled by higher inflation.
Many people have created their own businesses, often making and selling food, in order to make ends meet, said Mr Vilela.
"There are regions where unemployment is still a problem, like north-east Brazil, where the informal economy is not as big as in the rest of the country," he said.
"But on the whole, we are seeing a very tight job market."
It was spring 1995, and a team of us at the BBC were charged with creating the corporation's first web page.
My colleague Richard Taylor and I were put in charge, and we set up a skunkworks lab to investigate this new phenomenon.
We were lucky.
Despite the vast reach of the BBC, the organisation had, in those days, a relatively small number of people involved in new media.
So our team of about 12 was able to control the agenda.
We were joined by Martin Freethy, a brilliant young programmer who had been recruited from Oracle, and Anthony Howard, a designer who instantly understood what we were trying to do.
We were not trying to do anything very grand.
All we wanted to do was make sure the BBC had a web presence.
But we were fortunate in having an enlightened manager, Alan Chesters, who understood this new medium and gave us pretty much free rein.
We were also lucky that the web was so new that nobody really understood it fully, which meant we could pretty much make it up as we went along.
And so we did.

We took all the things we liked about the emerging web landscape – the things that seemed to make the most sense – and built a site that had most of the elements you would recognise in the BBC's web presence today: a top menu, a sidebar of links to internal pages, and a big promotion on the homepage to a major news story.
We added some other things that were novel at the time, such as a site-wide search engine and a daily updated list of "what's new".
And that was about it.
We weren't trying to "design" the site, because the idea of "user experience design" hadn't been thought of yet.
Nor were we trying to produce a "brand" experience, because again, that idea was still far in the future.
In fact, the word "brand" wasn't even used much in the BBC.
But despite this lack of design thinking, and working with incredibly primitive tools, it seemed to us that the site we were producing had a certain something.
In fact, looking back at it now, it seems pretty clean and crisp, and not that far off what we produce today.
And that, really, is the secret to the BBC's web success.
We got there first, and have remained there pretty much ever since.
The principles that guided us then – that less is more, that nothing should be unnecessary – have remained unchanged

A student who has been blind since birth can now see colours, following a groundbreaking surgery.
The surgery involved a unique "tongue display" which stimulated the brain, enabling the patient to see colours.
The patient, who was born with a form of congenital blindness that affects 1 in every 10,000 people, underwent the experimental surgery in November last year.

The operation, which was led by Dr. Ron Pelias, assistant professor of ophthalmology at Stanford University, stimulated the tongue's nerve fibres, which in turn stimulated the brain's visual cortex, allowing the patient to perceive colours.
"We're trying to work out the neural mechanisms of colour vision by stimulating the brain in this very precise way," said Dr Pelias.
The patient can now see colours, but still does not have any form of visual acuity, meaning they can't see shapes or outlines.
The surgery was carried out on a patient with complete colour blindness and involves a small, 1.5mm square electrode, which is placed on the tongue.
The electrode is linked to a small, wearable computer, which transforms images from a camera into "tongue maps", consisting of eight different regions, each stimulated by a different colour.
When the patient looks at an object, the computer converts the image into a "tongue map", which stimulates the brain in such a way that the patient can perceive colours.

"We're trying to stimulate the brain so that it interprets stimuli as colour, by coaxing neurons in the brain to respond in a way that would normally only occur when a sighted person sees colour," said Dr Pelias.
The device needs to be calibrated against a "tongue colour chart", which the patient uses to tune the colours on the device, ensuring they are seeing the right colours.
So far, the patient has been able to identify colours in experiments, but the team is still working on improving the clarity of the images produced.
"This is a very early stage of the research.
We're a long way from understanding how the brain encodes colour and even further from understanding how to restore that ability through electrical stimulation," Dr Pelias said.
"But it's a very exciting proof of concept that brings us a little bit closer to helping patients with congenital colour blindness.

"
The team hopes to carry out the procedure on other patients in the future and believes the technology could also be used to help people who have lost their sight to retinal degeneration.
Japan's economy has slipped into recession after it contracted by an annualised 2.3% in the third quarter of 2022, official data shows.
The figure was worse than many analysts had expected and followed a 0.8% drop in the previous quarter.
Japan has been hit by soaring energy prices and a strong currency, and is struggling to attract tourists as borders remain closed.
The latest data will increase the pressure on the government to do more to help the economy.
Japan's Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said the data was "extremely disappointing".
"I am fully aware that the Japanese economy faces serious challenges including inflation and will take all possible measures to overcome them," he said.
Earlier this month, Japan's central bank warned that the economy was likely to shrink further in the current quarter.
It also raised its inflation forecast, predicting that prices would rise by 3.0% this year, up from its previous forecast of 1.8%.
Japan has been hit by the same problems as other countries, including the war in Ukraine, but its response has been muted because it is a net importer of energy.
It has taken steps to try to cushion the blow to households by offering subsidies for electricity and natural gas, but economists say this has had little effect.
In addition, its export-heavy economy has been hit by the strong yen, which makes Japanese goods more expensive overseas.
And with its borders still closed to most foreign tourists, the country's service sector has been unable to benefit from the recent global tourism boom.
Courts in England and Wales have been given new guidance on how to handle cases where someone has been accused of burglary - with a particular focus on domestic burglary.
The Council of Circuit Judges issued the guidance - which includes urging judges to consider the psychological impact on victims.
It follows a campaign by the charity Victim Support and the Association of Police Officers.
Domestic burglary "has a profound and long-lasting effect on those left behind" the guidance says.
Judge David Rennie, who chaired the council, said the impact on victims was "often underrated".
The guidance says burglars who target people's homes "strike at the heart of the victim's privacy and security".

Judge Rennie said: "Victims of domestic burglary are, more often than not, deeply shocked and distressed by the invasion of their home; that intrusion is compounded by the fact the burglar usually enters the house when the occupant is in bed.
"This guidance recognises that fact and, I hope, will assist courts in ensuring that the impact of this particularly invasive crime is properly recognised when sentencing."

The guidance, which has been sent to all sentencing courts in England and Wales, gives examples of when judges might decide to impose a higher sentence - such as where the victim is particularly vulnerable, or where the burglar took steps to avoid being detected, such as wearing a mask or gloves.
It also reminds judges that older people are particularly vulnerable to burglary, and that these crimes often have a "devastating" impact on them.
Acting Deputy Chief Constable Paul Mills, who chairs the APCC Crime Prevention and Response Committee, said: "I very much welcome the publication of this guidance.
"It is vital that the impact of this invasive crime is properly recognised by the courts and that offenders are sentenced appropriately.

"

Rachel Griffin, from Victim Support, said: "We welcome the revised guidance which highlights the devastating impact that a domestic burglary can have on victims - particularly those who are older or more vulnerable.
"It is vital that all victims of burglary receive the support they need to recover, which is why we also welcome the emphasis on the need for courts to consider the provision of restorative justice."

Rebekah Brooks, editor of the Sun newspaper, which also published the texts, and News International have also been cleared of conspiracy to access Ms Kidman's emails and confidential information.

"

Disney has given its support to Sony's new high definition DVD format, a move which is likely to give the format a huge boost.
The decision is a major boost for the Sony HD DVD format, which is competing with a rival offering from Toshiba.
Disney's support will give the HD DVD format a huge lift, as the company controls some of the most popular films, including Star Wars and Pixar animations.
The format war has been going on for nearly two years, ever since Toshiba launched its HD DVD format, backed by Microsoft and Intel.
Sony later launched its own version, and now seems to be winning the battle, with a growing number of supporters.
Last week, US retailer Best Buy said it would stock the HD DVD players and movies in its stores.
This week, US director James Cameron said he had tested both HD DVD and Blu-ray and decided the HD DVD was superior.
"HD DVD is winning the format war, hands down," he said.
However, not all supporters of Blu-ray have given up hope.
Apple chief executive Steve Jobs, a strong backer of the Blu-ray format, said he believed that Blu-ray had broader support among consumers and he was confident it would prevail.
In a posting on Apple's website, Mr Jobs said that in addition to Best Buy, electronics giants Samsung and LG had also thrown their support behind HD DVD.
But he said that of the top six US electronics retailers, five were supporting Blu-ray, and that in Japan seven of the top eight electronics makers were backing the format.
"We think Blu-ray will prevail, based on its superior feature set and the growing number of Blu-ray players and titles available," he said.
House prices are expected to rise faster than incomes "for years to come" thanks to the stamp duty holiday and demand for more space post-pandemic, the Bank of England's governor has said.
Andrew Bailey said the property market had seen a rebound in demand since the first lockdown as people changed their behaviour.
But he said the boom had "clearly run ahead" of the banks' ability to assess the lending risks.
His comments came as figures showed home loan approvals had risen for a fourth month in a row in December.
The Bank estimated that house prices were between 5% and 7% higher than would have otherwise been the case because of the stamp duty holiday, which ended on 31 March.
The average house price is now £261,000, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
This is up 8.5% annually, but month-on-month prices fell by 0.5% in February.
Mr Bailey said that the demand for housing had "clearly been stronger than expected" over the past year.
But he added that the Bank's agents were "reporting that this boom had run ahead of their ability to assess lending risks".
The Bank's agents - a network of economists and experts who report back to the Bank - have also observed a decline in the number of properties available on the market, the governor said.

This could be driven by the trend of "working from home, and a desire for more space", which had been reflected in "very strong" growth in loan approvals for purchases of larger homes, Mr Bailey said.
However, he added that a slowdown in mortgage approvals since November "is consistent with the expectation that activity would slow given the stamp duty holiday ended".
Mr Bailey's comments came as the Bank released its monthly data on lending conditions and mortgage approvals.
The figures showed that approvals for house purchases rose to 71,000 in December, the fourth consecutive monthly increase.
But the figure was down from 74,000 in November, and still below the pre-pandemic monthly average of around 83,000.
Martin Beck, senior economic adviser to the EY Item Club, said: "Mortgage approvals recovered in 2020, despite the economy being in recession.

Europe is experiencing an unprecedented wave of bank withdrawals, with worried citizens withdrawing about $1.3 trillion in the last year alone.
This has led to an acute shortage of the largest denomination bank note - the €500 note - leading to worries that the very basis of the euro currency scheme could be threatened.
Many of the withdrawals are taking place in Greece, where a banking crisis has led to fears that the country could reintroduce its old currency, the drachma.
But other countries with high levels of non-cash payments, such as Denmark, Austria and the Netherlands, have also seen massive increases in the amount of cash being withdrawn.
The problem is set to be discussed at a meeting of central bankers from around the world in Washington DC on Friday.

"The sudden increase in demand… exceeds the capacity of the Eurosystem" said a paper prepared for the meeting by the European Central Bank, referring to the 19 central banks which together form the Eurosystem, and manage the euro.
The ECB has increased the number of €500 notes in circulation by more than 20% in the past year, but says it is still not enough.
And it is now asking central banks from outside the eurozone for help.
There are thought to be about 23 billion €500 notes in circulation, with a total value of about €1.1 trillion.
But some central bankers say that the demand is now starting to exceed the rate of reproduction.
"Increasing production of euro notes and coins is not enough to compensate for the exceptionally high demand," said the ECB.
"Consequently, inventories of euro notes and coins in some denominations are now at low levels and member banks may experience temporary shortages.

"

"That is why I am inviting national banks from non-euro area countries to make available their stocks of euro notes and coins," it added.
The extent of the shortage was demonstrated when the Dutch central bank put a limit on the number of €500 notes that could be withdrawn by individuals last month.
It said that the notes were being withdrawn "at an alarming rate".
The problem is not just a question of the amount of notes in circulation.
In many countries, banks are choosing to hold fewer notes in reserve, and are turning to other forms of deposit.
This has reduced the amount of notes in the system.
And the withdrawal of so many €500 notes - the largest denomination bank note in the eurozone - is making it difficult to replace them.

Ring of Fire hit co-writer Dean Jones dies at 84

Jones, who also wrote lyrics for The Monkees, died on Tuesday, his publicist said.
His songs were also performed by Frank Sinatra, Elvis Presley and Barbra Streisand.
The singer-songwriter died at his home in Los Angeles following a long illness, publicist Linda Petrie said.
Ring of Fire was a US chart-topping single for Johnny Cash in 1963 and received the Grammy Hall of Fame Award in 2014.
Jones co-wrote the song with husband-and-wife team Howard Greenfield and Sue Greenfield, known as the Greenfield Quartet.

Cash's version, about a love affair ending in betrayal and heartache, became one of the biggest hits of his career and saw him perform it in front of US President Lyndon B Johnson at the White House in 1968.
It was also honoured with a Grammy Award for best country solo performance.
Jones also wrote The Monkees' theme song and other songs for the band, and penned Love Shack for the B-52's.
His other compositions were performed by Sinatra, Presley, Streisand, The Grass Roots, The Everly Brothers and The Beach Boys.

The Bangalore-based company said it had made a profit of Rs 3,408 crore ($510m) in the three months to March, up 9.6% from a year earlier.
Revenue climbed nearly 10% to Rs 14,140 crore ($1.9bn), driven by strong performance in its banking, financial and insurance unit.
Analysts had on average expected profit of Rs 3,310 crore and revenue of Rs 13,910 crore, according to Refinitiv data.

"Our revenue growth is healthy and broad-based across industries and geographies.

"

Wipro, which has more than 220,000 employees, said it won a $1.5bn deal - its third largest - to digitalise the operations of US industrial firm Alcoa.

Mr Delaporte said the company was "winning large deals" and seeing renewed demand from customers.
"We are well positioned to capitalise on the robust digital transformation momentum, as reflected in our win rate and pipeline," he added.

But India - which imports most of its energy - has been keen to diversify its sources amid rising prices.
Mr Aiyar said the gas would start flowing in 2013 and India would make up any shortfall from Iran in the meantime by increasing imports from Qatar.
India already imports nearly two-thirds of its oil needs from the Gulf region.
New Delhi is also eager to develop nuclear energy and has signed a deal with France for the supply of nuclear plants.

The pop star, 54, will sing at the BBC's Broadcasting House in London for Radio 2.
It will be his first performance since he played at a charity concert for Greek disaster victims in Athens in November 2003.
Michael, who released his latest album Symphonica in March, will appear on Jo Whiley's show next Wednesday.
"I'm truly thrilled at the prospect of performing on Radio 2 - it's where I listened as a child growing up in Britain and it's where I listened when I first moved to London," he said.

The singer, who found fame with duo Wham!
in the early 1980s, last performed on BBC TV when he appeared on Comic Relief in 2011.
He joins a list of artists set to appear on Radio 2's Live in London season, which includes Kylie Minogue, Tom Jones and Paloma Faith.
The station's controller Bob Shennan said: "It is a huge honour that George Michael will be performing live on Radio 2 - a personal ambition for both of us.

"

A leading Pakistani cleric has issued a fatwa - a religious ruling - banning women in Pakistan from wearing helmets.
Maulana Abdul Aziz Jilani, who is the chairman of Pakistan's Ulema Council, argued that it was "un-Islamic" for women to wear helmets as it covered their hair.
His comments come after a young woman, who was riding a motorcycle with her husband when she was hit by a van, died as she was not wearing a helmet.
The couple's two-year-old son, who was on the back of the bike, survived with minor injuries.
Police said the couple were not wearing helmets and that this was a factor in the woman's death.
Motorcycle helmets are not mandatory for adults in Pakistan, but traffic police say they will launch a campaign to encourage their use following the death.
But cleric Maulana Aziz said that wearing helmets was against the teachings of the Quran and urged imams to spread this message.
"I request all imams to explain this issue to people and especially to women that wearing helmets on roads is against Islamic teachings and culture," he is quoted as saying by the Express Tribune.
He added that the traffic police should instead focus on ensuring that men wore helmets.
Clerics in Pakistan have issued several controversial fatwas in the past, including one banning the use of calculators because they were believed to "disturb the minds of students".

Spurs' football operations director Damien Comolli and first team coach Ryan Mason watched Finnsson in action earlier this month.

"

MANCHESTER UNITED cruised into the semi-finals of the League Cup with a comfortable victory over Nottingham Forest at Old Trafford.

First-half goals from Antony and Marcus Rashford and a late third from substitute Fred sealed United's victory and set up a last-four meeting with Nottingham Forest's East Midlands rivals Leicester City.
United dominated throughout, but struggled to find a way past a resolute Forest defence for the first 25 minutes.
The visitors survived an early scare when Tyrell Malacia's cross was inches away from curling into the far corner, with Anthony Martial unable to get a touch on it.
Moments later, Forest's Jason Cummings headed a cross narrowly wide from the left, but that was as close as the visitors came to scoring.
United took the lead a minute before the half-hour mark when Rashford cut the ball back for Antony, who produced a clinical finish to find the far corner from 18 yards.
And the hosts doubled their lead five minutes later when Rashford produced a fine finish from 10 yards out following a defensive mix-up.
Forest's best chance to get back into the game came five minutes into the second half when Cummings was played through on goal, but the forward's chip was too weak and easily saved by David de Gea.
United put the game beyond doubt with four minutes left when substitute Fred scored with a first-time finish from 20 yards out following a lay-off from another substitute, Jesse Lingard.
United could have added a fourth in the final moments, but Rashford's effort was too close to Forest goalkeeper Wayne Hennessey, who made the save.

"

Star Trek fans are fighting to save the show's original sets in California.
The sci-fi series debuted on US television 50 years ago this month.
An online petition has been launched to stop the original sets from being destroyed after the lease on the property where they are kept expired.
More than 275,000 people have signed it.
The sets are located at Vasquez Rocks Natural Area Park in Los Angeles.
They are protected by a large white tent, but fans want them made accessible to the public.
The petition says the "only thing worse than tearing down these sets... is to let them sit, decaying".
It was launched by Justin Lin, a director and producer on the Fox TV show The Exorcist.
He wrote: "We want to preserve these iconic sets so that fans today and in the future can enjoy them."
The petition adds that "the sets are in serious danger of being lost, as the lease on the property has expired and the new leaseholder does not appear to be interested in preserving them".
The campaign has been backed by some of the actors who appeared in the original series, including George Takei, who played Sulu.
In a video posted on Twitter, he said: "These sets are a landmark.
They were used to film episodes and movies that have brought joy to millions of people around the world.
"We have the opportunity to preserve them so that fans can enjoy them for generations to come.

"

The online petition is close to reaching its goal of 300,000 signatures.
The author of the petition has reached out to the park's administrators as well as local California politicians including city council members and state senators, according to the Los Angeles Times.
The newspaper also reports conservation experts have said the best option for preservation would be to remove the sets and store them, but that would be expensive.
Other options to save the sets include seeking heritage protection status or incorporating them into the park's visitor centre, the paper says.
Star Trek aired from 1966 to 1969 and spawned a franchise including TV series, movies and merchandise.
Arsene Wenger has admitted he is shocked that Newcastle United have not spent any money on new players in the January transfer window.

The Magpies have received bids for a number of their key players this month, including Joe Willock and Allan Saint-Maximin, but have not signed a player despite their dreadful form which has seen them slip to within two points of the Premier League relegation zone.
Manager Eddie Howe has claimed he is happy with the squad he has, but Wenger told BBC Radio 4: "It's a bit surprising.
"When you are in trouble, when you don't get results, the natural instinct is to say 'Let's change something'.
How much change?
Some clubs go for it and some clubs don't.

The clubs that don't, I think in the long term it's more dangerous because you risk getting into a spiral where the pressure from the fans, from the media, becomes stronger and stronger and the players themselves don't think they can get out of it.

"

Newcastle have been linked with a move for Burnley's James Tarkowski, but with the Clarets having received no offers for the 29-year-old centre-back, it appears he will remain at Turf Moor.
It has been reported that the Magpies have ended their interest in the England international.
Wenger believes January is an important month for clubs to strengthen their squads, with Champions League and title-winning teams often enhanced at this point.
"They (Newcastle) have gone seven or eight years without buying a player in January," he added.
"The last time they bought a player in January was Bruno Guimaraes, who has been a very good player for them.
"January is always a crucial month because when you look at the teams who have won the Champions League or the Premier League, they have bought in January.

Australian winemaker Foster's Group has increased its takeover offer for South Africa's Distell Group for a second time, after its initial bid was rejected.

Japanese banking battle at an end

Japan's biggest lender has reached a settlement in a long-running legal battle over compensation for customers who were wrongly charged for financial advice.
The bank said it would pay 101bn yen ($900m; £600m) to about four million customers.
It also agreed to establish a fund of about 50bn yen to handle future claims.
The move ends more than three years of legal battles with consumers and a powerful government regulator.
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) said the cost of the settlement was "huge".
But it said the move would help restore public confidence in the nation's banking system, which has been rocked by a series of scandals over the past year.
The central bank had been trying to get other banks to help pay for the settlement, but they have so far refused.
The bank has already set aside reserves for the settlement, which is expected to cost about 130bn yen.
The BOJ said it would work to improve its financial advisory services and strengthen its internal controls.
Veteran comic Cyril Fletcher has died at the age of 95.
The BBC radio and television comedian died in hospital in Poole, Dorset on Thursday, his agent said.
Fletcher, who was born in Lincolnshire, was one of the last surviving top comedians of the early radio days.

He became well-known for his catchphrase, "Hello, my dear!"; and his act often included singing a comic song, accompanied by his own piano playing.

Nigeria aims to boost cocoa production substantially in the next five years.

Its 'massive' expansion plan is aimed at reclaiming Nigeria's position as one of the world's top ten cocoa producers.
Nigeria - once a major cocoa producer - currently ranks below the main producers in West Africa.
These are Ivory Coast, which accounts for more than 40% of the world's production, and Ghana, which produces almost 20%.
Cocoa is the country's highest foreign exchange earner after oil and gas.
Nigeria hopes to raise production through the rehabilitation of abandoned plantations.
The NCB also plans to partner with the government to distribute high-yielding seedlings to farmers.
According to the International Cocoa Organization, Nigeria has the potential to be among the world's top three cocoa producers.

Players use a joystick to guide Master Chief through a series of military missions.

He said Xbox was considering adding a warning message to the game.
Halo 2 has become the fastest-selling game ever in the US.
More than 520,000 copies were sold in the first day, generating more than $125m in sales.
The original Halo, released in 2001, sold more than 20 million copies.

The company had warned in April that it would post a loss of $60m.

The company is now focused on patent and other intellectual property litigation.

Ipsos MORI's head of political research, Emily Gray, said it was "reassuring" that many knew "how they would vote" in an election.

"Sony hasn't declared victory yet but in practical terms it seems that Blu-ray has won," he added.
Toshiba said it was "disappointed" at Netflix's decision.
The company said it had no plans to pull the plug on its HD DVD players and recorders, and noted that it had recently released a new range of HD DVD products.
A Toshiba spokesman said the company was "committed to the HD DVD format and will continue to work with our industry partners to make HD DVD widely available to consumers".
The spokesman added that Toshiba had no plans to reduce the prices of its HD DVD players "at this time".
Amazon and Best Buy, two of the biggest US retailers, have already indicated they will stock Blu-ray products exclusively.
And software makers are increasingly releasing films only on Blu-ray, further undermining the already precarious future of HD DVD.
Berlin has honoured a South Korean director with a top cultural award for his contribution to fostering understanding and mutual respect between Europe and Asia.
Berlin-based Im Kwon Taek received the Goethe Medal on Tuesday for his "unwavering and passionate pursuit of cultural diversity and peace".
The medal is awarded annually by the German state to people who have actively promoted cultural understanding and exchange.
"In times of growing nationalistic and populist tendencies, Im Kwon Taek's work and life are more important than ever," the jury said.

The award-winning film-maker has lived in Germany for four decades and has made more than 60 films, including the 1986 epic Mandala, which was the first non-European movie to be nominated for an Academy Award in the best foreign language film category.
His other well-known films include the romantic drama Rosy Life, which won a Golden Bear - the top prize at the Berlin International Film Festival - in 2005, and the 2008 drama The Surrogate City.
Im Kwon Taek is the first film-maker to win the Goethe Medal since it was awarded to UK director Mike Leigh in 2010.
US employers added 233,000 jobs in May, according to the country's Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The figure was well above most economists' expectations.
And job growth for the previous two months was higher than first thought, the bureau said.
The data showed that the number of unemployed people looking for work decreased by 342,000 to 6.1 million.
The unemployment rate remained unchanged at 3.6% percent, near a 50-year low.
Average hourly earnings increased by 5.2% year-on-year, unchanged from April.
Price increases appear to be moderating, raising hopes that the Fed might pause its interest rate increases.
The jobs figures are good news for President Joe Biden, whose approval ratings have risen in recent months.

England centre Sam Burgess has joined his teammates in the treatment room after sustaining a calf injury in training, coach Steve McNamara has confirmed.

"It's really disappointing for Sam," said McNamara.

"

"

The PHE said the site was designed to be a "one-stop shop" for virus information, and would be regularly updated to reflect the changing threat.
It added that while the site was aimed at the general public, it would also be useful for healthcare professionals.

Dr Jenny Harries, the PHE's deputy director, said: "This new website is a vital tool in our fight against viruses, and will help to ensure that the public has the information they need to protect themselves and their loved ones.

"

Roger Federer claimed his eighth title in the Dubai Duty Free Tennis Championships with a straight-set victory over Felix Auger-Aliassime.

It was also the first time Federer had dropped a set in the tournament.
The 20-time Grand Slam champion eased through the opening set in 33 minutes but was broken three times in the second as Auger-Aliassime forced a tie-break.
Federer, who turned 40 last month, took an early 2-0 lead in the tie-break but lost the next seven points as Auger-Aliassime levelled the match.
Both players broke each other's serve early in the deciding set
but it was the veteran who earned the crucial break in the eighth game before serving out to love to seal the match in two hours and 21 minutes.
"It was tough, it was tough for me to play like this, especially after the year that I had," Federer said.
"The young guy is a terrific player with a great future ahead of him.
I think for me, it's just about staying healthy, recalibrating everything and trying to play more this year.

"

It was Federer's first title since the Swiss Indoors in October 2019 and his first outdoor hard-court title since Shanghai in October 2017.
Auger-Aliassime, who reached the final without dropping a set, has still yet to win a title after seven final appearances.
The Canadian has lost all three of his meetings with Federer, including in the quarter-finals of last year's US Open.
Households across the UK are to be bombarded with up to 50% more junk mail from tomorrow, Saturday 1 April, thanks to changes in the law governing the posting of letters.
From that date, postage costs for bulk mail will be reduced by up to 47%, resulting in an estimated extra 350 million items of junk mail every year.
The new rules are part of a European Union (EU) wide reform of the postal sector which aims to create a more level playing field for all postal operators across Europe.
But already some UK local councils are reporting that they are overwhelmed by the amount of junk mail they are receiving.
One council, in the London Borough of Richmond, says it is receiving up to 500 items of junk mail every day - equivalent to one delivery every six minutes.
Richmond Council says it is already having to spend £5,000 a year disposing of the unsolicited material.
Similar stories are coming from councils in Bristol, Edinburgh, and other towns and cities across the UK.

The Direct Marketing Association (DMA), which represents the UK's direct marketing industry, says it is aware of the concerns raised by local councils and is seeking discussions with them to find a way forward.
In a recent survey, 89% of respondents said they found junk mail an annoyance.
Almost as many - 87% - said they would like to receive less of it.
The survey, for the local authority-backed website moneymagpie.com, found that two-thirds of respondents said they usually throw junk mail straight in the bin, without even opening it.

According to the new rules, postage costs for bulk mail will be reduced because the price of a second class stamp is being cut from 36p to 25p, and the price of a first class stamp falls from 46p to 31p.
Prices have not changed since 2001.
Last year, 6.8 billion items of bulk mail were posted in the UK.
This figure includes junk mail.
Of these, 1.2 billion were door drops.
Almost all (99%) of local authorities report handling increased amounts of junk mail in recent years, according to the Local Government Association.
Council tax bills and other important documents could get lost in the flood of junk mail.
The new pricing structure was approved by the EU last December, and all 27 member states were obliged to implement the changes from 1 April.
Ireland and Greece have already introduced the new pricing structures, with Germany planning to do so later this year.
In the UK, the new prices were announced by Royal Mail

The manufacturing recovery is slowing, according to a new survey, which also shows that the number of firms reporting rising costs is at a record high.
The monthly survey by the CBI trade body found that its measure of manufacturing output slowed "significantly" in December, with firms reporting that uncertainty about the outlook had increased.
Orders books were described as "solid" by firms, the survey found, but added that they were "nowhere near" pre-pandemic levels.
In addition, the number of firms reporting rising costs reached a record high in December, according to the CBI.
It said that firms expected inflationary pressures to weaken, but "only slightly" over the next three months.
Rain Newton-Smith, the chief economist at the CBI, said that while output growth slowed in December, "that doesn't mean the manufacturing recovery is stalling".
"Output growth remains robust and firms are increasingly confident that conditions will improve in the year ahead," she said.
"But rocketing inflation and persistent supply chain disruption mean that Brexit is still a big drag on the sector.

"To overcome this, the government must do whatever it can to smooth relations with the EU, including exploring options for customs cooperation to help tackle the mountain of red tape exporters still face.

"

The survey echoed the findings of a similar poll by Make UK and PwC published on Monday, which found that manufacturing growth slowed in December as some firms struggled with supply chain problems.

The CBI survey of 231 manufacturers across the UK saw its total order book balance – based on a scale of -100 to 100, where -50 represents no change – fall to 28 in December, down from 39 in November.
Its output balance – which measures the percentage of firms reporting an increase in output – fell to 19 in December, from 23 in November.
A balance of 16% of firms said they expected to increase investment in plants and machinery over the next year – the highest level for a year.
But the proportion of firms reporting increased costs rose to 88%, the highest level since the CBI started collecting the data in 1988.

The survey comes a day after data from the Office for National Statistics showed that the cost of living increased at its fastest rate for 10 years in November, driven by higher prices for energy, fuel and second-hand cars.
US charity anthem 'We Are The World' is re-released with some of the original artists and some new stars.

Tobacco giants hail court ruling

Smoking cost the lives of 800,000 people in Europe every year, health experts have told the European Court of Justice.
The court in Luxembourg was hearing arguments on whether the EU should have the power to regulate tobacco products.
The tobacco industry argued that such legislation would represent an illegal interference with their trade.
Judges were told that smoking caused 600,000 deaths in the EU every year, with another 200,000 people dying from exposure to second-hand smoke.
The court's ruling is not expected before the summer.
The case was referred to the court by the French government which wanted to know if its own laws, banning smoking in public places, breached the tobacco firms' trade mark rights.
In court, the tobacco giants argued that there was no scientific proof that their products were dangerous and that smoking was a matter of personal choice.
They also argued that any laws aimed at reducing the number of smokers would amount to an illegal interference with their trade.

"There is no scientific consensus on the harmfulness of tobacco smoke and on the accuracy of the methods of measurement usually applied," said an alliance of British American Tobacco, France's Imperial Tobacco and Altadis, a Spanish-French group.

The World Health Organization (WHO), which was invited to speak as amicus curiae (a legal term meaning 'friend of the court'), argued that tobacco products were uniquely dangerous and that the case against them was "overwhelming".
The WHO said that smoking caused 600,000 deaths in the EU every year, with another 200,000 people dying from exposure to second-hand smoke.
"There are very few substances with which tobacco can be compared," it said in its submission.
"Even nitric acid, the substance with which the tobacco industry compares its products, is not as harmful as tobacco.

"

The court's ruling on the legality of any future EU laws on tobacco products will not be delivered until the summer at the earliest.

The euro hit a fresh 15-year high of $1.1378, while the Japanese yen and the British pound also strengthened against the greenback.
However, the Australian and New Zealand dollars slipped after their respective central banks raised interest rates by less than some had expected.
Meanwhile, bitcoin continues its recovery from its nearly two-year low last week, trading just below $17,000.
The latest slide in the dollar comes as investors look ahead to the release of US consumer price index (CPI) data, which is due out on 10 January.
Inflation data is also scheduled to be released in the UK, Canada and Europe.
"It appears that the stars are aligning for a major beat-down of the dollar in the coming weeks as the market prepares for a Fed pivot," said Edward Moya, senior market analyst at Oanda.
"The dollar's downfall won't be a straight line downward… The start of the year is setting up to be quite rocky for risky assets," he added.

Media organisations have asked a US judge to release the notes of a juror in the Michael Jackson trial so they can be considered for a possible new trial.
The singer was acquitted in 2005 of molesting 13-year-old Gavin Arvizo but convicted of enticing him to travel across state lines.
The media submitted a motion on Friday asking for the notes to be released under seal, meaning they would not be made public.
It is not clear when Santa Barbara Superior Court Judge Peter Busch will rule on the request.

The media motion comes about a month after the juror, who asked not to be identified, submitted a letter asking to be excused from the jury for Jackson's upcoming trial on charges of making illegal recordings of children.
In the letter, the juror said news reports about the case had brought back memories of the 2005 trial and "re-traumatised" her.
The judge denied the request, saying the jury had already been selected and it was too late to replace her.
In their motion, lawyers for media organisations including ABC, the BBC, the Los Angeles Times and the Press Association said the juror should be given an opportunity to explain her comments.
They said the note raised questions about the fairness of Jackson's trial, and the integrity of the jury that heard the case.
"This is not a situation where a juror is simply seeking to avoid further service by asserting that being on the jury has been a traumatic experience...
[she] expressly raised issues concerning her ability to be fair and impartial," the motion said.
Media lawyers also asked the judge to question the juror in court, but the judge has not yet indicated whether he will do so.

The Bees have taken seven points from their past three games and sit fifth in the table, level on points with fourth-placed Arsenal.

Sam Hamm has decided to withdraw his name from consideration for the post of US ambassador to the Vatican.
The move comes after some high-profile American Catholics, including members of Congress, raised objections to his nomination.
A statement from the US State Department said Mr Hamm had decided "this is not the right time for him to serve in this position".
Mr Hamm is a former adviser to President George W Bush.
His withdrawal comes as the US Senate prepared to vote on his nomination.
The Vatican has not had an ambassador from the US since 1984, when President Ronald Reagan chose William A Donohue for the post.
Mr Donohue's nomination was never confirmed by the Senate and he served as ambassador until 1986 without the post being filled.

The Vatican is considered a diplomatic priority for the US because it is the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church and because it is the seat of a global political organisation with ties to more than 100 countries.
Mr Hamm worked on President Bush's 2000 election campaign and later became a member of the White House staff.
He worked on social issues as deputy assistant to the president and director of the White House Office of Faith-Based and Community Initiatives.
In 2002 he was appointed by the US president to serve on the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom.

TV's future down the phone line

By Matt Wells, technology reporter

Published 1 hour ago

Updated 1 hour ago
The BBC is developing a way for people to watch television on their phones without eating into their mobile data caps.
Media player BBC iPlayer is to launch a new "data-free" iPlayer Radio app, offering listeners unlimited access to the BBC's radio output without it counting towards their data usage.
The app will automatically switch to using Wi-Fi networks if they are available, and will only use a mobile network if Wi-Fi is not available.
The BBC said the move would make its radio "more accessible than ever".
The app has been developed in partnership with mobile network operator EE, and will be available on iOS and Android phones.
The app will be available to all EE customers, as well as customers of BT and TalkTalk, which both use EE's network.
The app is not entirely data-free, however.
EE customers who use the app when they have run out of data or are not on an EE plan will have their data usage counted.
Customers of other networks will be charged for data usage if they have not bought a data add-on or are not on an unlimited plan.
The app is available to download now from the Google Play and Apple app stores.

A BBC spokesman said: "Data-free listening has been made possible following a deal between the BBC and EE, part of BT Group, to enable customers on EE, BT Mobile and TalkTalk Mobile to listen to BBC radio without impacting their monthly data allowance.
"The data-free version of the BBC iPlayer Radio app is the result of a groundbreaking partnership between the BBC and EE.

"EE has made it possible for its customers to use the app in a data-free way and the BBC has developed the technology that makes this possible."

Last month the BBC launched a "data-saving" version of its main iPlayer app, which reduces the amount of data used when people watch TV on their phones.
At the time, the BBC said it wanted to help people cut down on unexpected data charges.

"

"It shows that audiences are eager to get back to the movies if given the right opportunity.

"

"

Tech firm Shanda has bought a $586m stake in China's leading online media company Sina.

People in China can now send text messages to donate money to help victims of last month's earthquake in Nepal.

A new, pocket-sized device could help people with hearing loss communicate more easily with others.
The phone, called Sign, is being developed by a team at Harvard University's Wyss Institute, along with a Boston-based startup called MotionSavvy.
The device consists of a tablet with a screen the size of a smartphone, attached to a base that contains a camera.
That camera tracks the movements of the user's hands, allowing them to communicate in sign language.
The team at Harvard, who developed the technology, say it is the first time sign language has been translated into text and then spoken aloud, all in real time.
They hope it will make life easier for the estimated 36 million people in the US alone whose hearing is impaired.
The Sign device translates sign language into text, which it then speaks aloud, helping deaf people communicate with the hearing.
It does this through a sophisticated algorithm that can track hands and identify letters.
"It's a communication barrier that this technology breaks down," said MotionSavvy CEO Alex Dreger.
"It's a tool that lets them [deaf people] communicate onto the hearing world and empowers them to be more independent.

"

The device, which will cost less than $500, is not yet on the market, although the team is hoping to launch a smaller version later this year.
"It's a complex technology, it takes a lot of computational power," said Mr Dreger.
"And while we're very excited by it, we're taking our time to get it right.

"

The Sign device is one of a number of projects aimed at helping deaf people communicate more easily.
Another includes a glove fitted with sensors that convert sign language movements into text messages.

The EU and US appear no closer to resolving their trade dispute, after talks ended without agreement in Washington.
The two sides have been locked in a trade row for 18 months over allegations of unfair competition.
The US imposed tariffs on EU aircraft and other goods worth $7.5bn in 1997.
The EU currently imposes duties on US goods worth $4bn, on everything from jeans to motorcycles.

Russian pole vaulter Yelena Isinbayeva has set a new world record of 5.06m at a meeting in Zurich.

The 25-year-old broke her own record of 5.04m, set in February 2004, with her first attempt at 5.06m.

Her record tally now stands at 14 - the most ever by a female pole vaulter.

Suicide drones armed with nuclear warheads are an "imminent" threat and may have already been used, a report by a Russian think tank on the activities of Islamist militants has warned.
Moscow has been worrying about the possibility of nuclear terrorism for several years.

And recent concerns increased after Kazakhstan seized a uranium processing plant close to the border with Kyrgyzstan, which Moscow described as the "most dangerous" place in the world for storing nuclear materials.

Think tank Rusi's latest report concludes that "the threat of a nuclear strike by non-state actors is imminent", although it did not suggest that any particular group was ready to go ahead with such an attack.

It added that there was a risk that they had already deployed a nuclear device, with Pakistan being the most likely location for such an attack.

Prime Minister John Howard has thrown his support behind human stem cell research.
The Australian leader said on Tuesday that he did not support "destructive" cloning for stem cells, but he did back research on stem cells from embryos that are left over from IVF treatment.
Mr Howard's announcement is being seen as a move to head off a split within his government over the issue.
Several members of his government have called for legislation to be introduced to allow more research.
The prime minister said he would not introduce such laws, but his support for research on "spare" embryos was a significant shift from his previous position.
Embryonic stem cells

Mr Howard said he wanted to see legislation introduced to ensure that the embryos which were created for in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment and which were "spares" from IVF treatment were used productively for research.
"I think if we can find a use for these embryos that otherwise would be destroyed, then that is a good thing to do," he said.
"I don't think it is destructive to use them for research purposes provided that research is not destructive.

"

Mr Howard said he did not support the "destructive" cloning of human embryos for research purposes and he wanted to ensure that any legislation introduced to allow research on spare embryos made that clear.
"I think it would be a mistake to try to legislate for cloning of human beings for research purposes," he said.
"I think that would be a step too far and, to be frank, I don't think the public would support that."

He became a favorite of McDonald's founder, Ray Kroc, and was seen as a likely successor to him after he died in 1984.

The US created 235,000 jobs in February, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
That was the most jobs created in a month since March 2022.
But it is still considered slow growth, especially considering that the US economy needs to create roughly 150,000 jobs a month to keep up with the growth of the working-age population.
The unemployment rate remained flat at 3.6%, near a 50-year low.
Average hourly earnings increased 0.1% in February, raising wages by 5.1% from a year earlier, compared with a 5.7% annual increase in January.
The report showed that there are still more jobs than there are workers to fill them.
In February, there were 1.8 job openings for every unemployed person.
The labor force participation rate, which measures the share of working-age Americans who are working or looking for work, was 62.4% - unchanged from January.

Professional and business services added 74,000 jobs; transportation and warehousing added 60,000; education added 48,000; and manufacturing added 44,000.

However, the number of restaurant and bar jobs still has not returned to its pre-pandemic level.
The sector remains about 426,000 jobs below its February 2020 level.

The consumer price index rose 6.4% in January from a year earlier, the smallest increase in nearly a year.

A new report has revealed that nearly half of all mobile phones in the UK are now being used to access the internet.
The study, conducted by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), found that 49% of mobile phone users in the country are going online using their devices.

In 2018, only 41% of mobile phone users were accessing the internet on their devices, indicating a rapid shift in consumer behavior.
The ONS report also revealed that younger age groups are driving this surge in mobile internet usage.
Among 16 to 24-year-olds, a staggering 95% of mobile phone users are going online.
This age group has grown up with smartphones and is more likely to rely on them for various activities, including social media, online shopping, and entertainment.

With lockdowns and restrictions in place, people have increasingly turned to their mobile phones for work, education, and entertainment.

This shift in consumer behavior also presents opportunities for mobile app developers and digital marketers to create innovative and engaging experiences tailored to mobile users.
However, the report also highlighted the digital divide that still exists in the UK.

While mobile internet usage is on the rise, there are still segments of the population, particularly older age groups and those in rural areas, who may not have access to reliable internet connections or the necessary digital skills to fully utilize mobile internet services.
Overall, the ONS report paints a picture of a rapidly evolving digital landscape in the UK, with mobile internet usage becoming increasingly prevalent.
As technology continues to advance and mobile devices become more powerful, it is likely that this trend will continue to grow, shaping the way we access and interact with the online world.

The rise of high-definition technology has revolutionized the way we consume media, from television shows to movies.
With its crystal-clear picture quality and immersive audio, high-definition has become the new standard for visual entertainment.

However, this advancement in technology has also raised questions about the future of DVDs.

DVDs, once the go-to format for home entertainment, are now facing stiff competition from streaming services and digital downloads.
The convenience and accessibility of these platforms have made them increasingly popular among consumers.
But what does this mean for DVDs in the age of high-definition?
One of the main challenges for DVDs is their limited storage capacity.
High-definition content requires more space than standard-definition, resulting in a trade-off between picture quality and the amount of content that can be stored on a single disc.
This limitation has become more apparent as streaming services offer a vast library of high-definition content without the need for physical media.
Another factor affecting the future of DVDs is the rapid advancement of technology.
As new formats and devices emerge, the demand for DVDs has declined.
Blu-ray, a high-definition optical disc format, was once seen as the successor to DVDs.
However, even Blu-ray has struggled to gain widespread adoption, with many consumers opting for digital alternatives instead.
Despite these challenges, DVDs still have a loyal following.
Some consumers prefer the tangible nature of physical media, enjoying the experience of browsing through a collection of DVDs and selecting a movie to watch.
Additionally, DVDs can be played on a wide range of devices, including older models that may not support streaming services or digital downloads.
Furthermore, DVDs continue to be a popular choice for collectors and enthusiasts.
Limited edition releases, bonus features, and director's cuts are often exclusive to physical media, making DVDs a desirable option for those seeking a more immersive viewing experience.
In response to the rise of high-definition and the decline of DVDs, some companies have started to release "upgraded" versions of movies on Blu-ray or 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray.
These editions offer improved picture and sound quality, enticing consumers who want the best possible viewing experience.
In conclusion, high-definition technology has undoubtedly had an impact on the future of DVDs.
While streaming services and digital downloads have gained popularity, DVDs still have a place in the market, particularly among collectors and those who prefer physical media.
As technology continues to evolve, it remains to be seen how DVDs will adapt and whether they will continue to be a viable option for home entertainment.
