Diageo, the British multinational alcoholic beverages company, has announced plans to extend its partnership with India's leading beer company United Breweries (UB).
The company presently has a controlling stake of about 52% in the company.
The extended partnership between the two companies will result in a new entity, Diageo India, which will be 63% owned by Diageo and 37% owned by United Breweries.
The new partnership is expected to be completed by the end of fiscal 2024.
This move comes as part of Diageo's strategy to expand its presence in the fast-growing Asian beer market, which is estimated to be worth $70 billion.
United Breweries is one of the largest beer companies in India, with a portfolio of popular brands such as Kingfisher, Heineken, and Corona.
The company has a strong presence in the Indian market and has been expanding its operations in recent years.
Diageo's partnership with United Breweries began in 2015, when the company acquired a controlling stake in the company.
The new entity, Diageo India, will be well-positioned to capitalize on the growing demand for beer in the country.
Diageo is a global leader in the alcoholic beverages industry, with a portfolio of brands that includes Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, and Guinness.
The company has been expanding its presence in the Asian market in recent years and the new partnership with United Breweries is part of its strategy to grow its business in the region.
With the growing demand for beer in India and other Asian countries, Diageo is positioning itself to become a major player in the regional beer market.
The extended partnership between Diageo and United Breweries is expected to benefit both companies and help them to expand their operations in the growing Asian beer market.

With Diageo's expertise in the alcoholic beverages industry and United Breweries' strong presence in the Indian market, the new entity, Diageo India, will be well-positioned to become a leading player in the regional beer market.
Both companies expect the partnership to be completed by the end of fiscal 2024 and are excited about the future prospects of the new entity.

China has suspended approval for 26 coal-fired power projects in 13 provinces and regions that were already being implemented, according to an announcement by the National Energy Administration (NEA).
The move comes as part of the country's efforts to cut back on carbon emissions and improve the air quality.

The NEA's notice, dated 5 November, said that the suspended projects had a total planned capacity of 130 gigawatts (GW), which is equivalent to about 15% of the nation's existing installed capacity for coal-fired power.
The affected regions include the major coal-producing provinces of Shaanxi, Shanxi, and Inner Mongolia.
The NEA's notice stated that the suspension was necessary because many of the projects had not obtained proper permits and were in areas where coal consumption was already high.
The agency also said that some of the projects had been approved illegally or were being implemented in areas where they could pose a safety risk.
This move comes as China is under pressure to reduce its reliance on coal as a source of energy, due to its heavy carbon emissions and the impact it has on the country's air quality.
In recent years, the government has been trying to promote the use of renewable energy sources, such as wind and solar power, to reduce its dependence on coal.
The suspension of these projects is a significant step towards reducing China's carbon emissions and improving the country's air quality.
However, it may also have a significant impact on the country's economy, as the coal industry is a major source of revenue for many regions.
Japanese bank shares rose on speculation that the country's three mega-banks may consider merging.
Shares in Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMFG) and Mizuho Financial Group (MHFG) all rose on the Tokyo stock exchange on Thursday.
The move came after reports that Japan's three biggest lenders were in talks about possible mergers.
Local media said that the banks were planning to submit a formal proposal to the Japanese government about the merger plan.
The merger would create one of the world's largest financial groups with about $2.8 trillion in assets.
The move would be part of a government initiative to help Japan's biggest banks compete with their global rivals.
However, it is not clear how the merger would be structured or whether there would be any regulatory hurdles.
The dollar has fallen to its lowest level in 20 years against the euro, with other currencies also gaining ground.
The European Commission has warned that the weakening dollar could reignite the currency wars of the last financial crisis.
The dollar's decline accelerated after the US Federal Reserve last month signalled it was close to the end of its interest rate increases.
Many analysts think the Fed's move - which followed dovish signals from other major central banks - has triggered the dollar's fall.
But some see the start of a longer-term decline for the dollar, which would have serious implications for the US and the global economy.
The euro has risen above the key $1.20 level, hitting a high last seen in late 2002.
With the single currency now worth more than a dollar, holidaymakers travelling to the US are getting a bonus - their euros can buy more ice cream, burgers and beer than before.
But the European Commission, the EU's executive body, has warned that the dollar's decline is a cause for concern.

In its annual report on the international role of the euro, it said the euro's appreciation had been "particularly rapid" and warned that the "ongoing weakness of the US dollar" could have serious consequences for the global economy.
"The risk of competitive devaluations cannot be excluded," the report said.
Competitive devaluations are when countries deliberately reduce the value of their currencies in the hope of giving their exporters a price advantage.
This can lead to a "race to the bottom" as countries try to undercut each other by devaluing their currencies further.
This dynamic can destabilise the global economy.

The report did not explicitly say the US was responsible for the dollar's weakness, but the clear implication was that the Fed's decision to pause its rate hike cycle had triggered the dollar's decline.
Other major central banks, including the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan, have also shifted to more dovish stances, but the Fed's move was the most dramatic.
In effect, the report accused the US of deliberately weakening its currency to gain an economic advantage.
Over the years the US has frequently been accused of manipulating its currency, but it has always denied doing so.
The dollar remains the world's dominant currency, used in most international transactions.
As such, any shift in its value has wide-ranging implications for the global economy.

In the wake of the news that Google's parent company, Alphabet, has seen its market capitalisation drop below $1 trillion, analysts have observed a correlation between the selloff of tech stocks and the large number of employees who have exercised their stock options this year.

Data collected by Bloomberg shows that Alphabet and Microsoft Corp have lost about $84 billion in market value since the beginning of October, a period during which tech employees have sold twice as many shares as they did in the first nine months of the year.
The selloff has accelerated in recent days, with "a flood of trades" executed by employees following Alphabet's decision to cut its workforce by around 6% - or around 20,000 jobs.
The dip in share price has also been attributed to the Federal Reserve's continued interest rate hikes, which are expected to continue into next year, and growing concerns over the economic outlook.
The dip in share prices began in October, when Amazon announced it was laying off around 18,000 staff, and Meta announced its first-ever year-on-year decline in advertising revenue.
This was followed by Google's announcement of its own layoffs.
It is thought that the announcements of mass redundancies within the tech sector have triggered the selloff, with employees seeking to cash in their stocks before they lose their value.
Some analysts have said that the selloff is not surprising, given the scale of the layoffs in the tech sector and how expensive tech stocks have been in recent years.

Will Straf, a manager of Boston Consulting Group's U.S. innovation fund, said: "That was the bubble: valuations that didn't reflect the underlying fundamentals and a lot of expectations about perpetual growth."
However, others have argued that the selloff is an overreaction, with some analysts claiming that the redundancies represent a reset, rather than a sign of enduring economic pain.

A former Wall Street analyst, Eric Schiffer, said: "Stock price declines are necessary and a good thing as money shifts from overpriced and speculative back to safety and quality, where it should be."
As well as the selloff from employees, a large number of institutional investors have also sold off their tech stocks in recent days.
It is thought that investors are moving to other sectors in order to mitigate risk in the event of a recession.
Alphabet's current market capitalisation is around $913 billion.

The French suitor, Xavier Rolet, presented himself as a "true lover" of the London Stock Exchange as he wooed shareholders with promises of billions of extra pounds in revenue and a leap forward for the UK's financial standing.
The 57-year-old finished his presentation to investors at the London Stock Exchange's (LSE) annual meeting with a question and answer session that was at times tense.
"I'm confident that we have the right plan, the right strategy to deliver and achieve that £5bn vision," he said.
But several shareholders stood up and voiced their concerns, interrupting Mr Rolet as he tried to answer questions put to him by the chairman, Donald Brydon.
One shareholder asked if Mr Rolet planned to move the LSE's headquarters to Paris, to which he replied: "No, no, no.
This is not the plan.

"

Another shareholder accused him of "being vague" on the details of his strategy, before adding: "I am not convinced at all by you.

"

When another investor asked if he had visited the London Stock Exchange, Mr Rolet replied: "I spend most of my time in the office right next door to you.

"

The LSE's chief financial officer, Scott Evans, jumped in to clarify that Mr Rolet had in fact spent "a lot of time in this actual room".
In his opening remarks, Mr Rolet he had "profound respect" for the LSE and its history and traditions.
"The LSE means a lot to me, it's a thrilling adventure, and I did not hesitate to make it official and public by moving to London," he said.

"I fell in love with the LSE, this is a true love, and you don't fall in love with the LSE and then try to destroy it."

Earlier this year, the LSE agreed to a £32bn takeover by the Franco-Dutch rival Euronext.
Last month, the LSE's regulators cleared the deal, saying it did not harm the public interest.
The deal still needs the approval of about 600 shareholders, with a vote expected in the coming weeks.
The golden rule of foreign policy is "intact" and the UK will not "turn away from that", the former ambassador to Russia has said.
Dame Anne Pringle told the BBC the principle of "do as you would be done by" was as relevant now as it had been when laid down by Nelson Mandela.
Her comments came after the prime minister hosted a summit of African leaders aimed at boosting economic ties.
Asked if the foreign policy approach - to do unto others as you would have them do unto you - was at risk, Dame Anne said: "I don't think so.
"I think it
[the policy] is intact.
I can't immediately think of anything that would suggest otherwise.

"

But she did add that the UK was "turning away" from the "moral leadership" it had shown after the second world war.
The chief executive of Bombardier, Alain Bellemare, will step down from his role after nearly six years in the position.
Bellemare will be replaced by Éric Martel, the company's current president of aviation.
Martel will assume the role of president and CEO on 1 January 2023.
Under Bellemare's leadership, Bombardier underwent a significant restructuring, which included the sale of the company's rail business and a shift in focus towards the aviation industry.
These changes were made in an effort to streamline the company's operations and reduce its debt.
During his time as CEO, Bombardier also experienced significant challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic, which has impacted the aviation industry as a whole.
Despite these challenges, Bellemare has guided the company through a period of growth and transformation.

In a statement, Bellemare said: "With the turnaround plan nearing its end, I believe this is the right time to hand over the reins to someone with aviation experience to continue driving the transformation of Bombardier."

Bombardier's board of directors has expressed its gratitude for Bellemare's leadership and wishes him well in his future endeavours.
JPMorgan Chase has admitted that two of its predecessor firms benefited from slavery in the 19th century.
The bank said its ownership structure was "consistent with" that of slave owners, in a statement accompanying its annual report.
It comes after criticism from a UK-based campaign group, Spotlight on Slavery.
The organisation had called for banks to investigate their historical links to slavery.
Spotlight on Slavery's director, Christopher Brown, said the admission by JPMorgan was a significant step forward.

"There are still thousands of people around the world who are impacted by the legacy of slavery, so it is crucial that financial institutions like JPMorgan Chase take responsibility for helping to address the systemic economic inequalities which are still present today," he added.
The bank did not specify whether it would offer compensation.
It did, however, announce plans to allocate $350m towards a programme of initiatives addressing "systemic economic inequality" and "the legacy of slavery".
These will include funding job training, education and entrepreneurship among communities of colour.
The admission comes after increasing scrutiny of banks' historic ties to the slave trade.
In March, an investigation by Guardian journalists revealed that nearly two dozen global banks had been founded, or had their early growth funded, by investors with links to the slave trade.
These included Barclays, HSBC and Credit Suisse.
The findings led to calls for banks to pay reparations for the slave trade.

Earlier this year, a group of MPs and peers wrote to the Bank of England's governor, Andrew Bailey, urging the central bank to require banks to look into their historical links to slavery and make the results public.
Indian airline SpiceJet has signed a $1.8bn deal with Deccan Aviation's aircraft leasing company to acquire up to 155 aircraft.
Deccan Aviation's aircraft leasing firm, Deccan Charters, will supply 75 new Bombardier Q400 aircraft to SpiceJet, with the first delivery scheduled for the second quarter of 2024.
Under the agreement, Deccan Charters will also buy 50 new Boeing 737 MAX aircraft from lessor BBAM for delivery between late 2023 and 2028.
In addition, SpiceJet will buy 20 new Boeing 737 MAX aircraft directly from Boeing.
The deals are part of SpiceJet's plans to expand its fleet to more than 200 aircraft.
India's booming domestic air travel market has prompted airlines to place orders for more than 900 new aircraft over the past year.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) issued a warning on the impact of subsidies offered by countries on fisheries.
The impacts are detrimental to the sustainability of fish stocks and the ecosystems and livelihoods connected to them.
The warning follows a study on fisheries subsidies, a key issue behind overfishing.
The study was led by the FAO and conducted with the assistance of the European Union.
It found that approximately $14 billion in annual fisheries subsidies encourage continued overfishing.
Of this total, $1.3 billion dollars are offered by countries whose fisheries are already sustainably managed.
The study found that these subsidies contribute to declining fish stocks, with implications for the livelihoods of fishers and the food security and nutrition of billions of people.
The findings of the study were validated at a technical workshop attended by representatives from more than 30 countries.
The study concludes that the impacts of fisheries subsidies urgently need to be addressed through the rules of the World Trade Organization (WTO).
The WTO's Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (ASCM) establishes rules on the use of subsidies.
The study recommends that members of the WTO retain and strengthen the rules of the ASCM.
It also encourages members to agree on clear and effective rules to manage fisheries subsidies, with a particular focus on eliminating those subsidies that contribute to overcapacity and overfishing.
The study comes as the WTO continues to examine the issue of fisheries subsidies as part of its on-going fisheries subsidies negotiation.
The goal is to reach an agreement that reduces harmful fishing subsidies, leads to sustainable fisheries, and mitigates the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on the sector.
The FAO warns that the negotiators have a narrow window to reach an agreement that would contribute to a sustainable recovery of the sector.
The organization urges the members of the WTO to engage constructively and swiftly to ensure the negotiations reach a successful conclusion.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating troubled Marsh & McLennan over concerns that the insurance broker violated securities laws, according to people familiar with the matter.

The probe, which is in its early stages, focuses on whether Marsh & McLennan failed to disclose conflicts of interest when it recommended certain investment products to its customers, said the people, who refused to be named because the investigation is private.

The investigation comes on the heels of a similar probe of Marsh & McLennan by New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo, who in October accused the broker of failing to disclose millions of dollars in commissions it received for placing clients in investment products.
Marsh & McLennan has said it is cooperating with the attorney general's investigation.
It's unclear whether the company has been formally notified of the SEC investigation.
Shares of Marsh & McLennan fell 2.2% to $42.75 in New York Stock Exchange trading yesterday.
The Nasdaq exchange is planning a share sale that could raise around $100m (£85m) for its parent company Nasdaq Inc, according to reports.
The exchange operator is said to be considering a sale of around 10 million shares, which could increase its free float to nearly 20%.
If successful, it would be the first time Nasdaq has sold shares since it went public in 2002.
Nasdaq's parent company is currently owned by a group of investors including Silver Lake Partners, Bain Capital, and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan.
The news comes as the Nasdaq Composite index has risen more than 13% so far this year, due in part to the surge in technology stocks.
Last year, Nasdaq generated around $2.2bn in annual revenue, down from $3.4bn in 2019 before the pandemic.
The European Union is planning to use some of its budget for development aid more efficiently in order to boost investments in countries most vulnerable to the effects of climate change.
The EU is the world's largest aid donor and is planning to set up an international climate finance facility that would make $1.3 billion available for African countries between now and 2027.
The facility is expected to be up and running by the middle of 2024.
Depending on how well it works, the facility may be expanded to other regions.
The facility is one of several initiatives planned to help countries in Africa adapt to climate change without having to bear the costs of migration to Europe.
The EU has also been supporting Africa's green energy transition, including by funding solar power and wind power projects.
It has also been training young people in Africa to work in the green energy sector as part of its Green Deal program.

The facility is intended to help African countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, including by investing in early warning systems for disasters, climate-resilient infrastructure, and programs to help people move away from vulnerable areas.
According to the United Nations, climate change is set to push more than 100 million people into poverty over the next decade without assistance.
This number could be reduced by half if governments and businesses step up their efforts to help communities adapt.
The facility is also intended to help prevent further displacement of people as a result of climate change by providing funding to help communities adapt.
The UK has expressed interest in joining the facility once it has left the transition period following Brexit.
Being a part of this facility aligns with the UK's commitment to supporting developing countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change and could provide further funding for projects in Africa.
The Aston Martin brand has always been associated with luxury and performance, but until recently, it was missing from a prominent segment of the market.
That changed with the introduction of the DB11, which finally gave Aston a true competitor to the likes of the Porsche 911 and Audi R8.
With the release of the new Vantage, the company is now looking to take on the Porsche 718.
Although the Vantage is technically a successor to the previous Vantage, it's a completely different animal.
The new car is built on a modified version of the DB11's platform, and it shows.
It's lighter, tighter, and more agile than the old Vantage, and it's a true driver's car.
Under the hood, the Vantage is powered by a 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine that's shared with the DB11.
In the Vantage, the engine produces 503 horsepower and 461 lb-ft of torque, which gives the car a 0-60 time of just 3.6 seconds and a top speed of 195 miles per hour.
The Vantage's interior is typical Aston Martin, which is to say that it's luxurious and stylish, but not quite as fancy as you'd find in a Porsche.
The seats are comfortable and supportive, and the dashboard is simple and easy to use.
There's also a decent amount of space in the back seat, which is surprising for a car of this type.
Aston Martin has always been a bit of a niche brand, but with the DB11 and the Vantage, it's finally starting to become a real threat to the likes of Porsche and Audi.
If you're in the market for a high-performance sports car, the Vantage is definitely worth a look.
Beijing's municipal government recently announced plans to charge a fee for vehicle parking in order to control the number of cars on the road, but drivers aren't happy about it.
The new policy is set to take effect on October 1, and will include fees for both on-street and off-street parking.
For on-street parking, fees will be charged at a rate of 2 yuan ($0.30) for every half hour.
For off-street parking, fees will be charged at a rate of 3 yuan ($0.45) for every hour.
In addition, a monthly cap of 500 yuan ($72) will be set for on-street parking fees, and a daily cap of 10 yuan ($1.50) for off-street parking fees.
Drivers in Beijing have reacted with fury to the new policy, with many taking to social media to complain about the additional costs.

One driver, who asked to remain anonymous, said "I understand that the government needs to control the number of cars on the road, but why should we have to pay for the privilege of parking our own cars?

"

Another driver, who also asked to remain anonymous, said "I think the fees are fair, but the problem is that there are no enough parking spaces available.
So even if I want to pay for a spot, I often can't find one.

"

The municipal government has defended the policy, saying that it is necessary in order to reduce traffic congestion and pollution in the city.
A spokesman for the government said "The fees are necessary to encourage people to use public transportation and to reduce the number of cars on the road.

"

Despite the criticism, it appears that the policy will go ahead as planned.
Whether or not it will be effective in reducing traffic congestion and pollution in the city remains to be seen.

The troubled Italian dairy group Parmalat has sued 45 banks, alleging a "massive corruption and fraud" scheme that it says contributed to a dramatic decline in its fortunes and nearly bankrupted the company.
Parmalat, once Italy's largest dairy company, filed for bankruptcy in 2003 after revealing that it had found a $20bn hole in its finances.
The company has resurfaced under new ownership and now wants to recoup some of the losses it suffered.

"Parmalat collapsed as a result of a massive corruption and fraud scheme, conceived and orchestrated by the former management of the company, assisted by a number of financial institutions," the company said in a statement.
The company has filed lawsuits against banks including Credit Suisse, Bank of New York Mellon, Citibank, Deutsche Bank and Nomura.

Parmalat has claimed that the banks' involvement in the alleged fraud included "the fraudulent issuance, through an intricate web of offshore companies, of fake invoices for non-existent transactions".
The company said it had uncovered evidence that the banks "either knew, or should have known" about the alleged fraud.
Parmalat is seeking damages in an amount to be determined at trial, as well as interest payments on money it lost.
Japanese growth grinds to a halt in the third quarter as exports weaken and consumer spending declines, raising concerns about the outlook for the world's third-largest economy.
Economic growth in Japan ground to a halt in the third quarter as exports weakened and consumer spending declined, raising concerns about the outlook for the world's third-largest economy.

Data released on Monday showed that Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) remained unchanged in the three months through September from the previous quarter, compared to a median market forecast for a 0.2% contraction.

The world's third-largest economy has been struggling to recover from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, with its export-dependent manufacturers hit by a strong yen and slower global growth.
On a yearly basis, Japan's GDP grew 0.3%, compared to a median forecast for a 0.2% contraction and a 0.1% increase in the second quarter.
The data showed that private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's GDP, declined 0.1% in the third quarter, marking the second consecutive quarterly decline.
Investment in plants and equipment also declined, offsetting gains in government spending and exports.
Japan's economy has been struggling to recover from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, with the government's stimulus measures failing to boost consumer spending.
The country's economy has also been hit by the strengthening yen, which has made Japanese exports more expensive and reduced the income of exporters.
The war in Ukraine has also reduced demand for Japanese exports, particularly in Russia and Ukraine, which are major importers of Japanese goods.
Swedish home appliances maker Electrolux announced that it is to export hundreds of jobs from Europe to Southeast Asia, affecting workers in Sweden, Italy and Poland.
The company, which makes refrigerators and other appliances under the Electrolux, AEG and Frigidaire brands, said it would cut about 700 jobs in Europe, with most of the positions moving to Thailand.
The company employs about 85,000 people globally.
Electrolux has faced increased competition from cheaper Asian brands, as well as from American appliance giant Whirlpool, which has been able to keep costs down by producing in Mexico.
The company said it had taken the decision to optimize its European operations, and that the move would help to ensure its long-term competitiveness.
It added that it would help to "secure jobs in a sustainable way" in the long term.
Electrolux has already started discussions with employee representatives in the three countries, with the aim of minimizing the impact of the moves on workers.
An oligarch once praised as the richest man in Russia, Yukos oil boss Mikhail Khodorkovsky, is seeking political asylum in the US, citing fears for his safety if he returns home from a Siberian jail.
Mr Khodorkovsky, who has spent a decade in Russian prisons, was arrested again last month on a new set of charges.
His lawyer said on Tuesday that he had requested a visa to the US and asked for political asylum.
The former tycoon, once seen as a possible challenger to Vladimir Putin,  has "reasonable suspicions of his imminent persecution", his lawyer Vadim Klyuvgant said in a video statement.
The US State Department would not comment directly on Mr Khodorkovsky's request, but said it was "closely following" his case.
A decision will be made in coming days on whether to grant the oligarch a visa to visit the US.
Mr Khodorkovsky, who denies all the charges against him, was previously granted parole on condition that he remained in Siberia.
But last month a court in the region revoked his parole and sent him to a prison colony after he was accused of possessing a mobile phone, which he has denied.
A subsidiary of Russian oil giant Yukos has been hit with a $1.4bn claim from a group of banks, just two weeks after it was bought from bankruptcy.

The claim from a group of 10 banks, led by Credit Suisse and ING, is larger than the $1.3bn price tag for the purchase of YukosOil, which was bought by a group of businessmen backed by state-owned Gazprom.
The claim is being disputed by the new owners, who say they have already paid $300m of the $430m price.
The banks are claiming the remainder of their $1.4bn exposure is now covered by the new owners of Yukos, and that the sale was conducted properly.
The claim is further evidence of the difficulties surrounding the sale of Yukos, which was broken up and sold off after its bankruptcy.
The Russian government has said it will investigate the sale of YukosOil, and the former shareholders of Yukos have vowed to challenge the sale in court.
The new owners of YukosOil have said they will work with the Russian government to resolve the dispute, and that they have no plans to sell the company.
The latest data showing inflation in the US is running at its highest level since the early 1980s has sparked worries among economists and policymakers about the potential impact on the economy.
The consumer price index (CPI), which measures the cost of a wide-ranging basket of goods and services, rose to 6.8% in November from 6.2% in October, marking the fastest pace since June 1982.
The rise was driven by increases in the cost of shelter, used cars and trucks, and household furnishings, among other things.
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, has been trying to curb inflation by raising interest rates, but the latest data suggests that these efforts have so far had little effect.
Some economists are now predicting that the Fed will have to raise rates even higher in order to bring inflation under control, which could lead to a recession.
Others are calling for a more balanced approach, arguing that high interest rates could actually hurt the economy by slowing down consumer spending and business investment.
They say that the Fed should focus on targeting inflation in a more targeted way, rather than raising rates across the board.
Whatever course the Fed chooses, it will need to act quickly in order to get a handle on inflation.
With prices rising at such a rapid pace, the gap between the rich and the poor is widening, and the cost of living is becoming increasingly unaffordable for many Americans.
For now, the data suggests that the US economy is in for a rocky few months, and the coming year could be a challenging one.
Confidence among US consumers rose in October after three consecutive months of declines, according to a survey released on Tuesday.
The Conference Board's consumer confidence index increased to 102.5 in October, up from 99.0 in September.
The increase was driven by improvements in consumer attitudes towards current economic conditions and their expectations for the future.
Consumers were more optimistic about the labor market, with the percentage of respondents saying jobs are "plentiful" increasing from 18.3% to 20.3%.
Meanwhile, those saying jobs are "hard to get" declined, from 13.6% to 12.5%.
Conference Board economist Lynn Franco said, "Consumers' assessment of current conditions improved, and their expectations for the next six months rose to their highest level since April 2021.

"

The increase in consumer confidence comes as the Federal Reserve continues to raise interest rates in an effort to tame inflation.
However, the central bank has signaled that it may slow down the pace of rate hikes, which has been welcomed by investors and consumers alike.
Copper production in Chile, the world's largest producer of the metal, hit a record last year, according to government figures.
The country, which accounts for almost 30% of global copper output, mined 5.6 million tonnes of copper in 2022, the highest level yet recorded in its history.
Most of the copper mined in Chile is produced by large, privately owned mining companies, including BHP, Antofagasta and Glencore.
Copper is vital for the infrastructure of renewable energy systems, and rising demand for the metal has been driven by the green energy transition.
Chile's government has tried to increase its tax take from the copper mining sector, but has faced opposition from the companies.
Last year, the government agreed to reduce the amount of copper it charges companies a royalty on from 5% to 2% for large producers, in a bid to resolve a dispute over tax rules.
Companies including Antofagasta and BHP have also agreed to build refineries in Chile as part of the deal, which will lead to increased investment in the country's industrial sector.
GlaxoSmithKline is to dissolve its consumer health division, the company has announced.
The division makes over-the-counter medicines and products, including painkillers like Panadol and Nicorette nicotine gum.
Its chief executive, Brian McNamara, will leave by "mutual agreement" despite being praised for his "strong leadership".
The company said it would take at least three years and cost up to £1.5bn ($1.8bn) to shut down the division.
It expects to make one-off costs of about £2.4bn ($3bn) after taxes.
The decision comes as GSK's patent for asthma drug Advair is about to expire.
The drug is its biggest seller, bringing in £2.6bn ($3.2bn) in 2021.
Chief executive Emma Walmsley said the company wanted to focus on "innovative pharmaceuticals and vaccines".
She said the consumer health division had "delivered strong performance" but the company had decided to "prioritise innovation and growth" in its pharmaceutical business.
"The decision to separate the consumer healthcare business is a difficult one, but it allows GSK to more focused on our chosen priority areas of pharmaceuticals and vaccines," she added.
Mr McNamara said it had been a "great honour" to lead the consumer health division.
In a statement, he said the separation programme would "likely take three years or more to complete".
He added the division had "a broad portfolio and global scale" and was "well positioned for continued success".
It comes as GSK faces competition from other drug companies producing generic versions of Advair.
It is also feeling the impact of price increases for drugs coming off patent, and lower prices for vaccines in Europe.
Last year, GSK announced it would demerge the consumer health division and create a separate company.
But Ms Walmsley said on Wednesday that GSK had decided to instead "fully separate" the division.
A tsunami warning has been issued for banks in Sri Lanka after a large wave crashed into the island's coast, killing at least one person and injuring several more.
The wave, which measured over a metre in height, hit the coast south of the capital, Colombo, on Saturday night.
It was caused by a large underwater earthquake in the Indian Ocean, which measured magnitude 7.2.
The earthquake was centred approximately 570 kilometres (350 miles) south of Sri Lanka, but its impact was felt as far away as the island's capital.
The tsunami warning was issued for the island's entire coast, and police have been ordered to evacuate people from low-lying areas.
The country's disaster management centre said that the highest wave measured was 1.5 metres tall.
However, witnesses reported that the waves were even larger, with some saying they were as high as three metres.
The director of a company that owns a 20% stake in Manchester City has launched a legal challenge against the Premier League club's owners.
Estaban Roig Bajo, director of City Football Group (CFG), has asked a judge to stop the Abu Dhabi United Group from increasing its majority shareholding in CFG.
Mr Roig claims the proposed increase would breach rules on "acting in concert", which prevent anyone controlling more than 30% of a company.
The hearing continues in the High Court in London.
There is no suggestion that Manchester City, who are currently second in the Premier League, have done anything wrong.
In a statement, the club said they "note the claim" and "await a hearing on the matter".
CFG is the holding company for Manchester City and a number of other football clubs and related businesses around the world, all owned by the Abu Dhabi United Group.
Mr Roig, a Spanish national, is one of five directors of CFG, with the others representing the Abu Dhabi United Group.
His lawyers have written to the court alleging "a well-orchestrated plan to increase the ownership and control of CFG by the Abu Dhabi United Group".
They claim that, if the plan were to go ahead, it would be in breach of the "acting in concert" rules, which are an important part of corporate governance.

According to the CFG articles of association, "acting in concert" refers to "any agreement, arrangement or understanding, whether formal or informal" between two or more people to "act or agree to act together, in relation to the affairs of the company".
It is not clear what specific actions by the Abu Dhabi United Group Mr Roig's legal team are referring to, or whether they have asked the court to impose any specific sanctions.
In a statement, Manchester City said they "are aware of a claim by a minority shareholder of City Football Group which was filed in September 2022".
"The claim has been brought on behalf of that shareholder by a minority shareholder of City Football Group.
It relates to the proposed increase in the shareholding of the Abu Dhabi United Group in City Football Group," it added.
"That shareholding increase was approved by the City Football Group board, including the director who has brought the claim, and the independent directors.
"The club is aware of today's hearing and will continue to monitor the situation."
Shanghai, China -- Yangtze Electric Power's profits have more than doubled in the first nine months of the year, the company said on Sunday.
The world's largest hydropower enterprise reported that its net profits reached 5.25 billion yuan ($740 million), up 114% from a year earlier.

The Venezuelan government has launched a program to identify and take over "idle" farms in order to increase national food production and combat hunger.
The program, which is being led by the National Land Institute (INTI), aims to redistribute land to farmers who are willing to cultivate it.
According to INTI, there are thousands of hectares of land in Venezuela that are not being used to produce food, which is contributing to the country's hunger crisis.
The government hopes that by taking over these "idle" farms and giving them to productive farmers, it will be able to increase food production and improve the country's food security.
The program has already identified its first target, a farm in the state of Mérida that has been inactive for years.
The government plans to distribute the land to a group of local farmers who have already expressed interest in cultivating it.

While the program has received some criticism from those who believe that the government should focus on improving the country's economic and political situation before taking on additional initiatives, others have welcomed it as a much-needed effort to address the country's hunger crisis.

Ukraine has trimmed plans to privatise its state-owned assets amid opposition from key allies including the US, the UK and the EU.
The country had been expected to raise about $10bn from the sale of more than 700 state enterprises.
But a draft law now going through parliament has dropped a list of assets to be privatised.
The amended bill only mentions four state companies that would be put up for sale, raising about $233m.
The amendment was supported by the president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

In October, US secretary of state Antony Blinken said that Ukraine should not be in a hurry to sell state assets because corrupt officials could exploit the process to obtain them at undervalued prices.

Ukraine's prime minister, Denys Shmygal, said the sale was necessary to plug a budget deficit, which hit 6.1bn hryvnia ($185m) in the first 10 months of 2022 and is expected to reach 7.5bn hryvnia ($224m) by the end of the year.
The amended bill says the money raised from the privatisations will go towards servicing Ukraine's debt.

The original draft had identified hundreds of state firms for possible privatisation, including Ukraine's biggest bank, Privatbank, several regional banks, energy company Ukrgazvydobuvannya and its rival, Ukrenergo.
Also on the list were Motor Sich, the country's largest aircraft engine manufacturer and a key supplier to the Ukrainian military, and the state's stake in Ukraine's largest steel mill, Metinvest.
The interactive search engine Ask Jeeves is set to make a comeback later this year, as the company behind it hopes to capitalise on the growing popularity of voice-activated technology.
The UK-based firm said Ask Jeeves would be "voice-first", with a focus on answering search queries via smart speakers and other internet-connected devices.
It is the latest attempt to revive the brand, which has lain dormant since being sold to the US tech company IAC in 2010.
The new owners said they wanted to "revive and update" the well-known brand, which first launched as a pioneering search engine more than two decades ago.

At the time, it was known for its use of natural language processing, which allowed users to pose questions in normal English, with results drawn from a range of sources, rather than a list of blue links.
The new version will be "a voice-led, AI-powered discovery experience", according to the company, which said it would draw on the original features that made Ask Jeeves popular.

"We're going to bring back the original Ask Jeeves experience, but update it for today's users and for the modern era," said Doug Scott, co-founder and chief executive of Ask.com, which is owned by IAC.
"We believe in a world where asking questions is the easiest way to get things done and we're going to lead in that world."
The company said Ask Jeeves would launch in the US this year, with a global roll-out planned for 2024.
The announcement reflects the growing popularity of voice-activated technology, with sales of smart speakers such as Amazon's Echo and Google's Nest rising steadily over the past five years.

Other companies are also attempting to cash in on the trend, with Apple and Microsoft recently launching their own smart speaker devices, and Samsung and Sony also releasing updated versions of their products.

German stock exchange operator Deutsche Boerse has raised its dividend for the first time in three years after increasing profits, with chief executive Theodor Weimer saying the company is “back on track”.

The group – which owns the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, among others – increased its dividend for the fiscal year 2022 to 70 euro cents ($73 cents) per share, up from 50 euro cents the previous year, with the company saying it was resuming “its normal dividend policy”.

The move comes after Deutsche Boerse reported a 14% increase in its annual profits, with earnings reaching 727 million euros ($790 million) – helped by increased revenue from its clearing and settlement business.
“We exited the transformation phase with our data and analytics business and are back on track with a strong set of annual results,” Deutsche Boerse CEO Theodor Weimer said.
“All our businesses contributed to this success.”

The company reported that its revenue from its “data, analytics and index business” – which includes its Refinitiv platform – increased by 10% to 1.17 billion euros, with the company noting that it had achieved its goal of increasing recurring revenues to 65% of the unit’s total revenue.

Deutsche Boerse also reported increases in its revenue from its cash and derivatives markets, as well as its clearing and settlement business, with the company saying that it was benefiting from “increased client activity and higher revenues from partner workflows”.

However, the company said that it had incurred “significantly higher costs” in the fourth quarter of 2022, with Deutsche Boerse saying that it had invested in its “IT infrastructure as well as in the build-out of the new data centre in Frankfurt”.
Nevertheless, the company said that it was confident that it could continue to increase its profits in the future, with Mr Weimer saying: “We enter the new fiscal year with confidence.
“Our strong performance gives us comfort in reiterating our medium-term guidance of low to mid-single digit organic revenue growth and consistent annual increases in the dividend per share.”
Sunderland fans woke up today to the news of a takeover of the club by a foreign billionaire.
Within the space of three years, the club has risen from the brink of liquidation to the promise of great things to come.

This takeover will hopefully give the club the stability it needs to rise up the football league and reach the top of English football once more.

Bayer, the parent company of Monsanto, has been fined $1.5bn for bribery in Russia.
The German chemicals giant was charged with funneling cash to a foundation run by Russian intelligence services, with the aim of winning favour for Monsanto in the country.
The Kremlin said it was "ready to cooperate" with the German authorities in their investigation.
The Berlin prosecutor's office said Bayer had "made inaccurate statements" when it acquired Monsanto in 2018 and had "failed to comply with its obligations under the German foreign trade law".
The company said it would "vigorously defend itself against these allegations".
"There is no evidence that the payments in question led to an illegal benefit," it added in a statement.
The German authorities said the payments had been made between 2005 and 2013.
They said some of the cash had been donated to a foundation run by Russia's main intelligence service, the FSB, and later used for "political purposes".
TASS news agency reported that the funds were used to pay for equipment and infrastructure at a children's hospital in the city of Omsk.
The fine comes two years after Bayer bought Monsanto for $63bn, and is one of the biggest anti-corruption penalties ever imposed by German authorities.
The company has already faced massive lawsuits in the US over its Roundup weedkiller, which has been linked to cancer.
In a statement, Bayer said the fine would not affect its full-year outlook, and that it would not affect the sale of Monsanto products in Russia.
The average price of a UK home has fallen by £5,000 this month, to £296,000, according to a leading property website.
It said the market had "slowed down" following the festive period and buyers were "holding back" due to higher rates and inflation.
Rightmove said it was a reversal of the trend over the last few months, when prices rose.
The company's property expert said 2023 was "set to be the year of price corrections".
However, analysts said the falls were not as great as they first appeared, due to the time of year.
Rightmove's monthly house price index tracks asking prices for property advertised on its website.
It found that the average price of property advertised between 2 and 8 January was £296,000, down by 0.9% from £301,000 in the same period the month before.
The company said it was the first time in a year that prices had fallen month-on-month.
However, they were up by 6.3% on the same time last year.

"The market has slowed down following the frenzy of activity we saw on the back of the mini-budget, and the festive period is always a quieter time for trading, with buyers holding back ahead of New Year, which is compounded this year by the hike in interest rates and the impact of inflation on household budgets," said Tim Bannister, Rightmove's property expert.

" 2023 is set to be the year of price corrections, and the start of it has seen a re-balancing of asking prices, with some sellers being forced to adjust their asking price in order to effect a sale, and others deciding to take their property off the market for now and reassess later in the year.

"Those who have been through the buying and selling process a few times are familiar with the ebb and flow of the market, but first-time sellers can find it frustrating when prices aren't rising fast, as they were last year."

Nicky Stevenson, managing director at estate agent Fine & Country, said: "The monthly fall in the Rightmove index is not as significant as it first appears, as the market slows down over the Christmas holiday, making it difficult to accurately assess true pricing trends at this time of year.
"However the market has seen a significant shift in the last three months, and asking prices are now more likely to reflect realistic current values."
Standard Life has become the latest pension provider to cut policy bonuses, following a trend set by Prudential, Aegon, and Aviva.
The company said it would reduce the annual bonuses on its With-Profits policies to 3% from November, down from 3.5%.
The firm said its decision was based on a "lower expectation of future investment returns".

Standard Life hopes the reduction will encourage more policyholders to move their money into its new "With-Profits Cash Reserve Fund", where it expects better growth than on the With-Profits policies.
The fund, which offers a choice of eight investment strategies, was launched in May this year.
Its Mixed Growth strategy has so far delivered a return of 3.25%*, however, this is not a guarantee of future performance.
From October next year, the company will also reduce the number of strategies available for its With-Profits policies from three to two.
Rachel Adebo, a financial expert at the website www.moneysavingexpert.com, has urged policyholders not to panic.
She said that with-profits policies were long-term investments and that it was too early to tell what the impact of the bonus cut would be.

An ounce of gold for immediate delivery fell more than 1% to $1,710.00 on Thursday after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said it plans to sell 13 tons of gold, raising $778 million to help bolster its crisis-fighting resources.
The sale, announced late on Wednesday, marks the IMF's first sale of gold since early 2010.
In recent years, the IMF has made emergency gold sales to help fund aid to Ukraine and other countries.
However, the market was not expecting a sale this year.
The IMF last month said its current stockpile of gold was sufficient to protect its liquidity needs for the foreseeable future.
The market was caught off guard by the sale, on top of a faster pace of interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve, which has driven US bond yields and the dollar higher, pressuring gold.
"It does seem odd that they would sell at a time when gold is under pressure," said Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management.
"The market is pricing in a more aggressive Fed, so that is putting downward pressure on gold… and you've got rising bond yields," he said.
Gold has fallen more than 5% since hitting a two-month high on Monday as the prospect of faster interest rate rises kept the dollar firm, making gold more expensive for other currency holders.

The newest members of the European Union (EU) are underpinning growth in the region as their economies continue to expand, according to a report by the European Commission.

The report, which tracks the economic progress of the EU's newest members since their accession in 2004, found that the average growth rate of the 12 countries was higher than the EU average in the past two years.
It noted that this trend looked set to continue in the near future.

Among the countries cited as being particularly dynamic was Bulgaria, where a number of large-scale infrastructure projects are underway, and Romania, where the government has implemented a programme of reforms designed to attract investment.
The report also noted that the newest members have been able to take advantage of the single market to attract investment and create jobs, particularly in the automotive and electronics sectors.

However, it warned that the countries still faced challenges, including the need to improve their infrastructure and to address the issue of brain drain, with many of their most highly skilled workers moving to other EU countries in search of better opportunities.

The head of the Vatican's Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development said: "We have to accept that there was not enough questioning on the part of the church."

Decisions on when and how Turkey's customs union with the European Union will be updated have been put off until March, according to a joint statement agreed by Brussels and Ankara.

The statement, released early on Saturday, said the customs union would be "modernised" to take account of Turkey's various trade agreements with third countries.
However, the text made no mention of an emergency brake that Turkey had sought, which would allow it to re-impose tariffs on EU imports if it felt the deal was not being honoured.
The issue of the customs union - which removes tariffs on goods travelling between the EU and Turkey - had been one of the key sticking points in the talks.
Turkey wanted to retain the right to impose its own tariffs on imports from Europe if the EU did not allow it to upgrade its customs union agreement.
The joint statement said the EU and Turkey had agreed to "re-energise" their relations and gradually deepen their political dialogue.
It also said the EU would step up financial and technical assistance to help Turkey cope with the nearly three million refugees it is hosting, most of them Syrians.
The assistance would be worth €3bn ($3.4bn) over the next two years and would be released in stages, subject to progress on the refugee issue.

The statement also made reference to the "sensitive issue" of refugees being returned to Turkey from the EU, saying this would be done "in accordance with internationally accepted norms and standards".

It said the EU and Turkey had agreed to "accelerate" preparations for the deal to be implemented "as soon as possible" and that a first meeting to this end would take place at expert level in Brussels on Monday.
The aim is to seal the entire deal, including its financial aspects, by the end of March.

The row over who should be awarded a £10,000 arts grant given by the Welsh government in memory of a Jewish girl who died in a Nazi camp has been reignited.
Artist Robert Cohen died last week while awaiting the outcome of his legal challenge against the decision to give the grant to Mark Evans for his proposal using the name "Adolf" in the project.
Cohen, who originally applied for the grant, had argued that using the name would be inappropriate.
The 58-year-old from Merthyr Tydfil said it would be a "contemptuous insult" to Helen Pennant, the girl who died at Bergen-Belsen, and her family.
He launched an appeal against Arts Council Wales' decision to award the grant to Evans, but it was rejected by the High Court in July.
Despite the ruling, the row over the grant has continued.
A petition calling on the Welsh government to stop the award has received more than 17,500 signatures.

The grant, awarded as part of an arts programme named after the girl, was given to Evans, from Aberystwyth, to create the conceptual art piece using the name "Adolf" for a sculpture and performance piece.
The piece, entitled "The whole of Auschwitz was a sham", includes two stone tablets with the word "Adolf" carved into them.
The tablets will be placed in a wooden crate and buried in the ground near a synagogue.
Evans will then dig up and carry the tablets, wearing a uniform and holding a whip, towards the synagogue.
The work aims to challenge "anti-semitic representations" of Hitler by "humanising" the dictator through the performance, according to Evans' proposal.
The artist said the piece explores the "mythology" of Hitler and the "symbolism" of the tablets, which represent the "myth-making we see today in politics and the media".

Police have increasingly been issuing warnings that pubs should have the power to shut earlier in order to crack down on drunk violence, anti-social behavior, and noise pollution.
For years, police have been calling for stronger powers to tackle alcohol-related disorder in town and city centers, which have become no-go areas for many people living there.
With the Government preparing to announce its plans to tackle alcohol-related violence, police chiefs are again urging ministers to introduce a nationwide closing time of 11 pm.
While weekends see a majority of violent incidents, weekday evenings also produce their fair share of alcohol-related disorder and violence, particularly around closing time.

Police say that they are wasting valuable time and resources that could be better used elsewhere dealing with these incidents, which often result in hospital A&E departments being clogged up with drunken revellers.
According to the Association of Chief Police Officers (Acpo), the current licensing laws are "not fit for purpose" and are "hampering" the fight against alcohol-related violence.
Acpo is calling for the licensing laws to be simplified and for all premises to be classed as either a bar or a restaurant, with all bars required to close at 11 pm.
While the idea of giving police the power to close pubs earlier has received some support, there are those who believe that it is not the answer to the problem.

Some believe that the real problem lies in the fact that many young people now think it is acceptable to drink large quantities of alcohol and then behave badly, and that the answer lies in educating people about the effects of alcohol rather than in changing the licensing laws.

Others believe that the problem of alcohol-related violence is not confined to pubs and that the solution lies in tackling the issue of cheap, strong alcohol available in supermarkets and off-licenses.
They argue that the easiest way to reduce alcohol-related violence is to increase the price of alcohol through higher taxes.
The current system of Britain's £2.4bn annual rebate on its contribution to the European Union is unjustified and must be reformed, French President Jacques Chirac said today.
The rebate - which dates back to 1975 and was originally intended as a transitional measure - is unfair on other EU members, Mr Chirac said in an interview with the BBC's HARDtalk programme.
"It is not acceptable, it is not justifiable to have this rebate which creates imbalances, inequalities and which complicates the already difficult task of building a united Europe," he said.
Mr Chirac said the EU needed "a strong Britain" as a member, but that London must play by the rules.

"We need Britain because it is a great country, because it has a presence in the world which is important - maybe it doesn't want to play this role but it has it -, because it can be an important element in the construction of Europe and so we need Britain in the European Union."
But he added: "It is true that Britain benefits from the Union, it is true that Britain must respect the basic principles of the Union, and that is the only condition that must be fulfilled.

"

Mr Chirac said the French people - who voted against the European Constitution in a referendum last year - had simply wanted to send a message that Europe was moving too fast.
But he insisted they still believed in the EU project and that the Constitution - which has since been rewritten - would be ratified by all member states.

"I believe that the European Constitution, in one form or another, modified of course after the referendum in France and in the Netherlands, I think that this constitution, these basic texts, will be accepted by all the 27 countries," he said.
The former Labour prime minister, James Callaghan, has died at the age of 92, his family have announced.
One of the UK's most successful politicians, he served as a minister under every Labour prime minister from 1945 to 1976 - aside from Clement Attlee.
After Labour's defeat in 1970, he became the party's leader and prime minister from 1976 to 1980.
During his time in office, the UK suffered inflation, economic turmoil and extensive strikes - most famously the 1978-79 "winter of discontent".
The longest-serving Labour MP was among the final remaining figures of the post-war generation of politicians.
The Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has described a new wave toll for England as “shameful” and accused the UK government of being “totally insensitive”.
Her comments came after UK Transport Secretary Grant Shapps admitted that the estimated cost of the recent flooding in England was £1bn.

In Scotland, the cost of the storm which hit the west coast of the country over the New Year is estimated to be £200m.

Ms Sturgeon said this was “not an equal partnership” when she was asked if the Scottish Government could expect financial support from the UK government to recover from the storms.

The first minister was being interviewed on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme after Scottish Conservative leader Douglas Ross had also accused the UK government of being “totally insensitive” to the needs of Scottish fishermen who have suffered as a result of the storms.
Mr Shapps said that the UK government had “always” worked together with the Scottish Government.
He added that “all the mechanisms” were in place for the two governments to discuss further help for Scotland following the storms.
Supporters of a new rail link between Borders and Edinburgh gathered for a rally in the region today, amid a fresh push for the project.
Campaigners met at Carberry in the Scottish Borders, close to where an old railway line previously connected the region with the capital.
The group, which included local politicians and business leaders, hope a new rail link could transform the local economy.
The campaign has gained renewed momentum following confirmation that the Scottish Government is to hold an interim review of the transport links between Edinburgh and the Borders.
Meanwhile, the Scottish Borders Council confirmed it had submitted an application for funding to examine the case for a new rail line.
Council leader Mark Rowley said the region needed better transport links.

"There is clear and mounting evidence of the huge benefits that electrified rail links to Edinburgh could bring to the Scottish Borders in terms of stimulating economic growth, getting people to work, and improving tourism," he added.
The campaign group, Campaign for Borders Rail, has argued that the region has been "left behind" due to a lack of investment in transport links.
A feasibility study commissioned by the council last year found that a new rail link between Edinburgh and the Borders could lead to £322m in economic benefits.
The study said the project would deliver net benefits of £1.2bn over 30 years.
Supporters of the campaign have called for the Scottish Government to provide the necessary funding to deliver the project.

Local businessman and campaigner Richard Richardson said: "We have heard a lot of warm words from the politicians down the years but now is the time for them to put their money where their mouth is and for Scottish Borders Council to submit a robust business case to win Phase 2 funding from the UK and Scottish governments."
The Welsh NHS has been hit by its first strike today, as thousands of nurses and ambulance workers walk out in a pay dispute.
It is the first time the NHS in Wales has experienced a strike since 2004 when midwives took action.
Health minister Eluned Morgan said the strike was "hugely disappointing" and that the government had offered a "fair and affordable pay increase".
She warned that many NHS services would be "impacted" by the walkouts.
The dispute is over pay rises that have been offered to workers in Wales.
The Welsh government has offered NHS staff a pay rise of between 4% and 5%, but workers say they deserve a bigger increase.
They argue that they have been hit by a decade of austerity and need more money to keep up with the rising cost of living.
The strike will affect non-emergency services, with nurses and ambulance workers walking out on Monday and Tuesday this week, and then again on Monday, 21 November.
Emergency care will still be provided, but people are being warned to expect delays to routine appointments and procedures.
The Welsh government has said it is committed to reaching a deal, but that any increase in pay must be "affordable".
Government guidance on citizenship for faith schools is “confusing and complacent” and risks creating second-class citizens, a report by a group of MPs has warned.
The All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on British Muslims said the way in which faith schools approach citizenship can undermine the efforts of those seeking to promote social cohesion.
The report calls on the government to issue fresh guidance to help faith schools understand their legal duties around the subject.
And it urges local councils to be given stronger legal powers to intervene at faith schools where there are concerns over the quality of citizenship teaching.
The report's authors spoke to local authorities, schools, parents and civil society groups for their findings.
Their report said some faith schools gave greater emphasis to religious citizenship, such as teaching pupils about religious texts, than to secular citizenship, such as the rules of voting.
It said this reflected a “lack of understanding” of what good citizenship teaching involves, and of the legal duties of all schools to teach citizenship.
The report adds that “confusing and complacent” government guidance does not reflect the legal requirements set out in the Education Act 2002.
Author of the report, MP Yasmin Qureshi, said: “Citizenship is the only subject that is meant to level the playing field, to integrate our schools and bring people together.
“But our research has found that some faith schools are failing to properly teach citizenship, and in some cases, undermining it.
“The law needs to be strengthened to make this a legal requirement for all schools, and the government needs to reissue its guidance to make this clear.”
The report also found that some local authorities were unclear about their legal powers to assess, monitor and improve citizenship in faith schools.
The group is calling on the government to give local authorities the power to intervene in schools where concerns are raised over the quality of citizenship teaching.
A Department for Education spokesperson said: “Citizenship helps young people to develop their knowledge and understanding of democracy, including how to participate in society and elections.
“All schools, regardless of their faith status, must follow the curriculum and promote the spiritual, moral, and cultural development of their pupils.
“We have clear guidance available to help schools understand their responsibilities and further support will be provided to schools in the autumn.”
The UK has discriminated against Roma people from Central Europe, breaching their human rights, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled.
The complaint was brought by a Slovakian man, identified as M.H., who arrived in the UK in 2008 and claimed he faced discrimination when bidding to buy a plot of land in Yorkshire.
He claimed this was due to his Roma ethnicity.
The ECHR ruled that the treatment he received amounted to discrimination "on the basis of race".
The court ordered the UK government to pay M.H. €5,000 (£4,368) in damages for the discrimination, as well as €3,500 (£3,052) for costs.
Brits' voting habits are in flux as traditional parties see a significant drop in support, a survey suggests.
The finding comes in a study of voters in England, Scotland and Wales just over a year before the next general election.
It found more than a third of people (37%) said they did not trust politicians in the UK to tell the truth.
And 64% of those who selected the Labour Party as their first choice on the survey did not trust the Tories - the highest level of distrust among any group of voters for any other party.
The findings have been published by the BBC as part of its Voting Numbers series.
The latest analysis is based on a monthly phone survey of more than 100 people in Britain, carried out by polling firm Ipsos MORI.
The study - here - also found voters are now distributed across more parties than in the past, with 35% of people saying they have changed their vote in the past decade.
The analysis suggests the voting landscape has changed - with the traditional "big two" parties losing supporters to rivals on the left and right, and to independent candidates.
The survey suggests that in the 2005 general election, 67% of people voted for the Labour Party or the Conservative Party.
That figure is now just 51%.
At the same time, the study indicates the proportion of people who voted for the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru has increased.
The survey suggests that the Labour Party is currently the most popular party in Britain, with 38% of people saying they would vote for Sir Keir Starmer's party if there were an election tomorrow.
The Conservatives have seen their support increase since the autumn, when the party was chosen by 31% of people.
But the study suggests support for the Tories is not as high as it was in the spring of this year, when 42% of people said they would vote for Boris Johnson's party.
The findings also indicate there could be a close race between Labour and the Conservatives as the two largest parties in Britain.
Just three points separate the parties, with the Liberal Democrats on 19%, the Scottish National Party on 8% and Plaid Cymru on 4%.

The UK government has been criticised for its plans to send some migrants to a processing centre in Ascension Island thousands of miles away in the Atlantic.
The scheme - part of tougher immigration measures announced by Home Secretary Theresa May - is designed to discourage migrants from making dangerous journeys across the English Channel.
Ministers say the centre on the island, which is a British overseas territory, will be used to process migrants' claims "fairly and efficiently".
But Labour called the plan "inhumane".
Ascension Island is a volcanic island halfway between Africa and South America, with a population of fewer than 1,000 people and temperatures reaching up to 40C (104F).

It is part of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - best known as the location of the former prison camp where Boer prisoners of war were held during the Boer War in the early 20th Century.
The island has a naval base - long attached to the UK's interests in the South Atlantic - and is a stopping-off point for Royal Navy ships, as well as an important satellite ground station.
Building work is already under way to transform an abandoned US airbase on Ascension - which is twinned with Saint Helena - into a migrant processing centre.
The exact location has not been disclosed, but it is understood to be on the island's sweltering coastline.
The plans, first reported by The Times, have been criticised by politicians and charities.
Labour's shadow immigration minister, Stephen Kinnock, said the party was "urging the government to scrap this inhumane plan".
He added that Labour would "work with the government to find a humane alternative".
And the chief executive of the Refugee Council, Enver Solomon, said sending people "even further away from their families and support networks" was "not the answer".
The Home Office said the centre would "provide a safer environment for processing than the cramped conditions [migrants] are currently subjected to during their perilous journey".
The announcement came as part of a broader strategy aimed at limiting illegal migration after record numbers of people arrived in the UK across the Channel last year.
Mrs May announced the government would introduce legislation making it a criminal offence to enter the UK illegally and "obstructing removal" - with a maximum sentence of 12 months.
She also wants to make it easier to return illegal migrants to mainland Europe and improve immigration detention.

Microsoft has released patches for four zero-day vulnerabilities that are currently being exploited by threat actors.
The tech giant identified the vulnerabilities in its Windows, Exchange and SharePoint products and made emergency patches available to all customers.
It is believed that the vulnerabilities were being used by a state-sponsored group, which raises questions about whether the hackers could have used the bugs to assist in espionage activities.
The zero-day vulnerabilities were first discovered by cybersecurity company Mandiant, which reported that the vulnerabilities were being used in targeted attacks.
The attacks focused on stealing confidential information from target organizations, including private communications and data.
Microsoft has urged all customers to apply the patches as soon as possible in order to protect their systems from potential exploitation.
The company has also made additional resources available to help customers secure their systems and protect themselves from future attacks.
This latest incident highlights the increasing sophistication of cyberattacks and the importance of prompt patching of security vulnerabilities.
It also underscores the need for organizations to have robust cybersecurity measures in place to protect their systems and data from attack.

In a major breakthrough for the fight against software piracy, four Americans have been convicted of engaging in widespread copyright infringement by operating a pirate website.
After a seven-day trial, a federal jury in Texas found Denelle Dixon, David Bodher, Jeff Lundqvist, and Matthew Smith all guilty of conspiracy to commit copyright infringement.

The four defendants were the masterminds behind a popular peer-to-peer file-sharing website called "MegaUpload," which allowed users to store and share files, including copyrighted content such as movies, TV shows, music, and software, without permission from the copyright holders.
The site was shut down by the FBI in 2012 following an investigation that revealed the massive scale of copyright infringement taking place on the site.
The jury found that the defendants were aware of the widespread copyright infringement taking place on MegaUpload but took no meaningful action to prevent it.
In a statement, the U.S. Attorney's Office said that the defendants "profited handsomely from promoting and providing access to copyrighted content without the permission of the copyright holders...
the defendants enriched themselves while harming artists, filmmakers, musicians, authors, and other creators of copyrighted works."
The conviction comes as a significant victory for copyright holders in the ongoing battle against online piracy.
It is the first time that individuals have been held personally liable for copyright infringement committed through a peer-to-peer file-sharing website.

This includes the creation of a digital map of the city, which allows users to explore the ruins in a way that is not possible with traditional methods.
The map also includes detailed information about the city's history and architecture.
"Pompeii Virtual" also includes the creation of a digital museum, which will display artifacts and objects found in the ruins.
The museum will use holograms and other interactive technologies to bring the artifacts to life.
The project has been met with mixed reactions from the public.
Some have welcomed the addition of new technology to the ruins, while others have expressed concern about the potential impact on the site's historic integrity.

The concept of a low-cost, high-performance personal computer has intrigued Andrew Ritchie ever since he got involved in the fledgling UK PC industry back in the early 1980s.
Now, after several decades heading up UK consumer electronics company Raspberry Pi, Ritchie has come as close as anyone could to achieving that goal.
His new Pi Zero 2 W is a $15 PC with a 1GHz processor, 512MB of RAM and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, targeted at the same embedded and industrial markets as its predecessor, the original Pi Zero.
When the original Pi Zero was launched in 2015, it was hailed as a fully functional PC that sold for $5.
Its BCM2835 application processor, based on ARM's Cortex-A53 architecture, had been around since 2012, when it shipped in the first Raspberry Pi.
The Zero offered just 512MB of RAM and no wireless connectivity, but these seemed like reasonable trade-offs for such a low price.
Five years later, the Zero 2 W upgrades the CPU to a Cortex-A53-based Broadcom BCM2710, built on a more efficient 16nm process.
It also doubles the RAM and adds 2.4GHz 802.11b/g/n Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 4.2.
The $15 price remains the same.
The Zero 2 W has the same form factor as the original – the same size, the same number of USB ports, the same camera connector and display outputs.
According to Ritchie, changing any of those features would have required a complete redesign, which would have added considerable cost.
The Zero 2 W uses the same CPU as the Raspberry Pi 3B+, which itself inherited the CPU from the previous 3B model.
The 3B+ was already a pretty frugal design, so there were few obvious areas for Raspberry Pi to save money.
The company was able to achieve its price target in part by buying in bulk.
"It's a function of the quantity of silicon we're willing to buy," Ritchie says.
"We're pretty good at [negotiating] that now.
And the Zero 2 W is a very simple product.
There's no complexity in it at all.

"

Ritchie is keen to stress that the Zero 2 W isn't a general-purpose PC for everyday users.
It doesn't support 64-bit operating systems, has limited graphics capabilities and lacks the ports and connectivity of larger Raspberry Pi boards.
