The charity's accountants are also alleged to have removed money from the Foundation's accounts without permission.
Mr Fathy denies any wrongdoing and has promised to cooperate with the Charity Commission's investigation.
He says the money was paid to his son's company as a standard fee for consultancy work.
He claims the accountants were removed from the board after they made unauthorised donations to themselves.
Apple's Mac mini has always been a bit of an outsider in the company's desktop line-up.

The US duo behind the nation's first felony spam conviction were each sentenced to three years' probation yesterday for sending tens of thousands of junk e-mails.
Jonathan Buck, 35, and Daniel Krugler, 23, pleaded guilty in September to fraud and forgery charges for their part in an e-mail scam that harvested personal data from vulnerable computer users.
The pair, from Scottsdale in Arizona, sent more than 70,000 e-mails through a "spam farm" in India, offering victims a chance to make money by working at home.
When victims responded, they were sent a forged letter appearing to be from Microsoft, claiming that viruses had been detected on their computers.
The victims were then instructed to telephone a toll-free number, at a cost of $1.20 per minute, for assistance in removing the viruses.
The scam - believed to have been operated by a criminal gang in India - raked in at least $200,000 before it was shut down in March by federal investigators.
As part of the plea bargain, Buck and Krugler each surrendered a laptop, a computer server and a list of e-mail addresses of their customers.
They were also forced to hand over $42,000 in profits.
"This is a new kind of crime," said Thomas Collins, the attorney for Arizona.
"These are the first people in the US to be charged under state law with fraud for spamming.

"

Buck and Krugler could have faced up to 8.75 years in prison and $350,000 in fines.
But the judge imposed a more lenient sentence, saying that the pair had cooperated with the investigation.
The pair had been charged with forgery, computer tampering and conducting a scheme to defraud.
Buck pleaded guilty to all charges, while Krugler pleaded guilty to one count of forgery.
Judge Warren Granville told the pair that they had violated the public's trust by sending out spam.
"You sent out e-mails to hundreds of thousands of people who didn't want them," he said.
"It undermines the effectiveness of e-mail.

"

He added that the crime was "very serious" because some of the victims had spent large amounts of money on phone calls to the scam's helpline.

Lambert has had a close relationship with the band since first sharing the stage with them in 2009, when Queen founders Brian May and Taylor appeared as guests on the eighth season of American Idol, on which Lambert was a contestant.
The singer reflects on this experience in his own words: “I am thrilled to be continuing as Queen’s frontman, sharing the stage with these incredible rock legends.”
The Rhapsody Tour is set to begin on May 27 in Vancouver, with the first leg of the tour spanning 19 shows across Canada and the United States.
The tour will then pick back up in September, with dates scheduled across Europe and the UK into 2024.
The curtain has fallen on one of the most famous families to appear on TV, as MTV axes The Osbournes.
The show, which debuted in 2002 and turned the Osbourne family into reality TV stars, will not be coming back for a sixth season, a network spokesperson confirmed on Friday.
The announcement comes several months after Ozzy Osbourne, 67, revealed he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.
The series, one of the first in the reality TV boom of the early 2000s, followed the household's day-to-day life as they lived in Beverly Hills, California.
Apart from Ozzy – known for his decades-long career as the lead vocalist of heavy metal band Black Sabbath – the show also featured his wife, Sharon, and their two children, Kelly and Jack.
Sharon Osbourne, 68, told TalkTV in May she planned to step back from her television career to focus on her family, citing her husband's illness as the reason.
"I've worked my whole life and I really want to be with my husband and see to him and see to things at home," she said.
"I have absolutely no doubt that Sharon will be returning to work in the future, but for now she's going to be spending time with her family," her spokesperson told Variety at the time.
Last week, Ozzy – who disclosed his Parkinson's diagnosis in January – announced he was cancelling his upcoming tour dates citing his illness.
"It's the only tour I've ever cancelled," the singer said in a statement.
"Believe me, it hurts me to do this.
The father-of-three, who also suffers from emphysema and has suffered from injuries following a 2003 ATV accident, added he was "not physically capable" of performing.
"I'm desperate to get back on the road but I'm just not physically able to do it," he said.
The Muslim group attacked the TV drama 24 hours later.
The drama tells the story of a counter-terrorism officer who protects the U.S. president from a terrorist group that plans to attack America.
The Muslim group claimed that the TV drama 24 was offensive and promoted negative stereotypes about Muslims.
The group asked for a public apology from the BBC and for the drama to be removed from the BBC iPlayer.
The BBC responded by saying that the drama was not intended to be offensive and was meant to reflect the realities of working in counter-terrorism.
The BBC did offer to add a warning to the beginning of the show, however.
The BBC has secured the rights to host a special concert to celebrate the 65th anniversary of the Eurovision Song Contest.
The celebration, due to take place in Manchester next year, will see a number of the competition's "greats" going head-to-head.
The BBC has said it will release more details about the concert, including the line-up, at a later date.
The BBC has a good track record of securing the rights to host the Eurovision Song Contest's UK broadcasts.
The corporation has hosted the main competition nine times since the first UK win in 1967 and has regularly aired highlights packages of the event.
The Eurovision Song Contest is a yearly singing competition between member countries of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Each member country submits an original song to be performed on live television and radio.
Then, votes are cast by national jurors and, occasionally, a public tele-vote.
The country with the most points is then declared the winner.
The UK has competed in the contest since its inception in 1956 and has won it five times.
The first win was in 1967 with Sandie Shaw's performance of "Puppet on a String".
The latest win was in 1997 with Katrina and the Waves' performance of "Love Shine a Light".
The 65th Eurovision Song Contest will take place in May 2023 in the Netherlands, following the country's win in 2022 with the song "De Diepte" by the band Subwoolfer.
The latest film starring Will Smith as the titular character, Hitch, maintained its number one position at the US box office for the second week in a row.
Hitch, which co-stars Eva Mendes, has earned $76 million since its release two weeks ago.
The animated feature The Polar Express maintained its position at number two for the second week in a row.
Rounding out the top three is the latest James Bond installment, Die Another Day, starring Pierce Brosnan in his fourth, and final, turn as the world's greatest secret agent.
Overall, it was a quiet week at the box office, with no new releases making waves.
The week's biggest opener, Jack Frost, opened in the number eight spot with a mere $4 million.
Analysts are predicting a tight race next week, when eight new films open, including Bandido, All I See, and the long-awaited return of Steven Seagal in Flight of the Phoenix.
The BBC has confirmed a second season of "After Life", with creator, writer and director Ricky Gervais promising a "bigger and better" second season.
The six-part comedy first aired in April 2020 and was described as "warm, touching and occasionally laugh-out-loud funny" by BBC News.
The second series will again follow Tony, whose wife, Lisa, has died from cancer.
Gervais said the show would again "explore grief, inheritance, moving on and death".
He said: "I have never had a reaction like this before.
It's been a revelation.
"I didn't expect it, I never expected that level of emotion.
It's quite shocking really.

"

The writer, actor and director, who is best known for his comedy characters including David Brent and Derek Noakes, said the show had led him to think about "bereavement, grief and suffering".
He added: "I think the second series will be more hopeful.
It'll still be funny and sad but more hopeful.
"It's strange, having a drama about grief and death being the most hopeful thing I've ever done.
"I think the second series will be bigger and better and more ambitious.
I'm really proud of it."
Gervais, 57, also wrote and directed the show, and his character is largely based on his own experiences of losing his father, who died in 2012.
He said the first series had been "therapeutic" and had helped him come to terms with his loss.
"After Life" starred Gervais alongside Penelope Wilton, Tom Basden, Tony Way, Roisin Conaty, Diane Morgan, Ashley Jensen, Mandeep Dhillon and David Earl.
All are expected to return for the second series, which will again be set in the small fictional town of Tambury.
The show originally aired on Netflix and the streaming service will again work in partnership with the BBC to bring the show to audiences worldwide.
No release date has been announced for the second series.

Shorn of the emotion that was evident on both sides of the argument during the chaotic meeting that decided his fate, David Levy's final act as chairman of the Premier League was perhaps his most masterful.

Having successfully guided the top flight's biggest-ever restructuring through treacherous political waters, and with the £6.6bn sale of the Premier League's domestic television rights wrapped up, Levy effectively signed off with one last, crucial victory for the top flight in the shape of agreeing to a £2.5bn renewal of its UK live-streaming deal with Amazon.

That took the broadcaster's total spend on Premier League football to £30m a year, a five-fold increase on its previous deal, and completes a remarkable turnaround in the streaming giant's relationship with the game.
It also continued the Premier League's stellar commercial run, with UK television income up 11% (£1.4bn-£1.6bn) and international deals, worth £3.2bn, also increasing.
That financial clout helped persuade the required 14 clubs to finally back the sale of a £2.5bn stake in the league to a US-based investment fund.

Having failed to get the required 14 clubs to agree to the sale a year ago, when a small group of clubs led by Newcastle United's owners objected, the Premier League was finally able to get the deal over the line.
And, in a final act as chairman before handing over to Gary Hoffman, who takes over on Thursday, Levy was able to announce the Amazon deal at the league's quarterly meeting on Tuesday.
It brought to a conclusion a remarkable few years for Levy after what had been a turbulent start when he replaced Richard Scudamore as executive chairman in August 2019.
Having taken over Scudamore's role, Levy was quickly was confronted with the first Covid lockdown, which threatened the entire football economy.

He has had to deal with the fall-out from the attempt by the European Super League to create a breakaway league, which threatened the Premier League's position as the dominant domestic football competition and introduced government interference in the internal affairs of a previously sacrosanct organisation.

That resulted in a dramatic U-turn by the six Premier League clubs who had signed up to the ESL and a threat to try to block the sale of a stake in the league from going through the Football Association's owners' and directors' test.
That threat was dropped after the government indicated it would not intervene.
The iconic musician Elvis Presley has made a comeback to the top of the UK music charts after nearly 50 years, with his greatest hits album jumping from number 25 to number one.
The album, titled The Wonder of Elvis, has topped the charts for the first time since it was released in 1982, following a social media campaign by fans to get it to number one.
The campaign was sparked by a Twitter post by DJ Chris Evans, who suggested that the album was "the greatest ever" and encouraged his followers to get it to the top of the charts.
The move has paid off and the album has returned to the top spot nearly 50 years since it was first released.
The Wonder of Elvis album features iconic songs such as "Hound Dog" and " Suspicious Minds", as well as a cover of "My Way", a song made famous by Frank Sinatra.
The return to the top of the charts is a testament to the enduring legacy of Elvis Presley, who died in 1977.
It is not the first time that a social media campaign has resulted in a song or album topping the charts.
Fans of the musician Taylor Swift have previously used social media to get her songs to the top of the charts.
Many fans have expressed their delight at the return of the album to the top of the charts, and have celebrated the impact of social media in making it happen.
Others have suggested that the album deserves to be at the top of the charts and that it is a great example of the iconic musician's work.
It remains to be seen whether the album will continue to top the charts in the coming weeks.
The acclaimed director Parker has received a French honour for his contributions to cinema.
The award, which is given out by the French government, is a high distinction that recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the arts, literature, or science.
Parker, who is best known for his work on films such as "Birdman" and "Midnight Special", has been praised for his innovative and unique directing style.
His films have been noted for their technical brilliance and compelling narratives.
The French honour is a testament to Parker's contributions to the film industry and his impact on cinema.
It is a recognition of his ability to create thought-provoking and visually stunning films that have earned him critical acclaim and the admiration of audiences worldwide.
The BBC shares the news that a Briton has won an Oscar for the short film they produced.
The 92nd Academy Awards, hosted by Kevin Hart, celebrated the best in cinema during 2019.
The ceremony was held at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles on February 9, 2020.
Briton Anthony Hopkins, 82, best known for his role in The Two Popes, achieved a historic victory.
He became the oldest actor to win an Oscar in the Best Actor category.
After receiving the award, he thanked the Academy for the recognition and his two sons.
Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair has bought all the copies of the new Band Aid single so that the song can get to number one in the charts at Christmas.
The music industry veteran and philanthropist Sir Bob Geldof put together the latest version of the charity single to raise money for the Ebola appeal.
It features a host of British and Irish musicians including One Direction, Emeli Sandé, Paloma Faith and U2.
Sir Bob said: "Tony Blair has bought all the copies of the new Band Aid single to ensure it gets to number one.
"It's a smart thing to do.
Smart thinking, funny bloke."
The single will be released on Monday 16 November.
All proceeds will go to the Ebola appeal fund.
To date more than 10,000 people have died from the Ebola virus, which was first identified in 1976.
The virus is spread through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of an infected person.
It has an incubation period of two to 21 days and symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle pain and in some cases internal and external bleeding.
The new single is the follow-up to Do
They Know It's Christmas?, which was released in 1984.
That song featured George Michael, U2, Wham!
and Duran Duran.
Italian conductor Carlo Viotti has died at the age of 86.
A celebrated musician and conductor, Viotti was born in Milan in 1936 and began his music career as an assistant at the Teatro alla Scala opera house in his home city.
He went on to become musical director at the Maggio Musicale Fiorentino in Florence and the London Philharmonic, as well as chief conductor of the Royal Opera House.
Throughout his career, Viotti received many accolades and honours, including the Italian National Movie Award for lifetime achievement and the title of Commendatore of the Italian Republic.
He was renowned for his charitable work, particularly his efforts to raise money for cancer research.
Viotti's death was announced by the Teatro alla Scala, where he had been serving as honorary conductor.
The theatre said he would be remembered for his "immortal musicality".
Singer-songwriter Jack Knight has backed a song aiming to inspire hope in the wake of the Uvalde school shooting.
The 18-year-old musician, known for his singles Love Sick and Empty Room, is lending his vocals to Gun Control, a song written by Sarah Burmister.
All proceeds from the song will go to March For Our Lives, a charity founded in 2018 by survivors of the Stoneman Douglas High School shooting in Parkland, Florida.
The charity aims to end gun violence and create a safer future for all students.
The song features other artists including Grammy-winning singer-songwriter Lisa Loeb, actress and singer Ana Gasteyer and The Voice season 21 finalist Joshua Vacanti.
Mr Knight said it was a "true honour" to be asked to collaborate on the song.
"As a musician, I've always used my voice as a way to process the world, but this song felt different than anything I've done before," he said.
"I am thrilled to be able to lend my support to such an important organisation and meaningful cause.
The bodies of 19 children and two teachers were found in Uvalde in May after a gunman opened fire in an art classroom.
Miss Burmister, who is from Columbus, Ohio, but is currently living in London, said she was compelled to write the song in the hope of helping those affected by gun violence.
"When I heard about the shooting in Uvalde, it felt like another blow to an already incredibly heavy world," she said.
"I felt helpless and didn't know what to do.
I knew that I couldn't ignore what happened so I wrote this song as a way to process what occurred and hopefully help others too.

"
The single will be released on 3 March, with the aim of raising money and awareness for March For Our Lives.

"We are thrilled to have such talented artists supporting our work and helping to spread the message that change is possible when we come together to demand it," said March For Our Lives founder David Hogg.
"We must keep up the momentum to end the gun violence epidemic that is killing our children."
The Da Vinci Code, a book and a film which sparked a rush of interest in symbology and ancient history, is lousy history, according to a historian.
Professor Andrew Roberts, of Royal Holloway, University of London, said the best-selling novel was "full of errors".
Author Dan Brown, who has sold more than 80 million copies of the book, admitted at its launch that he had taken "huge liberties" with the facts.
But Professor Roberts said even basic errors were made, such as the location of an ancient church.
"It is full of errors and I think that people think it is much more historically accurate than it is," he said.
"Even basic things like the location of the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris - that's completely wrong.

Does it matter?
Professor Roberts said it was "quite amusing" to see how people had been taken in by the novel, but added that the inaccuracies had potentially negative consequences.

"They go to museums and they see things and they think they know the story, and they don't."

In the novel, which was made into a Hollywood film starring Tom Hanks, the central character, Robert Langdon, is a symbologist who uses symbols and codes to unravel a mystery surrounding the Holy Grail.
It claims that Leonardo Da Vinci's painting, The Last Supper, contains hidden symbols and that Jesus and Mary Magdalene were married and had children.

The release of a heavily disputed box set of Nirvana recordings has led to a sharply worded rebuke from the band's surviving members, who have called for it to be withdrawn.

The band's bassist, Krist Novoselic, wrote on Twitter that the release of the recording, which purports to feature demos of songs never released by the band, should be halted as it was unfinished and not ready for release.
He said the box set's release was a "cruel angle" on the 25th anniversary of the band's frontman Kurt Cobain's death.

Notorious for his versatility and emotional range, actor Sir Sean Connery forged a reputation as one of Britain's most recognisable stars, receiving plaudits and an Oscar for his performance in the title role of the 1962 adventure film Dr No.
He passed away on 31 October 2020, at the age of 90.
Allan Stewart paid tribute to Connery, saying he was "the greatest actor of all time", with Kenneth Branagh describing him as "my greatest mentor and inspiration".
The son of a cleaning lady and a factory worker, Connery was born in Edinburgh and raised in the city's Fountainbridge area.
He went to school at Royal High School in the city, but was expelled at the age of 13 and despatched to the National Defence Corps, where he remained until he was 16.
Connery then served in the Royal Navy, principally in the boiler room of a destroyer, before being discharged after three years due to a stomach ulcer.
He moved to London in 1953, working first in the building trade and then as a lifeguard, before becoming a model.

Connery's acting career began in the theatre, where he performed in a number of amateur productions and then several professional appearances in Shakespearean plays, including Macbeth and Richard III.
He then joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he gained positive reviews for his performances in a number of productions, including All's
Well That Ends

Well, Antony and Cleopatra and Henry V.

Connery's big break came when he was cast as James Bond in Dr No, a role that he would go on to play in five films, winning an Oscar for his performance in the 1983 film Never Say Never Again.
The late actor was considered a sex symbol, with his carousing, womanising, and hard-living persona making him an archetypal Bond.
His other film credits include The Name of the Rose, The Untouchables, and Robin and Marian, a film that marked his retirement from acting in 1981.
Connery received a knighthood in July 2000.
He was married to Diane Cilento from 1962 to 1973 and had a son, Jason.
He later married actress and former model Micheline Roquebrune, and had a stepson, Stefan.
The BBC's political correspondent, Chris Mason, says the expectation is that Tony Blair will call a general election for next Tuesday, with the formal announcement likely tomorrow.
The prime minister has told the House of Commons that he will make a statement outside No 10 at 1715 GMT.
All the indications are that he will announce the election, our correspondent says.
The election will be fought on the issue of trust, with Mr Blair's Labour Party portraying the Conservatives as reckless economic managers, our correspondent adds.
The UK economy is "stronger than forecast", according to the Office for Budget Responsibility.
It said in its latest forecast that the UK economy would return to its pre-pandemic level in April next year, three months earlier than previously expected.
The independent forecaster said that stronger-than-expected growth in the first half of this year had helped it to upgrade its outlook.
It now expects the economy to grow by 6.3% this year, compared with a previous forecast of 4.4%.
The OBR also upgraded its forecast for next year, predicting that the economy would grow by 1.8% in 2023, up from 1.5%.
However, it warned that the UK's recovery would be "tested" by rising energy prices and supply chain problems.
The forecast comes as the government is due to set out its budget plan on Wednesday.
Borussia Dortmund have been given hope that they may be able to rescue the season after reaching the last 16 of the Europa League and moving up to third in the Bundesliga.
A 1-0 win at Mainz on Saturday was their sixth successive league victory, meaning they are now nine points behind leaders Bayern Munich, who drew 0-0 at home to Cologne.
And on Thursday, a 1-0 win in Italy over Lazio means they go through to the last 16 of Europe's secondary competition as Group F winners.
"We have our goals in the Bundesliga and the DFB-Pokal, and now we've achieved our first goal in the Europa League," said Dortmund captain Marco Reus, who scored the winner in Rome.
Manager Edin Terzic added: "It wasn't easy today, we were without Jude Bellingham, Mahmoud Dahoud and Dan-Axel Zagadou.
We had a lot of young players in the squad.
It was an important step for the team.
Dortmund's hopes of retaining their title looked over in early November after losing to Bayern Munich, with the champions 11 points clear after 14 games.
But since then they have kept four clean sheets in six games, with goalkeeper Marwin Hitz, 35, playing every minute of that run.
"The team in front of me doesn't concede many chances in a game and that's why we've been able to keep so many clean sheets," said Hitz, who was voted man of the match after the win in Mainz.
"We're on a good run at the moment but we're not getting carried away.

We've got a tough game coming up next weekend and we're focusing on that now."

That tough game is at home to second-placed Union Berlin on Saturday, with the capital club two points ahead of Dortmund having played two games more.
The stars lined up for the Oscars luncheon on Monday, where the nominees for the most coveted film awards get a chance to swap gossip and tips ahead of the ceremony in March.
Best actress nominee Michelle Williams says she is revelling in the experience despite being snubbed in the past.
"For a long time I found it disappointing and it seemed like it was a systemic thing," the 41-year-old actress said of repeatedly being overlooked by awards voters.
"It seemed as if it was going to be very difficult to break through.
But I have found people to be generous and kind in the midst of their own struggle.

"

Williams is nominated for her role as a grieving mother in Kenneth Lonergan's Manchester By The Sea, which is nominated for six Oscars including best picture.
She paid tribute to her "brilliant and talented" co-star Casey Affleck, who is nominated for best actor.
"It has been a joy to watch him take this character on this journey and watch him transform into this character," she said.
"It is nothing any of us could have predicted, including Ken.
It's nothing that Casey could have predicted.
He really met the material and went to a place nobody knew he had in him.

"

Williams admitted she had not expected to be nominated, and only found out live on air while watching the announcement with her children.
"It was a nice way to hear it," she said.
"It is nice to watch it with the kids and share it with them...
They are the most important thing in my life.

"

Williams was joined at the lunchtime event by best actor nominee Andrew Garfield, who is nominated for his role in Hacksaw Ridge.
"It's just an overwhelming honour," he said.
"It's always lovely to be recognised by your peers, especially by the Academy.
I'm very proud to be here.

"

Garfield said he "couldn't care less" about winning an award, and that just being nominated was more than enough.
"It's nothing compared to the reward of making the film," he said.
"The most important thing to me is the process and the journey and working with inspiring, amazing people.
And I have been so blessed to work with so many incredible, talented people in my career.

"

Garfield said his six-year-old nephew was most excited about the prospect of winning an award, rather than him.
Singer Jamelia's hopes of representing the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest have ended after the BBC opted to withdraw from this year's event.
The soul singer, who last month announced she had submitted a song for the competition, said she was "disappointed" by the BBC's decision.
The broadcaster said it withdrew due to the event's alleged anti-LGBTQ+ policies.
Jamelia, 38, said in a statement posted on Instagram that "things happened" after she submitted her song, called "Wonder".
"I tried to fight for us all but unfortunately, it seems that things progress when things happen to certain people at certain times," she wrote.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which produces the event, has previously said it was committed to ensuring the contest is "open to all" following criticism over rules that prevented some participants from wearing rainbow colours or singing about gay rights.
In 2019, Ukraine's entry was banned from performing on stage in Tel Aviv after the country's broadcaster included a reference to Russia's invasion of Crimea in the song.
Jamelia, who rose to fame in the early 2000s with hits such as "Superstar" and "Beware of the Dog", said her Eurovision entry had been a "labor of love" and she was "so proud" of the song.
"I am aware of the BBC's decision to withdraw from this year's Eurovision Song Contest and I wholeheartedly support them in this," she said.
"I championed the values of the song and the importance of inclusivity within the competition and beyond."
The Eurovision Song Contest will take place in Turin, Italy in May.
England's Ben Stokes has compared Harry Douglas to "a younger version" of team-mate Moeen Ali, after signing the batsman for Indian Premier League side Rajasthan Royals.
The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) released Douglas, an attacking batsman and occasional off-spin bowler, from his contract this week to allow him to join the franchise.
He is expected to be available for the entire IPL season, which runs from March to May and has been moved to the United Arab Emirates due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic.
Stokes, who played with Douglas at Durham, said: "I've known Harry since he was a young lad coming through the system.
British condom maker SSL International is awaiting a firm bid from a private equity firm for its Durex brand, which it hopes will value the business at about £1.7bn.
US firm Carlyle has made a preliminary offer for SSL, which has been spun off from former parent company Unilever.
In May, SSL hired Credit Suisse to carry out a review of options for the business, which also makes the Femidom and Scholl plasters brands.
Its private equity owners, which bought an initial majority stake in 2014, were expected to sell their remaining shares this year.
SSL said it had received "a number of indications of interest" in Durex and the rest of its business, and that these were being "evaluated".
"No decision has been taken with respect to any offer and there can be no certainty as to the outcome of this process," it added.
SSL, which has its headquarters in London and a presence in more than 20 countries, reported annual sales of £393m in 2022.
Durex, which was founded in 1932, is the world's leading condom brand, selling more than 200 million condoms every year in more than 100 countries.
Labour has been accused of breaking a pledge to protect the pensions of retired miners after it emerged that a compensation scheme will not be extended to people in Wales, Scotland and Derbyshire.
More than 40,000 miners in England and some former pit communities in South Wales will receive payments worth £1,000 per year for the rest of their lives.
But the scheme, announced by Labour in 2005, will not be open to ex-miners in Scotland, Derbyshire and some former mining areas in South Wales.
The party promised miners in all areas nationwide that they would receive "fair compensation".
Labour said the scheme had always been intended to be a England-only initiative and it had expected the devolved governments to set up their own schemes.
Ex-miner and MP Ian Lavery said it was a "betrayal" and an "unforgivable broken promise".
The Deutsche Boerse has upped its offer for the London Stock Exchange Group to almost $35 billion as it looks to entice LSE shareholders with the promise of a higher cash offer.
Deutsche Boerse stated it is willing to pay 640 pence per share, equivalent to £24.4 billion ($33.7 billion).
The new offer is higher than the previous bid of 610 pence per share made in May.
This came after the LSE rejected a bid from the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) for £20 billion.
The LSE has stated it will consider the offer and is confident it can deliver growth alongside Deutsche Boerse.
This confidence may be due to the fact that the LSE has recently undergone a significant management shakeup that saw the departure of CEO David Schwimmer.
The LSE's management has claimed the previous bid was too low and didn't reflect the company's value.
Despite this, many shareholders were in favor of the original offer.
The increased offer comes after the LSE announced plans to delist from the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.
This move would result in the LSE becoming a wholly-owned subsidiary of Deutsche Boerse.
Many LSE shareholders were concerned about the original offer because it would have resulted in the LSE losing its independent status.
The new offer appears to have alleviated those concerns.
The deal is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first half of next year.
If successful, the merger would result in the creation of the largest stock exchange in Europe, with a market capitalization of over £130 billion.
This news comes after the EU recently proposed new rules that would make it easier for companies to list on multiple European exchanges.
The new rules are part of a broader push to create a single capital market in the EU and are intended to encourage cross-border investment and increase competition.
The LSE has also been in talks with the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Ltd (HKEX) about a potential merger.
However, those discussions have been put on hold while the LSE considers the Deutsche Boerse offer.
The battle for the LSE has been ongoing for several months and is not expected to end anytime soon.
With three major players vying for control of the LSE, shareholders can expect more offers and counteroffers in the coming months.

Inevitably, perhaps, it was the captain who made the difference as Scotland progressed to the knockout stages of the Euros with a tough 2-0 win over Croatia.

Callum McGregor's header just before half-time broke the deadlock in a tightly-contested match, with John McGinn adding a second just after the hour to ensure progress to the last 16 as one of the best third-placed teams.

There were loud cheers at Hampden Park when the final whistle confirmed the result, with Scottish fans delighted at the prospect of a trip to Copenhagen to face the world's number one team, Belgium, on Saturday.
And for Steve Clarke, the Scotland manager, it vindicates his bold move to change the system against the Czechs and play with three centre-backs behind a disciplined midfield.

There were echoes of Scotland's 2-0 win over England in 1977, with Clarke's team wearing the dark blue of Scotland and relying on two set-piece goals rather than the free-flowing performance that gave away nations a shock in the group stages of that year's World Cup.
"We can be proud of everybody, they are a great group and they have given the Scottish nation a lift," said Clarke.
"We can look forward to the game against Belgium with a lot of excitement."

It was seemingly inevitable that the internet would transform the way we give and receive presents but the extent of that change is surprising.
Seven out of every 10 pounds spent on UK Christmas gifts now originates online, a proportion that has doubled over the past decade, according to the Centre for Retail Research.

This shift has produced a boom in the fortunes of online retailers, yet another example of the upheaval in "the high street" as traditional retailers struggle to keep pace with the move to smartphones, tablets and computers.
The research, which was commissioned by payment services provider Worldpay, found that £19.3bn was spent online on Christmas gifts in the UK last year, a rise of more than £2bn on the year before.
Much of that growth is being driven by the rise of mobile phones as shopping devices.

Worldpay chief executive Philip Jansen said: "Over the past few years we have seen a significant increase in the use of mobile phones for online shopping, accounting for 52% of online sales in 2017, compared with 39% in 2015."
The most popular items purchased via mobile phones were clothes and footwear (£7.3bn), followed by games, toys and "hobby" goods (£4.8bn), and books, newspapers and stationery (£4.4bn).
Worldpay predicts that by 2021 the value of online sales will have reached £43bn, accounting for 42% of all retail sales in the UK.
Yet despite the rise of internet shopping, the research found that many consumers still prefer to make their final purchase in a shop.
Two-thirds of those who research gifts online still buy them in a store.
"The high street is still very important as a place to touch and feel the product, and importantly, for consumers to engage with the brand," said Mr Jansen.
"But the in-store experience needs to be seamless to cater for the 'always-on' consumer who wants a fully integrated shopping experience across all channels.

"

John Baulch, a director at the Centre for Retail Research, said: "The high street is changing from what it was 10 years ago.
It is all about experiences: you can go and have your hair done, you can have a coffee, you can meet your friends.
"The problem is that the multi-purpose nature of the high street is not compatible with the internet, which is very functional.
If you are looking for something specific, you are far more likely to go online."
The painting of 19th-century business magnate Henry Reynolds by Joshua Reynolds has gone on display at London's National Portrait Gallery.
The painting has been privately owned by direct descendants of the subject since it was created in 1789.
It was given on long-term loan to the gallery by the current owner, who wishes to remain anonymous.
Reynolds was a prominent figure in British industry, making his fortune from the Cornish mines.
He was painted by Joshua Reynolds in 1789, when he was 67.
The portrait shows the businessman in a brown coat against a stormy sky, with smoke rising from a chimney in the background.
National Portrait Gallery curator Dr. Hannah Fedorova said the portrait was "a brilliant example of a conversation between two generations of artists".
"The older Reynolds is depicted by the younger Reynolds and the result is a compelling portrait of a dynamic businessman and art collector, full of subtleties and contrasts," she said.
The painting will be on display in room 38 of the National Portrait Gallery from today until June 2023.

"

"

Queries about RFID tags have reached record levels in the UK, according to the country's national consumer advice centre.

"

Former British prime minister Tony Blair said US President George W Bush had to fight the "war on terror" alone after the 11 September attacks.

But in an interview with the BBC to promote the book, Mr Blair rejected the idea that the war had been a failure.

Mr Blair said the world had been "upended" by a series of events following the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.

Malaysia will remove a 30% limit on the share of Islamic banking assets for the country's banks, allowing them to grab a bigger slice of the sector as the government seeks to bolster financial inclusion.
The threshold, which has been in place since 2012, will be lifted from April 2022, Malaysia's finance ministry said in a statement on Monday.
Islamic banking follows religious principles such as bans on interest payments and pure monetary transactions.
The finance ministry said the move would provide more options and enhance financial inclusion in the country.
Malaysia, a Muslim-majority nation, has seen a rapid increase in Islamic banking assets since they were first offered to the public in the 1990s.
Sharia-compliant banking assets totalled 369.3 billion ringgit ($82.6 billion) as of September 2021, according to the central bank.

The body of a BBC news article titled "Text message record smashed":

The text message has become one of the most ubiquitous forms of communication in the modern world, with billions of messages sent each day.
But how much do you actually know about the history of the text message?
The first text message was sent way back in 1992, and it was just a simple message sent from one mobile phone to another.
It read "Merry Christmas".
This humble beginning paved the way for the text message revolution that would soon take the world by storm.
As text messaging became more and more popular, people began to realize its potential for communication.
It was quick, convenient, and could be done from just about anywhere.
As technology improved, so too did the capabilities of the text message.
Soon, we were able to send pictures, videos, and even voice messages.
But perhaps the most impressive milestone in the history of the text message is the record for the longest message ever sent.
This record was recently broken by a telecommunications company in the United Kingdom, who sent a message that was a staggering 263 pages long.
This record-breaking message was sent as a way to demonstrate the capabilities of modern text messaging technology, and it certainly did that.
It was comprised of a combination of text, images, and video, and it took over six hours to transmit.
The text message has come a long way since its humble beginnings in the early 1990s.
It has become an integral part of our lives, and it continues to evolve and improve as technology advances.
It's exciting to think about what the future holds for this powerful communication tool.

In Japan, the government said it would take "necessary measures" to protect the Japanese economy from the fallout from the euro crisis.

The co-writer of the Ring of Fire, one of the most successful songs in music history, has died at the age of 95.
Lou Christie, a singer and songwriter who was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018, passed away in his sleep on Sunday at his home in New Jersey, his publicist said.
Ring of Fire, which Christie co-wrote with June Carter Cash and others, has sold more than 35 million copies worldwide and was recorded by more than 200 artists.
A statement from his family said Christie's health had been failing recently, but the exact cause of his death was not immediately clear.
Christie's career spanned more than 60 years, and he recorded more than 40 albums.
He was born in Philadelphia in 1929 and served in the US Army during the Korean War.
He went on to become a disc jockey and is credited with introducing The Beatles to American audiences in 1964.
He began recording music in the early 1960s, achieving success with the single Rhapsody in the Rain, which sold more than 25 million copies.
He went on to work with other artists, including Elvis Presley, Frank Sinatra, and Barbra Streisand.
Christie was married to his wife Eileen for more than 50 years before her death in 2015.
He is survived by his son, daughter, and four grandchildren.
Even at the age of 95, Christie's love of music remained vibrant, and he was still performing and recording in the months leading up to his death, according to a statement from his family.
Indian IT giant Wipro has reported better-than-expected fourth-quarter results, with net profit rising to ₹3,408 crore, up 4.9% year on year.
The company said it had won deals worth $1.3bn in the three months to 31 March, helping its order book to rise for the sixth consecutive quarter.
Wipro's chief executive Thierry Delaporte said the company had "accelerated our transformation and delivered results ahead of expectations".
However, its revenue grew just over 1% year on year to ₹15,670 crore, slightly down on the ₹15,965 crore predicted by analysts.
Mr Delaporte said that the company was benefiting from investments in its digital, cloud and cybersecurity offerings.
"We are well-positioned to take advantage of growing demand for digital transformation and IT operations across industries," he said.
Wipro forecasts revenue growth in the fast range of 1.5 to 2.5% in the financial year to 31 March 2024, with a profit growth rate in fast range of 7.5 to 9.5%.
India has signed a $40 billion deal to import liquefied natural gas from Iran over the next 20 years as New Delhi seeks to boost its energy imports to meet the needs of its rapidly growing economy.

The deal, which was signed in New Delhi on Saturday by Indian Oil Corporation Chairman Sanjiv Singh and National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) Chairman Ali Akbar Salehi, will see India import 5 million tons of LNG a year from Iran for the next two decades.

India, the world's fourth-largest energy consumer, has been struggling to meet its gas needs as domestic production has failed to keep up with rising demand, forcing the country to increase its imports.

Saturday's deal will further strengthen economic ties between India and Iran, which have been growing closer in recent years due to their mutual opposition to Pakistan and common interest in stabilizing the region.
The deal is also a significant boost for Iran's nuclear deal with world powers, which allowed it to resume oil exports and opened the way for foreign companies to invest in its energy sector.
Iran has the world's second-largest natural gas reserves after Russia, but has been unable to capitalize on them due to decades of international sanctions over its nuclear program.

The start of LNG exports to India could open the way for other Asian countries to buy gas from Iran, which is looking to increase its LNG exports to help offset the loss of European customers following the nuclear deal.
While India has been slow to invest in Iran's energy sector due to remaining sanctions, Saturday's deal could open the way for other Indian companies to pursue energy projects in the country.

The Pakistani government has announced that it will no longer allow women to hide their faces in public.
The announcement comes after a recent spate of incidents in which women were attacked by men, with the attackers claiming that they were unable to see the women's faces.
The order, which will take effect in the next few weeks, will require all women in Pakistan to show their faces in public.
Those who do not comply will face a fine or a prison sentence.
The announcement has been welcomed by many in Pakistan, who have said that it is a necessary step to ensure the safety of women in the country.
However, others have criticized the order, saying that it is a violation of women's rights and that it will make them more vulnerable to harassment.
The order has also been criticized for being too vague.
It does not specify what constitutes a face being hidden, which could lead to confusion and abuse.
For example, it is not clear whether a woman wearing a scarf or a veil would be considered to be hiding her face.
Despite these concerns, the government has said that it is confident that the order will be a success and that it will help to improve the safety of women in Pakistan.

Star Trek fans are rallying to save the show, which they say has been a source of inspiration and representation for decades.

To understand the drama that is unfolding at St James’ Park it is important to appreciate the combustible mix of owners, directors and managers that have converged on Newcastle United this season.

On one side there is the consortium of buyers that comprises the Saudi Public Investment Fund, PCP Capital Partners, and RB Sports & Media, the group that completed their takeover of the club in October 2021.

It is an unlikely alliance of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund – the centrepiece of Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to diversify the country’s economy – and the Reuben Brothers, who built their property empire from scratch after arriving in the UK as refugees from Uganda.
It is easy to forget that the consortium’s offer to buy the club was accepted by Mike Ashley in April 2020, only for the deal to collapse when the pandemic hit.
It was revived and finally completed 14 months later with the buyers claiming to have pumped £350m into the club to clear debts and fund transfers.

On the other side there is the retained element of the old regime, chief executive officer Lee Charnley and executive director Kate Barnes, and more importantly, the man they appointed as manager in November 2020, Steve Bruce.
Bruce had been appointed eight weeks earlier, following the departure of Rafa Benítez, who had grown frustrated at the club’s failure to back his ambitions in the transfer market.

The new owners had every right to appoint their choice of manager and did so with a six-year contract, but in Bruce they chose a manager with no prior connection to the club, who had enjoyed only limited success at his previous clubs, and who had been relieved of his duties at Sheffield Wednesday and Newcastle United (the first time around).
Bruce said he needed “a proper chance” to prove himself and set himself a target of finishing 10th in his first season.
They finished 16th.
This season began with more change as Bruce’s trusted No 2, Graeme Jones, left to be replaced by Eddie Howe’s younger brother, Jason.
Early results were promising with four wins and a draw in the first eight games but that form was always going to be unsustainable given the limitations of the squad.
Since then just two more wins have come in the following 18 games before yesterday’s 3-0 defeat by Manchester City.
The longer the poor results went on, the more complicated the power struggle at the top
The European Central Bank has kept its main interest rate on hold at 2.5% but warned the economy was weakening more than expected.
In a statement, the bank said it was maintaining its rate "against the background of weaker economic activity".
The ECB had been expected to ease policy but economists predicted a cut might not come until July.
The eurozone's manufacturing and services sectors slowed in March, according to surveys released on Friday.
The ECB said interest rates were likely to remain at their current or lower levels until it saw inflation reaching its 2% target in a sustainable manner.
This is a change from its previous guidance, which said rates would remain low "for an extended period of time".
The ECB also said it would start buying euro-denominated securities issued by non-bank corporations on the secondary market.
The so-called corporate sector purchase programme (CSPP) is due to start in June.
The bank also said it would provide further details of the CSPP at its next meeting on 4 June.

The Japanese capital Tokyo on Monday warned that deflation was still a concern, even as the city announced a drop in consumer prices for October.
Prices in Tokyo fell 0.3% year-on-year in October, marking the first annual decline in nearly two years and ending a streak of more than 30 straight months of inflation.
The drop came as energy prices fell and the cost of food declined, offsetting a steady rise in the prices of goods such as clothing and household utensils.
The Tokyo metropolitan government said the rate of decline was smaller than in September, when prices fell 0.5% year-on-year, and smaller than the 0.4% drop that had been expected.
The data comes as the Japanese government has been struggling to combat deflation, which has been a major driver of the country's long-running economic slump.

While the central bank has implemented a series of measures to try to boost inflation, including negative interest rates and massive asset purchases, the measures have so far failed to produce the desired results.
Deflation has been a major drag on the Japanese economy, leading to a decline in consumer spending as people put off purchases in the hope of further price declines.
The Tokyo data was released as the Bank of Japan was holding a policy meeting on Monday, with the central bank expected to keep interest rates at their current low levels.

McConnell had claimed that Jim Inhofe's absence from the Senate chamber was due to the latter's "personal reasons".
Inhofe, however, claimed that McConnell had told him beforehand that Inhofe could miss the vote as he was "drunk".
Inhofe, who was reportedly sober, took to the floor of the Senate the next day to dispute McConnell's account.

The one-time pad, an encryption technique invented nearly a century ago, relies on short key phrases.
But a new study suggests that even when those phrases are nonsensical, their patterns can still be revealing.
Benjamin Sparrey and Daniel Hughes of the University of Bristol in the U.K. examined four famously secure messages encoded using one-time pads.
They found that, with enough contextual information about the authors and their backgrounds, they could guess at the content of the messages, despite having no knowledge of the key phrases used.
For instance, they were able to infer the content of a message that Soviet spy John Cairncross sent to Moscow in 1943, despite having no knowledge of the keyphrase that Cairncross used.
(They did have access to a 1987 book that gave six possible one-time pads that the author believed Cairncross might have used.)

The findings, presented last week at the IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy in Paris, underscore the importance of using appropriate one-time pads and cutting down on contextual information that might leak.
In an email to The Register, Sparrey wrote that the one-time pad remains a secure encryption technique if used properly.

"The reason why I performed this research is because I think it is important for people to realize just how secure the one-time pad is if used properly, and to understand the circumstances in which security may be broken," Sparrey wrote.
"I hope that this research can be used to further educate people on the strengths and weaknesses of this beautiful and elegant encryption technique."
Roger Federer claimed a historic crown in Dubai on Friday as the legendary Swiss star won his maiden title in the desert.
The world's most successful player had lost three previous finals in Dubai but defeated Felix Auger-Aliassime of Canada 7-6 (7-1), 6-3 to clinch the title.
It was Federer's very first tournament win in over a year and without a doubt one of the most special.
In an on-court interview after the match, Federer said "This is a dream come true.
I am happy for me, and I hope Dubai is happy as well.
This is just unforgettable.

"

With Novak Djokovic being deported from Australia earlier this year and Rafael Nadal missing from Dubai through injury, the 19-time grand slam champion had extra motivation.
Speaking on court, Federer said "There is more pressure since Novak isn't here and Rafa is hurt.
I know everybody is looking at me, maybe going, 'Okay, if Novak isn't there, maybe Roger can still do it.'
"But I think everybody was expecting me to maybe go far in this tournament, maybe even win the tournament, because of the situation.
"I honestly didn't think about that too much.
I just thought it would be amazing if I could win here again like 2003.

"

The win sees Federer move up to world No. 13 in the live rankings, just 405 points behind Nadal.
Liverpool have pledged to keep captain Steven Gerrard after the midfielder admitted he could leave the club in the summer.
The 32-year-old has been linked with a move to Real Madrid or Chelsea.
"It's not done any harm," said Liverpool manager Brendan Rodgers.
"It's shown the level of the player and how highly regarded he is.
"But for us it's not an issue.
He's a Liverpool player and we expect him to be here."
Gerrard, who has spent his entire career at Anfield, has won the Champions League, Uefa Cup, FA Cup and League Cup with the club.
He has made 695 appearances and scored 180 goals.
The England international admitted at the weekend he was considering his future, and said he would hold talks with the club as well as his family over the summer.
"I think it's the right time for me to speak to the club and see where we are and what happens next," he said.
"I've said before that I think it's the right time for me to cement my place in the England team and that would be a lot easier if I was playing every week.
"That's not happening at the moment and that's the reason why I'm thinking about things.
"I'm not sure how the club moves forward if they get an offer that's respectable.
That's something we have to think about in the summer and decide from there.

"
Liverpool chief executive Ian Ayre said the club would not sell Gerrard, and that the player would be going nowhere.
"Steven Gerrard is a Liverpool player and he will remain a Liverpool player, simple as that," said Ayre.
"There's no price we couldn't turn down - it's not going to happen.
"He's too valuable to the club, it doesn't matter who comes in for him.
"We've said all along we wouldn't sell him and we won't, so it's as simple as that."
The release of the documentary "Michael" signals the "end of an era", according to fans of the King of Pop, Michael Jackson.
The documentary, which premiered at the Sundance film festival, is billed as the final film in a trilogy, concluding over a decade's work by director Andrew Eastick.
But fans who have followed the singer's career believe the documentary could signal other things.
"It is the end of an era - the era of Michael Jackson, the greatest musician of a generation," one fan told the BBC.
"He survived the Beatles - yes the Beatles were huge but they hadn't anything like the global appeal of Michael Jackson," they added.
Another fan said: "He elevated pop as an art form and remained relevant even after his death.
"He's the greatest performer of all time and this documentary underlines that.
He is the epitome of cool."
But the fan, like many others who have been raving about the documentary on social media, believes the film signals more than just the end of Jackson's era.
"For me it signals the end of an era for documentaries," they said.
"It is brilliantly and beautifully made.
"It is respectful, and allows his work to speak for himself.
He was an extraordinary talent and this reflects that.

"

While some fans remain convinced Jackson's career spanned eras, the term "era" usually refers to a period of time within a musician's career when they produce music with a distinct style, and signal a new phase in their work.
The term can also refer to the length of a musician's career, and signal that a person's work is done.

Eastick's previous documentaries, "This Is It" and "Living With Michael", focused on Jackson's preparations for his final concerts, and the behind-the-scenes drama during the making of his album "Bad".
"Michael" includes never-before-seen archive footage of the singer, and explores his legacy.
Eastick said it was important to "show respect" to the singer, "a flawed genius".
"We wanted to show the man, not as anyone wanted to see him, but as he was," he told the BBC.
"He was a genius on many levels, not least of which was his ability to connect with audiences."

Sunderland are close to appointing former Scotland manager Steve Clarke as their new boss until the end of the season following discussions with the Football Association, but David Weir is poised to join their backroom team.

The Black Cats have been searching for a new manager since parting company with Phil Parkinson last week and have interviewed a number of candidates, but Clarke is set to be appointed ahead of Saturday's game against Burton.

The IMF has agreed to provide Turkey with a fresh loan of $5bn to support the country's economic recovery.
The announcement comes after Turkey's currency, the lira, reached a record low against the US dollar last week, amid a currency crisis and fears of an economic downturn.
The loan, which is subject to approval by the IMF's executive board, will comprise $3.3bn in emergency funding and $1.7bn in standby credit.

The IMF said the loan would provide critical support to Turkey's economy, helping to stabilize the country's currency and support economic growth.

"

Newcastle and Gloucester played out a thrilling draw at Kingston Park as the hosts scored a late penalty to earn a share of the points.

Thailands Pakorn Pornsaneewong retains his World Boxing Council (WBC) world minimumweight title with a unanimous points decision over Mexican Jose Javier Torres Sandoval in Bangkok.
The capacity crowd at the Indoor Stadium saw the champion outbox his game challenger in a battle of teenagers.

Men in the UK are set to live longer than women, but a new study suggests that they are failing to prepare for a longer retirement and as a result, risk falling into poverty in old age.
The study, based on research by the London School of Economics and Political Science, found that men were failing to save enough for retirement, despite having longer life expectancy than women.
The study's author, Dr. Claire Aston, said: "Living longer is a success story.
But with the state pension age rising, and a lack of savings, many men are at risk of falling into poverty in older age.

"Women have traditionally been less well-off in retirement, but recent increases in working rates and improvements in pension participation mean that they are now more likely than men to have adequate retirement savings."
The study found that women were now more likely to be in work than men, and as a result, were more likely to be contributing to a pension.
In addition, women were found to be more likely to receive a pension from their partner or spouse, which provided them with an additional income in retirement.
The study's authors called for more to be done to encourage men to save for retirement, including automatic enrollment into pension schemes and better financial education.

Ferguson hails Man Utd's resolve after Chelsea draw

"

Labour has been accused of creating "EU propaganda" for British citizens after it released a video urging people to vote to remain in the bloc.
The party's deputy leader, Angela Rayner, said the clip - which highlights the benefits of EU membership - was intended to "set the record straight" on the impact of Brexit.
But Conservative MP Alberto Costa called it "very misleading" and urged Twitter to remove it.
The video, released on Thursday, lists advantages of EU membership including cheaper phone bills, the right to live and work across Europe, and visa-free travel.
The voiceover says Labour is making the case to "defend our European future".
But in an letter to Twitter chief executive Jack Dorsey, Mr Costa, a Conservative MP for South Leicestershire, called for it to be taken down.
He said the video - which has been seen more than 120,000 times - was "very misleading" and broke the social network's rules on "misleading information".

"This is not the first time that Labour have pushed out this sort of propaganda and I strongly urge you to take immediate action in removing this video and to investigate Labour's behaviour in this matter," he wrote.
Ms Rayner said the video was intended to "set the record straight on the benefits of being in the EU".
"There are lots of benefits to being in the EU but the Tories want to deny that and just talk about immigration," she told the BBC's Newsnight.
"We're not going to let them get away with that.
We're going to talk about the benefits as well as the control and the security as well.
The video was also criticised by the pro-Brexit campaign group Leave Means Leave, which said it was an "attempt to brainwash people".
"With just five days to go until the referendum, we are clearly seeing the fear campaign from the Remain camp stepping up a gear," a spokesman said.
"It is frankly disgusting that Labour are now resorting to trying to brainwash people with this propaganda.

"

On Saturday, Labour's leader Jeremy Corbyn accused Prime Minister Boris Johnson of using "fear and lies" to make his case for Brexit.
The Labour leader said: "The Tories' campaign of fear and lies is exposing the worst of their corrupt, deceitful and undemocratic nature."
The Guantanamo Bay detention facility has been operating for 20 years.
In that time, according to official figures, 780 detainees have been through the prison, including a dozen or so who are still there.
In the summer of 2002, four men were brought to Guantanamo.

"

Kyrgios has been in fine form in 2018, winning his first title on home soil in Brisbane and reaching his first Grand Slam quarter-final at the Australian Open.

Melbourne, Australia (AFP) - Roger Federer produced a "magnificent" display to beat Russia's Marat Safin and reach the semi-finals of the Australian Open on Wednesday.
The Swiss master remained on course for a 10th successive Grand Slam title with a 6-3 7-6 (7/2) 6-2 victory over the former world number one.

The women's tournament will be decided on Thursday with Russia's Maria Sharapova taking on Belgium's Justine Henin in the final.

Glasgow: Scotland head coach Steve Robertson admits his side must beat Ireland in Sunday's decisive Euro 2021 encounter to have any hope of retaining their lure.
The Scots opened their campaign with a 19-0 defeat in Wales last weekend but Ireland suffered a heavier 41-8 loss to champions England.
"It is a must-win game.
The bonus point is important but the win is crucial," Robertson told BBC Scotland.
"Ireland were disappointed with their performance last week whereas we were really pleased with ours.

You have to take that into account but we are more concerned about what we do."

Having opened the tournament with a defeat for the second consecutive campaign, the Scots are under pressure to make it to the quarter-finals, where the top two in each group progress.
And Robertson, who took over from Shade Munro in January, says his players are better placed than in 2019 to progress.
"The first game is always tricky," he added.
"We are under no illusions that we need to beat Ireland to have a chance of topping the group.
"The tournament is quite tight.
There are probably six or seven teams who could win it.
We have just got to focus on our own performance and make sure we are accurate."
Liverpool midfielder Adam Tomlinson has signed a new contract that will keep him at the club until at least the summer of 2024.
The 20-year-old has made four senior appearances for Liverpool since making his debut against Aston Villa in April.
"It's been a long journey for me to get to this point, but I feel as though I'm ready now and hopefully I'll continue to show that," he said.
"I'm made up to be able to sign a new deal, it's been in the works for a little bit and to get it done before pre-season is a weight off my shoulders.

"

Tomlinson made his Champions League debut against AC Milan last season and was part of the squad that won the FA Cup and Carabao Cup.
He is part of Liverpool's pre-season training camp in Austria and could feature in their friendly against RB Salzburg on Saturday.
"It was a dream come true for me to play in the Champions League and it's something I learned a lot from," he added.
"Being around the first team has been great education for me, I've learned so much and hopefully I can keep pushing on."

UK Sport, the body that allocates funding to sports in the UK, has announced that it will be cutting funding for tennis by an estimated 41%.
This decision has prompted debate about the future of British tennis.
The funding cuts will take effect immediately, with elite players now needing to secure their own funding if they want to receive any sort of government support.
The Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) will receive approximately £6.5 million less than it expected to receive.
UK Sport stated that "an unacceptable gap between the funding needed to deliver success on the court and what is currently being delivered" was the reason for the cuts.
It also cited a lack of ranked players and poor results at Grand Slam tournaments as justification for the cuts.
The LTA has said it is "disappointed and surprised" by the decision, which it says will affect its ability to develop young players and compete on the global stage.
The LTA also claimed that the decision was taken without proper consultation.
The cuts are likely to have a significant impact on the future of British tennis, with many players and coaches now facing an uncertain future.

Is this the end of British tennis as we know it, or an opportunity for the LTA to reform and become more sustainable?

The official Rugby Football Union website carried a story entitled 'England plot granny rule twist to confuse Wales'.
It has since been removed but the Welsh camp were still aware of its contents when they arrived in Cardiff on Tuesday.
"It's not the professionalism that we've come to expect from the RFU," said Gatland.

"I don't know what their reasoning was for doing it
but it's not the professionalism that international rugby expects and it's not something we're used to from the RFU.
"I don't know what their reasoning is for releasing a statement like that

In 2003 World Cup final referee Andre Watson cited the 'granny rule' when sending off Wales' Richard Hibbard for a dangerous tackle on Australia's Elton Flatley.
The sanction appeared harsh at the time and Wales argued that Hibbard was entitled to a warning.
The 'granny rule' has never been used in a Six Nations match and Wales half-back Mike Phillips admitted on Tuesday that he was unaware of its existence.
"I heard about it when I came into training yesterday," said Phillips.
"It's not something we've spoken about.
"There was a bit of banter about it but that's as far as it went.
"It's one of those things that's not really worth talking about to be honest.
We're more worried about getting our own house in order and making sure we're ready for Saturday."

The International Tennis Federation (ITF) confirmed the ruling on Wednesday, saying the Russian's suspension will be backdated to 26 January, when she tested positive.

Hashimoto said it was "sad" they could not attend, but that she was determined to "make the Tokyo 2020 Games a complete success".
Her comments came as the Olympic flame arrived in Japan from Greece, after being taken around the world on an unprecedented journey delayed by Covid-19.
"I hope the flame can help lighten the mood," Hashimoto said at a welcoming ceremony at Tokyo's Haneda airport.
"Once the Olympic flame is lit inside the Olympic stadium, it will motivate athletes and encourage people around the world.

The pandemic has cast a long shadow over the Games, with a surge in cases prompting officials to impose a state of emergency in Tokyo, and athletes being warned to expect tough restrictions inside the Olympic Village.
On Friday, Japan's government said rising cases around the country were "extremely concerning" ahead of the Games.
Japan has recorded more than 14,000 deaths during the pandemic - a figure far lower than many other countries.
But the public appears divided over the Games, with opinion polls suggesting a majority believe they should be postponed again or cancelled altogether.
Small protests - mostly by anti-Olympic and anti-government groups - have taken place across the country.
Hashimoto admitted that she could "understand" why the Japanese public were concerned about the potential impact of the Games on the country's virus situation.
But she said organisers had put in place a range of measures to ensure the event would be safe.
"There are many reasons to support the Games," she added.
"The Tokyo Olympics will be remembered as the Olympics that conquered coronavirus.
I hope people can look back on these Games with warmth and affection."
Tim Henman has decided to quit the Davis Cup after eight years of service despite being picked for next month's final against Belgium.
The 30-year-old announced earlier this year that he was going to take a break from tennis following Wimbledon, but had not decided then about his future in the team competition.
However the British number one has now confirmed he will not play again, despite being part of successive promotions to the World Group.
In a statement released by the Lawn Tennis Association, Henman said: "It has been a difficult decision to make but I don't feel it would be right to play on.

"

The Welsh lightweight has fought - and lost - against better opponents than his record suggests because he has prioritised learning and development over results.
