Arsenal defeated Newcastle United on penalties to reach the FA Cup semi-finals on Saturday.
The match was goalless after extra time at Emirates Stadium, but Arsenal prevailed 5-4 in the shootout as Newcastle's Dan Burn blazed over the bar with the crucial fifth kick.
Saka, Bukayo Saka, and Emile Smith Rowe had earlier scored their penalties for the Gunners, while Rob Holding, Eddie Nketiah, and Aaron Ramsdale were also successful.
That meant Mikel Arteta's side progressed to the last four and a meeting with Manchester City after winning the shootout.
The first half of the match was goalless, with Burn having the best chance for the Magpies but failing with an acrobatic attempt.
Early in the second half, Newcastle almost broke the deadlock when Arsenal goalkeeper Ramsdale was forced to make a save from Sven Botman's header.
The visitors continued to create chances in the second half, but their finishing was poor.
Burn was denied by Ramsdale, while Miguel Almiron and Joelinton were off target with their attempts.
Arsenal almost won the game in the final minutes of normal time when Nketiah was brought down in the box, but Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang's penalty was saved by Magpies keeper Martin Dubravka.
Both sides had chances in extra time.
Nketiah hit the post with a header for Arsenal, while Newcastle's Allan Saint-Maximin had a shot cleared off the line by Holding.
The match ended 0-0, and penalties were required to decide the outcome.
Arsenal scored their first four penalties, with Saka, Smith Rowe, Holding, and Nketiah all finding the back of the net.
However, Newcastle's confidence appeared to crumble when Burn blazed over, and Ramsdale then saved from Matt Ritchie to seal victory for the Gunners.
England centre Emily Scarratt will become the women's game's highest ever Test scorer as she sets her sights on breaking the 5000-point mark in the Six Nations.
Scarratt, 34, currently has 3,527 points and needs just 23 points in this year's Six Nations to pass Katy Daley-Mclean's mark.
She will reach the milestone if she scores two tries and kicks seven conversions in England's first two matches.
"It's a honour," said Scarratt.
"When you look at the calibre of players that have come before, it's a proud moment.
"It's something I if hadn't have thought about, never mind something I probably wouldn't have imagined would happen when I started playing rugby.
"I feel incredibly lucky.

"

Before this year's Six Nations Scarratt needed 35 points to overtake Daley-Mclean's mark, but having been involved in England's recent Quilter Internationals against the USA and Canada, the centre has scored 60 points so far this season.
The England men's record is held by Jonny Wilkinson, who scored 1,246 points in his 95 Tests between 1998 and 2011.
If Scarratt reaches the 5000-point mark it will be thanks to her formidable penalty and conversion rates.
Of her 3,527 Test points, 2,577 have come from penalties and conversions.
Scarratt made her England debut in 2007 and has gone on to win 134 caps.
She has appeared at six World Cups and was named player of the match in the 2017 final, which England won.
She was also part of the England team that won the 2014 Women's Rugby World Cup.
Last year she was awarded an MBE for services to the game.
England play Scotland in their Six Nations opener on Saturday, with Wales their opponents in round two.
Liverpool chairman Tom Werner has warned the English game is "close to burning out" young players and says Academy chief Alex Inglethorpe has been asked to help protect against it.
Werner was speaking as Liverpool opened their state-of-the-art Academy on Friday.
The £50m complex, which sees the club return to Kirkby on a site close to Liverpool's old stadium, has been specifically designed to develop and nurture young players.
"One of the things we're concerned about is young players getting burned out," said Werner, who is also the Fenway Sports Group's chairman.

"We have discussions with Alex Inglethorpe, our academy director, all the time about weaning these young players so they can develop gradually, because that is what is required if they are to have long careers.
"It's pretty clear English football is close to burning out young players.
You see the numbers that get played at a young age.
The notion of 'super-sub' doesn't seem to exist in England.
In Germany and Spain, players are much more developed when they get to the first team.

"

Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp is among those to have expressed concern about the physical demands being placed on young players, who can struggle to cope with the expectation to perform well in their early games for the club while adapting to the step up in intensity from youth football.
Klopp has repeatedly called for reform of the schedule for young players in England to bring it in line with other countries.
Werner added: "It's not just Liverpool.
I think it's a problem across England.
"You have a player like Raheem Sterling, who is a tremendous athlete, and he was playing games at the age of 15.
"Think about that.
He's an extraordinary athlete but at 15 he was playing games for a big club.
"That doesn't happen in other countries.
These are the discussions we have to have, because the game is about the players.
It's our job to protect them so they can have long and successful careers."
Blackburn have rejected a third bid from Premier League side Burnley for central defender Scott Wharton.
The Clarets, who signed England international Ben Mee from Blackburn in the summer, returned with an improved offer of £4m for the 23-year-old on Thursday.

Rovers rejected it, just as they had done with an initial bid of £3m and a second offer of £3.5m.

Wharton has made 122 appearances for Blackburn since graduating from their academy, but has not played since April because of a hernia problem.
He signed a new contract last February that runs until the summer of 2023.
Spain's sporting daily As has criticised Barcelona midfielder Ivan Rakitic for his role in Croatia's victory over Spain at the UEFA Nations League final.
The newspaper said the former Barcelona player, now at Italian side SSC Napoli, did not make enough effort to mark Spanish midfielder Sergio Canales in the build-up to Spain's goal.
Croatia won the final after extra time and then beat Spain in a penalty shoot-out.
As says Rakitic "did not hurry" to get close to Canales, who it describes as "shorter and less physically imposing", in the build-up to the equaliser.
The paper adds that the 32-year-old, who spent six years at Barcelona, "did not appear to be in a hurry" to get back to his position and "it seemed he preferred to stay closer to Luka Modric".
Rakitic, who scored Barcelona's second goal in the 4-0 win over Liverpool in last season's Champions League semi-final first leg, was one of seven former La Liga players in the Croatia side.
As says the Croatian players "suffered" in the penalty shoot-out but "luckily for them their former Barcelona teammates were on the pitch".
Spain captain Sergio Ramos, who played with Rakitic at Barcelona between 2007 and 2011, missed the crucial fifth penalty for Spain with goalkeeper Unai Simon sending his shot wide.
As says Spain's players were not to blame for the defeat as they had controlled the game until Croatia's equaliser.
The newspaper concludes that Spain's players, including those who were only on the bench, were "close to tears" at the final whistle.
Fulham manager Roy Hodgson is enjoying the "stimulation" of European football and is happy that his side have been drawn against Roma and Basel in the Europa League.
The Cottagers, who finished sixth in the Premier League last season, face Roma in Italy in the first leg of their play-off on 20 August.
"I love being involved in these types of games, love the challenge," he said.
Hodgson spent seven years managing in Europe, guiding Fulham to the Europa League final in 2010, where they were beaten by Atletico Madrid.
"This is a short journey which we've undergone as a club in the last three years and I include ourselves as managers and coaches in that," he said.
"To go from where we were when we arrived, which was basically in the bottom three, to get into the (Premier League) top six and play in Europe again is a great achievement.
"To go into the draw and see who you're going to play and discover you've got Roma and then Basel, it's not as if we've been given a particularly difficult tie.
"It's still going to be very difficult but of course as a coach and a manager you want to test yourself against the best."
Hodgson believes English clubs are now better prepared for European football, particularly in the early stages of tournaments.
"The experiences that English clubs have had in the last few years, not only in Europe but in the FA Cup and the Carling Cup, they are far better equipped to deal with these situations," he said.
"A lot of the players in our squad have not played in these competitions before so it's a new experience for them.
It's one that we're all looking forward to.

"

Meanwhile, Hodgson has confirmed that he is looking to bring in "two or three" new faces before the start of the Premier League season.
"We're still looking for one or two players and I'm hoping that we can announce something in the next few days," he said.
"It's not going to be easy because a lot of clubs are looking for the same type of players as us.
We're looking for players who can improve the squad."
Scotland manager Steve Clarke has included Nottingham Forest's Scott McKenna and Kilmarnock's Stuart Findlay in his squad for next month's Euro 2020 play-off against Serbia.
The defenders have both recovered from injury problems that have kept them out since September.
McKenna has not played under Clarke, who took over from Steve Clarke in June 2019, due to a combination of injury and the form of his rivals.
Findlay has only made one appearance under the current Scotland boss, playing the entirety of the 2-0 defeat by Russia in September 2018.
The Scotland squad will meet up on Monday 24 January for a training camp at Dubai's Nad Al Sheba Sports Complex.
The squad will then travel to Belgrade for the play-off first leg on Thursday 3 February.

All Black magic: New Zealand rugby

They are universally recognised as the most successful international rugby union team of the modern era.
New Zealand's All Blacks have won more than 75% of their tests since 1905.
They have won the Rugby World Cup three times since the tournament was first held in 1987 and have finished as runners-up on another two occasions.
They are the only country to have competed at every Rugby World Cup and, alongside England, South Africa and Australia, one of only four teams to have made it to the semi-finals of every tournament.
New Zealand have also won the most matches at the Rugby World Cup, with 54 victories from 62 matches.
They have a winning percentage in test rugby of 77.92% and, as of November 2022, a total of 428 test victories - the most of any nation.
They have not lost a home test since 2009 - a run of more than 70 matches - and their away record is also impressive, with fewer than one in four tests away from home lost since 2010.
Add to that a hattrick of victories in the Bledisloe Cup - their annual contest with arch-rivals Australia - and it makes for quite a year for the All Blacks.

So what is the secret of their success?

'Leaving the jersey in a better place'
For All Blacks head coach Ian Foster, it is about 'leaving the jersey in a better place' - the mantra he uses to drive his team forwards.
"It's a mindset, it's a constant challenge to ourselves," he says.
"We've got a great history, we respect that, we know we're lucky to wear these shirts and the chance to make that better is something pretty special.

"That's the mindset of the team, we want to make the most of every day we train, every opportunity to get better, to make our fans and country proud of us, and ultimately to try and put a performance out on the park that reflects where we've been working hard to get to.

"

Respect for the jersey
That mindset, says Foster, is about respecting the jersey.

"If you don't have that, you're probably in the wrong sport, because ultimately, every guy in our team has that innate drive to want to be the best, to want to make their country proud and to wear the jersey the right way.

"

Andy Holmes secured a comfortable victory in the English Amateur Championship final at Royal Cinque Ports on Saturday.

It was Holmes' first major victory since he won the Amateur Championship at Royal Porthcawl in 2009, and denied Dean, who led after day one, a double.
The 22-year-old from Leeds was bidding to become only the second man to win both titles since they were split into separate events in 1989.
But he was never in the hunt on Saturday as Holmes, who finished fourth in the strokeplay section, built a three-hole lead after eight holes and turned with a two-hole advantage.
And he increased his lead to three after 14 holes before sealing the victory on the 16th with a par five.
"It's unbelievable really," Holmes told BBC Sport.
"I never expected it after the way I've played over the last few years.
"I've had a few ups and downs and thought about quitting a few times, so to win again is amazing.
"It's amazing what a difference a year makes.

Holmes, who turned professional after his 2009 success, failed to secure his card at his first attempt and returned to the amateur game.
"I decided to turn pro a bit too early," he said.
"I wasn't ready for it, I was still learning my trade as an amateur.
"It's been tough since then but to win again shows how hard I've worked."

"I'm disappointed not to win," he said.
"But I'm happy with how I played this week.

The UK economy is facing "major risks" from spiralling costs and inflation, the Bank of England's governor has warned.
Andrew Bailey said the economy was facing a "very large" shock, as the price of goods rose much faster than people's wages.
His comments came as the Bank decided to raise interest rates to 1% - the highest level in 13 years.
The increase - widely expected following recent spikes in inflation - is designed to try to curb price rises.
Mr Bailey said the Bank expected inflation to peak at a higher level than previously thought, reaching 11% in the spring, up from a previous forecast of 10%.
The governor added that he also expected the UK economy to shrink by 0.25% in 2023, in comparison to previous estimates.
The decision to increase the cost of borrowing to 1% - the sixth consecutive rise - takes the Bank rate to its highest level since February 2009.
Inflation - the rate at which prices rise - is currently at its highest point in 40 years, mainly as a result of the pandemic and the war in Ukraine.
The Bank's decision comes as thousands of workers are striking in protest over pay, with rail workers, nurses, paramedics, and lorry drivers all walking out.
Many unions have called for pay rises of around 10%.
Figures released on Wednesday showed that the cost of wholesale gas in the UK rocketed by more than 30% in just one day.
The price of oil has also jumped - rising above $100 a barrel for the first time since 2014.
The Bank's decision to raise interest rates is designed to increase the cost of borrowing money and reduce demand, which should help slow the increase in prices.
But it is expected that households will face further financial pressures with mortgage rates and borrowing costs set to rise.
Mr Bailey said that there was a risk that the Bank's actions "could end up being contractionary" - meaning that they could cause the economy to shrink.
He added that the Bank would "have to consider" whether to take further action at its next meeting in May.

Winter freeze keeps oil above $50

The US benchmark price for crude oil has stayed above $50 a barrel, as oilmen anticipate the impact of cold weather on supplies.
The price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) for February delivery rose 73 cents to $50.49 on Monday, reports the Associated Press.
Supplies of natural gas, which is used to heat homes and generate electricity, are expected to be lower than normal as temperatures drop.
That is because natural gas is also used in the drilling and extraction of oil.
"Drilling basically shuts down in extreme cold," said Tom Kloza, chief oil analyst at the Oil Price Information Service.
As a result, oil supplies will drop and prices will rise, he said.
"It's going to be nasty.
The forecast comes as US oil production has finally surpassed output from Saudi Arabia.
The US Energy Information Administration said that the US produced an average 11.6 million barrels a day in November, compared with Saudi Arabia's 11 million.
The figures are preliminary, but if they are confirmed, it would be the first time since October 2008 that the US has beat the Saudi kingdom in output.
The rise in US output has been driven by production from shale oil deposits, which are scattered across the country.
These deposits were once considered inaccessible, but advances in drilling technology, such as hydraulic fracturing ("fracking"), have made them viable.
The US oil boom has contributed to a global glut of oil, which has seen the price of crude fall from more than $100 a barrel in mid-2014 to less than $30 in early 2016.
However, prices have recovered to about $50 a barrel as output has slowed in countries such as Nigeria and Venezuela, and sanctions have been imposed on Iran.
Mr Kloza said that prices below $50 encourage US oil producers to drill more, which could send prices lower.
However, he said that prices above $50 ought to encourage producers to limit their output.
Brazilian stocks and currency have rallied in recent weeks, in a sign that markets are betting on the country's economic recovery.

His comments came as he unveiled a bronze of Smith in his hometown of Kirkcaldy, in Fife.

He added: "Adam Smith was a massive, incredible thinker who changed the way that people think about free markets and what have you, so I think he was a genius.

"

Smith wrote "The Wealth of Nations" in 1776, promoting the idea that the selfish actions of individuals can lead to societal benefits.
The concept, now synonymous with capitalism, was an alternative to earlier economic theories that centred on the state's involvement in the economy.
Smith is thought to have born in Kirkcaldy in 1723, but there is no record of his birth or baptism.
He went to Glasgow University at the age of 14 and graduated in 1740, before moving to Oxford University.
He returned to Scotland and lived in Edinburgh, before moving to Paris in 1764 - where he met fellow philosopher David Hume - and then on to London.
It was while living in the British capital that he published "The Wealth of Nations".
Smith died in 1790 and is buried in Edinburgh.
Despite his legacy, there has never been a statue of him in his hometown.
Local councillor Neil Crooks said it was "fitting" that a statue of Smith was finally being put up, describing him as "one of Kirkcaldy's most famous sons".
"It is incredible that someone who is so famous worldwide, someone who has influenced millions of people around the world in terms of economic thinking, is not recognised in his home town," he said.

"I think we will see a crisis in many of the humanities and social sciences," said Michael Woolcock, a professor of political science and international affairs at Yale University.
"AI is increasingly doing what anthropologists, sociologists and psychologists do, which is to help us to understand the behaviour of humans."

"We should be looking to collaborate with people from all sorts of different disciplinary backgrounds."

"If we are not careful, we could end up sleepwalking into a world where the engineering perspective dominates," said Woolcock.

"

The case will be heard in the General Court of the European Union, although a date for the hearing has not yet been set.
The mobile phone has changed a lot in 20 years, from bulky devices that could only make calls and send text messages to the multi-functional smartphones of today.
They have gone from being a luxury to a necessity, and from a novelty to an everyday item.
But one thing hasn't changed: the speed at which we upgrade them.
In the US, the average lifespan of a mobile phone is 22 months.
In the UK it is 18 months.
And it is not just phones.
In general, consumers upgrade their gadgets every three to four years.
This is having a big impact on the planet.
Electronic waste, or e-waste, is now the fastest-growing waste stream in the world, and it is increasingly ending up in landfills in developing countries.
The United Nations estimates that in 2016, the world produced 44.7 million tonnes of e-waste, and that this will grow to 52.2 million tonnes by 2021.
This is the equivalent of throwing away 800 laptops every second.
Most of this waste is not properly recycled, and the toxins in e-waste, such as lead, cadmium and brominated flame retardants, can pollute the air, water and soil.
And the carbon emissions produced during the manufacturing and disposal of electronic devices are significant.
One report estimated that the carbon footprint of the information and communications technology (ICT) industry is already equivalent to that of the civil aviation industry.
So what can be done to reduce the environmental impact of our love of gadgets?
One approach is to make them easier to repair.
A recent study in the US found that making smartphones easier to fix could significantly reduce the environmental impact of the gadget boom.
The study found that extending the life of a phone by just one year could reduce its carbon footprint by up to 30%.
This would have the biggest impact on the most-used devices, such as smartphones.
Another approach is to make phones using more sustainable materials, such as biodegradable plastics or fabrics made from recycled materials.
There are also many things we can do as consumers to reduce the environmental impact of our gadgets.

BBC news article - Domain system scam fear - by Andrew Jennings in Moscow Thursday 4 February 2010 GENERAL LISTINGS Check the general listings in your domain name registrar's control panel.
If you find a mysterious entry, it could be a sign that someone has gained access to your account and adjusted your settings.
It may be that the original owner set up the entry as a forward to another website, perhaps on behalf of a client.
But it could also be a red flag.
Forwarding to a dodgy site can harm your reputation and your search rankings, so it's always good to check.
BEWARE OF DOMAIN NAME SYSTEM HIJACKS Be aware that the domain name system can be hijacked in order to redirect users to scam sites.
It's unlikely that your domain name system (or nameserver) settings will be changed without your knowledge.
But if a hacker does get access, this is one of the things they can do.
This is a serious risk as it can affect your whole online presence.
Make sure you have your registrar's emergency contact details to hand so you can call quickly in case your site suddenly goes down.
ALSO READ - How to protect your website from hackers DON'T AUTOMATICALLY RENEW DOMAIN NAMES Automatic renewal is convenient, but it can lead to disaster.
If you forget to cancel the renewal of a domain name you no longer want, you may end up paying for two, or even more if the scammer has forwarded the extra domains to their site.
Check your domains one by one and decide whether you really need them.
If you no longer require a domain, cancel the renewal.
If you're not sure, hang on to it for now, but be aware that you may be charged for two years' renewal.
ALWAYS CHECK YOUR BILL
You will normally receive an annual bill for your domain name renewals well in advance of the expiry date.
Make sure you recognise all the domains on it and that the bill is in the correct amount.
If you are suspicious, contact your registrar immediately.
If someone has forwarded your domain to another site, you should receive an email alerting you to the change.
CHECK YOUR CONTACT DETAILS Make sure the contact details on your whois listing are up to date.
If you fail to keep your email address current, you may not receive important alerts from your registrar.

Napster has launched a subscription service offering access to millions of songs for a monthly fee.
The service, Napster Unlimited, is priced at $5 a month for broadband subscribers.
Napster, originally a free music file-sharing service, was shut down in 2001.
It was bought by Roxio, now known as Roxio/Napster, which hopes the new service will help it compete with market leader iTunes.
The service was announced at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas.
Napster Unlimited offers unlimited access to Napster's library of more than eight million songs.
Users will be able to play songs on up to three computers and burn up to three songs a day onto CDs.
The service will be available in the US before the end of January, with a UK launch to follow shortly afterwards, a Napster spokeswoman said.

Roxio competitor iTunes offers a subscription service in conjunction with phone company Verizon, but it is only available to Verizon broadband subscribers and is more expensive than Napster Unlimited.
iTunes is the market leader in legal digital music sales.
It sold more than 70 million songs in 2004 and accounts for more than 70% of online music sales, according to media analyst firm Nielsen SoundScan.
Roxio has struggled to compete.
It sold only about five million tracks last year, according to Nielsen SoundScan.
The new Napster service does not allow users to burn songs onto CDs without restrictions.
That is a marked difference from the original Napster, which made it easy for users to copy songs and gave the company its reputation as a piracy hub.
To burn more than three songs a day onto a CD, users will have to buy unlimited burning privileges for $5 more per month.
Roxio is hoping the new service will attract a large number of subscribers.
In a statement, Chris Gorog, chief executive of Roxio, said: "We think this is the right model at the right time.

"Given the choice, we believe that consumers prefer to rent their music on a monthly basis, with the ability to cancel their subscriptions at any time, rather than having to purchase their music collections.

"

To encourage users to sign up, Napster is offering a free 14-day trial.
The new service will be available in the US through all major broadband providers, including Comcast, Earthlink, and AOL Time Warner.

Smartphone cameras are "must-haves" - but they could be so much better.
That is the view of ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, who has designed phones including the iPhone.
Ive said smartphones were the most important photographic innovation in a century.
But he said their cameras were "terrible" and "embarrassing".
The designer, who now runs his own firm LoveFrom, said manufacturers were not trying hard enough.
LoveFrom is working with a charity that trains African photographers.
Ive said the firm would donate revenue from an upcoming product to the charity, which trains photographers in Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda.
"We have this extraordinary facility in our pocket which is the most important photographic innovation in a century, and yet the camera is terrible, it's embarrassing," he said.
"When you consider how this tool, the camera, is used worldwide today, it's primarily used for social approval.
How do I look?
How do I appear?
Who's with me?
Where am I?
What am I doing?
"The use of the tool is primarily about social approval.
And in that context, the quality is actually irrelevant.

"

Ive was giving a talk at the Royal Academy of Arts in London to promote a new book about his career.
The book features some of the products he designed alongside text written by the designer himself.
It is billed as "a visual autobiography" and all the profits will go to charity.
In a wide-ranging interview, Ive also discussed virtual reality, a technology he said he was "fascinated" by.
He said it had the potential to be "profoundly important" and compared it to the invention of the wheel.
But he said VR had been held back by the lack of a "defining" application, such as the telephone.

"

Intel has built a breakthrough new laser that could finally help bring extreme high-speed internet access to your home.
The chip maker has demonstrated a technology called "terabit silicon laser" that can transmit data at a staggering rate of 1.02 terabits per second over a distance of 2km (1.24 miles).
That's 50 times faster than the fastest fibre optics connection available today and speeds that even quantum computing cannot hope to match.
The silicon laser could be used to upgrade the infrastructure of internet service providers (ISPs) to enable speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second downstream from ISPs to homes.
Thereafter, the speed of data transmission would be dependent on the equipment inside consumers' homes.

Today, most homes in the UK have a broadband speed of 36Mbps, while those lucky enough to live in areas covered by Virgin Media's cable service can receive speeds of up to 1Gbps - less than 0.2% of the speed that the new silicon laser is capable of.
The technology relies on a new type of laser etching that allows data to be processed and transmitted using light, rather than electrical pulses.

Justin Rattner, Intel's chief technology officer, said: "For the data centre market, where optical interconnects are beginning to reach their limits, the terabit silicon laser demonstrates how scalable and compact optical I/O can be for future high-performance computing platforms."
He added that the technology could be used to connect computers within a data centre, connecting data centres themselves and providing internet access.
The silicon laser could also be used to provide the infrastructure for 5G networks and high-speed autonomous vehicles.

The latest version of the Opera web browser can now read aloud any news article or website you visit.
The Norwegian software firm behind Opera said the feature was introduced to make surfing the web more accessible.
The browser can also be given commands verbally, making it possible to browse the web without touching the keyboard.

"This introduces a new way of interacting with browsers, making web content more accessible and bridging the gap between sites and applications," said Håkon Wium, the company's chief technology officer.
"It makes the desktop web experience a lot more like using a tablet or smartphone.

"

To read text out loud, users simply need to select it with their mouse and click on a speaker icon that appears in the browser's address bar.
They can also click on any link and have the content read aloud without leaving the page they are on.
Opera's "native speech" technology is based on the same browser engine that is used by Google's Chrome browser, but Wium said Opera was the first to make use of it in this way.
"We are trying to make the PC experience more like how tablets work, where you can enjoy the web without having to stare at the screen all the time," he said.
"This is an important step towards that.

"

However, the speech function does not work with all websites because it relies on them to be written in a way that is compatible with the speech API in Opera.
At the moment, it works best with news articles and stories on e-commerce websites, Wium said.
"We support the W3C's speech API, but not all sites implement this API," he said.
"As this technology advances, we expect more sites to implement it, making more web content accessible.

"

Opera's new browser, version 15, is available as a free download for Windows and Mac computers.
The EU's plans to harmonise patent law for computer-implemented inventions have been delayed because of a lack of support.
The European Commission had proposed a law to clarify patenting rules for software.
But it was opposed by some member states, as well as by activists and open-source developers.
The commission will now try to reach a compromise ahead of planned talks on the issue next year.
"Nothing has been abandoned," a spokesman for the European Commission said.
"We are currently exploring ways to break the deadlock and we will continue doing so in the coming months."

The two-year-long debate over the patent law has highlighted a growing rift between traditional industrial players, who want to boost patent protection for software, and supporters of digital innovation, who fear the measures will stifle software development.
Patents grant inventors of products or processes exclusive rights to make, use or sell their inventions for a limited period.
The European Commission's proposal focused on the definition of what kinds of software should be eligible for patents and how software patents should be enforced across the EU.
But a coalition of activists, open-source developers and digital rights groups opposed the legislation, arguing that it would harm software innovation and saddle developers with licensing costs.

The coalition, which included the British Open Rights Group, the Foundation for a Free Information Infrastructure and the Pirate Party, urged members of the European Parliament (MEPs) to block the proposal.
"This patent proposal would have blocked small developers and stifled innovation," said Julia Reda, an MEP for the Pirate Party.
"Every developer and startup in Europe should be pleased that the EU institutions have listened to their concerns.

"

The proposal was also opposed by some larger member states, such as Italy and Spain, who are concerned that software patents could lead to endless court battles and additional costs for businesses.

The commission's spokesman said that the body was looking at "all options" to break the deadlock, including the possibility of reaching a compromise ahead of talks on the issue scheduled for next year.
"There are different views on this topic," the spokesman said.
"Some member states are in favour of moving ahead with the proposal, while others have expressed concerns.
We are exploring ways to break the deadlock and we will continue doing so in the coming months."
The commission's proposal was originally scheduled to be discussed by MEPs and EU governments in the coming weeks.

It sounds like a device straight out of a spy movie, but its makers say it is the future of mobile phones.
The Mobifone is a mobile phone with a difference - it has no screen or keypad.
Instead, it uses "eye music" - a system where the user glances at symbols on the lid to open messages, select music and pick up calls.
South Korean firm Pantech has developed the device, which goes on sale there this week.
The phone recognises up to 2,000 different glance actions - such as quick sideways glances, prolonged eye contact and blinking.
Pantech is one of South Korea's biggest mobile phone makers and launched the device at the CES technology show in Las Vegas this week.
The firm's CEO, Lee Jong-seok, said the device had been four years in the making and was a world first.
"This is the world's first eye-controlled mobile phone.
There are other eye-controlled computers but they don't have the mobility of a mobile phone," he said.
"The phone's lid becomes a new kind of mobile interface.
The user can glance over at the lid when they receive a message and then glance away when they have finished reading it.
"It has a learning function so it can remember the actions of individual users.
It is also possible to use eye contact to share content with other Mobifones.
The phone can even be used while it is still in a user's pocket.
"You can receive calls then use a blinking action to take the call or you can use a prolonged glance to switch to silent mode," said Mr Lee.
"It means you will never have to take your mobile phone out of your pocket again.

"

The device, which has a regular keypad and screen that can be accessed when the lid is opened, goes on sale in South Korea on Thursday.

Ringtone sellers face tougher rules on what they can sell, following a spate of complaints from customers.
The Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) has written to all major providers, telling them to stop selling ringtones as mobile content, and instead to treat them as premium rate telephone services.
The move follows a surge in complaints to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA).
Customers have been unhappy with the cost and difficulty of getting refunds after they bought a ringtone by text message and did not receive it.

The CAP said that because there had been so many complaints, it was taking immediate action on behalf of the ASA to ensure the ads were not misleading.

In a letter to ringtone providers, CAP said that all ads should make clear that customers will be charged for a telephony service and should not imply that the service is free or charged at a fixed rate.

The letter said: "Clearly, given the volume of complaints referred to the ASA and the seriousness of the issues raised, it would not be appropriate for the ASA to investigate individual cases prior to the implementation of the proposed changes.

"We understand that you will want to consider the details of the proposed changes and, if accepted, it will be for each of you to implement these as swiftly as possible."

CAP's proposals include a requirement that companies provide a free number for customers to call if they want a refund for a ringtone they did not want or receive.
In addition, customers should not have to go through more than one level of customer service to get a refund.

The letter said: "While we recognise that the cost of a ringtone is usually relatively low, the number of complaints indicates that there is clear public concern about the way these ads are currently being handled."

California has become the first state in the US to impose fines for the use of "spyware" on computers and other devices.
The state's top lawyer said the software, which can allow advertisers to track consumers' every move online, amounted to an invasion of privacy.
It follows a proposal earlier this year by the state's governor, Gavin Newsom, to control the use of such software.
The fines could be as much as $2,500 for each violation.
How does spyware work?
Spyware is typically installed on a user's computer or phone without their knowledge, often hidden inside legitimate software.
It can collect a range of sensitive information about users, including their browsing history, login details and personal communications.
This information can be used to target advertising directly at the user, or even sold on to third parties.
What did California do?
In a first for the US, the state has introduced fines of up to $2,500 for each violation of the law, which bans the use of non-consensual spyware on computers, phones and other devices.
It applies to everyone from multinational tech firms to small-time retailers, and anyone caught installing spyware on a device could face criminal charges.
California's Attorney General Rob Bonta said the law amounted to "an invasion of privacy, and nobody is free from this invasion".
"The bottom line is that no one should have to worry that their personal information is being harvested without their consent," he added.
How was it enforced?
In September, Governor Newsom signed a bill that gave the state's attorney general the power to enforce the new rules.
"California is paving the way to protect consumers' privacy and security online," Governor Newsom said at the time.
What else is being done about spyware?
In the UK, the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) has said that the use of spyware is unlikely to be legal.
And earlier this year, an investigation by The Washington Post revealed that a number of prominent charities and political groups had used such software.
Following the revelations, Apple issued an emergency software update to its devices to protect users from a type of spyware developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group.

Europe backs digital TV lifestyle

More than half of European homes have access to digital television, making it the fastest growing television platform, the European Commission says.
The growth in digital, both via satellite and cable, is destroying the old analogue way of watching TV, according to a study by the commission, the EU's executive body.
The study also found that Europeans think the switch to digital will give them better picture and sound quality and more channels to choose from.

Improved picture and sound quality was the most important reason for digital TV uptake in all countries, except the UK, where it was the fear of the analogue signal being switched off, the study found.

The study also found that the take-up of digital television is accelerating.

Microsoft has released fixes for 96 security flaws, including two zero-day vulnerabilities that are being exploited by malicious hackers.
The tech giant described the update, released on Tuesday, as its largest single monthly release of security fixes since it adopted its current format in 2019.
Many of the flaws were in Microsoft's Windows and Windows components, including the zero-day vulnerabilities.
They affect Microsoft Windows Graphic Component and the Windows Kernel, and could allow remote code execution.
This means that a hacker could gain access to a device, then run executable code, which could potentially include malware, without the user's knowledge.

Microsoft said one of the zero-days had been seen in "limited targeted attacks" and the other was being used as part of a targeted attack referred to as "Solorigate" or "Sunburst" by security researchers.
It is the second time in three months that Microsoft has issued security fixes for zero-day vulnerabilities that are known to be actively exploited.
The tech giant routinely releases patches on the second Tuesday of each month, which is known as "Patch Tuesday".
But in June it issued an emergency patch for a Windows flaw that was being exploited by a hacking group called Nobelium.
It is not known if the two zero-days released on Tuesday were also exploited by Nobelium.

Cyber-security expert Graham Cluley said it was concerning that Microsoft had again had to rush out an emergency patch, adding that it was "clear that more work needs to be done to get on top of vulnerabilities".

"It is also concerning that despite these patches having been released, we know that attackers are going to be scanning the internet to find systems that have not been updated, and are vulnerable as a result," he added.
Britons are spending an increasing amount of time using computers and smartphones, and less time sleeping and exercising, a study suggests.

It also found adults were spending an extra two hours a day in front of screens, with screen time now averaging eight hours a day.
In contrast, the study found sleep time had decreased from eight hours 18 minutes to seven hours 31 minutes a night.
Exercise had also decreased from 1.5 hours a day to 1.2 hours, on average.

"We need to go on a digital diet, and figure out a way to wean ourselves off these devices," she added.

Respondents in the UK spent nine hours 30 minutes a day online on average, compared with seven hours 51 minutes sleeping.

Smartphones were the most important device for a third of respondents, while a quarter (24%) said their laptop was the device they would miss most.
"People are blissfully unaware of how much time they spend on devices," Ms Bevan said.

Microsoft is urging computer users to patch a security vulnerability that could allow attackers to silently install malicious software onto their devices.

Microsoft said there had been no evidence that the vulnerability had been used by cyber-criminals.

"We know that nation-state actors, cybercriminals, and other malicious actors will always look for new ways to gain unauthorized access to networks and systems," said Phillip Misner, Microsoft's security group manager.
"Our recommendation is to immediately install the updates provided here," he added in a blog post.
The NSA tool, called EternalBlue, took advantage of a flaw in Microsoft software to collect data on targets.
It was part of a cache of hacking tools leaked by a group called the Shadow Brokers in April 2017.
Microsoft said it had released patches for the vulnerability in March 2017, but many computers remained unpatched because the flaw was "cherry-picked" by the NSA to exploit.
The agency then lost control of the tool, which was used in the massive WannaCry ransomware attack that hit the NHS and hundreds of thousands of other computers around the world.
CyberArk, a security company, said the newly-discovered vulnerability was similar to, but not the same as, EternalBlue.
It is another example of a broader trend in which malicious actors take advantage of "dual use" vulnerabilities - flaws in software that can be used for both good and bad purposes.

"An attacker can use this vulnerability to gain access to an entire corporate network if they successfully exploit it on a single computer that has access to that network," said CyberArk researcher Ben Seri.

"It's just one example of many 'dual use' vulnerabilities, which can be used by both attackers and defenders, and illustrates why responsible disclosure and handling of vulnerabilities is so critical," he added.
Text messages have become a key tool for relief agencies working to help victims of natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods.
Organisations such as the Red Cross and the United Nations use short messaging service (SMS) to coordinate relief efforts and to provide information to people in affected areas.

"It's immediate, you don't have to go and knock on doors, you don't have to worry about whether or not the infrastructure has collapsed, because everybody's got a mobile phone nowadays," he says.

"

"It's definitely no panacea, it's no silver bullet, but I think it's an important part of the toolkit for communicating with people in disasters," says Mr Dalby.

It seems obvious where the adverts are on Google - and indeed, where they are not.
Search for "holiday" on Google and the top of the search results are clearly marked as "ads" - paid-for links sold by Google to companies eager to catch people's eyes.
Yet a study suggests that many people still do not spot ads on Google - and that they increasingly do not realise when other information on the search results page is advertising either.
The study, by researchers at Columbia University, in the US, is based on experiments involving more than 1,000 Google searches.
They reached their conclusions by comparing the results of experiments involving Google with identical experiments involving a simpler search engine they created, called MobiliSearch.
In the MobiliSearch experiments, they deliberately inserted ads where users might not expect them, in an attempt to assess whether participants noticed the ads at all.
And they found that users were much better at spotting ads on MobiliSearch than on Google - even when the ads were in the same place on the page.
The results were the same, even when participants were given money to spend on the ads, and were told that the top results were ads.
"We were surprised that people were failing to notice the ads on Google," said Dr. Aaron Brown, who helped carry out the research.
"But given how ubiquitous Google is in people's lives, it makes sense that people have come to trust the platform, and that they are less sceptical of the results they get.

"

Google gave this response when asked about the study: "This study was not peer-reviewed, and conclusions drawn by the researchers about Google Search are inaccurate.

"

The company did not respond to requests for more detail about which conclusions it thought were wrong.
The researchers said that it was not clear whether the participants in their experiments had been searching on smartphones or computers.
But they said that Google's search results pages were much the same on both devices.
Dr. Brown said that it was possible that on smartphones, which have smaller screens, users might be less able to spot where ads began and organic search results ended.
He also said it was possible that Google's algorithms pushed ads further down the page on smartphones, making them less visible.
Columbia University has made the results of its experiments - due to be presented at the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems in May - available on the university's website.

This is a little more complicated.
United's net spend over the past six years has actually been around £77m after sales of players.

United's revenue is believed to be closer to £620m per year, with around half of that money going to player wages and the rest spent on infrastructure and keeping the club running.

Star Wars Battlefront 2 review

It's the game Star Wars fans have been waiting for, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.
Star Wars Battlefront 2 has plenty of bugs and some confusing design decisions, but if you can look past those there's plenty here to love.
It's taken three years and a change of developer, but we finally have a proper successor to the original Star Wars Battlefront games.
They're online multiplayer shooters, but with a Star Wars skin.
The original Battlefront games were essentially Battlefield games in disguise, and that's still true here.
The highlight is definitely the multiplayer modes - preferably played with a friend.
The meat of the multiplayer is made up of three different modes - Galactic Assault, Starfighter Assault and Strike.
They're basically your standard team deathmatch, vehicle deathmatch and conquest modes, but with a Star Wars skin.
They're simple, but still pretty exhilarating, especially when playing as or against iconic Star Wars characters and vehicles.
The controls are fairly simple, but it takes a while to get used to the floaty cover system.
The lack of a proper single player campaign is still pretty baffling though, and the one included here doesn't even come close to filling that void.
The campaign is a series of battles against the Empire, essentially a prolonged tutorial.
It's not particularly engaging, but at least it's short - lasting around two hours.
Battlefront 2 has some frustrating design decisions, but it has heart.
It looks gorgeous, and sounds amazing, but a lack of content and some baffling design decisions hold it back.
The original Battlefront games had a seemingly endless number of modes, but this one feels sparse in comparison.
The lack of a single player campaign is also confusing, especially when the one included here is so lacklustre.
But if you can look past those issues there's still a lot of fun to be had - especially when playing as a Jedi.
Star Wars Battlefront 2 was released on November 17 for PS4, Xbox One and PC.
Our review is based on the PS4 version.

Microsoft is launching a new search engine that it says can scour a user's computer in seconds, as it takes on Google in the battle for search.

Beastie Boys win sampling battle

The hip-hop group have settled a long-running lawsuit over their album Paul's Boutique.
The settlement means artists will be able to sample portions of other artists' work without fear of legal action.
Lawyers for the group and the record label Capitol Records agreed to settle the lawsuit over the group's 1989 album.
The settlement pre-empts a decision on the issue of copyright law that could have had far-reaching effects on the music industry.
It comes after a significant setback for the band last year when a federal judge in New York ruled that their sampling of classic rock songs amounted to piracy.
The judge said that the group had sampled portions of Aerosmith, James Brown and Elvis Costello songs without permission.

The group, comprising Mike D, Adam Horovitz and Ad-Rock, cross-sampled portions of dozens of songs for their album Paul's Boutique, which was an critical and commercial failure on release, but subsequently achieved cult status.

The band and their record company, Capitol Records, brought the action against subsidiary label, Rhino Records, which released a series of best-selling compilation albums also featuring sampled portions of artists' work.
The label argued that as the samples were brief, and the songs fundamentally different, no permission was needed.
A lower court agreed, but last year a federal judge reversed that ruling, sending the issue to the Supreme Court - which agreed to hear the case.

That decision turned a relatively minor dispute into a potentially far-reaching case on the legality of sampling portions of other artists' work - an issue that has split the music industry, and could have resulted in a flood of lawsuits.
But on Thursday, lawyers for the group and Capitol Records said they had settled the lawsuit, and promised to work together to allow the group to licence samples for future works.
"The parties consider the matter closed," read a short statement.
"Knowing they can now licence samples without fear of litigation, hopefully that will open up the creativity again and people can get back to making music," said group lawyer Peter Ross.
"It's too early to tell what the impact of the decision will be, but it seems likely that it will establish legal guidelines in this area of law," he added.
Scott has made a solid start to his independent career with his first album not tied to a major label, but it's not enough to capture the imagination.
The singer-songwriter has long been a curious figure in British pop, a critically adored artist who struggled to match his early promise with commercial success.
His debut album, 2013's Drugs, earned him a loyal fanbase and a reputation as an exciting new talent unafraid to tackle difficult subject matter in his lyrics.
But his second album, 2019's Scott, barely made a dent in the charts and prompted a split from his label, Universal.
Now, independently released, the musician born Jonathan Scott makes his boldest move yet with a conceptual, genre-hopping third album.
The album was written and recorded entirely in Los Angeles, where Scott now lives after a stint in Paris trying to launch his career in France.

The move seems to have paid off, with the album showcasing a more refined, polished sound, with nods to hip-hop and R&B.

The opener, 'Who Is Scott?' sees him teaming up with Denzel Curry, who delivers a fiery rap verse, over a swirling, hypnotic beat.
'Desperate Times' is a soulful mid-tempo groove, with Scott's vocals taking centre stage.
'Low', a collaboration with Tion Wayne, has already been a hit single.
'Basement Girl' has a more experimental edge, with a glitchy beat and eerie electronic effects.
It's a bold move that doesn't always pay off.
'Dangerous Woman' sees Scott returning to his indie rock roots, with a pounding beat and swirling guitars.
It's a welcome change of pace.
Overall, the album is a solid effort from Scott, who manages to retain his signature sound while exploring new genres and collaborations.
However, it's hard not to feel that he is still trying to find his place in the music industry.
While this album is a step in the right direction, it's not enough to make him a household name.
Despite some impressive collaborations and a more refined sound, this album fails to capture the imagination.
It's a solid start, but Scott still has work to do to live up to his early promise.

Plans to create a "super union" for journalists in the UK have been touted as a way to tackle the growing power of tech giants like Google and Facebook, following the collapse of the industry's regulator.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents UK news media outlets, made the proposal to merge the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) and the Broadcasting, Entertainment, Communications and Theatre Union (BECTU) at the weekend.
The plan would create a union of more than 40,000 journalists, making it the largest journalists' union in the world and one of the biggest in the UK.

It comes after the collapse of the News Media Association's regulatory body, the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO), following the departure of a number of major publishers including the Guardian, the Financial Times and the Daily Mail.

IPSO's demise has led to calls for a new system of independent press regulation, with some arguing that the UK needs a "super regulator" to tackle the dominance of tech giants like Google and Facebook, which have been accused of using their dominance to exploit news publishers.
The NMA's proposal for a "super union" would give journalists more power in negotiations with publishers and help them fight for better wages and conditions.
It could also give journalists a stronger voice in the debate over press regulation and help them campaign for a new system that is independent of both the government and the industry.
The idea of a "super union" has been welcomed by some journalists, with one NUJ member saying it was a "great idea" that would give journalists "more clout".
However, others have expressed concern that it could lead to a dilution of the NUJ's core values and a loss of its unique identity.
The NUJ's general secretary, Michelle Stanistreet, said the union would "consider any proposal that enhances our ability to better defend journalists and our industry".
BECTU's general secretary, Gerry Morrissey, said the union would "engage in constructive discussions" with the NUJ about the proposal.
It is not clear how the plan would be funded or how the two unions would merge their operations.

The new system would award points for factors such as a person's age, education, language skills, and job prospects.
A minimum number of points would be required to qualify for a work visa.

He proposed a new fast-track visa scheme for qualified scientists and researchers, which would allow them to enter the UK more quickly and easily.

He said the government would introduce a new income threshold for foreign workers, which would be set at a level equivalent to the national average wage.
Philp's speech marks the first major immigration policy announcement by the Conservative government, which has previously been criticized for its immigration policies.
The new immigration system is expected to be in place by the end of 2020.

The former prime minister Tony Blair and the former home secretary David Blunkett have announced a plan to help people in Sheffield with the cost of living crisis.
The initiative will offer practical advice on how to cope with rising bills and will be based in the city's Castle Market.
The pair, both Labour MPs, made the announcement during a visit to the city.
During the trip, Mr Blair described the decision to leave the European Union as "a mistake".
Speaking to journalists during the visit, the former prime minister said he was "not sure" the Labour Party could win the next general election if the party remained divided on the issue of Brexit.
"Obviously it's up to the Labour Party to decide where it goes, but I think to be an effective opposition you've got to argue for change, you can't just oppose change," he said.
"People want an effective opposition, they want a government that can change things for the better, that makes a difference.

"

Mr Blair said that Labour risked "getting into a position where you're opposing change, without offering any alternative change".
Mr Blunkett said the party had to move on from the "binary" argument over leaving the EU.
"People voted clearly - 17.5 million people sent a clear message - but once you've had that vote, once the referendum takes place, democracy requires that you then move on," he said.
"You've got to accept that decision, but also recognise democracy doesn't stop, you've then got to argue for what you believe.

"

The project they announced in Sheffield will offer "practical" help to people in the city who are facing financial difficulties as a result of the rising cost of living.
The advice hub, which will be based in the city's Castle Market, will offer people information on benefits they are entitled to and will help them to access debt advice.

"It's really practical... getting people into training, getting people into work, helping them if they're in work to move into better jobs, but also showing them how to manage their money properly, " said Mr Blunkett.

Dr Reddy's, an Indian pharmaceutical company, has reported a fall in quarterly profits after being hit by inflation and changes to its business model.

The firm - which has recently faced scrutiny over its drugs for Covid - said it made a net profit of 5.45bn rupees ($68m; £53m) in the three months to 31 December, down from 10.69bn rupees a year earlier.

In addition to rising prices, Dr Reddy's is also in the process of moving away from a "pure trading" model, which involved buying and selling medicines, to a "portfolio of products" approach.
This process "resulted in a significant decline in revenues in the quarter", the company said.
However, it added that the long-term impact of these changes would be "positive".
In December, the company was among a number of Indian drugmakers to receive a warning from the US health regulator over a failure to comply with manufacturing standards.
The warning came after the company's application to sell its Covid-19 antibody drug, which it had developed with Russian scientists, was rejected by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

The value of the Irish stock market has reached an all-time high, despite economic sanctions against Russia.
The Irish Stock Exchange's (ISE) main index, the ISEQ 20, ended 0.5% higher on Friday at a record 14,596.42.
It means the index has gained more than 22% since the start of the year, outperforming many of its European peers.
Darren McKinley, head of equity sales with broker Goodbody, said it had been "a phenomenal year" for the Irish stock market.

"We've had few IPOs (initial public offerings), but the big drivers have been the M&A (mergers and acquisitions) and the overseas investors looking to access the growth stories in the US and the bigger European markets," he said.
"There has been about €12bn invested in the Irish market in the last year.

"

Mr McKinley said the ISE was a beneficiary of global investors looking to reduce their exposure to Russian assets.

"We haven't seen any specific Russian sanctions but global investors who might have had an exposure to Russia historically might well have sold Irish stocks as they don't want to be exposed to any potential future Russian fallout," he said.

"

Among the big gainers on the ISE on Friday were grocery chain Tesco, which rose 1.1% to €2.60, and food group Kerry, which ended the day 1% higher at €128.40.
Oil prices have jumped more than 3% after the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies agreed to maintain supply increases ahead of winter.
The decision avoided a collapse in oil prices as the group considered either cutting output or failing to increase it by an expected 400,000 barrels per day.
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures rose 3.5% to $53.24 a barrel.
Earlier in the day, prices jumped more than 5%.
Brent crude futures rose 3.3% to $58.39 a barrel.

The contract earlier increased by more than 6%.

OPEC and its allies, including Russia, agreed on Thursday to stick to their plan to increase output by 400,000 barrels a day in January.
The group, known as OPEC+, has been gradually easing its output cuts since August as it aims to support prices and help clear a supply glut that has built up during the pandemic.

However, many analysts had expected the group to either abandon the plan for a modest output increase or to announce a bigger hike to address concerns about the impact of the Omicron variant of coronavirus and the possibility of strained oil balances in the first quarter of 2022.
Daily infections in Europe have reached an all-time high and forced governments to consider new Covid-19 restrictions, which could reduce fuel demand.
The OPEC+ meeting on Thursday was originally scheduled to take place last week, but it was delayed as experts sought more data on the Omicron variant.
The White House welcomed the decision by OPEC+ to boost supply, with spokesman John Kirby saying it was "consistent" with President Joe Biden's effort to lower prices.
"Overall, this is a decision that should give consumers some confidence that they are going to see more oil supplied to the markets," he told reporters.
Mr Kirby said the White House would "continue to monitor the markets" and "has tools" it could use if prices rose too high.
In October, the White House said it was co-ordinating with other consumer nations to keep oil supplies available for global economic recovery.
Mr Biden announced in November that the US and other major economies would release 60 million barrels of oil from their reserves in an effort to reduce prices.
Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger described the club's new signing, Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain, as "a very talented player" with "lots of potential".
"He's a player who's a good athlete, who's versatile, who can play in lots of different positions," said the Frenchman.
"He's young, still only 20, he has lots of potential and he will be an important member of our squad.

"

Wenger revealed he tried to sign the midfielder last summer but lost out to the Saints.
"We lost out on him to Southampton last year when we tried to take him from Southampton and we were monitoring him during the season," he added.
"We're pleased to get him signed now."

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown has faced criticism for his decision to return to the UK £340,000 in expenses paid by UK taxpayers for his office in Washington.
The sum, which was originally intended to cover the costs of his office in the US for two years, was deemed excessive after an investigation by the UK's cabinet office.
Brown, who was prime minister from 2007 to 2010, has faced criticism in the past for his use of public funds.
He repaid £125,000 after an inquiry found he had used a helicopter for trips to his Scottish home.
The former Labour leader received the £340,000 in question to cover the costs of his office in Washington, where he now works as a special United Nations envoy on global education.
But the cabinet office has now concluded that £160,000 of the funding was not needed, and has ordered Brown to repay the money.
Brown has said he will not do so, citing that the money was spent on promoting UK interests and that the cabinet office had not complained at the time of the expenditure.
The former prime minister said that the government should be thanking him, not demanding more money back.

Brown's spokesman said: "It is astonishing that the government is seeking to make a issue of this when at the time the then cabinet secretary sought and gained approval for the spending of public money.

"No one in government at the time, or subsequently, has suggested or believed that there has been any wrongdoing, and the government's own independent investigation has not suggested any wrongdoing either.
"What has happened is that a former cabinet secretary has changed the rules retroactively in order to create a problem for the office of the former prime minister.

"

At the time, the then cabinet secretary, Sir Gus O'Donnell, had told Brown that the funding was essential for the former prime minister's work in the US, and that without it, he would not be able to promote UK interests.
Doves' fifth album, 'The Universal Want', has reached number one in the UK album charts.
It is the Manchester band's fourth album to reach number one in the UK. '
The Universal Want' achieved gold certification - for sales of more than 100,000 - in under four weeks.
Doves released their debut, 'Lost Souls', in April 2000.
The band went on hiatus in 2010 before announcing their reunion in 2018.
Last month, they played a sold-out gig at Manchester's Heaton Park.
Frontman Jimi Goodwin said he was "overwhelmed" by the reaction to the album and thanked their fans for their support.
"It's been a crazy couple of years, huh?" he said.
"Thank you so much to everyone who's listened to the album, bought it, streamed it, borrowed it, or stolen it.
"This album was always about the big picture, but when the world gets as crazy as it is right now, it seems so trivial.
"For us, it's always been about trying to write songs that make people feel hopeful.
It's strange timing, but we'll take it."
'The Universal Want' marks the band's first release since they went on hiatus in 2010.
It is also the first time in years that Doves have been able to tour and promote a new release properly.
In the week of the release, the band played an intimate set for BBC Radio 6 Music at Manchester's Castle Hotel.
They also appeared on other shows across the BBC, including the BBC News Channel and BBC Breakfast.
Keyboardist and guitarist Jez Williams said it was "nice" to see their hard work pay off by reaching number one.
"It's nice that hard work sometimes is rewarded and somebody appreciates what you do," he said.
"We work hard on the records, for sure, and it's nice when people appreciate that work.
"I think people have maybe reconnected with the fact that doing stuff together is quite a nice thing to do.
"We're very fortunate that we have got a fanbase that has stuck with us for a long time.
We're very grateful for that."
BMW is to recall more than 342,000 diesel cars in Europe to fix a technical problem which the German carmaker said also affects its petrol models.
The European Commission had urged BMW to act after the German road authority found that exhaust emissions were higher than certified in some models.
The manufacturer said it would install new software to reduce emissions.
The issue relates to a so-called "defeat device" used by the carmaker.
Such devices are banned by the EU.
BMW's recall comes after Volkswagen admitted in 2015 that it had installed "defeat devices" in 11 million diesel cars to make models appear cleaner in tests than they were on the road.
The German carmaker said the recall would affect vehicles in Europe featuring BMW's popular 2.0-litre diesel engine, which powers a range of models, including the 320d, 520d and X3.
BMW said it was not planning a recall in the UK, but said that the software update would be offered to customers who wanted it.
The company said in a statement: "BMW never manipulated nor cheated on emissions.
It is incorrect to claim that BMW manipulated emissions values.

"

The manufacturer said the problem related to how the engine and its operating software reacted to temperature changes.
It said this could lead to an increase in emissions of nitrogen oxides, a pollutant that contributes to acid rain and smog.
BMW said its recall was not linked to the "dieselgate" scandal that has embroiled Volkswagen and other carmakers.
The European Commission said on Tuesday that it was taking BMW to court for failing to give information about the so-called defeat devices.
The German road vehicle authority, the KBA, found in March that some BMW models emitted far more nitrogen oxides in road tests than they had in official tests.
The KBA has been scrutinising emissions more closely since Volkswagen's "dieselgate" scandal.
BMW said it would install new software to reduce emissions and would suggest that customers have their cars checked.
The money spent on Britain's new e-university could have been better spent on widening participation in higher education, according to the head of the country's largest university.

In one of his first major speeches as head of the University of Warwick, Professor Nigel Thrift said that the £136m spent on the e-university could have paid for 30,000 extra students to go through the university system.
"It is a disgraceful waste of money which could have been spent on widening participation," he said.
The e-university was announced in 1997 as part of the government's strategy for increasing the number of people with access to higher education.
It was intended to be a "virtual" university, without a campus, offering courses predominantly through the internet.
But the project has been hit by a series of problems and has been the subject of criticism from academics who said that it would not attract students because of the lack of face-to-face teaching.
Last month, the government's spending watchdog said that there was no clear business plan for the e-university and that value for money was not proven.
The university's board is due to meet later this month to consider its future.
Professor Thrift said that he did not believe that the e-university concept was "a bad idea in principle".
But he added: "It is clear that it was conceived 11 years ago and that the world has moved on.
"The sums of money involved, £100m of public money and £36m of private money, could and should have been spent on widening participation.

"

The University of Warwick, which has more than 12,000 students, received £121m in income last year.
Professor Thrift said that the university intended to increase its intake of students from Britain's poorest backgrounds by 25 per cent over the next five years.
Three-time Olympic champion Asbel Kiprop will face an in-form Jake Wightman in the 3,000m at the Great City Games in May.
The announcement of the fields for the event, which takes place in Manchester on 7 May, was slightly premature as Kiprop has yet to confirm participation.
However, the man who has won three Olympic titles - including successfully defending his 1,500m crown in Tokyo last year - is expected to confirm soon.

Kiprop, who turned 35 on Wednesday, will be up against a 25-year-old Wightman, who has already set the fastest indoor time in the world this year in the mile and last weekend broke the British record for 5km.

Another notable addition to the fields is triple jumper Tornike Kakhidze, who has been added to a strong men's long jump lineup that already included Olympic champion Miltiadis Tentoglou and Olympic bronze medallist Juan Miguel Echevarria.
Kakhidze, who finished fourth in Tokyo, has only recently returned to action after a car crash in January left him with multiple fractures.

There are also entries from 2020 Olympic finalists in the women's long jump, such as Serbia's Milica Gardašević and Canada's Christabel Nettey, as well as Olympic 400m bronze medallist Marileidy Paulino of Cuba in the 150m.

The women's 100m will see Daryll Neita, who finished fourth in the Olympics last year running into a -10.7m/s headwind, up against Arthur Cissé, who finished fifth in the 100m for Senegal in Tokyo.
Great City Games director Andy Brooks said he was "thrilled" with the entries.
"Every single person who watched the Olympics will have recognised the quality of those athletes, so to have them competing in Manchester is a massive boost," he said.
Russian energy giant Yukos has lost a court battle with Deutsche Bank over $600m of debts.
Moscow's Arbitration Court ruled that Yukos must pay the bank the principal debt plus interest accrued, minus any proceeds from the sale of two Yukos subsidiaries.
The decision leaves the door open for further litigation between the two companies.
Yukos had sought to have more than $2.5bn of its debt to Deutsche Bank written off, claiming the bank pressured it into bad loans.
The energy firm declared bankruptcy in August and its main production unit was subsequently taken over by state-owned rival Rosneft.
Yukos has been battling a $3.4bn tax bill presented by the Russian government, which it says is politically motivated.
The case has pitted Russia's largest company against the German bank and concerned loans made in 2003 and 2004.
Yukos had claimed the bank pressured it into bad loans by threatening to withdraw credit lines, and that the bank had acted in collusion with the tax authorities.
But the court said in its ruling there was "no evidence" of this.
However, it did say that Deutsche Bank was in part to blame for the debt, because it had approved the loans after having been informed of the tax disputes.
The ruling suggested the bank would have been within its rights not to grant the loans at all, given the potential tax risks.
But the court ruled that Yukos had failed to prove its case for writing off the debt, and ordered it to pay up.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said it welcomed the decision, and said it would continue to "vigorously" defend itself against Yukos' "unfounded claims".
Yukos said it would study the ruling before deciding on its response.

Celebrity Big Brother star Sylvester Stallone has been evicted from the house.
The American actor was voted out by his fellow housemates in Friday's live show.
The 69-year-old starred in films including the Rocky series and Rambo.
He was the second celebrity to leave the house after model Chloe Ayling was removed by her fellow contestants on Monday.

Hundreds of fans gathered outside the airport terminal to greet him after he landed on Friday night.
In the house, the other contestants had voted to evict him instead of actress Sally Morgan, who was also up for eviction.
The show's hosts, Emma Willis and Rylan Clark-Neal, announced the result live on Friday evening.
Willis said: "By a majority vote, Sly has left the Big Brother house.

Singapore's economy grew an estimated 8.1% in 2004, driven by the booming semiconductor industry and a rebound in tourism, the government said.
The announcement released by the Trade and Industry Ministry on Friday showed that the growth rate was higher than the government's initial forecast of 7.5%-8.5% made in February last year.
For 2005, the ministry forecast that the economy would grow 3% to 5%, down from an initial forecast of 5% to 7%.

"The growth momentum is expected to slow largely due to the high base of 2004 and the expected moderation in the global economy," the ministry said.

2005 growth will also be affected by the tightening of monetary policies by major economies, weakening consumer sentiment and the high value of the Singapore dollar, the ministry said.
The government said it would release detailed figures on the economy later this month.

There's nothing else quite like it on the market - no other device packs as much power as it does into such a small and affordable package.
It's not a laptop, but a desktop computer, albeit a very small one.
You can hook it up to a separate monitor, keyboard and mouse, and it connects to the internet in the same way as a normal desktop machine.
The Mac Mini comes with Apple's M2 processor, which is an upgrade on the M1 chip that powered the previous version.
It's a significant step up in performance, and helps the Mac Mini compete with cheaper PCs.
It is, however, the price that is the most impressive thing about the Mac Mini.
The model we tested costs $599 (£569), which is less than many PCs, and considerably less than most Macs.
The Mac Mini comes with a lot of power for the price.
Our test model had 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, which is double what it had in the previous version.
This is serious amounts of memory and storage for a computer of this price.
PCs at this price tend to have much less of both, which can be a serious issue because Windows PCs tend to slow down considerably as they get filled up with files.
The Mac Mini doesn't slow down at all, even when it's running a dozen apps at once.
Windows PCs at this price do not have this amount of RAM, and the cheaper models can therefore feel very slow.
The Mac Mini also comes with an Apple GPU (graphics processing unit), which means it's good for basic gaming and graphical tasks such as editing videos and photos.
