UK retailer Next is to slow the rate of new store openings and the launch of its international websites after weak Christmas sales.
It said difficult trading conditions meant it would no longer reach its target of 650 stores.
Next currently has 540 stores and generates more than half of its £4.2bn sales online.
The retailer said sales in the 54 days since Christmas had been "strong" but added that the trading environment in the UK "remains challenging".
"In this environment we believe it is prudent to slow the rate of new space growth in the short term, and are today simplifying our store opening plans for the next financial year," the company said.
"We will open approximately 25 new stores during this period, compared to our original plan of c. 35.

"We will continue to open larger stores in our larger cities, but in the medium term will focus on meeting our customers' needs through our existing store estate, as well as enhancing our online offer.

"

Next also said the launch of its German website, planned for February, would be delayed.

It said the slowdown in store openings and the hold-up in the German launch were both "purely a result of the board's desire to maintain our strong financial position and to protect our profit margins".
The group said its full-year profit forecast of £790m remained unchanged.
Shares in Next fell more than 8% in early trading on Thursday.
The update comes as retailers face challenging conditions on the High Street.
Last week, rival Marks & Spencer reported a 0.9% fall in like-for-like clothing and home sales in the 19 weeks to January 5.
However, M&S said its overall sales were up 3.1% in the same period, helped by growth in its food division.
In its update, Next said its total sales in the 54 days since Christmas had risen by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018.
Within that, online sales were up 13.7% but in-store sales were down 5.2%.
The company said its clearance sale had been more successful than last year, with sales up by more than a third compared with 2018.
"We are pleased with our performance over the Christmas period," Next said.

"Our online business delivered growth in excess of our expectations whilst store like-for-like sales were in line with our planning.

"

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has confirmed that it will rule on whether to ban the Greek sprinters Kostadinos Kenteris and Katerina Thanou for allegedly taking performance-enhancing drugs.
The announcement came after a two-day hearing in Paris.
The athletes have consistently denied the allegations.
If found guilty, the pair face potential bans of up to two years.
The hearing panel will present its findings on Monday.

The case against the athletes - who are ranked first and second in the world - was based on evidence given by former coach, Nikolaos Sakelliadis, who testified that he had injected the pair with insulin in October 2001.
The IAAF had considered the case in 2004 but decided there was not sufficient evidence to bring charges.
However, it reopened the case last year based on new information provided by Mr Sakelliadis.
The Greek Athletics Federation (SEGNA) has always maintained that the pair were innocent and has backed its athletes throughout the process.
Last month, SEGNA unsuccessfully tried to have the case against them thrown out on a legal technicality.
The federation claimed that the IAAF had not followed correct procedures in reopening the case but this was rejected by the hearing panel.
If found guilty, Kenteris - who won the 200m at the 2004 Olympics - and Thanou, who won the 100m at the same Games, could become the highest-profile athletes to be banned for drug abuse.

Leyton Orient moved out of the League Two relegation zone after a tense 1-0 win at Mansfield.
The O's had not won away from home in the league since the opening day of the season but took the lead when striker Harry Smith scored his first goal for the club in the 38th minute.
Chances were at a premium in a game short on quality, but Orient had the better of the few chances.
They could have doubled their lead but substitute Aaron Drinan's shot was cleared off the line by Mansfield's George Lapslie.
The Stags' best opportunity came in the final moments but Orient goalkeeper Sam Sargeant tipped Christy Pym's shot behind.
Mansfield, who had been unbeaten in six league games, remain eighth in the table while Orient move up to 19th.
Wal-Mart Stores Inc has agreed to pay $14m to survivors of a 2012 shooting in Colorado in which a man using an assault-style rifle killed three people and wounded nine.
The agreement between the retailer and survivors of the attack in the town of Aurora concludes a liability lawsuit against the US's largest retailer.
The lawsuit alleged that Wal-Mart violated state and federal laws by failing to properly secure its firearms inventory.
It also alleged that the retailer violated local laws by failing to warn police that the shooter had bought an AR-15 rifle and large quantity of ammunition just a few days earlier.
The gunman, who died in the attack, bought the rifle over the counter at a Wal-Mart store in Thornton, Colorado, on 15 December, 2012.
He killed two people when he opened fire at a crowded screening of a Batman film.
Nine others were wounded.

"While no amount of money can adequately compensate them for their injuries, we believe this settlement makes good on our promise to support them and honours the memory of those they lost," Wal-Mart said in a statement.
The company's shares rose 60 cents to $69.89 in New York Stock Exchange trading on Thursday.
HSBC has signed a deal to buy a minority stake in a South Korean bank, in a move that will grant the British bank access to one of Asia's most vibrant economies.

The London-based banking giant will purchase a 19.9% stake in KB Securities, South Korea's fastest-growing investment bank, for $637m.

Once the deal has been approved, the two banks will aim to launch a retail investment joint venture, according to HSBC.
KB Securities was formed through the integration of Korea's two biggest securities firms, Korea Investment Banking and KDB Daewoo Securities.
While HSBC has had a presence in South Korea since 1915, the Asian country represents just a small portion of the bank's overall revenue.
The British firm recorded $12.7bn in Asia profits in the first half of 2022, of which just $404m came from South Korea.
By gaining a foothold in KB Securities, HSBC will hope to grow its presence in South Korea's banking ecosystem, despite tougher pandemic restrictions being reimposed in the country this week.
At the end of last year, HSBC came under pressure from an activist investor to consider splitting its operations between the UK and Asia.

The British Retail Consortium (BRC) said that total sales increased by just 0.1% in September, compared with the same month last year.
It said that the slowdown in sales growth was "particularly notable" amid tough comparatives with September last year, when sales rose 0.8%.

However, the BRC said that food sales had performed well, with more people dining out.

The BRC's survey came as retailers reported a tough month with consumers cutting back on spending, though the unseasonably warm weather helped boost sales of outdoor items.

She added that the BRC was "hopeful" that the upcoming Christmas season would help lift sales.

However, this was slower than the 10.2% growth seen in August.
The BRC said that the slowdown in online sales growth was in line with retailers' efforts to rein in the cost of delivering goods to customers' homes.

The UK's election watchdog has said that Wednesday's election could be a target for extremists.
Concerns about possible interference in the election increased after the Manchester Arena bombing in 2017.
The Electoral Commission's statement came as MPs voted 502 to 20 to pass a law to try to ensure the election could go ahead.
In a statement, a Commission spokesperson said: "Whilst we have seen no evidence of specific threats to the electoral process, we are aware of the wider security context.

"In recent months the Commission has been working closely with parliamentary authorities and the police to identify and mitigate potential risks to the election, and to ensure that all stakeholders are fully prepared for the election."

Defending the election, Home Secretary Priti Patel said on Tuesday that the threat level in the UK is "severe", meaning an attack is "highly likely".
"But severe is not the same as critical.
It means we have the plans in place, we have the capabilities in place to keep people safe," she added.
The election, which was originally scheduled for 2020 but was postponed because of the pandemic, is taking place on Wednesday, December 12.
Polling stations will be open from 07:00 GMT until 22:00, giving voters more time to have their say.
A total of 39,364,239 people have registered to vote, an increase of around 700,000 on the 2019 figure.

Atlanta, Georgia's OutKast started out as two high school friends playing the fraternity circuit, but they quickly rose to the top of the hip-hop world, becoming one of the most successful groups in the history of popular music.
They scored with songs like Hey Ya!, the crossover hit Mrs. Jackson and the infectious R&B of Roses.
Now, as the duo of André 3000 and Big Boi prepare for what promises to be their swan song, they speak to John Wilson about their story and their influences.
It all began at Joseph Wheeler High School in the Atlanta neighbourhood of East Point.
André 3000 and Big Boi were both wide receivers on the school football team -

André 3000 was named after the NFL star running back, Walter Payton - and they first got together as a musical duo in 1992, dubbing themselves OutKast, a name chosen, Big Boi says, "because it sounded like we were from outer space, or like we were aliens or something".
They were soon making waves in the city's vibrant hip-hop scene, and in 1993 were signed by the influential Atlanta producer and rapper Mr DJ, who took the pair to his LaFace Records label.
Their debut album, Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik, released in 1994, introduced the world to the OutKast sound, a tantalising mix of funk, soul, rock and roll and hip-hop.
Big Boi's booming delivery and André 3000's distinctive, versatile style combined to make a fresh, innovative sound that immediately stood out from much of the gangsta rap popular at the time.
"We always try to experiment," says André 3000.
"That's what OutKast is about.
It's about being free and trying different things.

"

The duo's follow-up album, ATLiens, released in 1996, established them as stars, and Aquemini, released in 1998, pushed their innovative streak even further, with songs like Rosa Parks and Slump featuring unusual sounds and samples.
But it was their next album that would truly transform the duo into international stars.

Speakerboxxx/The Love Below, released in 2003, was an inventive, imaginative album that became a huge commercial success, in no small part due to the monster hit Hey Ya! which quickly became a staple of pop culture.

"Flee" director Jonas Poher Rasmussen accepted the prize from Taron Egerton and Sheila Johnson.

Team GB's world champion Emily Diamond and fellow Olympic medallist Laura Muir have been named in a 56-strong squad to compete in the European Cross Country Championships in Turin next month.
The British team, which also includes Alex Bell and Josh Kerr, will be bidding for success in the Italian city when the championships take place on 11 December.

Muir, who won the 5,000m and 1,500m at this summer's Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, will be looking to improve on her third place in the opening event of the 2022-23 Cross Challenge series in London on Saturday.

"It is never easy selecting a team for these championships as we had some exciting performances over the country this season," said British Athletics cross country and mountain running coach Chris Jones.
"But the selectors and I are confident that those selected will give their all for their country and we wish them every success in Turin."
The Soros group has warned that Central Asia's booming economy is in danger of collapsing.
The Open Society Institute, founded by billionaire George Soros, says Kazakhstan is particularly vulnerable.
It says the country is too dependent on oil and too much wealth is being concentrated in too few hands.
The report comes as Kazakhstan's leader asks Russia for help in dealing with the economic crisis.

After the meeting, Mr Nazarbayev said he had asked Mr Putin to "render assistance" to Kazakhstan during the current economic crisis.
It is not clear what form this help would take.
The Open Society Institute, in its report on the five former Soviet Central Asian states, said the region's combined GDP had grown by 7% in 2007.

The region was already suffering from a fall in revenue from its main export, oil, because of the drop in world prices, the report said.
It added that the situation had been made worse by the weakening of the Russian rouble, as the Russian market is the main export market for the region's goods.

Barclays and Absa have been in talks about a possible sale of the British bank's African business, but have yet to come to an agreement, both banks said on Monday.
The statement followed a weekend newspaper report that Barclays was in advanced talks to sell its 53 percent stake in Barclays Africa to Absa for more than $1bn.
"Barclays regularly reviews the strategic options for our business to ensure that we are maximising returns to our shareholders," the bank said in a statement.

"As part of this process, we can confirm that Barclays and Absa have been in discussion about a possible sale of our majority shareholding in Barclays Africa, but these discussions are at an early stage and may not lead to any transaction."

Barclays has been divesting operations that it does not regard as core to its business since Chief Executive Jes Staley took over in 2015.
The bank has sold its Egyptian business, and spun off its Barclaycard and investment banking businesses into separate entities, leaving it focused on Britain and Africa.
Barclays also sold its stake in Barclays Africa in March, reducing its holding to 53 percent from 62 percent, for total proceeds of $1.75bn.
The bank said in June that it would continue to reduce its presence in Africa, but added that it did not plan to sell its remaining stake in Barclays Africa.
Absa, which is controlled by South Africa's Barclays Africa, said in a separate statement that there were "no imminent transactions" relating to the group.
Barclays shares were up 1.5 percent at 269 pence at 0900 GMT, while Absa Group's were unchanged at 179 pence.
Police in India have arrested at least 44 people on suspicion of using a fake ID service to circumvent coronavirus lockdown restrictions.
Police in the capital, New Delhi, detained the men - who included a couple of MPs - during a raid on a flat.
The flat's landlord, who rented it out as an office space, has also been held.
India has imposed a stringent lockdown to curb the spread of the virus, which has killed at least 357 people and infected nearly 17,000.
But the restrictions have unleashed a wave of desperate migrants trying to return to their home states.
With factories and businesses shut, millions have been left without work.
Many have walked or cycled from New Delhi - which is in the middle of the country - to their home states in the north and east.
At least eight people were killed on Tuesday when a truck ran over migrants as they slept on a highway in the state of Maharashtra.
The men arrested on Wednesday are suspected of using the fake service to move between states.
They were held after police received a tip-off about a website offering the service for thousands of rupees.
Officials said those using the service went to the flat, provided their personal details and pictures, and were provided with fake ID cards, bearing the name of a legitimate company.
Police have launched an investigation into the website and are trying to track those who paid for the service.
They are also trying to figure out how many people used the service and where they went.
"We will take action against these people for endangering public safety and spreading the virus," said Delhi police commissioner S N Shrivastava.
Microsoft has launched a search engine, Bing, in an attempt to challenge the dominance of Google.
The world's biggest software company hopes Bing, which has a £100m ($156m) marketing budget, will appeal to users who feel overwhelmed by the complexity of existing search technologies.
Bing has a simple interface with a background image that changes each day.
It also provides links to other Microsoft services and content from its partners.
Speaking at the launch in San Francisco, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer said: "We're launching Bing because we believe we can do better."
He added that the company had "invested in a deep technology stack" and promised a "decision engine" that would "deliver a relevant experience".
Mr. Ballmer said Microsoft had "no interest in doing a me-too search engine".
Bing's "decision engine" is designed to give more background information to help people make informed choices.
For example, if you search for a particular camera, Bing will list the item but also provide expert reviews and links to online shops where it can be bought.
It will also offer related searches - asking if users want cameras from other manufacturers, for example.
In addition, images are more prominent in Bing - the service displays photos from Flickr and Picasa, with links to the image owners.
Bing also aims to make it easier for people to search within websites.
At present, most search engines index only a few pages of a site.
Bing will have a feature called Deep Links, which will allow it to search within all the pages of a site.
Microsoft says it has signed up Amazon, eBay, Facebook and YouTube to participate.

Russian oil giant Yukos has asked a court to halt the sale of its main production unit, Yukos Oil Company.
The move comes after the company was denied an extension to a deadline to find a $10.8bn (£6.7bn) loan instalment.
Yukos was placed in bankruptcy administration last month after it failed to come up with the money.
The company has been plagued by legal troubles and is fighting numerous tax claims.
Last week, a court rejected Yukos's appeal to be given more time to find the money.
On Monday, the company asked the Moscow Commercial Court to halt the sale of Yukos Oil until it could hear the appeal.
If the sale does go ahead, Russian state oil firm Rosneft is widely expected to be the highest bidder.
Last week, Yukos received two offers for the oil company, but both were lower than the starting price of $8.8bn.
The offers came from Romania's Petrom and Russia's Sibneft, owned by Roman Abramovich.
The bodies, known as quangos, are accused of lacking transparency and accountability.
The government's quango watchdog, the Quango Commission, is to launch an attack on the "culture of secrecy" in some of the 1,000 public bodies.
Cabinet Office minister Francis Maude will demand that all quangos justify their existence.
The Tory MP said: "The age of the quango is over.

"

The coalition is examining all arms-length bodies, which cost £80bn to run every year.
The review could result in major reforms, with some institutions abolished and others have their powers transferred to ministers.
The Daily Telegraph has found that more than 200 quangos do not even have a website, making it impossible to find out who sits on their boards or how much they spend.
In addition, more than 150 do not publish their board members' attendance records - with some having not met for years.
More than 130 do not publish the salaries of their senior staff - with one boss reportedly earning £170,000 a year.
And more than 50 do not even publish their phone number or email address - including the Heritage Lottery Fund, which gives out £800m a year.
Some of the nation's biggest quangos, including the BBC, Channel 4 and the Arts Council, are exempt from the scrutiny.
The Quango Commission's attack on the "culture of secrecy" will be included in a report on the future of arm's-length bodies, which will be published next week.

It will also say that all quangos should have "a clear plan" for exiting government within a "reasonable" period of time.

Tim Henman and Andy Murray have been honoured by the Lawn Tennis Association after being voted as the top professionals in British tennis history.
Henman won the men's award ahead of Murray, who has won the award for the past two years, and Fred Perry.
Murray's mother Judy won the contribution award, while Leon Smith's coaching team took the team of the year award after guiding Britain's Fed Cup team to victory in April.
The LTA's annual awards, which were voted on by members of the association's council, were announced at a dinner in London on Friday.
Henman won 11 ATP titles and reached four Wimbledon semi-finals during his career before retiring last year.
"It's a great honour," the 37-year-old told BBC Sport.
"It's nice to be recognised by your peers, the people you have been competing against, and I'm very proud to be receiving an award like this."
Henman began working with the LTA last year in a part-time role as a talent identification adviser.
And he hopes to continue his involvement in British tennis following the recent appointment of new performance director Simon Timson.
"I'd like to think I can continue to make a contribution in some shape or form," added Henman.
"I've really enjoyed the work I've done with the LTA so far and I look forward to speaking to Simon about how I can help moving forward."
Murray, who won the men's award in 2011 and 2012, paid tribute to Henman, saying: "Tim had a fantastic career and was a great player.
"When I was growing up, he was the British player who was closest to winning one of the Slams and it's an honour to receive an award that he has previously won.

"

The 25-year-old Scot is currently training in Miami ahead of the defence of his Miami Masters title which begins on 31 March.
"I've had a good few weeks on the practice court and I'm looking forward to getting back into competition," said Murray.
"I've worked hard over the winter and I'm ready to get the season underway."

It is a rivalry which, despite the proximity of the two clubs, has not always been the most intense.
But in recent years, as both have competed in the Premier League and contested an FA Cup semi-final, tensions have risen.

It took the form of a "wrestling carnival", with athletes from the two clubs competing in a series of wrestling bouts, in front of a crowd of around 3,000 at Blackburn's Ewood Park.
The event was designed to raise money for local charities and the winners received silver cups donated by the Mayor of Blackburn, councillor WR Smith.

Former Prime Minister Sir John Major has accused Cherie Blair of launching a "vicious" attack on the Queen and US President George W Bush during the run-up to the Iraq war.
The accusation was revealed in Sir John's autobiography, due to be published on Thursday.
In it, he writes that the then prime minister Tony Blair's wife accused Mr Bush of "bullying" her husband ahead of the 2003 invasion.
And in a television interview to be broadcast on Thursday, Sir John says Mrs Blair accused the Queen of being "weak" for not standing up to President Bush.

Sir John writes that at a dinner party at Downing Street in February 2003, Mrs Blair - who was highly critical of the Iraq war - launched into a "long tirade" against the president, according to the Daily Mail, which obtained a copy of the book.
"For the first time in my life I saw Tony genuinely lose his temper," Sir John writes.
"It was startling and rather shocking to see.

"

The former Tory leader says Mr Blair rounded on his wife and told her: "For once in your life, keep your mouth shut.

"

Sir John says in the book that Mrs Blair "did not take kindly" to this rebuke, according to the Daily Mail.

And in the television interview with the BBC's Political Editor Nick Robinson, Sir John says Mrs Blair had also launched a "vicious" attack on the Queen - whom she accused of being "weak" in the face of President Bush.
"I was present in Downing Street when Cherie Blair launched a very vicious attack on the Queen, claiming that the Queen was weak," Sir John says.
"And when Tony challenged her, she turned on him...
I was standing astonished, I'd never seen anything like it in my life.

"

A spokesperson for Mrs Blair said: "This is fiction.
It never happened.

"

A spokesperson for Mr Blair said: "Tony Blair and John Major are friends and have always got on well and continue to do so.

and he's got nothing but respect for him as a person and a politician - but John's got a problem with New Labour and he's never really tried to hide that.
The head of Lloyd's of London has criticised a UK financial regulator for "over-regulation" of the city's insurance market.
In a speech, Richard Ward said the Financial Services Authority (FSA) had "lost its way" and that regulation had "gone too far".
Mr Ward said the cost of compliance with the FSA's rules was a burden, especially for small firms.
The City of London Corporation, which promotes the financial services industry, said Mr Ward's comments reflected "the concerns of the whole sector".

In his speech to the Lloyd's insurance market, Mr Ward, the chairman of Lloyd's, said there was a "growing sense that the FSA has lost its way, that regulation has gone too far and that the cost of compliance is becoming disproportionate to the benefits delivered".
"Over-regulation threatens to stifle the entrepreneurial spirit on which this market's success has been built," he added.
Mr Ward said that the cost of compliance with the FSA's rules was affecting Lloyd's small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which made up 80% of the market.
"This impact is particularly hard on the SMEs that form the backbone of our market... it is these companies that are most affected by over-regulation," he said.
"While the FSA's objectives are broadly right, its implementation is too often overly complex, burdensome and ineffective," he added.
A spokesman for the FSA said: "We are determined to reduce the burden on firms, particularly smaller ones, and we have already made substantial progress in this area.
"We will continue to focus on this in the months ahead and take on board the views of a wide range of firms," he added.
Mr Ward's speech comes after City minister Mark Hoban said in November that the government would conduct a "fundamental" review of financial regulation.
The review will consider whether regulation is "effective and proportionate", and assess its impact on competition and growth in the financial sector.
In a statement, the City of London Corporation said Mr Ward's comments reflected "the concerns of the whole sector about the level of regulation".
"The chairman...
[has] highlighted the need for proportionate regulation which supports market confidence without stifling innovation and growth," it added.

Japanese forward Daizen Maeda had opened the scoring with a first-time finish early on and Jota tapped in the fourth goal moments after coming on as a substitute.
Christie had hit the post early on but the Celtic midfielder made sure the hosts went in at the interval ahead when he fired beyond Danny Lennon's right hand from the edge of the box.

The former Aberdeen man produced a moment of magic to kill the game off with 20 minutes remaining, gathering possession deep in his own half before embarking on a mazy run that ended with a drilled shot beyond Brett Nixon.
Jota added further gloss to the scoreline with eight minutes left, the on-loan Benfica attacker tucking away a rebound after Nixon had done well to push away a shot from Liel Abada.

Ukrainian steel producers have been told to stop the illegal sale of steel products in Russia, by the country's prime minister.
Mykhailo Fridtyshyn said the metal was being sold "under the guise of humanitarian supplies".
He added that the steel was instead being used to rebuild infrastructure in Russian-occupied Crimea.
Crimea's Russian-backed government later said it would block the export of metal products from the region.
Since Russia's annexation of Crimea in March, Ukrainian steel producers have been selling their products at a discounted price.
Mr Fridtyshyn said the state budget had lost more than $500m (£300m) because of the "unlawful" trade across the Kerch strait between Crimea and Russia.
"We consider this illegal scheme of metal exports to Russia as a threat to Ukraine's security and budget," he said.
"Metal is sold under the guise of humanitarian supplies and then is used to rebuild the infrastructure in the temporarily occupied Crimea."
Mr Fridtyshyn also said that the Ukrainian government had asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate the illegal trade.
He said the court had confirmed that it would examine the case.
What's the solution?
To tackle the problem, Ukraine has decided to allow the export of steel and steel products only through ports in Ukraine-controlled territory.
Mr Fridtyshyn said that all other ports were now blocked for metal exports.
In a separate statement, the prime minister also called for an investigation into allegations of corruption in the metal trade.
Are there any counter arguments?
There has been no official response from the Russian side.
However, Crimea's deputy prime minister, Ruslan Balbek, later said that the region would also block the export of metal products from Crimea.
He said on social media that the move would prevent "uncontrolled price rises" and that the decision had been taken "to protect the people of Crimea".
What are the implications?
The statement by the Ukrainian prime minister is the first official acknowledgement of the large-scale export of steel products from Ukraine to Russia.
Previous statements by Ukrainian politicians referred only to the export of metal via the Kerch strait.
Metal producers in Ukraine have denied any wrongdoing.
They say the cheap metal is sold to Russian companies which then sell it on at market prices, making a profit.
Therefore, they say, the scheme is not losing money for Ukraine.

Iranian authorities have arrested and sentenced a prominent feminist blogger to more than a decade in prison on charges of harming the country's "cultural heritage" through her social media posts.
The reformist news website Kalame reported that Nazanin Serajeddini, better known as Nazanin Satrapi, was sentenced to 14 years in prison.
Ms Serajeddini had been detained since October 2021.
She is best known for her blog Girl in Red which she used to advocate for women's rights and against sexual harassment.
Her blog and posts on social media were highly critical of the Islamic Republic establishment and she supported the large protests that rocked Iran in 2017-18.
Ms Serajeddini, 39, faced a charge of "publishing obscene content" - a crime under Iran's cyber-crimes law - and three counts of "insulting Islamic sanctities" through her online work.
The blogger had also been vocal about the country's handling of the coronavirus pandemic.
Her mother, Fatemeh Satrapi, told the BBC's Service Persian that the blogger had been denied medical help for acute leukaemia during her time in detention.
Ms Satrapi said her daughter's prison sentence could be appealed against within 20 days.
Human rights activists have accused the Iranian government of using controversial cyber-crime laws to stifle dissent online.
Iran has been ranked among the top 10 prisons for women in the world, according to a report published in September by the London-based rights group Article 19.
UK house prices have risen slightly, according to a survey by lender Halifax.
The average cost of a home was up by 1.3% in November, marking the fourth consecutive month of growth.
However, prices are still 7.4% below their level a year earlier, before the stamp duty holiday prompted a surge in demand.
"It remains true to say that the housing market has now weathered the storm of the pandemic," said Russell Galley, managing director of Halifax.
The stamp duty holiday, which ended on 30 September, helped to boost property prices as buyers rushed to complete before the deadline.
Since then, the market has cooled slightly, but builders' merchants have reported healthy demand from homeowners opting to improve rather than move.
According to Halifax, November's rise took the average UK house price to £272,992.
That was up from £268,285 in October, but still below the £297,546 recorded in November 2020.
Mr Galley said that prices were now rising at a pace of 0.8% per month, which was "similar" to the average rate since 2015.
He added: "With opportunities for overseas travel restricted last year, it is no surprise that demand for bigger homes has risen sharply as more people work from home and seek more space."
However, he said that it was still too early to assess the impact of the new Omicron variant on the housing market.

"New housing market activity and price growth is likely to be more subdued in the coming months as inflationary pressures bite, and with the Bank of England predicted to raise interest rates next year, higher borrowing costs will also exert a cooling influence," he added.
Former Germany striker Jurgen Klinsmann has warned goalkeeper Jens Lehmann he risks becoming "the fall guy" if the national team's defensive problems do not improve.
Lehmann, 34, has been dropped by Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger but Germany boss Joachim Loew has kept faith with the keeper.
"Everybody is talking about our weaknesses in defence but nobody is talking about the goalkeeper -
he's the last man who can help," said Klinsmann.

"Lehmann is a great goalkeeper but if the defence is not doing their job then the goalkeeper becomes the fall guy."

The Germany squad gathered in Munich on Sunday ahead of their final Euro 2008 warm-up against Latvia on Wednesday.
Team director Franz Beckenbauer said he was confident the defending champions would improve as the tournament progressed.
"We have a good team and we know we have to get better match by match," he said.
"We have two difficult games against the Netherlands and Italy but we are confident for our group."
Germany open their Euro 2008 campaign against Croatia in Salzburg on 8 June.
And they will be without suspended midfielder Torsten Frings for that game after he picked up a yellow card in Germany's 2-2 warm-up draw with Hungary last weekend.
There has been no official announcement but it is expected that either Marcell Jansen or Sebastian Kehl will take Frings' place in the squad.
A "post-Christmas lull" in lending to British businesses has been described by a paint and varnish maker.
The managing director of Durham-based HMG Paints said he had applied for a £1m loan, but had been offered less than a quarter of that amount.
John Falder said the "lack of enthusiasm" from lenders left him worried about the health of the economy.
He said he had been told his firm's projections were "too optimistic".
It comes as official figures showed a sharp fall in approved lending to small and medium-sized firms.
According to the Bank of England, net lending rose by just £131m in November, the weakest growth since March.
The BBC has contacted the British Business Bank for comment.
Mr Falder said he had wanted to borrow £1m to invest in new technology, but that he had been offered less than £250,000 by his bank.
"I phoned up our bank manager and said 'what's going on?'
and he said 'oh, it's that time of year - it's a post-Christmas lull'," he said.
"I said 'look, can you lend us some money?'
and he said he'd see what he could do, and he went away and he actually came back and offered us less than a quarter of what we wanted.
"That does worry me in terms of the health of the economy… the fact that the banks aren't really enthusiastic at the moment about lending.

"

"I think they're being very, very cautious - they've been burnt with the property market, with Brexit and other things, and they're just holding back," added Mr Falder, who has run HMG Paints since 1987.
Figures from the Bank of England showed that net lending to small and medium-sized businesses rose to £131m in November from £1.38bn in October.
City analysts had expected a fall to about £1bn, but lending has been weaker than expected since the summer.
The Bank of England said that a slowdown in mortgage lending, as interest rates rose, had been offset by stronger consumer credit.
The annual growth rate of consumer credit, including credit cards and personal loans, rose to 10.4% in November from 9.7% in October, its highest since March 2016.
The Forum of Private Business said that the lending figures were "disappointing"
The European Central Bank has held its main interest rate at a record low to support the eurozone's post-pandemic recovery, despite inflation reaching a record high.
The ECB's governing council left the rate on its main refinancing operations at 0%, while the rate on its marginal lending facility remained at 0.25%.
The ECB also said it would accelerate its bond purchases under its 1.85 trillion euro ($2.1 trillion) pandemic emergency purchase programme (Pepp).
The moves came as inflation in the eurozone hit a record high of 5% in December, well ahead of the ECB's 2% target.
The central bank had already said it expected inflation to be higher for longer and that it would keep rates at their current, or lower levels until it saw inflation reaching 2% consistently.
Portugal's central bank chief, Mario Centeno, who is also the ECB's governor, said: "We are witnessing a phenomenon that is not a generalised inflationary spiral in the euro area.

"

He said that the ECB did not want to "surprise" markets by changing its policy stance prematurely and that any exit from its current policies would be gradual.
The Pepp is due to run until March, but the ECB has said it would assess whether its duration should be extended in light of the continued uncertainty over the outlook for the economy.
It has also said it would create a new tool to cope with government bond yields that "deviate substantially, and persistently" from their levels seen before the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
The ECB's move came on the same day as the US Federal Reserve increased its key interest rate by 0.25% to a target range of 4.5% to 4.75%, its highest level since 2007.
In the UK, the Bank of England also increased interest rates, raising them to 4% from 3.5%, their highest level in over a decade.

Sport betting rules in spotlight after Arsenal advance in Africa

Football's rule makers are to examine the situation around sports betting after criticism of the way gambling companies are tapping into the African market.
Arsenal's advance in the Champions League against PSV Eindhoven on Wednesday is the latest example of clubs and players being used in the marketing of betting firms.
The English Premier League club's shirt bore the logo of betting company SportPesa during their 2-0 win over the Dutch side.
And photographs of the match highlighted the presence of other operators' branding on advertising boards around the stadium in Eindhoven.
The issue has been highlighted by BBC Sport's football expert, Guillem Balague, who was commentating on the game for TV audiences in Africa.
Now, the sport's rule-making body, IFAB, has said it will "carefully review" the issue.
"Football and gambling companies operate in a symbiotic relationship," said IFAB, which is responsible for the laws of the game.
"Betting companies are increasingly using the profile of players and clubs to promote their products and to maximise their profits.
"In turn, football relies on income from these companies to further develop the game.
"The increasing presence of gambling companies in football brings its own risks, with concerns over the potential impact on fans and the game itself.

"

IFAB, which is composed of representatives from FIFA and the four British home football associations, said it had received three proposals to change the laws of the game relating to gambling.
But it said it did not currently plan to make any changes because of the "sensitivities and complexities of this matter".
Arsenal declined to comment on the issue when contacted by the BBC, while SportPesa did not immediately respond to an inquiry.
The BBC has launched its 'Focus on Africa' season, highlighting the issues that matter most to the continent.
For the next month, BBC News Africa will be showcasing the best journalists from the BBC and its partner networks across Africa.
It is the first time the BBC has devoted an entire month to news coverage from Africa.
A large proportion of the African population are young - more than 60% are under the age of 25.

England centre Emily Scarratt will lead out the Lions in Saturday's Women's Six Nations clash with Scotland at Murrayfield.

"

Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has called for the introduction of goal-line technology in the Premier League after Liverpool scored an injury-time winner against Everton from a clearly offside position.

Referee Anthony Taylor and his assistant on the near side were wrong to allow Mohamed Salah's 92nd-minute strike to stand, with the Egyptian forward inches offside as the ball was played forward by Trent Alexander-Arnold.
Title rivals Manchester City had beaten Southampton 6-1 earlier on Saturday to reduce the gap at the top to four points with one game remaining.

City have arguably been the biggest beneficiaries of contentious offside decisions this season, with their title victory last term aided by a number of key goals that have since been deemed to be offside.

That proved to be the decisive moment in the encounter, with City going on to win the game on the night and the tie overall to book a semi-final meeting with Paris St-Germain.

MP3 players are proving increasingly popular in the US, where more than 19 million have been sold, industry figures show.
The count, by the NPD Group consulting firm, includes not only portable music devices, but also MP3-capable cellular phones and iPod alternatives.
Some 11.8 million of the products sold were iPod derivatives, but units sold for MP3-capable phones number more than seven million, NPD said.
The most popular MP3 phone is Samsung's SCH-A990, which retails for $150 ($230 with camera) after a service contract with Cingular.
Some 58 million songs were downloaded legally in the US during the first half of 2005, more than double the amount downloaded during the same period of 2004, according to Nielsen SoundScan.
In contrast, some 95 million songs were downloaded illegally during the first half of 2005, according to BigChampagne, a media measurement firm.
iPods dominate the market for portable music devices in the US, but they face growing competition from phones that play music and cheaper devices that play MP3 files.
Apple sold more than 22 million iPods during the 2004 holiday season, but analysts say the device's sales are down as competitors enter the market.
The iPod's share of the portable music player market in the US has fallen to 73 percent from more than 90 percent during the 2004 holiday season, according to NPD.
Tech giants including Google and Amazon have welcomed "significant improvements" in a review of the body overseeing the web's domain name system.
The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers' (Icann) new chief executive took over in March amid concerns about its transparency and accountability.
In a blog post, Icann said it was seeking comments on an initial plan for a "significant overhaul" of its governance.
"We are seeking to make substantial changes to virtually all aspects of Icann's structures, policies, and procedures," it said.
The overhaul includes the creation of an "independent accountability mechanism" to handle complaints about the body, as well as term limits for board members.
Icann also plans to increase the diversity of its leadership, including reaching out to parts of the world that are currently under-represented, such as Africa.

In a joint statement, Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Yahoo welcomed the progress, and said the next step should be to establish a "stable funding source" to ensure the long-term sustainability of Icann.

"To foster the kind of predictable, stable, and broadly supported funding source that Icann needs, we urge the US government to work with Icann, and the broader internet community, to determine the best method for unleashing the kind of funding that will support Icann's mission for the long term," they said.
Icann is currently largely funded by registration fees for web domain names, but has warned that this model is becoming unsustainable.
The tech firms also urged Icann to modernise its "outdated" bylaws, and said any new mechanisms should be "simple, clear, and easy for all stakeholders to participate in".
Icann is responsible for managing the web's address system, and has faced criticism in recent years about its handling of online piracy and the rise of malicious websites.

Ukraine revisits state sell-offs

Ukraine's government is to sell off more state-owned enterprises as it seeks to raise money to tackle its debt mountain.
Prime Minister Volodymyr Groysman announced the new programme as he presented his government's programme for 2017 in parliament.
There are around 3,500 state-owned companies in Ukraine.
Previous efforts to sell them off have often been hampered by corruption.
Mr Groysman said the government would sell "at least" 100 of the companies this year.
They include aircraft maker Antonov and the state's stake in Ukraine's largest bank, Privatbank.
The prime minister said money raised from the sales would help reduce the country's debt, which amounts to about 80% of its GDP.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has demanded that Ukraine tackles its debt problem as a condition for continuing its $17.5bn (£12.7bn) loan programme.
Last year, the government raised $370m through sales of state enterprises, including Ukraine's largest steelmaker, Kryvorizhstal.
But Transparency International said the process was undermined by "systematic abuses", including companies being sold at below market value and to "unknown beneficiaries".
Lenovo's parent company Legend Holdings has reported a 97% drop in annual profit, causing it to miss its forecast.
The company said it had been hit by a "severe and complex" supply chain crisis, although the PC maker Lenovo had seen strong recovery.
Legend Holdings' profit was $98m (£82m), compared with $1.55bn the previous year.
The company had predicted a profit of $206m before paying dividends.
It said Lenovo's sales had been affected by a lack of components for PCs, as well as Covid-19 related lockdowns in China.

"The profitability of Lenovo was adversely affected by the substantial price increases of certain components stemming from the supply chain crisis and the depreciation of the Russian rouble," Legend said in its statement.

"Lenovo's operations in Russia and Ukraine accounted for approximately 2.5% of its revenue in the first half of 2022, and the company does not expect the situation to have a material impact on its full-year results," it added.
Despite the impact of the supply chain crisis on its parent company, Lenovo reported in August that its own sales had risen by 20% in the same period.
It said it had seen strong demand for its PCs due to coronavirus lockdowns which kept people at home and using digital devices.
This increased demand was during a time when other PC makers such as Apple struggled to meet targets due to supply chain issues.
Apple issued a warning over its sales targets in October, citing the impact of the pandemic and the war in Ukraine on its supply chain.
Last week, research firm IDC reported that Lenovo remained the world's largest PC maker in the third quarter, with a 24.2% market share, ahead of HP with 22.8% and Dell with 17.4%.
The UK's biggest civil service union will begin balloting members on strike action later this month.
The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union said tens of thousands of civil servants could walk out in March over a pay dispute.
It said it would launch the ballot on 24 January.
The PCS has urged its members to back a strike in protest at a below-inflation pay rise offered by the government.
The ballot will close on 17 February.
The first possible strike action would be on 1 March.
Civil servants at departments including Border Force, the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), and HMRC, as well as courts and job centres, could strike.
The PCS balloted members on strike action last year but the vote did not achieve the threshold needed by law for action to go ahead.
Union bosses said this time they were "confident" of reaching the threshold.
The government has so far made no offer to improve on its pay rise proposal.
A government spokesperson said ministers had "already put forward a fair pay offer" despite the cost of living challenges".
Disney has agreed to pay $2.8m to settle charges it misled investors about the size of its streaming subscriber base.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Disney distributed inaccurate information about its subscribers to investors.
The SEC said Disney distributed inaccurate information about the number of subscribers it had for its Disney+ streaming service shortly after its launch.
Disney had stated that it had more than 100 million subscribers when it only had approximately 26 million, according to the SEC.
Disney+ launched in November 2019 and the SEC said Disney knew its subscriber numbers were not as high as it was telling investors.
The settlement with the SEC does not mean the company has admitted to any wrongdoing.
Disney has not issued a comment on the settlement.
The SEC said its enforcement division found that Disney distributed inaccurate subscriber data in SEC filings and earnings releases between February 2021 and May 2021.
Disney+ launched in November 2019 and in early 2020 Disney told investors that its rollout had been highly successful, with nearly 34 million subscribers signed up.
The SEC said Disney knew its subscriber numbers after taking into account those who had received free promotional subscriptions were not as high as it was telling investors.
The regulator said Disney's filings inaccurately claimed that it had over 100 million total paid subscribers across its streaming services, when in fact it only had approximately 96 million.

The SEC said in a statement: "Disney misled investors by mistakenly including Disney+ Free Trial subscribers in its total subscriber count, when in fact Disney+ Free Trial subscribers do not provide Disney with any direct financial benefit, and were not counted as paid subscribers or as part of the total subscriber count pursuant to Disney's publicly-represented accounting policy.

"Disney's incorrect disclosures about the pace of Disney+ subscriber growth resulted from poor execution of a shift to a new subscriber reporting methodology, and not from any malicious intent or attempt to deceive investors.

"

Disney has recently been boosting its subscriber numbers through acquisitions such as its $73bn purchase of the bulk of 21st Century Fox in 2019.
It also owns cable sports network ESPN and recently launched a subscription based sports streaming service.

Oil prices have recovered after an unexpected build-up of US inventories slowed momentum on Monday.

The rebound came after unseasonably cold weather in the US and Britain kept buyers wary.

" Surprisingly large increases" in US fuel stocks driven by higher oil production and reduced demand kept prices down, said Commerzbank analyst Carsten Fritsch.
Despite the fluctuations, analysts said oil markets were generally supplied and there were no significant shortages.
Overnight, US crude oil inventories rose by 2.6 million barrels to 448 million, according to industry group the American Petroleum Institute (API).
Official data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) is due later on Wednesday.

Earlier this year, oil prices surged as investors worried that Russia would invade Ukraine.
The price of Brent crude climbed to more than $96 a barrel in the first week of February, up from about $70 a year earlier.
Mr Fritsch said that, for now, oil prices were unlikely to rise significantly higher, with Brent expected to average $90 a barrel this year.
"The market has already more or less priced in the threat to Ukraine, whereby the talks on Wednesday evening between Biden and Putin have calmed things down a bit," he added.

Former WorldCom chief Bernie Ebbers was aware that his company was engaging in fraudulent accounting practices prior to its collapse, according to testimony on Thursday from a former executive.

Ronald Beaumont, a Canadian who was vice-chairman of WorldCom, said that Mr Ebbers directed accounting staff to engage in fraudulent activity, such as moving normal operating expenses off the company's books.
"Bernie was aware of all the accounting shenanigans that were going on," Mr Beaumont told a court in New York.
Mr Beaumont was giving evidence in the trial of former WorldCom chief executive Bernie Ebbers, who has pleaded not guilty to fraud, conspiracy and filing false documents with regulators.
At the time of its collapse, WorldCom was the largest bankruptcy in US history, with debts of $107bn (£66bn).

Mr Beaumont, who has already pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit fraud for his own role in the WorldCom scandal, testified that Mr Ebbers directed the fraudulent accounting between 1999 and 2001, and was "very much aware" of it.
He said that Mr Ebbers instructed him to hire more staff for the company's accounting department, who were engaged in "accounting games".
"In order to meet the Wall Street expectations, we had to keep the expenses down as revenue grew," Mr Beaumont told the court.
"We were under pressure from Bernie to meet the numbers.
There was a lot of tension in the company as a result.

"

Mr Beaumont said that "everyone" in the company was aware that the practices were "not proper accounting".
He also alleged that Mr Ebbers had made a speech to staff in which he boasted about his knowledge of "how to cook the books".
Mr Ebbers denies all the charges against him.
The US government has estimated that the fraud at WorldCom amounted to $9bn.
Mr Beaumont was given immunity from prosecution in return for his evidence against Mr Ebbers.
The case against Mr Ebbers also includes charges of making false statements to auditors about $3.8bn in expenses that WorldCom shifted off its books.
US law enforcement agencies recently announced that they were seeking to recover $1.7bn in assets purchased with proceeds of the WorldCom fraud.
The assets include luxury yachts and homes in the US and the Caribbean.

As a minister, he played a key role in the negotiations which led to the Fresh Start Agreement, a deal between the DUP and Sinn Féin.
He returned to the Northern Ireland Assembly in May 2022 after winning a South Down by-election.

Small firms in the UK are being hit by rising costs due to inflation and increased energy prices, with some warning they are on the "verge of collapse", according to a new survey.

The Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) said its research indicated that smaller businesses were particularly exposed to fluctuations in energy prices as they typically operate on thinner margins than larger firms.
The FSB's research, based on a survey of its members, found that small businesses were paying on average £4,418 a year on their energy bills - a rise of 46% compared with 2018.

The organisation's national chairman, Mike Cherry, said: "Small businesses are on the verge of collapse due to energy costs, with many teetering on the edge of survival because of the worsening cost of doing business.
"The worst is yet to come in the next few months and thousands of firms could shut up shop unless urgent action is taken," he added.
"Small businesses have been hit by a perfect storm of rising costs, falling consumer confidence, and dwindling margins.

The FSB has called on the UK government to take immediate steps to help small businesses, including by bringing forward the date of the next business rates review, introducing more grants and easing the burden of debt.
The organisation also wants the government to work with the Bank of England to explore the possibility of a "small business emergency interest rate relief loan".
Mr Cherry said: "Small businesses have been neglected by this government.
They are suffering because of the after-effects of the pandemic and need support if they are to survive and get through the next few months.
"We need the government to show small businesses the same love and support that it gives to big business."
Aid agencies fighting one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters are using satellite maps of Sudan's Darfur region to help them decide where to distribute relief.
The maps, produced by American company DigitalGlobe, are updated every two weeks and are being distributed free of charge.
They are already being used by 10 organisations, including Unicef, the UN's children's fund, and Oxfam.
Oxfam uses the maps to assess the needs of displaced people in camps and to plan where to place water points.
"The current humanitarian crisis in Darfur is one of the most challenging situations facing the international community today," DigitalGlobe's chairman, Jeffrey R. Tarr, said in a statement.
"DigitalGlobe recognises the critical role that accurate geospatial information plays in helping the relief community to provide the necessary support to the people of Sudan.

"

The firm's satellites can image up to one million square km of the Earth every day and the maps it produces can be zoomed in up to 30m (98ft).
The firm has also made public additional high-resolution satellite imagery of the region dating back to early 2004.
This can be used to create a historical record of the destruction in Darfur and could be used in future war crime trials, analysts say.
DigitalGlobe, which is based in Colorado, says it is the only commercial provider of high-resolution satellite imagery and geospatial solutions.
Its clients include Nasa, defence and intelligence agencies and mapping companies.
The firm recently launched a satellite - called WorldView-2 - that can photograph objects as small as 0.7m anywhere on Earth.

Darfur crisis

The Darfur region has been devastated by violence between ethnic Africans and Arabs since 2003, when the Sudan government launched a counter-insurgency campaign against rebels.

Ford has reported a record first-quarter profit of $3.6bn, as strong finance results helped offset a fall in the value of its car portfolio.
The value of Ford's car portfolio fell by $1.4bn as a result of the semiconductor shortage, which has hit the car industry.

Ford's chief executive, Jim Farley, said the company was "aggressively managing" the impact of the shortage on its operations.

Ford said it would still be able to deliver between 1.1 million and 1.2 million vehicles this year, despite the chip shortage.

The shift away from petrol and diesel engines would result in the loss of around 12,000 jobs at Ford's European factories, the company said.

Korean carmaker Hyundai is to build a new factory in India to meet growing demand for cars in one of the fastest-growing car markets in the world.
The $1.2bn (£870m) plant is to be built in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu, Hyundai's biggest global production hub.
The factory is to produce 300,000 cars a year and will create thousands of jobs.
Construction is due to begin next year and the factory is expected to begin production in 2016, Hyundai said.
"India is one of the most important markets for Hyundai and we will continue to make investments to cater to the rising demand," Hyundai Motor India Director (Finance) Tae-lim said in a statement.
The announcement came as Hyundai reported its best monthly sales figures in India for September - at 38,205 units - due to new models and aggressive marketing.
Last month, Hyundai said it would invest $10m in India's largest online retailer, Flipkart.
The investment will be through Hyundai's subsidiary, Hyundai Mobis, which makes auto components.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is trying to boost foreign investment and manufacturing in India as part of an effort to revive the country's economic growth.

Boeing has secured a multi-billion-dollar order for dozens of jets from Japan's All Nippon Airways (ANA), in a boost for the US planemaker after its 737 MAX aircraft were grounded following two deadly crashes.
The deal for 30 Boeing 737 MAX 8 planes and 20 additional 737s, thought to be the 737-800 model, is worth about $9.5bn (£7.5bn) at list prices.
The announcement came on the eve of the opening of the Paris Airshow, one of the industry's largest events.
Boeing is struggling to restore public confidence in the 737 MAX, which was grounded worldwide in March following the crashes in Ethiopia and Indonesia that together killed 346 people.
The US manufacturer has already said it would cut production of the plane this month, although that move was planned before the second crash.
On Monday, Boeing said it would cut production by 20%, signalling that it did not expect the planes to return to service soon.
The company's fastest-selling jet, the 737 MAX, is a workhorse of the global aviation industry.
Its order book included nearly 5,000 planes, but some customers have begun to reconsider their orders following the crashes.
The deal with ANA, which is Japan's largest airline, comprises a firm order for 80 planes and a purchase right for an additional 40.

"We are proud to continue our tradition of delivering industry-leading aircraft to ANA as they introduce additional models of the Boeing 737 family to their fleet," said Boeing Commercial Airplanes president and CEO Kevin McAllister.

"These new airplanes will play an important role in ANA's plans to introduce new sightseeing businesses while continuing to promote popular tourist destinations in Japan and overseas," he added in a statement.
Earlier this month, ANA cancelled a booking for a 737 MAX 8 plane with Avolon, an Irish aviation leasing company.
Avolon said at the time that the cancellation was due to "continued uncertainty" around the reintroduction of the Boeing 737 MAX.
Tory MP Geoffrey Collins has told the BBC that former MP Neil Chambers should be reinstated.
Mr Chambers, who sits in the House of Lords as Lord Chambers of South East London, was suspended from the Conservative Party last week.
The peer, who was MP for Camberwell and Peckham until he lost the seat in the general election, was accused of bullying.
But Mr Collins, who won Camberwell and Peckham at the election, said: "I think we ought to bring him back into the fold."
He added that Lord Chambers had "apologised fully" and that he had "seen the error of his ways".
"I think he's been punished enough," the MP added.

'Not tolerant'
The peer was suspended from the party after he was accused of sending a stream of abusive and threatening emails to a local councillor.
Lord Chambers, who was appointed to the House of Lords in 2005, has not commented on the allegations.
But the BBC has learned that he has written to local Conservative members in Camberwell and Peckham to apologise for his behaviour.
In the letter, he said he was "deeply ashamed" of his conduct and that he had been under "enormous stress" at the time.
He also disclosed that he had been receiving treatment for bipolar disorder, which can cause aggressive behaviour.
Mr Collins said he did not believe that Lord Chambers' suspension from the party should be prolonged.
"I think we've got to be a little bit more tolerant - we're all human beings and make mistakes," he said.

'Not logical'
The MP also argued that his predecessor's suspension made "no logical sense".
"He hasn't been elected - he was given a peerage by the prime minister, so that's a matter for the prime minister," he said.
"I think it's up to the party to say 'look, you've apologised, you've seen the error of your ways, everybody makes mistakes, so let's move on'".
Mr Collins also revealed that Lord Chambers had offered to resign his peerage but that he had persuaded him to stay.
"I said 'look, you've done nothing wrong, you've been elected by the people of this area twice, you've done a lot of good things for the area, so let's just forget it and move on'," he said.

Former Australian Open champion Andre Agassi has given tennis' oldest tournament a vote of confidence - despite concerns from some players over court speed and the surface.
The 55th edition of the Grand Slam gets under way in Melbourne on Monday with top seed Rafael Nadal drawn to play American qualifier Ryan Harrison in the first round.
A number of players, notably David Ferrer, have criticised the pace of the court and warned that the tournament was putting players at risk of injury.
But American Agassi, who won the title in 1995, said he was confident that tournament director Craig Tiley and his team were doing everything they could to provide the best playing conditions.
"I have no doubt that they are doing everything they can to make sure the court is fast for the players, because that's what the players want," he said.
"But at the same time, you know, you can't please everyone.
Some people are going to like it faster, some people are going to like it slower.
As a player, you have to find a way to get it done.

"

Agassi added that he was confident that the courts would continue to play host to exciting matches.
"There were some great matches here last year," he said.
"You don't have too many tournaments where the defending champion loses in the first round and the tournament's still a great tournament.
"So I think they're doing a good job.
They're listening to the players, you know, and I think they're going to continue to make this place a great place to play.

"

Tiley has insisted that the courts were "absolutely perfect" and said he was confident that the tournament would produce a worthy champion.
"I think no matter who wins on Monday, the players will feel they've earned the right to be called the Australian Open champion," he said.

Sales of gadgets including mobile phones, MP3 players, and digital cameras will grow by more than a third to $714bn (£368bn) by 2005, driven by demand in China, Brazil and Russia, says US research group, Gartner.
It also said that Microsoft's Windows XP operating system had helped fuel sales of digital devices.
The study indicated that PC sales had risen by 14.6% in the final three months of 2004.
Gartner said it believed that sales of PCs would continue to grow in 2005, boosted by the arrival of Microsoft's Windows XP operating system, which was released in October.
The survey indicated that 386 million PCs were sold last year, with nearly 29 million in the last quarter of 2004.

"We believe the PC market in 2005 will be characterised by strong growth in portable PCs, robust growth in mature regions, and continuing growth, although at a slower pace, in emerging regions," said George Shiffler, a principal analyst with Gartner.
"We also believe that the fundamental growth drivers for the PC market will remain unchanged in 2005.

"

The research group also said it expected mobile phone sales to grow by 17.7% in 2005 to 988 million units, and for MP3 players to grow by 41.5% to 77 million.
Digital cameras are also expected to continue to do well, with sales up by 20.4% to 121 million units, it added.

She partnered India's Leander Paes in doubles in 2018 and 2019, winning the Wimbledon and US Open mixed doubles titles.

Russian oil giant Yukos has announced it is returning to US courts in a last-ditch attempt to overturn a $50bn arbitration award handed to a former subsidiary.
The move comes after a French court upheld the award earlier this month.
Yukos, once Russia's biggest oil firm, filed for bankruptcy in 1999.
Its main asset was sold to state firm Rosneft in 2004.
The case dates back to the early 2000s, when Yukos defaulted on $27bn in loans from a group of Russian banks and bondholders.
The creditors brought arbitration claims against the energy firm, which were eventually settled for $9.35bn in 2014.
However, a trio of hedge funds – GML, Inc, Bro-Drift and Veteran Partners – allege they own Yukos' debt, and brought a separate lawsuit demanding $114bn in 2008.
They won a $50bn arbitration award against Russia in 2014, though Moscow has always denied any involvement in the case.
Last month, a French court upheld the award, and rejected Russia's appeal to have the matter reheard.
In a statement on Friday, Yukos said it welcomed the decision, but pointed out that other courts had "expressly reserved" the company's right to challenge the award.
"Yukos intends to utilise this jurisdiction to request the annulment of the award, having regard to, inter alia, the decision of the French court," the firm said.
"Given the significance of the award, Yukos is entitled to pursue all available legal remedies.

"

Yukos cited "substantial grounds" for requesting the cancellation of the award, without giving further details.
However, it may ask the court to take into account the fact that most of the firms' assets were sold to Rosneft in 2004, and therefore it could not pay the award.
Yukos has repeatedly rejected the charges levied against it, describing the case as an attempt to "instrumentalise" the firm for political purposes.

Only two episodes of soap opera Coronation Street attracted bigger audiences.

Top of the list is The Apprentice, with an average of 10.2 million viewers.
The finale of the show attracted a peak audience of 13.3 million, the corporation said.
Only two BBC programmes attracted more viewers than Dirty Den's demise - the 1966 World Cup final, and a 1977 episode of Morecambe and Wise.
The top 10 is dominated by talent shows such as The X Factor and Strictly Come Dancing, and by dramas including Torchwood and Cranford.
The list contains no soap operas other than EastEnders.
Strictly Come Dancing attracted more than 12 million viewers to its final last year, as did The X Factor.
More than 11 million tuned into the final episode of Torchwood: Children of Earth.

People aged between 18 and 20 will be able to stand as MPs in the next general election, the Speaker's Committee has confirmed.
The change - affecting the next election, due by 2024 - was announced last year.

The committee's decision confirms the details of the plan and says the change is "reasonable".

MPs aged 18-20 would be entitled to salaries, allowances and office costs.
The committee - which makes rules for the House of Commons - also recommended allowing 16-year-olds to take part in select committee inquiries.
Its report said the change would mean "a more diverse range of people" would be able to take part in scrutiny of the government.
The plans, which are subject to approval by MPs, would not reduce the minimum age for voting, which is 18.
The committee's report said there was a "wide range of views" on the issue of lowering the voting age but that the decision had been made to "take a cautious approach".
It said "the crucial factor in the selection of the minimum age for candidacy is that the candidate should have the capability of being an effective member of Parliament".
The current minimum age of 25 for MPs was set in 1695, with the original reason being that MPs needed to be mature and experienced.
The plans for the next general election were announced by the then Prime Minister Boris Johnson in July 2022.

The proposal was among a number of measures aimed at improving access to politics, after the UK's first minister with learning difficulties, Deputy Prime Minister Dominic Raab, appointed a panel to advise on how politics could become more accessible.

Business groups have warned that the EU's economic growth is being hampered by regulations, red tape, and high energy prices.

The warning from business groups including BusinessEurope and Confitarma came as the EU's statistics agency, Eurostat, announced that the eurozone's economic growth had slowed to 0.2% in the second quarter of 2022, down from 0.8% in the first quarter.
BusinessEurope said that the second quarter growth figure was "another disappointing outcome".

"The European economy is suffering from a perfect storm of supply chain disruptions, rising energy prices, high inflation, and the ongoing pandemic," said BusinessEurope President Pierre-Olivier Mahieu.
Confitarma, which represents the European shipping industry, said that the EU's economic growth was being hampered by "overregulation" and "red tape".
"More than 36% of the regulatory burden imposed on the shipping sector in the last 12 years has come from the EU institutions," said Confitarma Secretary-General Andrea Morgante.

The European Commission has said that it is taking steps to reduce the regulatory burden on businesses, including a "one-in, one-out" rule that requires regulators to remove an existing regulation for every new one they propose.
However, business groups have said that the Commission's efforts are not enough to offset the economic impact of rising energy prices and high inflation.
"The European Commission's better regulation agenda has not yet delivered the reductions in red tape that were promised," said BusinessEurope's Mahieu.

US trade gap narrows as exports rise

The US trade deficit narrowed in November for the third straight month, as exports of agricultural products and machinery rose, official data shows.
The gap between what the US sells and what it buys from other countries fell to $67.0bn, a decline of nearly 11% from $75.4bn in October, the Commerce Department said.
The improvement was driven by a 6.2% rise in exports to $224.9bn, with soybean shipments rising ahead of the harvest in Brazil, and an increase in exports of capital goods.
Imports were up 0.9% at $292.9bn, with increases in foreign-made cars and consumer goods.
The monthly trade gap is closely watched as it is considered an important barometer of the US economy.
But it also matters because the gap represents the difference between what the US buys from abroad and what it sells to other countries.

When the trade gap is as large as it has been over the past year, it means the US is buying more from other countries than it is selling overseas, with the shortfall having to be financed by foreign capital.
That can contribute to a wider current account deficit, which means the US is paying out more money than it is taking in, increasing its need to attract foreign capital to finance the shortfall.
That can put pressure on the dollar, which fell after the release of the data on Thursday.

The improvement in the trade gap comes as central bankers and policymakers struggle to tackle inflation, which has been driven up by the supply chain problems and shortages caused by the Covid-19 pandemic and the recovery from the pandemic.

The Federal Reserve, which has kept interest rates low to support the economic recovery, has started to wind down its large-scale bond-buying stimulus scheme from November, and signalled that it plans to raise interest rates three times next year.
In the UK, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years this month, and analysts expect the Fed to raise rates at its meeting next month.

IBM has released 500 software patents into the public domain, in a move that could help accelerate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain and other emerging technologies.
The US computing giant said it was the first time such a large collection of patents had been made available without any strings attached.
"We're excited to see what's possible when man and machine collaborate," said IBM chief executive Ginni Rometty.
Patents cover a range of areas including cloud computing, AI, and internet of things.
Potential users do not owe IBM any royalties for using the technology.
IBM has been among the most aggressive in seeking patents for its inventions.
It tops the list of companies with the most patents granted by the US Patent and Trademark Office.
The patents being released are those that IBM determined it no longer needed for its own business purposes.
"Releasing patents is not something we do lightly," said IBM's general counsel, John Kelly.
"We spent decades investing in these inventions.
But today, we're taking steps to ensure they can accelerate the next generation of innovation.

"

IBM has already collaborated with Microsoft, Amazon and Google on open-source AI and quantum computing projects.
Last week, Microsoft announced it was making its patents available for free to "defend against patent trolls", a move followed by Google.
Patent trolls are companies that buy up patents from other companies and then sue other firms over alleged infringement.
At the time, Microsoft president and chief legal officer Brad Smith said the company was "taking a stand against those who would abuse the patent system".
IBM's patent giveaway is not entirely out of character.
The company has made smaller patent donations to other organisations in the past, including the Linux Foundation.
It has also contributed to standards bodies such as the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers and the World Wide Web Consortium.
But the move is a sign of a shift in IBM's attitude towards sharing its intellectual property, experts say.
