The bank's rate-setting council voted 8-1 to keep the rate on hold
It was the first time in a decade that a majority of members voted for no change
The Bank of England has kept interest rates on hold, following a split decision by its rate-setting committee.
It marked the first time in more than a decade that the majority of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to keep rates on hold rather than to cut them.
The bank's rate-setting council voted 8-1 to keep the rate on hold at 0.5%, amid signs that the UK economy is recovering from a Brexit-induced slump.
Only last month, the MPC reduced the base rate from 0.75% to 0.5% in response to a global economic slowdown and no-deal Brexit fears.
But data released since then appears to show that the UK economy is weathering the Brexit storm better than expected, and that employers are still hiring.

'No need to panic'
The MPC's decision was welcomed by businesses, with the Confederation of British Industry saying it would help to keep "confidence high".
"The Bank of England's decision to hold rates is important for businesses as it signals no need to panic over the economy," said CBI chief economist Rain Newton-Smith.
"Although we face challenges, the lower base rate and reduced uncertainty about the UK's future relationship with the EU have helped make our exports more competitive.

"

However, Ian Wright, chief economist at Britain's biggest business group, the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said that "many small firms will be disappointed" by the decision.
"The majority of firms would have liked to see the base rate cut to 0.25% to help them tackle the upfront costs of complying with Brexit," he said.

Low inflation
The MPC's decision was based on its assessment that inflation was likely to stay low, and that there was no need for a rate cut to help the economy as a whole.
However, it did acknowledge that the UK's departure from the EU was proving to be a drag on growth, and that the outlook for the economy was uncertain.

"The monetary policy response to Brexit, while significant, has been limited thus far, and remains contingent on the outlook for activity, inflation and the exchange rate," the MPC said in a statement.
"The Committee stands ready to adjust monetary policy accordingly as economic circumstances evolve."

Musicians including Sir Paul McCartney and Robbie Williams are among a group of artists who have backed a copyright treaty designed to help the music business survive in a digital age.
The "internet treaty" aims to create a simplified set of international rules to ensure that artists are paid when their songs are used online.
The two-year campaign for the agreement ended on Friday with a breakthrough at the Rome summit of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (Wipo).
Wipo's director general, Kamil Idris, said the new agreement marked "a historic moment".
He said: "It signals a new era of intellectual property protection on the internet.
It shows that multilateral organisations, such as Wipo, can adapt to the realities of the internet age."
Business and creative groups have welcomed the agreement, as have Google and Yahoo! - although both have said they are concerned that it does not go far enough.
The music industry has been hit hard by the growth of the internet, as it is increasingly easy for people to download music without paying for it.
The industry has been trying to combat this trend for several years.
In 1998, it succeeded in getting laws passed in the US that made it a crime to download music illegally.
However, many people have continued to download music, and the industry has recently stepped up its campaign for tougher measures.
It has also been pushing for the Wipo treaty, which it sees as a crucial step in ensuring that artists get paid for their work.
The agreement aims to make it easier for rights holders to monitor and manage their intellectual property on the internet.
It also aims to cut down on online piracy, by making it a criminal offence in many cases.
Among the musicians who have backed the agreement are McCartney, Williams, U2, Madonna, REM and Radiohead.
A statement by the musicians said: "The internet can provide great opportunities for artists and consumers alike.

"We welcome the efforts of the World Intellectual Property Organisation to find a balanced solution that will help the music industry to continue to invest in new artists and new music, while encouraging legal online music services.
The agreement still has to be ratified by at least 30 countries before it can come into effect.
But observers say they expect it to be approved, as it is in the interests of both the music industry and internet service providers.

Swiss food group Nestle has reported lower first-half profits owing to inflation, which has dampened sales growth for the world's biggest maker of instant coffee.
Net profit in the six months to 31 December fell 12% to SF2.3bn ($2.4bn) compared with the same period a year earlier.
Sales rose 7% to SF27.2bn, but missed expectations.
Nestle cited the impact of inflation on its pricing policy and "bad weather" in North America.
It also warned that it expected the strong Swiss franc to hit sales and margins in the second half of 2013.
In 2012, the company had warned that the strong franc - which hit a record high against the euro last year - would wipe CHF400m ($417m) off its 2012 full-year earnings.
The maker of KitKat chocolate bars, Nescafe coffee and Perrier water also announced an increase in its quarterly dividend to SF1.10 ($1.16) per share from SF1.05.
It also plans to spend SF13bn ($13.7bn) on shareholder returns, including the dividend and share buy-backs, this year.
In December, Nestle reported that its nine-month sales rose by more than 4% to SF21.2bn, driven by growth in emerging markets.
At the end of December, the group announced that it was selling its Yinlu peanut milk and canned rice business in China for an undisclosed sum.
Wall Street cheered on Wednesday as investors reacted positively to the election of George W Bush as president.
The tech-laden Nasdaq stock market index closed up 45.94 points at 1,919.60 - a gain of about 2.5% - on optimism about a Bush administration.
The broader S&P 500 index also closed up more than 2% on hopes of an economic revival under a Republican White House and Congress.
The gains reversed an early dip in share prices after an apparently narrow victory for Mr Bush, who inherits a struggling US economy from outgoing President Bill Clinton.

"This is a classic case of 'good news' for the economy and bad news for the nation," he added.
Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve, which is widely expected to cut interest rates when its policy-setting committee meets on 17 January.
"The Fed will be easing [interest rates] regardless of who won," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corporation.

The tax, which was introduced in 2003, is paid on properties bought for more than £125,000.
Party leader Ed Davey said it was "a tax on aspiration" that hindered young people being able to buy their first home.

"We are very confident that the Max will be recertified before the end of the year, allowing our customers to enjoy the savings these aircraft will provide," Mr O'Leary said.

The Ryanair deal will be a major boost for Boeing, which has been hit by a slowdown in orders due to the coronavirus pandemic.

Japanese technology investor Softbank has reported its first annual loss in 15 years, as the value of its investments in UK telecoms firm BT and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba slipped.
The company, which has invested in thousands of start-ups, logged a net loss of ¥921bn ($7.94bn; £5.3bn) for the year to 31 March.
It sold $10bn of Alibaba shares in December, but the value of its remaining stake fell to $20bn from $24bn a year earlier.
Softbank has invested heavily in British telecoms firm BT, but the value of its holdings dropped by £1.6bn.
It has also put money into US ride-hailing giant Uber, although that investment is held in its Vision Fund, which reports separately.

Uber's value also fell, leading the Vision Fund to write down its value by $1.9bn.

Indonesia has declined an offer from the G20 to have its debt frozen as it still has funds to pay its creditors, the country's finance minister has said.
Southeast Asia's biggest economy has been hit hard by the coronavirus pandemic, with strict lockdown policies pushing it into recession.

"We are not in an insolvency crisis, we have the funds to repay our debt," she said in an interview with the BBC.
Many countries have embraced the offer from the G20 to pause debt repayments as they grapple with the economic fallout from the pandemic.
Sri Mulyani said the offer - for debt suspension until the end of the year - would be reconsidered if Indonesia's economic situation took a turn for the worse.
"If in the second semester, or even in the next year, we see that our economic growth is not promising, then we will consider it," she said.
"We've seen that there are countries which have accepted the offer, and there are also countries that have not accepted it.

"

The former executives of two American companies went on trial in Milan on charges of murder and failure to protect the environment.
The trial of the former executives of mining companies Union Carbide and Dow Chemical got under way in Italy on Tuesday.
They are accused of failing to prevent the deadly explosion at the Bhopal plant in India in 1984, which killed thousands of people.
The defendants are also accused of failing to adequately dispose of hazardous waste at the site.
The seven executives include the chairman and chief executive of Union Carbide at the time, Warren Anderson, who has since died.
The others are ex-Union Carbide India chairman Kishore Kamdar, and former Dow Chemical CEO, Geoffrey H. Keys.
They all deny the charges.
The explosion of methyl isocyanate at the plant in the central Indian city released a toxic gas that killed thousands and injured more than 150,000.
The site had been owned by Union Carbide, but seven years before the disaster, the firm had sold it to Dow Chemical.
The long-awaited trial began after the Indian government finally handed over documents relating to the case that had been requested by Italian magistrates.
The defendants had been due to go on trial in Bhopal, but the Indian government failed to respond to requests for information about the incident.
That led the judges to issue an international warrant for the executives' arrest in 1992.

The warrant was executed in Switzerland five years later and the defendants have been on trial in Milan ever since, but the case was repeatedly delayed because the Indian government failed to provide documents relating to the incident.

A senior Welsh rugby union official has approached the Rugby Football League (RFL) about setting up a Wales rugby league training centre.
BBC Sport has learned that Wales would welcome a return to the full 13-a-side code for the first time since 1954.
The approach was made at a private meeting between Welsh unions and potential investors at a hotel in London on Tuesday.
The RFL said it wanted to see a "strong, stable and growing" league before committing to a new professional club.
A Welsh assembly member, Gareth Bennett, has already submitted a petition to the assembly calling for a Welsh professional rugby league.
And independent assembly member Delyth Jewell has tabled a motion calling on the Welsh government to "show leadership" by supporting the creation of a Welsh professional rugby league.
That motion will be debated in the assembly on Tuesday, 19 July.
In 2005, a proposed World League involving Wales, England, New Zealand and Australia fell through because the ARL in Australia did not want to participate.
And in 2007, a proposed eight-team European League, involving Wales, England, France, Ireland and Scotland fell through because of a lack of funding.
The most recent rugby league experiment in Wales - a nine-a-side Celtic League involving Welsh, Scottish and Irish clubs - lasted just one season, in 2010.
And since the end of the 2013 season, there has not been a professional club in either Wales or Scotland, with the end of the Super League licence of Welsh club Crusaders.
That means any new professional club in Wales would start in the Championship, the second tier of the English professional game below Super League.
A group from South Wales has already had preliminary discussions with the RFL about entering a team into the Championship, and those talks have now intensified.
The new group includes a Welsh rugby union official, rugby league backer Mike Lewis and businessman Steve Aizlewood, the owner of Welsh football side The New Saints.
Aizlewood, who also plays rugby league for Abercynon, near Cardiff, is a former board member of Crusaders.

Britain's Holmes selected for double bid

Holmes was already assured of a place in next month's World Championships in Beijing after winning the 1,500m and 5,000m at the British Championships in July.
The 26-year-old, who was a late addition to the British team for London, will now bid to repeat Sir Mo Farah's feat of winning both the 5,000m and 10,000m at successive Games.
"It shows the strength in depth now in British distance running," said Holmes.
"It's amazing to be given the chance to compete in both events in Beijing.
It was a no-brainer for me to take that opportunity.

"

Holmes' selection was confirmed at a British Athletics selection meeting in Birmingham on Saturday.
The double victory in London made Holmes only the third man to win both events at a single Games, after Farah and Finland's Lasse Viren, who achieved the feat in 1972 and 1976.

In Beijing, Holmes will aim to improve on his fifth-place finish in the 5,000m and challenge for a medal in the 10,000m.

"I think I've got as good a chance as anybody in the 10,000m," said Holmes.
"I've got a good shot at a medal in that and I'm going to go into it trying to win.
"Hopefully I can squeeze under 13 minutes in the 5,000m. That's the aim.

Playing on a GameBoy sounds like a blast from the past, but Polish musicians are using the handheld device in their performances.
They have even formed Blip-Pop - an international collective of GameBoy musicians and enthusiasts.
The group says the device is a "beautiful piece of raw hardware" which can be used to create "new and exciting" music.
GameBoy musicians can be seen and heard in this report, which features footage of a concert in Warsaw.
GameBoys have been used before by musicians, including chiptune artist Shirobon and the band 1-800-BIT-GYMS.
Blip-Pop co-founder Tomasz Szafranski said the device's sound is "really primitive and minimalistic".
"It's like taking a big synth and squeezing it in a small, eight-bit machine," he told the BBC.
The musician, also known as Xygen, added that the GameBoy was attractive as it could be used to create new sounds and "cross boundaries between genres".
The devices that Blip-Pop's members use vary from the original GameBoy, on which the Nintendo console games were played, to the GameBoy Pocket and GameBoy Advance.
The changes in the hardware can affect the digital and analogue signals, and the instruments can be pimped with additional electronics to modify the sound.
GameBoy music is created by sequencing the sounds - as the devices do not allow for live playing.
This means that a composition must be programmed into the device and then played back.
External electronics can be attached to allow for effects such as distortion.
Members of Blip-Pop - who are based in Poland, the UK and the US - have been touring clubs and festivals in Europe.
Mr Szafranski said the collective hoped to expand its membership and hold more live events.
Belle and Sebastian have been named the best Scottish band in a poll of music retailers.
The Glasgow group - who released their first album, Tigermilk, in 1996 - received the most votes in a poll of 70 Scottish music retailers, conducted by Scottish music magazine, The List.
The magazine's editor, Rory Foster, said all the bands in the top 20 have had an impact on the Scottish music scene.
"The fact that the poll was conducted by the people who know most about Scottish music, the retailers, makes me very confident that we have got it right," he said.
"And the good news for everyone is that all of these bands are still going strong, with new albums in the pipeline."

Foster said it was encouraging that the poll's top 20 included several newer acts, such as Glasgow indie rockers, Franz Ferdinand, and that no band had dominated the top of the chart since the days of eclectically-inspired rockers, Travis.
"There's no doubt that Belle and Sebastian are revered by the dealers, but so are a lot of other bands," he said.
"There isn't one band that the dealers think are brilliant and are selling in huge numbers. "
Travis topped the chart in 1997 and 1998, and came second last year.
This year the Glasgow band came sixth with their recent album, The Man Who, while Dundee's Gomez came second, down from first place last year.
Glasgow's Idlewild came third, with Moby, who recently opened a restaurant in Edinburgh, in fifth place.
Foster added that female-fronted bands were well represented in this year's chart.
"There are lots of great female musicians out there at the moment and quite a few featured in our poll," he said.
"Helene Rohner from the Delgados is possibly the most influential female musician in Scotland at the moment.

"

Rohner, who writes the group's lyrics and plays the guitar, emerged victorious in a recent battle with the group's record label, Warners, after complaining that the label were not doing enough to promote her as a songwriter.
She recently signed a new deal with Warners and is currently working on the follow-up to the Delgados' 1998 album, The Great Eastern.
A colourful character has won Britain's most prestigious gardening award.
The grey-haired, pink-clad Christopher Lloyd, who has been described as the "gardener of the century", picked up the top prize at the Chelsea Flower Show.
His garden, entitled The Dry Garden, won him a gold medal and the title of champion gardener.
The 82-year-old, who describes himself as "a gardener, writer and latter day hippy", took seven years to plan his garden.
And he celebrated winning the medal by doing a little dance round his garden.
He said: "I'm thrilled, excited, over the moon, and relieved.
"I think gardens are about enjoyment and this is such a lovely feeling - what a way to end my career."
Mr Lloyd, who is known as Christo, retired from gardening last year - but said at the time that he would continue to garden at his home, Great Dixter, in Northiam, Sussex.
The garden he created for this year's show is an imaginary one, but draws on his experiences of gardening in dry conditions in the Mediterranean and California, as well as in his own garden.
It is the second time that he has won the top prize at the show - he previously won it in 1998 with a garden featuring vigorous, large-leaved plants and trees.
This year he was up against another famous gardener, Diarmuid Gavin, who was favourite to win for the best show garden.
Mr Lloyd pipped him to the post with his dry landscape, which the judges described as "a tough, uncompromising, but incredibly beautiful garden".

Hacker threat to Apple's iTunes

Apple has urged hundreds of thousands of iTunes users to protect their accounts following claims that they had been hacked.
The tech company advised users to visit an account settings page on Apple's website and verify that their contact information was up to date.
It did not reveal any further details about the alleged security breach.
iTunes has more than 435 million users worldwide.
The tech giant said it was "actively investigating" the reported hacking of its iTunes Store, with "evidence" that the unauthorised access had been realised.
"We strongly encourage users to visit the Account Security area in their account settings to obtain the latest information and protect their accounts," Apple said in a statement.
"Apple takes the security of our users very seriously, and we are actively investigating the reported incident in order to protect our users and our service," it added.
News of the hack first emerged in a posting on the Hackernews website over the weekend.
It said that a number of users had received emails advising them that their accounts had been accessed by hackers, although it did not specify how many.
Apple would not say how many users had received such an email.
The hack is the latest in a string of high-profile breaches of internet firms.
Last month, Yahoo advised at least one billion users to change their passwords after hackers stole user data from its systems.
And in April, dozens of high-profile Twitter accounts were hacked in a major security breach.

Minister James Purnell has defended a poster campaign aimed at tackling anti-social behaviour.
The posters carry the slogan: "We're watching you - respect your community.

"

They have appeared in towns and cities across the UK, sparking criticism that they are an invasion of privacy.
The culture secretary told the BBC the posters were "a reminder" that people "should" behave.
The government says the campaign is aimed at reducing low-level crime and nuisance behaviour.
But the initiative has been called "chilling" and "sinister" by critics, including the Liberal Democrats and the National Council for Civil Liberties.
The chairman of the NCCL, Shami Chakrabarti, has called for an immediate withdrawal of the posters, describing them as "effectively a CCTV camera with a big red arrow pointing at it".
Are you happy with these new ads?
Mr Purnell said the posters were "not intended to be threatening".
"They're a reminder that in a civilised society people should behave, and if they don't behave then there are consequences for that," he told BBC One's Breakfast show.
"The ads are not intended to be threatening in any way, but they are a reminder of what people should be doing in our communities," he added.
The minister said he was "confident" that the posters were an effective deterrent, but added that there was "no hard evidence" to prove it.
"I don't have any evidence second-by-second, but it is a well-known fact that CCTV does reduce crime," he said.
"These ads... are a reminder that there are consequences to your actions.

"

The posters were commissioned by the Home Office and use the slogan: "We're watching you - respect your community."
They show an image of security cameras and carry the web address of the crime reduction charity Crimestoppers.
The charity's boss, Lord Ashcroft, has said the posters were an "effective" way of cutting anti-social behaviour.
Are these ads a good thing?
But the chairman of the NCCL, Shami Chakrabarti, argued that the posters were an "acknowledgement of failure by the government to tackle the causes of anti-social behaviour".
"Rather than creeping surveillance state, we need to resource programmes that work to prevent anti-social behaviour, rather than creeping surveillance state," she said.
England's Joe Cordina produced a stunning knockout of Andy Townend to become the new British lightweight champion.
The 28-year-old from Cardiff landed a huge right hand to floor his rival in the fourth round and then forced the referee to stop the contest as Townend tried to get up.
It was a second successful defence of his title for Cordina, who was fighting for the first time under new trainer Dominic Ingle.
His victory was one of the highlights on a historic night for Welsh boxing as four of his countrymen won Commonwealth titles.
It meant an unhappy ending to Townend's brave challenge as he was stopped for just the second time in his career and the first time since 2010.

Previously, Townend had earned the respect of Cordina with his persistence and toughness, but the Welshman always looked the more skilful fighter and he landed with some impressive left-handed counters in the third round.
However, it was a huge right hand which caught Townend early in the fourth which changed the course of the fight.
The Yorkshireman hit the canvas and although he made it to his feet he appeared unsteady and the referee stepped in to end the contest.

ABBA singer Agnetha Faltskog has entered the Sunday Times music rich list for the first time, with an estimated wealth of £26.2m.

The Swedish pop icon, 69, is the richest female musician in Sweden - ahead of Madonna and Beyonce.
Her fortune is largely due to her 50% share in ABBA's songs, which have enjoyed a revival thanks to the hit musical Mamma Mia! and the two films.

Her former husband and ABBA bandmate Bjorn Ulvaeus is the fifth richest musician in the UK, with an estimated £130m.

Agnetha, who lives in Stockholm, has not released an album since 2003's The Collection but has continued to tour with ABBA bandmates Bjorn, 76, Benny Andersson, 74, and Anni-Frid Lyngstad, 71.

They came second in the Eurovision song contest in 1974 with Ring and went on to become one of the most successful acts of the 1970s with a string of hits including Waterloo, Dancing Queen and Take A Chance On Me.
ABBA were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2010 and last year they were given a Bafta award for their contribution to cinema.
The Sunday Times Rich List is published on May 25.
Ben Scott has emerged as a surprise favourite to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond.
The Star Wars actor boasts a huge social media following and his inclusion in the conversation has seen betting odds on him replace Craig in the iconic role slashed.
Scott, 36, has gained a significant online following in recent years, primarily due to his resemblance to Craig, which has prompted fan campaigns for him to take on the role.
His chances have been boosted further by the recent news that producer Barbara Broccoli will have a key say in who the next Bond is.
She is said to be keen to shake up the formula and go for a younger, less well-known actor to play the legendary secret agent.
Scott has been a regular name in the betting to be the next Bond, but his odds have shortened from 25-1 to 6-1 in recent days.
Scott has yet to comment on the speculation.
The role is likely to be one of the most sought-after in Hollywood with Craig's fifth and final outing as Bond, No Time To Die, released in September.
Ukraine has reached a gas deal with Turkmenistan, ending its reliance on Russian supplies.
The deal was signed in Kyiv by Ukrainian Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko and his Turkmen counterpart Batyr Rejepow.
Russia has been Ukraine's main gas supplier since the collapse of the Soviet Union, but Kyiv has tried to diversify its energy imports.
Relations between Moscow and Kyiv have been at rock bottom since Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 and support for separatists in eastern Ukraine.
The new deal will see Turkmenistan export up to 1.5 billion cubic metres of gas to Ukraine annually, with supplies expected to start in 2024, according to the Turkmen government.
BMW has revealed details of a range of new electric vehicles which will launch across the next ten years as part of the company's ambitious plan to sell only fully electric cars by 2040.
The German carmaker said the new models would help it achieve sales of more than two million fully-electric vehicles by the end of that decade.
The most imminent new launch is the iX electric sports utility vehicle (SUV), which will go on sale before the end of this year.
It will be followed by the i4 electric saloon, which will go into production in the summer of 2021.
Both models will be assembled at BMW's plant in Munich.
The carmaker also revealed plans for a fully-electric version of its popular X1 model, which will be built in Leipzig, Germany, from 2023.
A larger electric SUV, the iNEXT, will be assembled in Dingolfing from 2021.
It will have a range of more than 600km (373 miles) and will be able to charge in just 30 minutes.
BMW's electric vehicle range will also be expanded to include a new model, the i7, an electric version of the 7 Series luxury saloon, which will go on sale in 2023.
The company's UK chief, Pieter Nota, said the announcements marked "a new era" for the company.
"We are going to introduce a few new architectures, new technologies, and a new mindset," he said.
"It's a big step going from being a leading provider of premium vehicles to becoming a leading provider of sustainable mobility.

"

As well as launching new all-electric models, BMW also plans to offer hybrid power trains on all its models by 2023.
The company currently offers hybrid engines on its 3 Series, 8 Series, X5 and X7 models.
The move towards electric power comes as carmakers across the world are committing to more environmentally-friendly vehicles.
Last week, Volvo said its entire range would be fully electric by 2030, while Ford announced plans to sell only all-electric cars in Europe by 2030.
Ford and BMW have also announced plans to work together on developing electric vehicles, with the two companies set to share technologies and work together to streamline development costs.
"We're taking significant steps towards making sure our vehicles are carbon neutral across the lifecycle by 2030," Mr Nota said.
"We're going to be open sourcing a lot of our e-drive technologies.

"

Shares in BMW rose sharply at the news of its electric vehicle plans.
They were up by 3.2%

England left-back Ben Chilwell could be out for the rest of the season after undergoing knee surgery, his club Chelsea said.
The 25-year-old had an operation on his knee cartilage injury on Monday and will start his rehabilitation soon.
Chilwell has been sidelined since late December when he damaged his knee in a 4-0 win against Juventus in a Champions League game.
He had made a good recovery from ACL surgery last summer and returned to training in September.
Chilwell has 18 months left on his current deal and is yet to begin discussions over an extension.
There is a major concern at Chelsea that Chilwell's injury is similar to the one which has kept England colleague Luke Shaw out of Manchester United's team since January.
Shaw, 27, had hoped to be back after the international break but has now suffered a setback in his recovery from a tendon injury.
United boss Erik ten Hag said the left-back, who has been linked with a move to Chelsea, will be out for "a while longer".

The 2003 French Open champion, who also won the ATP Finals that year and reached the world number one spot, does not mention 18-time major winner Nadal or Alcaraz, who rose to a career-high No 6 this week, by name.

Drinks group Diageo is to buy US wine company Beam Inc in a deal worth £13.4bn ($17.81bn).
The maker of Johnnie Walker whisky is paying £4.55bn ($6.4bn) in cash and shares for the maker of Jim Beam bourbon and Courvoisier cognac.
Shares in London-based Diageo closed up 1.5% on the news.
Diageo said the deal would transform it into the world's leading spirits company by "incremental sales".
The company said it would accelerate its expansion in key growth markets such as the US and China.
Diageo has been advised by Goldman Sachs, while JPMorgan and PJT Park Hill have worked with Beam on the deal.
The deal comes as the drinks industry faces slowing growth in Europe and increasing pressure from governments seeking to counter binge drinking.
Last year, Diageo held talks with Guinness maker Heineken over a possible merger of their drinks businesses.
However, those discussions broke down over price and because of the complexity of merging the two firms.
At the end of 2013, Diageo had sales of £6.7bn and operating profits of £2.7bn.
It employs about 30,000 people.
Beam, which is listed on the New York Stock Exchange, reported sales of about $4.3bn and operating profits of about $660m in the year to 31 March.
It employs about 5,000 people.

He said the cabinet had been told the election would be "tilted" towards older people, because of the pandemic - with a campaign run on the basis that "we must lock down or face chaos".
One minister told the BBC the government would argue that "we must have an election now so that we can clear out the blockage in Parliament and get the country behind the government's rescue plan".
Virgin Radio is launching a digital radio service that allows listeners to hear live radio while accessing 3G internet services on their mobile phones.

The service, created by digital radio firm Digital One, uses the digital audio broadcasting (DAB) protocol to offer Virgin Radio's existing analogue radio broadcast and a "parallel" digital broadcast.
Mobile phone users can listen to the digital radio stream through headphones while accessing internet services.
The service will be available in London from June 17, with a national roll-out planned for later in the year.

Digital One's commercial director, Andrew Harrison, said: "This service marks an exciting new development for digital radio in this country."

"We are offering a digitally-led, compelling consumer service that offers an 'always on', unlimited listening experience," he added.

How it works

Digital radio sounds like analogue radio, but with CD-quality sound.
It is broadcast from transmitters that offer better coverage than existing FM and AM frequencies, because they use lower frequencies than analogue radio.

To receive the digital signal, listeners need a digital radio or a digital radio receiver, which can be a stand-alone product or incorporated into another device, such as a mobile phone or MP3 player.
Digital One, which is owned by News Corporation and Broadcasting Development Fund, plans to offer dozens of digital radio services, including BBC stations and offerings from commercial radio firms.
The company has already launched more than 20 digital radio services, including five BBC stations - BBC Radio 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 Live.
Last month, Digital One struck a deal with Channel 4 to create a new digital radio station, called Channel 4 Radio, which will launch this summer.
The new station will be available on Digital One's DAB network, as well as via the internet and on digital television.

to reach the third round of the Italian Open on Wednesday.
The 39-year-old American great, a three-time Rome champion back in the 1990s, needed five match points to see off the 10th-seeded American teenager.
Top seed Roger Federer plays his second-round match against either Spain's David Ferrer or Italian wildcard Potito

Agassi looked to be coasting to a comfortable victory when he had four match points on Roddick's serve at 5-3 in the second set but the 19-year-old saved them all and went on to level at one set all.
The fifth seed looked tired at the end of his lengthy second-round victory over Australia's Lleyton Hewitt on Tuesday and his movement was clearly affected against Roddick.
Roddick looked confident early on, serving and stroking his way to a 3-0 lead but Agassi, backed by a large and enthusiastic Italian crowd, fought back to take the opening set.
The match turned in the 11th game of the second set with Agassi trailing 4-5 and facing three break points on his serve.
He saved the first with a fierce forehand winner but then double-faulted to give Roddick a fifth break point of the game.

Agassi, playing his first tournament since March, looked to be struggling but he broke Roddick in the very first game of the third set and went on to take a 2-0 lead.

He struggled through the third set before Roddick, who has yet to win a title this year, halted the match after only one game of the fourth.
Ex-France midfielder, now director of football development at Qatar Football Association, is in the running to be awarded the Knight of the Legion of Honour.
Henry, who played for France at World Cups in 1998, 2002, 2006 and 2010, has been appointed as the director of football development at the Qatar Football Association (QFA).
The 40-year-old's new role will see him oversee all aspects of football in the Gulf state, as Qatar invests billions in preparation for the 2022 World Cup.
If he is awarded the Knight of the Legion of Honour, Henry will be able to use the initials KLH after his name.
The former Juventus, Arsenal and Barcelona player was voted the world's best player in 2003 and was named the French player of the year three times.
He won the World Cup, European Championship and Champions League during his playing career.
"It was with emotion that I learned that I am likely to be awarded the Legion d'Honneur tomorrow," he said.

"I have proudly worn the blue, white and red jersey of my country during which I shared unforgettable moments with my teammates, whether it was in our great victories or in our most crushing defeats, especially in 2006.
"It's always been a boy's dream to play for his country and I was lucky enough to realise this dream."
Winter storminess in America has dropped to its lowest in 15 years, according to weather analytics company Planalytics.
The milder weather has led to a drop in demand for heating oil, prompting a surplus and driving down the price.
US oil prices have fallen 6% to $63.24 a barrel, the biggest one-day fall in a month.
"Oil prices have fallen quite a bit due to the weather - crude has actually fallen more than diesel and gasoline," said Rob Thummel, a portfolio manager at US Bank Asset Management.

"The weather has been incredibly warm this winter and if it continues to be warm, it is going to start to put pressure on energy prices, because you're not going to need as much fuel to heat homes and buildings," he added.
The drop comes as oil prices have hit their highest levels in years following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Global oil prices have surged by more than 30% since the start of the year, with benchmark Brent crude hitting $98 a barrel in March - a level not seen since 2014.
Mr Thummel does not expect the price of oil to fall significantly from here, given the underlying strength of the oil market.

"Oil prices still look pretty buoyant, especially when you look internationally, because a lot of countries are still trying to source oil and the logistics of getting oil from point A to point B - whether it be by ship or by pipeline - have become very challenging," he said.
In London, crude oil prices fell 1.1% to $86.23 a barrel, while in Asia, the price of oil slipped 0.8%.
Experts expect that the price of oil will remain high as Russia's actions continue to restrict the global supply.
The UK, US and Europe have all introduced bans on Russian oil in recent months as the war rages on.
And Opec, the group of major oil producing countries, has failed to replace Russian oil which is keeping prices high.

"With oil demand expected to grow faster in the second half of 2022 than in the first, due to the easing of Covid-19 restrictions and the reopening of China's economy, this tightening of oil supply is likely to keep oil prices elevated for the remainder of the year," said Hans van Cleef, senior energy economist at ABN Amro.
Police in Spain have received a bomb threat concerning football club Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium.
The country's civil protection agency confirmed it had received a warning, but said it was a "false" and "unfounded" alert.
It added that authorities were still investigating the origin of the message, which was sent to a mailbox used for such purposes.
Spanish media reported that an email sent to authorities cited the Islamic State group and threatened to carry out a bombing at the stadium during the Champions League final on 28 May.
The match pits Real Madrid against Atletico Madrid.
The email also warned of a car bomb in the capital Madrid, according to the reports.
Police are investigating the authenticity of the message, which was reportedly sent from Yemen.
The Bernabeu played host to the European Cup final in 2010 and 2014.
Two more senior executives have resigned from Fannie Mae, the US mortgage finance giant, as it continues to suffer heavy losses.
The latest departures came as Fannie Mae said it lost $2.2bn (£1.4bn) in the first three months of this year.
The firm has now lost more than $14bn over the past year.
The US government took over the firm in September 2008 after it suffered heavy losses on its mortgage loans.
Fannie Mae's chief executive, Michael Williams, resigned in March.
On Thursday, the firm's chief business officer, Stephen Swad, and its chief risk officer, Rob Van der Straeten, said they would leave Fannie Mae.
In a statement, the company said that Mr Swad, who had been with Fannie Mae for more than 16 years, was leaving to "pursue other opportunities".
Mr Van der Straeten said he wanted to "pursue opportunities in the risk management field".
Fannie Mae said its first-quarter losses included a $1.7bn pretax charge to reflect "deteriorating economic conditions" that have led to increasing levels of mortgage delinquencies and foreclosures.
The firm also said it would need about $6bn in additional federal funding this year on top of the $100bn it has already received from the US Treasury.
The US government has given the firm a total of about $188bn in aid.
Borussia Dortmund are "on the verge of bankruptcy", says the club's chairman Hans-Joachim Watzke.

The Bundesliga side have been struggling to cope with the financial fall-out from the coronavirus pandemic, as well as facing a 30m euro (£27m) fine from UEFA after they were found guilty of breaking spending rules.
Dortmund have qualified for the Champions League for a sixth consecutive season but CEO Hans-Christian Kolb said they "couldn't afford" to participate.
"We have to sort out this situation shortly," added Kolb, who admitted they had yet to decide whether to appeal against the sanction.
European football's governing body opened an investigation into the club's finances in February 2020 after they spent more than €100m on players in the previous two seasons.

Last month, the club were eventually sanctioned for "violations of the regulations on the break-even requirement" but the verdict ruled out a potential exclusion from the competition, leading Kolb to suggest they could withdraw if the fine was not reduced.
However, Watzke is now sounding more optimistic about the club's prospects.
"We have managed to achieve liquidity until 2024," he told German magazine Der Spiegel.
"We have negotiated a significant portion of our debts.
Those are now sustainable.
In June, we paid back a loan from Deutsche Bank with an interest rate of several percent.
That saved us €5m a year.

"

While the financial outlook has improved, Watzke did not hide the fact that the club could have been facing oblivion.
"It wasn't a matter of months, but a matter of weeks before we were insolvent," he added.
"Fortunately, we now have a sustainable economic plan in place.

"

The club recently sold England midfielder Jude Bellingham to Premier League side Manchester City for £97.5m but Watzke said any further sales would be decided on a "case-by-case basis".
They have been linked with a move for Arsenal's England striker Eddie Nketiah, who is out of contract at the end of the season.
"We have financial resources to make ourselves stronger if necessary," added Watzke.
"We're not going to spend £100m on a striker though.
Should we sell Bellingham for a lot of money?
I wouldn't say no.
Every player has his price."
Newcastle United are lining up a £3m bid for Chelsea's Nigeria international right-back Celestine Babayaro.
The Magpies' manager Graeme Souness sees the 24-year-old as the ideal replacement for injured England international Warren Barton.
Babayaro has struggled to establish himself in the Chelsea side since his move from Anderlecht two years ago.
He was linked with a move to Liverpool last season but stayed at Stamford Bridge - and has made just 12 starts for the Blues this season.

Ferguson fears Milan's cutting edge after Higuain arrival

 Ferguson confident despite Milan arrival 

Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson fears Milan's "cutting edge" after the arrival of striker Gonzalo Higuain from Real Madrid.
The Italian side signed the 25-year-old Argentine international for a fee of around £20m on Tuesday.
Ferguson said he was "confident" his players could cope with Higuain, 27-year-old Italy striker Filippo Inzaghi and 23-year-old Brazilian midfielder Pato.
"Milan have always been a club who have threatened in the three major competitions - the Italian league, the Champions League and the Italian Cup," said the United manager.
"They have bought well.
They are a dangerous side and Inzaghi was brilliant against us in Milan last season."
Inzaghi scored both goals in Milan's 2-1 win over United in the Champions League last 16, first leg at the San Siro last February.
The return game at Old Trafford was one of the great European ties, with United coming from two goals down to win 4-3 on penalties after a 3-3 draw over 90 minutes and extra time.
Ferguson believes Milan have become even stronger with the capture of Higuain, who has also been linked with United.
"We've got a lot of respect for Milan and what they have done," said the United manager.
"They have bought well in Higuain and he is one we thought a lot about.
"He's quick, he can score goals.
He can play as a single striker or with a strike partner.
He's versatile and he has been very successful."
Higuain scored 55 goals in 155 games for Real, winning the Spanish title three times and the Champions League once.
Ferguson believes the Milan link with Real could also benefit his own club in their pursuit of Brazil midfielder Kaka.
"There might be a chance there because of the relationship between the two clubs," said the United manager.
"We've been monitoring him for a long time and everyone knows how keen we are to get him."
The 26-year-old former Sao Paulo player has reportedly told Real he wants to move to United.

The US central bank signaled a readiness to begin reducing its holdings of government bonds next month, even as officials debated how fast rates might need to rise in the coming months to combat the sharpest surge in inflation in four decades.
The Federal Reserve said it would begin tapering its portfolio of bonds in February, reducing its balance sheet by $30bn a month, at twice the pace it used during a similar process in 2017 and 2018.
There was some disappointment that the central bank did not go further, and signal an immediate start to its balance sheet reduction, rather than in February.

Financial markets will take comfort that Fed officials' "dot plot" of their own economic forecasts continued to signal that they expect just three quarter-point rate rises this year - even as the so-called "dot plot" of individual officials' expectations pointed to as many as seven rate rises over the course of the year.

In the longer run, the median forecast saw the policy rate reaching 2.5% by the end of 2023, according to the dot plot, meaning that officials see another 75 basis points of rises after the expected lift in rates this year.
Fed chair Jay Powell told a news conference that the Fed was "of a mind" to raise rates at its meeting next month, and was "concerned" about inflation.
But he added that he would still like to see payrolls growth "solid" before increasing rates.
Stock markets initially rose following the release of the Fed's statement, but later gave up those gains.
Government bond yields also fell initially, but later moved higher.
Real Madrid have confirmed that they have signed striker Borja Iglesias from Real Sociedad on a six-year deal, after he allegedly tricked Reyes into thinking he was signing for Atletico Madrid.
The 24-year-old joined Sociedad from Deportivo La Coruna last summer for 6m euros and was widely expected to stay at the Anoeta until his release clause of 50m euros was activated.

However, he agreed a deal with Madrid on Tuesday evening after speaking with club president Florentino Perez and he will reportedly cost the European champions 30m euros.

Reyes, who was sold to Atletico by Madrid last summer, had believed that he had talked his former club into signing Iglesias.
The defender reportedly rang Iglesias, who was on holiday in Ibiza, on Tuesday to convince him to join him at the Vicente Calderon, but the player had already agreed terms with Madrid.
"I know it's difficult to believe but it's true," Reyes wrote on his Twitter page.
Madrid had been expected to fight for the signature of Valencia's David Villa, who scored 54 goals in 55 games for the Spanish side last season.

Belgium-based brewer InBev raised €13.2bn (£10.8bn; $16.6bn) in an share offering, as it seeks to reduce the company's debt ahead of its takeover of SABMiller.
InBev, which owns Stella Artois and Beck's, announced plans to buy SABMiller for about $100bn in November.
The company said it planned to spend the proceeds from the share sale - about $15bn - on paying down debt related to the takeover.
InBev's offering was priced at €65 a share, towards the top of the expected price range, and was more than 10 times oversubscribed.
The company said it would not be issuing any new shares.
InBev's takeover of SABMiller is expected to be completed in the second half of this year, pending regulatory approval.
SABMiller's brands include Fosters, Miller Lite, and Pilsner Urquell.
Upon completion of the deal, SABMiller shareholders will own about 42% of the combined group.
InBev said it had been approached by various parties interested in acquiring all or part of its business.
The company has said it will consider any "compelling" offers.
Greece's Olympic pole vault champion Rena Kerdenis has denied faking a road accident that reportedly left her with serious injuries just days before the Tokyo Games.
The 35-year-old, who won gold in Beijing in 2008 and bronze in London in 2012, suffered abdominal and neck injuries in the crash in Athens on Monday.
Greek news agency ANA said it appeared the airbags in her car had not been deployed.
In a statement posted on Instagram on Friday, Kerdenis said she was "surprised and annoyed" by the reports.
"I would like to express my annoyance at the misinformation, with ulterior motives, that has been circulated by certain media," she said.
"I have the accident report with all the details and the car that was involved.
Everything will be made public and I will donate the money from the car to a charity.
"It is without doubt that I will take all necessary legal action against those who slandered me.

"

The International Olympic Committee said it had "no reason to believe" that Kerdenis had not been injured in an accident.

"The IOC has been in contact with the Greek Olympic Committee, who confirmed that Rena Kerdenis had an accident on her way from training last Monday and sustained injuries, for which she was treated in hospital before being released the next day," it said in a statement.
"The IOC has no reason to believe that there is any truth to the rumours that have been appearing in the Greek media suggesting foul play.

"

Kerdenis, who also won the world title in 2007, finished fourth in Tokyo as Sweden's Mondo Duplantis took gold.
Prosecutors have launched an investigation into UK MP Ken Clarke over claims he compared the Jewish community to the Islamic State group.
The Conservative MP is alleged to have made the comment about the Board of Deputies, which represents British Jews, at a meeting in Westminster.
The Board of Deputies said it had reported the matter to the Metropolitan Police.
Mr Clarke, who was the justice secretary until last year, has yet to comment on the probe.
The Conservative Party has previously said the comments are "completely unacceptable".
The probe comes after Labour MP Naz Shah was suspended from the party over allegedly anti-Semitic Facebook posts.
In one post, she appeared to claim Jews controlled the media.
The 37-year-old, who represents Bradford West, has been the subject of an investigation by the Labour Party since February.
Party general secretary Jennie Formby wrote to her on 8 April asking her to explain the posts, which dated from 2014, within seven days.
Ms Shah apologised for the "completely unacceptable" posts on Saturday, adding that she had not intended to cause offence.
But Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has faced repeated calls to suspend her from the party.
On Sunday, nine Labour MPs and three peers called on him to take "decisive action" against Ms Shah.
In a letter to Mr Corbyn, they said her comments were "antisemitic and racist".
The MPs said Labour's "current procedures are incapable of dealing with cases involving anti-Semitism in a fair and timely manner".
The group - which includes former shadow minister Ian Austin and former deputy leadership candidate Lucy Powell - called for an independent inquiry into Labour's handling of anti-Semitism.
In response, a Labour Party spokesman said: "Jennie Formby has written to Naz Shah requesting she provides a full explanation of her comments as soon as possible.
"Once this response has been considered, Labour will decide what action to take.

"

The BBC has contacted Ms Shah for comment.
A new delay has hit EU efforts to impose restrictions on US tech giants, after a small country vetoed the EU's draft new digital markets law.
Austria said it wanted to defend its people's data against "unjustified access" by big tech companies.
The draft law, known as the Digital Markets Act (DMA), aims to create a level playing field for online platforms.
EU Industry Chief, Internal Market and Services Commissioner Thierry Brighton said: "I am very disappointed that the Council has not managed to adopt this important file".

"All member states, and in particular, those who blocked - deliberately, I think - this decision, simply to gain time, will have to explain to their citizens why they chose to let monopolisers thrive instead of reinforcing the digital single market".
Thierry Brighton, who is also vice-president of the European Commission, said negotiations would continue.
The DMA was proposed by the European Commission more than two years ago and was finally agreed by the EU Parliament in February.
But it has faced opposition from a number of EU member states, including Sweden, Denmark and Norway who have threatened to veto it.
Smaller countries with a thriving tech sector, such as Estonia, have also expressed concerns that the law will hinder innovation and entrench the dominance of big tech.

The DMA is one of a number of initiatives aimed at curbing the power of Big Tech in the EU, alongside the Digital Services Act, which aims to create a safer digital space, and the proposed Artificial Intelligence Act.
But all these projects have been hit by delays, with the DMA's adoption now pushed back by at least six months.
Former Southampton manager Harry Redknapp is set to return to the Premier League club in an advisory role.
The 70-year-old will work under director of football operations Richard Hill, with whom he worked at Saints between 2008 and 2009.
Redknapp guided Saints to promotion to the Premier League via the play-offs in his first season before leaving in December 2009.
He has also managed the likes of Bournemouth, West Ham, Portsmouth and Tottenham and has been out of management since leaving Birmingham City in the summer of 2017.

Southampton confirmed the appointment on social media, with Redknapp saying: "Delighted to be back where it all started for me management wise with Saints."

Hill added: "I am delighted to be working with Harry again.

I enjoyed working with him when I was a player and appreciate the expertise and knowledge he will bring back into the club."

Redknapp's return to St Mary's comes 18 years after he resigned as Saints manager in January 2004, with the club 16th in the Premier League table.
They were eventually relegated that season but Redknapp returned for a successful spell between 2008 and 2009, reaching the FA Cup final in 2002, where they lost to Arsenal.
The government has been accused of creating a new "culture of fear" after unveiling new measures to tackle terrorism.
The Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015 gives authorities extra powers to restrict terrorist suspects' freedom.
It allows for detention warrants, which can impose curfews and restrictions on movements.
The act, introduced in the Queen's Speech, will also restrict the freedoms of those who have returned from fighting in Syria.
They will be barred from mixing with members of the public unless they are with family members.
The measures have been widely welcomed by MPs, but human rights group Liberty has raised concerns.
Its director, Martha Spurrier, said the "sweeping" measures would create a "hostile environment" and a "culture of fear".
She added: "This will not make us safer.
It is time to bring the threat from terrorism back down to size.

"

The act will also introduce a new power to stop suspects from travelling abroad, with magistrates able to impose a range of travel restrictions.
These could include restricting an individual's movements within the UK or stopping them from boarding flights.
Ministers said the measures were needed to tackle the "evolving threat" from terrorism.
The legislation will be introduced when Parliament returns from its summer recess next week.
The government has already faced criticism for its plans to make it harder to return to the UK for people who have fought in Syria.
It plans to create a scheme which will allow the home secretary to strip the British citizenship of dual nationals if they receive a sentence of more than six years for terrorism-related offences.
The 28-year-old sister of one of the London Bridge attackers has asked not to be stripped of her British citizenship as she faces deportation from the UK.
Khawla Barghouthi, who has lived in the UK since she was a child, has 20 days to leave the country after her request for asylum was rejected.
Her brother, Said, was one of three attackers who killed eight people when they struck in June last year.

Volkswagen is considering opening a new factory in India to boost its production capacity amid a surge in demand for cars in the country, a senior company official has said.
Rudolf Hellwege, chief executive of Volkswagen India, said that the company was studying the possibility of setting up a new plant in India.
"We are studying the possibility of where and how to increase our production capacity in India.
Once we take a decision, we will inform you," Hellwege told reporters on the sidelines of an event in the southern Indian city of Chennai.
Volkswagen already has a plant in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh with an annual production capacity of 1.4 lakh cars.

The company has been witnessing a rise in demand for its cars in India, especially for its hatchback Polo and sedan Vento, amid a gradual recovery in the country's automotive industry from a pandemic-induced slowdown.
Hellwege said that the company was also considering setting up a battery manufacturing plant in India as part of its plans to introduce more electric vehicles (EVs) in the country.
"As part of our EV strategy, we are looking at components, whether it is batteries or others.
In that direction, we are studying possibilities and how to create a good ecosystem in India," he added.
US employers added 233,000 jobs in May, according to the country's Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The figure was well above most economists' expectations.
And job growth for the previous two months was higher than first thought, the bureau said.
The data showed that the number of unemployed people looking for work decreased by 342,000 to 6.1 million.
The unemployment rate remained unchanged at 3.6% percent, near a 50-year low.
Average hourly earnings increased by 5.2% year-on-year, unchanged from April.
Price increases appear to be moderating, raising hopes that the Fed might pause its interest rate increases.
The jobs figures are good news for President Joe Biden, whose approval ratings have risen in recent months.

UK's National Gallery in the pink

London's National Gallery has reopened after a major renovation of its main building, which has taken nearly five years and £215m.

The gallery in Trafalgar Square has been closed since August 2018, except for a brief period in the run-up to Christmas 2020, when it reopened for a few weeks.
The refurbishment of the Grade I listed building has seen improvements to ventilation, lighting and accessibility.
New spaces have also been created, including a Creativity Studio and dedicated spaces for learning and interpretation.
The gallery's directors said it was "an important moment for the National Gallery".
"This is, at heart, a project about access and inclusion," said Nicholas Penny, director of the National Gallery.
"We have created a beautiful space for everyone to enjoy.

"

The gallery boasts one of the greatest collections of European art in the world, with masterpieces from Leonardo da Vinci, Rembrandt, Vincent van Gogh and Claude Monet among its holdings.
Tiles in the main entrance have been cleaned or replaced, while ventilation has been improved in galleries and new lighting installed.
A new Learning Centre has opened on the ground floor, along with the Creativity Studio, a space for drawing and other creative activities for visitors of all ages.
A new entrance on Trafalgar Square has been created, while the St. Martin's Entrance off Orange Street has been renovated.
The East Wing has been partially reopened, with the new entrance on Trafalgar Square opening up that part of the building.
The East Wing will fully reopen in the autumn, along with the rest of the building.
The gallery said it had achieved a "world-class" environmental standard, and that it was on track to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2030.
Works of art from the collection have been lent to museums and galleries around the UK while the building work took place, with some due to remain on loan for several years.
The National Gallery is also due to open a new gallery at the Tate Modern in October, which will show experimental and interdisciplinary works from the collection.

DVD players equipped with Blu-ray's high-definition video will hit the US market on Tuesday, marking what many see as the final victory for the Blu-ray disc format in its two-year-long battle with HD DVD.
The decision by Sony to release the first batch of Blu-ray players in the US came just over a month after a similar move in Japan.
And with powerful Hollywood studios like Sony and Warner Bros backing the format with a steady stream of high-profile releases, the final death knell for the HD DVD seemed to sound.
The HD DVD camp, however, was not giving up without a fight.
A $99 (£50) player and an aggressive release schedule of big-name films, including Batman Begins and The Incredible Hulk, seemed to have reversed some of the momentum Blu-ray had built up.
And despite massive financial losses, HD DVD's backers were optimistic the format would eventually win out.
"This is a marathon, not a sprint," said a Toshiba America spokesman.
"When you look at the number of players sold worldwide, we are very confident the HD DVD format will prevail.

"

However, that confidence was dealt a blow yesterday when Netflix, the online DVD rental service, announced it was ending its HD DVD service immediately and focusing on Blu-ray.
The move by Netflix, which has over six million subscribers, is being seen as a major boost for Blu-ray.
"We think Blu-ray has now won the war," said Netflix chief executive Reed Hastings.
"Sony hasn't declared victory yet but in practical terms it seems that Blu-ray has won," he added.
Toshiba said it was "disappointed" at Netflix's decision.
The company said it had no plans to pull the plug on its HD DVD players and recorders, and noted that it had recently released a new range of HD DVD products.
A Toshiba spokesman said the company was "committed to the HD DVD format and will continue to work with our industry partners to make HD DVD widely available to consumers".
The spokesman added that Toshiba had no plans to reduce the prices of its HD DVD players "at this time".
Amazon and Best Buy, two of the biggest US retailers, have already indicated they will stock Blu-ray products exclusively.
And software makers are increasingly releasing films only on Blu-ray, further undermining the already precarious future of HD DVD.
Belgian tennis player Kim Clijsters is likely to play in the Australian Open in January, eight months after announcing her retirement, local media report.
The former world number one, 36, retired after the US Open in September but has since dropped the retirement clause in her tennis contract.
Organisers of the Australian Open expect her to compete in the tournament at Melbourne Park early in the new year.
Clijsters won the Australian Open in 2011 and the US Open in 2005, 2009 and 2010.
Her retirement in September ended her career 14 years after her Grand Slam debut in Paris in 2001.
Northern Irish band Snow Patrol have said they are "humbled" after being honoured with the lifetime achievement award at the Meteor Choice Music Awards in Dublin.
The four-piece from Bangor, County Down, received the trophy at Saturday's event at the 3Arena.
They joined other winners including Soulé, who was named best Irish act, and Taylor Swift, who won best international act.
Snow Patrol formed in 1993 and released a string of top 10 albums, including Eyes Open and Final Straw.
The band went on a hiatus in 2011 before reuniting in 2015.
"We are genuinely humbled by this, Snow Patrol have been a band for 21 years and we have been so lucky," said singer and songwriter Gary Lightbody as he accepted the award.
"We're a boy band," he joked, referring to the band's line-up of himself, Johnny McDaid, Nathan Connolly and Tom Simpson.
He added: "We've made something that has lasted... in Northern Ireland, in Ireland and in the UK and all over the world."
The band played a number of hits at the event, including Run, Chasing Cars and You're All I Have Left.
Their success has been echoed by other Northern Irish bands including Two Door Cinema Club and Ash.

"It's been an amazing year for Irish music and Irish musicians, not just the ones that have been successful for the last number of years, but also the new acts that are coming," said Radio 1 breakfast show host Greg James, who hosted the event.
"It is an absolute pleasure for me to be here...
it is one of my favourite places to come," he added.
Jamie Foxx and Hilary Swank have won the acting gongs at the Golden Globe awards.
Best actor in a drama went to Foxx for his role in Ray, while best actress in a drama went to Swank for her part in Million Dollar Baby.
Best actor in a musical or comedy was awarded to Leonardo DiCaprio for The Aviator, and best actress in a musical or comedy went to Annette Bening for Being Julia.
The awards were announced at a ceremony in Los Angeles.
Qatar has signed a $6.76bn deal with Shell to produce and sell liquefied natural gas (LNG) to the UK and Poland for the next 15 years.
The deal comes as many European countries are trying to wean themselves off gas supplied by Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.
Qatar is the world's biggest LNG exporter and has been steadily expanding its production facilities.
Shell said the deal with state-owned Qatar Energy would help provide UK and Polish customers with a reliable source of energy.
The deal involves the supply of three million tonnes of LNG annually to Poland and the UK from Qatar's North Field LNG expansion projects.
The first LNG is expected to be delivered in 2026.
A request from a group of activists for a massive peace demonstration in London has been rejected.
The Right to Demonstrate campaign had asked for permission to hold a 100,000-strong rally in the British capital later this year.
Home Secretary Theresa May said the request did not come from representative organisations.
The group had asked to hold the rally in November, to coincide with the International Day of Peace.
In a letter to the campaign, Mrs May said the request could not be granted as the activists were not "national campaign organisations".

The Home Office said such a demonstration would cause "significant disruption" and the request had not come from "national representative organisations or from bodies representative of the diversity of British society".
The letter, from Mrs May and Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg, added that there was "no mechanism in existence for assessing the merits of the proposal".
The Right to Demonstrate campaign had argued the demonstration was needed to demand an end to Britain's "foreign policy of conflict".
Spokesman Andrew Burgin said the group would consider its response before deciding on any future action.
"We are determined that the government should listen to the demand of the British people for a demonstration calling for peace," he said.
Film composer John Williams is to be honoured at the Academy Awards for his work in the movie industry.
The 95-year-old has composed the music for more than 100 films including Star Wars and Jurassic Park.
He will be awarded the Academy's highest honour, the Irving G. Thalberg Award.
The award is given annually to "a creative producer whose body of work has consistently reflected a devotion to excellence in film.

"

Williams has won five previous Oscars across a career that has spanned seven decades.
He has received 52 Academy Award nominations, second only to Walt Disney.
"John Williams is one of the greatest composers in the history of film music," said Ray Beckett, conductor of the Chamber Orchestra of Ireland.
"His music has been instrumental in the success of many films, and he has inspired generations of musicians and film-makers alike."
The composer has created many of the most recognisable film scores in history, from Jaws to Star Wars, Harry Potter to Jurassic Park.
His music has also been heard in many of the most popular movies of all time, including E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Superman, Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Schindler's List.
Williams has also composed the music for many award-winning documentaries and short films, as well as for television and theatre productions.
The composer retired from scoring film soundtracks in 2021.
The 64th Academy Awards will take place in Los Angeles on 27 March.

Google has signed deals with several major libraries to scan their collections and make them available online.
The libraries of Harvard, Stanford, University of Michigan, and the University of California at Berkeley will be digitised.
A statement from Google did not reveal the financial terms of the agreements.
The company said it planned to digitise "several million" pages per year.
The libraries will be scanned in the company's book scanning centre in Mountain View, California.
Google will then provide digital copies to the libraries, which can be viewed by people accessing their websites.
The project is part of Google's ongoing book partnership programme.
The company has already digitised more than 15 million pages from libraries in the US and from museums and other cultural institutions.
Ole Gunnar Solskjaer has raised hopes that he will one day return to manage Manchester United.
The Norwegian, who currently coaches Norwegian club Molde, made 207 appearances for United and scored 126 goals between 1996 and 2007.
"I'm a Man Utd fan forever and I'll always follow them and I've said that if one day the chance is there, then who knows?"
he told the BBC.
Solskjaer, 45, stepped down as manager of Cardiff City in 2014, shortly after a turbulent period in the Welsh club's history ended with relegation from the Premier League.
He was appointed as manager of Molde in 2015 and led the club to their first title in his first season in charge.
"I'm a Man U fan, of course I want them to win and I want Ole to do well, but it's not easy," he added.
"It's a hard job and I think he knows that.
It's a challenge for Ole, with the club and the players he's got."

Daniela Hantuchova reached the last eight of the Dubai Championships with a straight-set victory over Marion Bartoli.
The 27-year-old Hantuchova, who has slipped to 58 in the world rankings, beat the French sixth seed 6-2 6-4.

Sound baffles you, pictures fade into the daytime, and the screen itself is never quite big enough.
But help is now at hand - in the form of a £250,000 home cinema.
British company CinemaTech is offering an all-in-one home cinema in a box.

The company's founder, Julian Clarke, demonstrates in his demo room.

"

Egypt and Israel have agreed to a trade deal after more than a year of negotiations, Egyptian and Israeli officials say.
The deal, which was signed in Cairo, will see Egypt become Israel's largest trading partner in the Middle East, with total trade expected to reach $1bn (£640m) within five years.
Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed the deal ahead of a visit next month by US President Donald Trump.
Trump has urged stronger relations between the two countries.
Egypt suspended relations with Israel in 2007, following Israel's offensive in Gaza.
Full diplomatic ties were restored in March last year.

The latest deal will see tariffs on most products traded between the two countries cut to 0-10% within five years, and Israel will invest $500m in projects in Egypt over the next three years, according to Israeli officials.
Egypt is already Israel's largest African trading partner.
Last week, Sisi made a rare visit to an Arab country, travelling to the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
He agreed to forge closer economic ties with the UAE during his meeting with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Zayed al-Nahyan.
The UAE announced a $10bn fund for investment in Egypt a few days later.

The Norwich midfielder has been a key player for Scotland since Steve Clarke took over as manager and his absence will be a huge disappointment to the national coach.

Film director Spike Lee has backed a group of students who have been banned from filming a TV advert about racial profiling in the UK.
The College of Production Assistants (CPA) rejected the script for the short film, which features the experiences of three British Asian men.
The students, from the University of West London, plan to go ahead with the project.
Spike Lee, who won an Oscar in 2019, has offered to pay for the film to be finished.
The CPA, which licenses commercial production assistants in the UK, rejected the script for the short film because it was "too political".
The script for the film, called Trigger, features three British Asian men who share their experiences of being stopped by the police because of their race.
One of the men, Anjam Singh, said he was detained and strip-searched after being mistaken for a terrorist while travelling to London from India.
Another, Shahlaa Ahmed, said he was repeatedly stopped by police while driving a car with tinted windows.
The students have launched a crowdfunding page to raise money for the film and have received support from Spike Lee.
The Oscar-winning director has offered to finish the film if they are unable to do so.
In a tweet, he said: "I'm so excited & proud of u guys, u have accomplished what others couldn't, by making something real, raw & provocative!"
The students have raised more than £8,000 ($10,600) - double their original target - in just two days.
Mahad Ahmed, who is behind the project, said he was grateful for Lee's support.
"It means a lot, not only to me but to my colleagues as well, we're meant to be in our 20s and he's been in the industry for 50 years
and he's still passionate about the issues we're talking about right now," he said.
"We all grew up watching his films and cannot believe he has offered to pay for post-production services for our short."

Desktop photo printers are not new.

But an emerging trend toward producing professional-looking prints from desktop printers has prompted printer manufacturers to develop a new generation of photo printers that produce bigger, better-quality prints, in colours that last.
These new photo printers have a big advantage over the old ones.
They can print on a variety of media, not just on plain paper or special glossy photo paper.
With some units, you can print on canvas, transparent film for transparencies, and even T-shirts.

This versatility is expanding the market for photo printers beyond the traditional snapshooter to include professional photographers and artists who want to produce proofs, exhibition prints or prints for sale to customers.
These printers are also affordable.
You can buy a basic unit for less than £200 ($286).
Of course, if you want the best-quality prints, you have to pay more - perhaps £1,000 ($1,429) or more.
There are disadvantages, however.
Photo printers are slower than standard desktop printers.
They also use a lot of ink and special papers or cartridges can be expensive.
One of the biggest problems for photo printers is that the ink does not always dry quickly, especially on glossy paper.
Prints can also fade quickly, especially when exposed to light.
Finally, the prints from some printers sometimes have an uneven, streaky look, due to the way the ink is sprayed on to the page.

But despite these problems, desktop photo printers are getting better all the time and are likely to play an increasingly important role in the future as digital photography becomes more and more popular.

Lufthansa returns to profit as aviation industry recovers

Germany's Lufthansa has posted its first annual profit since 2019, as the easing of pandemic restrictions helped an increase in passenger numbers.
The airline said it made a net profit of €172m (£148m) in the 12 months to 31 December.
It was boosted by cost-cutting and the return of lucrative long-haul flights.
The group, which also owns Brussels and Swiss airlines, flew 71% of pre-pandemic capacity in 2022.
Chief executive Carsten Spohr said: "Despite the various headwinds prevailing in 2022, we achieved a respectable result.

"

The group, which is based in Frankfurt, accelerated its cost-cutting in 2022 as it struggled with rising fuel costs in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
It reduced its fuel bill by 26% after negotiating lower prices with suppliers.
Fuel is the biggest single cost at most airlines, often accounting for more than a quarter of their total operating expenses.

Lufthansa said it was too early to forecast whether it would achieve a profit in 2023, given the uncertainty created by the war in Ukraine, but it expected to reach break-even for the year as a whole.
The news comes as airlines struggle to cope with a surge in demand for flights after two years of Covid travel restrictions.
Airlines and airports have been plagued by cancellations and delays since the start of the year as they struggle to recruit enough staff after cutting thousands of jobs during the pandemic.
This has led to the cancellation of more than 2,700 flights from London's five main airports last week, according to data from aviation data specialist Cirium.
EasyJet on Tuesday raised its forecast for flight capacity in the first half of the year to 65-70% of pre-pandemic levels, up from 60-65%.
The budget airline said it had seen strong demand for holidays in the wake of the relaxation of Covid testing rules for travellers returning to the UK.
