The former England midfielder has been heavily linked with the vacancy at Goodison Park since Benítez's departure on 16 January.
Gerrard has made an impressive start to his managerial career since leaving Liverpool's Under-18s setup in November 2018 to take charge of Rangers.
He led the Ibrox club to the Scottish title in his first campaign and avoided defeat in his first 92 league games in charge before eventually losing his record unbeaten run in March 2021.
Gerrard is understood to have been keen on a return to the Premier League and the 41-year-old is regarded as the ideal candidate for Everton's new majority shareholder, Farhad Moshiri.
Benítez was appointed as Everton's manager in the summer of 2021 but after a bright start to his tenure, the team's form declined.

During the recent festive period, Everton won just one of their six Premier League matches and, despite their 2-1 victory over Chelsea on 28 December, Benítez ultimately paid the price for the Toffees' poor run of results.
Everton are currently 16th in the table, two points above the relegation zone, and face an uphill task to survive this season's relegation dogfight.
They have conceded a league-high 42 goals in just 21 matches and have scored fewer goals than all but two other top-flight teams.
Gerrard leaves Villa, who are 12th in the table, after just over three months in charge.
The former Liverpool captain led the club to an FA Cup third-round tie against Manchester United at Old Trafford on 8 January but they were knocked out following a 3-0 defeat.

The 41-year-old took over at Villa on 11 November following the sacking of Dean Smith, who had led the club into the Premier League via the play-offs the previous season but came under increasing pressure following a poor start to the campaign.
Gerrard won his first four matches at the helm but Villa then suffered three consecutive league defeats, including a 3-1 loss at home to Manchester City on 15 January.
Nigeria's Ese Brume has won Olympic silver and bronze medals in the long jump and Brume's compatriot, Tobi Amusan, has gone one better, taking Olympic gold in the women's 100 metres hurdles in Tokyo.
Now, they may have company.

Blessing Oborududu, who won a silver medal in the 96kg category in Tokyo, and Ese Brume have been named in a nine-strong squad that will represent Nigeria at the 2023 European Wrestling Championships in Moscow, Russia, from 23-30 April.

They are joined by 2018 Commonwealth Games champion Odunayo Adekuruoye, who will be aiming to add to her gold medal collection, including the 2019 African Games, the 2022 Commonwealth Games and the 2021 Islamic Solidarity Games.
Another standout name on the list is 1996 Olympic champion Chioma Ajunwa, who has been selected in the 68kg category.
The squad also includes 2016 Olympic finalist Sinivie Boltic, who will be aiming to go one better than her silver medal finish in the 68kg category when she competed at the 2019 World Championships.
Meanwhile, Commonwealth champion John Emmanuel has been named in the 74kg category alongside veteran wrestler Soso Tamarau, who has competed at four Olympic Games.
Their experiences will come in handy as Nigeria aims to improve on its best-ever finish of joint- seventh at the 2022 Championships in Budapest, Hungary.
England coach Eddie Jones blamed "laundry issues" after he made six changes to his starting line-up for Saturday's Test against France in Paris.
Jonny May and Jack Nowell - who both scored in the 44-8 win over Scotland - are two of those to drop out, with Joe Cokanasiga and Anthony Watson coming in on the wings.
There are also starts for Sam Underhill and Courtney Lawes in the forward pack, with Tom Curry shifting to number eight and Mark Wilson dropping to the bench.
England, who lead the Six Nations table with nine points, face France at 20:00 GMT on Saturday.

The announcement has been met with widespread praise, with many fans and athletes alike counting down the days until the game.
The north v south game is a historic sporting event that dates back to the early days of the Australian rules football league.
It is a game that pits the best players from the northern and southern states of Australia against each other in a thrilling display of athleticism and skill.
Past north v south games have produced some of the most memorable moments in Australian rules football history.
With the game now set to return in 2024, fans can expect to see even more thrilling action on the field.
Tickets for the game are expected to sell out quickly, so fans are encouraged to get in early to avoid disappointment.
With the game set to be held in Sydney's iconic Olympic Stadium, it promises to be a must-see event for sports fans everywhere.

Therapist Louis Thompson is the man responsible for the All Blacks' mental preparation and has been working with the team since 2008.
He is also the person who came up with the idea of using the ancient Maori war dance, the Haka, to focus the team's minds on the task at hand.
"It's a therapy that I've developed over the last eight or nine years working with the All Blacks," he said.
"It's a cognitive therapy, so it's a way of thinking about things and dealing with the mental side of sport.
It's designed to help players focus on the right things, to help them be in the present, to help them block out distractions and to help them perform at their best."
While the All Blacks have always incorporated the Haka into their pre-match routine, Thompson's addition of the war dance as a therapeutic tool has taken it to another level.
"We use the Haka as a therapy because it's such a powerful symbol of New Zealand and it's a great way to get guys thinking about what's important," he said.
"It's a great way to connect with our culture and our history and it's also a great way to energize ourselves and get ready for the game."

Thompson believes that the Haka therapy has been a key factor in the All Blacks' success in recent years, as they have won the last two Rugby World Cups and are currently ranked number one in the world.
"I think it's been a big part of our success," he said.
"It's helped us to focus on the right things and to block out distractions and it's helped us to perform at our best when it matters most."
Whether it's the Haka therapy or just the natural talent of the players, the All Blacks will be hoping that their magical secret weapon will continue to inspire them to success in the years to come.

Owen, who spent six years at Anfield after moving from Everton in 1996, is currently without a club having ended his brief stint at Manchester United at the end of last season.
The 32-year-old had been training with former club Newcastle in a bid to maintain his fitness but has still to decide his future.
Souness, the Reds' director of football, has not ruled out offering the striker a contract.
He said: "Michael is a Liverpool player in my eyes.
If he wants to come back to Liverpool I'd be inclined to try to do something.

"It might be that he just wants to play for a year and then finish, but if he is looking for a long-term contract I'd be interested."

Owen left Liverpool in 2004 and has since had spells with Real Madrid, Newcastle and Manchester United.
Rory O'Sullivan honed his skills on the snooker tables of his local working men's club as a teenager, now he is ready to burst onto the world stage at the sport's top tournament.

The 32-year-old from Cambridge will arrive at the Betfred World Championship as the biggest outsider in the field but with the confidence and potting prowess to cause a seismic shock at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield.
O'Sullivan has taken the back door into snooker's biggest event, having failed to win enough matches in other tournaments this season to automatically qualify for the World Championship.
But victory over experienced Australian Neil Robertson in the final qualifying round has given him a shot at the sport's biggest prize.
The tournament begins on Saturday with O'Sullivan facing Asian number one Ding Junhui, who is ranked sixth in the world.
Despite his lowly ranking of 29th, O'Sullivan goes into the match in confident mood.
He has been in fine form in qualifying, dispatching of Robertson, a former world number one, 3-1, and scoring a tournament high break of 142 in the process.
His run has galvanised a sport that has been searching for a new hero since the retirement of six-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan.

The prospect of a new rivalry between two players named O'Sullivan has the potential to capture the imagination of the sporting public and breathe life into a sport desperate for a lift after a year of financial uncertainty.
"It's amazing to have so many people wanting to come and watch me play, I suppose it's because of the name," said Rory O'Sullivan.
"But I'm sure they would rather it was a lower ranked player they were watching.

I'm just happy to have the opportunity to play and hopefully I can put on a good show."

O'Sullivan has been around the circuit for a number of years, but a combination of a debilitating illness and a lack of confidence has seen his progress stagnate.
But having got his body and mind into shape, he is now reaping the rewards.
"I was never a natural, I had to work very hard at the game from a young age," he said.
"My local club had one table and I would often queue up to play.
I was lucky if I got an hour's practice a day, but it was enough.
I have always had the dedication and application, but not the self-belief.
I think achieving that balance with my health has made a big difference."
The UK economy is facing a host of "major risks", the Bank of England's governor has said.
Andrew Bailey said the risks included high global inflation, rising interest rates and continuing supply chain problems.
He said the situation in Ukraine and China's Covid response were also among factors which posed a threat to the UK.
Mr Bailey's comments came as the Bank of England announced it was holding interest rates at their current record low of 0.1%.
Dairy group Parmalat will float on the Milan stock exchange next month, eight years after its biggest bankruptcy recovery in Italian history.
The company said shares would be sold in an initial public offering (IPO) at between €2.50 and €3 each, valuing the business at up to €8.5bn ($9bn).
The offering is expected to include a secondary sale of existing shares by its current owner, the Lactalis dairy group.
Lactalis bought Parmalat in 2011 for €1.5bn after it collapsed under the weight of a €14.3bn debt fraud.
The company was founded in 1961 by Sicilian entrepreneur Calisto Tanzi as a maker of stretched-curd cheeses, such as mozzarella.
It grew rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s through a series of acquisitions, becoming a global dairy giant.
However, it collapsed in 2003 after an audit revealed that Mr Tanzi had been using fraudulent accounting practices to conceal a €14.3bn debt.
The company was placed under administration and Mr Tanzi was sentenced to prison.
The administrator who oversaw the turnaround, Enrico Bondi, kept the company in private hands after Lactalis' purchase.
Parmalat returned to profit in 2013 and has paid off most of its debt.
The company's products include Lactalis' President brand of cheeses in France, as well as Parmalat-branded milk in Italy.
It also makes yoghurts and other dairy products.
Parmalat's IPO would be the biggest in Milan for three years and the largest ever IPO on the Italian stock exchange, according to Reuters.
The chairman of Euronext has reportedly written to the board of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) urging it to engage in discussions about a possible merger.
The letter from Stéphane Boujnah follows interest from the LSE in acquiring Refinitiv, the financial data provider that is currently owned by a consortium including Blackstone.

Blackstone has indicated it would prefer Refinitiv to be sold to a single buyer and sources close to the matter have said the LSE may be willing to sell its majority stake in Borsa Italiana to facilitate a deal.
Euronext's move marks the latest development in the potential overhaul of the $14 trillion global foreign-exchange market.
Refinitiv is the largest seller of market data to banks, providing stock market quotes, news and analytics.
Its subsidiary, Tradeweb, is one of the biggest platforms for trading bonds.
Sources close to the matter say that if the LSE pursued both Refinitiv and Borsa Italiana it would constitute a major step in the exchange's push to become a more global business.
It comes after the LSE abandoned its pursuit of Deutsche Börse in 2017 following a lengthy battle and concerns raised by the UK's competition authority.

Black Friday was nominally a week ago, but many retailers have extended their sales.
The BBC's Katie Hope was among the throng in London's West End on Saturday.

Kate Gibbs, from Gloucester, was among those making the most of the sales.
She had been up since 05:00 on Saturday morning, and had already been to several shops.

"

BMW is splashing out £100 million to future-proof the Mini plant in Oxford against the threat of Brexit.
The German car-maker said the investment will create about 1,000 new jobs by 2022 and secure the site's production outlook for the next decade.
The bulk of the money will be spent on upgrading and expanding the plant's facilities including body shops and paint shops.
About £50 million will be for a new "state of the art" paint shop that will be located at the southern side of the site.
The remaining £50 million will be used to upgrade the plant's infrastructure as well as "support an ongoing significant recruitment drive".
The investment comes after BMW warned that a bad Brexit deal could result in the company shifting production to the Netherlands.
Last month, the car-maker announced that it would close its plant in Swindon, with the loss of about 2,500 jobs.
The site in Oxford currently produces about 1,000 Minis a day.
The car plant was originally opened by the British Motor Corporation in the early 1960s.
It was later owned by British Aerospace and BMW took over in 1994.
Trade between China and Japan hit a record high last year, with Beijing displacing Washington as Tokyo's biggest trading partner, official data shows.
According to figures released by Japan's finance ministry, the country's trade surplus with China reached a record $159bn in 2022.
Japan's exports to China rose to $317bn, up from $196bn in 2021, while imports from China hit $158bn, up from $77bn.
The US came second, with Japan running a trade surplus of $103bn with America, down from $146bn the previous year.
Japan's trade surplus with the whole world came in at $911bn, up from $685bn a year earlier.
The data showed that Japan's overall exports rose to $1.4tn, up 20% on the year, while imports rose to $1.2tn, up 25%.
The figures showed that Japan's ratio of public debt to GDP rose to 257.2% in 2022, up from 231.9% in 2021.
Japan has struggled to keep its debt under control amid rising social security and medical costs, as well as the impact of rising energy prices following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

HSBC has become the latest bank to predict that the world's biggest economy will slip into recession next year, with analysts warning that soaring inflation and deteriorating consumer confidence could lead to a "perfect storm".

Although the bank's economists believe that the US Federal Reserve will succeed in bringing down inflation from the current level of around 8% to 4% by the middle of next year, they say that this will be achieved by "crushing" economic growth.
HSBC predicts that the US will slip into recession during the first half of next year, with the Eurozone following suit in the second half.
The gloomy forecast comes as major stock markets around the world enjoy a boom, with the latest example being the London Stock Exchange which earlier this week hit a new record high.
Last week, the chief economist at Goldman Sachs said that the US stock market was "overvalued" by 10-15%, based on comparisons with historical averages.
According to the Bank of America, current stock market levels are among the most overvalued ever, when compared to corporate earnings.
For the last decade, the biggest fight between Russia and the West has been over Ukraine.
But that could soon be eclipsed by a dispute that is decades old, but has taken on new life: the battle for control of Russia's oil and gas.
In the Kremlin, there is growing concern over the role that former Soviet countries play in Europe's energy supply.
Russia supplies more than 30% of Europe's gas and about a quarter of its oil.
Yet those numbers have been dropping.
For example, oil exports to Europe via the Druzhba pipeline, which travels through Ukraine and Belarus, have been declining since 2020.
The drop has been caused by increased competition from suppliers further away, such as Saudi Arabia and the United States.
But it has also been caused by increased political risk.
Belarus has been increasingly drawn into Russia's stand-off with the West over Ukraine.
This has included the Belarusian government's forced landing of a flight between Greece and Lithuania, which allowed the authorities to arrest a dissident journalist who was on board.
Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine have also accused Belarus of encouraging migrants to cross their borders.
In response, the European Union has imposed sanctions on Belarus.
This has caused a dispute with Russia, which relies on Belarus to transport oil to Europe.
In an apparent act of retaliation, Russian state oil company Rosneft announced that it would halt oil exports via the Druzhba pipeline from April 2022.
Europe has also been trying to wean itself off Russian gas.
Unlike oil, most of Russia's gas exports to Europe travel via pipelines that cross Ukrainian territory.
Western countries have accused Russia of using its gas exports as a political tool.
In January, Russian gas exports to Europe dropped to their lowest level since 2016.
The International Energy Agency has predicted that Europe could be free of Russian gas imports by the end of this year.
It says increased imports of liquefied natural gas from the US and Qatar, as well as increased production from Norway and Algeria, could achieve this.
Russia's response has been to accelerate the completion of two new pipelines that will bypass Ukraine.
The first of these, Nord Stream 2, directly connects Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea.
The second, the TurkStream, will go through Turkey and into southern Europe.
These pipelines represent a major geopolitical victory for Russia.
Yet they also undercut the country's main leverage point against the West: its control over gas transit through Ukraine.

Among the many fees that banks in China have been accused of charging without proper disclosure, the most common by far is something called a "financial holding fee" — in essence, a penalty for having money in an account.
In recent months, thousands of people have taken to social media to complain about being charged this fee, estimating that banks have taken billions of yuan from customers unfairly.
But in a country of 1.4 billion, where transparency on these charges is scarce, the exact number is difficult to ascertain.
Here's what little we know.

China's financial holding fees are essentially a way for banks to penalize depositors for holding above-threshold amounts of money in their accounts — in essence, a way to squeeze excess liquidity out of the financial system.
They were first introduced in 2013, and since then, the threshold — the amount of money that triggers the fee — has risen steadily.
This year, it stood at 123,000 yuan ($17,700) for urban banks and 87,000 yuan for rural banks, though the amount charged varies by bank.

China's central bank, the People's Bank of China (PBOC), has repeatedly urged banks to disclose these fees more clearly, warning that the lack of transparency could hurt the reputation of the financial system and undermine market confidence.
But so far, the PBOC has declined to say explicitly whether the banks are acting within the law, and regulators have yet to take any action against them.
House prices fell for the sixth month in a row in November, according to a survey of estate agents.
The average price of homes sold through estate agents was £296,000, down by 1.5% compared with October, said property website Rightmove.
It said the market had "definitely cooled" in the past month, with buyer demand falling to its lowest level since January.
Rightmove's house price index tracks the asking prices of property advertised on its website.
It is a closely watched measure of the health of the UK property market, but does not capture the entire market.
The figures come after Bank of England figures last week showed that mortgage approvals had fallen to their lowest level since June 2020.
Approvals for house purchases in October were 67,000, down from 71,000 in September, according to the Bank.
That was below the 12-month average of 72,000, and the lowest figure since June 2020, when the housing market was shut down for part of the month due to the Covid pandemic.
Martin Beck, senior economic adviser to the EY Item Club, said: "Households are increasingly worried about the rising cost of living, and this is starting to impact the housing market."

He said that higher interest rates and inflation, which is currently at a 40-year high, had "increased the squeeze on household budgets", meaning that people "have less money to spend on big-ticket items like homes".
But he said that it was not all "doom and gloom" for the property market, as there was still a "significant number" of people looking to buy a home.
"While the number of property sales has slowed, this will not be reflected in house prices until next year, as it takes time for transactions to work their way through the system," he said.

Separate figures from the Government's Land Registry, which records the final sale price of properties, showed that average UK house prices rose by 5.8% in the year to September, down from 7.3% in the year to August.

The sharp rise in fuel prices in recent months has had a significant impact on US airlines, with some carriers forced to cut flights and others struggling to keep up with the increased cost of operation.
The situation has been further exacerbated by the ongoing pandemic, which has reduced demand for air travel and made it difficult for airlines to raise prices to cover the increased cost of fuel.

One of the most affected airlines has been Southwest Airlines, which has been forced to cut its flight schedule by up to 20% in the coming months due to the increased cost of fuel and the decrease in demand for air travel.
The airline has also announced that it will be reducing its fleet by retiring older aircraft and delaying the delivery of new planes.
American Airlines has also been hit hard by the rising fuel costs, with the company's CEO, Doug Parker, stating that the airline is struggling to keep up with the increased cost of operation.
Parker has called on the US government to take action to help the airline industry, including the implementation of a tax break for airlines to help them cover the increased cost of fuel.
The rise in fuel costs has also had an impact on the price of airline tickets, with some carriers forced to raise prices to cover the increased cost of operation.
This has led to a decrease in demand for air travel, as many consumers have chosen to delay their trips until prices decrease.

Overall, the combination of rising fuel costs and the ongoing pandemic has had a significant impact on US airlines, with some carriers forced to cut flights and others struggling to keep up with the increased cost of operation.
It remains to be seen how the situation will develop in the coming months and whether government action will be taken to help the industry.
A group of investors including Microsoft Corp co-founder Paul Allen has admitted to bribing officials in Benin to allow them to build a controversial port in the West African country.
The project, which was negotiated in 2013, would see the construction of a much-needed deep-water port in the country but has been plagued by allegations of corruption.

The investors, which also include Israeli firm BSG and the Bolloré Group, a French transportation company, admitted to US authorities that they paid bribes to Beninese officials but claimed the bribes were commonplace in the country and essential to do business.
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) fined the group $778m.
The fine will be paid by BSG and Bolloré, with Allen's company, Vulcan, paying approximately $43m.
The fine is thought to be the largest ever levied against foreign officials.

Benin's government has claimed the port will bring much-needed jobs and infrastructure to the country but has faced stiff opposition from locals who say it will displace thousands of people and destroy cultural heritage sites.
The project is yet to begin and it is unclear if the latest developments will affect its status.
Sales and prices of homes in Britain have fallen for the first time since the pandemic began, industry figures show.
The price of a typical UK property fell by 0.9% in September, compared with a 0.4% rise in August, according to building society Nationwide.
It said the market had "lost some momentum" as lenders worried about the economic headwinds facing the country.
The number of mortgages approved for house purchases fell to their lowest level since April 2021, according to banking body UK Finance.
It does not expect the market to return to record levels seen earlier this year.
The trend is the same in London, where prices have fallen by 1.2% in September, compared with a 0.5% rise in August, according to the Nationwide figures.
The capital saw the biggest fall in activity, with the number of mortgages approved for house purchases in London dropping to its lowest level since December 2000.
Activity has slowed despite the government's recent decision to pause the imposition of a 1.25% tax on the value of people's homes in England that would have come into effect next month.
From next year, people buying a property in England worth more than £250,000 will have to pay an extra 2% in stamp duty, on top of the 3% they already pay.
But the tax holiday on the first £250,000 of any property purchase in England, which was due to end on 30 September, will continue until March next year.

The Korean government has announced a spending package worth $430bn as officials warned that without urgent measures, the economy would shrink by more than 1% next year and fall into a technical recession.
The announcement followed data showing that in the third quarter of 2022, the economy contracted by 0.4%.
It added to concerns that the economy is slowing after growth slowed to 0.7% in the second quarter.
"The economy is facing serious challenges," said finance minister Choo Kyung-ho.
"This package is a pre-emptive, transformational investment for the future.

"

The plan includes money for public sector pay rises, subsidies for heating costs, and a one-off payment for families with children.
There will also be funds available for small businesses struggling with the rise in interest rates, and extra government borrowing has been ruled out.
South Korea is a major player in the global economy as an exporter of semiconductors which are used in products ranging from smartphones to cars.
But its economy has been hit by the Covid-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and a slowdown in China, one of its major trading partners.
The government has been reluctant to restore its pandemic stimulus measures for fear of adding to rising inflation.
The central bank has raised interest rates six times since August last year, with the latest hike coming last week when it lifted them to 2.5%.

General Motors and Ford Motor Co. are cutting vehicle production amid falling sales and high inventories as higher borrowing rates, soaring inflation and the war in Ukraine continue to weigh on consumer demand.
GM said on Friday that it would temporarily halt production at eight North American plants for a total of six weeks during the quarter ending March 31.
The company said its daily production will be reduced by about 8,000 vehicles in the first quarter.
The reduction in output will begin this month and will impact truck and SUV plants in Michigan, Kentucky, Tennessee and Mexico.
The company plans to maintain production of its highly profitable full-size pickup trucks and SUVs.
Ford said on Thursday it would cut production of its F-150 pickup truck and two sport utility vehicles (SUVs) because of the falling demand.
Ford said it would shorten shifts at two F-150 assembly plants in Michigan and Missouri.
The company will also idle production lines at its Kentucky truck plant for four weeks in February and March.
Additional reductions are possible in the future, the company said in a statement.
France Telecom has confirmed it has received a approach from its largest shareholder, Orange, about a possible merger.
Orange, which owns more than 23% of the company, has made a number of proposals, France Telecom said in a statement.
These included an all-share merger, a purchase of the government's 15% stake, and the sale of France Telecom's mobile phone division to its rival.

General Motors (GM), the biggest US car maker, issues a profits warning for 2005 amid rising energy and commodity prices.
The warning comes as GM reports a 6% fall in third-quarter profits to $1.6bn (£0.7bn), partly because of a $460m (£230m) increase in steel prices.
In July, GM raised its outlook for the year, saying it expected to post a profit of $2.70 to $2.90 a share.

As a result, many insurers have withdrawn from the market, leaving homeowners with fewer options for coverage.
Those who remain in the market have had to raise their premiums significantly, making insurance unaffordable for many.
The UK government has been criticized for not doing enough to protect homeowners from the impacts of extreme weather.
With climate change expected to lead to more frequent and severe weather events, the situation is only expected to get worse.
Insurers are calling for more investment in flood defenses and other measures to protect homes and businesses from the growing threat of extreme weather.
Despite these challenges, the insurance industry continues to play a vital role in helping individuals and businesses recover from the impacts of extreme weather.
In the future, insurers will need to continue to adapt to the changing climate, with new products and services that address the increasing risk of extreme weather.

The Brazilian real has strengthened against the dollar, with experts suggesting the country's recession has come to an end.
The real gained more than 6% in October, reaching its strongest level in more than two years.
It came after the central bank raised interest rates to their highest level in more than a decade.
And government data showed that the country's inflation rate slowed for a tenth consecutive month in September.

Swiss drugmaker Novartis has agreed to buy France's Advanced Accelerator Applications (AAA) for $4.1 billion (£3.3 billion) to broaden its radiopharmaceuticals business.
Novartis has offered $2.43 billion (£1.95 billion) to buy all shares of AAA, and another $1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) to pay for its cash on hand.
The deal will allow Novartis to expand its expertise in radioactive medicine, which is used to diagnose and treat cancer.

AAA, based in Saint-Genis-Pouilly, near Paris, employs 950 people and specializes in diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceutical products.

Dairy group Parmalat has reported a surge in half-year profits as higher milk prices helped offset increased costs.
The Italian company said it had doubled its earnings to €194m ($208m) in the six months to 30 June, up from €96m a year earlier.
The world's largest dairy exporter attributed the rise to an increase in milk prices, which offset higher fertiliser, energy and feed costs.

South Korea's financial regulator said on Friday that it planned to sell troubled credit card firm Hyundai Card, the country's largest by assets, to bring down soaring household debt.

The Financial Services Commission (FSC) said it planned to sell Hyundai Card - owned by Hyundai Motor Group - to six firms, including Apple Inc, Amazon.com Inc and Samsung Electronics Co Ltd's financial unit, Samsung Financial Services.
The deal, which is expected to be worth about $6 billion, according to a Bloomberg report, will involve a cash injection by the new investors to shore up Hyundai Card's capital base.
The sale is subject to approval by cardholders, the FSC said in a statement.

Hyundai Card, with 6.5 million subscribers, has struggled with a decline in earnings and higher costs after the government capped interest rates on loans to ease debt problems amid rising household borrowing.
The cap has pushed up borrowing costs at Hyundai Card, causing its net profit to fall 91% year-on-year in the first half of 2022.
The six potential buyers will each acquire a 10% stake in Hyundai Card, with the possibility of increasing it to up to 42% depending on their performance, the FSC said.
The sale price for 10% of the firm is expected to be between KRW900 billion ($680 million) and KRW1,000 billion ($800 million), a source with knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
The FSC said the sale was aimed at helping Hyundai Card - whose parent Hyundai Motor Group also owns a stake in Hyundai Capital - to transform itself into a comprehensive financial firm.
The regulator also said it plans to announce a rescue plan for Hyundai Capital, Hyundai Card's sister firm, early next year.
South Korea's financial watchdog asked investors on Sunday to vote on a rescue plan for the country's sixth-largest lender, which some analysts say could trigger a banking crisis.

The Financial Services Commission (FSC) said it would provide a detailed plan this week on how to stabilise the economy after a local court ordered the liquidation of the struggling Savings Bank (SB) on Thursday.
The move sent shockwaves through South Korea's financial markets, prompting the FSC to announce it would work to minimise the economic impact.
Under the proposed plan, the FSC will set up a special purpose company (SPC) that will buy stocks of SB.
The SPC will then sell the bank's assets and liabilities to the government.
The FSC said the plan would "help ensure that there would be no further deterioration of SB's financial health".
It added that the voting process, which would be carried out by investors including the National Pension Service, would be completed by December 10.
Analysts have said the failure of SB could trigger a banking crisis in South Korea, where a series of credit card companies and a mutual savings bank have already been bailed out this year.
SB had been struggling to recover from a series of loan defaults by its shipbuilding clients, which were hit by a slowdown in the global marine industry.
The bank was also hit by allegations of fraud by a former employee, who is accused of forging documents to fraudulently gain loans.
The SPC will be funded by the government and investments from private creditors, and the state will eventually inject fresh capital into the bank, the FSC said.
The government said it would ensure that the stock trading plan would have no impact on the national budget.
But some analysts said the government may have to eventually increase its stake in SB.
"The government may have to turn SB into a public bank in the long run as its financial health would hardly improve," said Kim Dong-gon, a professor of finance at the University of Seoul.
The dollar has hovered around record lows against a basket of other major currencies as markets brace for a pivotal Federal Reserve meeting on Wednesday.

The UK economy is expected to have grown by around 6.5% in 2022, inflation is predicted to have fallen dramatically and unemployment is dropping.
The economy has been dubbed "strong" by ministers and independent forecasters alike, as the UK enjoys its longest period of continuous growth for nearly 200 years.
The question now is whether that strength will continue as the cost of living crisis begins to bite.
The economy grew by 6.7% in 2021 as it recovered from the Covid pandemic, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

It also makes Kahlua and Sauza tequila.
If the deal goes through, Paris-based Pernod Ricard's portfolio would swell to around 40 brands.

The Sunday Times revealed new information about the amount of damage the tsunami caused to Sri Lanka.
The monster wave, which erupted from the Indian Ocean following the eruption of an earthquake, caused devastation to communities along the coast of this Indian Ocean island.
The cost of the disaster has been assessed at $1.3bn.
This includes destruction to roads, buildings and bridges, as well as the country's port in Colombo.
An estimated £300m of this cost is believed to be insurance covered, whilst the remaining £950m will be recouped by foreign aid.
The United Kingdom have pledged to donate £450m, whilst the United States have pledged $200.
French ski equipment maker Rossignol has rejected an unsolicited takeover bid from its larger US rival Quiksilver, saying the offer "very significantly" undervalued the company.
Rossignol said the offer of €2.80 (£2.35) a share did not reflect its growth prospects.
The ski gear industry has been hit by a series of challenges, including the Covid pandemic and climate change.
Last year, Rossignol reported a 7.3% fall in revenue to €96.8m (£85m) for the first half of the year.
Quiksilver said its proposal - which was made on Tuesday - was an "opportunity to create a leading global adventure sports platform".
The US company added that the deal would help Rossignol's financial performance and strengthen its position in the market.

The board of Xstrata has urged shareholders to snub a improved £2.7bn bid from mining rival Glencore, describing the offer as “derisory” and “opportunistic”.

Glencore, which is backed by billionaire trader Marc Rich, made an improved cash-and-shares offer for Xstrata on Saturday, which values its rival at 820p a share, compared with the 800p it proposed earlier this month.
But Xstrata said the offer “significantly undervalued” the company and was “completely unacceptable” to its board.
It also said the offer “failed to address the concerns” it had previously expressed about the proposal.
Xstrata added that Glencore had made the offer at a time when the market was focused on the improving fundamentals of the copper market, where Xstrata is a major player.

It said the bid did not reflect the value of its diversified portfolio of assets and that Glencore’s offer “failed to recognise the value of the synergy benefits that would result from the combination of the two companies”.
Glencore has until 17:00 GMT on Tuesday to make a formal offer for Xstrata, although it can extend that deadline.
One of the biggest bankruptcies in Russian history has taken a new turn with the former oil company Yukos suing four multinational law firms for $20bn.

Yukos, once Russia's largest oil producer, was dismantled and sold off in 2009 after being hit with a $27bn tax bill, which supporters of former CEO Mikhail Khodorkovsky said was politically motivated.

The company is now suing US law firm Cleary Gottlieb, Russian firm Alfa-Law, UK firm Freshfields and Debevoise & Plimpton, claiming they were involved in what it says was a corrupt scheme to expropriate Yukos.
The case, filed at the UK High Court, is based on allegations that the law firms were "involved in, or culpable of, aiding and abetting a conspiracy to corruptly misappropriate assets from Yukos".
Yukos claims that the firms, which have all issued strong denials, were involved in a scheme to drain the company's assets through "the fraudulent scheme of 'trade mark' transactions".
These transactions allegedly involved the sale of Yukos' most valuable assets to firms linked to Moscow's tax authority, which then sold them back to Yukos at a much higher price.
The claims concern events that took place between 1999 and 2004, when Yukos was raided and eventually bankrupted.
Mr Khodorkovsky was jailed on fraud and tax evasion charges, and Yukos was declared bankrupt two years later.
The former executive, once Russia's richest man, is now living in Europe after being released from prison in 2013.
He has always maintained that his imprisonment was politically motivated, and that the charges against him were spurious.
Yukos has already recouped some $9bn from the Russian government, but the new litigation seeks compensation several times larger than that from the law firms.
The BBC has learned that the Chinese firm that was bidding to save Britain's last car maker MG Rover has had its offer delayed by the UK government.
The delay follows concerns being raised in parliament about the suitability of Shanghai Automotive Industry Corporation (SAIC).
It is understood that the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) wants more time to assess SAIC's plans for MG Rover, which went into administration in April.
The government wants to know how many of the company's workforce would keep their jobs, and where the cars would be built.
It is believed that SAIC has asked the DTI to keep the details of its rescue package confidential.
The Chinese company made a formal approach to the administrators several weeks ago and is thought to be the only party still in talks with them.
It is believed that SAIC wants to buy the Longbridge plant in Birmingham and retain a workforce of about 2,000 - mainly engineers - to help design a new range of MG sports cars.
The company also intends to use the site to build its own range of saloon cars which will be sold in Europe.
It is not thought that SAIC has made a formal offer for the company, but administrators PricewaterhouseCoopers (PWC) have said they are confident that a deal can be done.
It is understood that SAIC has requested that the DTI does not make any announcement about the nature of its plans for MG Rover until after the Shanghai motor show at the end of this month.
But a spokesman for the DTI said it was not prepared to make a statement about the Chinese firm's plans until it had carried out a thorough assessment of them.
"We have not been approached by SAIC asking for confidentiality on this matter," he added.
A PWC spokesman said: "We are talking to a number of parties interested in MG Rover and no-one has yet made an offer.
"We are confident that a deal can be done to save the company.

"

The future of MG Rover, which has been making cars at Longbridge for more than 80 years, has been uncertain since it stopped production in April.
More than 6,000 people have lost their jobs at the plant and at dealerships around the UK.
Japan has narrowly avoided slipping into a technical recession, with data showing the economy grew at a 1.2% annual rate in the last quarter.
The world's third-biggest economy contracted by an annualised 2.3% in the third quarter, meaning the latest data represent a rebound.
However, analysts warned that the recovery was fragile given the sharp fall in exports.
And they said the rebound owed much to stock rebuilding after low inventory levels, which could not be sustained in the coming quarters.
Japan's central bank has kept its key interest rate at -0.1% as it holds out hope that the slide in oil prices will finally push up consumer prices after years of deflation.
But it warned that slowing growth in China - a major trading partner - and the Ukraine war posed risks to the outlook.
The former Labour leader made his first speech in the upper chamber of the UK Parliament last week.
The 87-year-old crossbencher introduced a private member's bill - the Climate Change (Enforcement) Bill - on Thursday.
It aims to make sure the UK's target of net zero carbon emissions by 2050 is met.
The bill would criminalise any local or public authority in the UK which failed to draw up plans to meet its carbon emissions targets.
BNP leader Nick Griffin has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to harm.
The 43-year-old was detained at Birmingham Airport on Saturday afternoon.
West Midlands Police said the arrest was linked to an investigation into "alleged racist material" posted online.
The BNP issued a statement saying Mr Griffin had not been suspended and "fully expected" to be released without charge.
The statement added that the party believed the arrest was "motivated by political reasons and the forthcoming local elections".

Mr Brons, a member of the BNP's governing executive committee, is the father of two young children who was born in Britain to a German mother and a British father.
He works for a company making stainless steel equipment for the pharmaceutical industry.
As the BNP's health spokesman, he is a staunch advocate of vaccination against Covid-19.
British Prime Minister Brown has shrugged off fears of a recession, stating that the British economy is " remarkably robust".
Statistics released yesterday showed a surprise 0.2% growth in the last quarter of the year, despite the mounting uncertainty of Brexit and the recent interest rate rises.
Brown stated that he was "delighted" with the news, and that the government was "doing all we can to boost the economy".
The Office for National Statistics showed that the services sector, which includes banking and finance, construction and manufacturing, grew by 0.2% from October to December.
Construction output was particularly strong, with a growth of 2.1% in that sector.
However, economists have warned that the British economy is likely to weaken in the coming months, and that a recession is a strong possibility.
Brown's government has been criticised for its economic policies, with many blaming the recent interest rate rises and the uncertainty surrounding Brexit for the current economic problems.
Councils will be able to increase council tax by 5% without a vote from parliament, after the government dropped a clause from the Levelling Up Bill.
The change would save local authorities about £3bn in the next five years, ministers say.
But Labour, the Liberal Democrats and some Tory MPs criticised the move, saying it would hit poorer households.
The government said the change would give councils "certainty" and allow them to invest in services.
Under current rules, councils that want to raise taxes by more than a certain amount - this year 2% - must hold a referendum.
The government had proposed introducing a new upper limit on council tax increases of 2%, plus an additional 1% to fund social care.
But the plan, which was criticised by MPs on all sides of the House of Commons, was removed from the Levelling Up Bill last week.
Instead ministers introduced a new clause which would increase the existing 3% ceiling on council tax increases to 5%.
The change would mean councils could increase tax by an extra 2% without a vote - on top of this year's 2% rise.
Ministers said the change would save £2.3bn for councils over the next four years and £700m in the fifth year.
They said the savings would be equivalent to putting £170 back into the pockets of the average household by 2026.
But opposition parties have accused the government of putting money ahead of protecting the vulnerable.
Labour's shadow local government secretary, Steve Reed, said the change would have "far reaching consequences for councils and the services they provide".
He added: "Hard-up households will be dismayed that the government has sneaked out this change without any scrutiny, letting councils hike up council tax without a vote."
Lib Dem leader Ed Davey described the move as a "stealth tax bomb", while Tory MP Robert Halfon, who chairs the Commons education select committee, said it was "madness".
"Hard-working families are already feeling the pinch and it is unfair to ask them to pay even more," he added.
But local government minister Marcus Jones said the change would put councils on a "more stable financial footing".
"This gives councils the certainty they need to plan for the future, and the space to invest in their services and their local communities," he added.
The UK government has announced that it will press ahead with plans to introduce identity cards for citizens, despite strong opposition from privacy advocates and civil liberties groups.
The decision has been criticized for its high cost and potential for abuse, with some arguing that it will do little to address the issue of illegal immigration.

The government has argued that the cards will help to reduce crime and increase national security, as well as making it easier for citizens to access services such as healthcare and banking.

They have also raised concerns about the potential for abuse, such as the government using the cards to track citizens' movements and monitor their activities.

The announcement comes as the government faces increasing pressure to tackle the issue of illegal immigration, with recent figures showing that the number of people entering the UK without permission has reached record levels.
Despite this, many have argued that the introduction of ID cards is not the solution, and that the money would be better spent on more effective measures such as strengthening border security.
It remains to be seen whether the government will proceed with the scheme, which has been heavily criticized by both opponents and supporters of the Conservative party.
Britain's beleaguered prime minister is under fresh pressure after a leading backer threatened to withdraw support, and his own brother joined the growing calls for him to resign.

The pound fell sharply against the dollar on Thursday after a key ally of Boris Johnson warned that he could pull his support from the prime minister over a scandal involving Conservative MPs and "lockdown parties" held at Downing Street while ordinary citizens were unable to socialize.

The campaign behind the so-called "cold calls" made to voters in the run-up to the general election has been questioned by the head of the UK statistics agency.
Prof Sir Ian Diamond said the practice of making unsolicited phone calls to voters "undermines" public trust in statistics.
The Labour Party has admitted making " overcautious" calls to voters to check their details were correct.
The Liberal Democrats and Conservative Party have both received reports of similar calls.
In an interview with the BBC News website, Prof Diamond, the UK Statistics Authority (UKSA) chair, said making such calls was "not acceptable".

"It undermines that trust in official statistics and it's something that the Statistics Authority will be pursuing with the Office for Statistical Regulation."

"I think it is not acceptable to make these cold calls.

"

The Labour MP and former Speaker of the House of Commons, Betty Boothroyd, has called for a return to the traditional system of selecting the Speaker.
She said the current system, which sees the MPs elect the Speaker, introduced in 2005, reduces the likelihood of finding "the best person for the job".
Ms. Boothroyd, the first woman to be elected Speaker in the House of Commons in 1992, said the restoration of the old system where the Queen appoints the Speaker would be "much preferable".
Her comments come as the House of Lords is expected to elect a new Speaker tomorrow, with the Labour peer Baroness Hayman widely expected to get the job.
Ms. Boothroyd told the BBC that the prospect of a Labour peer becoming Speaker was a "strong argument" for electing speakers in the House of Commons.
"It's important that the Speaker is appointed by the whole house and it shouldn't be a partisan appointment," she said.

"The idea that the House of Lords has suddenly got itself a Speaker because they've got a vacancy and they've elected a Labour speaker - that's a strong argument, of course, for changing the system in the House of Commons.

"

Ms. Boothroyd served as Speaker from 1992 to 2000, during which time she was appointed by the Queen on the recommendation of the outgoing Speaker.
The system changed in 2005 following the enactment of the Parliamentary Elections and Referendums Act, which transferred the power to elect the Speaker from the Crown to the House of Commons.
Since then, MPs have elected the Speaker and the three deputy speakers from among their number, but Ms. Boothroyd said the new system had not served the country well.
"I think it is desirable to return to the former system," she said.
"Clearly, it is for the government of the day to decide, and I realize that there are arguments on both sides.

"But I think if you are going to have a fully elected House of Commons, then it does reduce the likelihood of getting the best person for the job if it is purely elected by the members of the House of Commons."
The former prime minister will appear before a judge to give evidence in a trial that could see him accused of misleading parliament over the Iraq war.
The Conservative former foreign secretary, Malcolm Rifkind, has also been called to give evidence to the special Iraq inquiry.

The documents, leaked to the BBC, show Blair's plans to win a third term for the Labour Party, despite being the most unpopular politician in the country at the time.
The leaked documents, labeled "Blair '05 election strategy" and dated Thursday, December 1, 2004, lay out a plan for a "core message" to be delivered by Blair during the campaign.
This message is centered around the idea that the general election in May 2005 would be a "once-in-a-generation chance to build a better Britain."

Blair's plans also include a "retail strategy," which involves targeting specific voter demographics, and a "communications strategy" for delivering the core message through various channels, such as television, radio, and the internet.
The documents also reveal that Blair's campaign would focus on the issue of trust, with the goal of making Blair the "trustworthy candidate" in the general election.
In addition, Blair's team planned to emphasize the threat of the Conservative Party, led by Michael Howard, to create a sense of urgency around voting for Labour.

The former Home Secretary has attacked the cost of asylum seekers to the UK, amid a rising number of Channel migrant crossings.
The government says it will change the law to make it a criminal offence to knowingly arrive in the UK without permission.
But Labour accused ministers of "criminalising asylum" and wanting to "hide from their failure to stop people making these dangerous journeys".
The BBC's Political Editor, Chris Mason, says it is likely the government will lose the vote, as it did on its plan to overhaul the asylum system last year.

"Or should we be saying to the people who are responsible for these individuals, 'It's up to you and your government to take care of these people and to provide the accommodation, not the British taxpayer'?"

He said the way to bring down overall costs was to "remove the incentive for people to come here illegally" by investing in "proper border protection".

The Government has announced the most significant changes to child access laws in decades, which supporters say will protect thousands of children from "abusive" parents.
Currently, the law says children should have contact with both parents after a separation, unless it is harmful to do so.
The new law will introduce a "primary carer" label for the parent who looks after the day-to-day care of the children.
The other parent will retain the right to contact, but it will be balanced against the right of the primary carer to protect the child from "intense or predatory" contact that could cause them harm.
The Government says the changes, which will be enshrined in law, will stop parents from using children as "pawns" during divorce proceedings.
Lord Wolfson, the minister for family support, said the reforms recognised that "children thrive best when they have both parents involved in their lives".
But shadow justice secretary Stephen Kinnock said the Government was "significantly weakening" the safeguarding of children.
He added that the Government had "totally failed to justify" the removal of the "proven framework" of the current law.
The announcement was also criticised by campaigners, with some warning the changes could put children at risk of abuse.
Rosie Canning, from charity Family Action, said the plans appeared to be based on the "misconception" that child abuse only happens when parents are divorced.
She added that the charity was "very concerned" that the changes would mean children being "rushed into having contact with a parent" without proper safeguards.
The Government said the changes would not represent a dilution of the safeguarding system but would introduce a more "sensitive" approach.
The Tory leader has unveiled a spending plan that he claims will boost the economy and help families with the cost of living.
Boris Johnson promised "a big package of measures" to help people cope with the impact of rising prices and energy bills.
The prime minister said the plan would "take the load off" people as Britain's economy encounters "serious headwinds".
Speaking at a Downing Street news conference, he promised details on Wednesday, after the Conservative Party conference ends on Tuesday.

Around midnight on Wednesday, a car pulled up outside the house of Sir Keir Starmer, Labour leader, in Camden, north London.
Daniel Kawczynski, a Conservative MP since 2005, got out and knocked on the door.
Starmer was in bed, but his wife, Victoria, answered, and invited the MP in.
He refused the offer of food and drink, and instead they sat in the kitchen, chatting.
Kawczynski had told his wife he was visiting a friend for "a drink and a chat", but in fact, he was moving MPs from the Conservative party to Labour.
It is a remarkable act of political rebellion – and an indication of the turmoil in the Tory party following the election of Boris Johnson as leader.
For years, Kawczynski had been a loyal Conservative, first as a member of the European Parliament, then as a member of the Polish community in Britain.
He was a strong supporter of Brexit and repeatedly attacked Labour as "the party of open borders".
But he became increasingly frustrated during the Tory leadership contest, as candidates veered to the right.
Michael Gove, who ultimately came third, promised to lead the party out of the European Convention on Human Rights; Johnson gave only a qualified commitment to the Northern Irish backstop.
Kawczynski believes the Conservative party has abandoned the one nation tradition of Toryism, and become an instrument to promote the interests of the wealthy and the privileged.
In Labour, he believes, he has found a party that reflects his beliefs, and those of many no-deal Brexiteers.
"The Labour party under Keir Starmer's leadership has changed dramatically," he told BBC News.
"Keir Starmer has shown he is a man of principle, who has managed to unite his party, and who is offering the country a vision of hope, a vision of unity.

"

Starmer was keen to recruit MPs to his top team, but had expected any who defected to be from the Conservative party's One Nation wing.
The arrival of Kawczynski, a committed Brexiteer, is a surprise, and a challenge.

The Labour leader has made clear he wants his MPs to represent all of Britain – Remainers and Leavers – and he hopes that Kawczynski will be able to talk to former Tory colleagues about the benefits of unity, and the dangers of Johnson's leadership.
