The UK is “heading in the wrong direction” in regards to its handling of COVID-19, Professor John Ashton, a former regional director of public health for north-west England, has said.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s World at One programme, he said that the UK had “lost its grip” on the epidemic and that the recent plan to scrap COVID-19 restrictions was “difficult to understand”.
He commented: “I think we are heading in the wrong direction
and I think we need to do something about it pretty quickly because this virus is not going to go away.”
Professor Ashton argued that a “middle way” was needed, whereby the government advises citizens on how to manage their risks.
This comes after Prime Minister Boris Johnson announced that mandatory masks, COVID-19 passports and social distancing would end in England on 27 January.
Speaking to MPs on Wednesday (04 January), the prime minister said the UK government “cannot keep the country indefinitely in a state of lockdown”.
He argued that the restrictions were having “damaging consequences” on people’s mental health and livelihoods.
However, Professor Ashton said that “locking down completely” was not under consideration and “nor should it be”.
Instead, he suggested that the government could be taking steps to slow the spread of the virus, such as advising people to work from home and introducing COVID-19 passports for large events.
On Tuesday (03 January), the UK Health Security Agency announced that COVID-19 cases had risen by 208,000 in England over the last week, with hospitalisations rising by 90% in the last month.
The latest data also shows that the total number of COVID-19 deaths in England have exceeded 150,000.
The EU is set to lift its embargo on weapons sales to China despite concerns from member states about human rights.
The EU imposed the arms embargo in 1989 following the Tiananmen Square crackdown.
But a new EU foreign policy chief, Josep Borrell, is leading efforts to lift it.
The move is part of wider efforts to improve EU-China relations and engage with Beijing.
But an EU source said a number of member states, particularly in Europe's east, were concerned about the plan.
The source said this included Baltic states and Poland, as well as Sweden and Denmark.
The embargo has been regularly reviewed since it was introduced.
And for years, Beijing has been demanding its removal.
In 2016, then-French President Francois Hollande said the ban was "obsolete".
And later that year, a governmental file classified by France as "secret" was found in a bin in Paris.
It suggested that the embargo would be lifted unless China's behaviour changed.
At the time, a Chinese government spokesman said the move would be a "positive step".
In 2017, China's President Xi Jinping visited the Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri, sparking speculation that Beijing was set to make major investments in the company.
Fincantieri is one of the world's largest shipbuilders and a major supplier of Europe's naval fleets.
An EU source said lifting the embargo was "controversial" and would be "very difficult".
The source said that any move to lift the embargo would require the agreement of all member states.
And that this was unlikely before the end of Germany's EU presidency in the second half of this year.

The BBC has learned that the Conservative Party has received a letter from the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) regarding their investigation into the Conservative Party and allegations of discriminatory and abusive behavior within the party.
This comes after the EHRC announced last week that it had opened a formal investigation into the Conservative Party for these very allegations.
In response, the Conservative Party has said that it will fully cooperate with the investigation.

A spokesperson for the party has said: 
"We are committed to ensuring that all those involved in the party participate in a respectful and open democratic culture.

"

This investigation comes just a few months after the Conservative Party was accused of racism and bullying by the former Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sajid Javid, along with other MPs.
The documents, which appear to be classified, were discovered in a London street by a member of the public on Sunday.
It is not clear how they came to be left in the street or how long they had been there.
The papers, which appear to be from the Ministry of Defence, contain sensitive information about the British military's plans in case of a no-deal Brexit.
They include details of how military equipment would be moved across the English Channel in the event of a no-deal Brexit.
The documents also include information about the British military's relationship with the EU and the United States.
The Ministry of Defence has confirmed that the documents are genuine and said that it is investigating how they came to be lost.
The police have also been informed of the discovery.
Sainsbury's, Britain's second largest supermarket group, will invest £50m in staffing and improve pay for thousands of workers as part of a shake-up of its store management structure.
The retailer said the changes, which include the creation of 2,000 shop floor jobs, would result in more than 35,000 workers receiving a pay rise.
Sainsbury's said it would also pay an annual bonus to shop floor workers for the first time.
From February, shop floor workers will earn between £10.10 and £11.40 an hour.
They currently start at between £9.50 and £10.75 an hour.

Siobhan McMullan, Sainsbury's retail and digital director, said: "Our shop floor colleagues do a brilliant job and are the key to our success, so we want to ensure they are appropriately rewarded for the fantastic work they do every day.
"When we created our new executive team last year, we gave ourselves the target of investing at least £100m in our colleagues over the next three years.
Today's announcement is a £50m down payment on that commitment.

"

The company, which also owns the Argos and Habitat brands, said it planned to change the way it runs its supermarkets, with managers currently working across several departments being replaced by specialists in each area.
Sainsbury's said the changes were likely to result in the creation of about 700 manager roles, with the rest of the roles replaced by the new shop floor roles.
The supermarket said it would also introduce an annual bonus for shop floor workers, to be paid in November each year, worth between 5% and 10% of their total pay.
Sainsbury's said it was investing in its stores after reporting strong Christmas trading last month.
The supermarket group, which has 2,000 supermarkets and convenience stores, said like-for-like sales, which strip out the impact of new store openings, were up by 6.6% in the 15 weeks to 8 January.
Sales were boosted by a strong performance in grocery, as shoppers spent more money on entertaining at home amid the cost of living crisis.
However, Sainsbury's warned of further increases in the cost of living this year, as it forecast that its costs would rise by about £660m in the next financial year.
The supermarket said it was able to absorb those costs through its size and scale, and by shoppers switching to own-brand products
Television debates between party leaders have become a regular feature of elections in many countries, but Britain has lagged behind.
That could be about to change, with the leaders of the three largest parties being urged to agree to a televised debate ahead of the next election.
The BBC's political editor, Chris Mason, has suggested that a debate between the party leaders could be arranged for next year.
While the BBC has not confirmed the proposal, nor has any other broadcaster, it would be a bold move and a big change from the usual format of election debates in the UK.
The TV debate would be a welcome addition to the political discourse in the UK and could help to engage more people in the election process.
It would also be a chance for the party leaders to showcase their ideas and policies to a wider audience.
Britain is set to vote in a general election for the third time in five years on Thursday.

The governing Conservatives have been campaigning hard on the message that the country risks being stuck in a perpetual cycle of elections if Labour wins and fails to get its Brexit plan through Parliament.

At the same time, the main opposition party has been warning that the Conservatives would put the NHS at risk by signing up to a trade deal with the US that would allow private healthcare companies to bid for contracts.
Labour has also been attacking the government over its record on tackling crime, promising to hire 10,000 more police officers if it wins.

This has been the nastiest campaign of the three elections, with both major parties trading blows over which of them has done more for the NHS and whether the leader of the opposition is fit to be prime minister.
One poll put the Conservatives seven points ahead of Labour, giving the party a healthy cushion over its main rival.
But another survey suggested that voters think neither party will win a majority, forcing another election.
The UK faces a crisis in the social sciences with experts warning that the country is falling behind international rivals, according to a study.
The report, by the Campaign for Social Science, says that the UK's ability to compete in the global economy is being put at risk by years of underfunding for research.
It calls for an increase in science funding for the social sciences to help the country to compete internationally.
The report singles out psychology and sociology for particular concern, noting that the UK's share of research publications in these fields has fallen significantly in recent years.
It warns that other countries are investing more in these areas, and that the UK is in danger of falling behind.
The report calls for increased funding for research in these fields, as well as for the wider social sciences.
The authors of the report argue that the social sciences are vital for understanding and addressing many of the challenges facing society today, such as climate change, poverty, and inequality.
They say that the social sciences can help to provide evidence-based solutions to these problems and that increasing funding for research in these fields is essential.
The report calls on the UK government to increase funding for research in the social sciences to at least match the spending of other leading countries.
Ed Mallon is a man on a mission.
The former Northern Ireland footballer has gone from being on the pitch to helping communities in Nigeria.
Now he's taking on a new challenge - campaigning for the SDLP in the upcoming assembly election.

Mr. Mallon grew up on a council estate in Belfast and went on to play for Manchester United, and he says that his background and experience have given him a unique perspective on the issues that matter to people.
He cited healthcare and housing as two of the biggest concerns for voters in the constituency he's hoping to win a seat in.
The SDLP is fielding candidates in all 18 constituencies in Northern Ireland, and Mr. Mallon is confident that they can make a difference.
"I think people are tired of the same old politics," he said.
"They want something different, and I think the SDLP offers that.
We have a positive message, and we're focused on the issues that matter to people."
The upcoming election is set to be a closely fought battle, with the SDLP, Sinn Fein, and the DUP all vying for seats.
Mr. Mallon is keen to focus on the issues that matter to voters, rather than getting caught up in the politics.
"I'm not interested in playing politics," he said.
"I'm interested in making a difference to people's lives."
Despite only joining the party in October, Mr. Mallon has received a lot of attention since being chosen as the SDLP candidate for the East Belfast seat.
With his background and experience, he could be a formidable opponent for the other parties.
One thing is for sure, the upcoming election is set to be an exciting one.
The Liberal Democrats have demanded a new inquiry into the handling of the coronavirus pandemic in the UK.
The call came as the party's leader, Ed Davey, warned the public had "lost trust" in the government's handling of the crisis.
Mr Davey accused ministers of "getting it wrong" on protective equipment for NHS staff, testing, and the pace of lifting lockdown restrictions.
The government has said it made "hard decisions" to protect the country.
Speaking at his party's autumn conference in Brighton, Mr Davey warned the country was "not out of the woods" with the pandemic "not done" and said his party would "hold their feet to the fire".
He added that the country "cannot afford to go on like this" with the NHS "on its knees" and the economy "in tatters".
The BBC has learned that the EU will not block the UK from spending billions on nuclear weapons despite the fact that the bloc is committed to nuclear disarmament.
The EU has no legal power to prevent the UK from spending money on nuclear weapons.
The EU is committed to nuclear disarmament and has created mechanisms to encourage countries to abide by this commitment.
However, the UK has opted out of these mechanisms which means even though it is a signed member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), it is not subject to the EU's oversight.
The disclosure comes after the UK government has announced it will increase its nuclear weapons stockpile.
This move has been met with criticism from non-proliferation experts who say it is a blow to global efforts to reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
MPs from several parties have demanded to know how a budget leak happened, as the government was forced into a U-turn over its plans to raise national insurance.
The Commons Treasury Select Committee said it wanted to hear from the Treasury and HMRC about the leak, which happened last weekend.
In Saturday's leak, a genuine-looking mock-up of the Budget document was posted online.
It showed that the government was planning to raise taxes to fund social care.
The Treasury has said it is investigating the leak, but MPs want to know the results of its probe by Friday.

The Conservative MP and committee chairman, Mel Stride, said it was "absolutely right" that the Treasury was investigating the leak but added that "it's important that the select committee follows this up as well".

He said the committee had written to the Treasury and HMRC "asking for further information on the extent of the leak, any evidence of where it may have originated from and the impact of this leak on the broader political debate".
"We would like to see a response to our inquiries by Friday of this week," he added.
The Liberal Democrats have called for an inquiry into the leak.
The party's Treasury spokesperson, Christine Jardine, said: "This was a disgraceful and dangerous leak, and the public deserve to know how it happened.
Britain has helped broker a deal between Norway and Turkey to help improve relations between the two NATO allies, Foreign Secretary Liz Truss has said.
The deal, signed on Friday in Oslo, aims to boost economic and military cooperation.
It comes after a dispute between the two countries last year over their opposition to Finland and Sweden joining NATO.
Turkey accused Norway of supporting Kurdish militants, while Norway accused Turkey of violating the human rights of its political opponents.
Ms Truss said the deal would bring the two countries "closer together" and help "maintain peace and stability in Europe".
She added that it would allow the two countries to work together to address some of the "biggest challenges facing the world today".

The deal follows a visit by Ms Truss to Norway last week, during which she discussed the importance of the two countries working together to address global issues, including the threat posed by Russia to Europe's security.
The foreign secretary has been touring European countries to promote Britain's global role as a diplomatic and military power following the completion of its exit from the European Union.
She has also been pushing for Britain to be admitted to the EU's Horizon Europe research and development programme.
Schools across the UK are being encouraged to take part in a mock election to help pupils learn about the democratic process.
The election, which is being organised by the UK Parliament, will take place in schools on the same day as the local elections in May.
Pupils will vote for candidates in a made-up constituency, with the results announced on the same day as the local election results.
The scheme is part of a programme to boost young people's understanding of democracy.
Parliament's Education Service has produced teaching materials on the election process to help pupils understand how it works.
The former cabinet minister, Mrs Theresa May, has been appointed to a senior position in the Conservative Party's election campaign.
The party's chairman, Mr Grant Shapps, said Mrs May had been chosen to lead the Conservatives' election effort in the key target seat of Chingford and Woodford Green in north-east London.
The seat is currently held by the Labour Party's Ms Stella Creasy.
Mrs May, who served as prime minister from 2016 to 2019, is a former constituency neighbour of Ms Creasy's and is favourite to win the seat back for the Conservatives.
During her time as prime minister, Mrs May was often seen as a cautious and pragmatic leader.
She took the U.K. out of the European Union in 2019 after delaying the original deadline she had set for Brexit several times.
Last year, Mrs May announced she was stepping down as an MP, having served the constituency of Maidenhead in Berkshire for nearly 20 years.
She is replacing Mr Andrew Selous as the Conservative candidate for Chingford and Woodford Green, who stood down earlier this year.
The Conservative party has pledged to offer every English primary school child access to free swimming and fitness lessons if it wins the general election next month.
The party said its plan - part of the Healthy Pupils Bill - would help combat childhood obesity.
Children would get free swimming lessons annually from the age of five - funded by a tax on sugary drinks - it said.
The party also promised to help the youngest school children learn about the benefits of healthy eating.
The Labour MP Jim McMahon has praised the Tory campaign for being more attentive to the needs of the country than the Labour Party.

In a column for the Sunday Telegraph, McMahon, who is the MP for Oldham West and Royton, stated that "the Conservative campaign has been more focused on the cost of living and giving people a clear explanation about what they will do to ease it, than we have been in Labour."

He continued, stating that "Labour has a comprehensive plan to help people with the cost of living, but we have not been explaining it well enough."
McMahon argued that the party needs to do more to make clear its plans to help with the rising cost of living, and to defend its record in government.
The MP concluded his column by saying, "I will be doing everything I can to make sure that Labour is listening and that we are offering the bold and radical plans that the country needs."
The UK should commit to a joint aid programme with the US and other G7 countries to fund global education, stop HIV and wipe out malaria, Gordon Brown has said.
The former UK prime minister said it was time for Britain to return to the forefront of international efforts to eradicate preventable diseases.
In a speech to the Centre for Global Development in Washington, he will call for a £5.5bn fund to tackle Aids, tuberculosis and malaria.
Mr Brown said that it was the "height of hypocrisy" for any government to talk about national security while failing to tackle diseases.
The fund would be used to target illnesses which have made a comeback due to coronavirus lockdowns and disruptions to health services around the world, according to the proposed plan.
It would include £1.7bn for a national plan to end Aids by 2030, £1.2bn for a global fund to fight tuberculosis, and £2bn for the elimination of malaria.
The price of petrol has been frozen for the twelfth month in a row, the chancellor has said.
Rishi Sunak said he would exercise his power to delay the inevitable increase in line with inflation until March next year.
The move will save motorists an average of £1.30 per litre, or £19 per tank.
The chancellor said the measure, which will apply to diesel and petrol, was part of the government's plan to help people with the cost of living.
Mr Sunak said: "We know that people are worried about the cost of living, so to help with that we're freezing duty on petrol," he said.
The decision mirrors last year's freeze, which was also announced in November and lasted until March.
The announcement was met with a mixed reaction from motoring groups.
The RAC said the move would provide some relief from record prices, but added it was "only a temporary solution".
"We need to encourage drivers to swap to electric cars, by improving charging infrastructure and offering financial incentives," said RAC fuel spokesman Simon Williams.
"But upfront costs need to be reduced too, especially as inflation is now starting to bite into household income.

"

However, the AA said the freeze would help consumers amid the "cost of living catastrophe".
"This move will help consumers when they most need it," said Luke Bosdet, the AA's fuel price spokesman.
"But freezing duty isn't a long-term fix.
The cost of filling up is largely determined by global oil prices, which showed little sign of easing as the chancellor spoke."
The announcement came as part of the chancellor's autumn statement, which included a package of measures to help with the cost of living.
This included a £2bn help package for households in England, comprising a £150 council tax rebate and £400 energy bill discount.
The former prime minister, Tony Blair, has said he is "confident" that a controversial government adviser who was fired last week will return to his role.
Stephen Reicher, a behavioural scientist, has advised the government on coronavirus messaging during the pandemic.
But he was dismissed on Tuesday following reports that he had called the prime minister "incompetent" and the government "disgraceful" in a Zoom call with colleagues.
Reicher has since said his comments were "not personal" but based on "evidence".
He added that he had "never experienced a worse example of government."
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Blair said Reicher had been "doing a very good job" and that his sacking was "a mistake".
The former Labour prime minister added that he believed Reicher would return to the position, saying there was a "better chance of him being brought back than somebody else being appointed".
It was meant to be a triumph for Manchester City and the Premier League.
Instead, the inaugural Premier League match at the club's magnificent new stadium was undermined by a cacophony of mistakes and blunders.
It started when the Premier League, in its official programme, listed the wrong kick-off time.
Then the stadium's PA system started malfunctioning.
Manchester City, who had asked for silence before their national anthem as a mark of respect for the Queen, suffered an embarrassing delay after the anthem had begun, as the sound cut out.
The match had barely started when the assistant referee was forced to abandon his position after he collided with a camera operator.
And City's frustrations were compounded when Eric Dier scored an unlikely equalizer for Tottenham with one of the goals of the season.
The mood was low as the teams walked down the tunnel at halftime.
Then a different sort of calamity occurred: a fire alarm went off, forcing everyone back up the tunnel and out of the stadium.
The malfunction was quickly fixed but it was another embarrassing setback.
City had hoped their new stadium would be a big step in their quest to match Europe's superpowers.
Instead, it served as a reminder of how far they still have to go.
"It was a lot of errors together," City manager Pep Guardiola said after the game.
"The people who are in charge of the kick-off time, they have to check with me if it is right.
The PA has to be better.
The fire alarm should not happen.
Especially when you want to host the Champions League, you have to solve these issues.

"

It seems Guardiola was being generous with his assessment.
Because while some of the issues were understandable gremlins in any new building, others were startling basic errors.
Take the wrong kick-off time, for example.
A simple check with Guardiola or City's chief executive, Ferran Soriano, would have revealed the error.
Instead, the Premier League's teams went into the match with different kick-off times on their team sheets.
It was a shoddy mistake that was easily avoidable.
As for the malfunctioning PA system, that too should not have happened.
City have an outstanding reputation for organizational excellence.
The club has presented itself superbly well in its first years of ownership by Sheikh Mansour.
So it's hard to believe they would get something as basic as the PA system wrong if they had applied the same attention to detail as they did, for example,
The former home secretary says his new autobiography covers "love, loss and politics, but not in that order".
The MP for Sheffield Brightside was home secretary from 2001 to 2004 under Tony Blair.
He said his book, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, covered "the stuff that politics misses".
It is the former cabinet minister's second autobiography.
The book is being published ahead of the expected publication of a report into the government's handling of Covid next week.
Blunkett was also a cabinet minister under John Major, serving as secretary of state for education between 1992 and 4 1997.
He spoke to BBC Radio 4's Today programme about the book, Blunkett - the New Labour Years.
The UK's highest-paid broadcaster has attacked the government's "pay later" budget, saying it would not help those most in need.

Speaking on the BBC's Andrew Marr show, the presenter Andrew Neil said the measures in the budget were "balancing the books in five years' time" and amounted to "giving voters a choice between a tax rise or a spending cut".
He added that the autumn statement was "an absolutely clear signal that the age of largesse is over".
His comments came as Chancellor Jeremy Hunt announced a squeeze on spending and a hike in taxes for millions of people.
Mr Hunt said he had made "difficult decisions" in order to restore confidence after the economic crisis caused by the pandemic and the war in Ukraine.
The Liberal Democrats have unveiled their general election slogan - "Boris gets Brexit done, Jo gets it done".
The party's leader, Jo Swinson, unveiled the phrase at a campaign event in London on Monday.
Ms Swinson said the slogan summed up the choice at the upcoming general election.
The prime minister has previously used the phrase "get Brexit done" as a reason for calling the election.
"Brexit is already causing damage to our economy and it will only get worse unless we can get a deal done," Ms Swinson said.
"And stopping Brexit is the most important step we can take to build a brighter future for our country.

"

Ms Swinson was appointed leader of the Liberal Democrats in July, taking over from Sir Vince Cable.

The party's new slogan echoes the famous "New Labour, New Life" campaign from the 1997 general election, when Tony Blair made a dramatic television appearance with his then-wife, Cherie, and their son, Leo.
The Supreme Court has ruled that ministers must give prisoners who want to be able to prepare their own meals with the necessary equipment to do so.
The decision has been made under the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to respect for private and family life, and cannot be overridden by legislation.
There are 15,000 prisoners across England and Wales who are currently required to slop out – or empty – their chamber pots rather than being given access to flushing toilets.
In 2013, three prisoners filed a legal case arguing that this constituted inhuman and degrading treatment, and that it violated their human rights.
The Ministry of Justice had argued that the current system, in place in British prisons since the 1830s, was necessary for security and good order.
Lord Reed, president of the Supreme Court, dismissed this argument, saying that the ministry had not provided sufficient evidence to support it.
The ruling could cost the ministry up to £40m per year to implement, however, campaigners have criticised the ruling for not going far enough.
A recent inspection found that not a single prison in England and Wales was adequately prepared for the upcoming ban on slopping out.
The clash between the Lord Chancellor, Liz Truss, and the Lord Chief Justice, Lord Burnett, over the government's plan to increase the use of fixed-term contracts for judges has escalated.
The Lord Chief Justice said the plan, which will make it easier to dismiss judges in the middle of their careers, would have a "chilling effect" on the independence of the judiciary.
He argued that the judiciary needed to be independent of government to rule fairly on matters such as the legality of asylum seekers or the release of terrorists.
In response, Ms. Truss said she had "huge respect" for the independence of the judiciary but that it was "not an absolute shield".
She argued that the government was entitled to have a say in who became a judge.
The former home secretary David Blunkett has told the BBC he is "confident" his review of police reform will succeed where previous attempts have failed.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said he would publish his plans within two months, and that he was "optimistic" about the government's response.
His review - announced in September - will consider the governance of police forces and whether the current system is "fit for purpose".
Mr Blunkett said the system was "broken", with forces "operating in silos".
Speaking to Newsnight's Kirsty Walk, the Labour life peer said his review would suggest ways the system could work better together.
This could include looking at whether police forces should collaborate more to deal with issues such as cyber-crime, he added.
Aid agencies have insisted that Friday's tsunami in the Pacific will not divert attention or resources from the humanitarian crisis in Africa.
The massive 8.9 magnitude quake, which struck off the coast of Samoa, triggered tsunami warnings across the Pacific.
There are fears that the wave could cause widespread damage in Samoa, Tonga and American Samoa - but aid agencies have stressed that the tsunami is not expected to directly affect Africa.
"Obviously we are watching very closely how this develops, but at this point it does not change our focus," UNICEF's regional director for west and central Africa, Elhadj
As Sy, told the BBC.
"For the moment we are not diverting any resources.

"

The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement also said that it was not halting its operations in Africa.
The organisation's director of international relations, Tarik Kadir, said that whilst they monitor the situation with the tsunamis, operations in Africa "remain our priority".
He added: "We have not had any requests for assistance regarding this earthquake or tsunamis, so at this point we are not diverting any resources."
The UK-based charity Oxfam also said it was "not aware" of any impact on its operations in Africa, but was "watching closely".

A spokesperson added: "We are not diverting resources away from east Africa at this point as the needs there are so critical and our operations are ramping up."

Earlier, the UN's humanitarian coordinator in Somalia, Mark Bowden, had said that the UN was "watching very carefully" but that the impact of the tsunami was not yet clear.
He added: "As far as I understand it's not directly a threat to Africa, but we're watching very carefully and if there is a request for assistance, then of course we will take a look at that."
Labour has been accused of creating "EU propaganda" for using the bloc's logo on documents setting out the potential benefits of remaining in the single market after Brexit.
The party used the logo of the European Union's executive, the European Commission, on a document published on its website and sent out to supporters.
But the use of the logo led to a row with Conservative MPs, who have demanded the party remove it.
One senior Tory said using the logo was "straight out of the Kremlin's playbook".
Another said the party had crossed the line from serious political debate to "propaganda".
Labour said the document, which had been published before the party's conference last month, had been intended to provide "a factual overview" of the UK's current trading arrangements with the EU.
But after criticism, it decided to take the document down and review its use of the logo.
The party said it had previously used the logo in the same way on a page outlining Labour's support for Remain in the 2016 referendum.
But Labour's use of the logo came as Conservative MPs warned the party was using "fearful" and "Project Fear" rhetoric over Brexit.
Former foreign secretary Boris Johnson accused Labour of trying to "derail" the Brexit process with "hysterical" warnings about leaving the EU.
And senior backbencher Jacob Rees-Mogg said the party was trying to "scare" voters with "fantastical" warnings that Britain would have lower food standards outside the EU.
British Airways and the UK's largest union for aviation workers, Unite, were heading for a High Court showdown over the suspension of a union representative.
The airline suspended Unite national secretary for aviation, Mark Richards, from operating flights because it said he had "damaged" the company.
Unite said it would seek an interim injunction in the High Court in London on Wednesday in a bid to get Mr Richards back at work.

The union is seeking an order under Section 145 of the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992 that states: "An employer shall not discriminate against an employee nor victimise an employee in relation to membership or activity on behalf of a trade union.

"

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Unite does not take this step lightly.
British Airways has pushed us into this situation and it has broad consequences for the whole trade union movement.
"An attack on one union is an attack on the whole trade union movement.
If British Airways gets away with this, it will have dire consequences for all working people.

"
British Airways said it could not comment on individual staffing matters.
The mobile phone has changed a lot in the past 20 years, but one thing has remained constant: our reliance on them.
According to a recent study, the average person will upgrade their phone every 2.5 years, with some people keeping their devices for as long as five years.
But no matter how long we keep our phones for, one thing is certain: we can't live without them.
In the early days of mobile phones, they were used primarily for making calls and sending text messages.
But today, they're used for everything from browsing the internet to paying for groceries.
As mobile phones have become more and more popular, so too have the number of apps available for them.
There are now millions of apps available for both iOS and Android devices, ranging from games to productivity tools.
While some people may argue that mobile phones are a distraction, there's no denying that they've become an integral part of our lives.

A study carried out by the University of Texas showed that people were unable to correctly identify the sponsored advertisements on search engine results pages (SERPs).
When shown screenshots of Google search results, participants pointed out advertisements as fewer than 25% of the time, despite the presence of cues like "Ad" or "Sponsored."

One of the authors of the study, Amanda Broderick, commented on the low number of participants able to discern between ads and search results, noting that "just because something is labeled 'Ad' doesn't mean that people will notice that it's an advertisement."
This failure to identify advertisements relates to a concept from psychology known as inattentional blindness, which causes people to miss obvious facts when their attention is focused elsewhere.
The authors of the study suggest that the low ability to recognize ads is due to the design of SERPs, which often place ads and search results in similar formats.
Additionally, people may be more focused on the search results themselves rather than the ads that appear on the page.
The authors suggest that search engine designers should make ads more distinct from search results to improve transparency and help users make more informed decisions.
The study's findings highlight the need for search engine users to be more vigilant in identifying advertisements and interpreting information on SERPs.
It is important to be aware of the potential for ads to influence search results and to consider the motivations of the companies behind the advertisements.

Overall, the study suggests that people are unable to reliably identify advertisements on SERPs, which has implications for the credibility of information and the influence of advertising on search engine users.

The incoming chief executive of Lloyd's of London has publicly challenged the City regulator over its plans to toughen capital requirements for insurers.
In his first major interview since being appointed, John Neal told the Financial Times that the Financial Services Authority's (FSA) review would "not improve consumer protection one iota".
He said that the review would unnecessarily increase the complexity of a simple product and force up prices.
His comments are the first public challenge to the FSA's proposals from the insurance industry.
However, industry sources have said that there are concerns about the plans within the Corporation of Lloyd's.
The FSA has proposed a "risk-based" approach to the capital that insurers must hold to reflect the harm they could cause to policyholders if they were to go bust.
At present, insurers must hold a flat £30,000 of capital for each policy they write.
The FSA has said that this approach is insufficient and has proposed a number of options for change, all of which increase the amount of capital that insurers must hold.
These range from a five-fold increase - £150,000 per policy - to holding capital equivalent to the average payout for the type of policy written.
The consultation on the proposals ended on Tuesday and the FSA is expected to publish its final rules later this year.
Mr Neal, who will take over as chief executive of Lloyd's next year, said that the corporation did not support any of the options put forward by the FSA.
"None of the options in the consultation paper currently stands up to scrutiny and I hope the FSA will take on board the points we have made," he said.
"This is not going to improve consumer protection one iota.
It is going to make the cost of simplification more expensive and it is not necessary.

"

A spokesman for the FSA said: "The cost of capital reform is a legitimate concern and one that we carefully considered when developing our proposals.
"However, any reforms also need to ensure that consumers are appropriately protected.

The UK's average house prices showed a slight increase in September, according to a report from the Halifax.
The bank found that prices rose by 0.1% in September, following a 0.3% increase in August.
This is the fourth consecutive month that house prices have risen, bringing the average price of a property in the UK to £261,922.
This is still 2.3% lower than it was in February 2022, before the start of the economic crisis.
The data also showed that the number of mortgages approved for house purchases rose slightly in September, to 81,000.
This is the highest level since March 2022, but still some way below the pre-pandemic average of 103,000.
Martin Ellis, the chief economist at Halifax, said that the housing market had 'weathered the financial storm' of the last few months.
He said that low-interest rates and a shortage of properties for sale had kept the market stable.
However, he warned that the economic crisis was not over and that house prices could fall further in the coming months.
'We are entering a prolonged period of uncertainty, which will weigh on consumer sentiment and activity,' he said.
Many homeowners have decided to stay put as the cost of living crisis deepens, with rising energy bills and food prices.
This has led to a boom in home improvements, as people invest in their current properties rather than trying to move up the property ladder.
At the same time, mortgage rates have fallen to record lows, with some lenders offering deals below 1%.
This has encouraged some first-time buyers to take their first steps onto the property ladder.

"Going forward, we expect a recovery in consumer borrowing, as households increasingly switch back to borrowing on credit cards, as opposed to their current preference for personal loans," he added.
Overall, consumer borrowing increased by £1.3bn in the three months to December, down from £6.7bn in the three months to November.

Please note that the figures for credit card and loan borrowing are seasonally adjusted.

The body of a BBC news article titled "Progress on new internet domains":

For decades, the internet has functioned using the domain name system (DNS), which divides the digital universe into separate parts, or domains, each preceded by "www" and separated by periods.
Examples include .com, .org, and .net.
There are also country-specific domains, such as .ca for Canada.
But despite the internet's rapid growth over the last three decades, the list of available domains has remained relatively stable.

That is, until the summer of 2016, when the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), the non-profit organization that oversees the internet's DNS, announced that it would be expanding the list of available top-level domains (TLDs).
ICANN's decision would open up the internet to potentially limitless new domains, ranging from .apple to .wine.
This announcement has sparked excitement and intrigue in the tech community.
Some believe that this expansion will lead to more innovation and creativity online.
Others are concerned that it will lead to more cybercrime and online harassment.

The change is certainly coming: in the first half of 2017 alone, ICANN received more than 1,900 applications for new TLDs, which came from a wide range of sectors, including banking, fashion, and agriculture.
There are also nearly 200 applications for non-Latin script domains, including Arabic, Chinese, and Cyrillic.
The process of reviewing and approving these new TLDs is rigorous.
Each application must meet a specific set of criteria, including technical and operational capability, and must be supported by a $185,000 application fee.
This means that the new domains are unlikely to launch anytime soon.
Nevertheless, the question remains: how will this expansion of top-level domains affect the way we use the internet?
Will it lead to a more diverse and inclusive internet?
Or will it lead to greater fragmentation and chaos?
Only time will tell.
But one thing is certain: the internet is about to enter a new era.

Small firms across the UK are reporting higher costs and struggling to pass these on to customers, a survey has indicated.
The Forum of Private Business said its research showed inflation was the biggest challenge for small and medium-sized companies.
Forum spokesman Toby Marshall said many were "struggling to manage" increases in the cost of energy, fuel and raw materials.
The forum's research showed 42% of firms had seen their energy bills rise in the past three months, while 36% had been hit by higher fuel costs.
Mr Marshall said: "Unfortunately, rising costs are now a fact of life for many small businesses.
"This is a particular challenge for those who have barely recovered from the economic impacts of the pandemic and are still trying to get back on their feet.
This comes amid expectations that the cost of living in the UK is set to rise further, with the price of energy expected to jump by as much as 50% in April.
About a third of the firms had put up their prices in the past three months, the research indicated.
Of these, about 60% managed to pass on all or most of the increased costs to customers, while the rest absorbed the rises.
The monthly survey by the forum is based on the responses of about 1,000 of its members.
Mr Marshall said the government needed to do more to help firms facing higher energy prices.
"We've long called for a permanent cut to VAT for the hospitality and tourism sector, which would help businesses manage higher energy costs," he added.
The suffering of the people in Sudan's Darfur region has been much documented in recent years, but the latest technology now promises to help alleviate their plight.
In an impressive example of international cooperation, a consortium of public and private organizations has launched an initiative to map the entire region using satellite imagery.

The project, which was spearheaded by the World Bank and the European Space Agency, will create a detailed map of Darfur that will serve as an invaluable tool for relief organizations operating in the region.
The map will include detailed information on the location of villages, roads, and other infrastructure, as well as the extent of damage caused by the ongoing conflict.
This information will help relief organizations to better target their resources and plan their operations more effectively.
"This is an excellent example of how space technology can be used for humanitarian purposes," said Simon Gray, the European Space Agency's project manager for the initiative.
"We are very pleased to be able to contribute to the effort to help the people of Darfur.

"
 
The project has already received widespread acclaim for its potential to improve the lives of the people of Darfur.
"This is an incredibly important project," said John Holmes, the United Nations' Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs.
"The detailed mapping of Darfur will be a valuable tool for relief organizations working to improve the situation in the region.
The initiative is also being praised for its potential to strengthen the peace process in Darfur.
By providing a detailed map of the region, the project will help to resolve territorial disputes between the various factions involved in the conflict.
"This is a very positive step towards improving the situation in Darfur," said Mohamed Ahmed, the Secretary-General of the Liberation and Justice Movement, one of the main factions in the conflict.
"We welcome any effort that will help to bring peace to our region."
With the initial phase of the project now complete, the consortium is turning its attention to the next step: creating a digital elevation model of the region.
This will involve collecting additional satellite imagery to supplement the data already acquired.

“We’d like to have Andy Murray playing here,” said Bruguera, the tournament director of the Barcelona Open.
“But I think that, seeing the extent of his injury and the nature of his surgery, it will be difficult for him to be here.”
Bruguera underwent a similar operation to Murray 20 years ago and he returned to competitive tennis six months later.
However, the Spaniard admitted he was not sure whether Murray’s recovery will be as straightforward as his own.
“My surgery was different,” he said.
“The recovery after that type of surgery now is faster than it was 20 years ago.
But we’ll see.”
The gadget market grew by 10% in 2004 as consumer electronics became more popular, according to research group NPD.

"Gadgets are becoming must-have items for today's consumers as they seek to enhance their digital lifestyle experiences," said Steve Gater, telecoms analyst at NPD.
"Increasingly they are looking for products which offer multiple functionality and enable them to access digital content such as music, photos and the internet, in a mobile environment.

"

He said the market for these gadgets had room to grow, but that it was facing increasing competition from other products such as games consoles and personal video recorders.

A judge has given the go-ahead for oil company Yukos to pursue $1.9bn in compensation from Russia in a Washington court.
The company was broken up and sold off after Russian tax authorities seized its assets.
The ruling in a Delaware court is the latest twist in a 15-year legal battle between Yukos and Russia.
The case will now proceed to trial unless the two parties reach a settlement.
Yukos was once Russia's largest oil producer.
It filed for bankruptcy in 1999 and was broken up after Russian tax authorities seized its assets.
The company's former shareholders sued Russia in a Washington court, arguing that the country had expropriated their investment in Yukos.
They also alleged that Russian authorities had colluded with Yukos's management to divert assets from the company.
In 2014, a US court ruled that Russia had violated Yukos's investors' rights by seizing its assets.
The court ordered Russia to pay $50bn in compensation.
Russia appealed against the ruling, and the case went to the Supreme Court.
In 2018, the Supreme Court ruled that the case should be reheard by a lower court.
Now, a judge in a Delaware court has given the go-ahead for Yukos to pursue $1.9bn in compensation from Russia.
The case will now proceed to trial unless Yukos reaches a settlement with Russia.
The demise of Dirty Den at the hands of his onscreen wife, Angie, is one of the most memorable moments in soap history.
It was watched by almost 14 million viewers, making it one of the most watched episodes of EastEnders ever.

The episode, which aired in April 1998, saw Den Watts (played by Leslie Grantham) discover that his wife, Angie (played by Anita Dobson), had been having an affair with his best friend, Ian Beale (played by Adam Woodyatt).
In retaliation, Den served Angie with divorce papers and slept with her sister, Sue (played by Sadie Frost).
However, their marriage was far from over.
Angie managed to convince Den to give their relationship another chance, and the couple reunited.
But their happiness was short-lived.
A year later, in April 1999, Den discovered that Angie had been lying to him about her affair with Ian.
Enraged, he flew into a rage and violently attacked her.
As he tried to strangle her with his bare hands, Angie's son, Ricky (played by Sid Owen), entered the room and tried to stop Den.
During the tussle that followed, Den fell back and hit his head on the fireplace.
Ricky and Angie looked on in horror as Den lay motionless on the floor.
Both realized that he was dead, and Ricky immediately called for an ambulance.
The episode ended with a shocked Angie looking at the body of her dead husband as the title sequence played.
The scene is widely regarded as one of the most iconic and memorable in the history of British soap operas.
The episode was watched by an average of 13.8 million viewers, with a peak of 15.1 million as Den fell to his death.
Italy's Ferrero said on Thursday it plans to cut more costs and revamp its operations following a difficult year in which the coronavirus pandemic hit sales of its Nutella spread and other products.
The maker of Ferrero Rocher chocolates and Kinder toys said it aimed to lift its operating margin to around 22% by 2023, up from 20.2% in 2019 before the pandemic.
Ferrero, which last year overtook Mars to become the world's fourth-biggest confectionery company, plans to reinvest savings from the cost cuts to step up marketing of its portfolio.
The company also plans to develop its business in China, where it began producing Kinder products in 2019 through a joint venture.
Ferrero's operating profit margin shrank to 14.5% in 2020 from 20.5% in 2019, as lockdowns forced the company to close factories and retailers to shut shops.
The Piedmont-based firm, which is controlled by the Ferrero family, has faced difficulties in integrating its recent acquisitions, such as the 2018 purchase of the U.S. confectioner Ferrara.
The company said it had streamlined its organisational structure and simplified its supply chain to cut costs.
It did not provide details on the size of the cost savings.
Ferrero also said it planned to improve sustainability in its supply chain by using only palm oil that is certified as sustainable by 2025.
The company buys around 185,000 tonnes of palm oil a year, it said.

The change forms part of the government's Youth Charter, which aims to give young people more say in the political process.
"This is a crucial step towards a more diverse and inclusive parliament," said Cabinet Minister Julia Lopez.

"

The ONS said that in the three months to October, the value of UK exports was up by £2.7bn compared with the three months to July, while imports were up by £2.2bn.

“We needed everybody,” Klopp said.
“Everybody who was available and that’s what the boys did.
It’s incredible.”
It was also a landmark night for Liverpool captain Jordan Henderson, who made his 400th appearance for the club in the win over Arsenal.

“I think today it hit home to be honest,” Henderson said.

Manchester United and England striker Ellen White has welcomed the news that her club has hired another female coach, following the appointment of Lindsey Horan as first-team coach.
White said "it's great to see" United "leading the way with having female coaches within the club".
The appointment of Horan, who joined United's coaching staff last month, followed that of Northern Ireland's Kenny Shiels as assistant manager last year.
United men's coach Michael Carrick said Shiels and Horan's appointments were "testament to the culture we have tried to create".
Meanwhile, United women's manager Marc Skinner praised the "unbelievable opportunity" Shiels and Horan have been given.
Skinner, who was appointed in December 2019, said it was critical for "coaching evolution" that managers and coaches "have an opportunity to coach men as well as women".

"
White, who has scored 32 goals in 94 England appearances, said "it is slowly starting to happen" regarding female coaches working in men's football.

White said she feels "100% fit" and is targeting success with United this season following the WSL's controversial decision to deny the club a licence for the new top-flight season.
"We've got a really good squad, with great players, a great manager and great staff, so I think we can achieve that [success]," she said.
"First and foremost we need to make sure we are playing in the right way, the style that Marc wants us to play, and then the success will come.

"

Wing Josh Adams and centre Jonathan Davies are included despite doubts over their fitness.

Speaking at Saturday's opening of the Greek Olympic Committee's new headquarters in Athens, Kolanidis said: "They (the doping samples) do not exist anymore.

The Greek Olympic Committee has previously said that samples taken from Kenteris and Thanou were destroyed because the Athens laboratory did not have the necessary permission from the IOC to store them.

Hong Kong has announced it will submit a proposal to host the 2011 Rugby World Cup.
The Hong Kong Rugby Union made the announcement at a news conference on Wednesday.
"We are going to take this opportunity to show the IRB (International Rugby Board) that we are ready, willing and able to host the tournament," said Union president Brian Kennedy.
"Hong Kong is a world city.
We have excellent infrastructure and communications and we are ready to share this with the international rugby family.

"

IRB rules require a candidate nation to have a stadium with a minimum capacity of 40,000.
The Union has approached the Hong Kong Government to seek approval for a new stadium with a minimum capacity of 50,000.
"So far we have had very positive discussions with the Government and I am confident we will reach an agreement," said Kennedy.
"If we are successful in our bid then this new stadium, which will be built specifically for rugby, will be a legacy for future generations of rugby players and fans in Hong Kong.

"

The Union has until 19 October 2007 to submit its formal proposal to the IRB.

IRB Chairman Bernard Lapasset said he was looking forward to receiving the bid.
"Over the years we have seen a tremendous growth in the game of rugby in Asia and the bid from Hong Kong, if successful, will further advance the sport's development."
Athens 2004 silver medallist Konstantinos Kenteris has avoided a jail sentence for speeding but has been given a suspended fine of $1,200.
The Greek sprinter was caught driving at 162km/h (100mph) in his Mercedes on a road with a 60km/h speed limit.
He and his coach, Christos Tsekos, had been due to appear in court in Athens on Tuesday but the judge delayed the verdict until next month.
The 30-year-old runner, who also won 4x100m silver at the Sydney 2000 Olympics, had pleaded not guilty to the speeding charge.
His lawyer, Michalis Dimitrakopoulos, said he expected his client to be found guilty of breaking the speed limit but avoided a prison sentence as it was his first offence.
"I expect he will be found guilty of breaking the speed limit... and most likely he will not go to jail as it is his first offence," Dimitrakopoulos told Greek TV.

"Secondly, there are issues of statute of limitations on the charges against him so we expect for him a suspended fine of about $1,200."

Kenteris, who won a total of six Olympic medals, including two golds in the relay, retired from athletics after the 2012 Olympics in London.
Antonio Santini has resigned as manager of Tottenham Hotspur.
The 59-year-old's departure ends a turbulent two-month period in charge of the Premier League club.
Santini was appointed in April as successor to Mauricio Pochettino but speculation has been rife about his future since the end of last season.
"I am sad that things have not worked out as we all hoped," he said in a statement.
"Unfortunately there has been too much negative speculation surrounding the club in recent months.

"

Although he achieved his primary target of keeping Tottenham in the top flight, Santini was never regarded as a long-term successor to Pochettino.
He was appointed as interim manager until the end of the season, with the club already beginning their search for a permanent boss.
"I wish Antonio Santini well for the future and thank him for his efforts over the past two months," said Tottenham chairman Daniel Levy.
England legend Lawrence Dallaglio believes he is fit enough to win a place on the Lions tour of South Africa.
The 36-year-old number eight has not played international rugby since 2005, but is "itching" to make a comeback.
The British and Irish Lions leave on 31 May for a month-long tour, playing four matches against Southern Hemisphere teams.
"If I get picked, it would be the pinnacle of my career," said the Wasps captain.
He added: "I'm as fit as I have ever been, and if I get the opportunity to play for the Lions I'll be very keen to take it."
Dallaglio has been selected for the Barbarians squad to play the Lions in Hong Kong on 2 June, the first of their warm-up games.
The veteran of 79 Tests for England has struggled with injuries in recent seasons, and underwent surgery on a disc problem in his back in March.
But the versatile back-row forward, who has played in three previous Lions tours, says he is now fully fit.
"I'm injury-free, which is a nice place to be," said Dallaglio.
"I've done everything that the Lions have requested of me in terms of fitness
and I'm in the best possible shape I can be.

"
The Lions play South Africa's A team in Pretoria on 8 June, followed by the first Test against the world champions on 20 June in Johannesburg, the second in Durban on 27 June and the third, which could be the decisive match, in Pretoria on 4 July.
Dallaglio would be competing with Scotland's Simon Taylor and England's Joe Worsley for the number eight spot in the Lions squad.
And the Italian-born forward says he would be happy to fill in elsewhere in the side.
"If it's at number six or number seven, I'm comfortable there as well," he said.

The UK economy grew faster than expected in the October-to-December quarter, despite worries about higher interest rates and falling consumer confidence.

Asian stock markets have defied expectations and risen in the wake of last week's earthquake in Japan as investors looked through the current turmoil and focused on the longer term prospects.
Japan's Nikkei index closed up 1.2% after falling as much as 2.5% earlier in the day.
In neighbouring South Korea the Kospi index rose 1.1%.
In Australia, the ASX/200 closed up 1.4%.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index ended the morning 0.3% higher.
And in China, where markets were closed on Friday for a public holiday, the CSI 300 index of the largest listed companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen rose 1.4% on Monday.
The resilience of Asian markets is in stark contrast to the reaction to the earthquake seven years ago.
After the earthquake in Tohoku, northern Japan, in March 2011, markets were jittery for months, said Yoshikiyo Shimamine, chief strategist at Daiwa Securities.
Back then, market participants were worried about the impact on the world's third biggest economy.
This time, they are more worried about the rest of the world, given the strong economic ties between Japan and its Asian neighbours.
"Investors are looking past the earthquake and thinking about the recovery of the Japanese economy," said Mr Shimamine.

"We are not concerned about the country's long-term economic outlook," they said.
Japan is a major exporter of cars and electronics and there are hopes that any slowdown in activity will be offset by a recovery in global demand as Covid-19 restrictions gradually get lifted.
The Bank of Japan's efforts to boost inflation are also likely to support the economy as it emerges from the shock, said Hiroaki Hashimoto, chief economist at Tokai Tokyo Research Institute.
"Looking at the bigger picture, there is no reason for the Japanese economy to be affected in the long term," he said.
And there is also hope that the planned $630bn stimulus package announced by the US government will give the global economy a big boost in the coming months.

Disruption to supply chains could affect the region's export-oriented economies.
And worries about the security of nuclear power plants could weigh on the recovery in Japan, analysts say.

Brussels has warned that mobile phone operators may be abusing their dominant position by charging for incoming calls.

The dollar has fallen to its lowest level in eight months, prompting concerns that the US currency's long-running decline could hurt economies worldwide.

Mrs Foley said there was particular concern about the Brazilian real, which has risen by 7% against the dollar since the start of the year.

In a research note, Morgan Stanley warned that the dollar's decline represented the "biggest risk" to global financial markets.
The dollar's fall "has been a key driver of global risk sentiment", the US bank said.

The German jobless rate has hit a new record high, despite predictions it would fall, official data shows.
The adjusted unemployment rate rose to 12.1% in October, up from 11.7% in September, the Federal Statistics Office said.
The unadjusted rate - which includes people who work fewer hours than they would like - was 18.1%, up from 17.5% in September.
Many market analysts had predicted a fall in the jobless rate, noting that the adjusted measure - which is the headline figure - had recently been coming in below market expectations.
However, the statistical office said that this was because it had changed the way it calculated the rate, and that the rise in October should be seen as a correction.
"We don't take too seriously this rise... because of the methodological changes," said Juergen Michels, chief economist at Citigroup in Frankfurt.
"We think the labour market is still improving, and we expect the unemployment rate to fall below 12% early next year.

"

The statistics office said that the rise in the unadjusted rate was due to an increase in so-called "inactive people" in the 16-64 age group, many of whom were giving up looking for work.
Germany has been hit less hard by the global economic crisis than many other European countries, in part because of its strong export focus, but it has not been immune.
The German economy contracted by 5.7% in the second quarter of this year, compared with the same period last year, according to the Federal Statistics Office.
At the same time, unemployment has been rising, and economists say that the government's wage support schemes, which have kept people in work, have hidden the true extent of the problem.
An Irish company has ended its involvement in a waste water treatment project in Iraq, following a report into the deaths of Iraqi civilians.
In 2016, the Iraqi government hired Irish firm Kentz to provide operational support for a waste water treatment project in the city of Basra.
But the firm announced on Tuesday that it had agreed with the Iraqi government to end its involvement in the project.
This came after a report by the Iraqi Human Rights Commission suggested that these contracts may have contributed to a crisis which saw hundreds of thousands of people forced to drink polluted water.
Kentz said it had conducted an extensive review of its involvement, and concluded its operations were "not the cause of the public health crisis".
But the company said it had ended its involvement in the project following a request by the Iraqi government.

London-listed shares in Oracle Co. fell after the U.S. business software company reported disappointing earnings and said it would lay off thousands of workers as part of its acquisition of healthcare tech firm Cerner.
Oracle said the layoffs were part of its integration plan for the $28 billion acquisition, which is the company's biggest deal to date.
The company did not specify the number of jobs that will be lost.
The news comes as Oracle reported fiscal second-quarter earnings that missed expectations.
The company reported earnings per share of $1.11, compared to the expected $1.14.
It also reported revenue of $11.25 billion, compared to the expected $11.26 billion.
Oracle said it expects the Cerner deal to close this year, and that it will contribute to its growth in the coming years.
The company also said it is confident in its ability to integrate Cerner and deliver value to customers and shareholders.
However, analysts were cautious about the company's outlook, with some pointing to the slowing cloud business as a concern.
"The core business is still growing at a healthy clip, but investors were hoping for more from Oracle's cloud unit," said Bob Peck, an analyst at SunTrust Robinson Humphrey.
"The Street is concerned about the company's near-term outlook as cloud growth is decelerating.

"

Overall, Oracle reported that its cloud services and license support segment revenue grew by just 6%, down from 20% growth a year earlier.
The company's total revenue grew by just 2% to $11.25 billion.
"Our overall revenue growth was impacted by the strengthening of the U.S. dollar index," said Oracle Chairman and CTO Larry Ellison.
"We expect currencies to stabilize at these new levels."
Many of the US supermarkets owned by the Dutch conglomerate Ahold have been accused of illegally importing seafood that was caught by slaves.
Prosecutors in Florida have filed a lawsuit against Delhaize America, the US subsidiary of Ahold, and its seafood supplier, Sea Delight.
The suit alleges that Sea Delight and its sister company, Locator Foods, were involved in "trafficking and forced labour" of fishermen in Indonesia.
Locator Foods and Sea Delight deny the allegations.
Delhaize America said it was "shocked and appalled" by them.
The lawsuit says that fishermen were forced to work up to 24 hours a day without pay or rest.
It claims that when workers resisted this treatment, they were threatened with beatings, knife stabbings and being thrown overboard.
Locator Foods provided seafood to Ahold's US supermarkets, including Stop & Shop, Giant Landover, and Hannaford.
Sea Delight also supplies restaurant chains and supermarkets including Whole Foods and Target.

The lawsuit was filed by a seafood importer and former Sea Delight sales manager, Jay LaTorre, who alleges that Locator Foods and Sea Delight knowingly imported seafood that was caught by fishermen working as slaves.
In an email to the BBC, LaTorre said that he hoped the lawsuit would help put an end to "systemic abuse".
"The horrific abuse inflicted on these fishermen is utterly reprehensible and has no place in a civilized society," he wrote.
"Those responsible for the trafficking and forced labour of these vulnerable fishermen must be held accountable for their actions.

"

The lawsuit alleges that Sea Delight and Locator Foods had been aware of the abuse since at least 2013 but did not act to stop it.
In a statement, Sea Delight said the allegations against it were "untrue and incorrect" and that it operated a "strict and rigorous policy on ethical sourcing and sustainability".
Locator Foods said it was not aware of any issues with its suppliers and that it took "these matters very seriously".
"We require all suppliers to comply with all applicable laws and conduct business in accordance with the highest legal and ethical standards," it added.
In a statement, Delhaize America said it was "committed to ensuring that no form of human trafficking or slavery is involved" in its supply chain.

Circuit City's board has not yet reviewed the letter and the company has not commented on it.

What's happening

Retailer Circuit City has received a letter from investor Richard L. Scott, proposing a takeover, the company said.
In a letter dated Thursday, Mr. Scott - whose firm is the largest shareholder in the electronics retailer - offered to acquire the company for $6.50 per share, or about $1.16 billion in cash.
Richard L. Scott's firm, Richmond, Virginia-based Ramius LLC, owns 9.2% of Circuit City's shares.

What they're saying

"The proposed transaction will provide certainty for shareholders and is superior to the current outlook for the company," Mr. Scott wrote in the letter.
"I do not see the prospects for the company improving in the near future," he added.
Mr. Scott also said that if a sale is approved, it would likely result in the majority of the company's stores being closed.
During the holiday shopping season, Circuit City - which has 567 stores nationwide - had offered steep discounts to attract buyers.
But the retailer, which has reported bigger losses in recent quarters, said earlier this month that it had seen a decline in same-store sales for the quarter that ended on January 31.
Could Yukos be a blessing in disguise?
For the last few years Russia's biggest oil company has been fighting for its life.
Yukos Oil Company is up to its neck in debt and last year saw its production slump to a 17-year low.
Now it has been hit with a massive tax bill which could ultimately send it bankrupt.
But some analysts think this could be a blessing in disguise, allowing the company to streamline its operations and come out fighting.
It has already announced plans to sell off its petrol station network.
And on Wednesday its chief executive, Aleksandr Dyukov, said the company was planning to tap its shareholders for as much as $8bn dollars as part of a restructuring plan.
He said the company would sell new shares and cut its massive debt by half.
But analysts say the company also needs to sell more of its key assets in order to survive.
"Yukos is losing its market position and must quickly sell non-core assets, and increase production and efficiency," said Andrei Kramarenko, an analyst with Renaissance Capital.
"Otherwise it will disappear.

"

The company has already signed a deal to sell its Nova television station and some property in Moscow.
But it could also be forced to sell its main production unit, Yukos Arktic, as well as its shares in the Siberian Light Oil Company and some refineries.
"All these assets are going to be sold.
The question is when and at what price," said Mr Kramarenko.
But he said the sale of Yukos's petrol station network would not be enough on its own to help the company out of its difficulties.

"It's nothing special, it's a typical market price, nothing extraordinary."

Yukos has been hit by a series of tax claims which have helped to push the company into debt.
The tax authorities say the company owes them $3.3bn dollars, a figure Yukos says is far too high.
But earlier this month a court in Moscow ordered the company to pay $315m dollars of the claim, and the tax authorities have said they will not rule out bankruptcy proceedings against the company.
The authorities have also put Yukos's main production unit up for auction in order to help pay the tax bill.
Yukos says this is illegal and has appealed to Russia's highest court.
But analysts say the battle with the tax authorities is also helping to strengthen Yukos's hand against its rivals.
