The head of the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has said his agency is considering changes to rules imposed in the wake of the Enron scandal.
They were brought in under former President George W Bush to boost oversight of shareholder votes.
But Gary Gensler said the rules had inadvertently led to fewer US-listed companies.
"We should reflect on whether those rules are still working as intended," he said.
Mr Gensler's remarks come as the SEC considers thousands of public comments after launching a review of the rules last year.
The rules, known as Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD), were introduced in 2000, in the wake of the Enron scandal.
They were designed to prevent selective disclosure of material information by companies to certain groups, such as favoured investors.
They established mechanisms to ensure that everyone gets the information at the same time, such as a safe harbour for forward-looking statements.
But Mr Gensler said last year that they may have had "unintended consequences" of leading to a fall in the number of listed companies in the US.
"One of the things that concerns me the most... is the decline in the number of public companies," he said in August.
"In 1996, there were more than 7,000 public companies in the US.
Today, there are barely 3,600."
Mr Gensler's comments came as the SEC published its first report into the review of Reg FD, together with a statement saying it had received more than 1,000 letters and e-mails on the subject.

The report did not make any recommendations, but said the SEC's next step would be to consider the comments it had received, and any further testimony from investors, public companies and other market participants.
US telecoms company Qwest Communications has made an unsolicited $6.75bn (£3.7bn) bid for its larger rival MCI, prompting a sharp rise in MCI's share price.
Qwest said it was offering $23.50 a share, mostly in cash, for the No 2 US long-distance telephone company.
The move could force rival US telecoms firm Verizon Communications to raise its bid for MCI, currently valued at $23.04bn.
Qwest said its offer, which represents a 37% premium on MCI's closing price on Friday, had the support of MCI's management.
"The management of MCI and the MCI board of directors supporting this transaction believe that it is in the best interest of MCI shareholders," Qwest said in a statement.

"Qwest has been informed that the MCI board will recommend that MCI shareholders accept the Qwest offer, subject to completion of definitive documentation."

Shares in MCI jumped $7.79, or 35%, to $29 in early trading in New York.
The firm has until 11 December to find a "superior" offer, and Qwest has until 18 December to sweeten its bid.
If no better offers come forward, MCI shareholders will have to approve the deal.
Qwest hopes to expand its operations through the acquisition of MCI, which has 22 million phone and data customers.
Qwest, which has 8.5 million customers, has been hit hard by the fall of the internet bubble and the collapse of carrier Sprint Corp's merger with Nextel Communications.
The firm has been looking to grow through acquisitions since it lost out on a deal to buy cable operator MediaOne for $48.5bn earlier this year.
The European Commission has recommended that member states should not impose cuts in 2023, and should instead aim for a modest fiscal expansion.
Many countries have been struggling with increased spending on energy support and rising interest rates as they battle inflation.
The recommendation represents a significant change in the EU's economic policy.
The commission said that its "economic outlook has deteriorated significantly" since it last made recommendations in July.
It said that "more ambitious" fiscal policies were needed to respond to "the unfolding energy crisis, persistent inflation, and the deteriorating economic activity".
Inflation in the eurozone is now lower than it was last year, but it is still very high by the standards of the last decade, with prices rising by 9.2% in December.

Energy prices have fallen from their peaks but are still nearly double what they were before the pandemic, and businesses and households are facing higher borrowing costs after the European Central Bank's recent interest rate rises.
The commission's recommendation to halt austerity is the first since 2010 when member states were battling the financial crisis.
It says countries with fiscal space, such as Germany and the Netherlands, should "take the lead" in spending to support the economy.
Those without that space, such as Italy, should use "all available means" to support households and companies, it adds.
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she would "study" the recommendations, adding that "we have always said that we are ready to do what is necessary to face the crisis".

The EU executive's advice is not binding, but it is used by the European Council to make its own recommendations, and by the Court of Justice to rule on whether national budgets are in line with EU rules.
The commission's President Ursula von der Leyen said "when times are tough, we must be tough".
"This is why we propose to our member states to suspend all fiscal rules and to revert to growth-friendly investments," she said.
The recommendation to halt austerity is likely to be welcomed by southern European countries, which have called for fiscal stimulus to help them through the energy crisis.
However, it is likely to be resisted by northern European countries, which have been pushing for continued spending discipline.
The commission's proposal will now go to the European Council for discussion at a meeting of finance ministers on 24 January.
US transportation officials are to meet on Friday to discuss travel chaos over the Christmas period, which was blamed on a severe storm that disrupted flights and road travel.
The Biden administration is to launch a "full investigation" into the incident, a Transportation Department (DOT) spokesperson told the BBC.
Thousands of holiday travellers were left stranded at airports around the US amid delays and cancellations due to severe weather, including heavy snowfalls and icy conditions.
There have been calls from lawmakers for the federal government to investigate how the storm impacted travel, as well as the role that climate change may have played in the severity of the weather.
According to flight tracker FlightAware, more than 9,000 US flights were delayed and almost 1,600 were cancelled on Saturday alone.
Five of the six busiest North American travel days of the year occur during the Christmas holiday season, according to the DOT.
A massive winter storm moved across the US ahead of Christmas, dumping snow from the Rocky Mountains to parts of the northeast.
As the storm advanced, the National Weather Service (NWS) issued winter storm warnings from the nation's capital, Washington, to parts of Maine.

In a statement released on Saturday, the Biden administration said they were "working closely with airlines and airport authorities to move towards normal operations, and actively working to understand any underlying issues with the extensive disruptions".
The statement added that the Biden administration "will take any appropriate action" to support passengers.
On Thursday, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas tweeted: "Perhaps a probe into how the winter weather was so poorly forecast & how best to prepare for future weather events?

"

After thousands of flights were delayed and canceled, Cruz added on Sunday that "the Biden Administration's failure to adequately prepare for Christmas week's winter storm hurt American travelers."
The Iranian government has approved next year's budget, which has been described as the country's most "social" budget yet.
The budget, worth about $40bn (£28bn), will not impose any new taxes and promises to create more than 800,000 new jobs.
It also plans to sell off hundreds of loss-making state companies.
Iran's economy has been hit by years of sanctions over its nuclear programme and the fall in oil prices.
Oil revenues make up about 80% of the Iranian government's budget.
Tehran has been trying to tackle its economic problems, including high unemployment and inflation, by boosting its exports and cutting back on its reliance on oil.
The 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and the six world powers - UK, US, France, Germany, Russia and China - lifted some economic sanctions in exchange for Tehran curbing its nuclear activities.
But Iran's economy has yet to recover, in part because of the US's withdrawal last year from the nuclear deal and its decision to reimpose sanctions.

China tightened the reins on its money supply in November, raising worries about the pace of economic growth.
Data from the central bank showed on Monday that the M2 money supply - a broad measure of the money supply - grew by 8.2% in November from a year earlier, compared with 8.6% in October.
The data also showed that China's new loans fell well short of expectations in November, as banks became more cautious about lending.
Some analysts said the move to tighten credit controls came as China's economy was showing signs of recovery.
"The credit data showed policy makers maintained a tight rein on credit growth in November as the economy continued to improve," said Zhang Zhiwei, chief China economist at Bank of New York Mellon.
"We expect credit growth to stay modest in the coming months as policymakers stick to their tight monetary policy stance.

"

The world's second-largest economy expanded by 7.8% in the third quarter, beating expectations and reversing a string of three consecutive quarterly declines.
But while the economy has been showing signs of recovery, China's leaders have moved to tighten credit controls in recent months to contain inflation and slow the rapid rise in property prices.
Data last week showed that China's consumer price index (CPI) rose to a 28-month high of 4.4% in November, driven by rising food and energy prices.
China's economy has been recovering from a soft patch earlier in the year, when it was hit by a downturn in its property market and a sharp fall in demand for its exports.
The government has set a growth target of around 7% for next year, but some analysts say that this may be difficult to achieve as policy makers continue to tighten credit controls.
Oil prices have risen to their highest level since 2014 on the back of hopes for a swift economic recovery in 2021 and continued production cuts by OPEC and its allies.
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures, the US benchmark, rose 2.5% to $63.37 a barrel on Tuesday, while Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 1.5% to $67.83 a barrel.
Strong manufacturing data from China and the US, as well as an upbeat assessment of the US economy by Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, have bolstered the case for a rapid recovery.
Mr Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on Tuesday that the US economy is poised to expand rapidly this year, adding that he expects inflation to pick up as the country reopens.
However, he said that any increase in prices would be temporary, and that the Fed would be patient in removing support from the economy.
In China, manufacturing activity rose to a eight-month high in March, according to a private survey released on Sunday.
The official manufacturing survey released on Saturday also showed a sharp improvement.
In Japan, manufacturing activity rose to its highest level since early 2011, according to a survey released on Friday.
OPEC and its allies, known as OPEC+, have also continued to cut production, with Saudi Arabia announcing plans to unilaterally cut an additional 1 million barrels per day in April.
The group has been cutting production since last year in an effort to support prices, and the cuts have been extended into March.
While the economic recovery has driven up demand for oil, supply has been limited by the OPEC+ cuts and by US sanctions on Iran and Venezuela.

However, In a statement on Monday, OPEC somewhat dampened the outlook, saying that "ongoing Covid-19 lockdowns in Europe and continuing restrictions in other parts of the world" could slow the recovery in oil demand.
The group said that it expects world oil demand to increase by 5.8 million barrels per day in 2021, down from its previous forecast of 6.0 million barrels per day.
Nevertheless, the outlook for oil prices remains bullish, with analysts forecasting that prices could rise further in the coming months.
Commodity trading firm Trafigura said in a report on Tuesday that it expects Brent crude to hit $70 a barrel by the end of June, driven by strong demand and limited supply.

Caption: Egypt to sell off state-owned bank - BBC News

Subcaption: A deal to sell a majority stake in the National Bank of Egypt (NBE) has been agreed
, officials say.
The bank's chairman said a number of investors would buy a 51% stake.
Details of the deal are expected to be announced later on Thursday.
The government is selling state firms to help reduce its debt.
The sell-off comes as Egypt battles inflation - which hit 18% in November - and a slump in the value of its currency.
The deal entails the participation of a number of strategic investors, the bank's chairman, Hisham Okasha, confirmed to Reuters news agency.
He did not disclose the identities of the buyers.
"It's a great day for the National Bank of Egypt," he was quoted as saying.
"We are selling at a good price and we are selling to strategic investors."
The bank's sale has been on the cards for years.
In 2017, the Egyptian government signed a memorandum of understanding with Saudi Arabian investors, but the deal never materialised.
A number of other, unsuccessful attempts to sell the bank have also been made.
The NBE is the largest of Egypt's state-owned banks.
It handles about half of the nation's banking transactions.
The bank's assets were about 1.7 trillion Egyptian pounds ($119bn; £95bn) at the end of 2020.
The Egyptian government has been trying to reduce its debt, which stood at 108% of GDP in the second quarter of 2021.
Last year, it sold its remaining stake in the Middle East's largest container handling company, Suez Canal Container Terminal, to the Dubai-based DP World.
This year, the government started selling state-owned enterprises in sectors including pharmaceuticals, chemicals and fertilisers.
Late last year, it launched a programme to sell off state-owned property.
In November, it sold a landmark government-owned property in Cairo.
The sale of state firms comes as Egypt battles inflation, which hit 18% in November - its highest level in 30 years.
The country's currency has also slumped from about 15 Egyptian pounds to the dollar in 2019 to about 20 pounds to the dollar now.
The Central Bank of Egypt has raised its key interest rate by 3% to curb inflation.
But it has faced criticism that its attempts to control rising prices have not been enough.
The dollar has slid ahead of the new year, as investors bet that interest rates will go up less quickly in the US than hoped.
The US dollar index, which measures the currency against six others, fell to a six-month low of 95.67 on Tuesday.
It has tumbled nearly 8% from its highest level this year in October, when markets were bracing for the Federal Reserve to hike rates by as much as 100 basis points in December.
However, Fed chair Jerome Powell's recent comments that smaller interest rate hikes would likely be appropriate "over the coming months" helped the dollar to rebound slightly.
But it came under pressure again on Tuesday, as easing inflation and weaker-than-expected retail sales reinforced the view that the Fed could take its foot off the gas when it comes to rate rises.
"The dollar is crumbling… as the Fed is falling behind the curve," Joseph Capurso, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, told Reuters.
"The market has priced out almost any chance of a 50 basis point hike in February and is pricing only about a 10% chance of a 25 basis point hike," he added.
The euro meanwhile has rallied and was trading at $1.0581 on Tuesday, a level not seen in six months.
Sterling also extended its gains to trade at $1.2346, a rise of more than 3.6% from its December low.
While the pound remains vulnerable to more volatility, it has been helped by data showing the UK is weathering the cost of living crisis better than expected.

It will be able to carry up to 10 million tonnes of crude a year - reducing the need to transport oil by ship.
The pipeline is expected to be operational from 2023.
The project, backed by the European Commission, will be financed by Italy's Eni, Bulgaria's Bulgargaz and Greece's DEPA.
Eni Chief Executive Claudio Descalzi said the pipeline would be "an important infrastructure for the security of European energy supply".
He said the pipeline would help "ensure diversification" of energy supplies.
Mr Descalzi said the project would help reach EU targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions as it would lower the amount of oil transported by ships.
French consumer spending is rising fast as households buy more online, eat in restaurants, and splash out on utilities and social activities, data shows.
According to the official data, household spending accelerated in January, up 1.1% from the same month a year earlier, and 0.8% higher than in December.
The figures were well above the 0.4% growth forecast by analysts.
The robust data points to healthy activity in the eurozone's second-biggest economy, says ING bank.
"The French economy surprises positively every time," said ING economist Charlotte de Montpellier.
"There is a catch, though: the data are extremely volatile and prone to large revisions.
But at this stage, it is difficult to see a big downward revision in the coming months," she added.
French consumers have been cautious since the 2008 financial crisis, with many holding onto their savings and looking to pay off debt.
But economists say they are increasingly spending some of their cash, in part because of low unemployment and rising wages.
The data showed a 1.4% rise in spending on transport, accommodation and food, as well as a 1.1% increase in spending on health, education and culture.
There was also a 0.8% rise in spending on leisure and communication, as well as a 0.5% rise in spending on clothing.
However, spending on housing, which accounts for more than a third of household spending, fell 0.6% in January.
This was the biggest fall since December 2012, and resulted in an overall 0.1% fall in household spending.

Air passengers win new EU rights

Passengers stranded by airline failure will automatically receive compensation from 2015, under new rules agreed by the European Parliament.
The parliament's transport committee voted to adopt rules that would see passengers offered vouchers for future flights or refunds.
Currently, they can wait up to several years to receive money from the Airline Insolvency Fund (AIF), which compensates passengers when an airline goes bust.
The new rules would also see passengers offered assistance, such as food, phone calls and hotel accommodation if there is a long delay or cancellation.
They could also get a full refund if they decide not to take a delayed flight.
Currently, airlines are not obliged to pay compensation in such cases.

The committee rejected proposals to introduce a Europe-wide passenger bill of rights, which could have seen passengers get refunds if their flight was delayed by more than three hours, and larger compensation if they were denied boarding.
UK airlines fear that such rules would cost them £500m a year.
Committee members also voted to scrap plans to force airlines to display information on the country of origin of their flights.
Several UK airlines had warned that the proposal would be costly and bureaucratic.
The committee's proposals must still be approved by the European Parliament and the 27 member states.

Music company EMI has warned its investors that rising costs mean it is unlikely to reach its profit target this year.
The British group, which is owned by Terra Firma, said it was facing increased recording and marketing costs, particularly at its Virgin Records label.
It also said the recession in the music industry and the war in Iraq had had an effect on artist recruitment.
EMI shares fell more than 11% on the London Stock Exchange following the warning on Thursday.
They have now fallen by about two-thirds since the company was bought by Terra Firma in August 2007.
In a statement, EMI said it now expected its operating profit - before exceptionals and tax - to be between £175m and £200m this year.
That is well below the target of £250m set by Terra Firma last year, and the £268m operating profit the company recorded in 2006.
EMI also said it was discontinuing the interim dividend to save money.
The group, whose stable of artists includes Coldplay, Kylie Minogue and Radiohead, said the performance of its flagship Virgin Records label had been particularly disappointing.

"Virgin Records has not performed as well as expected, as the costs of delivering a significant number of new releases, coupled with the costs of restructuring the business, have been greater than anticipated," it said.
"In addition, the continued difficult consumer environment has had an effect on artist recruitment.

"

However, EMI said its market-leading classical music operation, Warner Classics, had performed "extremely well".
It also said its Parlophone label, whose artists include Pet Shop Boys and Iron Maiden, had seen a strong performance, while its popular music output had been "solid".
India has unveiled one of the most ambitious budgets in its history, with a huge boost to spending on public healthcare and subsidies for poor households.
Many Indians living below the poverty line were already benefiting from cheap handouts of rice and wheat, but on Tuesday the government announced a new monthly payment for poor families.
This decision was one of the many ways that the government is trying to reduce poverty in the nation.
The plan will benefit an estimated 85 million poor people, at an annual cost of $20.6bn (1.23 trillion rupees).
About half of India's population lives on less than $2 a day, with many struggling to access basic healthcare and education.
Tuesday's budget raises spending on health care by 35% and on education by 22%.
There was also a boost for rural India, with an ambitious plan to electrify every single household by the end of 2022.
About 14 million households, or about 40% of all rural households, do not have electricity.
There were no big announcements on tax reforms or job creation - two other major challenges facing India.
The US trade deficit widened in October to the largest gap in a decade, with lower exports and higher imports.
The trade gap rose to $98.8bn (£74.4bn), up $2.2bn from September, the Commerce Department said.
The result was worse than expected and reflected a decline in exports of goods such as agricultural products.
It also reflected higher oil prices, which boosted the value of imports.
The wider trade deficit will weigh on US economic growth in the third quarter, analysts said.
The economy is already showing signs of slowing, in part because of an inflationary burst caused by supply chain problems that have now eased.

"The US trade deficit exploded in October as exports of agricultural products and capital goods declined, and higher oil prices boosted imports," said Ian Shepherdson, chief economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics.
"The deterioration... is not a positive development for fourth-quarter GDP growth.

"

OctOBer exports of goods and services fell 0.7% to $287.69bn, while imports rose 0.4% to $386.5bn, led by industrial supplies, such as petroleum products.
UK house prices fell by 0.1% in November 2022, according to a survey by Halifax.
It means prices have dropped for six months in a row, with values 6.9% higher than a year earlier, the mortgage lender said.
Halifax said that prices had been cooling noticeably since the start of the year, adding that the market had "definitely softened" in the last few months.

It added that a combination of inflation, rising interest rates, and a sudden increase in the cost of household goods had led to a sharp fall in disposable income, which had weighed on consumer confidence.
"Given the mounting pressure on household budgets, we expect house price growth to slow further in the coming months," said Halifax managing director Russell Galley.
The figures came as lenders approved the fewest mortgages for house purchases since April 2021, according to industry body UK Finance.
It said that there were 36,597 mortgages approved for house purchases in October, down from 39,327 a year earlier.
Mortgage approvals for home purchases are now at their lowest level since the onset of the Covid pandemic in spring 2020, UK Finance said.

Should the government introduce a cap on the amount of money individuals can donate to political parties?
A cross-party committee has recommended that the government should consider introducing a limit on political donations.
The House of Lords Appointments Committee said the current system "threatens the integrity and confidence of our political system".
It said the government should consider introducing a cap on the overall amount that can be donated by individuals, as well as a lower cap on the amount which can be donated in a single donation.

The committee's report said: "We are not convinced that a better alternative system to cap donations would deliver the improvements to transparency, fairness and confidence which would be needed to address the corruption risk and improve public confidence."

It added: "A lower cap on single donations could also help prevent corruption and improve confidence in the political system.
"Taken together, these measures have the potential to improve confidence in the system, but this would depend on how they were designed and implemented and how effectively they were enforced."
The committee also recommended that the government should lower the threshold at which political parties have to declare donations from £7,500 to £1,000.
And it said the next election should be "fully funded by the Treasury" to stop the parties competing to raise funds.
The committee's report comes after the PM announced that a public consultation on plans to reform the way political donations are handled will be launched.

Under current rules, political parties can receive donations of any size and do not have to declare them to the Electoral Commission unless they exceed £7,500.
The committee said the current situation had allowed wealthy individuals and companies to gain "undue influence" over political parties.
It added that while some of the largest donations were used to fund political campaigning, this was not always the case and some were used to pay off debt or cover running costs.

The report said: "We conclude that the current system does not provide adequate protection against corruption or the appearance of corruption and thereby threatens the integrity and confidence of our political system."

Barack Obama has helped re-elect Joe Sestak in Pennsylvania, improving the chances of the Democrats holding on to control of the Senate.

The UK government has introduced a new English language requirement for foreign nationals who want to marry British citizens.
From Thursday, those without a good grasp of English will have to take a test - at a cost of £1,000 ($1,270) - before they can get a marriage visa.
The measure is aimed at tackling so-called "sham weddings".
The test must be taken at one of the approved test centres in seven days.
The government says it is "determined to tackle illegal immigration" and protect the public against "marriages of convenience".

The test will be in addition to existing requirements for a foreign national who wants to marry a British citizen to prove they can speak English to a level equivalent to band A2 of the Council of Europe's common European framework of reference for languages.
This is the level expected of a basic user of English.
Officials say there are an additional 12 countries, including China and Russia, where applicants who wish to marry a British citizen must also prove they know English.
What has changed is that instead of providing evidence that they know English - such as through documents or testimonials - they must now take the speaking and listening test.
The test, which is run by language teaching body Trinity College London, lasts 20 minutes and applicants must achieve at least a pass mark of A2.
According to the college, the test is not designed to test applicants' knowledge of British culture or customs - it is a conversation on familiar topics such as family, hobbies and going out.
The Home Office says applicants who fail will be able to retake the test once, but they must pay the £1,000 fee each time.
Those who continue to refuse or fail to take the test will have their application for a marriage visa rejected.
The measure was announced in April as part of the government's wider strategy to reduce net migration.
The BBC has learned that ministers believe the measure will affect about 200 couples a year.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "The government is determined to tackle illegal immigration and protect the public against marriages of convenience, which are often used to circumvent immigration rules.
"That's why we have introduced tougher requirements for those who wish to come to the UK to marry, requiring them to prove their English language abilities and their knowledge of life in the UK.
"This is an important step in ensuring that those who come to the UK to marry are doing so for the right reasons

Mr Day is so concerned that he is taking an active role in the campaign against the law, and is even calling for the arrest of Tony Blair for the part he played in introducing it.

He added that he believed the law was being used to harass ethnic minorities and political dissidents.

"I think that the legislation is so broad and so draconian that it will catch legitimate political protest," he said.
"It's designed to catch terrorism but it's actually catching legitimate political dissent and that is unacceptable in any democratic society."
Mr Day added that he believed the law was being used to harass ethnic minorities.

At a federal court in western Texas on Tuesday, Jetflix's five founders were found guilty of conspiracy to commit copyright infringement.

Military forces around the world are taking part in exercises simulating war with a major power such as Russia or China.
The UK, US, Japan and Australia have all held exercises this year focusing on possible conflicts with great power rivals.
Russia and China have accused the West of stoking tensions.
The UK's Defence Secretary Ben Wallace said the war games were vital for planning.
Mr Wallace said Britain's military must be prepared to fight a "major conventional war" and that exercises were crucial for understanding "how we would fight and win".

The UK's series of war games this year - known as Cold Response - involved more than 15,000 troops from 27 countries, including two NATO members - Norway and Belgium - and two Nordic neighbours, Sweden and Finland.

It centred on a scenario involving a fictional country called "Aurora", which represented the kinds of challenges a state facing a hostile Russia might encounter, according to the UK's Ministry of Defence.
War games are also designed to test the limits of a military's ability to carry out missions, and identify where it needs to improve.
Exercise Northern Coast, held in Japan in January, prepared the country's Self Defence Forces for a Chinese invasion.
Some of the exercises mimicked a Chinese invasion of the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu islands in the East China Sea, which are controlled by Japan but claimed by China.
The US military carried out its own war games in South Korea in March, with the alleged aim of practising for a war with North Korea.
Thousands of American and South Korean troops took part in the exercises, which included simulated bombings and tank battles.
US and Australian troops also took part in exercises in Australia at the end of August, which aimed to prepare them for a conflict with China.
The exercises - known as Talisman Sabre - included computer-assisted command post exercises, air and sea deployments, and field training exercises.
China has repeatedly accused the US of stoking tensions in the region.

"The US is sending the wrong signal by dispatching military aircraft and warships in the South China Sea, and carrying out joint military exercises with countries outside the region," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said during a visit to Cambodia on Monday.
Russia has made similar complaints about Nato exercises.
Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov accused the alliance of "frequently holding provocative military exercises in Europe".

It sounds like a joke but it is a serious piece of malware which security experts say has caught thousands of people out.
The "joke" e-mail virus hides inside an attachment which claims to be a graphic image of a puppy or a kitten.
But the image is actually an executable file and opening it will launch the virus.
The attachment has a name like "cute_kitten.vbs".
Users should be suspicious of files with ".vbs" extensions as they are often used by viruses, security experts said.

The e-mail comes with a subject line such as "Look at this cute kitten!"

Once launched, the virus sends a copy of itself to all the people in the victim's address book.
It also disables several security features on the victim's machine and may make it vulnerable to further attacks.
The virus, which security experts have called "Funlove", appears to have been created by the same group which developed the "I love you" virus.
That was one of the most damaging viruses ever, which spread rapidly through e-mails with subjects like "I love you baby" or "Hello baby".
Experts believe the new virus is likely to spread rapidly in the next few days as people return to their desks after the Easter holiday weekend.

A popular Chinese lifestyle blogger known as "Sister Tao" has been grounded by her airline for posting a photo of herself wearing a bikini onboard a flight.
Tao Liang, who has more than 50 million followers on social media, posted the photo on June 25, posing in front of one of the plane's windows with the caption "summer vibe".
But it was the airline staff who were left feeling hot under the collar.
China's Hainan Airlines has banned Ms Liang from flying with the company for two years, and ordered her to undertake "corrective education" on air safety.

The company said in a statement that the move was made because the blogger had violated airline regulations on several occasions, including smoking in the plane's toilet, and not wearing a mask properly.
But Ms Liang hit back at the airline on China's Weibo social media platform, saying the bikini photo was taken after she had finished flying, and she was not wearing a swim suit on the flight.
"I never thought that my behaviour would be considered as not putting emphasis on civil aviation service morale, and I sincerely admit my mistakes," she said in a statement.
"I am willing to accept the punishment arranged by Hainan Airlines and promise to enhance my awareness of civil aviation services," she added.
The blogger has made headlines in the past for her controversial online content.
She shot to fame in 2016 for uploading videos of herself bragging about her wealth and buying expensive handbags.
But her online fame has not brought her happiness.
Ms Liang, from the southern city of Nanjing, has previously spoken about being bullied at school, and said in 2019 that she was being pursued by online trolls.
"I think at the very least, my happiness is taken into account," she said.
"I don't want to continue with this facade, to keep smiling."
Apple has filed a lawsuit in California against unnamed defendants it accuses of leaking confidential information about its products.
In the lawsuit, filed in Santa Clara County, Apple said it discovered in 2019 that "at least" six people had been leaking confidential information.
It did not name the defendants.
The lawsuit alleges that the defendants were in contact with Daniel Eran Dilger - a journalist who writes for Apple Insider.

"Apple has suffered and will continue to suffer irreparable injury and damage as a result of defendants' misconduct," the lawsuit added.

The steel structure is described as a "mega-dam" by Ukrainian officials and is being assembled near the capital.
It is hoped it will help protect the city from flooding as well as from Russian military attacks.
Work on the 25km (15 mile) structure began in August.
It is being constructed in stages, with the first section - almost 6km long - due to be completed by the end of the year.
The structure does not encircle Kyiv itself, but closes off a stretch of the Dnipro river to the east of the city.
Ukrainian officials say the barrier is necessary because of the low water level in the river, which makes it difficult to use floodplains as a defence against Russian troops.
"If the enemy succeeds in blowing up the dam, Kyiv will be flooded," said President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"That's why we are building a strong anti-flood barrier, a dam, which provides protection against floods and, importantly, against enemy shells and missiles.

"

The structure, which is being built by the Ministry of Infrastructure, is made up of more than 1,000 concrete elements, some of which are more than 6m high.
Once the first section is complete, work will begin on the next phase of the project, with a target completion date of 1 May.
Ukrainian officials have not revealed how much the project costs, but say that funds have been allocated from the state budget.

The virtual computer is an Android application that provides a basic desktop, complete with office applications.

Mr Wadongo came up with the idea in 2011 after visiting an internet cafe in Nairobi and realising that it was equipped with just three computers, yet more than 30 customers were jostling for space.
He had already experienced the frustration of unreliable electricity while studying mechatronics engineering at university in the US.
"I got tired of being in the computer lab and the power would go off.

Format wars between Blu-ray and HD DVD have "already damaged" the high definition DVD market in the UK, according to a retail study.
A survey by Retail Eyes found that the confusion among consumers over which format to buy caused sales of HD DVDs in the run up to Christmas to be "well below" expectations.
The study said that shoppers were put off buying machines capable of playing either Blu-ray or HD DVD, in case the format war ended up favouring the rival format.
"The format war has damaged consumer confidence in the whole category," the study said.
"Many consumers are reluctant to invest in a format that may become obsolete in the future.

"

The study found that just one in 200 UK shoppers purchased a high definition DVD player or recorder in the six weeks before Christmas.
Retail Eyes said that stock levels of the format were "generally good" but added that retailers should consider the impact of the format war when planning ahead for this year's Christmas season.
The study found that one in three shoppers would not buy any HD products because of the uncertainty surrounding the format war.
Last week, Japanese electronics giant Sony announced that it would buy out its rival Toshiba's share in a joint venture to produce HD DVDs.
The move all-but-ends the battle between Blu-ray and HD DVD to provide the next-generation optical disc for high definition movies and games.

Donald Gilligan, of EarthLink, warned that the coming of higher-speed wireless technology known as WiMax would increase the threat from opportunistic computer hackers with "nothing better to do".
His comments came as US telecommunications regulator, the FCC, voted to adopt rules to permit fixed and mobile WiMax deployment.
"Every time we introduce a new, faster service there are people out there who are going to use it for either good or evil," Mr Gilligan told the BBC.
"There is a whole category of people out there who did not have anything better to do before and now they do - and they can cause problems," he added.
WiMax, or 802.16, is a standards-based, broadband wireless technology that provides high-throughput data coverage over distances of up to 30 miles.

It allows users to connect without wires to the internet and is expected to be used for a wide range of services, from providing broadband coverage in rural areas to delivering high-speed access in airports, coffee shops and other public places.
The technology can also help networks cope with spikes in data use, such as when thousands of people try to access the internet during major events, Mr Gilligan said.
But he added that the growth of high-speed wireless internet would also create new opportunities for cyber criminals.

"There are people out there who are going to want to try to pretend to be your WiMax access point and if you log on through them, they can then intercept everything you are doing on the internet," he said.

Mr Gilligan said that WiMax technology included some "very good security" but that this would never be "good enough" to keep out a determined hacker.
The issue was further complicated by the growing popularity of Wi-Fi, or 802.11b, which allowed hackers to piggyback on networks from nearby locations, he said.

Apple has filed lawsuits against two people who allegedly shared copyrighted material, in what is believed to be the first time the technology giant has taken legal action against users of its operating system.
The file sharers were among a group of people who were monitoring the progress of the legal battle between Apple and Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite.
Apple said the two defendants, who live in Texas and Florida, had shared "trade secrets" and were in violation of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.
The company filed the lawsuits in US district court in California on Tuesday, but did not file against the other members of the group, which monitored the Epic Games case on the online forum Reddit.
In a statement, Apple said the two defendants, who have not been identified, had "gained unauthorized access" to its "internal bounty system" for reporting bugs and security vulnerabilities.
It said the move was part of an effort to "hold individuals accountable for their intentional misconduct".
"Apple never alleged the defendants disclosed any information about the operating system," the company said.

"The defendants are charged with violating Apple's endpoint security policy, which applies to all Apple employees, because they were actively running an unprotected instance of Apple's in-house file sharing service, despite multiple reminders to protect their sensitive data," it added.
Epic Games sued Apple in 2020, accusing it of acting as a monopoly with its online marketplace for apps on its iPhones and other devices.
The lawsuit was filed in US district court in Northern California and is still ongoing.
In recent months, a group of people on Reddit who call themselves "fuqyes" have been live-streaming and posting videos of themselves watching the legal proceedings.
The two defendants who were sued were members of the group, and posted a link to a file-sharing app, according to Apple.

The lawsuit said the two defendants had been reminded of their obligation to keep confidential information secure, but had continued to use the company's file sharing system in an "unauthorized and irresponsible manner".
"In doing so, they have flagrantly violated Apple's policies and ignored multiple reminders to address their misconduct," the company said.
Mobile phones are "not media players yet" because of the small screen size and lack of a keyboard, an Ofcom director has said.
Ed Richards said that the devices were currently "proving rather disappointing" as a way to access the internet.
He said that media companies had found it hard to establish a business model on the mobile platform.
The official called for more research into the way people use mobiles.
He said that mobile phones had been "pretty revolutionary" as a way to make phone calls while on the move, but that they had not yet lived up to their early potential as media players.
"As devices on which to make telephone calls whilst on the move, mobiles have been pretty revolutionary, but they haven't yet lived up to the early hype as media players," he said.
"Handset designers have struggled to come up with a device that is as easy to use as a remote control, with a screen at least as good as a pocket TV and with the same content as online.
"Until these problems are solved, mobiles are unlikely to become mainstream media players.
Media companies are also struggling to establish a sustainable business model for mobile content, just as they are with internet services.

"

The official called for more research into mobile phone use.
He said that mobile phone networks had carried out extensive research into how people use their phones, but that this information was "not as widely available as it might be".

"Given the importance of this still-emerging market, it's important that we know more about how users interact with mobile media services so that we can judge what works and what doesn't, and what might work in the future," he said.
Mr. Richards said that mobile phone users were still more likely to use their devices to make phone calls than to send text messages or access the internet.
He said this was likely to change in the future.
The official said that SMS text messaging had become the "first mainstream, non-voice mobile service".
Sony's latest products have won a prize for innovation at the CES technology show in Las Vegas.
The Japanese tech giant's new concept car and its latest robotic dog were among the winners at this year's event.
The concepts were recognised by the CES organisation as the best in floor innovation at the event.
The concepts were chosen from a wide range of products at the show, which showcases the latest tech developments.
The new concepts add to Sony's growing range of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics products for the home.
At last year's CES, Sony unveiled a new version of its Aibo robotic dog, as well as a new drone and a wearable robotic dog that can carry parcels.
At this year's show, Sony revealed a new version of its Aibo robot dog, as well as the Vision-S 02 concept car, which is a follow-up to last year's Vision-S 01.

The Vision-S 02 is a seven-seat electric vehicle (EV), with the same safety and driver assistance systems as the original Vision-S.

Sony scored a hat-trick of awards for its latest products, also winning best of innovation for its image sensor for smartphones and an energy efficient program for smart homes.
"Sony is definitely on a roll at the moment, having won three awards at CES this year for very different technologies," said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight.

Gamers could help unlock the secrets of a 500-year-old painting by Leonardo da Vinci
By designing virtual robots to scrub the surface of the painting in ultra-high definition, researchers aim to remove centuries of dirt and grime to reveal the masterpiece in all its glory

Experts hope the project will shed light on the techniques used by the Renaissance artist, and offer insights into the pigments he used

Gamers could help unlock the secrets of a €300m (£275m) Leonardo da Vinci painting newly unveiled at the Louvre.
French researchers are appealing to gamers to help clean up the surface of the restored Salvator Mundi by designing virtual robots to scrub the surface of the painting in ultra-high definition.
They hope the project will shed light on the techniques used by the Renaissance artist, and offer insights into the pigments he used, as well as the exact tone of the colours.
"There's never been a painting analysed in this way before," said Marc Vallière, the scientific director of the Opéra National de Paris, who is heading the initiative.
"We're going to scrub the surface of the painting in ultra-high definition and the painting itself is going to become a database," he told the BBC.

The project - which has been compared to Google's Street View - aims to remove centuries of dirt and grime that have built up on the surface of the painting, and could even help answer questions about its authenticity.

Over the past two years, the researchers have been examining the painting in minute detail - capturing everything from the cracks in the paint to the traces of restoration work carried out in the past.
They have created a digital replica of the painting, which has around 30 layers of tiny pixels - each one containing information about the colours used by the Italian master.
By comparing the replica with the original, the researchers hope to be able to scrub away the dirt and reveal the masterpiece in all its glory.
"We're going to clean the painting, not with solvents or any other material, but with pixels," said Mr Vallière.

The project - which has been described as "madness" by the Louvre - could also offer historians a chance to discover whether the painting has been tampered with over the centuries, and to find out more about how it was restored in the past.
"This is a painting that has been heavily restored, and so the underdrawing is not necessarily by Leonardo," said Mr Vallière.

Firefox browser takes on Microsoft

Early tests suggest Firefox's new browser is a formidable rival to Microsoft's Internet Explorer.
Mozilla, which pioneered the open-source movement, has made its new Firefox browser available for download.
It is the organization's first serious challenge to Internet Explorer since the mid-1990s.
And early tests suggest it is a formidable rival.
Although it will not be available on Windows XP, the new browser is being offered to users of Windows 7 and 8, as well as Apple's OS X and Linux.
It appears to be faster, especially at loading complex pages, than the current version of Internet Explorer (IE), which holds a 60% share of the browser market.
And it has some new features, such as a tool that blocks trackers that monitor users' behavior across the web.
Microsoft recently announced that it was releasing its new browser, IE11, last week to coincide with the release of Windows 8.1.
But that is only being made available for Windows 7 and 8 computers, and not for the much older Windows XP.
That means that there will be millions of users who will not have access to Microsoft's latest browser, but who will be able to use Firefox.
"If Firefox 38 is as good as it looks right now, then IE11 has a real fight on its hands," wrote one developer on his blog.
"I think we'll be recommending it to our users," added another.
But others have warned that the browser still has some way to go before it is ready for mainstream users.
"It feels a bit like a beta release, but that's not necessarily a bad thing," said one.
Mozilla, a non-profit organization, has been developing the Firefox browser for 15 years.
Its mission is to offer a free and open alternative to proprietary software such as Microsoft's.
Its browser is already very popular in some parts of the world, particularly in Europe where it has a market share of about 30%.
But in the US, it has struggled to make inroads against Internet Explorer and Google's Chrome browser.
A new computer worm has been discovered that uses the classic Soviet arcade game, Tetris, as a way of infiltrating and taking over a user's PC.
Researchers at California-based security firm, Kaspersky Lab, say the malware has so far been found only in Russia.
It is the first known case of a game being used in this way.
Experts believe the worm, which has been named Win32.Rmnet.12, is a test version of a tool that could be used for industrial espionage or other attacks.
The game is used to trick the user into launching the malware by clicking on an executable file that appears to be a harmless screenshot from the game.
"The malware is written in a compiled language and lacks any debugging symbols, which suggests it may be distributed as a commercial product," a blog post on Kaspersky's website said.
"There are a number of clues that suggest the authors are Russian speakers."
The firm said the worm had been detected on a relatively small number of computers so far.
It added that it was not yet being distributed via email and that the distribution method appeared to be "still a work in progress".
Researchers believe the worm is a test version of a larger piece of malware that could be used by criminal gangs or state-sponsored attackers.

"The fact that this particular piece of malware has not been observed in the wild yet, and the fact that it carries a debugging symbol, suggests that it may be a prototype or possibly a test version," Kaspersky said.
The use of gaming elements in malware is not common.
In 2010, the Storm Worm malware used images from the game, World of Warcraft, to deceive users.
The Win32.Rmnet.12 malware is significant because it uses an executable file that appears to be a screenshot from the game Tetris, which is a recognised and trusted brand, researchers said.

Europe backs digital TV lifestyle

More than half of European homes have access to digital television, making it the fastest growing television platform, the European Commission says.
The growth in digital, both via satellite and cable, is destroying the old analogue way of watching TV, according to a study by the commission, the EU's executive body.
The study also found that Europeans think the switch to digital will give them better picture and sound quality and more channels to choose from.

Improved picture and sound quality was the most important reason for digital TV uptake in all countries, except the UK, where it was the fear of the analogue signal being switched off, the study found.

In Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK, digital cable is the most popular digital platform but the study noted that digital satellite television is taking the lead in all other countries.
The study also found that the penetration rate of digital television in the EU reached 54% in 2005, almost double the figure for 2004.
Denmark tops the EU league with digital TV penetration of 97% while Romania and Bulgaria have yet to start digital switchover.
The study also found strong growth in the take-up of fixed broadband in Europe last year.
Denmark again tops the EU league with 39% penetration, followed by the Netherlands with 38% and Finland and Sweden with more than 30%.
However, despite this growth, take-up of fixed broadband in Europe is still below that of the US and Japan.

Brits lost £768m to so-called "phantom goods" scams in 2021, with fashion items, mobile phones, and electronics among the most popular targets for fraudsters, a report has found.
Action Fraud, the UK's national reporting centre for fraud and cyber crime, received 17,405 reports of these scams in 2021, with victims losing an average of £43.10 each.
The report found that fraudsters most commonly lured victims in with offers for Nike and Adidas trainers, as well as Apple products like iPhones and AirPods.
Electronics in general were the most likely to prompt victims to make a report, with nearly a quarter (24%) of all reports referencing this kind of item.
Second-hand goods were the most popular proposition - fraudsters offered these items at suspiciously low prices in order to incentivise quick sales.
Many victims reported being initially hesitant, but were then pressured by the scammer into going through with the purchase.
One victim told the BBC that they had lost £300 to a scammer, having found a supposedly rare pair of trainers being sold for a significantly lower price than usual.
They paid using PayPal, but never received the goods.
When they tried to contact the seller they found that the phone number had been disconnected.
PayPal refused to refund their money, and told the victim that they should have realised that the seller's account was fake.
"It's a hard lesson learned, but glad it was only £300 and not a mortgage payment or something else expensive," they said.
Fraudsters often asked victims to pay for items through online payment methods such as PayPal, bank transfer or with a virtual currency.
One victim told the BBC that they lost more than £1,000 after buying a car through eBay, which turned out to be nonexistent.

They are "grid computers" and instead of relying on a conventional power supply, they use the electricity generated by the sun.

The idea is an example of "grid computing", which links together thousands of PCs, or in this case, PCs and mainframes, to create a supercomputer.
It allows ECMWF to use its computers more efficiently, making it easier to model complex weather patterns and predict the behaviour of the atmosphere.
The centre currently has around 80 PCs, but that number is increasing all the time.
In the future, the grid could be used to model more complex scenarios, such as the spread of pollution or the development of weather patterns.
It could also be used to create more accurate models of the Earth's climate, which are needed to predict the effects of global warming.
Dr Bauer believes the grid will become more powerful and more efficient in the future.
He said: "We're limited by the speed of the individual computers.
The grid is making better use of our resources, but we don't see it as a final solution."

The "Brainwave" cap detects electrical activity in the brain caused by concentration and relaxation.
Users can perform simple tasks, such as turning a switch on and off, by thinking about it.
The device could be used to help people with movement disorders control equipment.
The researchers plan to trial the cap - dubbed "Brainwave" - on people with severe physical disabilities to see if it can help them to control computers.
"We were able to get some results that exceeded our expectations," said Dr. Tomoyuki Sato, who led the team at Yokohama National University.
"Using this device, we intend to continue research toward the realization of a new, interface that does not rely on the five senses," he added in a statement.
The device uses an electroencephalogram (EEG) to detect electrical activity caused by changes in brainwaves.
It then uses algorithms to analyze the brainwaves and trigger a switch in a computer.
In recent decades, brain-computer interfaces have been developed which let paralysed people use robotic arms or other equipment by thinking deliberately about moving.
The new device operates on a different principle - that of "event-related potential" (ERP), a spike in brain activity that occurs when a person senses a stimulus.
In this case, the researchers used an ERP called the P300 wave.
This is generated unconsciously when a person becomes aware of a stimulus - in this case, the switch being on or off.
The researchers asked 13 people to wear the Brainwave cap and try to turn on and off a virtual switch displayed on a computer screen.
Participants were asked to think "on" and "off" when a cue symbol appeared and to suppress the urge to blink.

Austrian internet users can now receive live local TV news free of charge on their computers - an indication of the shape of things to come, according to the channel's chief.
The Austrian Broadcasting Corporation (ORF) launched its internet TV service on Monday, in conjunction with Germany's Deutsche Welle and Switzerland's SRG.
The move follows a successful year-long trial project, and the new service is being hailed as a breakthrough on the path to "internet broadcasting".
Viewers can choose from a range of programmes, including the ORF's lunchtime and evening news bulletins, its TV magazine and a number of its popular entertainment shows.
They are broadcast in a multimedia format that includes streaming video and audio, as well as text and pictures.
Viewers can also opt to receive the channels as a continuous broadcast, like conventional TV, or they can choose the programmes they want to watch from an archive of content updated every hour.
The TV stations can be received free of charge by anyone with a high-speed internet connection.
ORF chief Paul Russ said the project indicated "which way the wind is blowing".
"I think we have a trend-setting product on our hands, a product that delivers television over the internet and, at the same time, makes use of the possibilities of interactive television," he said.

The world's fastest supercomputer, Japan's Fugaku, has broken another record, according to the Top500 project that ranks such machines.
Fugaku, which means "future" in Japanese, was developed by Fujitsu and Riken and has held the top spot since it was unveiled in June 2020.

The machine scored 415.5 quadrillion - or 415.5 million trillion - calculations per second (float-point operations per second, or FLOPS) in the Linpack benchmark, used to rate the performance of supercomputers.
That is nearly four times the 152.6 quadrillion calculations per second achieved by Summit, the previous record holder and holder of the No 2 spot in the Top500.
The back-to-back victories by Japanese machines mark the first time since 2011 that the world's fastest supercomputer has been continuously held by machines from the same country.
Fugaku achieved the record during a benchmark test carried out in May this year.
The supercomputer had been under development for years and was due to be completed in 2021.
However, the completion date was brought forward due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
It had been hoped the machine would help researchers develop a better understanding of the coronavirus and aid in the search for treatments and a vaccine.
"It's incredible how far we've come in just one year," said Satoshi Matsuoka, who leads the Riken Center for Computational Science, in a statement.

"Fugaku has demonstrated its capabilities as the world's fastest supercomputer, and we hope it will contribute greatly to the development of science and technology, not only in Japan but also around the world."
Fujitsu and Riken said they plan to make Fugaku available to researchers in Japan and around the world in 2021.
It is expected that the machine will be used to solve a wide range of problems, including those related to the pandemic, as well as climate change and other pressing challenges.
The Top500 project was started in 1993 and has been updated every six months since then, with the latest list released in June 2021.
It ranks the world's most powerful supercomputers based on their performance on the Linpack benchmark, which measures how well they can solve a series of linear equations.
The world's slowest internet speeds have been identified in a survey covering 132 countries.
The data, from the Speedtest Intelligence League Table, puts the UK at 69th globally, with an average download speed of 67.33 megabits per second (Mbps).
The league table's authors said just under a billion people had internet speeds of less than 4Mbps.
The fastest speeds were found in Singapore, with an average download speed of 165.53Mbps.
The UK's position in the league table has fallen from 39th place in the previous study, published in November 2020.
The UK's average upload speed has fallen slightly from 21.37Mbps to 20.48Mbps, according to the study.
This is still above the global average of 11.46Mbps.
The league table is based on the speeds experienced by users running Speedtest's testing software.
The researchers gathered data from tens of millions of tests taken between 1 April and 30 June 2021.
They said the actual number of people with access to the speeds shown in the league table was likely to be much lower, as faster connections were generally tested by a smaller subset of people.
The UK's average download speed has fallen from 72.12Mbps to 67.33Mbps in the past year.
Many UK households now have access to faster broadband speeds after a massive government infrastructure project to improve services - but uptake and availability of those speeds remains patchy.
The UK's ranking behind many other countries is explained in large part by the high cost of broadband in the country, according to Dan Howdle, consumer telecoms analyst at Cable.co.uk.
"The UK has improved its infrastructure in recent years, but the high price of connectivity is still a major inhibitor to faster broadband," he told the BBC.
"While nations including Singapore, Norway and Denmark have made clear progress in recent years, the cost of broadband in the UK has stalled progress.
"Until this issue is addressed, UK consumers will be denied access to the next generation of broadband technology, and the country will fall further behind its peers."
The study also highlighted the gap between mobile and fixed broadband speeds.
More than four out of five people - 85% of the world - have a faster mobile internet connection than a fixed one, the researchers said.
That is down from 92% in the previous study, suggesting greater growth in fixed broadband speeds than in mobile.

Number spoofing is a technique used by criminals to mimic the number of a trusted organisation, so that a call appears to be coming from a genuine source.

The term "digital footprint" often refers to the trail of information left behind on the internet by a particular person or organisation - a profile formed through social media posts, online purchases, and other data.
It can also refer to the bits of code that are inadvertently left behind by malicious hackers covering their tracks.
But British cybersecurity experts have given a new meaning to the idea of a digital footprint, as a way of fighting back against cyberattacks.

Dr. Daniel Smith and Prof. Ian Brown of the University of Bristol have developed software that can instantly analyse a cyberattack, and using an approach called "digital footprinting", can leave behind clues that reveal the attackers' identities.

At the moment, the team said, each time a cyberattack takes place, the victim - whether an individual or a company - is forced into a game of "cat and mouse", where they have to wait for an attack to happen before they can begin to work out who was responsible, and block them.
The new software does away with this by automatically analysing the techniques used by the attacker, and identifying them as the attacker.
It then leaves a digital footprint, or a set of clues, that can be followed by the victim to reveal the identity of the attacker.
"We are making it easier for victims to find out who is attacking them," said Smith.
"At the moment you can be attacked hundreds of times before you can work out who is attacking you, and work out what to do about it."
The software is designed for use by internet service providers (ISPs), who can use it to protect their customers, and could also be used by companies.

A prototype of the software was tested on a real network, and the team said that they were able to leave behind a digital footprint that revealed the attacker's identity, and suggested clues as to who they were, and where they were located.

Sir Ian Corbett, the former director-general of the BBC, has attacked the "dumbing down" of television, arguing that the public service channels are in danger of "losing their way".

The show features 22 of their hits including Waterloo, Dancing Queen and Voulez Vous.

He said he did not think the group, who split up 37 years ago, would have approved the show but that he was happy with it.

Movie makers from across the continent have descended on the German capital for the European Film Awards.
The winners of the Euromedia awards, which honour the best in European cinema, were announced at a glitzy ceremony in Berlin on Saturday.

The UK's Emily Blunt took the best actress award for her role in the drama The Girl in the Café, while the best actor award went to Spain's Javier Bardem for his part in the political thriller Mondays in the Sun.
The best film award went to Russian entry The Captain's Daughter, while the best documentary was given to the Danish/Swedish/Norwegian co-production The Swenkas.
The event was hosted by German actor Christian Ulmen and more than 500 guests attended.
They included renowned film-makers such as Britain's Mike Leigh and Terry Gilliam and Ireland's Jim Sheridan.
The awards are given out by the European Film Academy, which is made up of more than 2,000 film professionals from across the continent.
The academy says it aims to "promote and award the best in European cinema".
Its president, German director Wim Wenders, said this year's entries showed that European cinema was "as diverse, inventive and seductive as ever".
He added: "Even though national film funding is increasingly under threat, European cinema proves it has never been more needed and wanted by audiences all over the world."

Three people from Hull have repeated a charity's earlier success in crossing the Humber Bridge in their underwear.
Steve Clarkson, 44, Deborah Morgan, 40, and Andy Swift, 45, all from the city, took part in the challenge wearing only socks, shoes and hats.
They raised £400 for charity.

Mr Clarkson said: "Knowing there were lots of people supporting us, and knowing the reason we were doing it, made it easier."
He said the charity donations were an incentive to "keep going".
"We were freezing.
It was really cold but we had to keep going.
There was no chance to stop," he said.
The group chose to support the Teenage Cancer Trust, Macmillan Cancer Support and the Harry Potter-themed children's hospital in Birmingham.

Why did they do it?
The group repeated a charity challenge which three people known as the Humber Bridge Three carried out in 1992.
They raised £250,000 for charity when they walked over the Humber Bridge near Hull in just their underwear.

The Anglo-Nigerian writer Bernardine Evaristo has won the Booker Prize for her novel Girl, Woman, Other.
The novel tells the stories of 12 characters, mostly black women, living in Britain.
The 63-year-old reacted to winning the prize, worth £52,500 ($66,000), by lifting her arms in the air and laughing.
She described the book as "a celebration of heterogeneity".
The book is Evaristo's eighth novel and the judges called it "a dazzling, vivid and engaging novel".
The announcement was made at a dinner in London's Guildhall, with the shortlisted authors watching.
It is only the second time in the history of the prize that it has been won by a woman author.
The previous winner was Anna Burns in 2018 for her novel Milkman.
Organizers of the prize, which has been running for 51 years, said they made the decision to change the rules because "no woman has ever won the prize twice, or men either come to that".
They also wanted to encourage authors to enter their novels for the prize.
Prior to the rule change, authors could only win the Booker Prize once in their lifetime.
The change means that three previous winners - Margaret Atwood, Hilary Mantel, and John Banville - would now be eligible to win it again.
Atwood, who won in 2000 for The Blind Assassin, said she would "think about" entering her novel The Testaments, which follows on from The Handmaid's Tale, for the prize.
The Testaments was published in September and Atwood described it as a "sequel, not a sequel", because it picks up on characters from the earlier novel, but is also a standalone story.
The Booker Prize is open to writers of any nationality, writing in English.
The prize money for the Booker has increased this year from £50,000 to £52,500.
The increase marks the first time the prize has risen above £50,000 in its history.

Arthur Hailey has made a fortune from fiction.
His books have sold more than 170 million copies worldwide and have been translated into 40 languages.
He is the author of a string of bestsellers, including Hotel, Airport and Wheels.
The success of these books saw him dubbed "the king of the bestseller".
The one thing his readers could rely on was that Arthur Hailey would never surprise them.
His formula was simple.
Take a large organisation oozing with ambition, cynicism and greed.
Throw in a ruthless businessman as protagonist.
Add a strong female character as the moral compass.
Mix well and place in a container.
Then take a large pinch of suspense, a generous scoop of romance, and a heap of insider information about the workings of the organisation concerned.
Bake until the plot is thick and juicy, and serve in small portions.
A chapter a night is about right.
Some authors have admitted emulating Hailey's recipe for success.
Stephen King, for one.
"Hotel was one of the books that made me want to be a writer," he said.
"I thought, 'I can do this.
This is not rocket science.'

"

Others have criticised Hailey for making writing look easy.
Michael Crichton, creator of Jurassic Park, described Hailey as "a lazy writer".
"He works occasionally," he said, "but not hard.
The son of a police officer, Hailey was born in Luton in 1920.
After leaving school at 14, he had a variety of jobs - including as a vacuum cleaner salesman and a touring actor with the BBC's repertory company - before joining the RAF during World War Two.
After the war he worked as a journalist in London and, in 1951, moved to Canada where he wrote for the Toronto Star.
It was there that he started to write novels.
His breakthrough came with the publication of his seventh novel, Hotel, in 1965.
The book became an instant hit, turning Hailey into a millionaire.
He wrote a string of bestselling novels in the same vein - using real-life locations such as airports, railways and hospitals as the backdrop to his stories of big business and ambitious men.
His method was to carry out extensive research until he knew more about his subject than anyone else.
"I'm not a very bright fellow," he once said.
"But I stay with it until I know as much as anybody about it."

The magical nanny who swoops in to save the day has been a figure of fantasy for more than 50 years.
And now she is flying high in the West End in a £10m (£6.6m) musical extravaganza that has got off to a flying start.
The stage musical of Mary Poppins, starring former Royal Ballet principal ballerina Cynthia Erivo, has taken £450,000 in advance bookings alone.
It has been a long time coming for the famous nanny, who first appeared in a book by PL Travers in 1934 and on the big screen 16 years later in Walt Disney's classic animation.
Travers died in 1996 having never given her consent for a stage adaptation of her most famous creation.
Her estate finally gave its approval in 2008 and the show's co-director Richard Eyre says he is relieved the blessing has been granted.
"It's a daunting thing to take someone's work and adapt it for the theatre," he said.
"We were all nervous because we love the film so much.
It's a masterpiece of animation and design and we had to work out a way of doing it justice."
The musical features all the famous songs from the film, including Chim Chim Cher-ee, Jolly Holiday, Step in Time and Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious.
New songs have been written by the veteran team of George Stiles and Anthony Drewe.

Stiles and Drewe had been keen to work with Mary Poppins author Travers on a stage adaptation for more than a decade.

WTO members are trying to finalize texts on a proposal first made by India and South Africa in October 2020 to waive IP rights for COVID-19 vaccines and treatments.
United States President Joe Biden had previously backed the idea but Western pharmaceutical companies and EU nations have opposed it.
India's Ambassador to the WTO, Brajendra Navnit, told negotiators it was important to conclude talks on the waiver "in a timely manner".
"Given the scope, coverage and duration of the proposal, it represents a meaningful opportunity to address the pandemic and save lives," he said.
India and South Africa have argued that IP rights have created barriers to increasing the production of vaccines and other tools needed to fight the pandemic.
If agreed, the waiver would be the first ever of its kind under the WTO's Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property (Trips).
But talks have stalled, with a group of more than a dozen countries, including the UK, Switzerland and the European Union, opposing the plan.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that around 80% of the population in richer countries has received at least one vaccine dose, but this drops to around 15% in low-income countries.
Ambassadors from the WTO's 164 member states met in Geneva last month but failed to reach an agreement.
They are due to meet again on 29 June, with a final round of talks scheduled for 6-7 July.
India's role in the WTO talks is crucial as it is a major vaccine manufacturer.
It has produced more than 600 million doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine, widely used in the UK, and more than 110 million doses of the Covaxin vaccine, developed by Indian company Bharat Biotech.
Dr Soumya Swaminathan, the chief scientist at the WHO, said she hoped that India's strong role in the WTO talks would help find a solution.

The company, which returned to the London Stock Exchange in June, reported a loss of £43.9m ($61.8m) in the six months to 30 June, compared with a loss of £17.2m a year earlier.
The group has been hit by a number of factors, including the strong performance of the pound, weaker coal prices and "high production costs" at one of its sites.

The group added that it had made a "solid start" to the second half of the year, but uncertainty in the market meant it was "not recommending any dividend for the 2018 financial year".
UK Coal was taken over by a group of investors, including its former management, in April last year.
The firm was delisted from the London Stock Exchange in October 2013 after it was hit by falling coal prices and a tough market for coal miners.
However, it returned to the stock market in June this year, floating on the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM).
As part of the float, the company raised £3.5m through a placing of shares priced at 110p each.
The group's chief executive, Jon Meeching, said the company was "pleased" with progress in the first half of the year.
