Oil prices have fallen back from their recent highs as fears of a global economic slowdown outweigh concerns about supply.
Brent crude futures - the international benchmark for oil - were down 82 cents at $85.94 a barrel early on Tuesday.
US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures fell 89 cents to $80.35 a barrel.
Earlier this month, Brent crude touched its highest since early December 2014 at $86.71 a barrel, while WTI reached a seven-year high of $85.41.
But prices have dropped back in the last 10 days as analysts point to signs of weakening demand.
"The threat of demand destruction because of higher fuel prices is looming, with jet fuel demand already showing signs of weakening," said Louise Dickson, an analyst at Rystad Energy.
She added that higher prices, driven up in recent months by the Ukraine war, had also encouraged stronger output from outside the OPEC+ group of major oil producers.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, known as OPEC+, have been restricting supply to support prices for more than a year now.
However, the group decided to raise output by 400,000 barrels a day in December, with Russia's contribution being the biggest increase.
But as oil prices came off their highs at the start of the year, OPEC+ decided to stay with its current output plans, despite calls from the US and other nations to produce more oil.
Last week, US President Joe Biden urged OPEC+ to pump more oil in an effort to lower prices.
"While OPEC+ recently agreed to add production, uncertainties remain as to whether the group can actually reach its target," said Ms Dickson.

Sony has said it sold 3.5 million PlayStation 5 consoles during the device's first fiscal year - racking up a total profit of $157m.

The Japanese electronics giant had sold 30% more PS5s than the number of PS4s sold at the same point in its lifecycle.
But it sold fewer PS5 games, causing PlayStation's profit to fall short of management's expectations.
Sony blamed the global chip shortage, which it said had impacted sales.
The results covered the three months to 30 June 2021.
During that period, Sony sold 3.3 million PS5 consoles, taking the total number of consoles sold since launch to 3.5 million.
That compares to 10 million PS4s sold in the three months after it was launched in November 2013.
Sony said it had secured more PS5 units for the year to March 2022, and expected to sell more than seven million consoles during that period.
It also announced that its upcoming PlayStation VR2 virtual reality headset would launch in February, with pre-orders opening on 11 November.
Sony's overall game and network services division, which includes PlayStation, recorded revenue of $25.5bn for the year, up 27% year-on-year.
That was driven by strong sales of PlayStation 5 and PlayStation 4 software, as well as an increase in subscribers to PlayStation Plus, its subscription service.
Sony has 49 million subscribers to PlayStation Plus, game streaming and membership service PlayStation Now, and its PlayStation Vue television service.
While the gaming division performed well, Sony's overall profit fell short of its expectations.
It recorded a profit of $157m - far short of the $548m it expected to make.

The company blamed the shortfall on the cost of selling the PS5 at a loss due to the global chip shortage, as well as its decision to sell the PlayStation 4 at a lower price to shift excess inventory.
It also cited the impact of Covid-19 lockdowns in China on its semiconductor manufacturing.

The year's first major consumer electronics show, held in Las Vegas last week, showed a industry waking up to the fact that the MP3 player is now mainstream.
Last year, the MP3 player was the star of the show.
This year, it was taken for granted.
Instead, the buzz was about larger, higher-resolution screens and flashy new photo capabilities.
The new Pocket PC phones, with their colour screens, built-in cameras and MP3 players, got most of the attention.
But the star of the show was a handheld game console, not a phone or a music player.
The Nintendo DS, launched in the US last month, is a gaming handheld with two screens, one of which is a touchscreen.
Its most exciting feature, however, is its wireless connectivity.

Nintendo has partnered with a company called Broadcom to create an 802.11b Wi-Fi chip for the DS, which can be used to connect to the Internet, for multiplayer games, and eventually to download games and other content from the Web.

At the show, Nintendo demonstrated the device's Web browsing capabilities, although it was unclear when Nintendo plans to enable the feature, and whether Americans will be able to surf the net with it anytime soon.
The DS's Wi-Fi capabilities may be a prelude to a new generation of always-on, always-connected handheld devices.
Last year, when the MP3 player was the star, it was surrounded by devices, such as phones and PDAs, that could, in theory, do much more.
This year's show made good on some of those promises.
The most exciting products were not the star of the show, but they were also not the also-rans of last year.
They were simply cool, new gadgets that help us communicate, organise our lives and, of course, play music and games.

Singer Jane Weaver's documentary about folk music icon Shirley Collins will premiere at this year's Cambridge Film Festival.
The British singer-songwriter's film The Ballad Of Shirley Collins will open this year's festival, which runs from 14 to 23 September.
The film, described as a "musical odyssey", follows Collins' return to performance after decades away from the industry.
The Ballad Of Shirley Collins will open the festival on 14 September, with Weaver and Collins in attendance for a Q&A session following the screening.
The film will be released in UK cinemas on 22 November.
Collins, who is credited with preserving and documenting traditional English folk songs, released her first album, entitled Folk Songs Of England, in 1959.
She went on to record a further six albums, but retired from performing in the late 60s following the breakdown of her marriage and the emergence of folk rock.
The Ballad Of Shirley Collins features contributions from Collins' contemporaries, including Paul Brady, Martin Carthy, Aidan Moffat and Roddy Woomble.
The film's director, Weaver, is a former member of UK indie band Kill Laura.

Her film follows Collins as she returns to singing and prepares to release an album of traditional English folk songs, with contributions from contemporary musicians including Nick Cave, Robert Wyatt and Alasdair Roberts.
Tory MPs have criticised the prime minister for "U-turning" on plans to crack down on burglars.
The government had promised to increase the maximum sentence for burglaries - but plans to change the law have been dropped.
Conservative MP Pauline Latham described the move as a "U-turn" and called for the justice secretary, Chris Grayling, to resign.
Another Tory MP, Henry Smith, said he was "astonished" and vowed to press for legislation when Parliament returns from its summer break.
The government said the decision had been made because of concerns that the planned change could result in thousands of successful appeals against sentences.
Ministers had proposed doubling the maximum sentence for burglaries to 14 years, bringing it into line with warnings for other offences such as rape and manslaughter.
But under current laws, a judge who hands down a sentence which is considered by prosecutors to be too lenient can only increase it - not decrease it.

This led to concerns that if a judge considered the 14-year sentence as too lenient, they would be unable to increase it - resulting in successful appeals and potentially dangerous offenders being released.

Announcing the decision to drop the plans, Ministry of Justice minister Jeremy Wright said the government had "listened to concerns" and that the public should have "confidence in the criminal justice system".
He said the government would look at other ways of "ensuring dangerous offenders face severe penalties".
But Mrs Latham, the Conservative MP for Mid Derbyshire, said the government had "lost its way" and described the decision as a "complete U-turn and a failure of leadership".
"I think the justice secretary has got to consider his position.
He's clearly not capable of running a ministry," she added.
Mr Smith, the MP for Crawley, said he was "astonished that the ministry hasn't noticed this issue before".
"I think it's important that we get onto this as soon as possible when Parliament returns," he added.
Britain's terror laws are "absolutely necessary" to cope with the threat from al-Qaeda, former prime minister Tony Blair has said.
Speaking on the 10th anniversary of the 7/7 London bombings, Mr Blair said he had no doubt the legislation had saved lives.
The Labour ex-leader admitted aspects of the legislation - including some which had caused public concern - were "difficult".
But he said no government had "any alternative but to take the action we did".
The London bombings, in which 52 people were killed, prompted a revamp of the UK's anti-terror laws.
Speaking on BBC One's Breakfast show, Mr Blair - who was prime minister at the time of the bombings - said he had "no doubt at all" that the actions taken had saved lives.
"I believe the legislation we introduced has helped us to protect the British public but, as I say, it's not perfect and we need to keep improving it," he added.
Mr Blair said he had always tried to "balance" the human rights of individuals with the need to protect the public.
But he accepted that some of the measures - such as those allowing the detention without trial of suspects and the use of intercept evidence in court - had caused concern.
"I think any government has got to balance the need to protect the security of the public with the individual rights and that's what we did," he said.
"I think it's difficult, all of these things.
Every step of the way there's a balance to be struck and, yes, you do make difficult decisions.
"It's not easy to strike that balance but it's absolutely necessary."

"The Sash" is a 19th-century Irish folk song, which has become a anthem for Irish nationalists and Catholics.

"Sam Cole has decided to resign as a candidate for the Democratic Unionist Party in the forthcoming assembly election," a statement from the party said.

Sir Jeffrey has said that the caller's views were "not democratic, legal or reasonable" and that he had challenged them.

Anti-vaxxers are "dangerous" and "ignorant", Scotland's Health Secretary has said.
Humza Yousaf warned that people who spread misinformation about Covid vaccines were putting lives at risk.
He said some had wanted to "watch the world burn" during the pandemic.
Mr Yousaf spoke as NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde became the first health board in Scotland to surpass 1,000 Covid deaths.
The health secretary said the figure was "hard to digest" but put in context with projections at the height of the pandemic, it showed the success of measures such as vaccines.
Mr Yousaf paid tribute to the "heroic" efforts of health board staff - particularly during the recent "very challenging" spike in cases.
The majority of NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde's reported Covid deaths have occurred this year - 488 since 1 January.
Mr Yousaf said: "I don't think we can ever truly celebrate or applaud success when 1,000 families are grieving.
"It is really galling and frustrating for me at the same time as paying tribute to the heroic efforts of the staff at NHSGGC that this tragedy could have been avoided.

"A lot of the misinformation that is out there from some - I hesitate to use the word 'keyboard warriors' - but there are people out there who have actively wanted to watch the world burn during what is already a horrific pandemic."
He said health boards across Scotland had seen people presenting with more severe symptoms because of a delay in getting treated as a result of misinformation.

Mr Yousaf said it was not just anti-vaxxers spreading misinformation, but also people promoting "fake remedies" for Covid such as ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine - both of which have been discredited.
He said the Scottish government had a responsibility to continue to provide accurate information on health measures such as vaccines, but that he had no plans to make vaccines mandatory.
As of Thursday, 1,147 people have died within 28 days of a positive Covid test in Scotland.
About 80% of the 1,000 deaths in NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde involved people aged 75 or over.
The health board - Scotland's largest - has reported 1,354 deaths involving Covid since the start of the pandemic, but 53 of these were in people who died of other causes.

Air passengers in the European Union will now have stronger rights and protections thanks to new regulations approved by the European Parliament.
The new rules aim to ensure that passengers are treated fairly and compensated appropriately in the event of flight delays, cancellations, or denied boarding.

In such cases, passengers will be entitled to compensation ranging from €250 ($290) to €600 ($700), depending on the length of the flight and the delay caused by the denied boarding.
These new rights and protections are a significant step forward for air passengers in the EU.

Despite these concerns, the new EU regulations are a significant victory for air passengers.

The Trades Union Congress (TUC) has called for stronger protections for whistleblowers in the UK.

Wireless networks have become an integral part of our daily lives, providing us with the convenience of internet access without the need for physical connections.
However, a new threat has emerged that has experts concerned - the "evil twin" attack.
The "evil twin" attack is a form of wireless network hacking where a malicious actor sets up a fake wireless network that appears to be legitimate.
Unsuspecting users may connect to this network, thinking it is a trusted source, only to have their personal information compromised.
This type of attack is particularly concerning because it is difficult to detect.
The fake network will often have a similar name and appearance to a legitimate network, making it hard for users to differentiate between the two.
Once connected, the attacker can intercept and monitor all the data being transmitted, including passwords, credit card information, and other sensitive data.
To carry out an "evil twin" attack, hackers typically use specialized software and hardware to create a fake access point.
They may also employ techniques such as spoofing the MAC address of a legitimate network to further deceive users.
Once the fake network is set up, the attacker can launch various attacks, such as man-in-the-middle attacks or session hijacking, to gain unauthorized access to the user's data.
Experts recommend several measures to protect against "evil twin" attacks.
Firstly, users should always be cautious when connecting to wireless networks, especially in public places.
It is essential to verify the network's legitimacy by checking with the network owner or using a virtual private network (VPN) for added security.
Additionally, keeping devices up to date with the latest security patches and using strong, unique passwords can help mitigate the risk of falling victim to an "evil twin" attack.
Users should also be wary of any suspicious behavior, such as unexpected network disconnections or slow internet speeds, as these could be signs of a potential attack.
Wireless network providers and device manufacturers also play a crucial role in combating "evil twin" attacks.
They should continuously update their security protocols and educate users about the risks associated with connecting to untrusted networks.
As wireless networks continue to evolve and become more prevalent, it is essential for users to remain vigilant and take necessary precautions to protect their personal information.
By staying informed and implementing best practices, individuals can minimize the risk of falling victim to an "evil twin" attack and ensure their online safety.

Cybersecurity experts are warning the public about a new threat known as the "FBI virus".
This malicious software, also known as ransomware, has been targeting unsuspecting victims and demanding payment in exchange for unlocking their computers.
The virus disguises itself as an official FBI warning, claiming that the user's computer has been involved in illegal activities.
It then locks the computer and displays a message demanding a ransom to be paid within a certain timeframe.
Failure to comply with the demands can result in the permanent loss of data.
The FBI has issued a statement clarifying that they do not engage in such practices and that the virus is a scam.
They have advised users to be cautious and to report any instances of the virus to their local authorities.
Cybersecurity experts are urging the public to take precautions to protect themselves from this and other similar threats.
This includes regularly updating antivirus software, avoiding suspicious websites and email attachments, and backing up important data.
The "FBI virus" is just one example of the ever-evolving landscape of cyber threats, highlighting the need for constant vigilance and awareness.
Scientists have developed a groundbreaking "brainwave" cap that allows users to control a computer using their thoughts.

The cap, which is equipped with electrodes, can detect and interpret brain signals, enabling users to navigate through a computer interface without the need for physical input devices such as a keyboard or mouse.
The technology behind the brainwave cap is known as electroencephalography (EEG), which measures electrical activity in the brain.
By placing the cap on the user's head, the electrodes pick up the brain signals and transmit them to a computer for analysis.
The computer then translates these signals into commands that can be used to control various functions, such as typing, scrolling, or opening applications.

This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the way we interact with computers, particularly for individuals with physical disabilities or conditions that limit their ability to use traditional input devices.
For example, people with paralysis or motor impairments could benefit greatly from this technology, as it offers them a new way to communicate and interact with the digital world.
The brainwave cap also has potential applications in other fields, such as gaming and virtual reality.
Imagine being able to control a character in a video game or navigate through a virtual environment using only your thoughts.
This could enhance the immersive experience and make gaming more accessible to a wider range of individuals.
However, there are still challenges to overcome before the brainwave cap becomes widely available.
The technology is still in its early stages, and further research and development are needed to improve its accuracy and reliability.
Additionally, there are concerns about privacy and security, as the cap collects sensitive brain data that could potentially be exploited if not properly protected.
Despite these challenges, the development of the brainwave cap represents a significant step forward in the field of brain-computer interfaces.
It opens up new possibilities for human-computer interaction and has the potential to improve the lives of many individuals.
As researchers continue to refine and advance this technology, we can expect to see even more exciting applications in the future.
Laptop PCs are set to have a longer lifespan, thanks to a new initiative by the European Union.
The EU is aiming to reduce electronic waste and promote sustainability by introducing new regulations that will require manufacturers to make laptops that are easier to repair and upgrade.
Under the new rules, manufacturers will have to ensure that laptop batteries can be easily replaced, and that spare parts are available for at least seven years after a product is discontinued.
This move is expected to extend the lifespan of laptops by up to three years, reducing the need for consumers to constantly buy new devices.
The EU's initiative comes as electronic waste continues to be a growing concern globally.
According to the United Nations, around 50 million metric tonnes of electronic waste is generated each year, with only 20% of it being recycled.
By making laptops more repairable and upgradable, the EU hopes to reduce the amount of electronic waste that ends up in landfills or is illegally exported to developing countries.
In addition to the environmental benefits, the new regulations are also expected to benefit consumers.
Repairing and upgrading laptops will become easier and more affordable, as spare parts will be readily available for a longer period of time.
This will not only save consumers money but also reduce the demand for new laptops, ultimately leading to a more sustainable and circular economy.
However, not everyone is on board with the new regulations.
Some manufacturers argue that making laptops more repairable and upgradable could lead to compromises in terms of design and performance.
They also claim that it could increase the risk of counterfeit spare parts entering the market.
Nevertheless, the EU remains determined to push forward with its plans, believing that the benefits outweigh the potential drawbacks.
The new regulations are expected to be implemented in the coming years, giving manufacturers time to adjust their production processes and supply chains.
It is hoped that other countries will follow suit and introduce similar measures to promote sustainability and reduce electronic waste.
With laptops set to have a longer lifespan, consumers can look forward to a more sustainable and environmentally friendly future.
The next generation of internet technology is set to be rolled out across the globe, promising faster speeds and improved connectivity.
Known as 5G, this new network is expected to revolutionize the way we use the internet and pave the way for advancements in various industries.
5G, or fifth-generation wireless technology, is the successor to the current 4G network.
It is designed to provide faster download and upload speeds, lower latency, and increased capacity.
With speeds up to 100 times faster than 4G, 5G will enable users to download large files, stream high-definition videos, and play online games with minimal lag.
One of the key advantages of 5G is its ability to handle a massive number of connected devices simultaneously.
This is crucial in the era of the Internet of Things (IoT), where everyday objects are connected to the internet.
With 5G, smart homes, autonomous vehicles, and industrial automation will become more efficient and reliable.
The deployment of 5G networks is already underway in several countries, with major telecommunications companies investing heavily in infrastructure upgrades.
South Korea became the first country to launch a nationwide 5G network in April 2019, followed by the United States and China.

Other countries, including the United Kingdom, Germany, and Japan, are also making significant progress in rolling out 5G.

However, the widespread adoption of 5G is not without challenges.
One of the main concerns is the cost of infrastructure upgrades required to support the new network.
Building the necessary infrastructure, including new cell towers and fiber optic cables, can be a costly endeavor.
Additionally, there are concerns about the potential health effects of increased exposure to radiofrequency radiation emitted by 5G networks.
Despite these challenges, the benefits of 5G are expected to outweigh the drawbacks.
The faster speeds and improved connectivity offered by 5G will open up new possibilities for industries such as healthcare, transportation, and entertainment.
From remote surgeries to self-driving cars, 5G has the potential to transform various sectors and improve the quality of life for people around the world.

As the rollout of 5G continues, it is important for governments, telecommunications companies, and consumers to work together to address the challenges and ensure a smooth transition to the next generation of internet technology.
With its promise of faster speeds and improved connectivity, 5G is set to revolutionize the way we live, work, and communicate in the digital age.

A heated debate has erupted over the use of peer-to-peer (P2P) advertising, with critics arguing that it poses a threat to consumer privacy and could potentially enable illegal activities.

P2P advertising, which involves individuals promoting products or services directly to their peers, has gained popularity in recent years due to its cost-effectiveness and ability to reach a targeted audience.
However, concerns have been raised about the lack of regulation and oversight in this form of advertising.
One of the main concerns surrounding P2P advertising is the potential for invasion of privacy.
Critics argue that when individuals promote products or services to their peers, they may inadvertently share personal information without the knowledge or consent of the person being targeted.
This could lead to a breach of privacy and potentially expose individuals to unwanted solicitations or scams.
Another issue raised by opponents of P2P advertising is the potential for illegal activities to be facilitated through this platform.
As P2P advertising often operates outside of traditional advertising channels, it can be difficult to monitor and regulate.

This opens the door for unscrupulous individuals to promote illegal products or services, such as counterfeit goods or illegal substances, without facing the same level of scrutiny as traditional advertisers.
Proponents of P2P advertising argue that it offers a more authentic and personalized approach to marketing.
They believe that individuals are more likely to trust recommendations from their peers, leading to higher conversion rates and customer satisfaction.
Additionally, P2P advertising allows for a more targeted approach, as individuals can tailor their promotions to specific groups or communities.
However, critics argue that the lack of regulation and oversight in P2P advertising undermines consumer protection.
They argue that without proper guidelines and enforcement, individuals may be exposed to misleading or deceptive advertising practices.
This could lead to financial loss or harm to consumers who are not adequately informed or protected.
The debate over P2P advertising is likely to continue as the industry grows and evolves.
It remains to be seen whether regulators will step in to address the concerns raised by critics or if the industry will self-regulate to ensure consumer protection.
In the meantime, consumers are advised to exercise caution when engaging with P2P advertising and to be aware of the potential risks and pitfalls associated with this form of marketing.

A supercomputer has shattered the speed record for processing power, marking a significant milestone in the field of computing.
The machine, named "Quantum Lightning," achieved an unprecedented level of performance, surpassing all previous benchmarks.
Developed by a team of scientists and engineers, Quantum Lightning utilizes cutting-edge quantum computing technology.
Unlike traditional computers that rely on binary bits, quantum computers leverage quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in multiple states simultaneously.
This unique characteristic allows quantum computers to perform complex calculations at an exponentially faster rate.
The supercomputer's record-breaking achievement was made possible by harnessing the power of quantum entanglement.
By entangling qubits, Quantum Lightning can process vast amounts of data simultaneously, leading to a remarkable increase in computational speed.
This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize various industries, including finance, healthcare, and scientific research.
Quantum Lightning's speed record is a significant leap forward in the race to develop more powerful computing systems.
It opens up new possibilities for solving complex problems that were previously deemed intractable.
For instance, the supercomputer's enhanced processing capabilities could accelerate drug discovery by simulating the behavior of molecules and predicting their interactions with precision.
Furthermore, Quantum Lightning's breakthrough could have profound implications for cryptography and data security.
Quantum computers have the potential to crack currently unbreakable encryption algorithms, posing a challenge for cybersecurity experts.
However, this development also presents an opportunity to develop new encryption methods that are resistant to quantum attacks.
While Quantum Lightning's achievement is undoubtedly groundbreaking, there are still challenges to overcome before quantum computing becomes widely accessible.
Quantum systems are highly sensitive to environmental disturbances, requiring extremely low temperatures and stable conditions to operate effectively.
Additionally, scaling up quantum computers to handle larger and more complex problems remains a significant hurdle.
Nevertheless, the record-breaking speed of Quantum Lightning represents a significant milestone in the advancement of computing technology.
As scientists and engineers continue to push the boundaries of what is possible, the potential applications of quantum computing are becoming increasingly tangible.
The race to develop even more powerful supercomputers is now more intense than ever, with the promise of solving some of the world's most complex problems within reach.

Pirates who have been illegally downloading and playing the popular video game Half-Life 2 have been hit hard by a recent ban.
The ban, which was implemented by the game's developer Valve, has resulted in a significant decrease in the number of pirated copies of the game being played.
Half-Life 2, released in 2004, is a highly acclaimed first-person shooter game that has garnered a large and dedicated fan base over the years.
However, like many popular games, it has also been a target for piracy.
Valve, the company behind Half-Life 2, has been actively combating piracy by implementing various measures to protect their intellectual property.

Cybersecurity experts are turning to a new method to combat attacks on computer networks - net fingerprints.
These unique digital signatures are being used to identify and track hackers, making it easier to catch and prosecute them.
Net fingerprints are created by analyzing the behavior of network traffic.
By examining patterns in data packets, experts can identify the unique characteristics of a particular attacker.
This information can then be used to build a profile of the hacker, including their methods, tools, and even their location.
One of the key advantages of net fingerprints is their ability to track attackers across different networks.
Traditional methods of tracking hackers often rely on IP addresses, which can easily be masked or changed.
Net fingerprints, on the other hand, are based on the behavior of the attacker, making them much more difficult to hide or alter.
This new approach to cybersecurity has already proven successful in several high-profile cases.
In one instance, a hacker responsible for a major data breach was identified and apprehended using net fingerprints.
The evidence gathered from the fingerprints was crucial in securing a conviction and bringing the perpetrator to justice.

As hackers become more sophisticated, they are finding ways to evade detection and manipulate their digital signatures.
This means that cybersecurity experts must constantly adapt and update their methods to stay one step ahead of the attackers.
Despite these challenges, net fingerprints offer a promising solution to the growing problem of cyber attacks.
By using this innovative technique, experts can not only identify and track hackers, but also gather valuable intelligence on their methods and motives.
This information can then be used to strengthen network defenses and prevent future attacks.
As the threat of cyber attacks continues to grow, it is crucial that we explore new and effective ways to combat them.

Cybersecurity experts are warning that many public Wi-Fi networks are woefully insecure, leaving users vulnerable to hacking and data theft.
A recent study conducted by a leading cybersecurity firm found that a staggering 83% of public Wi-Fi networks in major cities around the world lack basic security measures.
This means that anyone connected to these networks could potentially have their personal information intercepted by hackers.

The study also revealed that many public Wi-Fi networks are not properly encrypted, making it easy for hackers to gain access to users' devices and steal sensitive data such as passwords, credit card information, and personal documents.
In addition, the lack of security measures on these networks makes it easier for hackers to launch attacks on connected devices, potentially compromising the entire network.
One of the main reasons for the woeful state of Wi-Fi security is the lack of awareness among both users and network providers.
Many people are unaware of the risks associated with using public Wi-Fi networks and assume that they are secure.
Network providers, on the other hand, often prioritize convenience over security, failing to implement basic security measures such as encryption and authentication.
To protect themselves from these risks, cybersecurity experts recommend that users avoid connecting to public Wi-Fi networks whenever possible.
If connecting is necessary, they advise using a virtual private network (VPN) to encrypt internet traffic and protect sensitive data.
It is also important to ensure that devices are updated with the latest security patches and that strong, unique passwords are used for all accounts.
In response to the study's findings, some network providers have pledged to improve the security of their public Wi-Fi networks.
However, experts warn that more needs to be done to address this issue.

They call for increased awareness and education about the risks of using public Wi-Fi networks, as well as stricter regulations and standards for network providers to ensure the implementation of basic security measures.
In conclusion, the woeful state of Wi-Fi security on public networks is a cause for concern.
Users must be vigilant and take necessary precautions to protect their personal information from potential hackers.
Network providers also need to prioritize security and implement basic measures to ensure the safety of their users.
Only through collective efforts can we hope to improve the security of public Wi-Fi networks and safeguard against cyber threats.

The highly contagious variant has led to renewed lockdowns and travel restrictions in several countries, dampening fuel demand.

The group plans to gradually raise output by 400,000 barrels per day from August until December.

However, the Delta variant's spread has cast doubt on these projections, leading to a more cautious outlook for oil consumption.
Additionally, concerns about inflation and the potential for central banks to tighten monetary policy have also contributed to the decline in oil prices.

Former US President George W. Bush has pledged to take a 'tough' stance on the country's deficit, amid growing concerns about the state of the American economy.

"

"

Brazil's Congress has given the green light to a significant overhaul of the country's bankruptcy law, aimed at increasing the survival rate of companies facing financial difficulties.
The reform is expected to boost the economy by improving the business environment and encouraging investment.

The new legislation, approved on Wednesday, simplifies the reorganisation process for businesses on the brink of bankruptcy, making it easier for them to negotiate with creditors and avoid liquidation.
It also provides more protection for creditors by allowing them to take over the management of the distressed company if necessary.
The reform is part of a broader economic recovery plan put forward by President Jair Bolsonaro's government, which is seeking to revive the economy after it was hit hard by the Covid-19 pandemic.
"The approval of the bankruptcy reform is a major step forward in improving the business environment in Brazil," said Economy Minister Paulo Guedes.
"It will provide more security for creditors and give companies a second chance to recover and grow.

"

Under the new law, small businesses will have a simplified and faster bankruptcy process, with the possibility of presenting a reorganisation plan within 60 days of filing for bankruptcy.
This is expected to help many small businesses survive and maintain jobs.
The reform also introduces a new mechanism for dealing with the debts of large companies.
They will be able to negotiate their debts with creditors in a court-supervised process, which is expected to speed up the resolution of bankruptcy cases.
The new legislation also includes measures to encourage the purchase of assets from bankrupt companies, by providing legal protection to buyers and making the process more transparent.
The bankruptcy reform has been welcomed by business groups and economists, who believe it will help to attract more investment and stimulate economic growth.
"The new bankruptcy law is a positive development for the Brazilian economy," said Roberto Campos Neto, president of the Central Bank of Brazil.
"It will make the process of corporate restructuring more efficient and will contribute to the recovery of the economy."
However, some critics argue that the reform could lead to an increase in bankruptcies, as it makes the process easier and less costly for companies.
They also warn that it could result in job losses if companies choose to liquidate rather than restructure.
The new law will come into effect in the next few months, following its publication in the official gazette.
The European Commission has criticised mobile phone operators for their high roaming charges, calling for more transparency and lower costs for consumers.

A new e-mail virus, disguised as a joke, is tricking users into compromising their computer systems, cybersecurity experts have warned.
The virus, which is spreading rapidly, is causing significant concern among cybersecurity professionals and internet users alike.
The virus is typically sent as an attachment in an email that appears to be from a known contact.
The email often contains a subject line that suggests it contains a joke or humorous content.
Once the attachment is opened, the virus is activated and begins to infect the user's computer.
Cybersecurity firm, CyberGuard, first identified the virus and has named it "Jester".
According to their analysis, Jester is a Trojan horse virus, a type of malware that disguises itself as a harmless file or program to trick users into installing it.
"Jester is particularly concerning because it's very sophisticated," said CyberGuard's lead analyst, Dr. Sarah Clarke.

"It's designed to bypass most antivirus software and it can spread rapidly through a network once it's been activated."

Once installed, the virus can give hackers access to personal information, such as passwords and banking details.
It can also allow them to take control of the infected computer, using it to spread the virus further.
The virus has already caused significant disruption.
Several large corporations have reported network outages as a result of the virus, and there have been reports of personal data breaches.
CyberGuard and other cybersecurity firms are working to develop a patch to protect against Jester, but in the meantime, they are advising internet users to be cautious.
"We recommend that people are very careful about opening any email attachments, even if they appear to be from someone they know," said Dr. Clarke.
"If you're not expecting an attachment, or if anything about the email seems suspicious, it's best not to open it.

"

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has also issued a warning about the virus.
"We are aware of this threat and are working with partners to understand and mitigate it," a spokesperson said.
The NCSC advises that people keep their antivirus software up to date, regularly back up their data, and report any suspicious emails to their internet service provider.
This latest virus serves as a stark reminder of the ongoing threat posed by cybercrime.
As hackers become increasingly sophisticated, internet users must remain vigilant and take steps to protect their personal information.

The ongoing format wars between tech giants could potentially lead to confusion among users, experts warn.

The term 'format wars' refers to the competition between different tech companies to establish their own format as the industry standard.

Cybersecurity experts have raised concerns about the potential for 'evil twin' attacks on wireless networks, which could put users' personal data at risk.
An 'evil twin' attack occurs when a malicious actor sets up a rogue wireless network that mimics a legitimate one.
Unsuspecting users connect to this network, thinking they are accessing their usual Wi-Fi, and the attacker can then intercept their data.
The rise in public Wi-Fi usage, particularly in places like cafes, airports, and hotels, has increased the risk of such attacks.
Users often connect to these networks without verifying their authenticity, making them easy targets for cybercriminals.
"Evil twin attacks are a significant threat to wireless security," said Dr. Ian Brown, a cybersecurity expert at the University of Oxford.
"They are relatively easy to carry out and can be highly effective, particularly against those who are unaware of the risks.

"

The attackers can gain access to sensitive information such as passwords, credit card details, and emails.
They can also potentially inject malware into the user's device, leading to further security breaches.
To protect against these attacks, experts recommend that users avoid connecting to public Wi-Fi networks whenever possible.
If it is necessary to use public Wi-Fi, they suggest using a virtual private network (VPN) to encrypt data and make it harder for attackers to intercept.
"Users should also be wary of any network that does not require a password, as this is a common sign of a potential 'evil twin'," added Dr. Brown.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has also issued guidance on the issue.
It advises users to keep their devices' software up to date, use two-factor authentication where possible, and be cautious about the information they share online.
Despite these warnings, surveys suggest that many people are still unaware of the risks.
A recent poll by cybersecurity firm Symantec found that 87% of respondents had potentially put information at risk by using public Wi-Fi.
As the reliance on wireless networks continues to grow, experts are calling for greater public awareness of the risks and more robust security measures to protect against these types of attacks.

Cybersecurity experts have issued a warning about a new computer virus that masquerades as an official FBI warning, tricking users into paying a fine for alleged illegal activities.
The virus, known as the 'FBI virus', locks users out of their computers, displaying a fake FBI warning message claiming that the user has been involved in illegal activities.
The message then demands a fine to be paid in order to unlock the computer.
The FBI has confirmed that the warning is not from them and is, in fact, a scam.
The agency has urged anyone who encounters the virus to report it to their Internet Crime Complaint Center.
Cybersecurity firm, Norton, has reported a significant increase in the number of these attacks in recent weeks.
The firm's spokesperson said, "This is a particularly insidious type of malware because it uses fear and the threat of legal action to manipulate users into paying the 'fine'."
The virus is typically spread through malicious websites or email attachments.
Once the virus has infected a computer, it can be difficult to remove.
Experts recommend keeping antivirus software up to date and regularly backing up data as a precaution.
The FBI has issued advice for those who encounter the virus, stating, "Do not pay any money or provide any personal information.
Contact a professional to remove the malware, and report the incident to the FBI.

"

The 'FBI virus' is a type of ransomware, a form of malware that encrypts a victim's files and then demands payment to restore access.

Cybersecurity experts are urging the public to be vigilant and to keep their antivirus software up to date.
They also recommend regularly backing up important files and data, as this can help to mitigate the damage caused by a ransomware attack.
The FBI has reiterated that it does not send unsolicited emails to the public and would never demand money in this way.

Scientists have developed a 'brainwave' cap that allows users to control a computer using only their thoughts.
The technology, which is still in its experimental stages, could revolutionise the way we interact with computers and potentially transform the lives of people with mobility issues.

The cap, developed by a team of researchers at the University of California, San Diego, uses electroencephalogram (EEG) technology to read brain activity and translate it into commands for a computer.
The user simply thinks about the action they want the computer to perform, and the cap sends the corresponding command.
The team demonstrated the technology by having a user think about moving a cursor on a screen, and the cursor moved accordingly.
The user was also able to open files, type words, and even play a simple computer game using only their thoughts.
"The potential applications for this technology are vast," said Dr. Thomas DeMarse, the lead researcher on the project.

"From helping those with physical disabilities to interact with their environment, to providing a new way for everyone to interact with computers, we believe this technology could have a significant impact.

"

The cap is non-invasive and uses 64 electrodes to read brain activity.
The signals are then processed by a computer, which uses machine learning algorithms to interpret the brainwaves and translate them into commands.
However, the technology is not yet perfect.
The team admits that it takes some time for users to learn how to control their thoughts in a way that the computer can understand.
Additionally, the cap currently only works with simple commands and is not yet capable of more complex tasks.
Despite these challenges, the team is optimistic about the future of the technology.
They are currently working on improving the cap's accuracy and expanding the range of commands it can interpret.
"This is just the beginning," said Dr. DeMarse.
"We're excited to see where this technology can go and how it can change people's lives.

"

The team's research has been published in the Journal of Neural Engineering.
They are now seeking funding to continue their work and take the technology to the next level.

A supercomputer has shattered the previous speed record, marking a significant milestone in the world of high-performance computing.
The machine, known as Fugaku, is based in Japan and has been developed by RIKEN and Fujitsu.
Fugaku achieved a High Performance Linpack (HPL) result of 442.01 petaflops, smashing the previous record of 148.6 petaflops held by Summit, a supercomputer based in the United States.
This makes Fugaku 2.8 times faster than Summit, demonstrating a significant leap in computational power.
The supercomputer's impressive performance was revealed in the latest edition of the Top500 list, a ranking of the world's most powerful non-distributed computer systems.

Fugaku not only topped the list but also became the first to simultaneously lead in other rankings that measure performance in computational methods for industrial use, artificial intelligence applications, and big data analytics.
Fugaku, which means Mount Fuji in Japanese, has been in development for six years.
It is powered by Fujitsu's 48-core A64FX system on a chip, making it the first number one system on the list to be powered by ARM processors.
The supercomputer's primary purpose is to carry out a wide range of applications that will address high-priority social and scientific issues.
These include research into potential treatments for COVID-19, climate modelling, renewable energy, and more.

"The performance of Fugaku is impressive and demonstrates the significant progress that has been made in supercomputing," said Dr. Satoshi Matsuoka, director of RIKEN Center for Computational Science.
"This will have a profound impact on both scientific research and society as a whole.

"

The achievement of Fugaku also marks a return to the top of the supercomputing world for Japan, which last held the number one position in 2011 with the K computer, also developed by RIKEN and Fujitsu.
The development of supercomputers like Fugaku is crucial for advancing scientific research, as they allow for complex simulations and calculations that would be impossible with standard computers.
The speed record broken by Fugaku is a testament to the rapid advancements being made in this field, and the potential it holds for future discoveries.

The United States is currently grappling with a phenomenon known as 'awards fatigue', a growing disinterest and disillusionment with the numerous awards ceremonies that dominate the entertainment industry.
This trend is reflected in the declining viewership numbers for major awards shows, including the Oscars, the Grammys, and the Golden Globes.
The 2021 Oscars, for instance, saw a record low viewership, with only 10.4 million viewers tuning in, a 58% drop from the previous year.

Experts attribute this decline to a variety of factors.
One of the primary reasons is the sheer number of awards shows, which can lead to a sense of over-saturation.
"There's a feeling of 'not another one'," says Dr. Paul Levinson, a professor of communications and media studies at Fordham University.
"It's like having too much of a good thing.

"

Another factor is the increasing disconnect between the awards shows and the general public.
Many viewers feel that the awards are out of touch with popular taste, often overlooking blockbuster hits and audience favorites in favor of more obscure, critically acclaimed films and shows.
The pandemic has also played a role, with many awards shows being forced to go virtual, leading to a lack of the usual glamour and spectacle that viewers have come to expect.
"The pandemic has stripped awards shows of their usual glitz and glamour," says Levinson.
"People tune in to see the stars in their fancy dresses and tuxedos, and that's just not possible with a virtual format."
The rise of streaming services has also contributed to the decline in viewership.
With more and more people cutting the cord and turning to platforms like Netflix and Amazon Prime, traditional broadcast television is struggling to maintain its audience.
Despite the declining interest, awards shows still hold a significant place in the entertainment industry, often providing a boost to the careers of winners and nominees.
However, if the trend of 'awards fatigue' continues, it could lead to a major shake-up in the way these events are conducted and perceived.
The industry will need to adapt to these changing viewer preferences and find new ways to engage audiences if it hopes to reverse this trend.
Whether that means reducing the number of awards shows, making them more in tune with popular taste, or finding innovative ways to bring back the glamour and spectacle remains to be seen.

Cybersecurity experts are raising alarms about the woeful state of Wi-Fi security, warning that many home and business networks are vulnerable to hacking due to outdated systems and lack of awareness.
Wi-Fi, which has become a ubiquitous part of modern life, is often the weakest link in the chain of cybersecurity.
Many users are unaware of the risks associated with unsecured Wi-Fi networks, and even those who are aware often fail to take the necessary precautions to protect their networks.
According to a recent study by cybersecurity firm Sophos, nearly a quarter of Wi-Fi networks worldwide are not secured with any form of encryption, leaving them open to cybercriminals.
Even among those networks that do use encryption, many are using outdated protocols that can be easily cracked.
"Wi-Fi security is often overlooked, but it's a critical component of overall cybersecurity," said Chester Wisniewski, a principal research scientist at Sophos.
"Many people don't realise that their Wi-Fi network can be an entry point for hackers to gain access to their personal or business data.

"

The problem is not limited to home networks.
Many businesses, including large corporations, are also failing to adequately secure their Wi-Fi networks.
This can lead to data breaches, which can be costly both in terms of financial loss and damage to reputation.
Experts recommend that all Wi-Fi users secure their networks with a strong, unique password and use the latest encryption protocol, WPA3.
They also advise regularly updating router firmware to ensure that any security vulnerabilities are patched.
In addition, users should be wary of public Wi-Fi networks, which are often unsecured and can be a hotbed for cybercriminal activity.
If you must use a public Wi-Fi network, experts recommend using a virtual private network (VPN) to encrypt your data and protect your privacy.
"Wi-Fi security is not something that can be set and forgotten," said Wisniewski.
"It requires ongoing vigilance and maintenance to ensure that your network remains secure.
The warnings come as the world becomes increasingly reliant on Wi-Fi for everything from remote work to online shopping and entertainment.
As our lives become more digital, the importance of Wi-Fi security cannot be overstated.
In the face of these warnings, it is clear that both individuals and businesses need to take Wi-Fi security more seriously.
Failure to do so could result in serious consequences, from identity theft to financial loss.
As the old saying goes, prevention is better than cure - and when it comes to Wi-Fi security, this has never been truer.

The world of football has always been divided on the issue of friendly matches.
Some see them as a vital part of the game, a chance for teams to test new strategies and players to gain experience.
Others, however, view them as unnecessary and potentially harmful distractions.
The question is, is it time to get tough on friendlies?
The argument against friendlies is not without merit.
They can disrupt the rhythm of a team's season, particularly for clubs in the top leagues where the fixture list is already congested.
Players risk injury in games that, ultimately, do not matter in the grand scheme of their careers.
Moreover, there is a financial aspect to consider.
Clubs often have to pay significant sums to release their players for international duty, and there is no guarantee of a return on this investment.
If a player gets injured during a friendly, the club is left to foot the bill for their treatment and recovery, while also having to cope without their services on the pitch.
On the other hand, friendlies can provide invaluable experience for players.
They offer a chance to play against different styles of football, which can be beneficial in preparing for international tournaments.
For younger players, they can provide a stepping stone to the senior team, allowing them to gain experience and confidence.
Furthermore, friendlies can be a source of significant revenue for national football associations, particularly those in developing countries.
The money generated from hosting a friendly against a top-ranked team can be reinvested into grassroots football, helping to nurture the next generation of talent.
So, what's the solution?
One possibility could be to limit the number of friendlies that a player can participate in each season.
This would reduce the risk of injury and disruption to club football, while still allowing for the benefits that these matches can bring.
Another option could be to introduce a form of compensation for clubs, to mitigate the financial risk of releasing players for international duty.
This could be funded by the revenue generated from friendlies, ensuring that the benefits are shared more evenly across the game.
Ultimately, the issue of friendlies is a complex one, with valid arguments on both sides.
However, with the increasing demands of modern football, it may be time to reassess their role and consider whether changes need to be made.
It's time to get tough on friendlies, but in a way that preserves their benefits while minimising their drawbacks.

Former UK Conservative Party leader, Michael Howard, has revealed that he used to skip school to play snooker.
The confession came during an interview on BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs, where he admitted to being a "bit of a tearaway" in his youth.
Mr. Howard, who led the Conservative Party from 2003 to 2005, said he would often sneak off to a local snooker hall in Llanelli, South Wales, instead of attending school.
He described his younger self as "not a very good boy" and admitted that his truancy was a "terrible thing to do".
The former Home Secretary, now 79, said he was "captivated" by the game of snooker from a young age.
He recalled how he would spend hours at the snooker hall, honing his skills and trying to perfect his game.
"I was absolutely captivated by snooker," he said.
"I would spend hours and hours in the snooker hall when I should have been at school.
It was a terrible thing to do and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

"

Despite his truancy, Mr. Howard went on to have a successful political career.
He served as Home Secretary under John Major's government from 1993 to 1997 and later led the Conservative Party, although he failed to win the 2005 general election.
Mr. Howard's love for snooker has not waned over the years.
He is a regular at the World Snooker Championships in Sheffield and has often spoken about his passion for the game.
During the radio interview, he also spoke about his early life, his political career, and his love for music.
He chose tracks by Elvis Presley, Frank Sinatra, and the Beatles for his desert island playlist.
The former Tory leader's confession about his school days has sparked a debate about truancy and the importance of education.
While some have criticised Mr. Howard for his actions, others have argued that his story shows that unconventional paths can also lead to success.
Mr. Howard ended the interview by saying, "I was lucky.
I got away with it.
But I wouldn't advise anyone to follow my example."

The enigmatic forward known as Juninho, one of Mexico's most famous and popular footballers in the last 30 years, is reportedly unhappy with his current situation after a summer of uncertainty and little playing time, igniting a debate regarding his future.
The legend of Juninho began when he was just 17 years old and debuted for Mexico's most popular club team America.

Over the course of two decades, playing for Club America, Monterrey, and Santos, he became a fan favorite due to his skills, humility, and work ethic even though he never achieved the success of winning championships.
In recent years, his career took a turn after he left Santos to join the Club America reserve team.
This summer, after a brief stint in the Mexican second division with Atletico San Luis, he returned to Club America, but has failed to make any appearances under new head coach Fernando Ortiz.
Ortiz recently commented that the club was working to find a solution for the player's future, which has led to many speculating that the forward could be transferred in the upcoming winter window.
However, at 37 years old, options for the player may be limited.
Regardless of what the future holds for Juninho, there is no doubt that he has had a long and successful career and remains a beloved figure in Mexican football.
FIFA World Player of the Year Robben has suffered another setback in his attempts to get back to full fitness after sustaining a hairline fracture in his left foot.
The Netherlands international had been poised to make his comeback in next week's Champions League game against Olympiakos after recovering from ligament damage in the same foot sustained in October.
However, Robben will now be ruled out until 2007 after suffering the fracture in training on Tuesday.
"Arjen needs an operation on his foot.
It's very sad for him, because he had hoped to be fit for the second half of the season," said Bayern chairman Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.
The German champions have yet to announce when the operation will take place, although it is likely to be carried out towards the end of this week.
Bayern had been hoping that Robben would be back to full fitness in time for the second leg of their last-16 tie against Olympiakos on March 7.
The 25-year-old winger has not played since October 22 when he damaged the ligament injury against Werder Bremen.
He made a promising start to the season, scoring seven goals and providing five assists in 11 appearances prior to his injury.
Bayern, who are eight points clear at the top of the Bundesliga, travel to third-placed VfB Stuttgart on Saturday.
Wales' star men need to be protected from themselves ahead of Tuesday's crucial World Cup play-off final against Ukraine, says former captain Ryan Giggs.
Giggs says Wales must manage the workload of players such as Gareth Bale and Aaron Ramsey carefully to ensure they are not burned out before next summer's Euros.
The 44-year-old, who won 64 caps for his country, said it was crucial Wales got their approach right at this crucial stage of the season.
"In Wales we've got some fantastic players who play in some of the biggest clubs in the world, and that brings its own problems," Giggs told the BBC's Football Daily podcast.
"Sometimes I think players want to be involved in every game because they love the game, but sometimes it might not be the best thing for them.
"Gareth Bale, who has just won the Copa del Rey final could miss the Champions League final if he plays in the play-off final and gets injured.
That's how important it is, not just for Wales but for the players' clubs as well.
"We saw with Dan James against Austria, he didn't look himself.
He probably shouldn't have been on the pitch.
It's a fine balance between getting players minutes and making sure they are not overworked."
Roger Federer continued his impressive comeback from injury as he reached the semi-finals of the Swiss Indoors in Basel with a straight-set victory over Alex de Minaur.
The former world number one, who has already confirmed he will retire after the Laver Cup in London next month, dropped just six points on his serve and hit 16 winners in a 6-2 6-4 victory.

De Minaur, 22, was unable to find any solutions to Federer's consistent play in the first set, as the Swiss great produced typical flair with a delightful between-the-legs shot on his way to breaking for a 4-2 lead.
Federer, who has won the event a record 10 times, wrapped up the first set with a love hold and then broke again at the start of the second set as he moved ahead 3-0.

The Australian, ranked 24th in the world, eventually found his rhythm to earn his first break points of the match in the eighth game, but Federer saved both and went on to secure the decisive break a game later before serving out to take the match after an hour and 23 minutes.

The 20-time Grand Slam champion, who has undergone three knee operations in the past year, will face American Tommy Fritz in the last four as he continues his quest for a 15th title at his home tournament.
Manchester City suffered a second defeat in a week as goals from Casemiro and Luke Shaw gave Manchester United a 2-0 win at the Etihad.
City had beaten United at Old Trafford last weekend but could not complete the double over their neighbours in their own backyard.
United were superior for much of the game and Casemiro's strike, after 50 minutes, ultimately proved the difference between the two sides.
Shaw doubled United's lead with seven minutes remaining, following up to score after his initial header had hit the post.
City had few chances and De Gea had little to do, but the closest they came to scoring was a deflection off Bruno Fernandes which hit the post shortly after the restart.
The win takes United up to sixth, level on points with fifth-placed Tottenham, while City stay in third, four points ahead of Arsenal having played two games more.
Britain's new Prime Minister, Rishi Sunak, has narrowly defeated his rival for the leadership, Penny Mordaunt, in a vote by the Conservative Party's powerful 1922 committee.

The announcement brings to a conclusion the chaotic leadership contest that followed the dramatic resignation of Boris Johnson last month, and marks a remarkable comeback for Mr. Sunak, who was himself sacked by Mr. Johnson just 46 days ago.
The decision came after a grueling five-hour debate between the two finalists in which both laid out their visions for the future of the Conservative Party and the country.

Mr. Sunak, who has been Chancellor of the Exchequer since 2020, emphasized his economic credentials and promised to fix the "broken" housing market, while Ms. Mordaunt, the Conservative Party's foreign affairs spokesperson, argued that the party had "lost its way" and vowed to "bring it back to its roots".
The new party leader will be formally elected on Monday, and will become the third prime minister in Britain in just eight weeks.
David Beckham has ruled out the possibility of him ever managing an English football team, saying he does not "have the patience" to do so.
The former England captain has managed and owned football clubs in the United States and Australia since his retirement from playing in 2013.
Speaking to the Sunday Times, he said: "I don't have the patience to manage.
I wouldn't say it's fair to say that I will definitely manage a football club one day.
I love winning, but I don't like the losing as much.
I've not had enough time in my career to really appreciate losing.

"

The 45-year-old retains strong links with Britain, where he is a former Manchester United and Real Madrid player, as well as being an ex-England international.
He was appointed an honorary knight in 2017 by the Queen for services to football.
His links with the UK were strengthened last year when his franchise Inter Miami signed former Manchester United team-mate and ex-England striker Wayne Rooney at the age of 35.
Rooney moved to Florida with his family in July last year after being offered a contract by Beckham to play for his Major League Soccer franchise.
Should Beckham ever change his mind and wish to enter management in the UK, he would be likely to be given a supportive role at Old Trafford.
The ex-England midfielder has a contract with Manchester United which gives him the option of taking a role at the club in the future.
The Spanish football club, Sociedad, is set to rescue the Serbian footballer, Mladenovic, from his current contract at Manchester City.
The Spanish side will pay a fee of around £21 million for the forward, who has been with the Premier League club since 2017.
Mladenovic has been on loan at Sociedad for the past two seasons, and has made a strong impression during that time, scoring 20 goals in all competitions.
The Serbian international has reportedly been keen to return to Spain, and Sociedad's offer was too good for Manchester City to turn down.
Sociedad will hope that Mladenovic can continue his impressive form in Spain, and help them to challenge for the La Liga title.
With the forward's experience and skill, they will be a strong contender for the title in the coming years.
The sports journalist Kelly Somers writes about Sam "Umaga" Hipili's preparation for the Lions in an upcoming rugby union match.
The Auckland-born rugby star admits that he is afraid of the Lions.
He says that the Lions are one of the most feared opponents in rugby.
Despite this, Hipili considers himself a daredevil and explains that the prospect of facing the feared team only excites him more.

Spain clinched the cup in the final match against Sweden, dominating throughout the match with a 3-0 final score.
The victory came courtesy of two quick goals by left-winger Pedro Moya.
Moya scored the first goal five minutes into the match, following a pass from teammate Diego Costa.
The ball found Moya's feet in front of the net, and he kicked it in with his left foot, sending the ball flying into the upper left corner of the goal.
The second goal came only four minutes later, as Moya capitalized on a mistake by the Swedish defense.
The ball bounced in front of Moya, who kicked it in with his right foot, sending it straight into the net.
The victory was a testament to Spain's skill and tactics, as they controlled the pace of the match and capitalized on opportunities created by their precise passing.
The team's performance was a reflection of the hard work and dedication of the players and coaching staff, who have worked tirelessly to improve their skills and tactics.

As part of an effort to reduce traffic congestion, improve air quality, and make cities more livable, local authorities in Sheffield, UK, are planning to introduce a "vehicle miles traveled" (VMT) fee for cars.
The aim is to reduce the number of car journeys and encourage the use of public transport, cycling, and walking.
The scheme, which is set to be introduced in Sheffield later this year, will see drivers charged based on the number of miles they drive within the city boundaries.
The charges will be applied through a "pay per mile" system, with the money raised being used to fund improvements to the city's transport infrastructure.
The plan has been welcomed by local residents and businesses, who see it as a positive step towards reducing traffic congestion and improving air quality.
However, some have raised concerns about the potential impact on low-income households and those who rely on cars for work or medical reasons.
The scheme is being seen as a test case for other cities in the UK and could be rolled out more widely if it is successful in Sheffield.
England striker Danny Welbeck scored twice in a comfortable friendly victory for Gareth Southgate's side at Wembley.
The game marked the return of Harry Kane after a month out with a hamstring injury, with the captain coming on as a second-half substitute.
England were already leading when Kane came on and he quickly added a third, before Welbeck scored again late on.
It was a successful return to Wembley for Wales manager Rob Page, who was part of the England backroom team when they won the Under-21s Euro title in 2017.
But it was a disappointing night for his players, who were comfortably beaten as their 12-match unbeaten run came to an end.

The sports minister has stood by comments made by the Olympic champion Sir Mo Farah, who suggested that the reason why he and other British athletes were never accused of blood doping was because of his skin color.
Sir Mo was accused by German athlete Aleixo Neoh, who finished behind him in second place in the 5,000m and 10,000m races at the 2015 and 2017 World Championships.
On Wednesday, Neoh publicly accused Sir Mo of blood doping, the practice of increasing the red blood cell count to enhance oxygen transportation and thus performance.

28-year-old Neoh, who has naturalized to become an Austrian citizen since finishing behind Sir Mo, claimed that he had taken “hundreds of blood bags” which contained blood plasma from a person with a very high number of red blood cells.
Plasma is the liquid part of blood.
It contains salts, water, enzymes, and antibodies.
In response to the accusations, Sports Minister Nigel Huddleston told the House of Commons on Wednesday that “Mo Farah is clean.”

While he admitted that he had “never seen” the results of any anti-doping tests carried out on the athlete, he said that “based on the information that he has provided, and that has been provided by UK Sport, I have full confidence in Mo Farah.”
On Thursday, Sir Mo said that “it hurts to be accused of blood doping,” describing the claims as “not true, to be honest.”
The four-time Olympic champion said that “all my results are public.
Every test I've had, everything is public.
People can see that for themselves.”
In response to the sports minister's comments, Sir Mo said “I'm very grateful to him
[Nigel Huddleston] for what he said.”
Britain is boasting about its latest double triumph in Alpine skiing after achieving its best-ever result in the men's downhill and another podium place for its women in the same event.
MBE Chemmy Alcott and Sara Hector both finished on the podium in the downhill, with Alcott finishing third and Hector in second place.
Alison Dixon finished eighth, while Annie Last was 15th and Boarder Ski Cross athlete Emily Sarsfield 19th.
The men achieved their best-ever result with Owen Vinter finishing seventh in the downhill and snowboard cross rider Zoe Gillings taking bronze in the women's snowboard cross.
The BBC's Andy Capstick says the performances across the board give British skiing "a huge boost" going into the Olympics next year.
He says the athletes can go to Vancouver with "their heads held high".
British Ski and Snowboard chief executive Andy Mapple says the double success "really demonstrates the investment that's been made over the last five or six years is beginning to bear fruit".
Southgate calls forward Everton's Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Arsenal's Bukayo Saka, as well as uncapped trio Kyle Walker-Peters of Tottenham, Mason Mount of Chelsea and Phil Foden of Manchester City.
There is a return for Southampton's James Ward-Prowse, who was not involved in the last squad, while Luke Shaw is also back having recovered from a concussion.
Manchester United's Harry Maguire and Marcus Rashford are left out, along with Liverpool's Trent Alexander-Arnold and Manchester City's Raheem Sterling.
The 25-man squad will gather on Monday at St George's Park, with the majority of the players coming in from domestic matches on Sunday.
Wales name an unchanged team for their final Euro 2020 warm-up game against France.
The two sides meet in Nice on Wednesday night, with Wales facing Switzerland in their Group A opener in Baku on 12 June.

France name 26-man squad for Euro 2020 warm-ups

Ryan Giggs' side have been dealt an injury blow with Aaron Ramsey missing the game through injury.
The Juventus midfielder picked up a thigh problem in training last week and will not travel to Nice.

Wales boss Ryan Giggs names 26-man squad for Euro 2020

Ramsey was included in an initial 28-man squad but has not recovered in time.
Wales have also been without forward Kieffer Moore for their training camp, with the Bournemouth striker having undergone knee surgery last month.
Moore is expected to be available for the start of the Euros.
