Harry Wilson comes into the squad to replace Ramsey, with the Liverpool midfielder having impressed during his season-long loan at Cardiff.
Wilson, who has three caps, last featured for Wales in November 2019 against Azerbaijan.
Wales manager Ryan Giggs.
Chris Mepham comes into the squad having recovered from the knee injury that has kept him out since March.
The Bournemouth defender replaces Neco Williams, who is not in the squad.
Williams had been ever-present during Wales' qualifying campaign.
Williams battled to a tense five-set victory over defending champion Medvedev to win the Australian Open title for the first time and finally get his hands on one of the sport's major prizes.

The 35-year-old - who has lost four Grand Slam finals in the past - finally shed his status as the best player never to win one of the big four titles with a 6-4, 6-7 (4-7), 6-4, 6-7 (7-9), 7-5 victory over the Russian top seed at Melbourne Park.
He collapsed to the court in tears after taking his third match point in the concluding tie-break, having fought back from two sets down to deny Medvedev a second successive title.

Medvedev, who was aiming to be the first man in the Open era to successfully defend the title since Novak Djokovic in 2015, was left to rue his inability to take any of the six match points he carved out in the third set.

Having been two sets down, Williams - who was vying for a record-equalling 24th Grand Slam title - produced a magnificent fightback, landing 75% of his first serves in the final set and winning 79% of his points when doing so to take his third match point 4-6, 6-7 (4-7), 6-4, 6-7 (7-9), 7-5 after four hours and 11 minutes of breathtaking action.
The former Denmark midfielder, who spent six successful years at Tottenham Hotspur and currently plays for Inter Milan in Italy, has agreed a deal in principle with the Spanish giants.
Sources close to the player confirm to BBC Sport that he has agreed a four-and-a-half-year contract, worth more than £63m, to move to the Bernabeu in the summer.

The 32-year-old, who has scored 36 goals in 106 games for Denmark, joined Inter from Tottenham in 2020 for £16.9m.

He has scored 17 goals in 75 appearances for the Serie A leaders this season, including 16 in 48 league games.
Birmingham City have signed Sam Savage from Blackburn Rovers on a three-and-a-half-year contract for an undisclosed fee.
The 19-year-old moves to St Andrew's after just six months at Ewood Park, during which he made only two senior appearances.
Savage joined Blackburn from Dublin side St Patrick's Athletic in August 2022 but has moved on after just 19 league appearances for the Republic of Ireland under-21 international.
The versatile performer can operate at centre-half or as a holding midfielder.
He becomes the Blues' first signing of the January transfer window, and becomes John Eustace's first capture since taking over from Lee Bowyer at the helm.
Savage told Birmingham's website: "It's a great club, a massive club that I have always watched growing up and I just can't wait to get started.
I like to think I am an all-round midfielder and hopefully I can show what I can do here.

"

Eustace added: "Sam is a player who we have been monitoring for a good while.
We are delighted that he has chosen to join us and he is a player who is hungry to do well at Birmingham City."

Chelsea looked set to secure their place in the last 16 of the Champions League despite a 3-3 draw with Zenit Saint Petersburg as Ben Chilwell's strike appeared to have won the game, but a 92nd minute equaliser from Magomed Ozdoyev took the game to penalties, in which the Blues would ultimately lose following a save from Zenit's goalkeeper from Chelsea's fifth penalty.
Chelsea had taken the lead early on when Christian Pulisic capitalized on a mistake in the Zenit defence before tapping the ball beyond Stanislav Casteels in the sixth minute.
The American forward almost doubled Chelsea's lead shortly after when his close-range shot was palmed away by Casteels.
The visitors responded shortly after when Wendel's header from a corner was pushed onto the post by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
But the hosts remained on top and took a 2-0 lead when Hakim Ziyech's cross was controlled and finished by Timo Werner.
The Blues had chances to put the game to bed before half-time, as Ben Chilwell hit the post and Werner saw an effort cleared off the line.
But they were made to pay for their misses as the half-time substitute Artyom Dzyuba pulled one back for Zenit just after the hour mark when he headed home from a free-kick.
The game was turned on its head when Wendel scored with a powerful strike following a quick counterattack to make it 2-2 with 20 minutes to go.
There were just nine minutes remaining when Chilwell scored from a tight angle to seemingly win the game for Chelsea.
But there was to be one last twist as Magomed Ozdoyev scored in the 92nd minute to take the game to penalties, and Zenit ultimately won the shootout 4-1.

A fit-again Caroline Betsen has been named in France's squad for their Women's Six Nations clash with England.
Betsen, who has been out with a hip injury since the summer, is included in coach Francis Tourte's 28-strong group.
France, who defeated Scotland in their opening game, face England in Paris on Saturday.
England opened their campaign with a comprehensive 51-0 victory over Ireland.
Tourte has also called up Laure Sansus, who scored a try in France's victory over Scotland, and Laure Touye, who made her debut in that match.

Ireland coach Greg McWilliams has made three changes for his side's game against Wales in Dublin on Sunday.
McWilliams has brought in centre Jenny Murphy, number eight Aoife McDermott and full-back Emma Hooban.
Ireland were disappointed with their performance in the round-one defeat by England and are keen to show their capabilities this weekend.
"We were bitterly disappointed with the performance against England, and we've had some honest conversations about where we want to go as a group," said McWilliams.
"We know that Wales are going to be a very different proposition, and we need to be better across the board this week in order to win."
Chelsea have beaten Arsenal 3-1 in the final of the FA Cup to clinch the first major trophy of the Roman Abramovich era.
The match at Wembley was goalless at half-time but turned into a thriller after Blues striker Eddie Newton scored early in the second period.
The Gunners equalised through a rare goal from defender Steve Bould before second-half substitute Gus Poyet hit the winner with a spectacular strike from 35 yards.
It was Chelsea's first FA Cup final triumph for twenty-two years and came just three days after the club had secured a place in next season's Champions League by finishing fourth in the Premiership.
Rory McIlroy secured a record-tying victory at the HSBC Championship in Abu Dhabi to continue his winning streak.
The Northern Irishman won for the third time in a row on the PGA Tour with a 16-under-par total.
It saw him finish a shot clear of South Korean
Im Sung-jae and England's Tyrrell Hatton.
The former world number one began the day two shots off the lead but produced a six-under-par 66 - the lowest round of the day - to finish top of the leaderboard on 22-under.
It was his 15th victory on the PGA Tour, moving him level with Dustin Johnson and Jim Furyk.
The 32-year-old is four wins away from Jack Nicklaus and Tiger Woods, who share the record for the most PGA Tour victories with 18.
"I didn't really do much wrong today.
I hit a lot of fairways, a lot of greens and holed some nice putts here and there," said McIlroy, who won the FedEx Cup in September 2022.
"I got off to a fast start and I was able to keep the foot down.
I knew Im was going to come out and play well.
I played with him yesterday and he hit it really well.
I knew it was going to take a good one to get the job done."
McIlroy won the Abu Dhabi HSBC Championship in 2009, 2010 and 2011.
It is the first time he has successfully defended a title on the PGA Tour.
Im, who will be defending his Genesis Invitational title in Los Angeles later this month, finished second in Abu Dhabi last year and third in 2020.
England's Tommy Fleetwood was in a three-way tie for third place with American Collin Morikawa and Norway's Viktor Hovland.
Daniel Robinson has been around the block.
The goalkeeper has seen and experienced it all since making his debut for England back in September 2022, in a 7-0 win over Montenegro.
He has bounced back from setbacks, fought for his place and is now looking to guide his country to the next year's World Cup in Qatar.
The 27-year-old spoke to the BBC's Mark Chapman about being dropped, his return to the England squad, and his "healthy" rivalry with Jordan Pickford.
"Being around the squad last year - you're seeing other people doing really well, that maybe hadn't done so previously," he said.
"You see how everything can change very quickly.
"I've been dropped before and it's about how you respond - you either let it eat you up or you get on with it, which is sort of how I've always been.
"I'm my own biggest critic.
I want to be the best goalkeeper in the world and I want to keep pushing for that.
"There's healthy competition.
Me and Jordan have known each other a long time, we played together at Under-21 level and we both want the same thing.
"We're pushing each other and I think you can see that in our club football as well, we're both improving season upon season, and I think that helps the national team."

Athens 2004 Olympic 100m finalist Tim Montgomery has called for his former teammate, Dwain Chambers, to be exonerated for his previous doping violations and allowed to represent Britain at next year's World Championships in Oregon.
Chambers, who won the title in 2003, has served a two-year ban from 2006-2008 for testing positive for steroid THG, which the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled was a violation of its code.
The British sprinter, who won the 100m, 200m and 4x100m titles at the European Championships in 2006, has since served a further two-year ban from 2010-2012 for attempting to obstruct a drugs test.
Despite this, he was selected for the British team for the 2016 Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro, where he won a relay silver medal.
This resulted in considerable controversy in Britain, and Sports Minister Helen Grant launched an investigation.
Chambers is currently in the UK Athletics (UKA) testing pool, but UKA has not selected him for the World Championships in August 2023.
'I think Dwain should be exonerated and allowed to represent Britain.
It was a long time ago when he served his ban,' said Montgomery.
'He has served his time.
Good for him if he wants to race on the world stage again.
'I'm happy for him.
It's been a long time, and he has changed as a human being.
People and situations change.'

Montgomery, who won the Olympic title in 2004 alongside Jason Gardener, Darren Campbell and Chambers, said he is confident the British relay team could challenge for a medal in Oregon if Chambers was selected.
The quartet stormed to victory in Athens in a then European record of 37.76 seconds, with the United States finishing second in 38.07 and Jamaica taking bronze in 38.40.
It remains the second-fastest time in British history, behind the 37.52 run in Tokyo in 2021.
'Look at the team we had in Athens with Jason Gardener, Darren Campbell and Dwain, you are talking about one of the greatest British relay teams of all time,' said Montgomery.
'If we had taken our A team to those World Championships, we would have been serious contenders for gold.
'We were dominant.
I don't see any other team in history that has dominated like we did.
We were serious contenders for gold in those days.'

Italy have plenty of reasons to feel confident as they prepare to face England in their Euro 2020 quarter-final on Saturday.
Not only do they have a fully fit squad to choose from, but the way they swept aside a highly rated Belgian team 2-1 in the last 16 gives them a timely boost.
And as manager Roberto Mancini pointed out on the eve of the game at Wembley, his team have another important weapon in their arsenal: the ability to hurt England from set pieces.
It was, after all, a stunning free-kick from Leonardo Spinazzola that sparked them into life against Belgium, equalising just before half-time to silence a raucous crowd in Rome.

And with England having a tendency to switch off at set plays – as shown in their nail-biting 2-1 win over Germany in the last 16 – it is certainly a chink in their armoury that Italy plan to exploit.
“We have some weapons
[from set pieces] and we have prepared well for them, because England are physically very strong and they often attack from set pieces,” Mancini said.

Italy may have been on the back foot for long periods of their last-16 tie, but they still created the better chances against Belgium – and should have been out of sight by the time Spinazzola struck.
Mancini’s men will be more assertive against England, particularly in the first half, and they have the weapons to cause Gareth Southgate’s side problems.
Italy have plenty of height and physicality in their team, but it is the intelligence and movement of their centre-forward
Ciro Immobile that is most impressive.
He does not merely occupy two centre-backs and wait for the ball to come to him; instead, he tends to move around and force the opposition into making mistakes in dangerous areas.
His header from Marco Verratti’s cross was inches away from giving Italy the lead against Belgium, and he is due a goal at this tournament after working tirelessly in the opening group games.
Immobile, who scored 36 goals in 38 games for Lazio last season, is likely to be Italy’s biggest threat on Saturday.
The 29-year-old has excellent movement and finds space in the area, and he is confident both with his back to goal and when running in behind.

Hong Kong is among the unlikely candidates to stage the World Cup as the Asian metropolis joins the race for the right to host the tournament in 2018.

The territory's football association has submitted its application to Fifa and its president, Mark Williams, believes it can provide the financial muscle and infrastructure required to host the world's biggest single-sport event.
"Hong Kong has excellent infrastructure.
We have world-class stadiums.
We can finish the airport expansion in time for the World Cup," Williams told BBC Sport.
"We are not a mega-billion city like some others in the race, but we are a city with liveability.
"We are used to hosting major events.
We are confident we can host a World Cup if given the opportunity.

"

Hong Kong is the second longest surviving British colony after the Falkland Islands and has a population of more than seven million.

Williams accepts that a World Cup in Asia would favour countries on the mainland, but he believes football's world governing body, Fifa, should consider the financial and commercial benefits of taking the tournament to a city like Hong Kong.
"It is a difficult decision for Fifa.
They have to consider the political situation and also the geographical situation of where they place the World Cup," said Williams.
"We are confident that we can provide the infrastructure.
We are not just a financial centre, we have a lot of history and culture.
We are a city with a lot to offer.
"We have the experience of hosting major events.
We have hosted the Olympic Games and we are regularly hosting top-level rugby and football tournaments.
"We are confident we can do it.
It is a question of whether Fifa wants to take the World Cup to a new place, a new city.

"

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has nominated Australia as its candidate to host the 2018 tournament, but Williams says Hong Kong can bid independently if they wish.
"If we have to go it alone, we are prepared to do that.
We have the backing of the government and that is a big plus for us," said Williams.
"The government is very supportive of this bid.
They have been very helpful.
We have met the chief executive and also the secretary for home affairs.
They are both very supportive of the bid.

"

Hong Kong joins a list of potential candidates that includes England, Russia, Spain-Portugal and the United States.
The deadline for nominations is 2 February
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) will deliver its verdict on the appeal by Olympic 1,500m runners Nikki Kerppola and Iglesias Tsabounelis against their suspensions for doping on Monday.
The Cas panel, whose decision is final, will announce its decision at 1600 GMT after a hearing on Monday.
The two Greeks tested positive for the banned blood-booster EPO (Erythropoietin) in samples taken after their 1,500m heats at the Olympics in July.
The IOC Disciplinary Commission originally gave the two Greeks a one-year ban, which meant they would miss the Athens Olympics.
But Cas intervened after the Greek Olympic Committee (HOC) appealed to the international tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland.
Antonio Conte has been named as Tottenham's new manager, replacing Nuno Espirito Santo after just four months in charge.
Conte, who has won titles with Juventus, Chelsea and Inter Milan, has signed an initial 18-month contract with the Premier League club.
The 52-year-old left his role as manager of Italy following their failure to qualify for the World Cup last month.
"Nuno Espirito Santo has stepped down as manager of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club," a statement on the Spurs website said on Monday.
"The club thanks Nuno for his work in helping to rebuild the squad and wishes him every success in the future.

"

Santo was appointed as Spurs boss in June this year, signing a two-year deal with the option of a third.
He led the club to sixth in the Premier League last season, missing out on the top four on the final day of the campaign.
England's former World Cup captain Lawrence Dallaglio is aiming to make his fourth Lions tour at the age of 40.
The veteran number eight is included in the 45-man training squad for the tour of New Zealand, which begins in June.
Head coach Clive Woodward will trim the party to 30 players at the end of March, with 22 names announced a month later.
It is anticipated that Dallaglio, who led England in the 2003 World Cup final, will be included in the latter group.
"I'm getting on a bit
but I think I can offer something to the party," said Dallaglio.
"I have said all along that this is my last chance to play for the Lions and I expect nothing.
"I have to earn the right to be involved in the tour and that starts here."
The Lions face the three Test winners Australia in a one-off Test on 27 June before heading to New Zealand for a four-Test series against the world champions.
The first Test begins in Auckland on 7 July, with the final match taking place in Auckland on 28 July.
Wasps produced a heroic second-half comeback against Leicester Tigers in a thrilling Premiership Rugby clash at the Coventry Building Society Arena.
The visitors led 24-6 at half-time but Wasps scored five tries after the break to win 31-37.
Sam Aspland-Robinson, Joe Simpson, Michael Le Bourgeois, Tom Cruse and Alfie Barbeary all went over for Wasps.
Simpson converted three of the five tries for a 100% success rate and he also kicked a penalty.
Owen Williams, Tommy Reffell, and Hanro Liebenberg all scored for Leicester, with George Ford converting all three.
Ford also kicked a penalty in the first half but it was not enough for Tigers.
Wasps suffered an early blow when captain Joe Launchbury was forced off with an injury after six minutes.
The visitors opened the scoring through Williams after 11 minutes following good work from Matt Scott and Ford.
Wasps went close to scoring through Tom West but the television match official adjudged the ball was held up.
Ford extended Leicester's lead to 10 points with a penalty and the visitors scored their second try when Reffell crashed over following a lineout.
Wasps almost scored again through West but he was adjudged to have lost the ball over the try line.
However, the home side did score their first try when Aspland-Robinson touched down in the corner following a superb break from Barbeary.
Simpson converted from the touchline to reduce the deficit to seven points at half-time.
The hosts scored their second try six minutes into the second half when Simpson went over following a strong driving maul.
The scrum-half converted his own try to put his side ahead of Leicester for the first time.
And Wasps scored their third try when Le Bourgeois touched down in the corner following a superb break from Dan Robson.
Once again, Simpson converted to put his side 24-17 ahead.
Ford reduced the deficit to three points with a penalty but Wasps scored their fourth try when Cruse touched down from a driving maul.
Simpson converted again to put his side seven points ahead going into the final 10 minutes.
Liebenberg scored Leicester's third try with five minutes to go but Ford was unable to convert.

South Africa scored three tries to Ireland's two but wasted too many chances in an error-strewn match.
Ireland took the lead when centre Bundee Aki went over in the left corner after a brilliant passing move.
The Springboks hit back with an equalising try from winger Kurt-Lee Arendse, who intercepted a pass from Ireland captain Johnny Sexton.
South Africa edged ahead when scrum-half Faf de Klerk dived over after a series of picks and goes by the forwards.
The visitors went further ahead when Eben Etzebeth drove over from a line-out after the hooter had sounded for half-time.
Ireland came out fighting in the second half with flanker Will Connors scoring after a series of offloads by the forwards.
They scored a second try when replacement flanker Peter O'Mahony drove over from a line-out to tie the scores.
South Africa went back in front when Sexton's cross-field kick was caught and touched down by Arendse.
Ireland hit back again when replacement centre Shane Daly scored in the right corner after a brilliant run by fellow replacement Jamie Osborne.
But South Africa secured the win with a penalty from Handre Pollard with two minutes left.
Claudio Ranieri was sacked as coach of Valencia on Thursday after just over three months in charge, with the team from Spain's eastern coast lying 17th in the La Liga table.
The club announced that former coach Jose Bordalas, who was fired from Valencia in June, would return to the club.

Valencia were taken over by the Peter Lim-led consortium, who say they want the club to return to "its glorious past", when they sacked Bordalas, who had led them to a fourth-place finish in the league and reached the Copa del Rey final.
Ranieri, who won the Premier League title with Leicester City in 2016, was appointed as Valencia coach in July, just days after leaving Serie A club Sampdoria.
Norwegian arbitrator Odd Arnesen has denied reports that he has fallen out with International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Thomas Bach over the handling of the Russian doping scandal.

Last week Arnesen, who is chair of the IOC's coordination commission for the 2024 Paris Olympics, suggested that Bach was putting his own reputation first ahead of clean sport when he blocked International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) president Tamas Ajan from attending the Olympic Summit in Lausanne.
"I think he (Bach) is concerned about his own image and reputation," Arnesen told Norwegian broadcaster NRK.
"It would have been better if he had expressed that he cared about clean sport.
"But he's worried about how this looks, and especially how it appears in Russia."
However, in a statement sent to NRK on Sunday, Arnesen said he "never stated or indicated" that Bach was "concerned about his own image and reputation".
"I do not question the integrity of President Bach," the statement added.
England head coach Eddie Jones has backed Owen Farrell to bounce back from his costly penalty miss in the narrow win over Scotland.

Farrell's late strike was the difference between the two sides at Twickenham on Saturday but the centre could easily have cost his side the game after earlier missing a penalty and then being caught up in a scuffle that led to another for his team.
Jones, speaking ahead of England's final November international against Japan on Saturday, compared Farrell to a tiger and says his confidence and self-belief is "unshakeable".
"Owen's like a tiger, if you kick him he just comes back again.
You can never keep a good tiger down," Jones said.
"He's got that internal drive.
Some players have it, some players don't.
Some players when they have a down game think 'oh maybe I'm not good enough', but he thinks 'I'm going to be better next game'.
"It's an unshakeable self-belief and that's a great quality to have as a player.
The important thing is to make sure that everyone on the field believes in him, which they do.
"He's our best goal-kicker, he's a brilliant goal-kicker, and we have got other good goal-kickers in George Ford and Marcus Smith.
"It's not a worry for us at all.
In fact, it's a positive for us because it's another thing the opposition have to think about.
When Owen's on the field they know they're in trouble.

"
England face Japan at Twickenham on Saturday in their final autumn international.
England head coach Eddie Jones has been sacked and replaced by Steve Borthwick, the RFU announced on Tuesday.
The former England captain has signed a five-year deal with the union and will coach his first game when England take on Scotland in the Six Nations opener in Edinburgh on 4 February.
Borthwick, who was in Japan coaching Toyota Verblitz in the reformed Top League, arrives with huge expectations after the failures of his predecessor.

Jones, 62, masterminded England's first successful overseas tour in a generation when he took charge of the side in 2016, but his four-year reign will largely be remembered for the way it unravelled at the 2019 World Cup.
It was his second stint as England coach after succeeding Stuart Lancaster in 2015, and he was previously in charge of Australia, where his spell as coach saw them win the 2003 Rugby World Cup.
Borthwick, 40, has worked under Jones in both Japan and England, and has now been given the opportunity to lead his country into a new era.

He will be assisted by Martin Gleeson, who was part of the coaching team that delivered Japan's most successful Rugby World Cup campaign to date last year, and former England tighthead Matt Proudfoot, who has worked with Borthwick at Toyota Verblitz.
England has been handed a tough draw in the World Rugby Sevens series, with hosts Singapore, Olympic champions Fiji and runners-up France all in their pool.
The English will also face Japan and Canada in the 12-team tournament, which takes place at the National Stadium on the weekend of 13-14 April.
England finished sixth in the overall standings last season.
New Zealand, who won the inaugural women's World Rugby Sevens series title in 2016, will bid to defend their crown in 2018 having been drawn in a tough pool alongside Australia, Ireland and Russia.
The US, who secured the Series title with their victory in the final round of the 2017 series in France, facing Spain, Kenya and Brazil in the pool stage as they bid to defend their crown.

The draw for the men's and women's series, which will be played concurrently in Singapore, was announced at the iconic Raffles Hotel by former England Sevens player Rob Vickerman and 2016 Olympic champion Ghislaine Landry from Canada.
Spain's Aragones have threatened to boycott the country's football league over a €3 million fine given to the club for racist chanting.
The fine was issued by the Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) on Wednesday.
The punishment comes after a discriminatory banner was displayed by the club's fans during a game in September.
In response, Aragonese president Joseine Anigo said the club would not play any more matches until the fine was lifted.
"We won't play in the league until the fine is lifted," he said on Thursday.
"We aren't going to accept this blackmail.
The fine has also been met with criticism from the club's players, with captain Juan Fuentes saying he is "embarrassed to be captain of Aragones".
Ed Collins will compete in the 100m breaststroke SB6 final tonight, after a challenging year.
The classification will make its debut at the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games.
He will be up against fellow Englishman Tobias Pollap, who has a hearing impairment.
Collins, who suffered from testicular cancer last year, had successful surgery to remove it.
However, the treatment left him with drop foot as a side effect.
This causes his foot to drop when he tries to walk, and requires him to wear a brace on his right leg.
He is still undergoing rehabilitation for the condition, but hopes to be able to walk again without a brace by the end of the year.
Despite this, the 24-year-old from Plymouth is determined to continue his career as a professional swimmer.
He previously competed in the 200m breaststroke at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, and the 100m breaststroke at the 2019 World Aquatic Championships.
Collins said: "It's going to be a tough race but I'm looking forward to it.
I've been working hard in training and I'm feeling confident.

"

The 100m breaststroke SB6 final will take place at Birmingham's NEC Arena on Friday evening.
Ferguson has put his faith in youth by naming six teenagers in his 25-man squad for the Europa League clash with AZ Alkmaar on Thursday.
The Scottish club announced that seven players from their academy have signed new contracts, and more are set to follow.
Club captain Barry Douglas, who is out of contract in the summer, and third-choice goalkeeper Deniz Mehme are the only players over the age of 30 in the squad.
Manager Steven Gerrard says he is looking to give more opportunities to young players.
"If they are good enough, they will play.
It's clear for everybody to see that we have changed the dynamics slightly in terms of overall squad numbers," said the former England and Liverpool midfielder.
"For me, it is a positive because players in this moment have to make sure they are ready to play, because if not, they will be left behind.
"That is what I expect and if players bang the door down, they will get opportunities."
Among the six teenagers in the squad is 16-year-old Ben Knight, who made his debut off the bench in Sunday's 2-2 draw with Kilmarnock.
Knight is a versatile midfielder, who can also play centre-back and suffered a serious knee injury last season.
He has recovered from his injury and signed a contract extension until 2025.
"Ben is a fantastic talent, one of many that we have in the academy," said sporting director Ross Wilson.
"He is still a young boy but has a fantastic future in the game.

His versatility, attitude and application are all important traits for any player and he has embraced the opportunity given to him this season." 

Also included in the squad is 17-year-old striker Leo Donnell, who has already made four appearances this season.
"Leo is a natural finisher and has impressed at youth level.
He has made the step up to the first team seamlessly this season and we are excited to see him develop further," said Wilson.
"We are delighted Leo has committed his future to the club."
Eighteen-year-old forward Darren Ramsey, who scored against AZ Alkmaar in October, has also signed a new deal until 2025.
"Darren is a strong, powerful and versatile attacker and has made great strides this year," said Wilson.
"He has a great future ahead of him and we are delighted he has committed to the club for the long term."
Midfielder Adam Devine, 17, and 16-year-old striker Rory Wilson have also signed new deals.
Following a disciplinary process, Chelsea have parted company with striker Adrian Mutu.
The Romania international was suspended in September after admitting himself into rehab.
Mutu was also fined £7.8m, £3.6m of which was payable to Chelsea and £4.2m of which was suspended.
The 31-year-old, who was the subject of a failed bid by Juventus in August, has been given permission to train with other clubs to maintain his fitness.
He has scored 17 goals in 76 appearances for the Blues.
Italy were utterly humiliated by a red-hot Wales side in Rome on Sunday, as the visitors ran in seven tries to seal the largest win a Welsh side has ever achieved against the Azzurri.

By the time that the final whistle sounded, Italy had shipped 38 points without reply and would have lost by more if it were not for two tries that they managed to scratch together deep into injury time.
It was a shocking performance from the hosts, who had entered the clash on the back of an improved run of results in the Championship but were completely outclassed on this occasion.
Wales, meanwhile, leapfrog Ireland into second place in the table and continue their rapid improvement under coach Warren Gatland.
Italian coach Conor O' Shea will be horrified by the manner of his side's defeat, with the defending woeful and the attacking non-existent.
They will also be concerned by the lack of composure shown by half-backs Stephen Varney and Alessandro Fusco, who kept gifting Wales possession with needless turnovers.
Wales, meanwhile, showed few signs of rustiness despite having not played together in a month, with their attacking play increasingly slick and their set piece solid.
They scored their first try within two minutes through centre Jonathan Davies after Italian indiscipline handed them an easy platform to attack from, and never looked back from there.
The visitors scored their next try just after the half-hour mark, with flanker Josh Navidi charging down an Italian clearance and winning the race to the touchdown.
The floodgates opened in the second half, with Wales running in four more tries in a devastating display of attacking rugby.
Italian frustration finally boiled over with 10 minutes to go, when replacement prop Andrea Lovotti was shown a red card for a high tackle on Wales captain Alun Wyn Jones.
It summed up a miserable day for the hosts, who will need to improve considerably if they are to avoid a swift return to the Championship next year.
Williams will continue to race in Formula One despite a dispute between the team's owners.

The British outfit have been owned by Dorilton Capital since 2020 but their partnership with Williams was thrown into doubt following concerns from the family of Sir Frank Williams, who founded the team.
Chief executive officer James Bower said "it is not going to be anything dramatic" with regards to the ownership of the team, and that Williams will be able to "continue to race".
Williams have won 114 races and seven constructors' championships since their debut in 1977, but have not won a race since 2012 and finished last in the constructors' championship in 2022.
The team are currently preparing for the first race of the 2023 campaign in Bahrain on 5 March.

The former secretary of state for the environment, George Eustice, has endorsed the controversial candidacy of Liz Truss to be the next leader of the Conservative Party and Britain’s next prime minister.
In an article for the Telegraph, Eustice praised Truss’s economic programme, and specifically her pledge to reverse the rise in corporation tax announced by the current chancellor, Rishi Sunak.
“In the eyes of many Conservative supporters, the prime minister’s U-turn on national insurance and corporation tax was a step too far,” he wrote.
“They believed it was a breach of trust and that it would shrink the income of households and businesses.
Many remain unconvinced that higher taxes are necessary.”
Truss, the foreign secretary, is expected to formally launch her campaign on Thursday with a speech in the northwest of England.
Having come through their qualifier against Felixstowe, Yeading FC face a daunting trip to St James' Park to face Newcastle United in the third round of the FA Cup.
The fans have spoke of their excitement of facing a Premier League side and the revenue it will generate for the club.
However, with the team struggling in the National League and the Magpies flying high in the top flight, it looks like it could be a long afternoon for the visitors.
Yeading manager Jimmy Gray has worked wonders with the club since joining them in 2021 and believes that his team aren't just making up the numbers.
He said: "We've got nothing to lose.
We might not have the star names that Newcastle have got, but we can cause an upset.
On any given day, any team in any league can beat another team.
We've got to believe that we can do it.

"

Newcastle United come into the game off the back of a 4-0 win over Fulham in the Premier League and will be hoping to continue their fine form.
The Magpies have a rich history in the competition, having won it on six occasions.
Manager Eddie Howe knows that the FA Cup is a competition that the fans have a deep affection for and wants to do well in it.
He said: "The FA Cup is a competition that we'd like to win.
It has huge resonance, and we'll do everything we can to be as successful as we can.

"

One to watch from Yeading is forward Joe Gardner, who has been in fine form this season, scoring 10 goals in all competitions.
He says that the team are excited about the opportunity to test themselves against Premier League opposition.
Gardner said: "It's a great draw for us.
We want to test ourselves against the best and see where we're at.
Of course, we respect Newcastle and the quality they've got, but we're not going there just to make up the numbers.
We'll give it our best shot and see where it takes us.

"

Newcastle will be hoping that their main man, Callum Wilson, will be able to continue his fine goalscoring form.
The forward has scored seven goals in his last six games across all competitions and will be keen to add to his tally.
This game has all the ingredients to be a classic FA Cup tie.
The magic of the cup is well and truly alive.

The doping probe into British Cycling and Team Sky began today, with a detailed examination of medical records and data at the British Cycling headquarters in Manchester.
The investigation, commissioned by the UK Anti-Doping agency and headed by Richard Freeman, will look at whether the team used banned substances.
The probe will focus on rider Sir Bradley Wiggins, a five-time Olympic gold medallist and the first Briton to win the Tour de France.
In a statement, UKAD said "it is fair to say the sport of cycling, and more specifically the GB cycling team, has never been bigger than it is now in this country.
That is why it is essential that British cycling, a leading light in the sport, is not only winning clean, but is seen to be winning clean."
Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois has joked that his childhood dream was to become a dentist, and not a professional footballer.
The former Chelsea stopper joined the La Liga giants in August 2018 for £35m, winning the Champions League last season under Zinedine Zidane.
But the Belgian, speaking at a charity event, said: "I always thought of being a dentist and that is why I went to study dentistry at university.

"

Courtois studied at the Catholic University of Leuven prior to joining Genk's youth set-up in 2004.
At the event in Madrid - organised by the anti-poverty charity Child Fund - Courtois also spoke of his desire to have a lasting impact on the city.
"When I arrived here, I said to myself that I wanted to win everything, the league, the Copa del Rey, the Champions League...
and we did," he added.
"But now I think that, as a team, we have to keep winning because that is what the fans deserve and we owe it to them.
Madrid must keep winning.

"

Courtois and his team-mates face a crucial week, with Madrid hosting Barcelona in the Clasico on Sunday, 24 November.
The following Wednesday, they travel to Munich to face Bayern Munich in a decisive Champions League group game.
Andy Murray's former coach, Mark Davenport, has criticized the Wimbledon organizers for failing to honor the Scottish tennis star.
Davenport claimed that Murray, who has won the tournament twice, was treated unfairly due to his recent lack of success compared to other players.
"It's unfair and it's not what Wimbledon is about," Davenport told the BBC.
"There are going to be greats of the game in 20 years' time going through the same situation as Andy Murray is going through now, and they should be treated with more respect.

"

Davenport argued that Murray should have been given more consideration due to his record at the tournament, including his consecutive wins from 2013 to 2016.
He also noted that Murray was the first player to compete in an Olympics and then immediately play at Wimbledon.
The BBC reported that Davenport said he stood by his comments, claiming that "Wimbledon controls the narrative."
It is unclear if Wimbledon organizers have responded to the criticism.
Davos delegates face a crowded agenda this year with climate and pandemic emergencies competing for their attention.
For the first time since the pandemic began, the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum (WEF) is being held face-to-face.
Organisers said they expect more than 2,000 politicians, business leaders and journalists to attend the event in the Swiss ski resort this week.
As well as focusing on Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the meeting will look at how climate plans have been affected by the cost of living crisis.

With the pandemic largely moving into an endemic stage, delegates face a twin challenge of tackling the huge disruption Covid-19 has caused, while taking steps to decarbonise in line with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

This year's meeting will also examine the role of business in promoting sustainable and inclusive economic growth, while addressing the vulnerabilities that have been exposed by the pandemic and other global crises.
The former director of telecommunications giant WorldCom gave a detailed account on Tuesday of how the company cooked its books prior to its collapse and admitted lying under oath.

Bernie Ebbers, who served as chief executive of WorldCom until 2003, pleaded guilty to engineering a $11 billion accounting fraud at the company, then the nation's second-largest long-distance phone company.

The 65-year-old Canadian, who resigned when the fraud was revealed, testified in U.S. district court in New York City on Tuesday as the prosecution began presenting its case in the trial stemming from the accounting scandal.
Mr. Ebbers is charged with securities fraud, conspiracy and filing false documents with regulators.

Prosecutors claim that beginning in 1999, Mr. Ebbers directed a scheme to falsely inflate WorldCom's earnings, including by capitalizing ordinary expenses such as executive bonuses as a way to boost the company's bottom line.

Mr. Ebbers attorney, Reid Weingarten, has indicated that he will argue that Mr. Ebbers was deceived by the company's former chief financial officer, Scott Sullivan, who has already pleaded guilty to fraud.
Mr. Ebbers testified that he repeatedly lied to Wall Street analysts about the company's financial health, including by falsely claiming personal responsibility for the company's books.
He also claimed that he had been "deceived" by Mr. Sullivan and others at the company.
"I trusted Scott Sullivan from the first day I met him," Mr. Ebbers said.
"I trusted him with my life."

Mr. Ebbers also testified that he had hired Mr. Sullivan because he was "good with numbers" and had a "financial mind", however Mr. Ebbers admitted that he had not understood the details of WorldCom's financial statements.
When asked by a prosecutor why he had not taken steps to ensure the accuracy of the company's financial statements, Mr. Ebbers responded: "I relied on the people that I trusted."

Mr. Ebbers also admitted that he had lied under oath in testimony before a congressional committee in 2004, and had not been truthful with prosecutors or the FBI when first questioned about the fraud in June 2002.
"Every time I testified, I lied," Mr. Ebbers said.
"I lied to Congress."
Prosecutors have claimed that Mr. Ebbers' false statements to Congress demonstrated that he had taken steps to conceal the fraud at WorldCom.
British biotechnology firm Phytopharm has signed a deal with Arizona-based Cactus Botanics to market its fat-fighting cactus extract.
Tucson-based Cactus Botanics will incorporate the extract into its line of diet supplements and weight-loss products, which are sold by retailers including Wal-Mart, Target, and Costco.
The extract, which comes from the Opuntia ficus-indica cactus species, inhibits the breakdown and absorption of fat in the gut.
It could be incorporated into capsules, tablets, and liquids, with sales starting in the second half of next year.
Phytopharm, based in Hampshire, said the five-year deal could be worth more than $500m (£378m).

The company's chief executive, Dr. Roger Leggett, said "clinical studies" - most presumably referring to a trial involving a dozen overweight people announced in 2005 - had shown the cactus extract safe and effective.
He added that he did not know of any other such product on the market.

"We are confident that we have an attractive business opportunity, whereby Phytopharm's clinical expertise and sales and marketing know-how are combined with Cactus Botanics' capabilities in ingredient supply," he said.
Cactus Botanics, a division of BioActive Nutritional Ingredients, employs 145 people and has an annual turnover of $25m.

The BBC News article "Brazil plays down Varig rescue" discusses how the Brazilian government has been criticized for its handling of a recent rescue operation of a commercial airplane that crashed in the Amazon.
The plane, which was owned by the Brazilian airline Varig, was flying from Rio de Janeiro to Belém when it crashed, killing all 97 people on board.
The Brazilian government has been accused of not providing enough resources and support to the rescue operation, which was conducted by the military.
The government has played down the significance of the crash, with the president, Jair Bolsonaro, claiming that the media is exaggerating the story.
The crash has raised concerns about the safety of air travel in Brazil, as Varig has had a history of crashes and safety issues.
It has also called into question the government's ability to respond to emergencies and crises.
The Iraqi government will invite international telecommunications companies to submit bids for a licence to operate a mobile phone network in Iraq, officials said.
The move follows a vote by parliament last week to approve the plan.
A source at the communications ministry said a notice would be published "soon" in the official journal, inviting companies to apply for the licence.

Giving a lecture at Cambridge University, Sir Anthony, who was responsible for radio programmes such as Desert Island Discs and The Archers, spoke of his fears for the future of serious television.
He said television had taken a direction "completely contrary to the idea of an intelligent democracy".
The 83-year-old argued that there were some exceptions, such as Channel 4's coverage of the Iraq war, but that these were "becoming isolated islands in a sea of triviality".
"I worry about the future of serious television.
I worry that it could disappear altogether," he said.

Sir Anthony criticised the trend towards reality shows and panel games, which he said allowed participants to behave badly towards each other, and the increasing use of sexualised female presenters in order to attract viewers.
"Is there any other explanation for the number of female presenters in mini-skirts presenting programmes about decorating your home or trying on clothes?"
he asked.
"These are not role models for young women, nor for young men," he said.
"They merely provide an excuse for more sexism and more exploitation.

"

The broadcaster argued that serious issues were being marginalised, saying that the BBC's flagship current affairs programme, Newsnight, had been pushed from its 10pm slot to midnight in Scotland.
And he claimed that an earlier generation of journalists would be "appalled" at the way news was presented now, with the emphasis on the visual rather than the story.
"In the old days, you had reporters who could write, and could describe what was going on.

"The priority is to get pictures, and the pictures are often shown repeatedly... with a voice-over which may have nothing to do with the pictures.
"I think the journalists of my generation would be appalled at the priorities, and the techniques, of many television journalists today.

"

Sir Anthony said he did not believe that television had been entirely taken over by "the stupid, the coarse and the venal".

For more than a decade, the BBC's Marc Settle has been worrying about the security of the many Wi-Fi networks he's been forced to connect to.
They're not just in coffee shops, but also in hotels, conference centres, and on trains.
"Some are completely wide open, and some have a flaky password that you can quickly glean from the guy at the front desk when you check in," he says.
So, what can be done to improve the situation?
"You basically have two choices," says Mr Settle.
"You can either stuff the network in a box, by using a VPN
[virtual private network] app, or you can operate your own router as a firewall.
"The stuff-it-in-a-box solution is the easiest thing to do, but it's also pretty unsatisfactory," he says.
Once you're connected to the VPN, you have to be careful which websites you access, because your IP address is now hidden and you're effectively operating in secret online.
"VPNs are a little bit like the old days of Tor, when you had to carefully choose your browser to access the internet safely," says Mr Settle.

"It's better than nothing, but it's not a great solution."

Operating your own router as a firewall is technically challenging, he says, and you also need an internet connection that's stable enough to support it - which can be a problem on trains, for example.
So what can be done about the poor state of Wi-Fi security in public places and hotels?
The industry is slowly waking up to the problem, says Mr Settle, but change is slow.
"In the meantime, I'd like to see people thinking more carefully about security when they set these things up," he says.
"If you're running a network, please don't set the password on the front desk.
And if you really must do that, make it a long password using all sorts of weird characters, not just 'hotelwireless'.
"And turn off guest access to the network unless it really needs to be on."

The BBC's flagship technology show, Click, recently ran a story about the MP3.
They rightly pointed out that "whatever happened to the MP3?"
The answer is simple: almost everything.
Today, MP3 technology is everywhere.
It's in your phone, your car, your home, your fridge, your watch, and your fitness tracker.
There are billions of MP3-playing devices around the globe.
Chances are, you're listening to an MP3 file as you read these words.
The MP3 story is an interesting one and worth retelling.
The technology that delivers music to your phone or PC has a rich history and a bright future.
In the early 1980s, the Fraunhofer Institute in Germany developed a way to compress audio files.
The idea was to reduce the size of audio files to enable faster transmission over the internet while retaining acceptable quality.
At the time, there were many competing audio formats, but the MP3 stood out.
It was developed by MPEG, the same group that gave us the MPEG video standard.
The first MP3 player was unveiled in 1997.
It was a portable music player that could hold enough music to rival the Sony Walkman.
The Apple iPod launched in 2001 and quickly became the world's most popular MP3 player.
Since then, MP3 has become the de facto standard for digital audio.
It's used in every device that plays digital music, from your phone to your car.
There are billions of MP3 files stored on devices and computers worldwide.
But the MP3 is more than just a file format.
It's a technology that has changed the way we listen to music.
It has made it possible for us to carry our music collections with us wherever we go.
It has made it possible for us to share our music with friends and family.
It has made it possible for us to discover new music.
The MP3 is here to stay.
Thanks to ever-improving audio technology, the MP3 continues to evolve.
We can expect to see higher-quality MP3 files and more features that enable us to do more with our music.
That's why the BBC was right to ask, "whatever happened to the MP3?"
